paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovich Karamazov (people sometimes called him Alyosha) was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a landowner who was pretty famous in our area back in his day. People still talk about him because of the dark and dramatic way he died thirteen years ago—but I’ll tell that part of the story later. For now, I’ll just say that Fyodor Pavlovitch—everyone called him a “landowner” even though he barely spent any time on his own property—was a very strange man. You actually see people like him pretty often around here: he was selfish, mean, and reckless, yet somehow not exactly stupid. In fact, he was good at looking after his money and business, just not much else. For example, Fyodor Pavlovitch started out poor, with almost nothing, always begging for meals at other people’s houses and sucking up to them. But when he died, he left behind a hundred thousand roubles in cash! Still, everyone agreed he was one of the weirdest, most foolish people in the district. But it wasn’t that he was dumb—lots of people like him are actually smart in their own way. It was more like he had a special kind of Russian craziness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was married twice and had three sons. The oldest, Dmitri (Mitya), was from his first wife. His other two sons, Ivan and Alexey (Alyosha), were from his second wife. His first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, came from the Miüsov family—a rich and respected noble family who also owned land in our area. No one really understood why such a smart, independent, and beautiful heiress would marry someone as weak and useless as Fyodor Pavlovitch. I once knew a woman from the last “romantic” generation who, after years of being in love with a man she could have married anytime, invented all kinds of reasons not to, and finally threw herself into a river one stormy night just to be dramatic—kind of like Shakespeare’s Ophelia. If the riverbank hadn’t been so beautiful, maybe she wouldn’t have done it. I think Adelaïda Ivanovna’s decision was similar—she was influenced by other people’s ideas and maybe just wanted to prove she could make her own choices, no matter what her family thought. Maybe, for a brief moment, she imagined that Fyodor Pavlovitch was a bold, clever man of his time—when really, he was just a mean clown. The marriage was even more exciting to her because they ran away together first, which she found romantic. Fyodor Pavlovitch was desperate to improve his life, so marrying into a good family and getting a dowry sounded great to him. But there was really no real love between them, not from her or him, even though Adelaïda Ivanovna was beautiful. Strangely, she was probably the only woman Fyodor Pavlovitch wasn’t attracted to—he usually chased after any woman who gave him the slightest bit of attention.

Right after they ran away and got married, Adelaïda Ivanovna realized she only felt contempt for her husband. Their true feelings showed quickly, and even though her family soon accepted the marriage and gave her the dowry, the couple’s life together was a mess, full of constant arguments. People said Adelaïda Ivanovna was far more generous and dignified than Fyodor Pavlovitch, who, as everyone knows now, grabbed all her money—twenty-five thousand roubles—as soon as she got it, and she never saw it again. He also tried to get the house in town and the village that were part of her dowry signed over to him, using every dirty trick he could. He might have succeeded, since she was so tired of him and disgusted by his constant begging, but her family stepped in and stopped him. They fought a lot, and actually, it was said that she beat him, not the other way around, since she was strong, impatient, and quick-tempered. Finally, she left him and ran away with a poor theology student, leaving little Mitya, who was just three, behind with Fyodor Pavlovitch. As soon as she was gone, Fyodor Pavlovitch filled his house with women and started partying and drinking all the time. In between, he’d drive around the province, whining to everyone about how Adelaïda Ivanovna had left him, sharing embarrassing details about their marriage that no husband should ever tell. He actually seemed to enjoy playing the part of the poor, abandoned husband, making his story even more ridiculous for attention.

“Looks like you got a promotion, Fyodor Pavlovitch—you seem happier now, even though you say you’re upset,” people joked with him. Some even said he enjoyed getting to act silly in a new way, and that he pretended not to notice how ridiculous he looked just to make it funnier. But maybe he was just simple-minded. Eventually, he managed to find out where his runaway wife had gone—she was in St. Petersburg with the theology student, living a wild and free life. Fyodor Pavlovitch started getting ready to go after her, though even he probably didn’t know exactly what he wanted to do when he got there. He might have actually gone, but once he decided, he used it as an excuse to drink even more. Right at that time, Adelaïda Ivanovna’s family got word that she had died suddenly in St. Petersburg, either from typhus or, according to another rumor, from starvation, all alone in a tiny attic room. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard she’d died, and some people say he ran out into the street, cheering and shouting, “Lord, now let Your servant go in peace!” But others say he broke down crying like a little kid, and people actually felt sorry for him, even though he usually disgusted them. Maybe both stories are true: he was happy to be free, but also sad about the person who freed him. Honestly, people—even the bad ones—are usually much more innocent and simple-hearted than we think. And so are we.

You can probably guess what kind of father someone like Fyodor Pavlovitch (let’s call him Fyodor) would be, and how he would raise his kids. He was exactly the kind of dad you’d expect: after marrying Adelaïda Ivanovna, he completely ignored their son, Dmitri (Mitya). It wasn’t because he was angry or wanted to hurt the boy—it was just that he forgot about him. While Fyodor was busy making everyone around him miserable with his constant whining and wild parties, a loyal family servant named Grigory took care of three-year-old Mitya. If Grigory hadn’t stepped in, there wouldn’t have been anyone to even change the boy’s shirt.

What’s more, Mitya’s relatives on his mother’s side didn’t remember him at first either. His grandfather had died, his grandmother (Mitya’s mom’s mom) was in Moscow and seriously ill, and her daughters were all married. So for almost a whole year, Mitya lived with old Grigory in the servants’ cottage. Even if Fyodor had thought of him—which he probably did, at least a little—he would’ve just sent him back to the cottage, since Mitya would have gotten in the way of his wild lifestyle. Then a cousin of Mitya’s mom, named Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, came back from Paris. Pyotr was young, proud of his European ideas, and had traveled to lots of big cities. Later, he became a well-known Liberal and loved to talk about the time he almost joined the fighting during the Paris Revolution of 1848. He was rich, with a huge estate near the town and right next to the famous monastery—which started a never-ending argument with the monks about fishing or woodcutting rights (the exact details aren’t important here). Pyotr believed it was his duty to challenge the church and act like a modern thinker. When he heard about Adelaïda Ivanovna (whom he remembered and once liked) and learned that Mitya existed, he decided to help, even though he looked down on Fyodor. He met Fyodor for the first time and told him straight out that he wanted to take care of Mitya’s education. Later, Pyotr liked to tell people that when he brought up Mitya, Fyodor acted confused, as if he didn’t even know he had a little son at home. Maybe Pyotr exaggerated, but it was probably close to the truth.

Fyodor was always a bit of an actor—he liked to surprise people by acting strangely or unexpectedly, even if it didn’t help him at all, like in this situation. Lots of people are like that, even smart ones, not just Fyodor. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed things forward and was made joint guardian of Mitya (along with Fyodor). Mitya had a little property, a house, and some land from his mother. So Mitya went to live under Pyotr’s care, but since Pyotr didn’t have a family and wanted to get back to Paris as soon as possible, he left Mitya with one of his cousins, a woman in Moscow. Eventually, Pyotr settled in Paris for good, and he forgot about Mitya too, especially once the 1848 Revolution started—a memory that stuck with him forever. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya moved in with one of her married daughters. I think he changed homes a fourth time after that. I won’t go into all the details now, since there’s much more to say later about Fyodor’s oldest son. For now, I’ll just stick to the main facts about him, since they’re important for the story.

First of all, this Mitya (really named Dmitri Fyodorovitch) was the only one of Fyodor’s three sons who grew up believing he had his own property and would be independent when he turned eighteen. His childhood and teenage years were all over the place. He didn’t finish school, went to a military academy, then to the Caucasus, fought a duel, got demoted, then promoted again, lived wildly, and spent lots of money. He didn’t get any money from Fyodor until he became an adult, and got into debt before that. Mitya first met his father when he was old enough to claim his inheritance and came to settle things. He didn’t seem to like his dad, didn’t stay long, and left quickly—getting only some cash and making an agreement for more money in the future. But he never got a clear statement of what the estate was actually worth. For the first time, Fyodor noticed (and this is important) that Mitya had a very vague and overblown idea of his own property. Fyodor liked this, since it fit with his own plans. He realized Mitya was reckless, impatient, wild, and just wanted quick cash, even if it wouldn’t last. So Fyodor started sending him small amounts of money now and then. Finally, four years later, Mitya came back, fed up, wanting to settle things for good. To his shock, he found out he had nothing left. It was hard to even get a proper account from Fyodor. It turned out that, bit by bit, Fyodor had already given him everything he was owed, and maybe even more, so by some agreements Mitya had signed, he couldn’t expect anything else. Mitya was crushed, thought he’d been tricked, and was almost out of his mind with anger. This set off the chain of events that is the main story of my first chapter—or at least, the outside part of it. But before I get to that, I need to talk a bit about Fyodor’s other two sons and where they came from.

Not long after Fyodor Pavlovitch (sometimes called “Papa Karamazov”) sent his four-year-old son Mitya away, he married again. His second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, was also very young and came from another part of the country, where Fyodor had gone on a business trip with a Jewish man. Even though Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunk and led a wild life, he was oddly good at making money—though he wasn't exactly honest about it. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of a poor church deacon and had been an orphan with no family since she was a child. She grew up in the house of a rich old general’s widow, who both helped and tormented her. I don’t know the whole story, but I heard that once, the gentle and quiet Sofya tried to hang herself in the attic because the old lady nagged and bullied her so much. The old woman wasn’t truly evil, but she was so bored and bossy that she made Sofya’s life miserable.

Fyodor Pavlovitch proposed to Sofya, but when people asked about his reputation, he was turned down. Still, just like with his first wife, he convinced Sofya to run away with him. She probably never would have married him if she had known what kind of man he really was, but she lived far away and was only sixteen. She thought life would be better anywhere than with the old widow. So, she left one cruel “benefactress” for a new “benefactor.” This time, Fyodor didn’t get any money for marrying her—the old widow was furious, gave them nothing, and cursed them both. But Fyodor didn’t care about a dowry; he was drawn to Sofya’s beauty, especially her innocent look. That was a big attraction for someone like him, who usually preferred women who were more rough around the edges.

“Those innocent eyes cut right through me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch would say later, with a nasty laugh. For a man as twisted as he was, this probably just meant he was attracted to her looks. Since he got no money with Sofya and had “rescued her from hanging,” he didn’t treat her with any respect. He acted like she owed him something and took advantage of how gentle and obedient she was, doing whatever he wanted and ignoring even the basic rules of marriage. He invited other women to the house and threw wild parties right in front of her. Things got so bad that even Grigory, the grumpy, stubborn servant who had hated Fyodor’s first wife, took Sofya’s side. Grigory stood up for her, scolded Fyodor, and one time even kicked all the rowdy women out of the house. Eventually, Sofya, who had lived in fear since she was a child, became seriously ill—she had fits and lost touch with reality, much like some peasant women who people said were “possessed.” Even so, she had two sons with Fyodor: Ivan and Alexey (Alyosha). Ivan was born in the first year of marriage, Alyosha three years later. When Sofya died, Alyosha was only four, but he somehow remembered his mother all his life, though it was more like a dream. After her death, the two boys were forgotten and abandoned by their father, just like their older brother Mitya had been. Grigory took care of them in his cottage, and that’s where the old widow who had raised Sofya found them. She was still alive after all those years and hadn’t forgotten the insult. She had kept track of Sofya’s miserable life, and when she heard about her illness and how horribly she was treated, she said more than once to her servants:
“She got what she deserved. God punished her for being ungrateful.”

Three months after Sofya Ivanovna died, the old widow suddenly showed up in town and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. She stayed only half an hour, but caused quite a stir. It was evening. Fyodor, who hadn’t seen her in eight years, came in drunk. Right away, without saying a word, the old lady slapped him hard on both cheeks, grabbed a handful of his hair, and shook him up and down three times. Then, still without talking, she marched to the cottage where the boys were. She saw right away that they were dirty and unwashed, so she smacked Grigory, too, and announced that she was taking the children. She wrapped them up just as they were in a rug, put them in her carriage, and drove away. Grigory, loyal as ever, took the slap quietly, and when he helped her into the carriage, he bowed low and told her, “God will reward you for caring for the orphans.” But as she left, the old lady yelled back, “You’re a fool anyway!”

Fyodor Pavlovitch, after thinking it over, decided this was for the best and didn’t object when the old widow made arrangements for the boys’ education. As for the slaps she’d given him, he went around town telling everyone about it.

The old lady died soon after this, but she left each boy a thousand roubles in her will, making it clear that the money should be used only for their education, and that it should last until they turned twenty-one. She even wrote something odd in her will like, “If other people want to waste their money, let them.” I haven’t read the will myself, but I heard it was written in a funny way. The main heir was Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility for the province, and he turned out to be an honest man. He wrote to Fyodor Pavlovitch and quickly saw that he would get no help from him for the boys’ education (even though Fyodor never directly said no, he just kept making excuses, and sometimes even pretended to care). So Yefim Petrovitch took a personal interest in the boys, especially the younger one, Alyosha, who lived with his family for a long time. Please remember this—it’s important. Thanks to Yefim Petrovitch, who was unusually generous and kind, the brothers owed more to him than anyone else for their upbringing. He kept the two thousand roubles safe, and by the time they were adults, the money had doubled with interest. He paid for their education himself and spent more than a thousand roubles on each of them. I won’t go into all the details of their childhood, but I’ll mention the most important things. The older brother, Ivan, was quiet and serious, but not shy. By the time he was ten, he understood that they lived on charity and that their father was someone shameful. Ivan was a really smart kid, and everyone noticed his talent for learning. For some reason, when he was barely thirteen, he left Yefim Petrovitch’s family and went to a school in Moscow, boarding with a famous teacher who was an old friend of Yefim’s. Later, Ivan would say this was all because Yefim Petrovitch was obsessed with the idea of genius—he wanted Ivan to learn from the best. But neither Yefim nor the teacher was alive by the time Ivan finished school and started university. Because Yefim hadn’t sorted out the old lady’s will, the money for Ivan’s inheritance was delayed by paperwork—so Ivan really struggled during his first two years at university, having to support himself while studying. He never even tried to contact his father—maybe out of pride, maybe because he knew he’d get nothing, or maybe just because he was realistic. Either way, Ivan didn’t let it get him down. He started by tutoring for a little money, then got work writing news stories for the papers under the name “Eye-Witness.” His stories were so good and interesting that editors published them right away. This showed how talented he was compared to all the other struggling students just begging for translation jobs. Once he got into the world of journalism, Ivan kept up his connections, and in his last years at university, he wrote great book reviews and became well-known. But in his final year, he wrote an article that really made people notice him. He had just finished university and was about to travel abroad on his inheritance, when he published a strange article in a major magazine. The topic was the church courts—something everyone was talking about at the time, even though Ivan was a science student. He discussed different opinions and then explained his own. The article’s tone and surprising ending made it stand out. Church leaders thought he was on their side, but even atheists liked it. Some people thought he was just making fun of everyone. I mention this because Ivan’s article made it all the way to the famous monastery in town, where the monks got really confused by it. When they found out the author was from their town and was “that Fyodor Pavlovitch’s son,” they were even more interested. And around that time, Ivan himself showed up in town.

I remember wondering at the time why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come to visit. This visit later turned out to be the start of a lot of important events, but I never quite understood his reasons. It seemed strange that such a smart, proud, and careful young man would suddenly visit a father who had ignored him all his life—a father who barely knew him, never thought about him, and would never give him money. Fyodor Pavlovitch was always worried that Ivan or Alyosha would ask him for money, but here was Ivan, actually living in his father's house and getting along with him. He’d been there for two months, and they seemed to be on good terms. This surprised a lot of people, not just me. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, the cousin of Fyodor's first wife, was visiting the area again. He usually lived in Paris, but now he was back. Miüsov was even more surprised than anyone when he met Ivan—he found him fascinating and even compared himself to Ivan (sometimes feeling a little jealous).

“He’s proud,” Miüsov would say. “He’ll never be poor. He has enough money to travel if he wants. So why is he here? Everyone can see he didn’t come for money, since his father would never give him any. He doesn’t drink or party, but his father can’t seem to do without him. They get along so well!”

That was true—Ivan really did have a strong influence on his father. Fyodor Pavlovitch actually behaved better when Ivan was around, and sometimes even seemed to follow his son’s lead, though just as often he acted difficult and stubborn.

Later we learned that Ivan had come partly because his older brother Dmitri (Mitya) asked him to, for a reason that mattered more to Dmitri than to Ivan. Ivan and Dmitri met for the first time during this visit, though they had written letters before about something important (which you'll find out about later). Even when I learned this, Ivan still seemed mysterious to me.
I should add that Ivan seemed to be acting as a peacemaker between his father and his older brother Dmitri, who were fighting so badly that Dmitri was even thinking of suing their father.

For the first time, the family was all together, and some of them were meeting each other for the first time. The youngest brother, Alexey (Alyosha), had already been in town for a year—he was the first of the three brothers to arrive. It’s hardest for me to talk about Alyosha in this introduction, but I have to say something about him, especially to explain a strange fact: I have to introduce my main character to you as a novice monk. Yes, Alyosha had spent the past year living in our monastery, and it looked like he planned to stay there for the rest of his life.

Alyosha was only twenty years old then, his brother Ivan was twenty-four, and their oldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First, I want to make it clear that Alyosha wasn’t some kind of fanatic, and, at least in my opinion, he wasn’t even a mystic. Let me be honest from the start: he just loved people, even from a young age, and he decided to join a monastery because, at that time, it seemed like the perfect way to escape the darkness of the world and find the light of love. What really drew him in was meeting Father Zossima, a famous elder at the monastery, who became like a hero to him, and Alyosha loved him with all the warmth of his heart. Still, I can’t deny that Alyosha was a bit strange, even as a little kid. I’ve already said that, even though he lost his mother when he was four, he remembered her all his life—her face, her hugs—“as though she stood living before me.” Some people remember things from even earlier, but for Alyosha, this memory was like a bright patch in a faded painting—everything else was gone, except this one piece. He remembered a summer evening: the open window, golden sunlight coming in, an icon in the corner with a lamp burning, and his mother on her knees, crying and praying in front of the icon, hugging him tight and holding him out to the Mother of God as if asking for protection. Suddenly, his nurse ran in and took him away from his mother, who seemed frantic but beautiful to him. Alyosha rarely talked about this memory. Even as a child, he wasn’t chatty, but not because he was shy or grumpy. It was more like he was busy with deep thoughts that mattered so much to him, he sometimes forgot about everyone else. Yet, he liked people and trusted them, but no one ever thought he was foolish or simple. There was something about him that let everyone know he would never judge or criticize others. He accepted people as they were, without condemning anyone, though he sometimes felt deep sadness. Even as a young man, nothing seemed to shock or frighten him. When he came to live with his father at twenty, the house was full of wild parties and bad behavior, but Alyosha, who was pure and innocent, just quietly left the room when things got too bad, never showing any disgust or anger. His father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was usually quick to take offense, at first didn’t trust Alyosha and was cold to him. “He doesn’t talk much,” he’d say, “but he thinks a lot.” But after only two weeks, Fyodor started hugging and kissing him all the time, even when he was drunk, and really did seem to care about Alyosha in a way he never had for anyone before.

Everyone liked Alyosha wherever he went; this had been true ever since he was a little boy. When he moved in with his benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he quickly became a part of the family, as though he was their own son. He was so young when he arrived that it wasn’t because he was trying to win anyone over. It was just his nature—he made people love him without even trying. It was the same at school, even though he was the kind of kid others sometimes teased or didn’t trust. He was dreamy and often liked being alone, reading in a corner, but he was still a favorite with everyone. He wasn’t playful or cheerful like some kids, but it was clear that he wasn’t sulky. In fact, he was friendly and easy to get along with. He never tried to show off, and maybe because of that, he wasn’t afraid of anyone. The other boys could see he wasn’t proud of being brave; it was just who he was. He never got angry when someone insulted him. If someone was mean, he’d still talk to them an hour later as if nothing had happened—not because he forgot or was pretending to forgive, but because he honestly didn’t see it as a big deal. This attitude won the boys over. There was one thing about him, though, that made the others want to tease him—not to be mean, but because it was funny to them. Alyosha was extremely modest and shy, especially about anything to do with girls or women. At school, boys sometimes talked about things they were way too young to really understand, and when Alyosha covered his ears, they’d pull his hands away and shout even louder, while he tried to hide without saying a word. Eventually, they stopped teasing him and just felt sorry for him, thinking it was a weakness. Alyosha was always one of the best students, but he was never at the very top.

When Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha still had two more years left at school. The widow left for Italy with her daughters and other women, so Alyosha went to live with two distant relatives of Yefim Petrovitch, even though he’d never met them before. He didn’t really think about what kind of arrangement this was; it just wasn’t something that bothered him. This was very different from his older brother Ivan, who had worked hard to pay his own way through university and always felt uncomfortable living off someone else. But with Alyosha, you couldn’t really blame him; anyone who met him would see that he was the kind of person who, if he suddenly became rich, would probably give everything away to charity or even to someone trying to trick him. He didn’t really understand the value of money—not literally, but he didn’t think much about it. When he got pocket money (he never asked), sometimes he’d spend it all at once, other times he’d keep it for weeks without using it.
Later on, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov—a man who really cared about money and honesty—gave his opinion about Alyosha after getting to know him:

“Here’s probably the only man in the world you could leave alone in a huge city with no money, and he’d be fine—he wouldn’t starve or freeze, because people would help him without him even asking. And they wouldn’t mind; in fact, they’d probably enjoy it.”

Alyosha didn’t finish school. A year before graduation, he told the ladies he was going to see his father because he had an idea he wanted to talk about. They didn’t want him to go, but the trip wasn’t expensive, and they wouldn’t let him pawn his watch (a goodbye gift from his benefactor’s family). They gave him plenty of money and new clothes, but he gave back half the money, saying he’d travel third class. When he got to town, he didn’t answer his father’s question about why he’d come before finishing school, and people said he seemed unusually thoughtful. Soon, it was clear he was looking for his mother’s grave. He almost admitted that was the main reason he’d come, though probably there was more to it—maybe he didn’t even fully understand himself why he suddenly felt called in a new direction. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t know where his second wife was buried; he hadn’t visited the grave since the funeral and had forgotten where it was.

By the way, Fyodor Pavlovitch hadn’t been living in town for a while. Three or four years after his wife died, he moved south and ended up in Odessa for several years. He joked that he first met “a lot of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and later became friends with rich and poor Jews alike. It was probably during this time that he got good at making and saving money. He only came back to town three years before Alyosha arrived. Old friends saw he looked much older, even though he wasn’t really that old. He acted with more shamelessness now than before, and he enjoyed making fun of people. His bad behavior with women was even worse than before. He opened a bunch of new taverns, and it was obvious he had maybe a hundred thousand roubles, or close to it. Lots of people owed him money—and he made sure they gave him good security. He looked puffy and seemed less responsible, starting one thing and then doing something else, as if he didn’t care anymore. He got drunk more often. If it hadn’t been for Grigory, his old servant (who was getting pretty old himself), Fyodor Pavlovitch could have gotten into real trouble. Alyosha’s arrival seemed to affect him, as if something inside him had woken up after being dead for a long time.

“You know,” he’d often say, looking at Alyosha, “you look like her, ‘the crazy woman’”—that’s what he called Alyosha’s mother. It was Grigory who showed Alyosha where his mother was buried. He took Alyosha to the cemetery and pointed out a simple but well-kept iron tombstone in a quiet corner, with her name, age, and a short poem on it. Alyosha was surprised to learn that Grigory had paid for the tombstone himself, after Fyodor Pavlovitch went to Odessa and forgot all about the grave. Alyosha didn’t show much emotion when he saw the grave. He listened quietly to Grigory’s serious explanation about setting up the tombstone, bowed his head, and left without saying a word. He didn’t return to the cemetery for about a year. Still, this episode had an effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—a really strange one. Suddenly, he took a thousand roubles to the monastery to pay for prayers for the soul of his wife—not for Alyosha’s mother, the “crazy woman,” but for his first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, who used to hit him. That evening, he got drunk and made fun of the monks to Alyosha. He himself was not religious at all; he probably never even lit a candle in front of an icon. People like him often have sudden, random feelings and ideas.

I mentioned that he looked puffy. His face showed clear signs of his wild lifestyle: big fleshy bags under his small, sneaky, mocking eyes, lots of deep wrinkles in his chubby face, and an Adam’s apple hanging under his sharp chin like a thick lump, which made him look strange and kind of creepy. He had a long, greedy-looking mouth with thick lips, and you could see little black stumps of rotten teeth when he talked. He drooled whenever he spoke. He actually liked making jokes about his own face, though I think he was proud of it. He liked to point out his nose, which wasn’t big but was thin and hooked. “A real Roman nose,” he’d say. “With my goiter, I look just like a Roman nobleman from ancient times.” He seemed proud of this.

Not long after visiting his mother’s grave, Alyosha suddenly said he wanted to join the monastery, and that the monks were willing to take him as a novice. He said this was really important to him, and he was seriously asking for his father’s permission. Fyodor Pavlovitch knew that Father Zossima, who lived in the monastery, had made a big impression on Alyosha.
“That’s probably the most honest monk there,” Fyodor said, after listening to Alyosha and not seeming too surprised by the request. “So, that’s where you want to be, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and a slow, tipsy smile spread across his face, a little sly. “Hmm... I kind of guessed you’d end up like this. Would you believe it? You were heading straight for it. Well, at least you have your own two thousand roubles. That’s your dowry. And I won’t abandon you, my angel. I’ll pay whatever they want for you at the monastery—if they ask. If not, why bother them? You barely spend anything—like a canary, just a few grains a week. You know, near one monastery, there’s a place outside town where everyone knows ‘the monks’ wives’ live—thirty women, I think. I’ve been there myself. It’s interesting, in its way, as something different. The funny part is it’s so Russian—no French women there. Of course, if they found out, they’d come, since there’s plenty of money. But there’s nothing like that here, just two hundred honest monks. They keep the rules, I admit it... So, you want to be a monk? And, you know, I’m sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I’ve really grown fond of you? Well, it’s a good chance. You’ll pray for us sinners—we’ve sinned enough. I’ve always wondered who’d pray for me, if anyone would. My dear boy, I’m clueless about that. You wouldn’t believe how clueless. Every now and then, I think about it. I imagine the devils won’t forget to drag me to hell with their hooks when I die. And then I wonder—hooks? Where do they get them? Iron? Do they have a foundry? The monks probably think hell has a ceiling. I could believe in hell, but without a ceiling. That would be classier, more modern, like the Lutherans. But really, does it matter if there’s a ceiling or not? Still, there’s a tricky question: if there’s no ceiling, there can’t be hooks; and if there are no hooks, the whole story falls apart. But that’s unlikely—there have to be hooks, or else how would I get dragged to hell? There’s no justice if I don’t! They’d have to invent the hooks just for me—if you only knew, Alyosha, what a scoundrel I am.”
“But there aren’t any hooks,” Alyosha said, looking at his father kindly and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That’s how a Frenchman described hell: ‘I drank the shadow of a coachman who with the shadow of a brush cleaned the shadow of a carriage.’ How do you know there are no hooks, darling? Once you’ve lived with the monks, you’ll probably see things differently. Still, go find out the truth and come tell me. It’s easier to face the next world if you know what’s there. Besides, you’ll fit in better with the monks than here, with a drunk old man and young women... though you’re like an angel—nothing seems to touch you. Maybe nothing will touch you there either. That’s why I’m letting you go, because I hope for that. You’re smart—you’ll go through the fire and come out the other side, healed, and come back. And I’ll be waiting. I feel like you’re the only person in the world who hasn’t judged me. My dear boy, I feel it, I really do. I can’t help it.”
And then he started crying. He was sentimental. He was wicked, but he was also sentimental.

Some readers might think Alyosha was a sickly, overly dreamy kid—maybe pale and weak, always lost in his thoughts. But actually, at nineteen, Alyosha was healthy, with red cheeks and bright, clear eyes. He was good-looking too: graceful, a bit taller than average, with dark brown hair, an oval face, and wide, shining grey eyes. He always seemed calm and deep in thought. Some might say that even healthy people can be fanatics or mystics, and that’s true. But I think Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Sure, he believed in miracles at the monastery, but realists aren’t troubled by miracles. If a true realist doesn’t believe in miracles, nothing will make him. Even if he sees one, he’ll doubt his own senses before admitting it’s real. If he finally accepts it, he just calls it a natural event he doesn’t understand. For a realist, faith doesn’t come from miracles—miracles come from faith. If he does believe, though, he has to accept miracles too. Remember how the Apostle Thomas said he wouldn’t believe until he saw Jesus, but when he did, he cried out, “My Lord and my God!”? It wasn’t the miracle that made him believe—he believed because he wanted to, maybe even before he saw anything.

Some might also argue that Alyosha was stupid or immature, or that he didn’t finish his education. It’s true he didn’t finish school, but it would be unfair to call him dumb. Like I said, he chose this path because it inspired him, and seemed like the best way to escape from darkness to light. Plus, he was a young man of his time—honest, searching for truth, and ready to give everything for it, even his life. But these young men often don’t realize that giving up your life can sometimes be easier than giving up a few years of youth to hard study, just to serve your cause better in the end. Alyosha took a different path, but with the same need for quick results. As soon as he really thought about it, he became convinced God and immortality existed, and he told himself, “I want to live for immortality. I won’t settle for anything less.” If he’d decided there was no God or immortality, he would have become a total atheist and a socialist right away. Socialism, to him, wasn’t just about workers—it was mostly about atheism, about building a world without God, not to reach heaven, but to invent heaven on earth. Alyosha couldn’t have just kept living the same way. Remember: “Give all you have to the poor and follow Me, if you want to be perfect.”

Alyosha thought to himself: “I can’t just give a little and pretend that’s enough. I can’t just go to church instead of really following Him.” Maybe memories of childhood, like his mom taking him to mass at the monastery, or the sunlight shining on the holy icons she showed him, still influenced his imagination. Maybe that’s why he came to the monastery—to see if he could truly give up everything, or just a little. There he met the elder. I should explain what an “elder” is in Russian monasteries, though I’m not an expert. The idea of elders is only about a hundred years old in Russia, though it’s much older in places like Sinai and Athos. It may have existed in ancient Russia, but was forgotten after all the wars and disasters. It was brought back by a great ascetic, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his students, but even now, not many monasteries have elders, and some people in Russia saw it as a risky new idea. It was especially important at the famous Kozelski Optin Monastery. I don’t know exactly when our monastery got elders, but there had been three, and Zossima was the last. He was very sick, and there was no one to take his place. This was a big deal for the monastery, because it wasn’t famous for anything else—no saintly relics, no miracle-working icons, no heroic history. Its only claim to fame was its elders, who drew thousands of pilgrims from everywhere.

So, what is an elder? An elder is someone you trust so much that you give up your own will to follow his. When you choose an elder, you agree to obey him completely and give up your own wants. This is done willingly, as a way to really master yourself, hoping that after a life of obedience, you’ll find true freedom by letting go of your ego. The elder system isn’t some theory—it’s based on a thousand years of practice in the East. The commitment to an elder is much more than the usual obedience in Russian monasteries. It means confessing everything to your elder, and forming a deep, unbreakable bond with him.

There are old stories about this. For example, once in early Christian times, a novice disobeyed his elder and left his monastery for Egypt. There, he did amazing things and died a martyr. But when the church tried to bury him as a saint, the coffin was mysteriously thrown out three times, until they realized he’d broken his vow to his elder. Only after getting the elder’s forgiveness could he be buried properly. That’s just a legend, but here’s a more recent example.

Once, a monk was ordered by his elder to leave Mount Athos, a place he loved, and go first to Jerusalem and then to Siberia. The monk, heartbroken, went to the Patriarch in Constantinople to ask if he could be released from this duty. But the Patriarch said only the elder who gave the order could release him, and no one else had the power to do it. That’s why elders sometimes have incredible authority. Because of this, some monasteries almost persecuted the idea at first. But ordinary people loved the elders. Crowds of both simple and important people visited them to confess, ask for advice, or share their pain. Critics said this made confession less serious, but the regular talks with elders weren’t the same as the sacrament. In the end, elders became more accepted in Russia. Of course, giving up your will to another can be risky—it could make someone truly humble, or it could make them proud and controlling, turning freedom into another kind of slavery.

Elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a landowning family, was an army officer when young, and served in the Caucasus. Alyosha was probably drawn to something special in his spirit. Alyosha lived in Zossima’s cell, and the elder cared for him and let him help out. Alyosha wasn’t forced to be there—he could come and go as he liked, even though he wore the monk’s robe by choice. Maybe he liked it, or maybe he was inspired by the elder’s power and reputation. People said that so many visitors had come to Father Zossima for advice or confession that he could sense what strangers wanted or what troubled them just by looking at their faces. Sometimes he amazed and even scared people by knowing their secrets before they spoke.

Alyosha noticed that most people went to see the elder nervous and uneasy, but left with happy, peaceful faces. He was especially impressed that Father Zossima was never strict or gloomy—instead, he was almost always cheerful. The other monks said he was drawn to the biggest sinners, and the worse someone was, the more he cared about them. Of course, a few monks disliked or envied him, but most loved him deeply. Some were so devoted, they whispered that he was a saint, and since he seemed close to death, they expected miracles and fame for the monastery after he died. Alyosha believed completely in the elder’s miraculous powers, just as he believed the story of the flying coffin. He saw people bring sick children or relatives to the elder, asking for his prayers, and later come back in tears, thanking him for healing them.

Alyosha never questioned whether these healings were real or just natural recoveries—he believed totally in his teacher’s spiritual power and was proud of his fame. His heart would race with excitement when the elder came out to the gates to greet the crowds of pilgrims, many of them poor, who had traveled huge distances just to see him and get his blessing. People would fall at his feet, kiss the ground he walked on, and weep. Mothers would lift up their children to him, and the sick were brought to him as well. The elder would speak to them, say a short prayer, bless them, and send them away. He’d gotten so weak lately that sometimes he couldn’t leave his cell, and the pilgrims would wait days just to see him. Alyosha completely understood why people loved and worshipped him so much. For the poor, tired Russian peasants, worn out by hardship and the endless unfairness and sin in the world, it was a huge comfort to have someone holy to look up to.

“Yes, there’s sin and injustice everywhere,” they thought, “but somewhere on earth, there’s someone truly holy. He knows the truth, so truth isn’t dead—it will come to us someday and rule the world as promised.”

Alyosha knew this was exactly how people felt. He understood it, and he had no doubt that Elder Zossima was this saint, the keeper of God’s truth—just like the weeping peasants and the sick women who brought him their children. Alyosha was even more certain than anyone else that after the elder’s death, great miracles and glory would come to the monastery. Lately, his faith and excitement had been burning even brighter in his heart. He wasn’t bothered at all that the elder was the only example he could look up to.

“It doesn’t matter. He’s holy. He has the secret to make everything new, to bring truth to earth so that everyone will be holy and love each other. There won’t be rich or poor anymore, no one above or below—everyone will be children of God, and Christ’s true kingdom will come.” That was Alyosha’s dream.

The arrival of his two brothers, whom he’d never really known before, made a big impression on Alyosha. He became friends with his half-brother Dmitri (Mitya) more quickly than with his full brother Ivan, even though Dmitri came later. Alyosha was very interested in Ivan, but even after two months in town and several meetings, they weren’t close. Alyosha was quiet, almost as if he was waiting for something or maybe a little embarrassed. At first, Ivan had looked at him curiously, but soon seemed to lose interest. Alyosha noticed this and felt a bit awkward—maybe it was because Ivan was older and better educated, but maybe there was another reason Alyosha didn’t understand. He kept thinking Ivan was obsessed with something important inside himself, some goal that was hard to reach, and that’s why he didn’t pay attention to Alyosha. Alyosha also wondered if Ivan, as an atheist, might secretly look down on him, the naive monk. He knew Ivan was an atheist, but he couldn’t be offended if his brother looked down on him. Still, Alyosha waited anxiously for Ivan to get closer to him. Dmitri always spoke of Ivan with great respect and seriousness. From Dmitri, Alyosha learned all the details about the “important matter” that had recently brought the two older brothers together. Dmitri’s high opinion of Ivan was even more impressive since Dmitri was much less educated, and the two brothers were so different in personality and character, you couldn’t find two people less alike.

Around this time, the whole strange Karamazov family finally got together in Father Zossima’s cell—the man who had such a big influence on Alyosha. The reason for this meeting wasn’t real. At that point, the fight between Dmitri and their father Fyodor Pavlovitch was at its worst, and they couldn’t stand to be around each other. Fyodor Pavlovitch was the one who suggested, as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima’s cell. Maybe, without asking for his help directly, they could work things out under the elder’s calming influence. Dmitri, who had never met the elder, thought his father was just trying to scare him, but since Dmitri felt guilty for losing his temper with his father recently, he agreed to the meeting. Dmitri didn’t live with his father, but on the other side of town. At the same time, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was in the area, got interested in the idea too. Miüsov was a liberal atheist from an older generation, and maybe he was just bored or looking for some fun. He also had a lawsuit with the monastery and thought this was a good excuse to talk to the Superior and maybe come to an agreement. As a visitor with “good intentions,” he’d likely get more respect than if he admitted he was just curious. People inside the monastery asked the elder—who was sick and hardly saw anyone anymore—to agree to the meeting, and finally he said yes, and the date was set.
“Who made me a judge over them?” was all Father Zossima said to Alyosha, smiling.

Alyosha was really worried when he heard about the meeting. Of everyone coming, only Dmitri seemed likely to take it seriously. The others, he knew, were coming out of boredom or even to make fun of the elder. Ivan and Miüsov, he feared, would come just to satisfy their curiosity, maybe even to be rude, and Fyodor Pavlovitch would probably try to pull some kind of prank. Alyosha understood his father perfectly, even though he never said anything. People thought Alyosha was simple, but he wasn’t. He waited for the meeting with a heavy heart, always thinking about how to end the family’s fighting, but most of all, he worried about the elder. He was afraid the elder would be disrespected, especially by Miüsov’s polite sarcasm and Ivan’s clever, superior comments. Alyosha even thought about warning the elder, but changed his mind and kept quiet. The day before, he just sent a message to Dmitri through a friend, saying he loved him and hoped he’d keep his promise. Dmitri wasn’t sure what promise that was, but he wrote back that he’d do his best not to “get provoked by nastiness,” and that even though he respected both the elder and Ivan, he suspected the meeting was just a trap or a joke.
“Still, I’d rather bite my tongue off than disrespect the holy man you care about so much,” Dmitri wrote at the end. Alyosha didn’t feel much better after reading the letter.

It was a warm, sunny day near the end of August. The meeting with the elder was set for half-past eleven, right after the late church service. The visitors skipped the service and arrived just as it finished. First, an expensive open carriage pulled up, carrying Miüsov and his distant relative, a young man named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov, who was twenty and planning to go to university. Miüsov, who Kalganov was staying with, was trying to convince him to study abroad in Zurich or Jena, but Kalganov hadn’t decided yet. He was thoughtful, sometimes lost in his own world, and had a habit of staring off into space—even at people—without really seeing them. He usually kept quiet and seemed awkward, but when alone with someone, he could suddenly become talkative, even laughing at nothing. Still, that energy would disappear just as quickly. He always dressed very well and seemed wealthy, expecting to inherit even more one day. He was also friends with Alyosha.

In an old, bumpy, but spacious rented carriage drawn by a pair of tired pinkish-gray horses, Fyodor Pavlovitch arrived with his son Ivan, following far behind Miüsov’s carriage. Dmitri was running late, even though he'd been told the time the night before. The group left their carriage at the hotel outside the monastery grounds and walked to the monastery gates. Except for Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of them had ever been to the monastery before, and Miüsov probably hadn’t even been to church in thirty years. He looked around with curiosity, trying to act casual, but found nothing interesting inside except for the church and the regular-looking buildings. Worshippers were leaving the church, bareheaded and making the sign of the cross. Among them were some people of higher rank—a couple of ladies and a very old general, all staying at the hotel. As soon as the visitors arrived, a group of beggars surrounded them, but no one gave them anything except for young Kalganov, who nervously pulled out a ten-copeck coin and handed it quickly to an old woman, saying, “Split it between you.” No one commented on his action, which only made him feel more embarrassed.

It was strange that no one seemed to be expecting their arrival, and they weren’t greeted with any special respect, even though one of them had recently donated a thousand roubles and another was a wealthy landowner who could decide the monastery’s fishing rights in an ongoing lawsuit. Still, no official came out to meet them.

Miüsov glanced absent-mindedly at the tombstones near the church and almost made a sarcastic remark about how the dead must have paid good money to be buried in such a “holy place,” but he held his tongue. His usual sarcastic attitude was quickly turning into real annoyance.
“Who on earth are we supposed to ask for help in this ridiculous place? We need to figure this out—time’s running out,” he muttered, mostly to himself.

Suddenly, an older, bald man with eager, twinkling eyes approached. He wore a full summer coat and, tipping his hat, introduced himself with a soft, syrupy voice as Maximov, a landowner from Tula. He immediately jumped in to help the visitors.
“Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, apart from the main monastery, about four hundred steps away on the other side of the woods.”
“Yes, we know it’s past the woods,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch. “But we don’t remember the way. It’s been a long time since we visited.”
“This way, through this gate, and then straight across the woods… the woods. Come with me, if you like! I’m headed there myself. This way, this way.”
They left through the gate and turned toward the woods. Maximov, who was about sixty, hurried along, almost running and glancing sideways at them with wild curiosity, his eyes practically bulging.
“You see, we’re visiting the elder for our own business,” Miüsov said sternly. “He’s agreed to meet us, so while we appreciate your help, we can’t ask you to come with us.”
“I’ve already been there, un chevalier parfait!” Maximov said, snapping his fingers in the air.
“Who’s a chevalier?” Miüsov asked.
“The elder—the wonderful elder! Zossima! He’s the pride and honor of the monastery. Such an amazing elder!”
But before Maximov could say more, a very pale, thin-looking monk of medium height, wearing a monk’s cap, caught up to them. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.
The monk gave a deep, respectful bow and announced:
“The Father Superior invites all you gentlemen to lunch with him after you visit the hermitage. At one o’clock, no later. And you too,” he added, nodding to Maximov.

“Of course, I’ll be there!” Fyodor Pavlovitch said, obviously pleased with the invitation. “And believe me, we’ve all promised to be on our best behavior here… And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you come too?”
“Yes, of course. Why else would I be here except to learn about your customs? The only downside for me is having your company…”
“True, Dmitri Fyodorovitch hasn’t shown up yet.”
“Honestly, it would be great if he didn’t come. Do you think I enjoy all this, especially with you here? Anyway, we’ll come to lunch. Please thank the Father Superior,” he told the monk.
“Actually, I’m supposed to take you to the elder now,” the monk replied.
“In that case, I’ll just go straight to the Father Superior… to the Father Superior,” Maximov babbled.
“The Father Superior is busy right now. But as you wish…” the monk hesitated.
“Annoying old man!” Miüsov said out loud as Maximov hurried back toward the monastery.
“He reminds me of von Sohn,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.
“Is that all you can think about? How is he like von Sohn? Have you even met von Sohn?”
“I’ve seen his portrait. It’s not his looks, but something about him. He’s a second von Sohn. I can always tell from someone’s face.”

“Sure, you’re an expert at that. But listen, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you just said we promised to behave. Don’t forget it. I’m warning you—if you start acting up, I’m not getting involved. You see what he’s like,” he said to the monk, “I’m actually afraid to be seen with him in public.” The monk gave a small, knowing smile, but didn’t reply, clearly out of politeness. Miüsov looked even more annoyed.
“Ugh, what a farce!” Miüsov thought. “All this fancy tradition built up over centuries, and underneath it’s just nonsense and trickery.”
“Here’s the hermitage! We made it!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “But the gates are shut.”
He crossed himself several times, bowing to the saints painted above and beside the gates.

“When in Rome, do as the Romans do,” he joked. “There are twenty-five saints living here, saving their souls, staring at each other, and eating cabbages. Not a single woman is allowed through this gate, which is interesting. But I heard the elder does see ladies,” he added, looking at the monk.

“There are some women from the local towns lying in the portico waiting right now. But for higher-class ladies, there are two rooms built next to the portico but outside the main grounds—see those windows? The elder goes out to them through a special hallway if he’s well enough. They’re never allowed inside. There’s a woman from Harkov, Madame Hohlakov, waiting with her sick daughter right now. He probably promised to see her, though lately he’s been too weak to meet even the regular people.”

“So there are loopholes to get around the rules after all, to see the women. Don’t get me wrong, Father, I’m not criticizing. But did you know that at Athos, not only are women not allowed to visit, but not even female animals—no hens, turkey-hens, or cows?”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, I’m warning you: I’ll turn around and leave if you keep this up. They’ll kick you out as soon as I’m gone.”
“But I’m not bothering you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look,” he suddenly pointed as he stepped inside, “what a beautiful garden they have here!”

Even though it was autumn and there were no roses, there were lots of rare and pretty flowers blooming wherever there was space. Someone obviously took great care of them. Flowerbeds surrounded the church and were even between the graves. The elder’s one-story wooden house was also surrounded by flowers.

“Was it like this when the last elder, Varsonofy, was here? He wasn’t into fancy things. I heard he used to jump up and whack even ladies with a stick,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said as he went up the steps.

“Elder Varsonofy did act a little strange sometimes, but most of the stories about him are just rumors. He never hit anyone,” the monk replied. “Now, gentlemen, if you’ll wait a minute, I’ll announce you.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, this is your last warning—remember our agreement. If you embarrass us, I’ll pay you back for it,” Miüsov muttered.

“Why are you so nervous?” Fyodor Pavlovitch teased. “Are you worried about your sins? They say he can tell from your eyes why you’re here. And you care so much about their opinion—for someone who’s so modern and Parisian, I’m surprised.”
Miüsov didn’t get a chance to answer the sarcasm because they were invited inside. He walked in, clearly irritated.
“Why am I so annoyed?” Miüsov thought. “I’m going to lose my temper, start arguing, and end up lowering myself and my beliefs.”

The group entered the room just as the elder, Father Zossima, came in from his bedroom. Already waiting inside were two monks from the hermitage: the Father Librarian, and Father Païssy, who was known for being very smart but was rather sickly, though not old. In the corner stood a tall young man, about twenty-two, dressed in regular clothes. He was a theology student who lived at the monastery. His face was broad and fresh, with sharp, narrow brown eyes that seemed to notice everything, and he looked at the elder with a mix of respect and self-confidence. Because he wasn’t considered equal to the guests, he didn’t bow when they came in.

Father Zossima entered with a novice and Alyosha (Alexey, sometimes called Alyosha). The two monks stood up and greeted the elder with deep bows, their fingers touching the floor, and then kissed his hand. The elder blessed them, bowed just as deeply in return, and asked for their blessing too. The whole ritual was done with serious emotion, not just as a daily habit. But Miüsov thought it was all a bit too dramatic and put-on. He stood in front of the others, remembering that he should probably go up and get the elder’s blessing, or at least bow politely, since that was the custom—even if he didn’t want to kiss the hand. But when he saw all the bowing and hand-kissing, he changed his mind. With a stiff, formal bow, he moved to a chair. Fyodor Pavlovitch copied him, making fun of Miüsov like a monkey. Ivan bowed with dignity and politeness but didn’t offer his hands, while Kalganov was so flustered he didn’t bow at all. The elder lowered his hand, bowed again to the group, and asked everyone to sit down. Alyosha blushed deeply. He was embarrassed—his worries were coming true.

Father Zossima sat on an old, worn mahogany sofa covered in leather. He had his guests sit in a row on four mahogany chairs, their black leather seats looking shabby. The monks sat, one by the door and one by the window. The theology student, the novice, and Alyosha stayed standing. The small room looked faded and simple, with only the bare necessities for furniture, all cheap and rough. In the window were two pots of flowers, and in the corner, several religious icons—one huge, ancient icon of the Virgin with a lamp burning in front of it. Next to it were two more icons in bright frames, carved cherubs, some porcelain eggs, a Catholic ivory cross with a statue of the grieving Virgin Mary, and a few old Italian engravings. Right next to these priceless artworks were some cheap Russian prints of saints and martyrs, the kind they sell at fairs for almost nothing. Other walls had portraits of Russian bishops, both past and present.

Miüsov glanced quickly at all these “standard” decorations, then stared hard at the elder. He thought pretty highly of his own judgment—maybe too highly, but he was fifty, and men with experience often take themselves seriously. Right away, he didn’t like Zossima. To be fair, there was something about the elder’s appearance many people might not like. He was short, hunched, with weak legs, and even though he was only sixty-five, he looked at least seventy-five. His face was very thin, covered in fine wrinkles, especially around his quick, shining, light-colored eyes. He had some gray hair at his temples, a pointed, scraggly beard, and lips so thin they looked like two threads. His nose wasn’t long but was sharp, almost like a bird’s beak.
“He seems like a mean-spirited man with too much pride,” Miüsov thought, feeling unhappy to be here.
A cheap little clock on the wall hurriedly struck twelve, and that gave them a reason to start talking.

“Right on time!” Fyodor Pavlovitch exclaimed. “But still no sign of my son, Dmitri. Please forgive him, holy elder!” (Alyosha shuddered at the words “holy elder.”) “I’m always on time myself, to the minute—because being punctual is the sign of a king...”
“But you’re not a king, anyway,” Miüsov muttered, unable to hold back.

“True, I’m not a king. Would you believe, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I know that about myself!” Fyodor Pavlovitch said, putting on a sad voice. “I always say the wrong thing. Father, let me introduce myself: I’m a clown, seriously! It’s a bad habit, but I can’t help it. If I say silly things, it’s just to entertain people and be liked. People like someone who’s fun, right? Years ago, I was in a little town on business and made friends with some merchants. We went to the police chief to invite him to dinner. He was tall, fat, and cranky—dangerous type. I tried to joke with him and said, ‘Mr. Ispravnik, be our Napravnik.’ He looked grumpy. I explained, trying to be clever, that Mr. Napravnik is a famous orchestra conductor in Russia, and our group needed someone like that for harmony. He just replied, ‘I’m an Ispravnik, and don’t make puns about my job.’ He left, and I followed, calling, ‘You’re Ispravnik, not Napravnik!’ He shot back, ‘You called me Napravnik, so now I am one!’ That ruined everything. I always put myself in trouble by trying to be funny. Another time, I told an important man that his wife was a ‘ticklish lady,’ meaning sensitive. He asked, ‘Did you tickle her?’ and I, trying to be polite, said yes—so he tickled me, right there! That was long ago, so I’m not embarrassed to say it. I always mess up like this.”
“You’re doing it again,” Miüsov muttered, disgusted.
Father Zossima silently looked at both of them, studying them.

“Am I? Would you believe, I knew you’d say that, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. As soon as I start talking, I can tell when my joke isn’t working. Both my cheeks feel tight, like they’re being pulled down—happens every time. It’s been this way since I was young, when I had to make jokes to earn my keep in noble households. I just can’t help it, it’s like a curse. Maybe it’s a little devil inside me—just a little one, a bigger devil would have found a better place to live! But you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, aren’t much of a prize either. Still, I do believe in God, even though I’ve had doubts lately. Now I’m just sitting here, waiting for wisdom. I’m like the philosopher Diderot, Father. Did you ever hear how Diderot went to see Metropolitan Platon during Empress Catherine’s time? He walked in and said, ‘There is no God.’ The bishop pointed his finger and said, ‘The fool says in his heart there is no God.’ Diderot fell down at his feet and cried, ‘I believe! I want to be baptized!’ So he was—Princess Dashkov was his godmother, Potyomkin his godfather.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, this is ridiculous! You know you’re making that up, the whole Diderot story is fake. Why are you acting like this?” Miüsov cried, voice trembling.

“I’ve always suspected it wasn’t true,” Fyodor Pavlovitch declared, sounding sincere. “But here’s the real truth, everyone. Great elder, forgive me—the part about Diderot’s baptism, I just invented that right now. I never thought of it before. I only made it up to make the story more entertaining. I act the fool, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to be liked—but sometimes, I don’t even know why I do it. As for Diderot, I heard the ‘fool says in his heart’ part a dozen times from the local gentry. I even heard your aunt, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, tell it. They all still believe Diderot the atheist argued about God with the Metropolitan Platon...”
Miüsov jumped up, forgetting himself in his anger. He was furious—and aware of how silly he must look.

What was happening in the cell was honestly shocking. For decades, ever since the days of previous elders, no one had ever entered this cell without deep respect. Every visitor felt honored just to be allowed in. Some even stayed kneeling the entire visit. Many visitors had been high-ranking, well-educated people—even some who didn’t believe in God—but all had shown the utmost respect and care. Money wasn’t the issue here—just love and kindness on one side, repentance and deep questions on the other. So this clowning around stunned the onlookers, or at least some of them. The monks, faces calm, waited seriously for the elder to speak, although they looked like they might stand up any second, just like Miüsov. Alyosha stood with his head down, almost in tears. What hurt him most was that his brother Ivan, the one he’d hoped would help and who could control their father, just sat there, calm and interested, as if he was just waiting to see how it would all play out. Alyosha didn’t dare look at Rakitin, the theology student—he knew Rakitin’s thoughts better than anyone else at the monastery.

“Please forgive me,” Miüsov said to Father Zossima. “It probably looks like I’m part of this embarrassing nonsense. I made a mistake thinking even Fyodor Pavlovitch would know how to behave when visiting someone as respected as you. I never thought I’d have to apologize just for coming with him...”
Pyotr Alexandrovitch couldn’t say any more. He was so embarrassed he was about to leave the room.

“Please don’t upset yourself,” the elder said. He got up on his weak legs and took Pyotr Alexandrovitch by both hands, making him sit down again. “Please, I ask you, don’t worry. Be my guest.” He bowed and went back to his old sofa.
“Great elder, tell me! Am I bothering you with my liveliness?” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly shouted, gripping his chair like he might jump out of it if the answer was bad.

“I truly ask you not to worry, and not to be anxious,” the elder said, his voice serious. “Don’t trouble yourself. Make yourself comfortable. Most importantly, don’t be so ashamed of yourself—that’s really where your trouble comes from.”

“Make myself at home? Be my real self? That’s too much, but I accept it happily. You know, holy Father, you might regret inviting me to be myself. I warn you—it could be risky! I won’t go that far, for your sake. Anyway, what happens next is still a mystery, though plenty of people would love to describe me for you—right, Pyotr Alexandrovitch? But as for you, holy man, let me tell you, I’m overflowing with excitement.”

He got up and, throwing his hands in the air, exclaimed, “Blessed be the womb that bore you, and the breasts that fed you—the breasts especially! When you just said, ‘Don’t be so ashamed of yourself, that’s at the root of it all,’ you hit me right in the heart. You read me completely. Honestly, every time I meet people, I feel lower than everyone and think they all see me as a clown. So I say, ‘Fine, let me really be a clown—I’m not afraid of your opinions, because you’re all worse than me.’ That’s why I act the fool. It’s because of shame, holy elder, just shame. If I could ever believe that everyone thought I was the kindest and wisest man, oh, what a good person I’d be! Teacher!” Suddenly, he dropped to his knees. “What must I do to get eternal life?”
Even now, it was hard to tell if he was joking or actually moved.
Father Zossima looked up at him and smiled.

“You’ve known what to do for a long time. You’re smart enough: Don’t get drunk, don’t talk too much, don’t give in to lust or greed, and most of all—don’t lie. And close your taverns. If you can’t close them all, then at least two or three. And above all, don’t lie.”
“You mean about Diderot?”

“Not just about Diderot. Most of all, don’t lie to yourself. A man who lies to himself and believes his own lies gets to a point where he can’t tell what’s true inside of him or around him. Then he loses respect for himself and other people. Without respect, he can’t love. To distract himself from this emptiness, he turns to passions and rough pleasures, and sinks into bad habits—all because he keeps lying to himself and to others. Someone who lies to himself is more easily offended than anyone. Sometimes, it actually feels good to be offended, doesn’t it? A man can know that he hasn’t really been insulted, but he makes up an insult in his own mind, exaggerates it, grabs onto a word, and makes a mountain out of a molehill. He knows it’s made up, but he’ll be the first to get offended and will enjoy nursing that resentment, until it turns into real anger. But please, get up and sit down. All of this, too, is just acting...”
“Blessed man! Let me kiss your hand.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch jumped up and quickly kissed the elder’s thin hand. “It really is pleasant to take offense! You said it better than I’ve ever heard before. Yes, my whole life I’ve taken offense just to feel special—sometimes it’s not just pleasant, it’s even fancy to be insulted! You forgot that, great elder—it’s elegant! I’ll remember that. But I’ve been lying—really lying—my whole life. Every day, every hour, I’m a liar, and father of lies. Well, maybe not the father. I’m mixing up my Bible quotes. Let’s just say the son of lies—that’s enough. But... my angel... can I sometimes talk about Diderot? That can’t hurt, right? Still, sometimes just one word can hurt. Great elder, by the way, I almost forgot—I’ve been meaning to ask you this for two years. Please tell Pyotr Alexandrovitch not to interrupt me. Here’s my question: Is it true, Father, that in the Lives of the Saints, there’s a story about a holy man who, after his head was cut off, got up, picked up his head, and ‘courteously kissed it’ before walking a long way with it in his hands? Is that true or not, Father?”
“No, that’s not true,” the elder replied.
“There isn’t anything like that in the Lives of the Saints. Which saint are you talking about?” asked the Father Librarian.

“I don’t know which saint. I don’t know at all. I was fooled. Someone told me the story. And you know who told me? Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who just got so angry about Diderot. He’s the one who told it.”
“I’ve never told you that. I don’t even speak to you at all.”

“It’s true you didn’t tell me directly, but you told the story when I was in the room. It was three years ago. I only mention it because that silly story shook my faith, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You didn’t even know it, but I went home with my faith shaken, and I’ve been losing it more ever since. Yes, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you’re the reason for my fall. That wasn’t a Diderot!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch sounded upset and emotional, even though by now everyone could tell he was just acting again. Still, Miüsov was annoyed by his words.

“What rubbish, it’s all nonsense,” Miüsov muttered. “Maybe I told it at some point... but not to you. I heard it myself in Paris from a Frenchman. He said it was read at our mass from the Lives of the Saints... He was a smart man who studied Russian statistics and lived here for years... I’ve never read the Lives of the Saints, and I don’t plan to... People say all sorts of things at dinner—we were eating then.”
“Yes, you were eating, and so I lost my faith!” Fyodor Pavlovitch said, mimicking him.
“Why would I care about your faith?” Miüsov was about to shout, but he stopped himself, then said with disgust, “You ruin everything you touch.”

The elder stood up. “Excuse me, gentlemen, I need to leave you for a few minutes,” he said to everyone. “I have other visitors who arrived before you. But don’t start lying while I’m gone,” he added to Fyodor Pavlovitch, good-naturedly. Then he left the cell. Alyosha and the novice hurried to follow him down the steps. Alyosha was out of breath—he was glad to leave, but also relieved that the elder wasn’t upset. Father Zossima headed to the porch to bless the waiting people, but Fyodor Pavlovitch tried to stop him at the cell door.

“Blessed man!” he called out, sounding emotional. “Let me kiss your hand one more time. Really, I could talk with you for hours. Do you think I always lie and joke like this? Believe me, I’ve been putting on an act this whole time to test you. I wanted to see if I could get along with you. Is there space for my humility next to your pride? I’ll give you my word—you’re easy to get along with! But now, I’ll be quiet. I’ll sit in my chair and keep my mouth shut. Now it’s your turn to talk, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You’re the main character now—for the next ten minutes.”

Near the wooden porch outside the monastery wall, about twenty peasant women were gathered. They had heard that Father Zossima (the elder) was finally coming out, so they waited together, excited and hopeful. Two ladies, Madame Hohlakov and her daughter, were also out on the porch, but in a special section reserved for upper-class women.

Madame Hohlakov was a rich woman, still young and pretty, always dressed nicely. She was pale, with lively black eyes. She wasn’t older than thirty-three, and she’d been a widow for five years. Her fourteen-year-old daughter was partly paralyzed and hadn’t been able to walk for six months, so she was rolled around in a reclining wheelchair. The girl’s face was thin from sickness, but she was cheerful, and her big dark eyes sparkled with mischief. Madame Hohlakov had wanted to take her daughter abroad since spring, but business with their land had kept them in town all summer. They had been in town for a week, mostly for business, but had already visited Father Zossima three days earlier. Even though they knew the elder rarely saw anyone, they came again today, begging to “see the great healer just once more.”

The mother sat on a chair next to her daughter’s wheelchair, and two steps away stood an old monk—not one from this monastery, but a guest from a small, distant monastery in the far North. He also wanted Father Zossima’s blessing.

But when Father Zossima came out onto the porch, he went straight to the peasant women crowded at the bottom of the three steps. He stood at the top step, put on his stole (a priest’s scarf), and began blessing the women pressing around him. One woman, who seemed mentally ill, was brought to him. As soon as she saw the elder, she started screaming and twisting around like she was in pain. Father Zossima laid his stole on her forehead, said a short prayer, and right away she calmed down and became quiet.

I don’t know how it is now, but when I was a child, I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in villages and monasteries. They’d be brought to church, making animal noises so loud that everyone could hear. But when the holy sacrament was brought out and they were led up to it, their “possession” would stop, and they’d calm down for a while. As a child, this amazed me, but later, some grown-ups told me these women were just pretending to avoid work, and that being strict with them would cure it. But after hearing from doctors, I was surprised to learn it’s a real illness, especially common among Russian peasant women, caused by their hard lives, tough labor, abuse, and suffering. The quick “healing” when they were brought to the sacrament wasn’t a trick, but something natural: the women and those around them truly believed the evil spirit would leave if she bowed before the sacrament. The sick woman, expecting a miracle, would often have a strong reaction and seem healed, at least for a little while. That’s exactly what happened now, when Father Zossima touched the sick woman with his stole.
Many women in the crowd started crying with joy, moved by what they saw. Some tried to kiss the edge of Father Zossima’s robe, while others chanted or sang out.
He blessed them all and spoke with some of them. He already knew the “possessed” woman—she was from a village only six miles from the monastery and had been brought to him before.

“But here is someone from far away,” Father Zossima said, pointing to a woman who wasn’t old but was very thin, her face dark from being outside so much. She was kneeling, staring at the elder with wild, desperate eyes.
“From far away, Father, from far away! Two hundred miles from here. From far away, Father, from far away!” The woman began to chant, rocking her head and resting her cheek in her hand.

There is quiet, hidden suffering among peasants, but sometimes grief is too much and bursts out in tears and wailing, especially with women. This crying doesn’t make the pain lighter; it actually hurts more, but it comes from the need to keep feeling the loss. This kind of grief doesn’t want comfort—it feeds on its own hopelessness and the need to keep the wound open.
“Are you from a family of tradesmen?” Father Zossima asked, looking at her closely.

“We’re town people, Father, but still peasants even though we live in town. I came to see you, Father! We heard about you. I buried my little son, and I came on a pilgrimage. I went to three other monasteries, but they told me, ‘Go, Nastasya, go to them’—meaning you. I was at the service yesterday, and today I’ve come to see you.”
“Why are you crying?”

“I’m grieving for my little son, Father. He was three years old—almost three years and three months. For my little boy, Father, I’m in pain. He was our last child. Nikita and I had four, but now they’re all gone. I buried the first three and was sad, but I could move on. Now, after the last one, I can’t forget him. I see him everywhere. He’s always in my mind. My heart is broken. I look at his tiny clothes—his shirt, his boots—and I cry. I lay out his things and wail. I said to Nikita, my husband, ‘Let me go on a journey, husband.’ He’s a driver. We’re not poor, Father, we have our own horse and carriage. But what good is any of it now? Nikita will start drinking while I’m away—he always does when I leave. But I don’t think about him anymore. I left home three months ago. I’ve forgotten him, forgotten everything. I don’t want to remember. What would life be for us now anyway? I’m done with him, done with everyone. I don’t care about the house or our things. I don’t want to see anything at all!”
