“Listen, mother,” said the elder. “A long time ago, a holy saint saw a mother like you crying in the Temple for her only child who had died. The saint told her, ‘Don’t you know how bold these little ones are before God’s throne? There’s no one bolder in Heaven. They say, “Lord, you gave us life, but you took it back so soon!” They keep asking and asking, so God makes them angels right away.’ So, mother, you should also rejoice and not cry, because your son is with the Lord and the angels. That’s what the saint said, and he wouldn’t have lied. So remember, your child is with God, happy, praying for you. So don’t cry, but be happy.”
The woman listened, looking down, her cheek in her hand. She let out a deep sigh.

“My Nikita tried to comfort me with the same words as you. He said, ‘Don’t cry, our son is probably singing with the angels before God.’ He tells me that, but he cries too. I see it. I told him, ‘I know, Nikita, where else would he be but with God? But he’s not here with us anymore, not sitting with us like before.’ If only I could see him just once—just a peek, not even talk to him, just watch him for a minute, hear him playing outside, calling, ‘Mommy, where are you?’ If only I could hear his little feet running around the house one more time, just once. I remember how he used to run to me, laughing. If I could hear his footsteps, I’d know it was him! But he’s gone, Father, he’s gone, and I’ll never hear him again. Here’s his little sash, but I’ll never see or hear him anymore.”
She pulled out her son’s small embroidered sash from her dress, and when she looked at it, she started shaking and sobbing, covering her eyes with her hands as tears streamed down.

“It’s like Rachel from the Bible,” said Father Zossima, “crying for her children and refusing to be comforted because they’re gone. That’s the sadness mothers must bear on earth. Don’t try to be comforted. You don’t need it. Cry and don’t stop, but remember every time you cry that your son is now one of God’s angels. He sees you from heaven, rejoices at your tears, and shows them to God. You’ll carry this sadness for a long time, but one day it will become a quiet joy, and your tears will turn into gentle sorrow that heals your heart. I will pray for your boy’s soul. What was his name?”
“Alexey, Father.”
“That’s a beautiful name. Was he named after Alexey, the man of God?”
“Yes, Father.”

“He was a great saint! I’ll remember your son Alexey and your grief in my prayers, and I’ll pray for your husband’s health. But it’s wrong for you to leave him. Your son will see from heaven that you’ve left his father and will be sad. Why make him unhappy? He’s still alive—his soul lives forever—and even if he’s not in the house, he’s near you, unseen. How can he come home if you hate the house? Who will he come to if you and his father aren’t together? He visits you in dreams now, and you grieve. But then he’ll send you gentle dreams. Go back to your husband, mother—go today.”

“I’ll go, Father, because you told me to. I’ll go. You’ve touched my heart. My Nikita, my Nikita, you’re waiting for me,” the woman chanted softly. But Father Zossima had already turned to an old woman dressed like a townsperson, not a traveler. Her eyes showed she had something to say. She told him she was the widow of a non-commissioned officer and lived nearby. Her son Vasenka worked in the commissariat and had gone to Irkutsk in Siberia. He’d written twice, but it had been a year since his last letter. She didn’t know where to ask about him.

“Just the other day, Stepanida Ilyinishna—a rich merchant’s wife—told me, ‘Go, Prohorovna, put your son’s name down for prayers in church and pray for his soul as if he were dead. His soul will be troubled, and he’ll write you a letter.’ She said this always works, it’s been tried many times. But I’m not sure... Oh, Father, is this right or wrong?”

“Don’t even think about it. It’s wrong to pray for the soul of someone who’s alive—especially your own son! That’s a big sin, almost like magic. But since you didn’t know, you’re forgiven. It’s better to pray to the Holy Mother for his health, and ask her to forgive you for your mistake. And one more thing, Prohorovna—your son will either come home soon or send you a letter. Go and be at peace. Your son is alive, I promise.”
“Thank you, Father! May God reward you, you who pray for all of us and our sins!”
But the elder had already noticed two bright eyes watching him in the crowd. A young peasant woman, looking sick and thin, was staring at him quietly, her eyes pleading but afraid to come closer.
“What is it, my child?”
“Please, Father, forgive my soul,” she whispered, then slowly knelt at his feet. “I have sinned, Father. I’m afraid of my sin.”
The elder sat down on the lowest step. The woman moved closer to him on her knees.

“I’ve been a widow for three years,” she whispered, trembling. “Life with my husband was hard. He was old and beat me badly. When he was sick, I thought, if he gets better, what then? And then I had a terrible thought—”
“Wait,” the elder said, leaning closer so only he could hear.
She continued in a very quiet voice, so soft almost no one could hear. She finished quickly.
“Three years ago?” the elder asked.
“Three years. At first, I didn’t think about it, but now I’m sick and can’t stop thinking about it.”
“Did you come from far away?”
“Over three hundred miles.”
“Have you confessed this sin?”
“I have. Twice.”
“Have you taken Communion?”
“Yes. But I’m still afraid. I’m scared to die.”

“Don’t be afraid, and don’t worry. If your repentance is true, God will forgive everything. There is no sin on earth so big that God won’t forgive someone who truly repents. No sin is greater than God’s love. Keep repenting, but let go of fear. Believe that God loves you more than you could ever imagine—even with your sin, in your sin. It’s said that there’s more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ten good people. Go, and don’t be afraid. Don’t be bitter towards others, even if they hurt you. Forgive your dead husband for what he did to you. Make peace with him in your heart. If you’re truly sorry, you love, and if you love, you belong to God. Love can make up for everything, can even help save others. If I, a sinner too, can feel for you, how much more will God? Love is so precious that it can save the world, not just your own sins, but others’ too.”
He blessed her three times with the sign of the cross, took a small icon from his own neck, and put it on her. She bowed to the ground without saying a word.
He stood up and smiled at a healthy peasant woman holding a small baby.
“We’re from Vyshegorye, Father.”
“You came five miles with your baby? What brings you here?”

“I just wanted to see you. I’ve come before—don’t tell me you forgot me! You must be forgetting things if you did. We heard you were sick, so I thought I’d come see for myself. But you’re not sick! You’ll live another twenty years. May God bless you! So many people pray for you—how could you be sick?”
“Thank you for everything, daughter.”

“I do have a small request. Here are sixty copecks. Please, Father, give it to someone poorer than me. On my way here, I thought it’d be better to give it through you, since you’ll know who needs it most.”
“Thank you, my dear, thank you! You have a good heart. I love you. I’ll make sure to do it. Is that your little girl?”
“Yes, Father, my daughter Lizaveta.”
“May God bless you both, you and your baby Lizaveta! You’ve made me happy, mother. Goodbye, dear children, goodbye, my dears.”
He blessed everyone and bowed deeply to them all.

A visitor was watching the scene as the elder talked to the peasants and gave them his blessing. She started to cry quietly, wiping her tears away with a handkerchief. She was a sensitive woman from high society, sincerely kind in many ways. When the elder finally approached her, she greeted him with excitement.

“Oh, how moved I’ve been, watching this touching scene!...” She couldn’t finish because she was so emotional. “Now I understand why people love you so much. I love the people, too. I want to love them even more. Who wouldn’t love our wonderful Russian people, so simple and yet so great?”
“How is your daughter feeling? You wanted to talk with me again?”

“Oh, I’ve been begging for this! I even prayed for it! I was ready to kneel outside your window for three days until you let me in. We’ve come, great healer, to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. You healed my Lise—she’s completely better, just from your prayers and when you laid your hands on her last Thursday! We rushed here to kiss your hands, to show our gratitude and respect.”
“What do you mean, healed? She’s still sitting in her chair.”

“But her night fevers have completely stopped since Thursday,” the woman said quickly. “And that’s not all. Her legs are stronger. This morning she woke up feeling good; she slept all night. Look at her rosy cheeks, her bright eyes! She used to cry all the time, but now she laughs and is happy. Today she even insisted on standing up, and she managed a whole minute without help. She bets she’ll be dancing in two weeks! I called Doctor Herzenstube, and he just shrugged and said, ‘I’m amazed; I don’t understand it.’ So how could we not come to thank you? Lise, thank him—come on!”

Lise’s pretty, laughing face suddenly turned serious. She sat up as much as she could in her chair, folded her hands together, and looked at the elder. But then she couldn’t help herself and started laughing.
“It’s him,” she said, pointing at Alyosha, annoyed with herself for laughing.
If anyone had looked at Alyosha, standing just behind the elder, they would have seen him blush instantly. His eyes sparkled and he looked down.
“She has a message for you, Alexey Fyodorovich. How are you?” the mother continued, reaching out her gloved hand to Alyosha.
The elder turned and looked closely at Alyosha. Alyosha stepped forward to Lise and, smiling awkwardly, held out his hand to her too. Lise suddenly acted very serious.
“Katerina Ivanovna asked me to give you this,” she said, handing him a small note. “She really wants you to visit her as soon as possible. She says she’s counting on you and you must come.”

“She wants me to come see her? Me? Why?” Alyosha said, clearly shocked. He looked worried. “Oh, it’s about Dmitri Fyodorovich and everything that’s happened recently,” the mother explained quickly. “Katerina Ivanovna has decided something important, but she has to talk to you about it... I don’t know why. But she needs to see you right away. You must go—it’s your Christian duty.”
“I’ve only met her once,” Alyosha said, still confused.
“But she’s such a noble, amazing woman! Think of how much she’s suffered... and what she’s going through now! What’s going to happen to her! It’s all so awful, so awful!”
“Alright, I’ll go,” Alyosha said after reading the brief, mysterious note, which just begged him to come without any explanation.

“Oh, that’s so kind and good of you!” Lise suddenly burst out. “I told Mom you wouldn’t go, that you were too busy saving your soul. You’re wonderful! I always thought so. I’m so glad I can finally tell you!”
“Lise!” her mother said with emphasis, but smiled after saying it.
“You’ve completely forgotten about us, Alexey Fyodorovich,” she said. “You never visit anymore. And yet Lise has told me twice that she’s only happy when you’re around.”

Alyosha looked up, blushing again, and smiled—he himself didn’t know why. But the elder was no longer paying attention to him. He had started talking to a monk who had been waiting near Lise’s chair. The monk was clearly from a poor peasant background, narrow-minded but sincere and stubborn in his faith. He said he had come from far in the north, from Obdorsk, from Saint Sylvester’s monastery, which only had ten monks. The elder blessed him and said he could visit his cell whenever he wanted.
“How can you claim to perform miracles like this?” the monk suddenly asked, pointing at Lise. He meant her “healing.”

“It’s too soon to speak of miracles. Feeling better isn’t the same as a cure, and there can be many causes. But if there was any healing, it was only by God’s will. Everything comes from God. Please visit me, Father,” he added to the monk. “I don’t get many visitors—I’m sick, and I know I don’t have much time left.”
“Oh, don’t say that! God won’t take you from us. You’ll live a long, long time,” the lady cried. “But what’s wrong with you? You look so well, so cheerful and happy.”

“I do feel much better today. But I know it won’t last. I understand my illness now. If I seem happy to you, that’s the best compliment you could give me. People are made for happiness, and anyone who is truly happy can say, ‘I am doing God’s will on earth.’ All the saints and martyrs were happy.”

“Oh, how you talk! Such strong and inspiring words!” the lady exclaimed. “It’s like your words cut right through me. But happiness—where is it? Who can say they’re truly happy? Oh, since you’ve been so kind to see us again today, I want to tell you something I couldn’t say before. I’m suffering! Please, forgive me—I’m suffering so much!”
Overwhelmed with emotion, she clasped her hands in front of him.
“What are you suffering from, exactly?”
“I suffer... from lack of faith.”
“Lack of faith in God?”

“Oh no, no! I don’t even dare to think about that. But the afterlife—it’s such a mystery! No one can explain it. Listen, you’re a healer, you know people’s souls so well, and I know you might not believe me, but I swear I’m being serious. The idea of life after death drives me crazy with fear and sadness. I don’t know who to turn to, and I’ve never dared to ask anyone until now. I have to ask you. Oh God, what must you think of me?”
She folded her hands together.
“Don’t worry about what I think,” said the elder. “I truly believe that your suffering is real.”

“Oh, thank you! You see, sometimes I close my eyes and wonder, if everyone believes, where did faith come from? People say it’s just because of fear of nature, and that none of it is real. And then I think, ‘What if I’ve believed all my life, and when I die, there’s just weeds growing on my grave?’ I read that somewhere, and it scares me! How can I get my faith back? I only really believed when I was little, and that was automatic, without thinking. How can I prove it’s real? That’s why I came to you—to lay my soul open and ask you. If I miss this chance, I’ll never get another answer. How can I convince myself? I’m so unhappy! I look around and see that almost no one else cares; it’s only me who can’t stand not knowing. It’s killing me!”
“No doubt. But you can’t really prove it—though you can be convinced.”
“How?”

“By actively loving others. Try to love your neighbors, always and tirelessly. The more you grow in love, the more sure you’ll be that God and your soul’s immortality are real. If you can forget yourself in loving others, you’ll believe without any doubts. This has been tested. It’s true.”

“Active love? But I have another question—an important one! You see, I love humanity so much that sometimes I dream of giving up everything, leaving Lise, and becoming a nurse. I close my eyes and imagine helping the sick, and at that moment nothing scares me—not wounds, not infections. I could clean them, take care of the suffering, maybe even kiss their wounds.”
“It’s good that you have these dreams, not bad ones. Maybe one day, without realizing it, you’ll actually do something good.”

“Yes, but could I keep it up for long?” the lady went on passionately. “That’s my biggest worry. I shut my eyes and ask, ‘Would you keep helping if the sick person you’re caring for wasn’t grateful but instead was rude and demanding and complained about you to your boss—which happens a lot when people are suffering—would you keep loving them or not?’ And I realized, to my horror, that if anything could destroy my love for people, it would be ingratitude. Deep down, I want to be rewarded right away—with praise, with love in return. Otherwise, I can’t really love anyone.”
She was almost attacking herself with guilt, and when she finished, she looked at the elder with challenging determination.

“A doctor once told me the same thing,” the elder said. “He was older and very smart. He was honest, though he spoke with a kind of bitter joke. ‘I love humanity,’ he said, ‘but I’ve noticed that the more I love people in general, the less I can stand individual people. I’ve dreamed of doing great things for humanity—even being crucified if I had to. But I can’t stand being in the same room with someone for two days. As soon as someone is close, they annoy me and take away my freedom. After a day, I start hating even the best people—one takes too long eating, another keeps blowing his nose. I get angry as soon as anyone’s nearby. But the more I dislike people one-on-one, the more passionately I love humanity as a whole.’”
“But what should you do then? Is there any hope?”

“Don’t despair. The fact that you’re upset about this is already something good. Do what you can, and that will count for a lot. You’ve already come far if you can understand yourself so deeply and honestly. But if you’re only talking this way to get praise for your honesty, like you just did with me, then you won’t really achieve real love—it’ll just stay as dreams, and your life will pass by like a ghost. Then you’ll probably stop worrying about the afterlife, and you’ll get used to it and feel calmer in the end.”
“You’ve really hit me hard! Only now, listening to you, do I realize that I was just looking for your approval when I said I couldn’t stand ingratitude. You’ve made me see the truth about myself!”

“Are you being honest? Well, after such a confession, I believe you really are sincere and good at heart. If you don’t find happiness, remember you’re on the right path—just try not to leave it. Most importantly, don’t lie to yourself or to others. Watch out for your own dishonesty and notice it constantly. Don’t look down on anyone—not others, not yourself. When you notice your own faults, that alone will help you become better. Don’t be afraid, either—fear comes from lying. Don’t be scared if it’s hard to love people. Don’t worry too much about your own mistakes. I’m sorry I can’t comfort you more, but love in action is a hard, tough thing compared to love in dreams. Love in dreams wants quick, showy results; people will even die for a cause, as long as it’s fast and with everyone watching and cheering. But real love is hard work, patience, and maybe even a science. But I predict that just when you feel you’re failing, when you feel farther than ever from your goal—that’s when you’ll finally reach it and see how God has been loving and guiding you all along. Sorry, I can’t stay longer—they’re waiting for me. Goodbye.”
The lady was crying.
“Lise, Lise! Bless her—bless her!” she cried, suddenly jumping up.
“She doesn’t deserve to be loved. I’ve seen her mischief for a while now,” the elder said jokingly. “Why have you been laughing at Alexey?”

Lise really had been making fun of him the whole time. She’d noticed before that Alyosha was shy and avoided looking at her, which she found hilarious. She waited for him to meet her gaze, and when he finally looked, she grinned at him triumphantly. Alyosha got even more embarrassed and upset, finally turning away and hiding behind the elder. After a few minutes, unable to resist, he looked back—and saw Lise leaning out of her chair, peeking at him, eager to catch his eye. When he did, she laughed so much that the elder had to say, “Why are you teasing him, you naughty girl?”
Lise suddenly blushed. Her eyes flashed and her face got completely serious. She started speaking quickly and nervously, sounding both warm and upset:

“Why did he forget everything? He used to carry me around when I was little. We used to play together. He used to come teach me to read. Two years ago, when he left, he promised he’d never forget me, that we’d be friends forever! And now he’s suddenly afraid of me. Do I bite? Why doesn’t he want to come near me? Why doesn’t he talk? Why won’t he visit us? It’s not like you’d stop him—we know he goes everywhere. I can’t invite him myself, that’s not proper. He should’ve thought of it if he hasn’t forgotten me. No, now he’s too busy saving his soul! Why did you put that long robe on him? If he runs, he’ll trip!”

Then she covered her face with her hand and started laughing so hard she could barely breathe. The elder listened with a smile and blessed her warmly. As she kissed his hand, she suddenly pressed it to her eyes and began to cry.
“Don’t be mad at me. I’m silly and useless... Maybe Alyosha’s right not to want to visit such a ridiculous girl.”
“I’ll make sure he comes,” said the elder.

The elder had been away from his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was already past twelve-thirty, but Dmitri—the reason they were all gathered—still hadn’t shown up. Oddly enough, everyone seemed to have forgotten about him, and when the elder returned to his cell, he found his guests deep in conversation. Ivan and the two monks were leading the discussion. Miüsov was trying to join in eagerly, but he wasn’t having much luck. No one paid much attention to his comments, which only made him more irritated. He’d had debates with Ivan before and hated how Ivan could be so offhand with him.
“I used to be seen as one of the most forward-thinking people in Europe, and now these young people act like I don’t even exist,” Miüsov thought to himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had promised to sit quietly, had actually been still for a while. But he watched Miüsov with a mocking little grin, clearly enjoying seeing him struggle. Fyodor Pavlovitch had been waiting for a chance to get back at him, and now he couldn’t resist. Leaning over, he started whispering to Miüsov to tease him again.

“Why didn’t you leave earlier, after all that polite kissing? Why did you stick around with such ‘bad company’? It’s because you felt insulted and want to prove yourself by showing off how smart you are. You won’t leave until everyone sees your intelligence.”
“You again?... Actually, I’m just about to go,” Miüsov replied.
“You’ll be the last one to leave, you’ll see!” Fyodor Pavlovitch whispered, just as Father Zossima came back into the room.

The conversation paused for a moment as the elder sat back down in his usual spot. He looked at everyone, almost as if he was encouraging them to keep talking. Alyosha, who knew all the elder’s expressions, could tell he was extremely tired and pushing himself hard. Lately, he’d been having fainting spells from exhaustion. His face was pale, and his lips looked white, like they always did before these episodes. Still, he clearly didn’t want to send everyone away. It seemed like he had a special reason for keeping them there. Alyosha watched him closely, trying to figure out what it was.

“We’re talking about this gentleman’s fascinating article,” said Father Iosif, the librarian, pointing to Ivan as he spoke to the elder. “He brings up some new ideas, but I think the argument can go both ways. The article was written as a reply to a book by a church leader about the question of church courts and their authority.”
“I’m sorry I haven’t read your article, but I’ve heard about it,” said the elder, giving Ivan a sharp, focused look.
“He’s got an interesting point of view,” Father Iosif went on. “When it comes to church authority, he’s actually against separating the Church from the State.”
“That’s interesting. But what do you mean by that?” Father Zossima asked Ivan.
At last, Ivan answered, not in a condescending way like Alyosha had feared, but with humility and sincerity. He seemed genuinely friendly and had no hidden agenda.

“Here’s where I’m coming from: this mixing up of Church and State—these two different things—will keep happening forever, even though they can’t really mix, and nothing normal will ever come from it, because it’s built on a lie. Trying to compromise between the Church and State, especially about things like authority, just doesn’t work. The church leader I’m responding to says the Church has a clear, limited place in the State. But I think the Church should include the whole State, not just a small part of it. And if that’s not possible right now, it should at least be the main goal for the future of Christian society!”
“Exactly right,” agreed Father Païssy, the quiet, scholarly monk, with real passion.
“That’s pure Ultramontanism!” Miüsov burst out impatiently, crossing and uncrossing his legs.

“Well, we don’t have any mountains here,” Father Iosif joked. Then he turned back to the elder: “Look at how Ivan answers these ‘fundamental’ points from his opponent—a churchman. First, that ‘no social group should have the power to control its members’ political rights.’ Second, that ‘criminal and civil authority shouldn’t belong to the Church, because it goes against its nature as a religious group.’ And third, that ‘the Church is a kingdom not of this world.’”

“That’s a terrible misuse of words for a churchman!” Father Païssy interrupted. “I’ve read the book you responded to,” he said to Ivan, “and I was shocked at the phrase ‘the Church is a kingdom not of this world.’ If it isn’t of this world, then it can’t exist on earth at all. In the Gospel, that phrase doesn’t mean what he says. Twisting words like that is wrong. Jesus Christ came to establish the Church on earth. The Kingdom of Heaven is, of course, not of this world, but it’s only reached through the Church, which is on earth. So joking about it like that is unforgivable. The Church really is a kingdom and meant to rule, and in the end, it must become the kingdom that rules over the whole earth. We have God’s promise for that.”
He suddenly stopped, as if he’d caught himself going too far. Ivan listened closely and respectfully, then continued, speaking to the elder with calmness and real friendliness:

“The main point of my article is that for the first three centuries, Christianity was only the Church—it had no other form. When the pagan Roman Empire became Christian, it included the Church, but it stayed pagan in many ways. That was bound to happen. But Rome the State kept a lot of pagan ideas and ways of running things. When the Christian Church became part of the State, it couldn’t give up its core beliefs or its mission from God, which includes trying to bring the whole world, and even the old pagan State, into the Church. So, the Church shouldn’t just settle for a corner in the State like any other group, but should aim for the whole State to become the Church, giving up any goals that don’t fit with the Church’s mission. This wouldn’t lower the State’s honor or the honor of its leaders, but would turn it from a wrong path to the right one, the only one that leads to eternal life. The writer of the book on church authority would have been right if he’d said that the current way is just a temporary compromise for our sinful times. But when he claims these are the eternal foundations, he’s going directly against the Church and its true purpose. That’s what my article is about.”

“So, to sum up,” Father Païssy said, carefully choosing his words, “some modern theories say the Church should turn into the State, as if that’s moving up from something lower to something higher—so that the Church disappears and is replaced by science and modern ideas. And if the Church resists, it’s pushed into a corner under State control—which is what’s happening in many European countries. But Russian ideas say the State shouldn’t swallow the Church; instead, the State should become the Church and nothing else. So be it! So be it!”

“Well, I must admit you’ve made me feel a little better,” Miüsov said, smiling and crossing his legs again. “If I understand you, this ideal is so far off that it’ll only happen when Christ comes back. That’s fine. It’s like a beautiful dream—no more war, diplomacy, banks, and so on—almost like socialism. But I thought you were talking about something real, that the Church might start judging criminals and sentencing them to prison or even to death.”

“But if the Church courts were the only courts, even now the Church wouldn’t sentence anyone to prison or death. The way we see crime would change—not instantly, but fairly quickly,” Ivan replied calmly.
“Are you serious?” Miüsov shot him a sharp look.

“If everything was part of the Church, then the Church would just exclude people who did wrong—it wouldn’t execute them,” Ivan explained. “And what would happen to someone excluded? He’d be cut off not just from people, but from Christ. By committing a crime, he’d be sinning against the Church, not just against people. That’s true even now, but it isn’t always said clearly, and criminals often convince themselves: ‘I steal, but I’m not against the Church or Christ.’ That’s what they tell themselves today. But if the whole world was the Church, it would be much harder for a criminal to say, ‘Everyone else is wrong—I’m the only real Christian.’ That’s almost impossible. Now, think about how the Church sees crime: shouldn’t it move away from just cutting people off to protect society, and instead really try to help the person change and be saved?”
“What do you mean? I don’t get it at all,” Miüsov cut in. “Is this another dream? What is excommunication? What exactly do you mean by exclusion? Are you just joking, Ivan Fyodorovitch?”

“No, but you know, that’s actually how it is now,” said the elder suddenly, and everyone turned to him. “If it weren’t for the Church of Christ, nothing would really hold a criminal back from doing evil—except for the mechanical punishments we already talked about, which mostly just make people bitter. The only real punishment, the only one that works, comes from a person’s conscience when they recognize their sin.
“How’s that?” Miüsov asked, now genuinely interested.

“Well,” the elder began, “all these punishments—sending people to labor camps, or in the past, flogging—don’t actually reform anyone, and hardly scare criminals off, either. Crimes just keep increasing. So society isn’t really any safer. When one criminal is sent away, another just takes his place, sometimes two. If anything protects society or helps a criminal change, it’s the law of Christ in his conscience. Only by realizing he’s sinned against the Church—as a member of a Christian group—does he understand his guilt. So it’s only against the Church, not the State, that today’s criminal can really feel he’s sinned. If the Church had real authority, it would know when to bring someone back and welcome them again. Right now, the Church doesn’t have that power, so it just gives moral advice and never really punishes. It doesn’t officially cut anyone off, but keeps encouraging and caring for them instead. The Church even tries to keep up a relationship with the criminal—letting him come to services, take communion, giving him help, treating him more like someone in trouble than a convict. Imagine if the Church also rejected him the way the law does—what would happen then? There could be no greater despair, at least for a Russian criminal, since many still have faith. But if the Church was harsh too, maybe they’d lose even that faith, and then what? So the Church, like a loving mother, stays away from punishing, since the civil law is already so harsh, and someone needs to have pity. The Church stays apart because its judgment is the only true one, and it can’t really be mixed with any other kind of judgment, not even as a temporary solution. She won’t make deals about that. In other countries, they say criminals rarely repent, because modern ideas tell them their crimes are just reactions to unfairness. Society cuts them off and doesn’t care what happens to them, and there’s no help from the Church, because in many places, the Church has turned into just another part of the State. So criminals don’t feel like they’re part of the Church and fall into despair. If they come back to society, they often hate it so much that society rejects them again. It can happen here too, but the difference is that, besides the courts, we still have the Church, which always tries to keep a bond with the criminal. Even if it’s only in thought, the Church’s judgment is still alive as a dream for the future, and the criminal probably senses it deep inside. It’s true, as was just said, that if the Church had full authority and society itself became the Church, not only would the Church’s judgment have a much bigger effect, but there would probably be far fewer crimes. And the Church would treat both criminals and crimes differently, helping to bring people back, stop those planning evil, and change those who have fallen. Of course,” said Father Zossima with a gentle smile, “Christian society is still weak, resting on just a handful of truly righteous people, but as long as they’re there, the Church will survive, waiting to become a single, universal, all-powerful Church. So be it! Even if it takes until the end of the world, it’s meant to happen! And we don’t need to worry about when. Only God knows the right time, and what seems far off to us may be close at hand for Him. So be it, so be it!”
“So be it, so be it!” Father Païssy echoed, with seriousness and respect.
“Strange, very strange!” Miüsov said, not angrily, but with a quiet sense of outrage.
“What do you find so strange?” Father Iosif asked carefully.

“Why, it’s unbelievable!” Miüsov burst out. “You want to get rid of the State and turn the Church into the new State. That’s not just Ultramontanism, it’s even more extreme! Even Pope Gregory the Seventh never dreamed of this!”

“You’ve got it all wrong,” Father Païssy said sternly. “The Church isn’t supposed to turn into the State. That’s Rome’s idea. That was the devil’s third temptation. No, the State is supposed to become the Church, to rise up and become a Church for the whole world. That’s the opposite of Ultramontanism, and it’s the destiny of the Orthodox Church. This star will rise in the east!”

Miüsov stayed silent, looking extremely dignified, with a smug, condescending smile. Alyosha was deeply moved by the whole conversation, his heart beating fast. He glanced at Rakitin, who was standing quietly by the door, listening with his eyes downcast. But Alyosha could tell from Rakitin’s flushed cheeks that he was just as stirred up, and Alyosha knew why.

“Let me tell you all a little story,” Miüsov said, in a grand, important way. “A few years ago, after the December coup in Paris, I was visiting a very powerful government official and met an interesting man at his house. This man wasn’t exactly a detective, but he was in charge of a whole group of political detectives—a pretty important job. I was curious, so I talked to him. Because he saw how his boss treated me, he was willing to share a little, though he was more polite than open, the way Frenchmen can be, especially to a foreigner. Still, I understood him. We talked about the socialist revolutionaries who were being persecuted then. I’ll just tell you one thing he said: ‘We’re not really worried about all these socialists, anarchists, atheists, and revolutionaries. We watch them and know what they’re up to. But there are a few odd men among them who believe in God and are Christians—and socialists at the same time. Those are the ones we’re really afraid of. They’re dangerous! The Christian socialist is scarier than the atheist socialist.’ That stuck with me, and now it came back to me as we were talking.”
“Are you saying you see us as socialists?” Father Païssy asked directly.

But before Miüsov could answer, the door opened, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch—the guest everyone had been waiting for—finally walked in. People had almost given up on him, so his sudden arrival took them by surprise.

Dmitri Fyodorovitch (or Mitya), a young man of twenty-eight, was of average height and had a pleasant face, but he looked older than he really was. He was strong and muscular, but something about his face seemed unhealthy. His cheeks were thin and hollow, and his skin had a yellowish tint. His big, dark eyes looked determined, but also a bit distant and distracted. Even when he got angry or started talking loudly, his eyes didn’t always match his mood; sometimes they seemed to show the opposite of what he was feeling. People who saw him often said, “It’s hard to know what he’s really thinking.” His eyes could look serious and gloomy, but then he’d suddenly burst out laughing, showing that he had much lighter and happier thoughts than he seemed. Right now, his face looked tense, which was understandable. Everyone knew about the wild and troubled life he’d been living lately and the huge fights he’d had with his father. There were lots of stories going around town about him. It was true that he got angry easily and was “unstable and unbalanced,” as the local judge, Katchalnikov, liked to say.

Dmitri was dressed sharply and neatly in a perfectly buttoned suit. He wore black gloves and carried a top hat. He’d only recently left the army, so he still had a mustache but no beard. His dark brown hair was cut short and brushed forward at the sides. He walked with the long, confident steps of a soldier. He paused for a moment at the door, looked at everyone in the room, and walked straight over to Father Zossima, guessing he was the leader. He bowed low and asked for his blessing. Father Zossima stood up and blessed him. Dmitri kissed his hand with great respect and emotion, almost seeming angry as he spoke:
"Please forgive me for keeping you waiting so long. Smerdyakov, my father's servant, told me twice that the meeting was at one o’clock. Now I suddenly find out—"
"Don't worry about it," Father Zossima interrupted gently. "You’re a little late, but it doesn’t matter."
"Thank you very much. I expected nothing less from your kindness."

After saying this, Dmitri bowed again. Then, turning quickly to his father, he bowed to him just as deeply and respectfully. It was obvious Dmitri had planned this, thinking it was his duty to show respect and good intentions.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was surprised, but didn’t miss a beat. He jumped up from his chair and bowed just as low to Dmitri, his face suddenly looking very serious—almost angry. Dmitri then bowed to everyone else in the room, walked over to the window with his long, determined stride, sat down in the only empty chair next to Father Païssy, and leaned forward to listen to the conversation he’d interrupted.
Dmitri’s entrance had only taken a couple of minutes, and then the conversation continued. But now, Miüsov decided not to answer Father Païssy’s persistent and slightly annoyed question.
"Let me step out of this discussion," Miüsov said coolly. "It’s a tricky topic anyway. Ivan Fyodorovitch is smiling over there—maybe he has something interesting to say. Why don’t you ask him?"

"Nothing special, just a quick comment," Ivan said immediately. "A lot of European liberals, and even our own Russian ones, often mix up the results of socialism with those of Christianity. That’s a pretty common mistake. But it’s not just liberals—even the police, especially foreign police, make that mix-up. Your Paris story fits perfectly, Pyotr Alexandrovitch."

"I’d rather just drop this topic completely," Miüsov repeated. "Instead, let me tell you all something interesting about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Just five days ago, at a gathering here—mostly with ladies—he argued that there’s nothing in the world that makes people love each other. There’s no natural law that says you should love your neighbor, and if people have ever loved others, it’s only because they believed in life after death. Ivan Fyodorovitch even added that all natural law is based on that faith, and if you got rid of belief in immortality, not only love but everything that keeps the world alive would disappear. Then, nothing would be wrong anymore—everything would be allowed, even cannibalism. And that’s not all. He went on to say that for anyone who doesn’t believe in God or immortality, the rules of morality should flip to the exact opposite of religious rules, and selfishness—even crime—would be not just allowed but expected and even respected. That’s just one of the wild ideas our eccentric friend Ivan Fyodorovitch has!"

"Excuse me," Dmitri suddenly shouted. "Did I hear correctly—that crime should not only be allowed but is actually the logical and inevitable result for anyone who doesn’t believe in God? Is that right or not?"
"Exactly right," said Father Païssy.
"I’ll remember that."
Dmitri stopped as suddenly as he had started. Everyone looked at him with curiosity.
"Is that really what you believe will happen if people stop believing in life after death?" Father Zossima asked Ivan suddenly.
"Yes, that’s what I think. There can’t be real goodness if there’s no immortality."
"You’re lucky if you believe that—or maybe very unhappy," the elder replied.
"Why unhappy?" Ivan asked, with a smile.
"Because, most likely, you don’t actually believe your own soul is immortal, nor what you wrote in your article on Church law."
"Maybe you’re right!... But I wasn’t entirely joking," Ivan admitted suddenly, blushing.

"You weren’t just joking, that’s true. This question is still bothering you, deep down, and you haven’t found an answer. Sometimes, people who are suffering try to distract themselves with their own pain. You do the same, writing articles and debating in society, even though you don’t really believe your own arguments—and you secretly mock them even as you say them. That question is still unanswered for you, and it hurts, because it demands an answer."
"But can I answer it? Could I answer yes?" Ivan asked strangely, still looking at the elder with that odd smile.

"If you can’t answer yes, you’ll never be able to answer no, either. That’s the trouble with your heart, and all its suffering comes from that. Still, be grateful to God for giving you a heart that can think and seek higher things—for our true home is in heaven. May you find the answer on earth, and may God bless you on your journey."

The elder raised his hand as if to make the sign of the cross over Ivan. But Ivan stood up, went over to him, received his blessing, kissed his hand, and quietly returned to his seat. He looked serious and determined. Ivan’s action, and their strange conversation, made everyone feel the importance of the moment, and things grew quiet. Alyosha looked almost scared. Suddenly, Miüsov shrugged his shoulders, and at the same moment, Fyodor Pavlovitch jumped up from his chair.

"Most holy elder," Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, pointing at Ivan, "that is my son—my own flesh and blood! He’s my most loyal Karl Moor, so to speak, and this son who just came in, Dmitri, is the rebellious Franz Moor—they’re both characters from Schiller's play The Robbers, and that makes me Count von Moor! Judge us and save us! We need not just your prayers, but your prophecies!"
"Speak seriously, and stop insulting your family members," the elder said in a weak, tired voice. He was getting more and more exhausted.

"What a ridiculous scene—I knew this would happen when I came!" Dmitri shouted angrily, jumping up. "Forgive him, Father," he said to the elder. "I’m not an educated man, and I don’t even know how to address you properly, but you’ve been tricked and too kind to let us all meet here. My father just wants a scandal, and only he knows why. But I think I do—"

"They all blame me—every one of them!" Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted back. "Pyotr Alexandrovitch here blames me too! You’ve been blaming me, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you have!" He turned to Miüsov, who hadn’t said a word. "They all accuse me of hiding the kids’ money and cheating them, but isn’t there a court that can figure it all out? They’ll show, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, from your notes and letters, how much money you had, how much you spent, and how much is left. Why won’t Pyotr Alexandrovitch judge for himself? Dmitri isn’t a stranger to him! It’s because everyone is against me, while Dmitri Fyodorovitch actually owes me thousands of rubles—I have proof. The whole town gossips about his wild behavior, and even before, at his post, he spent thousands trying to win over some respectable girl. We know all about that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, every detail. I’ll prove it. And get this, Father, he’s won the heart of a very honorable young lady, the daughter of a colonel who was his commanding officer—an honored man. He promised to marry her, but now she’s an orphan here, and even though she’s engaged to him, he’s running after another woman right in front of her! And that other woman, even though she lived with a respectable man without being married, is strong and proud—like a real wife, and she’s virtuous, I tell you! Dmitri wants to win her over with money, and that’s why he’s rude to me now, trying to get more money, even though he’s already wasted thousands on her. He’s always borrowing money for it. Guess from who? Shall I say, Mitya?"
"Be quiet!" Dmitri shouted. "Wait until I’m gone! Don’t you dare insult a good woman in front of me! You talking about her is shameful, and I won’t allow it!"
He was out of breath.
"Mitya! Mitya!" Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, almost in tears. "Does your father’s blessing mean nothing to you? What if I curse you, then?"
"Shameless liar!" yelled Dmitri, furious.

"He says that to his own father! His own father! Imagine what he’d do to strangers! Gentlemen, just picture this: there’s a poor but honest man here, with a big family—a captain who lost his job in the army, but not because of any disgrace. And three weeks ago, Dmitri grabbed him by the beard in a tavern, dragged him into the street, and beat him up, just because he worked for me as an agent in a little business of mine."

"It’s all a lie! It may look true, but inside it’s a lie!" Dmitri was shaking with rage. "Father, I don’t excuse what I did. Yes, I admit it—I acted like a beast to that captain, and I’m ashamed of my violent anger. But this captain, your agent, went to the woman you call an enchantress and tried to get her, on your behalf, to collect my IOUs that you had, and threaten to put me in jail if I kept asking you for my inheritance. Now you blame me for caring about her when you’re the one who pushed her toward me! She told me herself and laughed at you. You tried to get me thrown in jail because you’re jealous I care about her, and I know you tried to force your attentions on her, too—she laughed at you for that as well. So here’s this man, my father, who calls me a disgrace! Please forgive my anger, but I knew this sneaky old man would try to cause a scene. I came here ready to forgive him if he wanted forgiveness, to make peace. But since he just insulted not only me but a good woman I respect so much I won’t even speak her name, I’m going to expose his lies, even if he is my father..."

Dmitri couldn’t speak anymore. His eyes flashed and he was breathing heavily. The whole room was tense. All the guests except Father Zossima stood up nervously. The monks looked strict but waited for the elder to guide them. He sat quietly, pale—not from excitement but from sickness. A gentle, pleading smile came over his face, and he raised his hand now and then, as if to calm everyone, but he seemed to be waiting for something and watched them closely, as if trying to figure out what was really going on. Finally, Miüsov felt completely embarrassed and ashamed.

"We’re all to blame for this shameful scene," he said angrily. "But I didn’t see it coming, even though I knew who I was dealing with. This needs to stop now! Believe me, Father, I had no idea about the things we just heard—I didn’t want to believe them, and I’m hearing them for the first time. A father is jealous of his son’s relationship with a woman with a bad reputation, and actually tries to get his own son thrown in jail because of her! And I’ve been forced to be here for all this! I was tricked. I swear to you all, I was as fooled as anyone."

"Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly yelled, his voice wild and unnatural, "if you weren’t my son, I’d challenge you to a duel right now... with pistols, three steps apart... across a handkerchief!" He stamped his feet for emphasis.

Old liars like him sometimes get so caught up in their performances that they actually tremble or cry real tears, even though, inside, they know they’re faking. They might even whisper to themselves, "You know you’re lying, you shameless old fraud! You’re putting on a show now, pretending to be so angry."
Dmitri glared at his father with deep disgust.

"I thought... I thought," he said softly and with effort, "that I was coming home to take care of my father in his old age, with the angel of my heart—my fiancée—and instead I find nothing but a disgusting, immoral clown."

"A duel!" the old man shouted again, gasping for breath. "And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, let me tell you—there’s never been a more honest, better woman in your whole family than this ‘creature’ you dared to insult! And you, Dmitri, left your fiancée for that ‘creature,’ so you must think she’s better than your fiancée. That’s the woman you call a ‘creature’!"
"Disgraceful!" said Father Iosif.
"Shameful and disgusting!" Kalganov shouted, his face red and voice shaking. He hadn’t said anything until now.

"Why does such a man even exist?" Dmitri muttered, beside himself with rage, his shoulders hunched until he looked almost deformed. "Tell me, how can anyone let him keep polluting the earth?" He looked at everyone, pointing at his father, and spoke slowly and clearly.

"Listen to that, monks—he’s threatening to kill his own father!" Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, running to Father Iosif. "That’s your answer to ‘disgraceful’! What’s so disgraceful? That ‘creature,’ that ‘immoral woman,’ might actually be holier than any of you monks! Maybe she made mistakes when she was young, because of her tough life. But she loved much, and Christ forgave the woman who loved much!"
"Christ didn’t forgive her for that kind of love," Father Iosif said, losing his patience.
"Yes, he did—for exactly that kind of love! You save yourselves here by eating cabbage and think you’re so righteous. You eat a little fish every day and think God will be impressed by that!"
"This is unbearable!" people said all around the room.

But the chaos was interrupted in a totally unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly stood up. Alyosha, almost panicking for the elder and everyone else, managed to catch him by the arm. Father Zossima walked over to Dmitri and, reaching him, fell to his knees. Alyosha thought he had collapsed from weakness, but instead, the elder deliberately and clearly bowed down until his forehead touched the floor at Dmitri’s feet. Alyosha was so shocked he didn’t move to help when the elder got up again. There was a faint smile on Father Zossima’s lips.
"Goodbye! Please forgive me, all of you!" he said, bowing to everyone.

Dmitri stood frozen in amazement. Bowing to him—what did it mean? Suddenly he cried out, "Oh, God!" covered his face with his hands, and ran out of the room. All the guests hurried out after him, so confused that they didn’t say goodbye or bow to their host. Only the monks stayed to receive the elder’s blessing.

"What did that mean, bowing at his feet like that? Was it a symbol or what?" Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, suddenly calm, trying to start up a conversation but not really talking to anyone. They were all leaving the hermitage at that moment.
"I can’t explain a madhouse or madmen," Miüsov answered grumpily, "but I’m going to avoid your company forever, Fyodor Pavlovitch. Where’s that monk?"
"That monk"—the one who’d invited them to lunch with the Father Superior—was waiting for them at the bottom of the steps, as if he’d known exactly when they’d be coming.

"Father, please do me a favor," Miüsov said sharply to the monk. "Tell the Father Superior that I deeply regret I can’t attend lunch with him today because of unexpected circumstances, even though I would have liked to."

"And of course, that ‘unexpected circumstance’ is me," Fyodor Pavlovitch interrupted right away. "Did you hear that, Father? This gentleman just can’t stand to be around me, or he’d come right away. Go on, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, go apologize to the Father Superior and bon appétit. I’ll be the one to decline, not you. I’m going home. I’ll eat at home—I don’t feel up to staying here. My dear relative Pyotr Alexandrovitch!"
"I’m not your relative and never have been, you awful man!"

"I said that on purpose to annoy you, because you always deny being related, even though you actually are, and I can prove it with the church calendar. Ivan, stay if you want. I’ll send the horses for you later. Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you must go to the Father Superior to apologize for the mess we made..."
"Are you really going home, or are you just lying?"

"Pyotr Alexandrovitch! How could I possibly stay after what just happened? Forgive me, gentlemen, I got carried away! I’m upset, too! Honestly, I’m ashamed. Some people have the heart of Alexander the Great, and some have the heart of a little dog. I’m the little dog. I’m ashamed! After a scene like that, how could I go to lunch and eat fancy monastery food? I’m embarrassed, I can’t stay. Please excuse me!"
"Who knows, maybe he’s lying," Miüsov thought, still hesitating and watching Fyodor Pavlovitch leave with suspicion. Fyodor noticed him watching and blew him a kiss.
"Well, are you coming to the Superior’s lunch?" Miüsov asked Ivan suddenly.
"Why not? I was especially invited yesterday."

"Unfortunately, I feel like I have to go to this annoying lunch," Miüsov grumbled, not caring that the monk could hear. "We ought to apologize for the disturbance and explain it wasn’t our fault. Don’t you think?"
"Yes, we have to make it clear it wasn’t our fault. Besides, father won’t be there," Ivan pointed out.
"Well, I certainly hope not! What a stupid lunch!"

Still, they all kept walking. The monk listened quietly. As they walked through the woods, he said only that the Father Superior had been waiting a long time and they were over half an hour late. No one answered. Miüsov glared at Ivan with hatred.
"Look at him, going to lunch like nothing happened," Miüsov thought. "He’s shameless, just like a true Karamazov!"

Alyosha helped Father Zossima to his bedroom and sat him down on the bed. The room was small and plain, with just what was needed—an old iron bed with a thin felt mattress, and in the corner under the religious icons, a little desk with a cross and a Bible on it. The elder collapsed onto the bed, completely worn out. His eyes were bright and he was breathing heavily. He stared at Alyosha, like he was thinking something over.
“Go on, my dear boy, go now. Porfiry can stay with me. Hurry up, they need you over there—go wait at the Father Superior’s table.”
“Can’t I stay here?” Alyosha begged.

“You’re needed more over there. That place has no peace right now. Wait with them, and help if you can. If things get tense, just say a prayer. And remember, my son”—the elder often called him that—“this is not where you’ll belong in the future. When God calls me, you must leave the monastery. Leave for good.”
Alyosha was shocked.

“What do you mean? This isn’t the right place for you, not for now. I bless you to serve in the world. You’ll go on a long journey, and someday you’ll even have to marry. You’ll have a lot to face before you come back. There’s much to do. But I trust you, so I send you out. Christ is with you—don’t leave Him, and He won’t leave you. You’ll see great sadness, but even in sorrow, you’ll find happiness. This is my last message: in your sadness, look for happiness. Work, work without stopping. Remember my words, because even though I’ll talk to you again, my time is almost up—not just days, but hours.”
Alyosha’s face showed how much this affected him. His mouth trembled at the corners.

“What’s wrong now?” Father Zossima asked, giving him a gentle smile. “People in the world cry over the dead, but here we are happy for the father who is leaving us. We celebrate and pray for him. Now go, I need to pray. Hurry. Stay close to your brothers—both of them, not just one.”

Father Zossima lifted his hand to bless Alyosha. Alyosha wanted to protest and stay, but he couldn’t. He also wanted to ask why the elder had bowed to Dmitri earlier—the question was right on his lips—but he was afraid to say it. He knew Father Zossima would have explained if he wanted to. That action had left a deep impression on Alyosha; he believed it was mysterious, maybe even frightening.

As Alyosha rushed out of the hermitage toward the monastery to help at the Father Superior’s dinner, he suddenly felt a sharp pain in his heart and stopped. He could almost hear Father Zossima’s words again, predicting his own death. If the elder had said it so clearly, it must really happen—Alyosha believed that with all his heart. But how could he live without him? Where would he go? The elder told him not to cry, and to leave the monastery. Oh God! Alyosha hadn’t felt so lost in a long time. He hurried through the woods between the hermitage and the monastery, looking up at the tall old pine trees to calm himself. He only had about five hundred steps to go and didn’t expect to see anyone, but right at the first turn in the path, he saw Rakitin waiting for someone.
“Are you waiting for me?” Alyosha asked as he caught up.

“Yeah,” Rakitin grinned. “You’re rushing to the Father Superior, right? He’s having a big dinner. There hasn’t been one like this since the Bishop and General Pahatov visited, remember? I won’t be there, but you go hand out the sauces. Listen, Alexey, what does that scene mean? That’s what I want to ask.”
“What scene?”
“When Father Zossima bowed to your brother, Dmitri. Didn’t he even touch his forehead to the floor?”
“You mean Father Zossima?”
“Yes, Father Zossima.”
“He touched the ground?”
“Well, maybe that’s not the most respectful way to say it, but you know what I mean. What do you think it meant?”
“I don’t know what it means, Misha.”

“I knew he wouldn’t tell you! It’s nothing special, just the usual holy show. But he did it for a reason. Soon, all the religious folks in town will be gossiping about it, trying to figure out what it meant. If you ask me, the old man has a sharp sense—he smelled trouble coming. Your family reeks of it.”
“What kind of trouble?”
Rakitin clearly wanted to say more.

“There’s going to be a crime in your family. Between your brothers and your rich old father. So Father Zossima fell on the ground to prepare for whatever might happen. If something does happen, people will say, ‘Ah, the holy man predicted it!’ though all he did was bow. ‘It was a sign,’ they’ll say, ‘an allegory,’ and who knows what else! People will remember it and say, ‘He predicted the crime and pointed out the guilty one!’ That’s how it always goes with these religious fanatics—they pray at the bar and throw rocks at the church. Your elder beats up the innocent and bows to the guilty.”
“What crime? What murderer? What are you talking about?”
Alyosha stopped in his tracks, and Rakitin stopped too.

“What murderer? As if you don’t know! I bet you’ve thought about it before. That’s interesting, by the way. Alyosha, you always tell the truth, even when you’re caught between sides. Have you thought of it or not? Tell me.”
“I have,” Alyosha said softly. Even Rakitin was surprised.
“What? Really?” he burst out.
“I... I didn’t exactly think it,” Alyosha muttered, “but when you started talking like this, it felt like maybe I had thought it myself.”
“See? (And you said it so well!) Looking at your father and your brother Mitya today, you thought about a crime. So I’m not wrong?”
“Wait, just a minute,” Alyosha interrupted, uneasy. “What made you see all this? Why do you care so much? That’s the first thing I want to know.”

“That’s really two questions, but fair enough. I’ll answer them one at a time. What made me see it? Well, I figured it out because suddenly, I understood your brother Dmitri completely. I saw right into him with just one clue. Honest but wild people have a line they can’t cross. But if they do, he’d attack your father with a knife. Your dad’s a drunken, wild sinner who never knows where the line is—if they both lose control, it’ll end badly for both.”
“No, Misha, no. If that’s all, you’ve made me feel better. That won’t happen.”

“Then why are you shaking? Listen, Mitya may be honest (he’s dumb, but honest), but he’s a sensualist. That’s who he is, deep down. He gets that from your father—low desires. I’m amazed you’ve stayed pure, Alyosha. You’re a Karamazov, too! Your family’s weakness for pleasure is almost like a disease. And now, these three pleasure-lovers are all watching each other, ready to fight. The three of them are at each other’s throats, and you might be the fourth.”
“You’re wrong about that woman. Dmitri—doesn’t respect her,” Alyosha said, shivering a little.

“Grushenka? No, he doesn’t despise her. He’s left his fiancée for her—he can’t despise her. There’s something here you don’t get yet. A man can fall in love with a beautiful woman, or even just a part of her (a sensualist would understand), and he’ll abandon his kids, sell his parents, even betray his country for her. If he’s honest, he’ll steal; if he’s kind, he’ll kill; if he’s faithful, he’ll cheat. Pushkin, the poet, even wrote poems about women’s feet! Others don’t write about it, but they still get excited just looking at their feet—and not just their feet. You can’t help it with contempt, not even if he does look down on Grushenka. He does, but he can’t let her go.”
“I get that,” Alyosha blurted out suddenly.

“Really? I bet you do understand, since you just let it slip,” Rakitin said sharply. “That was honest, and so it’s even more valuable. So you’ve thought about this stuff—about sensuality! Oh, you innocent soul! You act quiet, Alyosha, but who knows what’s in your head and what you’ve done! You’re pure, but you’ve seen the darkness... I’ve been watching you. You’re a real Karamazov—your dad was all desire, your mom was a little crazy and holy. Why are you shaking? Is it true, then? You know, Grushenka keeps begging me to bring you to her. ‘I’ll take off his monk’s robe,’ she says. You can’t imagine how much she wants to meet you. She’s a strange woman, really!”
“Thank her and tell her I’m not coming,” Alyosha said, forcing a small smile. “Finish what you were saying, Misha. I’ll tell you my thoughts after.”

“There’s nothing else to say. It’s the same old story, brother. If even you’re a sensualist deep down, imagine your brother Ivan. He’s a Karamazov too. All you Karamazovs are pleasure-seeking, greedy, and wild! Ivan writes religious articles as a joke, for some strange reason, even though he’s an atheist—and he admits it’s fake. That’s your brother Ivan. He’s trying to steal Mitya’s fiancée, and I think he’ll succeed. What’s more, Mitya will let him, just to get rid of her and run off to Grushenka. He’ll do it even though he’s supposed to be noble. Watch out for people like that! They know they’re wrong and do it anyway! And your father is getting in Mitya’s way now. He’s suddenly obsessed with Grushenka and acts like a lovesick cat. He made that scene earlier just because Miüsov called her a ‘loose woman.’ At first, she just worked for him at his bars and in other shady ways, but now he’s crazy about her. He keeps annoying her with offers—not marriage, of course. So, father and son are about to clash over her! But Grushenka isn’t choosing either of them—she’s playing them both, trying to see who’ll give her more. She could take money from the old man, but he’d never marry her, and might get cheap in the end. That’s where Mitya comes in—he’s broke, but he’ll marry her. Yes, marry her! He’d leave his fiancée, Katerina Ivanovna, who’s rich and beautiful, for Grushenka, who used to be the lover of a sleazy old merchant, Samsonov, a rough, uneducated local mayor. Some violent disaster could happen, and your brother Ivan is just waiting for it. That would be perfect for him. He’ll steal Katerina Ivanovna, who he’s crazy about, and take her sixty thousand ruble dowry. That’s a lot for a nobody like him. And he won’t even be hurting Mitya—he’ll be doing him a favor. I know for a fact that last week, when Mitya was drunk with some gypsy girls, he yelled that he didn’t deserve Katya, but Ivan did. And Katerina Ivanovna won’t say no to Ivan in the end—she’s already torn between them. Why does everyone worship Ivan? He’s just laughing at you all.”
“How do you know? How can you be so sure?” Alyosha demanded, frowning.
“Why do you ask, and why does my answer scare you? You know I’m telling the truth.”
“You don’t like Ivan. Ivan wouldn’t care about money.”
“Really? But what about Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty? It’s not just the money, but sixty thousand is tempting.”
“Ivan’s above that. He wouldn’t go after anyone just for money. It isn’t about money or comfort for him. Maybe he wants to suffer.”
“What a wild idea! Oh, you aristocrats!”
“No, Misha, he has a storm inside him. He’s trapped by his own mind. He’s driven by a huge, unanswered question. He’s the kind of person who doesn’t want millions, but wants an answer.”

“That’s not your own thought, Alyosha. You’re just repeating what your elder says. Ivan gave you a puzzle, huh?” Rakitin said, sneering. His face changed and his mouth twitched. “And it’s a dumb puzzle, not worth guessing. His article is ridiculous. Did you hear his theory before—if there’s no life after death, then nothing matters, and anything is allowed. (Remember how Mitya yelled, ‘I will remember!’) That’s just an excuse for bad people! (Sorry, that’s rude.) Not just for crooks, but for know-it-alls who like to show off their doubts. It’s all fake! People can still live good lives, even if they don’t believe in life after death. They’ll do it for freedom, equality, and brotherhood.”
Rakitin was getting worked up, but suddenly, as if he remembered something, he stopped.
“Okay, enough of that,” he said, grinning even wider. “Why are you smiling? Do you think I’m just some loudmouth?”

“No, I never thought you were a fool. You’re smart, but... never mind, sorry for smiling. I get why you care so much, Misha. I think, from how passionate you are, that you like Katerina Ivanovna yourself; I’ve suspected it for a while, brother. Is that why you dislike Ivan? Are you jealous?”
“And jealous of her money too? Why not say that?”
“I won’t talk about money. I’m not here to insult you.”
“I believe you, since you say so, but forget you—and your brother Ivan, too. Why should I have to like him? He talks down to me, you know. Why can’t I talk back?”
“I never heard him say anything about you, good or bad. He doesn’t talk about you at all.”

“But I heard that just two days ago, at Katerina Ivanovna’s, he was bad-mouthing me the whole time—you see how interested he is in me. So who’s jealous now? He even said that if I don’t become an archimandrite or a monk soon, I’ll end up in Petersburg writing for some magazine, and after ten years, I’ll own the magazine, make it liberal and atheistic, with a little bit of socialism, but always watching my own back, playing both sides, fooling everyone. He said I’d save up my profits, invest with the help of some Jewish businessman, then build a big house in Petersburg and rent out the top floors. He even picked the spot—near the new stone bridge they’re supposed to build.”
“Misha, you know, that probably is exactly what will happen, every bit of it,” Alyosha laughed, unable to help himself.
“So now you’re mocking me too, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
“No, no, I’m just joking, forgive me. I was thinking of something else. But, tell me, who told you all this? You couldn’t have been at Katerina Ivanovna’s when Ivan was talking about you?”

“I wasn’t, but Dmitri Fyodorovitch was. I heard him tell it myself; he didn’t tell me directly—I just overheard him by accident, because I was sitting in Grushenka’s room and couldn’t leave since Dmitri was in the next room.”
“Oh right, I forgot she’s your relative.”
“Relative? Grushenka, my relative?” Rakitin yelled, turning red. “Are you crazy? What’s wrong with you?”
“Wait, isn’t she related to you? I thought I heard that.”

“Where did you get that? You Karamazovs love to brag about being an old noble family, even though your father was just a clown at other people’s tables and barely allowed in the kitchen. I may just be a priest’s son, and nothing to fancy people like you, but don’t insult me like that. I have honor, Alexey Fyodorovitch—I couldn’t be related to Grushenka, a common prostitute. You should know that!”
Rakitin was really angry.

“I’m sorry, really, I had no idea... but how can you call her a prostitute? Is she really like that?” Alyosha blushed. “I’m telling you, I heard she was related to you. You visit her a lot, and you said yourself you’re not her lover. I never thought you’d look down on her like that! Does she deserve it?”

“I have my own reasons for seeing her. That’s none of your business. But as for family, your brother or even your father is more likely to be related to her than me. Anyway, we’re here. You’d better go to the kitchen. Whoa, what’s going on? Are we late? They can’t be done with dinner already! Have the Karamazovs made trouble again? Looks like it. There’s your father and your brother Ivan leaving the Father Superior’s. And look, Father Isidor is yelling something after them from the steps. And your father’s shouting and waving his arms—probably swearing. And there goes Miüsov driving off in his carriage. See, he’s leaving. And there’s old Maximov running! There must have been a fight. Maybe there wasn’t even a dinner. Did they attack the Father Superior? Or maybe they got beaten up? Honestly, it would serve them right!”
Rakitin’s surprise made sense. There really had been a scandal—a wild scene that no one expected. It all happened in a flash.

Miüsov, who prided himself on being a polite and cultured man, felt embarrassed as he and Ivan walked up to the Father Superior’s house. He was ashamed for losing his temper earlier. He thought he should have just ignored Fyodor Pavlovitch, that awful man, instead of letting him get under his skin during their visit to Father Zossima’s cell. “The monks didn’t do anything wrong,” he told himself as he climbed the steps. “If these people are decent—and I hear the Father Superior is a nobleman—why not just be friendly and polite? I won’t argue. I’ll go along with whatever they do, impress them with my good manners, and make it clear I’m not like that clown Fyodor Pavlovitch. I was tricked into this whole thing, just like they were.”

Miüsov decided right then to drop his lawsuit with the monastery and give up his claims to the forest and fishing rights. He was even more willing because those rights weren’t worth much anymore, and honestly, he didn’t even know exactly where the forest and river were.

These good intentions only grew stronger when he walked into the Father Superior’s dining room—even though it wasn’t really a dining room, since the Father Superior only had two rooms total. These rooms were bigger and more comfortable than Father Zossima’s, but they weren’t luxurious. The furniture was old-fashioned mahogany with leather, the floor wasn’t stained, but everything was spotless, and there were lots of beautiful flowers in the windows. The fanciest thing was the table, which was set with a clean cloth, shiny dishes, three kinds of bread, two bottles of wine, two of delicious mead, and a big jug of kvass—all made in the monastery and famous in the area. There was no vodka. Rakitin later told everyone there were five dishes: fish soup with little pies, then boiled fish, then salmon cutlets, ice pudding, compote, and finally blancmange. Rakitin found all this out by sneaking into the kitchen—he always found a way to poke his nose everywhere. He was restless and jealous, always thinking he was smarter than everyone else, and he was sure he’d be important one day. Alyosha liked Rakitin but was bothered that his friend didn’t even notice how dishonest he really was—Rakitin thought that just because he didn’t steal money, he was the most honorable guy around. No one could change his mind.

Rakitin, of course, wasn’t important enough to be invited to the dinner. Only Father Iosif, Father Païssy, and one other monk from the monastery were invited. They were already waiting when Miüsov, Kalganov, and Ivan arrived. Maximov, the other guest, stood to the side, also waiting. The Father Superior came into the middle of the room to greet them. He was tall and thin but still strong, with black and gray hair and a serious, thin face. He bowed silently. This time, the guests came forward for his blessing. Miüsov even tried to kiss his hand, but the Father Superior quickly pulled it back. Ivan and Kalganov, though, went through the whole ceremony and kissed his hand just like peasants do.

“We must apologize, your reverence,” Miüsov began, smiling politely and speaking in a formal, respectful way. “Please forgive us for coming without Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom you invited. He felt he had to decline your invitation, and for good reason. In Father Zossima’s cell, he lost his temper during an argument with his son and said some things that were... well, not appropriate.” He glanced at the monks. “I’m sure your reverence has already heard. Because he knows he was wrong, he feels truly sorry and ashamed. He asked me, and his son Ivan, to bring you his apologies and regrets. He hopes he can make it up to you later. He asks for your blessing and begs you to forget what happened.”
As he finished his speech, Miüsov felt completely at ease again, and all his earlier anger disappeared. He felt full of love for humanity once more.
The Father Superior listened to him calmly and, nodding slightly, replied:
“I’m very sorry he couldn’t come. Maybe if he’d joined us, we might have come to understand each other better. Please, gentlemen, have a seat.”
He stood in front of the holy icon and began to say grace out loud. Everyone bowed their heads respectfully, and Maximov clasped his hands in front of him, looking especially earnest.

Right then, Fyodor Pavlovitch decided to pull one last stunt. He really had meant to go home, and he did feel it would be wrong to show up at the Father Superior’s dinner after his outrageous behavior in Father Zossima’s cell. Not that he was all that sorry—probably the opposite—but he knew it wasn’t the right thing to do. But as soon as his old carriage was brought to the hotel steps and he got inside, he suddenly changed his mind. He remembered what he’d said in the elder’s cell: “Whenever I meet people, I feel lower than everyone else, and they think I’m a clown—so I act like one, since you’re all even stupider and lower than me.” He wanted to get back at everyone for his own bad behavior. He also remembered how someone once asked him, “Why do you hate so-and-so so much?” and he’d answered, “He never did anything to me. But I played a nasty trick on him, and ever since then, I’ve hated him.”

Thinking about that now, he grinned in a mean, sneaky way, hesitating for a second. His eyes flashed, and his lips trembled. “Well, I’ve started, so I might as well keep going,” he thought. What he felt most strongly at that moment could be summed up like this: “There’s no fixing my reputation now. So I’ll embarrass them as much as I can and show them I don’t care what they think. That’s all!”

He told the driver to wait, then hurried back to the monastery and straight to the Father Superior’s house. He didn’t really know what he would do, but he knew he couldn’t control himself, and if someone pushed him, he might do something outrageously rude—but nothing criminal, nothing he could get arrested for. He knew he could always stop himself at the last moment, and he was sometimes amazed by that. He walked into the Father Superior’s dining room just as the prayer ended and everyone was moving to the table. Standing in the doorway, he looked around at everyone and, with his long, mocking laugh, stared them all boldly in the face. “They thought I’d gone, but here I am again!” he shouted.

For a moment, everyone just stared at him in silence, and instantly, everyone could tell something shocking and awful was about to happen. Miüsov immediately went from feeling friendly to being furious. All his old anger came rushing back.
“No! I can’t put up with this!” Miüsov shouted. “Absolutely not! I just can’t!”
His face turned red, and he started to stutter. He didn’t care how he sounded—he grabbed his hat.

“What is it he can’t do?” Fyodor Pavlovitch called out. “What exactly is it he absolutely can’t and certainly can’t do? Your reverence, should I come in or not? Will you let me join you as your guest?”

“You are welcome, with all my heart,” answered the Father Superior. “Gentlemen,” he added, “I ask you, please, to put aside your arguments and be united in love and family harmony as we pray at our humble table.”
“No, no, this is impossible!” Miüsov shouted, completely losing it.

“Well, if it’s impossible for Pyotr Alexandrovitch, then it’s impossible for me, too, and I’m leaving. That’s why I came. I’ll stick with Pyotr Alexandrovitch everywhere from now on. If you leave, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I’ll leave too; if you stay, I’ll stay. You upset him with your talk of family harmony, Father Superior—he refuses to admit he’s my relative. Isn’t that right, von Sohn? There’s von Sohn. How are you, von Sohn?”
“Do you mean me?” Maximov muttered, confused.
“Of course I mean you!” Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted. “Who else? The Father Superior can’t be von Sohn.”
“But I’m not von Sohn, either. I’m Maximov.”

“No, you’re von Sohn. Do you know who von Sohn was, Father Superior? He was part of a famous murder case. He was killed in a brothel—that’s what you call those places, isn’t it? He was killed and robbed, and even though he was old, they nailed him up in a box and shipped him from Petersburg to Moscow. While they nailed him in, the prostitutes sang songs and played the harp—well, actually the piano. So this is the same von Sohn, back from the dead, isn’t it, von Sohn?”
“What’s happening? What is this?” voices whispered among the monks.
“Let’s go,” Miüsov said to Kalganov.

“No, excuse me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch interrupted loudly, stepping further into the room. “Let me finish. In the cell, you said I was disrespectful just because I talked about eating fish, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Miüsov, my relative, prefers to sound noble instead of honest, but I prefer to be honest instead of noble—forget nobility! Right, von Sohn? Father Superior, I may be a clown, but I have a good heart, and I want to say what I think. Yes, I’m honest, while Pyotr Alexandrovitch is just upset because his pride is hurt. I came here to speak my mind. My son, Alexey, is here, trying to be saved. I’m his father, and I care about what happens to him—it’s my job. While I was acting the fool, I was listening and watching, and now I want to give you the finale. Do you know what it’s like with us? Once something falls, it stays down forever. But I want to get up again. Father Superior, I’m upset with you. Confession is a great sacrament, and I respect that, but in the cell, everyone kneels and confesses out loud. Is that right? The holy Fathers said confession should be in secret—that’s the only way it’s a mystery. How can I tell everyone the things I’ve done—sometimes it’s not fit for public ears! That’s a scandal! You could turn people into Flagellants with this stuff... I’ll write to the Synod about it, and I’ll take my son Alexey home.”
