It’s important to mention that Fyodor Pavlovitch knew just where to poke to cause trouble. There had been rumors before—even the Archbishop heard them—that elders in monasteries were too respected, sometimes undermining the authority of the Superior, and that elders abused confession. These were silly accusations that had faded away. But Fyodor Pavlovitch, caught up in his own wild, nervous energy, brought up this old slander. He didn’t really understand what he was saying—especially since no one had confessed out loud or knelt in the elder’s cell that day. He was just repeating confused gossip he’d heard before. But as soon as he finished his ridiculous rant, he realized how foolish he sounded and wanted to prove that he hadn’t been talking nonsense. Even though he knew he was just making things worse, he couldn’t stop himself and kept going.
“How disgraceful!” Miüsov shouted.

“Please forgive us,” said the Father Superior. “It was said long ago, ‘Many have begun to speak against me and said bad things about me. And when I heard it, I told myself: it’s the Lord’s way of humbling my proud soul.’ So we thank you, honored guest,” and he made a deep bow to Fyodor Pavlovitch.

“Tut-tut-tut—empty words and fake respect! The same old speeches and gestures. The old lies and fake bows. We know all about those. A kiss on the lips, a knife in the back—just like in Schiller’s Robbers. I don’t like lies, Fathers. I want the truth. But the truth isn’t in eating fish, and I say that out loud! Why do you monks fast? Are you expecting a reward in heaven? For a reward like that, I’d fast too! No, holy monk, try being good out in the real world, helping people without hiding in a monastery at other people’s expense and waiting for a reward above—you’ll find that’s a lot harder. I can talk sense, too, Father Superior. What do we have here?” He walked up to the table. “Old port wine, mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. Wow, Fathers! That’s better than fish. Look at the bottles you brought out! Ha ha! And who paid for all this? The Russian peasant, the worker, brings his hard-earned coins here—money that’s hard to get from his family and taxes! You bleed the people, holy Fathers!”
“This is too disgraceful!” said Father Iosif.
Father Païssy stayed stubbornly silent. Miüsov rushed out, and Kalganov followed him.

“Well, Father, I’ll follow Pyotr Alexandrovitch! I’m not visiting you again. Even if you beg me, I won’t come. I sent you a thousand roubles, and now you’re watching me! Ha ha! No, I’m done. I’m getting payback for my youth, for all the humiliation I suffered.” He banged the table with his fist, pretending to be upset. “This monastery has been a big part of my life! It cost me many tears. You turned my crazy wife against me. You cursed me with bells and prayers, you spread rumors about me. Enough! This is the age of Liberalism, steamships, and trains. You won’t get a thousand, or a hundred roubles, or even a hundred kopecks from me!”

Truthfully, the monastery had never been important in his life, and he had never cried over it. But he got so caught up in pretending to be emotional that for a moment, he almost believed it himself. He was almost in tears. But right then, he realized it was time to stop.
The Father Superior bowed his head at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s spiteful lie and spoke with dignity again:
“It is also written, ‘Bear patiently and cheerfully the shame that comes to you through no fault of your own. Don’t be embarrassed and don’t hate the one who shamed you.’ And so we will.”

“Tut, tut, tut! More old sayings and speeches. Think it over, Fathers, I’m leaving. But I’m taking my son Alexey away from here for good—because I’m his father. Ivan Fyodorovitch, my loyal son, I order you to come with me. Von Sohn, what are you sticking around for? Come see me in town. It’s fun there. It’s only a short ride; instead of boring monastery food, I’ll give you roast pig and porridge. We’ll have dinner with brandy and liqueur... I’ve got cloudberry wine. Come on, von Sohn, don’t miss your chance!” He stormed out, shouting and waving his arms.
At that moment, Rakitin spotted him and pointed him out to Alyosha.
“Alexey!” his father yelled from across the yard when he saw him. “You’re coming home with me today for good. Bring your pillow and mattress—leave nothing behind.”

Alyosha stood frozen, watching the whole scene quietly. Meanwhile, Fyodor Pavlovitch got into the carriage, and Ivan started to follow him, grim-faced, without even saying goodbye to Alyosha. But just then, something even crazier happened. Maximov suddenly appeared at the carriage, running up, out of breath, afraid he’d be left behind. Rakitin and Alyosha saw him running. He was in such a hurry that he accidentally stepped on the same step as Ivan and grabbed the carriage, trying to jump in. “I’m going with you!” he kept shouting, giggling nervously with a wild look on his face. “Take me too!”

“See!” Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted, delighted. “Didn’t I say he was von Sohn? It’s really him, back from the dead! How did you get away? What vonsohn thing did you do there? How could you leave the dinner? You must be a real rascal! I’m like that myself, but you surprise me! Get in, get in! Let him through, Ivan. It’ll be fun. He can lie down at our feet. Will you lie at our feet, von Sohn? Or ride up front with the driver. Go on—get up there, von Sohn!”
But Ivan, who was already inside, suddenly punched Maximov hard in the chest, knocking him back. Maximov almost fell, but managed to keep his balance.
“Drive on!” Ivan shouted angrily to the coachman.
“What are you doing? Why did you do that?” Fyodor Pavlovitch protested.
But the carriage was already driving away. Ivan didn’t answer.
“Well, you’re a real character,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said again.
After about two minutes, he glanced sideways at his son and said, “You’re the one who got this whole monastery thing started. You pushed for it, you agreed to it. Why are you mad now?”
“You’ve talked enough nonsense. You should be quiet now,” Ivan muttered grumpily.
Fyodor Pavlovitch was silent for another two minutes.
“A bit of brandy would be good right now,” he commented, but Ivan didn’t reply.
“You can have some, too, when we get home.”
Ivan still said nothing.
Fyodor Pavlovitch waited another two minutes.
“But I’m still taking Alyosha out of the monastery, even if you hate the idea, my dear Karl von Moor.”
Ivan shrugged, looking annoyed, and turned away to stare at the road. They didn’t speak again for the rest of the ride home.

The Karamazov family’s house wasn’t right in the middle of town, but it wasn’t way out in the countryside either. It was an old, cozy two-story house, painted gray with a red metal roof. There was plenty of space, and the house looked like it could last for many more years. The place was full of odd little cupboards, closets, and twisting staircases. There were even rats, but Fyodor Pavlovitch (their father) actually didn’t mind them much. “It’s less lonely at night with rats around,” he used to joke. He liked to send all the servants out to the lodge in the yard overnight, locking himself inside the big house alone. The lodge itself was sturdy and roomy, and that’s where the servants cooked all the food—even though there was a kitchen in the main house—because Fyodor Pavlovitch hated the smell of cooking. No matter the season, they carried the dishes across the courtyard into the house. The house was built to fit a big family and their staff, but right now, only Fyodor Pavlovitch and his son Ivan lived inside. The only people in the lodge were three servants: old Grigory, his wife Marfa, and a young man named Smerdyakov. Let’s talk about these three for a moment. You already know a bit about Grigory: he was stubborn and determined, always sticking to what he decided was right, even if his reasons didn’t make much sense. He was honest, and nobody could buy him off. Marfa Ignatyevna, his wife, always did whatever Grigory wanted, but after the serfs were freed, she kept bugging him about moving to Moscow and opening a small shop with their savings. But Grigory made up his mind—he thought, “Women are all dishonest, and leaving our old master would be wrong.” So, he decided they had to stay and serve Fyodor Pavlovitch, no matter what.
“Marfa Ignatyevna, do you even know what duty means?” Grigory asked her.
“I know what duty is, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Marfa replied firmly. “But I’ll never understand why staying here is our duty.”
“Well, you don’t have to understand. But that’s how it’s going to be. And keep quiet about it.”

And that’s how it stayed. They didn’t leave, and Fyodor Pavlovitch promised to pay them a small wage—and he actually paid on time. Grigory knew he had real influence over his master. Fyodor Pavlovitch was stubborn and clever in his own way, but even though he could be strong-willed about some things, in other situations he was surprisingly weak and scared. He understood his own faults, and they worried him. Sometimes, you really need someone trustworthy to watch your back, and Grigory was that person. More than once, Fyodor Pavlovitch only avoided getting beaten up because Grigory stepped in—and each time, Grigory would scold him afterward. But Fyodor Pavlovitch wasn’t just afraid of physical threats. Sometimes, when he was drunk or acting especially badly, he got hit by these weird, almost physical waves of fear—like a panic attack. “My soul’s shaking in my throat in those moments,” he’d say. When he felt like that, he needed to know that someone loyal and strong—someone good, not like himself—was nearby, someone who knew all his secrets but wouldn’t judge or threaten him, just be there if needed, ready to defend him from some unknown danger. Sometimes, late at night, Fyodor Pavlovitch would even wake Grigory up and bring him over for no real reason, just to talk about nothing in particular, and then send him back. Afterward, Fyodor Pavlovitch would go to bed, sometimes cursing, but sleep peacefully. When Alyosha (also called Alexey) came to live with him, Fyodor Pavlovitch felt something similar. Alyosha “touched his heart” simply by living there, seeing everything, and never judging. Alyosha brought a kind of kindness Fyodor Pavlovitch had never known before—he was naturally devoted to his father, who didn’t deserve it at all. This shocked Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had cut himself off from his whole family and never cared for anyone except “evil.” After Alyosha left, he realized he’d learned something new—something he’d never wanted to learn before.

I already mentioned that Grigory hated Adelaïda Ivanovna, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s first wife and Dmitri’s mother, but he defended Sofya Ivanovna, the poor “crazy woman,” against Fyodor Pavlovitch and anyone else who talked badly about her. His sympathy for that unhappy woman had become almost sacred to him—even twenty years later, he couldn’t stand to hear anyone say anything negative about her and would stop them right away. On the outside, Grigory seemed cold, dignified, and quiet, choosing his words carefully and never being silly. You couldn’t really tell if he loved his obedient wife, but he did, and she knew it.

Marfa Ignatyevna wasn’t dumb; in fact, she was probably smarter than her husband, or at least more practical about real-world issues. Still, she always did what he said, never questioning or complaining, and she respected him for being more spiritual than her. They hardly ever talked to each other—just about the daily necessities. Grigory always thought through his problems alone, and Marfa got used to not being asked for advice. She felt her husband respected her for not talking much, and she saw it as a sign of her good sense. He had only ever hit her once, and it was barely anything. It happened a year after Fyodor Pavlovitch married Adelaïda Ivanovna: all the village girls and women (who were then serfs) were called to sing and dance outside the house. They started singing “In the Green Meadows,” and Marfa, who was young back then, jumped out and danced the Russian Dance—not like the peasants, but the way she’d learned when she worked for the rich Miüsov family, where they had a real dance teacher from Moscow. Grigory saw her dance, and an hour later, at home, he gave her a “lesson” by pulling her hair a bit. That was the only time, and after that, Marfa stopped dancing.

They didn’t have children. They had one baby, but it died. Grigory really liked children and never hid it. When Adelaïda Ivanovna ran away, Grigory took care of little Dmitri, who was only three, washing him and combing his hair, and watched over him for almost a year. Later, he also looked after Ivan and Alyosha—for which the general’s widow slapped him, but I’ve already told that story. The only happiness his own child gave him was before it was born. When the baby arrived, Grigory was shocked and heartbroken—it had six fingers. He was so upset that he stayed silent and hid in the garden until the christening. It was spring, and he spent three days digging in the kitchen garden. On the third day, when everyone, including Fyodor Pavlovitch (the godfather), had gathered for the christening, Grigory suddenly announced, in a flat voice, that the baby “shouldn’t be christened at all,” staring right at the priest.
“Why not?” the priest asked, surprised but friendly.
“Because it’s a dragon,” Grigory muttered.
“A dragon? What do you mean, a dragon?”
Grigory stayed quiet for a while. “It’s something messed up in nature,” he finally said, clearly not wanting to explain more.

Everyone laughed, and of course, they christened the poor baby anyway. Grigory prayed hard at the font, but he never changed his mind about the child. He didn’t interfere or try to stop anything, but as long as the sickly baby lived, he barely looked at it or even went into the cottage. After two weeks, the baby died of thrush. Grigory himself laid the child in its little coffin, looked at it with deep sorrow, and when they filled the tiny grave, he knelt down and bent to the earth. For years, he never mentioned his child, and Marfa never spoke of the baby in front of him—if she talked about it at all, it was only in a whisper when he wasn’t around. Marfa noticed that since the burial, Grigory had thrown himself into religion, reading the Lives of the Saints alone and in silence, always putting on his big round glasses. He almost never read aloud, except maybe during Lent. He especially liked the Book of Job, and he’d found a copy of the sermons of “the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian,” which he read over and over for years, barely understanding it, but maybe loving it all the more because of that. Lately, he’d started listening to the teachings of a group called the Flagellants who lived nearby. They really affected him, but he decided it was wrong to join them. All his theological reading made him seem even more serious.

Maybe Grigory was always drawn to mystical things. The birth and death of his deformed child seemed to be linked to another strange, almost miraculous event—something he said later “left a mark on his soul.” On the night after his child’s funeral, Marfa was woken by the sound of a newborn baby crying. She was scared and woke Grigory. He listened and thought it sounded more like someone groaning—maybe a woman. He got up and dressed. It was a warm night in May. As he went down the steps, he clearly heard groans coming from the garden, but the garden gate was locked, and the whole place was surrounded by a tall, strong fence. Grigory got a lantern and the garden key, ignored Marfa’s panicked fear that it was her own baby crying for her, and went out into the night. Right away, he realized the sounds were coming from the bath-house near the garden gate, and they were definitely a woman’s groans. He opened the door and was shocked by what he saw. Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya (people called her “Stinking Lizaveta”), a girl with intellectual disabilities who wandered the streets and was known to everyone in town, had gotten into the bath-house and just given birth. She was dying, with her newborn baby beside her. She couldn’t say anything—she’d never been able to speak. But her story deserves its own chapter.

There was one thing about Lizaveta that really caught Grigory’s attention and made him suspect something awful. Lizaveta was tiny—“not even five feet tall,” as the old women in town would say sadly after she died. Her wide, healthy red face looked blank and empty, and her eyes, even though they seemed gentle, had a strange, fixed stare that made people uncomfortable. Lizaveta wandered around all year, barefoot and wearing only a rough, scratchy shirt made from hemp. Her thick, almost black hair was super curly, like lamb’s wool, and it looked like a giant messy hat on her head. It was always dirty and full of leaves, twigs, and bits of wood, since she usually slept outside on the ground. Her father, Ilya, was a homeless and sickly drunk who had lost everything and spent years working for rich shopkeepers. Her mother had died a long time ago. Ilya was mean and sick, and whenever Lizaveta came home, he would beat her terribly—but she rarely went back, because almost everyone in town looked after her, thinking she was special to God because of her mental disability. Ilya’s bosses and other townspeople, especially the shopkeepers, tried to dress her warmly for winter, giving her big boots and a sheepskin coat. She let them dress her, but then she’d just go to the cathedral porch, take off all the clothes they’d given her—scarf, coat, skirt, and boots—leave them there, and walk away barefoot in her simple shirt again. Once, a new governor came through town and saw Lizaveta. He was shocked and said it was unacceptable for a young woman of about twenty to walk around in only a shirt, and that it shouldn’t happen again. But after he left, nothing changed. When her father died, the religious people in town liked her even more now that she was an orphan. In fact, everyone seemed to care about her—even the boys, who were usually troublemakers, left her alone. She’d walk into strangers’ houses, and no one chased her out. People were always kind and gave her things. If she got a coin, she’d put it straight into the church or prison donation box. If someone gave her bread or a bun at the market, she’d hand it to the first child she saw, or sometimes give it to a rich lady, who would happily accept it. Lizaveta herself ate only black bread and drank water. If she went into a fancy shop full of expensive things and money, nobody worried—everyone knew she wouldn’t take anything, not even a penny. She almost never went to church. She slept in the church porch or climbed over fences—there were lots of hurdles in town—into people’s gardens. Once a week, she’d show up at her father’s old employers’ house, and in winter she went there every night to sleep in the hallway or cow shed. People wondered how she survived such a hard life, but she was used to it and, even though she was small, she was very tough. Some townsfolk said she acted this way out of pride, but that didn’t really make sense—she could barely talk, only making strange noises now and then. How could she have been proud?

One clear, warm night in September, many years ago, five or six drunk men were leaving the club very late, at least by our town’s standards. They took the back way, which ran between people’s gardens, with hurdles on each side, and led to a bridge over a long, stinky pond that people called a river. In the weeds and tall plants near the fence, they saw Lizaveta asleep. The men stopped, laughed, and started making crude jokes. One of the younger guys even asked if anyone could ever see someone like her as a real woman, and so on. They all said, with disgust, that it was impossible. But Fyodor Pavlovitch (let’s call him Fyodor for short), who was with them, jumped in and said it wasn’t impossible at all—in fact, he thought there was something “interesting” about it, and so on. At the time, he was playing the clown, trying really hard to make everyone laugh. He liked to act like he was part of their group, but really, he was trying to impress them. This was right after he found out his first wife had died in St. Petersburg. He wore black ribbon on his hat for mourning, but was drinking and acting so wild that even the craziest people were shocked. Of course, the others laughed at Fyodor’s opinion, and one even dared him to prove it. The rest said no way, but still laughed, and finally, they moved on. Later, Fyodor always insisted he left with them—and maybe he did, no one knows for sure. But five or six months later, the whole town was gossiping angrily about Lizaveta’s condition, trying to figure out who had done this to her. Suddenly, everyone was saying the culprit was Fyodor Pavlovitch. No one knows who started the rumor. Of the drunken group, five had moved away, and the only one left was an older, well-respected councilman with grown daughters, who wouldn’t have spread something like that. Still, the rumor stuck to Fyodor, and people wouldn’t stop talking about him. He didn’t really care—he wouldn’t bother arguing with shopkeepers. Back then, he was proud and only talked to the officials and nobles, the people he entertained at his house.

At the time, Grigory defended his boss fiercely. He got into arguments and fights to protect Fyodor’s reputation, and even convinced a few people. “It’s the girl’s own fault,” he insisted, blaming a man named Karp, a dangerous escaped convict who had been hiding in town. This seemed believable, since Karp had been around that fall and had robbed three people. But all this talk didn’t make people care less about poor Lizaveta. People looked after her even more. A wealthy merchant’s widow, Mrs. Kondratyev, took Lizaveta into her home at the end of April, determined not to let her leave until after the baby was born. They watched her closely, but on the very last day, she managed to escape and got into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. No one could explain how she climbed over the tall, strong fence in her condition. Some people thought someone must have helped her; others whispered about something supernatural. Most likely, since Lizaveta was used to climbing fences to sleep in gardens, she just managed to do it herself, even though she was pregnant, and hurt herself jumping down.

Grigory rushed to get Marfa and sent her to Lizaveta, while he ran to find an old midwife who lived nearby. They managed to save the baby, but Lizaveta died at sunrise. Grigory took the baby home, sat his wife down, and put the newborn in her lap. “A child of God—an orphan belongs to everyone,” he said, “but especially to us. Our own lost child has sent us this one, who comes from the devil’s son and a holy innocent. Take care of him and don’t cry anymore.”

So Marfa raised the child. He was baptized Pavel, but everyone quickly added Fyodorovitch (son of Fyodor) to his name. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t mind any of this—he even found it funny, though he always insisted he wasn’t the father. The townspeople liked that he took in the orphan. Later, Fyodor gave the boy a last name: Smerdyakov, after Lizaveta’s nickname.

That’s how Smerdyakov became Fyodor Pavlovitch’s second servant, living with Grigory and Marfa in their house when our story begins. He worked as the cook. I should really say more about Smerdyakov, but I’m sorry to keep you focused on these ordinary folks for so long. I’ll return to the main story, but I’ll talk more about Smerdyakov later.

Alyosha stood there, unsure of what to do after hearing his father yell at him from the carriage. Even though he felt nervous, he didn’t just stand around – that wasn’t his style. He went straight to the kitchen to figure out what his dad had been up to upstairs. Then he set off, hoping he’d find some answer to the questions bothering him while he walked. By the way, his father’s loud orders for him to come home “with his mattress and pillow” didn’t scare Alyosha at all. He totally understood that his dad was just putting on a show, trying to make himself seem important—like the shopkeeper in town who, when he didn’t get more vodka at his party, smashed his own plates, tore up the curtains, and broke windows, just to be dramatic. Of course, the next day, he regretted it all. Alyosha knew his father would probably let him go back to the monastery the next day, or maybe even that evening. He was sure that while his father might hurt other people, he’d never actually hurt him. In fact, Alyosha felt certain no one in the world would ever want—or be able—to hurt him. He just took that for granted, and it helped him keep moving forward without any fear.

But right then, a different kind of worry started to bother him, and it was worse because he couldn’t really put it into words. He was nervous about seeing a woman, Katerina Ivanovna (Katya), who had sent him an urgent note through Madame Hohlakov, asking him to come see her about something important. Ever since he got that request, he’d felt uneasy, and even after everything that happened at the hermitage and with the Father Superior that morning, the feeling just got worse. It wasn’t because he didn’t know what she’d talk about or how he’d answer—he wasn’t scared of women in general. He’d actually grown up around women until he joined the monastery. It was something about Katerina Ivanovna herself that made him nervous. Ever since he’d first met her, he’d been a little afraid of her. He’d only seen her a couple of times and barely spoken to her, but he always thought of her as beautiful, proud, and a little intimidating. It wasn’t just her looks that unsettled him—it was something more, something he couldn’t explain, and that made it worse. He knew she was trying to help his brother Dmitri out of pure kindness, even though Dmitri had treated her badly. Still, even when Alyosha respected all her good intentions, he felt a chill run down his back as he got closer to her house.

He realized Ivan (his close brother) wouldn’t be there with her, since Ivan was definitely with their father right now. He was even more sure Dmitri wouldn’t be there, and he had a bad feeling about why. That meant he’d be talking to Katerina Ivanovna alone. He really wanted to go see Dmitri before facing her, just to talk things over, even without showing him her letter. But Dmitri lived far away, and Alyosha figured he probably wasn’t home anyway. Alyosha paused for a second, crossed himself out of habit, smiled, and then walked bravely toward the house of the woman who scared him.

Alyosha knew exactly where her house was. If he went around by the High Street and through the market, it would take a long time, because the town—even though it was small—was really spread out and the houses were far apart. Plus, his father might still be waiting for him and could get mad if Alyosha took too long. So, Alyosha decided to take a shortcut through the back way, since he knew every path and fence in town. He’d have to climb over some fences, cut through people’s backyards, and say hi to neighbors who all knew him, but it would let him reach the High Street much faster.

The shortcut took him past a garden next to his father’s property. The garden belonged to a shabby little house with four windows. Alyosha knew the owner was an old woman who was bedridden, living with her daughter. The daughter had once worked as a maid for rich families in St. Petersburg, but now she’d been home for a year taking care of her sick mother. She always wore fancy clothes, even though she and her mother were so poor they went every day to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen for soup and bread, which Marfa always gave them. Still, even though the daughter came for food, she never sold any of her dresses—one even had a long train, which Alyosha had heard from Rakitin (who always knew all the gossip). Alyosha had forgotten about the dress until now, but as he reached the garden, he remembered it, lifted his head from his thoughts, and saw something he totally didn’t expect.

Over the fence in the garden, Dmitri (Mitya) was standing on something, leaning over, waving his arms excitedly and signaling Alyosha to come closer. He was clearly trying not to make a sound so no one would hear him. Alyosha ran over to him.
“Good thing you looked up—I almost yelled for you,” Mitya whispered, sounding happy and urgent. “Climb over here, quick! I can’t believe you showed up—I was just thinking about you!”

Alyosha was thrilled too, but he wasn’t sure how to get over the fence. Mitya reached over with his strong arm and helped him up. Alyosha picked up his cassock and jumped over the fence as easily as if he were a street kid used to climbing things.
“Nice job! Now come on,” Mitya whispered, full of excitement.
“Where are we going?” Alyosha whispered, looking around. There was nobody else in the little garden—the house was at least fifty steps away.
“There’s no one here. Why are you whispering?” Alyosha asked.

“Why am I whispering? Oh, forget it!” Dmitri suddenly shouted. “It’s so weird how you start whispering just because you’re doing something secret, even when there’s no need. Never mind, let’s go. Over there. But stay quiet for now. I want to give you a hug.
I was just wishing for that before you showed up.”

The garden was about three acres, but there were only trees planted along the four sides—apple, maple, lime, and birch. The middle was just grass, which they’d cut for hay in the summer and sold for a few rubles. There were also raspberry, currant, and gooseberry bushes around the edges, and a kitchen garden planted near the house.

Dmitri took Alyosha to a hidden corner in the garden, where there was an old, falling-apart green summer-house surrounded by lime trees and thick bushes of black currant, elder, snowball, and lilac. The summer-house was really old and falling apart—the floorboards were loose and rotting, and it smelled musty. There was a green wooden table stuck in the ground, and some green benches you could still sit on. Alyosha immediately noticed that Mitya seemed strangely cheerful, and he also saw half a bottle of brandy and a glass on the table.
“It’s brandy,” Mitya laughed. “I see you looking at me—like, ‘He’s drinking again!’ But don’t worry, it’s not what you think.

I’m not drunk, I’m just ‘indulging,’ like your friend Rakitin says. He’ll probably be some big official one day, but he’ll still be talking about ‘indulging.’ Sit down. I wish I could grab you and squeeze you until I broke your ribs! Because, honestly, in the whole world—really, truly—(can you even believe it?) I love nobody but you!”
He said those last words with real passion.

“No one but you—and one woman who’s brought me to ruin. But being in love isn’t the same as loving someone. You can be in love with a woman and still hate her. Remember that! I can still joke about it for now. Sit here by the table and I’ll sit next to you—I just want to look at you and talk. You just listen and let me talk, because I need to. Actually, I should keep my voice down, just in case someone’s listening. I’ll explain everything. I’ve been dying to see you these last five days I’ve been hiding out here. Because you’re the only one I can tell everything to, the only one I trust. Tomorrow, everything will change for me—life will end and begin all at once. Have you ever had a dream where you’re falling off a cliff into a deep pit? That’s how I feel, except it’s not a dream. And I’m not even scared—or maybe I am, but I like it. Actually, I’m terrified, but also kind of thrilled. It’s weird, but that’s just how I am! Look at this day—the sun, the blue sky, the green leaves—it’s still summer, it’s so peaceful. Anyway, where were you going?”
“I was on my way to father’s, but I planned to visit Katerina Ivanovna first.”

“Her—and father? What a coincidence! Want to know why I was waiting for you, wanting to see you so badly? Because I wanted you to go to father and to her, Katerina Ivanovna, to sort things out with both of them. I could have sent anyone, but I wanted to send an angel. And here you are, already on your way to them!”
“Wait—did you really mean to send me?” Alyosha said, looking upset.
“Hold on! You already knew, didn’t you? I can tell you get it. But just be quiet for now—don’t feel bad, and don’t cry.”
Dmitri stood up, thought for a second, and tapped his forehead.
“She asked you, wrote you a letter, right? That’s why you’re going to see her? You wouldn’t be going otherwise?”
“Here’s her note,” Alyosha said, pulling it from his pocket. Mitya read it quickly.

“And you took the back way! Thank God for sending you this way, just like the golden fish in that old story! Listen, Alyosha, listen, brother! I’m going to tell you everything, because I have to tell someone. I’ve already told an angel in heaven; now I need to tell one on earth. You’re my angel on earth. You’ll listen, judge, and forgive me. That’s what I need, forgiveness from someone better than me. Listen! If someone is about to leave everything behind—run off into the unknown, or ruin themselves—and before they go, they come to a friend or brother and ask for a favor they’ve never asked before, something huge, who could say no?”
“I’ll do it—just tell me what you want, and hurry up,” said Alyosha.

“Hurry up! You’re always in a rush, Alyosha. There’s no need to hurry now. The world’s different now. Ah, I wish you understood what it’s like to feel ecstatic! Actually, what am I saying? Of course you understand! ‘Be noble, O man!’—who says that?”
Alyosha decided to just wait. He could sense that maybe this was where he was supposed to be. Mitya leaned on his elbow, resting his head in his hand, and both of them sat silent for a moment.

“Alyosha,” Mitya said, “you’re the only one who wouldn’t laugh at me. I want to start my confession with Schiller’s ‘Hymn to Joy,’ An die Freude! I don’t know German, I just know that’s what it’s called. Don’t think I’m talking nonsense because I’m drunk—I’m not. Brandy’s fine, but I’d need two bottles to actually get drunk:

I haven’t even drunk a quarter of a bottle, and I’m not Silenus, even if I am strong. Sorry for the dumb joke; you’ll have to forgive a lot more than jokes today. Don’t worry, I’m not dragging this out. I’ll get to the point soon. Wait, how does that poem go again?”
He lifted his head, thought for a second, then started reciting with excitement:
Mitya suddenly started sobbing and grabbed Alyosha’s hand.

“My dear brother, I’m so messed up. There’s so much pain and suffering in the world. Don’t think I’m just a brute in an officer’s uniform, lost in drinking and bad behavior. I really do think about miserable, fallen people—if I’m not lying to myself. I hope I’m not lying or just trying to show off. I think about those people because I am one of them.

The problem is, how do I stay connected to the earth forever? I don’t hug it, I don’t cling to it. Am I supposed to become a peasant or a shepherd? I keep moving forward and I don’t know if I’m headed for shame or for light and happiness. That’s the puzzle—life is full of puzzles! Every time I fall into the worst kind of mess (and it happens a lot), I read that poem about Ceres and people. Does it make me better? Never! Because I’m a Karamazov. When I mess up, I do it all the way, and I even feel proud of it. But even in the middle of all that, I start praising God. Let me be cursed, let me be disgusting, just let me touch the edge of the veil that covers God. Even if I’m following the devil, I’m still Your son, Lord, and I love You—I feel the joy that the world can’t survive without.

Enough poetry! I’m crying—just let me cry. Maybe it’s stupid, and everyone else would laugh at me. But you won’t. I can see your eyes shining, too. Enough poetry. Now I want to talk about the “insects” God gave “sensual lust” to.

I’m that insect, brother. All of us Karamazovs are. And even though you’re an angel, you have that insect in you too, and someday it’ll stir up a storm in your blood. Because desire is like a storm—a wild, uncontrollable storm! Beauty is both wonderful and terrifying! It’s scary because no one really understands it—God just gives us mysteries to solve. Life is full of contradictions. I’m not well-educated, but I’ve thought a lot about this. There are so many mysteries that weigh people down. We each have to try and make sense of them, and try not to drown. Beauty! I hate the idea that a man can start out worshipping the Madonna and end up obsessed with Sodom. Even worse, someone with Sodom in his soul never gives up dreaming about the Madonna. His heart can still burn with that pure dream, even after he’s been corrupted. People are just too complicated. I wish they were simpler! It’s impossible to make sense of—what our minds call shameful, our hearts call beautiful. Is there beauty in Sodom? Believe it or not, most people find their idea of beauty in Sodom. Did you know that? The scary thing is, beauty is both mysterious and terrifying. God and the devil are fighting for our hearts, and the battlefield is right there inside us. But enough about that—let’s get to the real facts.”

“Back then, I was living wild. Dad just said I spent thousands of roubles on seducing young girls. That’s a disgusting lie—nothing like that happened. And even if it did, I wouldn’t have needed the money just for that. For me, money was just extra—something to throw around because I felt like it, not the point itself. One day, I’d be with a classy lady; the next, just some random girl from the street. I spent money like crazy on music, parties, and gypsies. Sometimes I gave cash to the girls too—they never turned it down, that’s for sure. Some ladies liked me—not all, but it happened. But I always liked going off the main path, finding little adventures in the shadows—where you dig up surprises, even valuable things in the mud. I’m talking in metaphors, you know. The town didn’t really have dark alleys, but there were plenty of shady situations. If you were like me, you’d get it. I loved doing bad things, loved the shame of it. I liked being cruel sometimes—am I not a bug, a gross little pest? A true Karamazov! Once, a bunch of us went on a winter picnic in sledges. It was dark, and I started flirting with a girl, even forced her to kiss me. She was the daughter of an official, sweet and gentle. She let me do what I wanted in the dark. She thought I’d propose the next day (people thought I was a good catch), but I ignored her for five months. At dances, I’d see her in the corner, watching me with hurt, angry eyes. That just entertained the twisted part of me. Five months later, she married someone else and left town—probably still mad and maybe still in love with me. Now she’s happy. Notice, I never told anyone. I never bragged about this stuff. Even though I have low desires, I’m not dishonorable. You’re blushing—your eyes flashed. Let’s stop with this filth. And honestly, all this was nothing—just little random stories. But the dark side in me was already strong. I have a whole collection of these memories. God bless those girls. I always tried to end things peacefully. And I never told anyone. But enough about that. You didn’t think I brought you here just to talk about this nonsense, right? I want to tell you something more interesting. And don’t be shocked that I’m actually glad to tell you, not ashamed.”
“You say that because I blushed,” Alyosha said suddenly. “But I didn’t blush because of what you did or said. I blushed because I’m just like you.”
“You? Come on, that’s pushing it!”

“No, it’s not,” Alyosha said seriously (clearly, he’d thought about this before). “It’s like a ladder. I’m on the bottom step, and you’re way up, maybe on the thirteenth, but it’s the same ladder. Anyone on the first step could end up at the top.”
“Then people should never step on it at all.”
“If they can help it, they shouldn’t.”
“But can you?”
“I don’t think so.”

“Quiet, Alyosha, quiet, my dear! You’re so sincere, I could kiss your hand. That tricky Grushenka noticed you, you know. She once told me she’d eat you alive one day. But don’t worry—I won’t! Let’s leave this rotten stuff behind and move on to my real tragedy, which is just as dirty. Even though Dad lied about me seducing innocent girls, there actually was something like that in my story—just once, and it didn’t even happen the way he thinks. He doesn’t know about it; I never told anyone before. You’re the first—well, except Ivan. Ivan knows everything; he knew before you. But Ivan’s like a tomb.”
“Ivan’s a tomb?”
“Yeah.”
Alyosha listened very closely.

“I was a lieutenant in an army regiment, though I was still kind of watched, like a convict. But people in the town really liked me. I spent money everywhere and everyone thought I was rich—I thought so too. But I must have had other things going for me. Even though people gossiped about me, they still liked me. The colonel, the head officer, suddenly disliked me. He was always picking on me. But I had powerful friends and the town was on my side, so he couldn’t really hurt me. Still, it was my own fault—I refused to respect him properly. I was too proud. The colonel, who was actually a good, kind man, had been married twice—both wives dead. His first wife, who came from a humble background, left behind a daughter just like her. She was about twenty-four when I was there, living with her dad and her mom’s sister, her aunt. The aunt was simple and uneducated; the daughter, Agafya Ivanovna, was simple but lively. I like to say good things about people. I never met a woman with a better character than Agafya. And she wasn’t bad-looking for a Russian woman: tall, round, good eyes, though a bit rough around the face. She hadn’t married, even though she’d had two suitors, but she was always cheerful. I was close to her, but not in “that” way—it was just friendship. I’ve often had innocent friendships with women. I used to talk to her very openly, and she’d just laugh. Some women like that, and she was still a girl, so it was fun. You couldn’t really see her as a regular young lady. She and her aunt lived with the colonel in a sort of humble way, not acting like they were equal to others. Agafya was popular and useful—she was great at making clothes, and she’d do it for free, though she’d take money if offered. The colonel was a big deal, though—one of the most important people in the area. He had guests all the time, threw dinners and dances. When I joined the battalion, everyone was talking about his second daughter, a real beauty, coming home from a fancy school in the city. This second daughter is Katerina Ivanovna. She was the child of his second wife, who was from a famous general’s family, but I heard she didn’t bring any money either. Just connections, that’s all. Maybe they hoped for more, but it didn’t happen.

“But when the young lady came home from boarding school, the whole town got excited. The most important women—two titled ladies and the colonel’s wife—and everyone else followed their lead, throwing parties for her. She was the star of all the dances and picnics, and they even put on plays for charity. I ignored it all, kept living wildly, and did something stupid that got the town talking. I saw Katerina Ivanovna watching me at a party, but I didn’t go up to her—like I was too good for her. Later, I did speak to her at another party. She barely looked at me and just pressed her lips together, looking down on me. I thought, ‘Just wait, I’ll get back at you.’ I acted like a complete idiot back then, and I knew it. It was worse because I could tell that ‘Katenka’ wasn’t just some clueless schoolgirl—she was strong, proud, and really smart, everything I wasn’t. You think I wanted to propose to her? No, I just wanted revenge because I thought I was a big deal and she didn’t care.

“Meanwhile, I kept drinking and partying until the lieutenant-colonel put me under arrest for three days. Right then, Dad sent me six thousand roubles after I sent him a letter giving up any claim to his money—kind of settling things between us, saying I wouldn’t expect more. I didn’t understand any of it at the time. Even now, I barely get my money situation with Dad. But never mind, we’ll talk about that later.

“Just as I got the money, a friend wrote to me about something really interesting. The higher-ups were unhappy with our lieutenant-colonel. He was suspected of doing shady things, and his enemies were planning something big. Then the division’s commander showed up and caused a huge fuss. Soon after, the lieutenant-colonel was forced to retire. I won’t explain all the details—he definitely had enemies. Suddenly, everyone in town turned against him and his family. His friends abandoned him. That’s when I made my move. I ran into Agafya Ivanovna, my friend, and said, ‘Did you know your father’s accounts are short 4,500 roubles of government money?’
“‘What do you mean? Why are you saying that? The general was here recently, and everything was fine.’
“‘It was then, but not now.’
“She got really scared.
“‘Don’t scare me!’ she said. ‘Who told you that?’

“‘Don’t worry,’ I told her, ‘I won’t tell anyone. You know I’m as silent as the grave. I just wanted to say that, if they demand that 4,500 roubles from your father and he can’t pay, he’ll be put on trial and sent to be a regular soldier in his old age—unless you secretly send me your young lady. I’ve just gotten money. I’ll give her 4,000 and keep it secret, I promise.’
“‘You scoundrel!’ That’s what she said. ‘You wicked scoundrel! How dare you!’

“She stormed off, furious, while I shouted after her that I’d keep the secret. Agafya and her aunt, I should say, acted like absolute angels through all of this. They honestly adored their ‘Katya,’ thought she was way better than them, and did everything for her. Agafya told her about my conversation—I found out later. She didn’t hold it back, which was exactly what I wanted.

“Then the new major arrived to take over the battalion. The old lieutenant-colonel suddenly got sick, couldn’t leave his room for two days, and didn’t hand over the government money. Dr. Kravchenko said he really was sick. But I knew for sure—and had for years—that he never kept the money except when the Commander came to inspect. He’d lend it to a trustworthy local merchant named Trifonov, an old widower with a big beard and gold glasses. Trifonov would go to the fair, use the money to make a profit, then return the full sum to the colonel, plus a little gift and some interest. But this time (I heard about it from Trifonov’s useless son), Trifonov brought nothing back. The colonel rushed to him. ‘I never got any money from you. Impossible,’ Trifonov said. So now the colonel is stuck at home, with a towel on his head, with his family putting ice on him. Suddenly, an orderly shows up with the order to ‘hand over the battalion money immediately, within two hours.’ The colonel signs the book (I saw it later), says he’ll get dressed, goes to his room, loads his gun, takes off his boot, and tries to pull the trigger with his foot. But Agafya, remembering what I’d told her, got suspicious. She sneaked in and saw him just in time. She jumped on him from behind, grabbed him, and the gun went off—hitting the ceiling, not anyone. The others ran in, took away the gun, and held him down. I heard all this later. I was home, getting ready to go out—dressed up, hair brushed, nice-smelling handkerchief in hand, and about to leave, when suddenly Katerina Ivanovna walked into my room.

“It’s weird how things happen. No one saw her on the street, so the whole town didn’t know. I lived with two old ladies who took care of me. They were super helpful and, when I asked, kept silent like statues. Of course, I understood right away what was going on. Katerina Ivanovna walked in, looked me straight in the eye, her eyes determined and kind of challenging, but her lips and mouth looked unsure.
“‘My sister told me,’ she started, ‘that you’d give me 4,500 roubles if I came to you myself. I’m here...give me the money!’
“She couldn’t keep it up—she was out of breath, scared, her voice cracked, and her mouth trembled. Alyosha, are you listening, or did you fall asleep?”
“Mitya, I know you’ll tell the whole truth,” Alyosha said, really emotional.

“I am telling it. If I tell you exactly what happened, I won’t go easy on myself. My first reaction was a true Karamazov one. Once, a centipede bit me and I was sick for two weeks. Well, I felt like a centipede was biting my heart then—a poisonous bug, you know? I looked her up and down. You’ve seen her, right? She’s beautiful. But she was beautiful in a different way then. At that moment, she was beautiful because she was noble and I was a jerk; she was so generous and brave for her father, and I was like an insect! She was totally at my mercy, body and soul. She had no way out. I’ll be honest: that evil thought took over my heart—I almost couldn’t resist it, like I would act like a bug, cruel and without pity. I could barely breathe. But I would have gone the next day to ask for her hand, to make things right, so no one would know. Because, even though I have base desires, I’m honest. But suddenly, it was like I could hear a voice whispering, ‘But tomorrow, if you propose, she’ll have nothing to do with you. She’ll have the coachman kick you out. “Tell the whole town,” she’ll say, “I’m not afraid of you.”’ I looked at her and could tell that’s exactly how it would be. I could see from her face that I’d be thrown out. My pride was hurt. I wanted to take revenge—to sneer at her, and right where she stood, humiliate her with some nasty comment.

“‘Four thousand? What are you talking about? I was joking. You were too quick to count on that, Miss. Two hundred, maybe, sure, but not four thousand for something like this. You’ve wasted your time.’

“I would’ve lost, of course. She’d have run away. But it would have been a cruel revenge, and it would almost have been worth it. I’d have regretted it forever, but just to pull that trick! Believe it or not, I’ve never felt that way about any other woman. At that moment, I looked at her with real hatred—the kind that’s just a hair away from crazy love!

“I went to the window and pressed my forehead against the frozen glass. I remember it burned like fire. Don’t worry, I didn’t keep her waiting long. I turned back, went to the table, opened a drawer, and took out a five-thousand rouble note (it was in a French dictionary). I showed it to her, folded it, handed it over, opened the door for her, and bowed deeply—a really respectful, serious bow, believe me! She shivered, stared at me for a second, turned white as a ghost, and suddenly, not quickly but gently, bowed to my feet—not a silly schoolgirl curtsy, but a real Russian bow, touching her forehead to the floor. Then she jumped up and ran out. I was wearing my sword; I drew it and almost stabbed myself with it right there—no idea why. It would’ve been really stupid. Maybe it was just from the rush of it all. Can you understand feeling so much that you might kill yourself from joy? But I didn’t. I just kissed my sword and put it back—which I didn’t really need to tell you, but whatever. Maybe I’m making myself sound better than I was, but so what. Anyway, that’s what happened with Katerina Ivanovna. Now Ivan knows, and you know—no one else.”
Dmitri stood up, paced around in his excitement, wiped his forehead with his handkerchief, then sat back down—not where he was before, but on the other side so Alyosha had to turn to face him.
“Now,” said Alyosha, “I get the first part.”
“You understand the first part. That part was a drama, and it happened over there. But now the second part is a tragedy, and it’s happening here.”
“And I don’t understand anything about that second part yet,” said Alyosha.
“And do you think I understand it?”
“Wait, Dmitri. There’s something important I need to know. Tell me, were you engaged? Are you still engaged?”

“We weren’t engaged right away—not until three months after that whole mess. The next day, I told myself it was over, done, that nothing else would happen. I thought it would be sleazy to propose to her. She didn’t reach out to me at all for the six weeks she stayed in town; well, except for one thing. The day after she visited, her maid came by with an envelope for me. I ripped it open—it was the change from the banknote. Only four thousand five hundred roubles were needed, but there was a discount of about two hundred for exchanging it. She only sent me around two hundred sixty. I can’t remember exactly, but there wasn’t a note, not even a word of explanation. I checked for any kind of message—nothing! Anyway, I used the rest of the money to party so hard that my new commanding officer had to warn me about my behavior.

“Well, the lieutenant-colonel came up with the battalion money, and everyone was shocked because nobody thought he still had it. As soon as he paid, he got sick, took to bed, and three weeks later his mind started failing. He died five days after that. He got a military funeral, since he didn’t get discharged in time. Ten days after the funeral, Katerina Ivanovna, her aunt, and her sister left for Moscow. And, believe it or not, the day they left (I didn’t see them off or say goodbye) I got a tiny note—just a thin piece of blue paper with one line written in pencil: ‘I will write to you. Wait. K.’ That was it.

“Let me explain the rest quickly. In Moscow, their luck changed almost like magic, like something out of a fairy tale. Their closest relative, a general’s widow, suddenly lost her two nieces—her heirs—both died of smallpox in the same week. The old woman was heartbroken and took Katya in like a daughter, her last hope. She changed her will to leave everything to Katya. But that was for later. Right away, she gave her eighty thousand roubles as a dowry, letting her use it however she liked. The old lady was dramatic and emotional. I met her in Moscow later.

“Then, out of nowhere, I got four thousand five hundred roubles in the mail. I was completely shocked, as you can imagine. Three days later, I got the promised letter. I still have it—you should read it. She offers to marry me. She says, ‘I love you madly. Even if you don’t love me, it’s okay. Be my husband. Don’t be afraid. I won’t get in your way. I’ll be your property. I’ll be the carpet under your feet. I want to love you forever. I want to save you from yourself.’ Alyosha, I can’t repeat those words properly—they’re too beautiful for me, and I just make them sound cheap. That letter still hurts me. Do you think I don’t care? I wrote back to her right away, since I couldn’t go to Moscow in person. I wrote her with tears in my eyes. But there’s something I’ll always be ashamed of—I mentioned her being rich and having a dowry, and that I was just a poor loser. I shouldn’t have brought up money, but I did. Then I wrote to Ivan, told him everything in a six-page letter, and sent him to her. Why are you looking at me like that? Yes, Ivan fell in love with her; he’s still in love with her. I know it. Maybe I did a stupid thing, but maybe it’ll save us all in the end. Don’t you see how much she respects Ivan? When she compares us, do you really think she could love a guy like me, especially after everything that’s happened?”
“But I’m sure she really does love someone like you, and not someone like him.”
“She loves her own goodness, not me.” Dmitri blurted this out, almost bitterly. He laughed, but a moment later his eyes flashed, his face turned red, and he slammed his fist on the table.

“I swear, Alyosha,” he yelled, truly angry with himself, “you might not believe me, but as God is holy, and Christ is God, I swear that even though I just made fun of her high ideals, I know I’m a million times worse than her, and her ideals are as real as an angel’s. That’s the real tragedy—I know it’s true. So what if people put on airs sometimes? Don’t I do it too? But I am sincere. And as for Ivan, I can imagine him cursing fate now—with his intelligence! To see her pick me—me, who’s engaged but can’t stop behaving badly, right in front of my fiancée! And yet she picks me, not Ivan. Why? Because she wants to sacrifice herself out of gratitude. It’s crazy! I’ve never told Ivan any of this, and he’s never said anything to me either. But fate is fate. The best man will win, and the one who doesn’t deserve her will disappear into his own miserable corner forever—his filthy back alley, where he belongs, and where he’ll rot by his own choice. I’m just rambling now. I can’t say it right, but that’s how it’ll be. I’ll drown in that back alley, and she’ll marry Ivan.”

“Stop, Dmitri,” Alyosha interrupted anxiously. “There’s still something you haven’t explained: you’re still engaged, aren’t you? How can you break off the engagement if she—your fiancée—doesn’t want to?”

“Yes, officially and properly engaged. It all happened when I got to Moscow, with a big ceremony, icons, everything done right. The general’s wife blessed us and—would you believe it?—even congratulated Katya, saying, ‘You’ve made a good choice. I can see right through him.’ And—can you imagine?—she didn’t like Ivan and barely even greeted him. I talked a lot with Katya in Moscow. I told her everything about myself—honestly, straight up. She listened to all of it.
Though, to be honest, there were some proud things said too. She forced me to promise I’d become a better person. I made that promise, and now—”
“What?”
“Well, I called you out here today—remember that—to send you—yes, today—to Katerina Ivanovna and—”
“What?”
“To tell her I’ll never come see her again. Say, ‘He sends you his regards.’”
“But is that even possible?”
“That’s exactly why I’m sending you instead of going myself—because it’s impossible. How could I face her?”
“So where are you going?”
“To the back alley.”
“To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha said sadly, putting his hands together. “So Rakitin was telling the truth? I thought you just visited her, and that was it.”

“How could a guy who’s engaged go visit someone like that? Is that even possible, especially with a fiancée like Katya, and everyone watching? I do have some honor! As soon as I started seeing Grushenka, I stopped being engaged and honest. I get that. Why are you looking at me? See, I went there at first to confront her. I’d heard—and now I know for sure—that my father’s agent, that captain, had given Grushenka an IOU of mine so she could make me pay up and ruin me. They wanted to scare me. I went to fight her. I’d seen her before. She doesn’t impress you at first. I knew about her old lover, the merchant who’s sick now, paralyzed, but leaving her some money. I also knew she loved money, hoarded it, and lent it out at crazy high interest, and that she’s a pretty ruthless cheat. I went to fight her, and I stayed. The whole thing hit me like a disease. I’m still sick, and I know I’m finished, that nothing good is left for me. That’s my situation. And even though I’m broke, by chance I happened to have three thousand roubles in my pocket right then. I went with Grushenka to Mokroe, about twenty-five miles from here. I brought in gypsies and champagne, got all the peasants drunk, and spent everything. In three days, I was broke, but I felt like a hero. Do you think I got what I wanted from her? Not a bit. I’m telling you, Grushenka is tricky—she has this way about her, you can even see it in her little toe. I saw it, and I kissed her foot, but that’s all, I swear! ‘I’ll marry you if you want,’ she said, ‘but you’re broke. Promise you won’t beat me and will let me do whatever I want, and maybe I’ll marry you.’ She laughed—and she’s still laughing!”
Dmitri jumped up, furious. He suddenly looked almost drunk, and his eyes turned bloodshot.
“And do you really want to marry her?”

“Right away, if she’ll have me. And if she won’t, I’ll stay anyway. I’ll be the doorman at her house. Alyosha!” he shouted, grabbing Alyosha by the shoulders and shaking him hard. “You have no idea, innocent boy, how crazy this all is—there’s a tragedy here. Look, Alexey, I might be a low person with rotten desires, but Dmitri Karamazov is not a thief or a pickpocket. But let me tell you: I am a thief and a pickpocket. That same morning, just before I went to fight with Grushenka, Katerina Ivanovna secretly asked me to go to the main city and mail three thousand roubles to Agafya Ivanovna in Moscow, so no one here would find out. So I had that three thousand roubles in my pocket when I went to see Grushenka, and it’s that money we spent at Mokroe. Later, I pretended I’d mailed it, but I didn’t show her a postal receipt. I said I’d sent the money and would bring proof, but I haven’t. I just forgot. Now what do you think you’re going to tell her today? ‘He sends his regards,’ and she’ll ask, ‘What about the money?’ You could have told her, ‘He’s a messed-up guy who wasted your money because he couldn’t control himself. But at least he’s not a thief—here’s your three thousand, you send it to Agafya Ivanovna. And he says “he sends his regards.”’ But as it is, she’ll ask, ‘But where’s the money?’”
“Mitya, you’re really suffering, yes! But not as badly as you think. Don’t torture yourself with all this misery.”

“What, do you think I’d shoot myself because I can’t pay back three thousand? No way. I’m not going to kill myself. Not right now, anyway. Maybe later. For now, I’m going to Grushenka. I don’t care what happens.”
“And then what?”
“I’ll be her husband if she’ll have me. And when she has lovers visit, I’ll just go in the next room. I’ll polish their shoes, heat their tea, run their errands.”

“Katerina Ivanovna will understand everything,” Alyosha said solemnly. “She’ll see how big this problem is and she’ll forgive you. She’s a great person. No one could be more unhappy than you. She’ll understand.”
“She won’t forgive everything,” said Dmitri, with a twisted smile. “There’s something here that no woman could ever forgive. Do you know what the best thing would be?”
“What?”
“Pay back the three thousand.”
“Where would we get it? I have two thousand. Ivan will give you another thousand—that’s three. Take it and pay her back.”

“And when would you get your three thousand? You’re not even old enough, and besides, you have to—absolutely have to—take my message to her today, with or without the money, because I can’t keep dragging this out. Things have gotten so bad. Tomorrow is too late. I’ll send you to Father.”
“To Father?”
“Yes, to Father first. Ask him for three thousand.”
“But, Mitya, he won’t give it.”
“Of course he won’t! I know he won’t. Do you know what real despair is, Alexey?”
“Yes.”

“Listen. Legally, he doesn’t owe me a thing. I’ve already gotten everything from him; I know that. But morally, he does owe me something, right? He started with twenty-eight thousand roubles from my mother’s money and turned it into a hundred thousand. Let him just give me three out of that twenty-eight thousand, and he’ll save my soul, and it’ll pay for a lot of his sins. For that three thousand, I swear, I’ll end all this, and he’ll never hear from me again. This is his last chance to act like a father. Tell him God Himself is giving him this chance.”
“Mitya, he won’t give it, no matter what.”

“I know. I know it perfectly well. Especially now. And that’s not all. I know something else. Just a few days ago, maybe even yesterday, he finally realized for sure (really realized) that Grushenka might actually not be joking and really might marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows how she is. Do you think he’ll give me money to help make that happen when he’s obsessed with her himself? And there’s more. I know that in the last five days, he took out three thousand roubles from the bank, changed it into hundred-rouble notes, put them in a big envelope, sealed it five times, and tied it with red string. See how much I know? On the envelope, he wrote: ‘To my angel, Grushenka, when she comes to me.’ He wrote it himself in secret, and no one knows the money’s there except his servant, Smerdyakov, who he trusts completely. So now he’s been waiting for Grushenka to come for the last few days; he hopes she’ll show up for the money. He sent her a message about it, and she replied that maybe she’d come. If she actually does visit him, how could I marry her after that? Now you understand why I’m here in hiding and what I’m watching for.”
“For her?”

“Yes, for her. Foma has a room in this house—he’s from our area, used to be a soldier in our unit. He does odd jobs here. He’s the night watchman and hunts during the day. That’s how he lives. I’m staying in his room. Neither he nor the women in the house know my real secret—that I’m here watching.”
“So only Smerdyakov knows?”
“No one else. He’ll let me know if she goes to the old man.”
“So he’s the one who told you about the money?”

“Yes. It’s a dead secret. Even Ivan doesn’t know about the money, or anything else. The old man is sending Ivan to Tchermashnya for two or three days because someone wants to buy the copse for eight thousand. So Father keeps asking Ivan to go work out the deal. It’ll take two or three days. That’s what Father wants—so Grushenka can come while Ivan’s away.”
“So he’s expecting Grushenka today?”

“No, she won’t come today; I can tell. She definitely won’t,” Mitya suddenly said. “Smerdyakov thinks so too. Father’s drinking now. He’s at the table with Ivan. Go to him, Alyosha, and ask for the three thousand.”
“Mitya, what’s wrong with you?” Alyosha cried, jumping up and staring at his brother’s wild face. For a second, Alyosha wondered if Dmitri had gone crazy.
“What is it? I’m not crazy,” said Dmitri, looking at him seriously. “Don’t worry. I’m sending you to Father because I know what I’m saying. I believe in miracles.”
“In miracles?”
“Yes, in a miracle from God. God knows my heart. He sees my despair. He sees everything that’s happening. He won’t let something terrible happen. Alyosha, I believe in miracles. Go!”
“I’m going. Will you wait for me here?”

“Yes. I know it’ll take some time. You can’t just go straight at him. He’s drunk right now. I’ll wait three hours—four, five, six, seven. Just remember, you have to go to Katerina Ivanovna today, even if it’s midnight, with or without the money, and say, ‘He sends his regards.’ I want you to say that to her: ‘He sends his regards.’”
“Mitya! And what if Grushenka comes today—or if not today, tomorrow or the next day?”
“Grushenka? If she comes, I’ll see her. I’ll rush out and stop it.”
“And if—”
“If that happens, it’ll be murder. I couldn’t handle it.”
“Who would be killed?”
“The old man. I wouldn’t kill her.”
“Brother, what are you saying?”

“Oh, I don’t know... I don’t know. Maybe I won’t kill, maybe I will. I’m afraid that when I see his face at that moment, he’ll disgust me so much. I hate his ugly neck, his nose, his eyes, his gross smirk. I feel sick just thinking about it. That’s what I’m afraid of. That might be too much for me.”
“I’ll go, Mitya. I believe God will make things turn out right, that nothing horrible will happen.”
“And I’ll sit here and wait for a miracle. And if

When Alyosha (Alexey) arrived, he found his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, still sitting at the table. Even though the house had a dining-room, they always set the table in the drawing-room, which was the biggest room and decorated in an old-fashioned, showy way. The furniture was all white and very old, covered in faded red silk. Between the windows hung big, fancy mirrors with gold and white frames carved in old styles. On the white wallpaper—which was torn in lots of places—there were two big portraits: one of a prince who used to be the district governor thirty years ago, and another of a bishop who had died long ago. In the corner across from the door were several religious icons, and every night they lit a lamp in front of them—not really to pray, but just to light the room. Fyodor Pavlovitch stayed up very late—sometimes until three or four in the morning—and would wander around the room or sit and think in an armchair. This was his routine. He often slept alone in the house, sending the servants to sleep in the lodge, except Smerdyakov, who usually stayed and slept on a bench in the hallway.

When Alyosha came in, dinner was already finished, but coffee and some preserves were on the table. Fyodor Pavlovitch enjoyed eating sweets and drinking brandy after dinner. Ivan was there too, slowly drinking his coffee. The servants, Grigory and Smerdyakov, stood nearby, and everyone seemed strangely cheerful. Fyodor Pavlovitch was laughing loudly. Before Alyosha even entered, he could hear his father's high-pitched laugh and could tell from it that his father was in a good mood—happy, but not yet really drunk.

“Here he is! Here he is!” Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted happily when he saw Alyosha. “Come, join us. Sit down. Coffee is allowed during Lent, and this is hot and good. I won’t offer you any brandy since you’re fasting. Or do you want some anyway? No, better yet, I’ll get you our famous liqueur. Smerdyakov, go to the cupboard, second shelf on the right. Here are the keys. Hurry up!”
Alyosha started to say no to the liqueur.
“Never mind. If you don’t want any, we’ll drink it ourselves,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said, still smiling. “But wait—have you had dinner?”
“Yes,” Alyosha answered, though he had really only eaten some bread and had a glass of kvas in the Father Superior’s kitchen. “But I’d be happy to have some hot coffee.”

“Good for you, my boy! He’ll have some coffee. Does it need reheating? No, it’s boiling hot. This is excellent coffee—Smerdyakov made it. My Smerdyakov is a master at making coffee, fish pies, and fish soup too. You have to come over for fish soup one day. Just let me know ahead of time... Oh, and didn’t I tell you this morning to bring your mattress and pillow and everything? Did you bring your mattress? Ha ha ha!”
“No, I didn’t,” Alyosha answered, smiling himself.

“Ah, but you were scared this morning, weren’t you?” Fyodor Pavlovitch laughed. “Don’t worry, my boy, I’d never do anything to upset you. You know, Ivan, I just can’t help it—when Alyosha looks me right in the face and laughs, it makes me laugh too. I really love him. Alyosha, let me give you my blessing—a father’s blessing.”
Alyosha stood up, but Fyodor Pavlovitch had already changed his mind.

“No, no,” he said. “I’ll just make the sign of the cross over you for now. Stay seated. We’ve got something special for you—a treat you’ll like. It’ll make you laugh. Balaam’s donkey has started talking to us here—and what a talker!”

By “Balaam’s donkey,” he meant the servant Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov was about twenty-four, very unsociable and quiet. He wasn’t really shy—more like he thought he was better than everyone else and looked down on people.

Let’s pause for a moment and talk about Smerdyakov. Grigory and Marfa raised him, but Grigory always said the boy “never showed any gratitude.” Smerdyakov was unfriendly and always seemed suspicious of everyone. When he was a kid, he liked to hang cats and then bury them with a lot of ceremony. He’d dress up in a sheet like it was a church robe, sing, and swing something over the dead cat like it was incense. He did all this in secret. One time Grigory caught him and gave him a good beating. Smerdyakov sulked in the corner for a week. “He doesn’t care about you or me,” Grigory would say to Marfa. “He doesn’t care about anyone. Are you even human?” he said to the boy. “You grew out of the mold in the bath-house, that’s what you are.” Smerdyakov could never forgive him for that. Grigory taught him to read and write, and when Smerdyakov turned twelve, he began teaching him the Bible. But that didn’t last: at the second or third lesson, the boy suddenly grinned.
“Why are you grinning?” Grigory asked, glaring at him over his glasses.
“Oh, nothing. It’s just—God made light on the first day, but the sun, moon, and stars on the fourth day. Where did the light come from on the first day?”

Grigory was stunned. Smerdyakov looked at him with a sarcastic, almost smug expression. Grigory lost his temper. “I’ll show you where!” he shouted, and slapped the boy hard on the cheek. Smerdyakov didn’t say anything, but hid in his corner for days. About a week later, he had his first seizure of the illness that would follow him all his life—epilepsy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard about it, his attitude toward Smerdyakov changed right away. Before that, he barely noticed the boy—though he never scolded him and always gave him a coin when he saw him. Sometimes, if he was in a good mood, he’d send Smerdyakov a sweet from his table. But after he heard about the illness, he suddenly got involved: called a doctor, tried different treatments, but nothing worked. The seizures happened about once a month, sometimes more or less. Sometimes they were mild, sometimes very serious. Fyodor Pavlovitch strictly told Grigory never to hit the boy again, and let Smerdyakov start coming upstairs. He also stopped him from being taught anything for a while. When Smerdyakov was about fifteen, Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed him looking at the books behind the glass in the bookcase. Fyodor Pavlovitch had over a hundred books, but nobody had ever seen him read. Right away, he gave Smerdyakov the key. “Go ahead, read. You can be my librarian. Better to read than hang around the yard. Try this one,” and Fyodor Pavlovitch handed him Evenings in a Cottage near Dikanka.
Smerdyakov read a little of it but didn’t like it. He didn’t smile once, and just ended up frowning.
“Why? Isn’t it funny?” Fyodor Pavlovitch asked.
Smerdyakov didn’t answer.
“Answer me, you fool!”
“It’s all made-up,” the boy muttered with a grin.
“Then get out of here! You’ve got the mind of a servant. Here, read Smaragdov’s Universal History instead. That’s all true. Read that.”
But Smerdyakov didn’t read even ten pages of Smaragdov. He thought it was boring. So the bookcase was locked up again.

Not long after, Marfa and Grigory told Fyodor Pavlovitch that Smerdyakov was becoming extremely picky. He would sit in front of his soup, pick up his spoon, stare into the soup, lean over to inspect it, then take a spoonful and hold it up to the light.
“What is it? A beetle?” Grigory would ask.
“Maybe a fly,” Marfa would add.

Smerdyakov never answered, but he did the same thing with his bread, his meat, and everything he ate—holding up each piece to the light, staring at it closely, and only after thinking it over for a while, finally putting it in his mouth.
“Such fancy behavior!” Grigory would mutter, shaking his head.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard about Smerdyakov’s new habits, he decided to make him his cook and sent him to Moscow to train. Smerdyakov spent a few years there and came back looking a lot older than before—his face was wrinkled, yellowish, and he looked kind of weak. But his personality hadn’t changed much: he was still as unfriendly as ever and didn’t want to be close to anyone. In Moscow, people said, he barely talked or took interest in anything. He went to the theater once and came back silent and unhappy about it. On the other hand, he returned well-dressed, in a neat coat and clean shirt. He brushed his clothes carefully twice a day and loved polishing his smart shoes with special English polish so they shined like mirrors. He turned out to be a great cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, most of which Smerdyakov spent on clothes, hair cream, cologne, and things like that. He seemed to dislike women as much as men—he kept his distance and hardly spoke to them. Fyodor Pavlovitch started to respect him more. But Smerdyakov’s seizures were getting worse, and on the days he was sick, Marfa had to cook, which Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t like at all.
“Why are your fits getting worse?” Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, eyeing his new cook. “Do you want to get married? Want me to find you a wife?”

Smerdyakov turned pale with anger and didn’t say a word. Fyodor Pavlovitch just waved him off. The important thing was that Fyodor Pavlovitch completely trusted his honesty. One time, when he was drunk, he dropped three hundred-rouble notes in the muddy yard—money he’d just received. He didn’t notice they were missing until the next day and was just about to check his pockets when he saw the notes lying on the table. How did they get there? Smerdyakov had picked them up and brought them in the day before.

“Well, I’ve never met anyone like you,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said simply, giving him ten roubles. Not only did he trust Smerdyakov’s honesty, but for some reason, he even liked him, even though Smerdyakov always looked at him (and everyone else) with the same gloomy silence. He hardly ever spoke. If anyone had wondered what interested him or what he was thinking, they wouldn’t have been able to tell just by looking. Sometimes he would just stop suddenly in the house, or outside, and stand there for ten minutes, completely lost in thought. If a face reader had looked at him, they’d probably say there was nothing going on—no thinking, just blank staring. There’s a famous painting by Kramskoy called “Contemplation”—it shows a peasant standing alone in a snowy forest, looking lost in thought, but not really thinking, just sort of existing. If you touched him, he’d snap out of it and look confused, but he’d be fine right away; if you asked what he’d been thinking, he wouldn’t remember. Still, deep down, he kept those moments inside him, maybe without even realizing it. One day, after storing up all those impressions for years, he might suddenly go on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to save his soul, or maybe he’d set fire to his village—or even do both. There are a lot of “contemplative” people like that among the peasants. Smerdyakov was probably one of them, quietly collecting thoughts and feelings without knowing why.

Suddenly, Smerdyakov (let’s call him Smerdyakov for short) spoke up—like Balaam’s donkey in the Bible, which surprised everyone. The topic at the table was strange that day. Earlier, Grigory had gone shopping and heard from the shopkeeper, Lukyanov, a story in the newspaper about a Russian soldier. The soldier had been captured in a far-off part of Asia and told he would be horribly killed if he didn’t become Muslim and give up Christianity. But the soldier refused to give up his faith. He was tortured and skinned alive, but he died praising Christ until the end. Grigory told this story at lunch. Fyodor Pavlovitch (the father) always liked joking and chatting after dinner, especially if Grigory was around. That afternoon, Fyodor Pavlovitch was in an extra good mood, sipping his brandy and listening to Grigory’s story. He joked that they should make the soldier a saint and bring his skin to a monastery—“That would draw crowds and bring in loads of money.”

Grigory frowned, seeing that Fyodor Pavlovitch wasn’t moved at all, but as usual was just making fun of a serious story. At that moment, Smerdyakov, who was standing by the door, smiled. Smerdyakov often waited on them at the table during the end of dinner, and ever since Ivan had arrived in town, he did this every day.
“What are you grinning at?” Fyodor Pavlovitch snapped, immediately noticing Smerdyakov’s smile and knowing he was reacting to Grigory.

“Well, here’s what I think,” Smerdyakov said suddenly and loudly. “If what the soldier did was so great, then I think it wouldn’t have been a sin if, at such a desperate moment, he had just said he wasn’t a Christian to save his life—and then tried to make up for it later by doing good deeds.”
“How could that not be a sin? That’s nonsense. For that, you’d go straight to hell and get roasted like a lamb,” Fyodor Pavlovitch interrupted.
