Just then, Alyosha (Alexey) came in, and as we know, Fyodor Pavlovitch was thrilled to see him.
“We’re talking about your favorite topic!” Fyodor Pavlovitch said, chuckling and motioning for Alyosha to sit and listen.
“About roasting like a lamb—that’s not right. There’d be no punishment for this, and there shouldn’t be, if we’re being fair,” Smerdyakov insisted.
“What do you mean, ‘if we’re being fair’?” Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, even more cheerful, nudging Alyosha with his knee.
“He’s just being a troublemaker!” Grigory suddenly blurted out, glaring angrily at Smerdyakov.

“Hold on, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov answered calmly. “Think about it: if I was captured by enemies of Christianity and they told me to curse God and give up my faith, I’d have the right to use my own judgment. And there would be no sin in doing so.”
“But you’ve said that before. Stop talking and prove it,” Fyodor Pavlovitch demanded.
“Soup-maker,” Grigory muttered under his breath.

“Wait a second before calling me a soup-maker, Grigory Vassilyevitch. Think about it without insulting me. The moment I say to those enemies, ‘No, I’m not a Christian, and I curse my real God,’ then right away, by God’s law, I’m instantly cut off from the Church—like a non-believer. Not just when I say it out loud, but even when I think about saying it. Isn’t that true, Grigory Vassilyevitch?”
Smerdyakov looked at Grigory with satisfaction, even though he was really answering Fyodor Pavlovitch’s question, and he knew it, but he pretended Grigory had asked.
“Ivan,” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly called, “lean over here so I can whisper. He’s putting on this act for you. He wants you to praise him. Go on, praise him.”
Ivan listened seriously to his father’s excited whisper.
“Hold on, Smerdyakov, be quiet a minute!” Fyodor Pavlovitch interrupted again. “Ivan, come closer.”
Ivan bent down again, his face completely serious.
“I love you just as much as Alyosha. Don’t think I don’t. Want some brandy?”
“Sure—but you’re pretty drunk yourself,” Ivan thought, looking steadily at his father.
Ivan was watching Smerdyakov with great curiosity.
“You’re already accursed, as it is,” Grigory suddenly exploded. “And how dare you argue after that, you scoundrel—”
“Don’t yell at him, Grigory, don’t yell,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut him off.

“You should wait a bit, Grigory Vassilyevitch, and listen, because I’m not done yet. The moment I become accursed, right then, I’m just like a non-believer, and my baptism means nothing. Isn’t that true?”
“Hurry up and finish, boy,” Fyodor Pavlovitch urged, enjoying his wine.

“And if I’m not a Christian anymore, then I wasn’t lying to the enemy when they asked me if I was Christian—since God Himself, just from the thought, had already taken away my Christianity before I even said a word. And if I’m already dismissed from it, how could I be judged as a Christian in the afterlife for denying Christ, if I’d already lost my faith just by thinking it? If I’m not a Christian anymore, then there’s nothing left to deny. Who would blame some non-Christian Tatar in heaven for not being Christian? No one would punish him for how he was born. God wouldn’t say a Tatar was a Christian just because! That would be a lie, and can God ever lie, even once?”

Grigory was stunned and stared at Smerdyakov, his eyes wide. He didn’t really get everything Smerdyakov said, but he caught enough to be totally shocked, like someone who’d just hit his head. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his glass and burst out laughing.

“Alyosha! Alyosha! What do you think of that? Ah, you trickster! He must have been hanging out with Jesuits somewhere, Ivan. Oh, you sneaky Jesuit, who taught you this? But you’re talking nonsense, pure nonsense. Don’t cry, Grigory—we’ll shut him up in a second. Tell me this, you donkey; maybe you’re right with your enemies, but you still gave up your faith in your heart, and you admit that you became accursed right then. And if you’re accursed, they’re not going to reward you in hell. What do you say to that, you clever Jesuit?”
“There’s no question I gave up my faith in my heart, but there’s nothing special about that. Or if it is a sin, it’s just an ordinary one.”
“How’s that just an ordinary sin?”
“You’re lying, you cursed man!” Grigory hissed.

“Think about it yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov went on, calm and confident, almost feeling sorry for Grigory. “The Bible says if you have faith as small as a mustard seed, and you tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move. Well, Grigory Vassilyevitch, if I don’t have faith and you say you have so much, then try telling that mountain—not to move into the sea, that’s far away, but just to move to the little river at the bottom of the garden. You’ll see, it won’t move, no matter how much you yell at it, which shows you don’t really have faith, and just like to yell at others. And anyway, no one these days—not just you, but nobody, from the highest to the lowest—can move mountains except maybe one or two people in the whole world, who are probably hiding somewhere in the Egyptian desert. If everyone else has no faith, will God curse the whole world except those two desert hermits? Or, because God is merciful, won’t He forgive at least some people? So I think that even if I doubted, I’ll be forgiven if I truly repent.”
“Wait!” Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted, delighted. “So you actually think there are two people who can move mountains? Ivan, write it down! That’s so typically Russian!”
“You’re right—that’s just how common people think,” Ivan said, smiling approvingly.
“You agree, so it must be true. Right, Alyosha? That’s the Russian faith, isn’t it?”
“No, Smerdyakov doesn’t have the Russian faith at all,” Alyosha said seriously.
“I don’t mean his faith. I mean the idea that there are two holy men out there. That’s Russian, right?”
“Yes, that’s totally Russian,” Alyosha said, smiling.

“You’ve earned a gold coin for that, you donkey, and I’ll give it to you today. But everything else you said is just nonsense. Let me tell you, we’re weak in faith only because we’re busy and don’t have time—even to sleep, much less to repent. But you denied your faith when you had nothing else to worry about except proving your faith! So, I’d say that’s a sin.”

“Maybe it is a sin, but consider this, Grigory Vassilyevitch: it’s not as bad as it sounds. If I’d truly believed, like I should, then yes, it would be sinful to give up my faith instead of suffering for it. But if I had that much faith, I could just tell the mountain, ‘Move and crush my enemies,’ and the mountain would do it, and I’d walk away praising God. But suppose I tried that and nothing happened, even while I was being tortured—how could I not start doubting at such a terrible moment? And if the mountain didn’t move for me, it means my faith wasn’t so great, so why would I let them skin me alive for nothing? Even if they started torturing me, the mountain still wouldn’t move. In a moment like that, anyone could start doubting or even lose their mind from fear. So why blame me for wanting to save my own skin when there’s no reward here or in heaven? I’d just hope that God’s mercy would forgive me anyway.”

The argument was over now. But, strangely, Fyodor Pavlovitch (let's call him Fyodor) suddenly stopped acting cheerful and started to frown. He drank more brandy, even though he’d already had too much.

“Get out of here, Jesuits!” he yelled at the servants. “Go away, Smerdyakov. I’ll send you that gold coin I promised, but leave now! Don’t cry, Grigory. Go see Marfa—she’ll take care of you and help you to bed. These rascals never let us relax after dinner,” he complained grumpily as the servants hurried out.
“Smerdyakov always tries to hang around after dinner now. He’s really interested in you,” Fyodor said to Ivan. “What did you do to get his attention?”

“Nothing at all,” Ivan replied. “He just thinks highly of me for some reason. He’s just a servant and kind of a nasty person. But I bet people like him will be the first to join a revolution when it happens.”
“A revolution?” Fyodor asked.
“Yeah, there will be better people joining too, but at first, you’ll get guys like Smerdyakov. The better ones come later.”
“And when’s this going to happen?” Fyodor pressed.
“Maybe never. Maybe the revolution will just fizzle out. The peasants don’t really care about these troublemakers yet anyway.”
“But people like Smerdyakov—they keep thinking and thinking, and who knows what they come up with?” Fyodor said.
“He’s collecting ideas,” Ivan said, smiling.

“I know he can’t stand me, or anyone else—not even you, Ivan, even though you think he likes you. He really hates Alyosha. But at least he doesn’t steal, and he’s not a gossip. He keeps quiet and doesn’t tell everyone our business. Plus, he makes great fish pastries. Still, why are we even talking about him so much?”
“Yeah, there’s no point,” Ivan agreed.

“And as for his ideas—Russian peasants just need a good beating. I’ve always said that. They’re a bunch of cheaters and don’t deserve pity. It’s a good thing they still get flogged sometimes. Russia has plenty of birch trees, and if we lost those, the country would fall apart. I’m all for the smart people. We stopped beating the peasants because we think we’re clever, but really they just end up hurting themselves instead. ‘With whatever measure you use, it’ll be used on you again,’ or something like that. Anyway, justice happens. But Russia is a mess. Honestly, if you knew how much I hate Russia—well, maybe not Russia itself, but all the bad stuff in it. Or maybe I do mean Russia. It’s all just a pigsty. You know what I like? I like people who are clever.”
“You’ve had enough to drink. That’s enough now,” Ivan said.

“Wait, just a bit more. One more glass, then another, then I’ll stop. Don’t interrupt. At Mokroe, an old man told me, ‘We love sentencing girls to be whipped, and we always make the young guys do it. The same guy who beats a girl today will propose to her tomorrow. So the girls don’t mind either.’ Can you believe that? They’re like the Marquis de Sade, but it’s kind of smart, in a way. Should we go check it out? Alyosha, are you blushing? Don’t be shy, kid. I wish I’d stayed for dinner at the monastery and told the monks about the girls at Mokroe. Alyosha, don’t be mad that I insulted your elder this morning. I lost my temper. If there’s a God, then, of course, I’m guilty and will have to answer for it. But if there isn’t a God, what do your monks deserve? Just killing them isn’t enough—they hold back progress. You probably don’t believe I really feel bad about it, Ivan. I can see in your eyes you think I’m just some clown. Alyosha, do you think I’m just a clown?”
“No, I don’t think that,” Alyosha said.

“And I believe you—you look honest and you talk honestly. But not Ivan. Ivan acts all superior. Still, I’d get rid of your monks, even so. I’d wipe out all that mystical stuff from Russia, make everyone think clearly. And just think of all the gold and silver we’d get!”
“But why get rid of it?” Ivan asked.
“So Truth can win. That’s why.”
“Well, if Truth wins, you’d be the first one to get robbed and silenced,” Ivan said.

“You’re probably right. I’m such an idiot!” Fyodor said, smacking his forehead lightly. “All right, Alyosha, your monastery can stay. We ‘smart’ people will just enjoy our brandy. Ivan, this must be the way God planned it. Ivan, seriously, is there a God or not? Tell the truth. Why are you laughing?”
“I’m laughing because you just said something smart about Smerdyakov believing in two saints who could move mountains.”
“So, am I like him now?”
“Pretty much,” Ivan replied.

“Well, that means I’m Russian too, I guess. Even you, the philosopher, could end up like that. Maybe I’ll catch you out tomorrow. But really, be honest: is there a God or not? I want you to be serious.”
“No, there’s no God,” Ivan said.
“Alyosha, is there a God?” Fyodor asked.
“There is,” Alyosha answered.
“Ivan, is there any kind of immortality? Even just a little bit?” Fyodor went on.
“No immortality either,” Ivan said.
“None at all?” Fyodor pressed.
“None at all.”
“So there’s just complete nothingness? Maybe there’s at least something? Anything is better than nothing!”
“Complete nothingness,” Ivan said.
“Alyosha, is there immortality?”
“There is,” Alyosha answered.
“So, God and immortality?”
“God and immortality. Immortality is in God,” Alyosha said.

“Hmmm. Ivan is probably right. Wow, just think how much passion and strength people have wasted for thousands of years on that dream. Who’s laughing at people for this? Ivan, one last time: is there a God or not? I’m asking for the last time!”
“And for the last time: there isn’t,” Ivan replied.
“Then who’s laughing at mankind, Ivan?” Fyodor asked.
“It must be the devil,” Ivan answered, grinning.
“And the devil? Is he real?”
“No, there’s no devil either.”
“That’s a shame. I’d love to punish the person who first invented God. Hanging them would be too easy.”
“There wouldn’t be any civilization if people hadn’t invented God,” Ivan said.
“Really? No civilization without God?”
“Nope. And there wouldn’t be any brandy, either. But I’m still taking your brandy away from you.”
“Wait, wait! Just one more glass, please. I hurt Alyosha’s feelings. Are you mad at me, Alyosha? My dear Alexey!”
“No, I’m not angry. I know what you’re thinking. Your heart is better than your head,” Alyosha said.
“My heart’s better than my head, huh? Oh, wow! And from you, too. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?”
“Yes,” Ivan replied.
“You need to love him,” Fyodor said, now clearly drunk. “Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. I was just worked up. But that elder is smart, don’t you think, Ivan?”
“He probably is,” Ivan said.
“He is, he is. There’s something clever about him. He’s like a Russian Jesuit. He’s honest, but underneath, he’s angry about having to pretend to be holy.”
“But he definitely believes in God,” Ivan pointed out.
“Not at all. Didn’t you know? He tells all the smart people who visit him. He told Governor Schultz, ‘I believe, but I don’t know in what.’”
“Really?” Ivan asked.

“He really did. But I respect him. He’s a bit like Mephistopheles, or maybe that character Arbenin... I forget the name. He’s such a sensualist that I’d worry if my wife or daughter went to confess to him. When he tells stories, you can’t help but laugh. Last year, he had us over for tea with liqueur (ladies send him liqueur), and he told stories about the old days—like how he cured a paralyzed woman. He said, ‘If my legs weren’t bad, I’d show you a dance.’ What do you think of that? ‘I’ve done plenty in my time,’ he said. He once tricked the merchant Dernidov out of sixty thousand.”
“What, he stole it?” Ivan asked.

“He said, ‘Hold this money for me, friend, the police will search my house tomorrow.’ Then he kept it, saying, ‘You gave it to the Church.’ I told him, ‘You’re a scoundrel.’ He said, ‘No, I’m just broad-minded.’ But actually, that story was about someone else. I got mixed up. Come on, one more glass and that’s enough. Take the bottle, Ivan. I’ve been lying. Why didn’t you stop me, Ivan?”
“I knew you’d stop yourself,” Ivan said.
“That’s not true. You just did it to spite me. You look down on me. You come here and look down on me in my own house.”
“Well, I’m leaving. You’ve had too much to drink,” Ivan said.
“I begged you, for Christ’s sake, to go to Tchermashnya for a few days, and you won’t go.”
“I’ll go tomorrow if you really want me to,” Ivan replied.
“You won’t go. You want to keep an eye on me. That’s why you’re staying, you spiteful guy.”
The old man wouldn’t drop it. He was now drunk enough that he wanted to pick a fight and prove himself.

“Why are you staring at me? Why do you look at me like that? Your eyes say, ‘You ugly drunk.’ You don’t trust me. You look down on me. You came here with a plan. Alyosha’s eyes are different—they shine. Alyosha doesn’t look down on me. Alexey, you shouldn’t love Ivan.”
“Don’t be mean to my brother. Stop picking on him,” Alyosha said firmly.
“Fine, whatever. Ugh, my head hurts. Take the brandy, Ivan. This is the third time I’ve told you.”
Fyodor sat thinking, then a sly grin spread over his face.

“Don’t be mad at a weak old man, Ivan. I know you don’t love me, but don’t be angry. You have no reason to love me. Go to Tchermashnya. I’ll come visit you and bring you a present—a young girl I’ve had my eye on. She still runs around barefoot. Don’t look down on barefoot girls—they’re real treasures!”
He kissed his hand loudly.

“If you ask me,” he perked up suddenly, almost sobering up when he started talking about women, his favorite topic. “If you ask me... Oh, you boys! You kids! I never thought any woman was ugly—that’s my rule. You can always find something interesting in every woman if you know how to look. That’s a talent! There’s no such thing as an ugly woman. Just the fact that she’s a woman is enough. Even old maids—you can find something in them that makes you wonder why men ignored them. Barefoot girls, plain girls—you just have to surprise them, catch them off guard. Didn’t you know that? Make them feel amazed that someone like you would pay attention to them. It’s good that there are always masters and servants in the world—there will always be a maid and her master, and that’s all you need for happiness. Listen, Alyosha, I used to surprise your mother, but in a different way. I’d ignore her, then suddenly, when the moment was right, I’d be all loving, kneel and kiss her feet. She’d always end up with this weird, quiet, nervous laugh. That’s how I knew one of her fits was coming. The next day she’d start screaming like crazy, but that little laugh wasn’t real happiness, just a sign. The secret is to know how to handle everyone. Once, Belyavsky—a good-looking, rich guy—liked to visit her. One day, in front of her, he slapped me. And your mother—who was usually so gentle—almost attacked me for it. ‘Now you’re beaten, you took a blow from him,’ she said. ‘You tried to sell me to him. And how dare he hit you in front of me! Don’t come near me again! Go challenge him to a duel!’ I took her to the monastery to calm her down. The Fathers prayed for her. But I swear, Alyosha, I never insulted her—only once, maybe, in the first year. Back then, she loved to pray, especially on holy days, and would kick me out of her room. I thought I’d cure her of that mysticism. ‘Here’s your holy icon,’ I said, ‘I’ll spit on it, and nothing will happen to me!’ When she saw that, I thought she’d kill me. But she just jumped up, wrung her hands, then covered her face and fell to the floor, shaking all over. Alyosha, Alyosha, what’s wrong?”

The old man jumped up, worried. As he started talking about Alyosha’s mother, Alyosha’s face changed—he turned red, his eyes lit up, his lips trembled. Fyodor kept talking, not noticing, until suddenly something strange happened: Alyosha reacted just like his mother used to. He jumped up, wrung his hands, hid his face, and collapsed back in his chair, shaking with silent, intense sobs. The way he looked just like his mother really shocked Fyodor.
“Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! He’s just like her, exactly like his mother. Spit some water on him—that’s what I used to do to her. He’s upset about his mother, his mother,” he mumbled to Ivan.

“But she was my mother, too, right? Wasn’t she?” Ivan said, unable to hide his anger and disgust. Fyodor shrank back from Ivan’s fierce glare. For a moment, it was like Fyodor had forgotten that Alyosha’s mother was Ivan’s mother too.

“Your mother?” Fyodor muttered, confused. “What do you mean? Which mother are you talking about? Was she… Oh, right! Of course she was yours too! Wow, my mind has never been this fuzzy before. Sorry, Ivan… heh heh heh.” He trailed off, his face spreading into a wide, drunken, half-conscious grin.
Just then, a huge crash and shouting came from the hallway. The door burst open, and Dmitri stormed into the room. The old man rushed over to Ivan in terror.
“He’ll kill me! He’ll kill me! Don’t let him near me!” Fyodor screamed, grabbing Ivan’s coat.

Grigory and Smerdyakov rushed into the room right after Dmitri. They had tried to hold him back in the hallway, following orders from Fyodor Pavlovitch from a few days earlier. As soon as Dmitri stopped for a second to look around, Grigory ran around the table, slammed shut the double doors on the other side of the room leading to the inner part of the house, and stood in front of them with his arms wide, like he was ready to fight to the death to keep anyone from getting by. Seeing this, Dmitri let out a wild scream and charged at Grigory.
“Then she’s in there! She’s hiding in there! Get out of my way, you jerk!”

Dmitri tried to shove Grigory aside, but the old servant pushed him right back. Furious, Dmitri punched Grigory as hard as he could. Grigory dropped to the floor like a heavy sack, and Dmitri jumped over him, smashing through the door. Smerdyakov stood at the back of the room, pale and shaking, pressing close to Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“She’s here!” Dmitri yelled. “I just saw her heading for the house, but I couldn’t catch her. Where is she? Where is she?”
That shout—“She’s here!”—had a crazy effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch. Suddenly, he wasn’t scared anymore.

“Stop him! Hold him back!” he shouted, and ran after Dmitri. Grigory had gotten off the floor but was still dazed. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. In the third room, something crashed to the floor—it was a big glass vase on a marble stand that Dmitri knocked over as he ran by.
“Get him!” the old man yelled. “Help!”
Ivan and Alyosha grabbed their father and pulled him back by force.
“Why are you chasing after him? He’ll kill you for sure,” Ivan said angrily to his father.
“Ivan! Alyosha! She must be here. Grushenka’s here. He said he saw her running.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was choking. He hadn’t expected Grushenka to come, and now the idea that she was here made him lose control. He was shaking all over, almost crazy.
“But you saw for yourself she hasn’t come,” Ivan said.
“But maybe she came through the other entrance.”
“You know that entrance is locked, and you have the key.”

Dmitri suddenly came back into the drawing-room. He had found the other door locked, of course, and the key was in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s pocket. All the windows were closed, so there was no way Grushenka could have come in or left.

“Stop him!” Fyodor Pavlovitch screamed as soon as he saw Dmitri again. “He’s been stealing money in my bedroom!” He broke free from Ivan and rushed at Dmitri. But Dmitri threw up his hands, grabbed the two patches of hair on the old man’s temples, yanked them, and threw him hard to the floor. He kicked his father in the face two or three times with his heel. The old man let out a piercing moan. Ivan, even though he wasn’t as strong as Dmitri, grabbed him and pulled him away with all his strength. Alyosha helped too, holding Dmitri back from the front.
“Are you crazy? You’ve killed him!” Ivan shouted.
“He deserves it!” Dmitri yelled, breathing hard. “If I haven’t killed him, I’ll come back and finish the job. You can’t protect him!”
“Dmitri! Leave, right now!” Alyosha ordered.
“Alexey, tell me. You’re the only one I trust. Was she here just now or not? I saw her sneaking this way by the fence from the lane. I called out, and she ran away.”
“I swear she hasn’t been here, and no one was expecting her.”

“But I saw her… so she must have… I’ll find out where she is right now. Goodbye, Alexey! Don’t say a word to Æsop about the money. But go to Katerina Ivanovna right away and tell her, ‘He sends his compliments to you!’ Compliments, just compliments! Tell her about all this.”

Meanwhile, Ivan and Grigory had picked up the old man and put him in an armchair. His face was bloody, but he was awake and listened hungrily to Dmitri’s shouts. He still thought Grushenka might be hiding somewhere in the house. Dmitri gave him a hateful look as he left.
“I don’t regret making you bleed!” Dmitri shouted. “Watch out, old man, watch out for your dream, because I have my own dream, too. I curse you and I disown you completely.”
Dmitri ran out of the room.
“She’s here. She must be here. Smerdyakov! Smerdyakov!” the old man croaked, barely able to speak, motioning with his finger for Smerdyakov to come over.
“No, she’s not here, you crazy old fool!” Ivan yelled at him angrily. “Look, he’s fainting! Water! A towel! Hurry, Smerdyakov!”

Smerdyakov ran to get water. They finally got the old man undressed and into bed, wrapping a wet towel around his head. Tired from the brandy, the wild emotions, and the beating, he closed his eyes and fell asleep as soon as he hit the pillow. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing-room. Smerdyakov cleaned up the pieces of the broken vase while Grigory stood by the table, staring at the floor in a dark mood.
“Shouldn’t you put a wet cloth on your head and go to bed, too?” Alyosha said to Grigory. “We’ll take care of him. My brother really hurt you—with that blow to the head.”
“He insulted me!” Grigory said gloomily and clearly.
“He insulted his father, not just you,” Ivan said with a forced smile.
“I used to wash him in his tub. He insulted me,” Grigory repeated.
“Honestly, if I hadn’t pulled him away, he might have killed him. It wouldn’t take much to finish off Æsop, would it?” Ivan whispered to Alyosha.
“God forbid!” Alyosha said.
“Why should God forbid?” Ivan whispered back, making a bitter face. “One snake eats another. They both deserve it.”
Alyosha shuddered.
“Of course I won’t let him be murdered, just like I didn’t just now. Stay here, Alyosha. I’m going for a walk in the yard. My head is killing me.”

Alyosha went to his father’s bedroom and sat by his bed, behind the screen, for about an hour. Suddenly, the old man opened his eyes and stared at Alyosha for a long time, clearly remembering and thinking. Suddenly, his face showed wild excitement.
“Alyosha,” he whispered nervously, “where’s Ivan?”
“He’s outside. He’s got a headache. He’s keeping watch.”
“Give me that mirror over there. Give it to me.”
Alyosha handed him a small round folding mirror from the chest of drawers. The old man looked at himself—his nose was really swollen, and there was a big red bruise on the left side of his forehead.
“What does Ivan say? Alyosha, my dear, my only son, I’m afraid of Ivan. I’m more scared of Ivan than the other one. You’re the only one I’m not afraid of…”
“Don’t be scared of Ivan either. He’s angry, but he’ll protect you.”
“Alyosha, what about the other one? He’s gone to Grushenka. Tell me honestly, was she here just now or not?”
“No one saw her. It was a mistake. She hasn’t been here.”
“You know Mitya wants to marry her—to marry her.”
“She won’t marry him.”
“She won’t. No way, she won’t marry him! Not ever!”
The old man was so happy it was like he was fluttering with excitement. He squeezed Alyosha’s hand and pressed it to his heart. His eyes even sparkled with tears.

“That icon of the Mother of God I was telling you about—take it home with you. Keep it for yourself. I’ll let you go back to the monastery… I was kidding this morning, don’t be mad. My head hurts, Alyosha… Alyosha, comfort me! Be an angel and tell me the truth!”
“You’re still asking if she’s been here?” Alyosha said sadly.
“No, no, I believe you. But listen: go to Grushenka yourself, or see her somehow. Go quickly and ask her—find out for yourself who she’s going to pick, him or me. Okay? Can you do that?”
“If I see her, I’ll ask,” Alyosha mumbled, embarrassed.
“No, she won’t tell you,” the old man interrupted, “she’s tricky. She’ll start kissing you and say she wants you. She’s a liar, a shameless woman. You mustn’t go to her!”
“No, father, it wouldn’t be right at all.”
“Where did he send you just now? He shouted ‘Go’ as he left.”
“To Katerina Ivanovna.”
“For money? Did he send you to ask her for money?”
“No. Not for money.”

“He’s got no money—not a penny. I’ll settle down for the night and think things over, and you can go. Maybe you’ll run into her… Just promise to come see me tomorrow morning. Promise me. I have something I need to tell you. Will you come?”
“Yes.”
“When you come, just pretend you’re coming to check how I’m doing on your own. Don’t tell anyone I asked you to. Don’t say anything to Ivan.”
“Okay.”
“Goodbye, my angel. You defended me just now. I’ll never forget it. I have something to tell you tomorrow—but I need to think about it.”
“And how are you feeling now?”
“I’ll get up tomorrow and be perfectly fine again, just wait and see!”

Crossing the yard, Alyosha found Ivan sitting on a bench by the gate, writing something in his notebook with a pencil. Alyosha told Ivan that their father was awake, aware, and had said he could go back to the monastery to sleep.
“Alyosha, I’d really like to see you tomorrow morning,” Ivan said warmly, standing up. Alyosha was surprised by how friendly he sounded.
“I’ll be at the Hohlakovs’ tomorrow,” Alyosha replied. “I might go to Katerina Ivanovna’s too, if I don’t find her now.”
“But you’re going to see her now, right? For that ‘compliments and farewell,’” Ivan said, smiling. Alyosha looked uncomfortable.
“I think I get what all his shouting was about just now, and what happened before. Dmitri asked you to go to her and say he’s—well, basically—saying goodbye to her?”
“Brother, how will all this end between father and Dmitri?” Alyosha asked.
“No one can say for sure. Maybe nothing will happen; it could just fade away. That woman is trouble. Either way, we have to keep the old man inside and not let Dmitri in the house.”
“Brother, let me ask you one more thing: does anyone have the right to look at others and decide who’s worthy to live?”
“Why talk about ‘worthy’? People usually make up their minds about others for reasons that are a lot more personal. And as for rights—who doesn’t have the right to wish?”
“You mean, wish for someone else’s death?”

“Even that—wish for someone’s death. Why pretend otherwise, since that’s how people really feel, even if they can’t help it. Are you talking about what I just said—that one snake eats another? Then let me ask you, do you think I’m like Dmitri, and could actually kill Æsop?”
“What are you saying, Ivan? That never even crossed my mind. I don’t think Dmitri could do it either.”

“Thanks, at least for that,” Ivan said with a smile. “Just know, I’d always defend him. But in my thoughts, I keep all my options open in this case. Goodbye till tomorrow. Don’t judge me, and don’t think I’m a bad person,” he added, smiling.
They shook hands warmly—warmer than ever before. Alyosha felt his brother was finally reaching out to him, and that Ivan definitely had some special reason for doing so.

Alyosha left his father's house feeling even more tired and upset than when he’d arrived. His thoughts were all over the place, and he was afraid to piece them together, as if he couldn’t handle the whole truth of what had happened that day. He felt close to despair—a feeling he’d never experienced before. The biggest, most impossible question looming over everything was: how would things end between his father, his brother Dmitri (Mitya), and this terrible woman? He’d seen it all himself now, witnessed them face to face. Yet, of all of them, only Dmitri seemed doomed to be truly miserable—he was heading for disaster. And there were other people involved, more than Alyosha had realized. Something mysterious was going on. Ivan had finally reached out to him, which Alyosha had wanted, but now that it happened, he felt nervous about it. And the women involved? Strangely enough, although he’d been embarrassed to visit Katerina Ivanovna that morning, he now felt no embarrassment at all—if anything, he was rushing to her, hoping she could help him sort out what to do. Still, the task he’d come for—delivering Dmitri’s message—felt harder than ever. The business with the three thousand rubles was settled, and now Dmitri, feeling disgraced and hopeless, might do something terrible. Dmitri had also told him to describe to Katerina Ivanovna everything that had just happened with their father.

It was already seven in the evening and getting dark when Alyosha entered Katerina Ivanovna’s large, well-kept house on High Street. Alyosha knew she lived with two aunts. One was not very educated—she had looked after Katerina’s half-sister Agafya Ivanovna back when they lived at her father's house. The other aunt was a stylish lady from Moscow, though she wasn’t rich. People said both aunts let Katerina Ivanovna do whatever she wanted; they were only there to act as chaperones. Katerina Ivanovna herself didn’t let anyone tell her what to do, except for her benefactor, the general’s widow, who was sick in Moscow and required Katerina to write her detailed letters twice a week.

When Alyosha entered the hall and asked the maid to let them know he was there, it was clear everyone already knew he’d arrived. Maybe someone had seen him from the window. Alyosha heard footsteps rushing and the sound of skirts swishing—two or three women, it sounded like, had just run out of the room.

Alyosha thought it was odd that his arrival caused such a stir. Still, the maid led him straight into the drawing-room. The room was big and decorated with style—not at all like a small-town home. There were several comfortable sofas and chairs, tables of different sizes, paintings on the walls, vases and lamps on the tables, lots of flowers, and even an aquarium by the window. It was getting dark, so Alyosha could only just make out a silk shawl tossed on the sofa, showing people had just been sitting there. On the table sat two half-finished cups of hot chocolate, cakes, a dish of blue raisins, and another with candies. Alyosha realized he’d interrupted some visitors and frowned. Just then, the door curtain was swept aside and Katerina Ivanovna hurried in, smiling brightly and holding out both hands to greet him. At that moment, a servant brought in two lit candles and put them on the table.
“Thank goodness! You’re finally here! I’ve been praying you’d come all day! Sit down.”

Alyosha had been impressed by Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty three weeks earlier, when Dmitri had first introduced them at her request. They hadn’t really talked—Katerina Ivanovna had focused on Dmitri to spare Alyosha, thinking he was shy. Alyosha had been quiet, but he’d noticed a lot. He was struck by her commanding presence, her confidence, and her proud attitude. He was sure he wasn’t exaggerating. Her dark, glowing eyes looked amazing against her pale, slightly yellowish, long face. But there was something in her eyes and lips—something that Dmitri might fall madly in love with, but maybe not love forever. After their visit, when Dmitri insisted Alyosha share his honest thoughts about his fiancée, Alyosha had said as much.
“You’ll be happy with her, but maybe not peacefully happy.”
“You’re right, brother. Some people never change; they don’t give in. So you think I won’t love her forever?”
“No, maybe you will love her forever. But you might not always be happy with her.”

Alyosha had said this, blushing and feeling embarrassed for speaking so boldly about a woman. Right after, he thought his own opinion was foolish. Now, however, as he saw Katerina Ivanovna running in to greet him, he realized he might have been totally wrong. She looked genuinely kind and warm-hearted, her face lit up with sincerity. The pride and haughtiness he’d noticed before now just seemed like honest energy and a strong belief in herself. Right away, Alyosha sensed that she was fully aware of the tragic situation with the man she loved, maybe she already knew everything. But even with all this, her face shone with hope and confidence in the future. Alyosha immediately felt guilty for misjudging her. He was won over at once. Plus, he noticed that she was extremely excited—almost overjoyed.
“I was so eager to see you because only you can tell me the whole truth. No one else.”
“I’ve come,” Alyosha stammered, still nervous. “He sent me.”

“Ah, he sent you! I knew it. Now I understand everything—everything!” Katerina Ivanovna said, her eyes flashing. “Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ll tell you why I wanted to see you so badly. You know, I might know more than you think, so there’s no need for you to fill me in. What I want is your real, last impression of him. I want you to tell me honestly, in plain words—even harsh ones if you must—what you thought of him today, and what you think of his situation after your meeting. That would be better than talking to him directly, since he doesn’t want to come to me. Do you get what I mean? Now, just tell me exactly what message he sent with you—I knew he’d send you.”
“He told me to give you his compliments—and to say he’ll never come again—but to give you his compliments.”
“His compliments? Did he use that exact word?”
“Yes.”
“Maybe he just picked the wrong word by accident?”
“No, he told me to say that word, exactly. He reminded me two or three times not to forget.”
Katerina Ivanovna blushed deeply.

“Help me now, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I really need your help. Let me tell you what I think, and you can say if it’s right. Listen! If he’d just casually sent ‘his compliments’ without making you repeat the phrase, that would mean everything is over. But if he insisted you use those words, and told you to remember them, maybe he was upset and not thinking clearly. Maybe he’d made his decision and was scared of it, not walking away calmly but running. Maybe he was just putting on a brave face.”
“Yes, yes!” Alyosha said, getting caught up in her hope. “I think that’s it.”
“And if that’s true, he’s not hopeless. I can still save him. Wait! Did he mention money—three thousand rubles?”

“He did talk about it, and that’s what’s crushing him most. He said he’d lost his honor and that nothing matters now,” Alyosha replied, feeling a burst of hope and thinking maybe his brother could still be saved. “But do you know about the money?” he asked, and suddenly stopped, unsure.

“I’ve known about it for a long time. I sent a telegram to Moscow to check, and found out ages ago the money hadn’t arrived. He never sent it, but I kept quiet. Last week I learned he was still desperate for money. My only reason for all this was to show him who his real friend is. But he doesn’t see that I’m his truest friend; he just sees me as a woman. I’ve spent the whole week worrying about how to keep him from feeling ashamed in front of me about the three thousand. Let him feel ashamed in front of others, but not me. He can tell God everything, no problem. Why can’t he see how much I’m willing to put up with for him? How can he not know me after everything? I want to save him forever. He can forget me as his fiancée. Yet here he is, afraid he’s disgraced in my eyes. Why, he wasn’t afraid to be honest with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Why don’t I deserve the same?”
She ended in tears, and they poured from her eyes.
“I have to tell you,” Alyosha began, his voice shaking, “what just happened between him and my father.”

And Alyosha described the whole scene—how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how he’d forced his way in and knocked their father down, and then insisted Alyosha deliver his compliments and farewell. “He went to see that woman,” Alyosha added quietly.

“And he thinks I can’t handle that woman? Does he really think so? But he won’t marry her,” Katerina Ivanovna suddenly laughed, a little crazily. “Could a passion like that really last forever for a Karamazov? It’s just passion, not love. He won’t marry her, because she won’t marry him.” She laughed again, strangely.
“He might marry her,” Alyosha said quietly, looking down.

“He won’t marry her, I’m telling you. That girl is an angel. Do you know that? Do you?” Katerina Ivanovna suddenly burst out. “She’s one of the most unusual people ever. I know how charming she is, but I also know she’s kind, strong, and noble. Why are you looking at me like that, Alexey Fyodorovitch? You think I’m exaggerating, don’t you? Agrafena Alexandrovna—my angel!” she suddenly called into the next room, “come in here. This is a friend—this is Alyosha. He knows all about what’s going on. Come show yourself.”
“I’ve just been waiting behind the curtain for you to call me,” came a soft, sweet, almost syrupy woman’s voice.

The curtain lifted and Grushenka herself walked in, smiling. Alyosha was shocked. He stared at her, unable to look away. This was the terrible woman—the “beast” Ivan had just called her. Yet, standing there, she seemed so ordinary—just a pretty, friendly woman. She was certainly very attractive, with the kind of Russian beauty that many men adored. She was a bit shorter than Katerina Ivanovna, who was very tall, but still taller than most. Grushenka had a full figure and moved softly, almost silently, her movements gentle and smooth, just like her voice. She didn’t walk with Katerina’s bold steps, but instead moved quietly—her feet made no sound. She sank gracefully into a low chair, her luxurious black silk dress rustling as she settled, her white neck and broad shoulders wrapped in a fancy cashmere shawl. She was twenty-two, and her face looked exactly that age—very pale, with a faint pink blush in her cheeks. Her face was a little wide, and her lower jaw stuck out a bit. Her upper lip was thin, but her lower lip was much fuller and stuck out in a pout. But her thick, dark brown hair, dark eyebrows, and beautiful gray-blue eyes with long lashes would make anyone stop and stare. What caught Alyosha most was the childlike goodness in her face—her eyes sparkled with innocent happiness. She came to the table, her whole face lighting up with excitement and curiosity. The happiness in her eyes lifted Alyosha’s spirits. There was something else about her, too—something he couldn’t quite describe. Maybe it was the softness and smoothness of the way she moved, that catlike quietness, even though she was full-figured and strong. Her body had the curves of a statue, though maybe a bit exaggerated, and experts in Russian beauty would probably predict she’d lose her looks early, get puffy and wrinkled by thirty, her skin growing rough. But Alyosha didn’t think of any of that. He was both fascinated and a bit unsettled, wondering why she spoke so slowly and sweetly, as if on purpose. It felt fake, a result of poor upbringing and a mistaken idea of what was elegant. Still, her sugary way of talking didn’t match the simple, innocent happiness on her face. Katerina Ivanovna immediately made her sit facing Alyosha and kissed her several times on her smiling lips, looking totally smitten.

“This is the first time we’ve met, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Katerina Ivanovna said, almost bursting with excitement. “I wanted to meet her, to see her. I was about to go visit her, but as soon as I said so, she came to me. I knew we would sort everything out together—my heart told me so. People begged me not to do this, but I knew this was the right way out, and I was right. Grushenka explained everything to me, told me her plans. She came here like an angel, bringing peace and joy.”
“You didn’t look down on me, sweet, wonderful young lady,” Grushenka said in her slow, sing-song voice, her smile warm as ever.

“Don’t talk like that to me, you little witch! As if I would look down on you! Here, I need to kiss your lower lip again. It looks swollen, and now it’ll be even more so. Look how she laughs, Alexey Fyodorovitch! Seeing this angel does my heart good.”
Alyosha blushed, and a nervous chill ran through him.
“You’re treating me too kindly, dear young lady, and maybe I don’t deserve your kindness at all.”

“Not worthy! She says she’s not worthy!” Katerina Ivanovna cried, just as warmly. “You see, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we’re both a little stubborn and proud inside. But we’re generous, we’re noble too. We’ve just been unlucky. We were willing to sacrifice everything for a man who maybe didn’t deserve it, a man who changed his mind. Once, five years ago, there was a man—an officer—we loved him, gave up everything for him. He’s forgotten us now, married someone else. Now he’s a widower, he’s written, and he’s coming here. And you know, Grushenka has loved no one but him all this time, all her life! When he comes, Grushenka will be happy again. She’s been miserable for five years. But who can blame her? Who can say they’ve really had her heart? Only that sick old merchant, and he’s more like a father, a friend, a protector. He found her when she was desperate, abandoned by the man she loved. She almost drowned herself, but the old merchant saved her—he saved her!”
“You’re defending me so kindly, dear young lady. You’re always in such a hurry,” Grushenka said with her slow drawl.

“Defend you? As if I need to defend you! Grushenka, angel, give me your hand. Look at her sweet, soft little hand, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It’s brought me happiness and lifted me up. I want to kiss it, both sides, here, here, here!”
She kissed Grushenka’s admittedly chubby but lovely hand three times, almost lost in her own happiness. Grushenka held out her hand with a musical, nervous giggle, and seemed to enjoy the attention.
“Maybe this is a little too much excitement,” Alyosha thought, blushing again. He felt uncomfortable the whole time.
“You won’t make me blush by kissing my hand like that in front of Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
“Did you think I was trying to make you blush?” Katerina Ivanovna asked, surprised. “Oh, my dear, you don’t understand me at all!”

“And maybe you don’t really get me either, dear young lady. Maybe I’m not as good as you think. I have a bad heart—I like to get my own way. I flirted with poor Dmitri Fyodorovitch that day just for the fun of it.”
“But now you’ll save him. You promised me. You’ll explain everything to him. You’ll tell him you’ve loved another man for a long time, and now he’s asking for your hand.”
“Oh, no! I never promised I’d do that. You kept saying it, but I didn’t promise.”
“Then I misunderstood you,” Katerina Ivanovna said slowly, turning pale. “You promised—”

“Oh no, angel, I didn’t promise anything,” Grushenka interrupted gently, still smiling. “You see, I’m much more stubborn than you. If I want to do something, I do it. Maybe I did promise you something just now, but now I’m thinking: maybe I’ll go back to Mitya. I liked him a lot once—almost for a whole hour. Maybe I’ll go tell him to stay with me forever. I’m so changeable, you see.”
“But just now you said—something completely different,” Katerina Ivanovna whispered faintly.
“Yes, just now. But you know, I’m such a soft-hearted, silly thing. Just think what he’s been through because of me! What if I go home and start feeling sorry for him? What then?”
“I never expected—”

“Oh, you’re so good and generous compared to me! Maybe you won’t like someone as silly as me, now you know what I’m really like. Give me your sweet little hand, angel,” Grushenka said softly, taking Katerina Ivanovna’s hand with a sort of awe.

“Here, dear young lady, I’ll take your hand and kiss it like you kissed mine. You kissed mine three times, but I should kiss yours three hundred times to make it fair. But let’s just leave it at that. I’ll do whatever God wants. Maybe I’ll be your slave and do whatever you want, like a real slave. Whatever happens, happens. What a sweet hand—what a beautiful hand you have! You incredible beauty!”
She lifted the hand to her lips slowly, as if her real goal was to “even the score” with kisses.

Katerina Ivanovna didn’t pull her hand away. She listened, hopeful, to Grushenka’s last words, even though the promise to be her slave sounded a bit strange. She looked into Grushenka’s eyes and saw the same innocent, trusting look, the same bright happiness.
“Maybe she’s just too naïve,” Katerina Ivanovna thought, with a flicker of hope.
Meanwhile, Grushenka kept admiring the “sweet hand.” She lifted it close to her lips but paused for a couple of minutes, as if she was reconsidering.
“You know, angel,” she finally said in an even sweeter, slower voice, “I think I won’t kiss your hand after all.” She gave a little happy laugh.
“Whatever you want. What’s wrong with you?” Katerina Ivanovna asked, suddenly startled.
“So you’ll remember that you kissed my hand, but I didn’t kiss yours.”
There was a sudden sharp look in Grushenka’s eyes. She stared intensely at Katerina Ivanovna.
“You insolent thing!” Katerina Ivanovna shouted, as if she’d just figured something out. She blushed all over and jumped up from her seat.
Grushenka stood up too, but calmly.
“So I’ll tell Mitya you kissed my hand, but I didn’t kiss yours. Imagine how hard he’ll laugh!”
“You filthy slut! Get out!”
“Oh, shame on you, young lady! Shame! That’s not a word for someone like you to use.”
“Get out! You’re nothing but a woman for sale!” Katerina Ivanovna screamed, her face twisted in rage.
“For sale? You used to visit men at night for money—you sold your beauty too. See, I know.”
Katerina Ivanovna shrieked and nearly lunged at her, but Alyosha held her back with all his strength.
“Don’t move, don’t answer! Don’t say a word. She’ll leave—she’ll go right now.”
Just then, Katerina Ivanovna’s two aunts and a maid rushed in at her cry. They all crowded around her.
“I’ll go,” Grushenka said, picking up her shawl from the sofa. “Alyosha, darling, walk me home!”
“Go—please, quickly!” Alyosha begged, wringing his hands.
“Sweet Alyosha, walk me home! I have a funny story to tell you on the way. I put on this whole scene just for you, Alyosha. Come with me now—you’ll be glad you did later.”
Alyosha turned away, twisting his hands in frustration. Grushenka ran out of the house, laughing musically.
Katerina Ivanovna had a hysterical fit. She sobbed and shook uncontrollably. Everyone rushed to comfort her.

“I warned you,” her older aunt said. “I tried to stop you. You’re too impulsive. How could you do this? You don’t know people like her—they say she’s worse than any of them. You’re just too stubborn.”
“She’s a tiger!” Katerina Ivanovna yelled. “Why did you hold me back, Alexey Fyodorovitch? I would have beaten her—beaten her!”
She didn’t bother to control herself in front of Alyosha; maybe she didn’t even care.
“She should be whipped in public, right in the square!”
Alyosha moved toward the door.

“But my God!” Katerina Ivanovna cried, wringing her hands. “He! He! He could be so dishonorable, so cruel! He told her what happened that cursed day! ‘You brought your beauty for sale, dear young lady.’ She knows all about it! Your brother’s a scoundrel, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
Alyosha wanted to say something but couldn’t find the words. His heart hurt.
“Go away, Alexey Fyodorovitch! This is awful for me! Please, I beg you, come tomorrow. Don’t judge me. Forgive me. I don’t even know what I’ll do with myself now!”
Alyosha staggered out into the street. He felt like crying, just as she had. Suddenly, the maid caught up to him.
“The young lady forgot to give you this letter from Madame Hohlakov. It’s been here since dinner.”
Alyosha took the small pink envelope automatically and put it in his pocket without thinking.

The monastery was less than a mile from the town. Alyosha walked quickly down the empty road. It was nearly night, and so dark he couldn't see much ahead. About halfway, he reached some crossroads, where a single willow tree stood alone. Under that tree, Alyosha saw someone. As soon as he got closer, the figure rushed out at him, yelling wildly:
“Your money or your life!”
“Mitya! So it's you!” Alyosha shouted, shocked and startled.

“Ha ha ha! You didn't expect to see me, did you? I wondered where to wait for you. Near her house? There are three roads from there—I'd probably miss you. Then I thought, if I wait here, you'll have to pass by. There's no other way to the monastery. So, tell me everything. Crush me if you want. But—hey, what's wrong?”

“Nothing, brother—you just scared me. Oh, Dmitri! What happened with Father just now…” (Alyosha started crying. He'd been holding back tears for a while, but now he couldn't help it.) “You nearly killed him—cursed him—and now here you are, making jokes, shouting, ‘Your money or your life!’ ”
“So what? Is that not proper? Not fitting for someone like me?”
“No, I just—”

“Wait. Look at this night. See how dark it is, how wild the wind is, and all these clouds. I was hiding under the willow, waiting for you. And honestly, I suddenly thought, why keep living in misery? What's the point? I have a willow, a handkerchief, a shirt—I could make a rope in a minute, with my braces too. Why keep dragging myself through life, shaming the world with my rotten existence? Then I heard you coming—and it felt like something swooped down and saved me. There was someone I loved—my little brother, the only person I love in this world. I loved you so much at that moment, I wanted to hug you right away. Then I got this dumb idea to joke and scare you. I yelled, ‘Your money!’ Forgive me, I was just being stupid. I didn't mean anything by it, my soul's not as bad as my joke. Anyway, tell me what happened. What did she say? Hit me, crush me, don't hold back! Was she furious?”
“No, not that… It wasn't like that, Mitya. I found them both there.”
“Both? Who?”
“Grushenka was at Katerina Ivanovna's house.”
Dmitri was left speechless.
“No way!” he cried. “You're crazy! Grushenka was with her?”

Alyosha told him everything that had happened since he went into Katerina Ivanovna’s house. It took him about ten minutes. He didn’t tell it smoothly, but he got all the important points across, and even described his own feelings with just a word or two. Dmitri listened silently, staring at him with a hard, intense look, but Alyosha could tell that he understood everything. As the story went on, Dmitri’s face became not just dark, but actually threatening. He frowned, clenched his teeth, and his stare got even scarier—until suddenly, his angry, wild face completely changed. His lips pulled apart and Dmitri Fyodorovitch broke into wild, uncontrollable laughter. He shook with it and couldn’t speak for a long time.

“So she wouldn’t kiss her hand! So she didn’t kiss it, she just ran away!” he kept repeating, giggling almost hysterically; it would’ve been rude if it hadn’t been so real. “So the other one called her a tigress! And that’s what she is! She should be whipped in public? Yes, yes, she should! I agree, she deserved it long ago. That’s just how she is! But first, I need to get better. I totally get the queen of rudeness now. That’s Katya for you! You saw what she was like with the hand-kissing, that little devil! She’s amazing in her way! So she ran home? I’ll go—I’ll run to her! Alyosha, don’t blame me, I agree, even hanging is too good for her.”
“But what about Katerina Ivanovna?” Alyosha said sadly.

“I see her now, too! I see right through her, clearer than ever! It’s like discovering a whole new continent—no, five! What a stunt to pull! That’s so Katya, she was never afraid to stand up to rude, nasty officers and risk being insulted, just to save her father! But the pride, the craziness, the way she dares fate—she never stops! You said her aunt tried to stop her? That aunt is super bossy herself. She’s the sister of the general’s widow in Moscow, but even snobbier. Her husband got caught stealing government money and lost everything, so the proud wife had to accept it and hasn’t gotten over it. So she tried to stop Katya, but Katya wouldn’t listen! Katya thinks she can do anything, that everyone will give in to her. She thought she could charm Grushenka if she wanted, and she actually believed it herself! She’s always acting out her own fantasy—whose fault is that? Do you think she kissed Grushenka’s hand first on purpose, with some plan? No, she really was mesmerized—not by Grushenka, but by her own dream. It was all in her head! Alyosha, how did you get away from those two? Did you grab your robe and run? Ha ha ha!”

“Brother, don’t you see you insulted Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about that day? And Grushenka just threw it back in her face—that she went to men in secret to sell her beauty! What could be worse than that kind of insult?”
What bothered Alyosha most was that, as unbelievable as it seemed, his brother seemed happy about Katerina Ivanovna’s humiliation.
“Ugh!” Dmitri growled, hitting his forehead with his hand. Only now did he really realize what Alyosha had just told him—the insult, and Katerina Ivanovna shouting, “Your brother is a scoundrel!”

“Yeah, maybe I did tell Grushenka about that ‘fateful day,’ like Katya calls it. Yeah, I remember! It was that time at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing… But I was sobbing, kneeling, praying to Katya’s picture, and Grushenka understood. She got it then—I remember, she even cried herself… Ugh! But things are different now… Back then she cried, but now, it’s like ‘a dagger in the heart’! That’s how women are.”
He looked down and fell silent, lost in thought.

“Yes, I’m a scoundrel, a real scoundrel,” he suddenly said in a low, miserable voice. “It doesn’t matter if I cried or not—I’m a scoundrel! Tell her I accept the title, if it makes her feel better. Alright, that’s enough. Goodbye. There’s no point in talking anymore. It’s not fun. You go your way, I’ll go mine. And I don’t want to see you again, unless there’s no other choice. Goodbye, Alexey!”
He squeezed Alyosha’s hand tightly, still looking down and not raising his head, as if he was forcing himself to leave. Then he quickly turned towards the town.
Alyosha watched him go, not able to believe he would really leave like that.

“Wait, Alexey, I have one more thing to confess, just to you!” Dmitri suddenly turned back. “Look at me—really look. You see here, right here—something shameful is coming for me.” (As he said “here,” Dmitri hit his chest with his fist, like the disgrace was right there, maybe in his pocket or hanging around his neck.) “You know me now—a scoundrel, an open scoundrel—but I’ve never done anything before, and never will again, that’s as low as the shame I’m carrying right now. I could stop it. I could. I could save at least half my lost honor tomorrow. But I won’t stop it. I’m going to do it, and you’ll be my witness that I told you before it happened. Darkness and destruction! No need to explain—you’ll find out soon enough. The dirty alley and the she-devil. Goodbye. Don’t pray for me, I’m not worth it. And I really don’t need it… I don’t need it! Go away!”
This time he turned and left for real. Alyosha walked toward the monastery.
“What? I’ll never see him again? What is he talking about?” Alyosha thought, confused. “Of course I’ll see him tomorrow. I’ll go look for him. What does he mean?”

He walked around the monastery and crossed through the pine woods to the hermitage. Even though nobody was usually let in at that hour, they opened the door for him. Alyosha’s heart was trembling as he entered Father Zossima’s cell.

“Why did he have to go out there? Why did Father Zossima send him into the world? There was peace here—holiness. But outside, there was just confusion and darkness, where people lose their way so easily…”

In the cell, he found Novice Porfiry and Father Païssy, who came every hour to check on Father Zossima. Alyosha was alarmed to learn that Father Zossima was getting worse. Not even the usual evening talk with the brothers could happen that day. Normally, after evening service, the monks would gather in Father Zossima’s cell and confess their sins, thoughts, and even arguments from the day. Some even confessed on their knees. The elder would forgive, advise, give penance, bless them, and send them away. Some people didn’t like this group confession—they even said it was disrespectful to the real sacrament of confession, maybe even a kind of blasphemy. They told the church leaders it did more harm than good, and actually led to sin. Many monks disliked going to the elder, but went anyway because everyone else did, and they didn’t want to be accused of pride or rebellion. People said some monks would even agree in advance—“I’ll confess I got mad at you this morning, and you can admit it”—just to have something to say. Alyosha knew this really happened sometimes. He also knew some monks were mad that letters from relatives were always opened and read by the elder before they got them.

Everyone acted like it was voluntary and done in good faith, as a way of obeying and getting good guidance. But in reality, there was a lot of faking and pretending. Still, the older, wiser monks stuck to their beliefs, saying, “For those who came here honestly looking for salvation, this kind of obedience and sacrifice will definitely help; for those who find it annoying and complain, they’re not real monks and should be out in the world. Even in church, you’re not safe from sin and the devil, so there’s no point worrying about it too much.”

“He’s weaker now, and getting sleepy,” Father Païssy whispered as he blessed Alyosha. “It’s hard to wake him, and we shouldn’t try. He woke up for about five minutes, sent his blessing to the brothers, and asked them to pray for him tonight. He wants to take communion again in the morning. He remembered you, Alexey. He asked if you’d gone away, and we told him you were in town. ‘I blessed him for that task,’ he said, ‘his place is there, not here, for now.’ That’s what he said about you. He remembered you with love and worry; do you see how much he honors you? But why does he want you to spend time in the world? He must see something in your future! Remember, Alexey, if you go back to the world, it should be for the duty your elder gave you, not for fun or worldly things.”

Father Païssy left. Alyosha was sure now that Father Zossima was dying, even if he might last another day or two. Alyosha decided, with all his heart, that no matter what he’d promised his father, the Hohlakovs, or Katerina Ivanovna, he wouldn’t leave the monastery the next day—he’d stay with his elder until the end. He felt a deep love and blamed himself for ever forgetting, even for a second, the man he honored most in the world, who was lying here dying. He went into Father Zossima’s bedroom, knelt, and bowed all the way to the floor before the elder, who slept quietly, his breathing soft and peaceful.

Alyosha went back to the other room, where Father Zossima had greeted guests that morning. He took off his boots and lay on the narrow, hard leather sofa he always used as a bed, with just a pillow. The mattress his father yelled about that morning—he hadn’t slept on it in ages. He took off his cassock and used it as a blanket. But before lying down, he knelt and prayed for a long time. In his prayer, he didn’t ask God to make things easier or clearer—he just wanted the joy and peace he always felt after evening prayers. That joy always helped him sleep well. As he prayed, he suddenly felt the little pink note in his pocket—the one the servant gave him when he left Katerina Ivanovna’s. He felt uneasy, but finished his prayer. Then, after hesitating, he opened the envelope. Inside was a letter to him, signed by Lise, Madame Hohlakov’s young daughter, who had teased him in front of Father Zossima that morning.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she wrote, “I’m writing this without anyone knowing, not even Mama, and I know it’s wrong. But I can’t keep my feelings inside anymore, and only you and I can know about this for now. But how can I say what I want to say? People say paper never blushes, but I swear this page is as red as I am right now. Dear Alyosha, I love you. I’ve loved you since childhood, since our days in Moscow, when you were so different from now. I’ll love you all my life. My heart has chosen you, so we can spend our lives together until we’re old. But only if you leave the monastery. By the time we’re old enough, I’ll definitely be strong and able to walk and dance—no doubt about it.”

“You see, I’ve thought of everything. There’s only one thing I can’t imagine: what you’ll think of me when you read this. I’m always joking and acting up—I made you mad this morning, but I swear, before I started writing, I prayed to the Mother of God, and now I’m praying again, almost crying.”

“My secret is in your hands. When you come tomorrow, I don’t know how I’ll look at you. What if I start laughing again, like today? You’ll think I’m just making fun of you, and you won’t believe my letter. So please, if you care about me at all, when you come tomorrow, don’t look me straight in the face. If I meet your eyes, I’ll definitely start laughing, especially with you in that long robe. Just look at Mama or out the window for a while…”

“I’ve actually written you a love letter. Oh no, what have I done? Alyosha, don’t hate me, and if I’ve done something awful or hurt you, forgive me. Now my secret—maybe ruining my reputation forever—is in your hands.”
“I’m definitely going to cry today. Goodbye until our meeting—our terrifying meeting. —Lise.”
“P.S.—Alyosha! You have to, have to, HAVE TO come! —Lise.”

Alyosha read the letter, amazed. He read it twice, thought for a moment, and then let out a soft, happy laugh. He stopped himself—laughing felt wrong. But a minute later, he laughed again, just as softly and happily. He slowly put the letter back in its envelope, made the sign of the cross, and lay down. His worries faded right away. “God, have mercy on them all—look after all these unhappy, restless souls, and guide them to the right path. All roads are yours. Save them as you know best. You are love. You will bring them joy!” Alyosha whispered, crossing himself, and soon drifted peacefully off to sleep.

Alyosha was woken up early, before the sun came up. Father Zossima had woken feeling very weak, but he wanted to get out of bed and sit in a chair. His mind was clear, even though his face looked tired. Still, he seemed almost happy, with a kind and cheerful expression. “Maybe I won’t live through today,” he told Alyosha. He wanted to confess his sins right away and take communion. He always confessed to Father Païssy. After communion, they held the anointing service for the sick. The monks gathered in the tiny cell, which soon filled up with people from the hermitage. By then it was morning, and people began arriving from the main monastery. When the service was over, Father Zossima wanted to say goodbye and kiss everyone. Because the room was so small, the first visitors left to let others come in. Alyosha stood next to Father Zossima, who was back in his chair, talking as much as he could. His voice was weak but steady.

“I’ve spent so many years teaching you, and so many years talking, that I’ve gotten used to speaking out loud,” Father Zossima joked, looking at everyone with emotion. “Now it’s almost harder for me to stay quiet than to talk, even though I’m so weak, dear Fathers and brothers.”

Alyosha later remembered some of what Father Zossima said. Even though he spoke clearly and his voice was steady, his speech jumped from topic to topic. He talked about many things, as if, right before dying, he wanted to say everything he hadn’t said in his life—not just to teach, but as if he was desperate to share his happiness and joy one last time with everyone and everything, to open his heart completely.

“Love each other, Fathers,” Father Zossima said, as Alyosha remembered it. “Love God’s people. Just because we’ve come here and shut ourselves behind these walls doesn’t mean we’re holier than people outside. Actually, it means we’ve admitted to ourselves that we are worse than everyone else on earth… And the longer a monk lives here, the more he has to realize that. Otherwise, why come here at all? When a monk realizes he’s not only worse than others, but also responsible for everyone else’s sins—every human sin, big or small—then our purpose here is fulfilled. Everyone is responsible for everyone else, not just because the world is sinful, but each person is responsible for all people, personally. This is the highest truth for a monk or any person. Monks aren’t a special kind of person—they’re just what everyone should be. Through this knowledge, our hearts fill with endless love. Then you’ll have the power to win the world with love and wash away its sins with your tears… Always keep watch over your heart, and confess your sins to yourself. Don’t be afraid of your sins, as long as you’re truly sorry, but don’t make deals with God. Don’t be proud—not to anyone, big or small. Don’t hate those who reject you or insult you. Don’t hate atheists or people who teach evil, not even the worst ones. Pray for them: ‘Save, O Lord, all those who have no one to pray for them, and save those who won’t pray.’ And add: ‘I don’t pray this out of pride, Lord, for I am lower than all men…’ Love God’s people, and don’t let outsiders steal them away, because if you become lazy or greedy, they will. Teach the Gospel to the people all the time… Don’t be greedy. Don’t love money… Have faith. Hold up the banner and lift it high.”

But Father Zossima spoke even more disjointedly than Alyosha remembered later. Sometimes he had to stop talking to catch his breath and regain some strength, but he seemed almost lost in a joyful trance. Everyone listened with emotion, though some were confused by his words. Later, they all remembered them.

When Alyosha left the cell for a moment, he noticed how excited and tense the monks outside were. Some showed their anticipation by looking anxious, others by acting serious and prayerful. Everyone expected something miraculous to happen right after Father Zossima died. In a way, this hope seemed almost childish, but even the strictest monks felt it. Father Païssy looked the most serious of all.

A monk quietly came to get Alyosha to see Rakitin, who had come from town with a strange letter for him from Madame Hohlakov. In the letter, Madame Hohlakov told Alyosha about something strange and amazing. The day before, an old woman from town, a sergeant’s widow named Prohorovna, had come to get Father Zossima’s blessing. She asked if she could pray for her son Vassenka, who had gone to Irkutsk and hadn’t sent word in over a year. Father Zossima had answered her very strictly, saying she should not pray for someone who was alive as if he were dead—that was like witchcraft. Later, he forgave her because she didn’t know any better, and then (as Madame Hohlakov put it, “as if reading the future”) he comforted her: “Her son Vassya is definitely alive, and he will either come back soon or send a letter, and she should go home and wait for him.” Madame Hohlakov wrote excitedly, “Would you believe it? The prophecy came true, and even more than that!” As soon as the old woman got home, she received a letter from Siberia that had been waiting for her. And that’s not all—in the letter, written as Vassya was traveling from Ekaterinenburg, he told his mother he was coming back to Russia with an official, and that three weeks after she got the letter, he hoped “to hug his mother.”

Madame Hohlakov begged Alyosha to tell the Superior and all the monks about this new “miracle of prediction.” “Everyone should know!” she finished. The letter was written in a rush—you could tell Madame Hohlakov was very excited. But Alyosha didn’t have to tell anyone, since everyone already knew. Rakitin had asked the monk who brought Alyosha the message to also tell Father Païssy, “with all respect, that he, Rakitin, has something so important to say to him that he can’t wait, and asks forgiveness for being bold.” Since the monk had already delivered Rakitin’s message to Father Païssy before giving Alyosha the letter, all Alyosha had to do was hand the letter to Father Païssy to confirm the story.
Even Father Païssy, who was strict and careful, couldn’t hide his feelings as he read the news of the “miracle.” His eyes lit up, and a serious but joyful smile appeared on his lips.
“We shall see greater things!” he burst out.
“We shall see greater things, even greater things!” the monks around him repeated.

But Father Païssy, frowning again, asked everyone not to talk about it yet, “until it’s more fully confirmed, since people are so easily fooled these days. And honestly, this could have happened naturally,” he added, sounding cautious, though it was clear even he didn’t quite believe his own doubts—and everyone could tell.

Of course, within an hour, the “miracle” was known all over the monastery and among the visitors who had come for mass. No one seemed more impressed than the monk who’d arrived the day before from St. Sylvester, the little Obdorsk monastery in the far North. He was the same monk who, standing near Madame Hohlakov the previous day, had asked Father Zossima about the “healing” of Madame Hohlakov’s daughter, saying, “How can you dare to do such things?”

Now, this monk was puzzled and didn’t know whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont, who lived alone behind the beehives, and the visit had really shaken him. Father Ferapont was an old monk, famous for his strict fasting and silence, who already had a reputation for being against Father Zossima and the whole idea of “elders,” which he considered a dangerous and foolish new trend. He was a powerful opponent, though he hardly ever spoke because of his vow of silence. What made him really influential was that quite a few monks felt the same as he did, and many visitors considered him a great saint and ascetic, even though some thought he was a little crazy. But that craziness was part of his appeal.

Father Ferapont never visited Father Zossima. Even though he lived in the hermitage, no one forced him to follow the usual rules, mostly because he acted so strange. He was at least seventy-five, and lived in an old, crumbling wooden cell beyond the beehives. The cell had been built for another famous ascetic, Father Iona, who had lived to be 105, and whose holy deeds were still talked about in the area.

Father Ferapont had managed to get himself assigned to that remote cell seven years earlier. It was basically a peasant’s hut, but it looked like a chapel because it was filled with icons and always had lamps burning in front of them—these were offerings people had brought to the monastery. Father Ferapont was supposed to take care of the icons and keep the lamps burning. People said (and it was true) that he ate only two pounds of bread every three days. The beekeeper, who lived nearby, brought him the bread, but Father Ferapont rarely said a word even to him. He got four pounds of bread a week, plus sacramental bread sent by the Father Superior every Sunday after mass. That was all he ate. His water was changed every day. He almost never showed up at mass. Visitors who came to honor him sometimes saw him kneeling in prayer all day, never looking up. If he spoke to them, it was always short, strange, and usually rude. On rare occasions, he would say something mysterious, but he never explained himself. He wasn’t a priest, just a simple monk. Some of the less educated people believed Father Ferapont could talk to heavenly spirits and only spoke to them, which is why he was so silent with humans.

The monk from Obdorsk, after getting directions from the grumpy beekeeper, went to Father Ferapont’s cell. “Maybe he’ll talk to you since you’re a stranger, or maybe he’ll say nothing,” the beekeeper warned. The monk later said he approached very nervously. It was late in the evening. Father Ferapont sat on a low bench at his door, under a huge old elm tree whose leaves rustled in the cool air. The monk from Obdorsk bowed before the old man and asked for his blessing.
“You want me to bow to you, monk?” Father Ferapont said. “Get up!”
The monk stood up.
“Blessing, be blessed! Sit next to me. Where are you from?”

What surprised the monk most was that, even though Father Ferapont fasted so strictly and was so old, he still looked strong. He was tall, stood up straight, and his thin face looked healthy. He clearly still had a lot of strength and was well built. Surprisingly, he wasn’t even completely gray yet—his thick hair and full beard, once black, still had color. His eyes were gray, big, and bright, but they stuck out a little. He spoke with a thick accent. He wore a long, reddish peasant coat made of rough cloth, tied with a rope. His chest and throat were bare. Under his coat, his shirt was so dirty it looked almost black, since he hadn’t changed it in months. People said he wore thirty pounds of iron chains under his coat. He didn’t wear socks, just old, falling-apart slippers.
“From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester,” the monk answered humbly, keeping his nervous, sharp eyes on the hermit.
“I’ve been to your Sylvester’s. I used to stay there. Is Sylvester well?”
The monk hesitated.
“You’re a clueless bunch! How do you keep the fasts?”

“Our food follows the old monastery rules. During Lent, we don’t have meals on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday. On Tuesday and Thursday, we have white bread, fruit with honey, wild berries, or pickled cabbage and porridge. On Saturday, cabbage soup, noodles with peas, and kasha, all with hemp oil. On the other weekdays, dried fish and kasha with cabbage soup. From Monday until Saturday night in Holy Week, we only have bread and water—and not much of it—and sometimes skip food altogether, just like the first week of Lent. On Good Friday, nothing at all. On Holy Saturday, we fast until three o’clock, then have a little bread and water and one cup of wine. On Holy Thursday, we drink wine and eat something without oil, or not cooked at all, since the old church rules say not to break the fast on Holy Thursday. That’s our fasting. But what is that compared to you, holy Father?” the monk added, getting more confident, “since you only eat bread and water, even at Easter, and what we eat in two days lasts you a whole week. Your fasting is truly amazing.”
“And mushrooms?” Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
“Mushrooms?” the monk repeated, surprised.

“Yes. I can give up their bread, don’t need it at all, and just go live in the forest eating mushrooms and berries. But they can’t give up bread, so they’re slaves to the devil. These days, people say there’s no need to fast like this. Their pride and dirtiness shows in their judgment.”
“Oh, that’s true,” sighed the monk.
“And have you seen devils among them?” asked Father Ferapont.
“Among them? Among who?” asked the monk, nervously.

“I went to the Father Superior on Trinity Sunday last year—I haven’t been since. I saw a devil sitting on one man’s chest, hiding under his robe, only his horns sticking out; another had one peeking out of his pocket with sharp eyes, afraid of me; one devil was in a man’s dirty belly, another was hanging around someone’s neck, and he carried it without even knowing.”
“You can see spirits?” the monk asked.

“I’m telling you, I can see them. When I left the Superior’s room, I saw one hiding from me behind the door—a big one, about a yard and a half tall, with a long gray tail. The tip of its tail was caught in the door, and I was quick and slammed the door on it. It squealed and struggled, but I made the sign of the cross over it three times, and it died right there like a squished spider. It must have rotted in the corner and is stinking, but they don’t notice. I haven’t been back for a year. I’m telling you this because you’re a stranger.”
“Your words are frightening! But, holy and blessed Father,” said the monk, getting braver, “is it true, like people say even far away, that you actually talk to the Holy Ghost?”
“He does fly down sometimes.”
“How does he come? What does he look like?”
“As a bird.”
“The Holy Ghost as a dove?”
“There’s the Holy Ghost and there’s the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can come as other birds—sometimes a swallow, sometimes a goldfinch, sometimes a blue-tit.”
