“How do you know it’s not just a regular blue-tit?”
“He talks.”
“How? In what language?”
“In human language.”
“And what does he say?”
“Well, today he told me a fool would visit and ask me improper questions. You want to know too much, monk.”
“Your words are frightening, most holy and blessed Father,” the monk said, shaking his head. But his nervous eyes looked uncertain.
“Do you see this tree?” Father Ferapont asked, after a pause.
“I do, blessed Father.”
“You think it’s an elm, but to me it looks different.”
“What does it look like?” the monk asked, waiting for an answer.
“It happens at night. See those two branches? At night, it’s Christ reaching out His arms to me, searching for me. I see it clearly and I tremble. It’s terrible, terrible!”
“What’s terrible if it’s Christ Himself?”
“He’ll grab me and carry me away.”
“Alive?”
“In spirit, in the glory of Elijah—haven’t you heard? He’ll take me in His arms and carry me off.”

Even though the monk returned to his shared cell confused, in his heart he now respected Father Ferapont even more than Father Zossima. He strongly believed in strict fasting, so it wasn’t surprising to him that someone who fasted like Father Ferapont would “see marvels.” His words sounded strange, but who could know what God hid in such words? The story about pinching the devil’s tail, he was eager to believe, even literally. He had, before visiting the monastery, already disliked the whole idea of “elders,” thinking it was a bad new invention. Soon after arriving, he noticed some shallow brothers secretly grumbling about the elders. He was a nosy, curious man, always poking into things. That’s why the news of Father Zossima’s new “miracle” left him totally confused. Alyosha remembered later how this guest from Obdorsk kept wandering from group to group, listening and asking questions among the monks crowded around the elder’s cell. But at the time, Alyosha didn’t pay much attention to him—he only remembered this later.

Alyosha had no time to think about that anyway, because when Father Zossima felt tired and went back to bed, he thought of Alyosha as he was closing his eyes and asked for him to be brought in. Alyosha hurried in. Only Father Païssy, Father Iosif, and the novice Porfiry were there. The elder opened his tired eyes and looked closely at Alyosha, then suddenly asked:
“Is your family expecting you, my son?”
Alyosha hesitated.
“Don’t they need you? Didn’t you promise someone yesterday to see them today?”
“I did promise—to my father, my brothers—others too.”

“You see, you have to go. Don’t be sad. I promise I won’t die before you come back to hear my last words. I’ll say them to you, my son, as my last gift. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go keep your promise.”

Alyosha left right away, even though it was hard. But the promise that he would hear Father Zossima’s last words, and that they would be a gift just for him, filled Alyosha with excitement and joy. He hurried to finish his errands in town and come back quickly. Father Païssy also said something to him as they left the cell that surprised and touched Alyosha deeply.

“Remember this always, young man,” Father Païssy started, without any introduction. “The science of this world, which has become so powerful, has especially in the last century picked apart everything that was once sacred and handed down to us in the holy books. After this harsh analysis, the scholars have ruined what was once holy. But they only analyzed the pieces and missed the whole, and that blindness is amazing. Yet the whole thing still stands before them, and the gates of hell won’t defeat it. Hasn’t it lasted nineteen centuries? Isn’t it still alive, both in individual hearts and in crowds? It’s still just as strong and living, even in the hearts of atheists who have tried to destroy everything! Even those who attack Christianity still secretly follow its ideals, because, so far, neither their cleverness nor their passion has been able to come up with a better ideal of humanity and goodness than what Christ gave us. When people have tried, the results have been ridiculous. Remember this, especially since your elder is sending you out into the world. Maybe, remembering this day, you won’t forget my words, spoken from the heart to guide you, because you are young, and the world’s temptations are strong and hard to resist. Now go, my orphan.”

With these words, Father Païssy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and thought about what he’d heard, he realized he had found a new, unexpected friend—a warm and loving teacher in this strict monk who had always seemed stern. It was as if Father Zossima had left him in Father Païssy’s care, and “maybe that’s exactly what happened,” Alyosha thought. The deep thoughts he’d just heard showed how much Father Païssy cared for him. The monk was in a hurry to prepare Alyosha’s mind for the temptations of the world and to protect his young soul with the strongest defense he could offer.

Alyosha headed straight to his father’s house. On the way, he remembered that his father had told him yesterday to visit without letting his brother Ivan know. “Why would he want that?” Alyosha wondered. “Even if my father wants to talk to me alone, why sneak around? He was probably just worked up yesterday and didn’t mean it.” Still, he was relieved when Marfa Ignatyevna opened the garden gate for him and told him that Ivan Fyodorovitch had gone out two hours earlier. She also mentioned that Grigory was sick in bed at the lodge.
“And my father?” Alyosha asked.
“He’s up, drinking his coffee,” Marfa replied, sounding a little annoyed.

Alyosha went inside. His father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, was sitting alone at the table, wearing slippers and a worn-out old coat. He was flipping through some bills, but not paying much attention to them. The house was empty except for him; Smerdyakov had also gone out shopping. Even though Fyodor Pavlovitch had gotten up early and was trying to act tough, he looked tired and weak. His forehead was covered with big purple bruises that had come up overnight, and he had wrapped a red handkerchief around his head. His nose was swollen and covered with smaller bruises, making his whole face look mean and sour. He knew he looked bad and glared at Alyosha as he walked in.
“The coffee’s cold,” he snapped. “I’m not giving you any. I only ordered some Lenten fish soup today. I don’t want anyone joining me. Why are you here?”
“I wanted to see how you’re doing,” Alyosha answered.
“Yes, and I told you to come yesterday. Doesn’t matter now. You didn’t have to bother. But I knew you’d show up eventually.”

He said this with a harsh tone. Then, almost right away, he stood up and checked his reflection in the mirror (probably for the fortieth time that morning), focusing on his nose. He started adjusting the red handkerchief on his forehead so it looked a bit better.
“Red looks better. White makes me look like I’m in a hospital,” he said seriously. “So, how are things at the monastery? How’s your elder?”
“He’s really bad. He might die today,” Alyosha replied. But his father wasn’t really listening and forgot his question immediately.

“Ivan’s gone out,” he said suddenly. “He’s trying his best to steal Mitya’s fiancée. That’s the only reason he’s still here,” Fyodor Pavlovitch added in a nasty tone, twisting his mouth and staring at Alyosha.
“Did he actually tell you that?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes, he did. Ages ago. Would you believe it, he told me three weeks back? You don’t think he came here to kill me too, do you? He must have had some reason for showing up.”
“What do you mean? Why are you saying things like that?” Alyosha said, worried.

“He doesn’t ask for money, but he’s not getting a single penny from me. I plan to live as long as I can, Alexey Fyodorovitch, so I need every bit of my money, and the older I get, the more I’ll need. I can still pass as a man at fifty-five, but I want to keep that going for another twenty years. When I get older, I’ll look awful. Girls won’t come to me for free, so I’ll need money for that. That’s why I’m saving more and more, just for myself, my dear son. You should know that. I’m going to keep sinning till the end, let me tell you. Sin is sweet; everyone complains about it, but everyone lives in it—some just do it in secret, while I do it out in the open. That’s why other sinners hate me, because I’m honest about it. And your paradise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, isn’t for me, let me tell you; it’s not a place for a gentleman, even if it exists. I think you just fall asleep and never wake up. Pray for my soul if you want, or don’t, I don’t care! That’s what I believe. Ivan spoke well here yesterday, even though we were all drunk. Ivan acts all high and mighty, but he doesn’t know that much... he isn’t really educated. He just sits there, silent, smiling at everyone—that’s how he gets by.”
Alyosha listened quietly.

“Why won’t he talk to me? If he does, he acts all superior. Your Ivan’s a scoundrel! And I’ll marry Grushenka in a second if I want to. If you’ve got money, Alexey Fyodorovitch, you just have to want something and you can have it. That’s what Ivan’s afraid of—he’s watching to make sure I don’t marry her, and that’s why he’s pushing Mitya to marry Grushenka himself. He hopes that’ll keep me away from her (as if I’d leave Ivan my money if I don’t marry her!). Besides, if Mitya marries Grushenka, Ivan thinks he can steal Mitya’s rich fiancée. That’s his plan! He’s a scoundrel, your Ivan!”
“You’re so upset! It’s because of yesterday. You should go lie down,” Alyosha said.

“See, you say that,” his father said suddenly, as if it just hit him, “and I’m not angry with you. But if Ivan said it, I’d get mad. You’re the only one I can be nice to; otherwise, you know I’m a mean man.”
“You’re not mean, just twisted,” Alyosha said with a smile.

“Listen. This morning, I was planning to get that thug Mitya locked up, but now I don’t know. These days, parents are seen as just old-fashioned, but even now the law won’t let you drag your old father around by the hair, kick him in the face in his own house, and talk about killing him in front of witnesses. If I wanted, I could destroy him and have him arrested for what he did yesterday.”
“So you’re not going to press charges?”
“Ivan talked me out of it. I usually wouldn’t listen to Ivan, but there’s something else.”
Leaning in close to Alyosha, he started whispering confidentially.

“If I send that thug to jail, she’ll hear about it and run straight to see him. But if she hears he beat me—an old, weak man—nearly to death, she might give up on him and come to me instead... She always does the opposite of what you’d expect. I know her completely! Want a little brandy? Take some cold coffee, and I’ll pour in a little brandy—it’s delicious, my boy.”

“No, thank you. But I’ll take that roll if I can,” Alyosha said, putting a small French roll in his cassock pocket. “And you probably shouldn’t have brandy either,” he added, worried, looking at his father.
“You’re right, it makes me more nervous instead of calming me down. Just one small glass. I’ll get it from the cupboard.”
He unlocked the cupboard, poured himself a glass, drank it, then locked the cupboard and put the key back in his pocket.
“That’s enough. One glass won’t hurt me.”
“See, you’re already in a better mood,” Alyosha said, smiling.

“Hmm! I love you even without the brandy, but with scoundrels I act like a scoundrel. Ivan isn’t going to Tchermashnya—why? He wants to see how much I give Grushenka if she comes. They’re all scoundrels! But I don’t even recognize Ivan, I don’t know him at all. Where does he come from? He’s not one of us, not really. As if I’d leave him anything! I’m not making a will at all, you know. And I’ll crush Mitya like a bug. At night, I squash black beetles with my slipper; they make a nasty sound when you step on them. Your Mitya will get squashed too. Your Mitya, because you love him. Yes, you love him, and I’m not afraid of that. But if Ivan loved him, I’d be worried for myself. But Ivan doesn’t love anyone. Ivan’s not really one of us. People like Ivan are just clouds of dust. When the wind blows, they’re gone... I had a silly idea when I told you to come today; I wanted to ask you about Mitya. If I gave him a thousand rubles—maybe two—do you think the miserable guy would agree to leave for five years, or better, thirty-five, and give up Grushenka for good, huh?”
“I—I’ll ask him,” Alyosha mumbled. “If you gave him three thousand, maybe he—”

“That’s ridiculous! Don’t ask him, there’s no need! I changed my mind. It was a dumb idea. I’m not giving him anything, not a penny—I want my money for myself,” his father shouted, waving his hand. “I’ll crush him without it. Don’t say a word to him or he’ll start hoping. You don’t need to stay here. Is that fiancée of his, Katerina Ivanovna, who he’s hidden from me all this time, going to marry him or not? You went to see her yesterday, didn’t you?”
“Nothing will make her leave him.”

“See how much those fancy young ladies love a wild guy and a scoundrel? They’re weak, I tell you, those pale girls—not like... Ah, if I had his youth and the looks I had at twenty-eight (I was better looking than he is), I’d be a real hero just like him. He’s a lowlife! But he’s not getting Grushenka, no way! I’ll crush him!”
His anger flared up again as he said this.
“You can go. There’s nothing else for you to do here today,” he barked.
Alyosha walked over to say goodbye and kissed his father on the shoulder.
“What’s that for?” The old man looked a little surprised. “We’ll see each other again, or do you think we won’t?”
“No, nothing like that. I didn’t mean anything by it.”

“Neither did I, it didn’t mean anything,” his father said, watching him go. “Hey, listen!” he shouted after Alyosha. “Come back soon and I’ll get some real fish soup for you, not like today. Make sure you come! Come tomorrow, all right, tomorrow!”
As soon as Alyosha left, Fyodor Pavlovitch went straight to the cupboard and poured himself another half-glass of brandy.
“No more now!” he muttered, clearing his throat. He locked the cupboard, put the key in his pocket, went into his bedroom, lay down exhausted, and fell asleep within a minute.

“Thank goodness he didn’t ask me about Grushenka,” Alyosha thought as he left his father’s house and started walking toward Madame Hohlakov’s place. “If he had, I might have had to tell him about meeting Grushenka yesterday.”

Alyosha couldn’t shake the feeling that since yesterday, both his father and Dmitri were even more fired up, and their hearts had turned cold again. “Father is angry and spiteful—he’s come up with some plan and he won’t give it up. And what about Dmitri? He’ll be even tougher and angrier than before, and he’ll have a plan too. I have to find him today, no matter what.”

But Alyosha didn’t have much time to think. Something happened on the way that, even though it seemed small, really stuck with him. After he crossed the square and turned onto Mihailovsky Street—which was separated from the main street by a little ditch—he noticed a group of schoolboys, probably nine to twelve years old, standing by the bridge. They were heading home from school, some with bags slung over their shoulders, some with leather satchels, some in jackets, and others in coats. A few wore those fancy high boots with folds at the ankles—the kind spoiled kids with rich dads liked. They were all talking excitedly, as if having a meeting. Alyosha always noticed children, ever since his days in Moscow, and he especially loved little kids, but liked older boys too. Even though he was worried today, he felt drawn to them. He glanced at their excited, flushed faces and immediately noticed that all the boys were holding stones. About thirty paces away, across the ditch, another schoolboy stood by a fence. He also had a satchel and looked about ten—pale, thin, with sharp black eyes. He was staring anxiously at the group, clearly his classmates, but it seemed like they were in a fight.
Alyosha went up to the group and spoke to a fair, curly-haired, rosy-cheeked boy in a black jacket.
“When I used to carry a satchel like yours, I always wore it on my left side so my right hand was free. You’ve got yours on your right side, so it’ll be hard to reach.”

Alyosha hadn’t planned this comment—it just came out naturally. But this kind of practical talk is the best way for an adult to connect with kids, and especially with a group. You have to treat them seriously, like equals. Alyosha just knew this instinctively.
“But he’s left-handed,” answered another boy, who looked about eleven and seemed strong and healthy. The rest stared at Alyosha.
“He even throws stones with his left hand,” added a third boy.
Just then, a stone flew into the group, just missing the left-handed boy. It had been thrown hard by the boy on the other side of the ditch.

“Get him, hit him back, Smurov!” the others shouted. But Smurov, the left-handed boy, didn’t need encouragement—he threw a stone right back, but missed and hit the ground. The boy across the ditch, whose coat pocket bulged with stones, threw another one. This time it hit Alyosha hard on the shoulder.

“He aimed at you, that was for you! You’re Karamazov, Karamazov!” the boys yelled, laughing. “Come on, everyone throw at him at once!” Six stones flew at the lone boy. One hit him on the head and he fell down, but he jumped up right away and started throwing stones back fiercely. Both sides kept throwing stones nonstop. Many in the group had their pockets full as well.
“What’s going on? Aren’t you ashamed? Six against one! You’ll hurt him!” Alyosha shouted.
He rushed forward, putting himself in front of the stones to shield the lone boy. Three or four boys stopped throwing for a moment.

“He started it!” yelled a boy in a red shirt, sounding angry and childish. “He’s a monster. He stabbed Krassotkin in class with a penknife the other day—there was blood. Krassotkin didn’t tell on him, but he needs to be taught a lesson.”
“But why? Do you tease him or something?” Alyosha asked.

“There, he hit you in the back again—see, he knows you!” some of the boys cried. “He’s throwing at you now, not us. Come on, everyone, aim at him again, don’t miss, Smurov!” And the stone-throwing started up again, more vicious than before. The boy across the ditch got hit in the chest. He screamed, started crying, and ran up the hill toward Mihailovsky Street. The group shouted, “Ha! He’s running away, scaredy-cat! Wisp of tow!”
“You don’t know what a monster he is, Karamazov. Killing him wouldn’t be enough,” said the boy in the jacket, his eyes flashing. He looked the oldest.
“What’s wrong with him?” Alyosha asked. “Is he a snitch or what?”
The boys looked at each other with mocking grins.
“Are you going that way, to Mihailovsky?” the oldest boy continued. “Catch up to him. Look, he’s stopped—he’s waiting for you and watching.”
“He’s looking at you,” the others chimed in.
“Ask him if he likes being called a ‘wisp of tow.’ Do you hear? Ask him!”
All the boys burst out laughing. Alyosha looked at the group, and they stared back at him.
“Don’t go near him, he’ll hurt you,” Smurov warned.
“I’m not going to ask him about the ‘wisp of tow’ thing—I’m guessing you tease him with that,” Alyosha replied. “But I will try to find out why you all hate him so much.”
“Go ahead, find out!” the boys shouted, laughing.
Alyosha crossed the bridge and started up the hill by the fence, heading straight for the lone boy.
“Watch out!” the boys called after him. “He’s not afraid of you. He’ll stab you just like he did Krassotkin, when you least expect it.”

The boy waited and didn’t move. When Alyosha got closer, he saw that the boy was about nine, small and sickly looking, with a thin pale face and big dark eyes full of anger. His shabby old overcoat was way too small for him, and his bare arms stuck out past the sleeves. There was a huge patch on his right knee, and his right boot had a big hole at the toe, colored in with ink. Both pockets of his coat were weighed down with stones. Alyosha stopped a couple of steps away, looking at him curiously. The boy could tell from Alyosha’s eyes that he wasn’t going to hit him, so he relaxed a little and spoke first.
“I’m alone, but I’ll beat all six of them by myself!” he said suddenly, his eyes blazing.
“I think one of the stones hurt you pretty badly,” Alyosha said gently.
“But I hit Smurov on the head!” the boy yelled.
“They told me you know me, and that you threw a stone at me on purpose,” Alyosha said.
The boy glared at him.
“I don’t know you. Do you know me?” Alyosha pressed.
“Leave me alone!” the boy snapped, but he didn’t move, as if waiting for something. His eyes were still full of anger.
“Alright, I’m going,” Alyosha said. “But I don’t know you, and I’m not teasing you. They told me how they make fun of you, but I’m not here to do that. Goodbye!”

“Monk in silk trousers!” the boy yelled after him with the same angry, defiant look, getting ready as if to fight. But Alyosha just turned, looked at him, and walked away. He hadn’t gotten three steps before the biggest stone from the boy’s pocket hit him hard in the back.

“So you hit people from behind! I guess they were telling the truth when they said you attack people when they’re not looking,” Alyosha said, turning around. This time, the boy threw a stone right at Alyosha’s face. Alyosha managed to block it, but it hit his elbow.
“Aren’t you ashamed? What did I ever do to you?” Alyosha cried.

The boy stood his ground, sure that Alyosha would attack him now. But when Alyosha still didn’t move, the boy’s rage exploded like a wild animal’s. He charged at Alyosha, grabbed his left hand with both hands, and sank his teeth into Alyosha’s middle finger. He bit down hard for about ten seconds before letting go. Alyosha yelled in pain and pulled his finger free. The boy backed away. Alyosha’s finger was bleeding badly, almost to the bone near the nail. He pulled out a handkerchief and wrapped it tightly around the wound, taking a whole minute to do it. The boy waited, watching him the whole time. When Alyosha finished, he looked up at the boy with gentle eyes.
“Alright,” he said. “You see how badly you bit me. Isn’t that enough? Now tell me—what did I ever do to you?”
The boy stared at him, stunned.

“Even though I don’t know you and this is the first time I’ve seen you,” Alyosha continued calmly, “I must have done something to you. Otherwise, you wouldn’t have hurt me like this. So what did I do? How did I wrong you? Tell me.”

Instead of answering, the boy burst into loud, tearful sobs and ran away. Alyosha slowly walked after him toward Mihailovsky Street. For a long time, he could see the boy running in the distance, still crying and not even glancing back. Alyosha decided he’d find out more about the boy when he had time and solve this mystery. Right now, though, he had too much to do.

Alyosha quickly arrived at Madame Hohlakov’s house, which was a big, impressive two-story stone building—one of the nicest in town. Even though Madame Hohlakov spent most of her time at her other estate in a different province, or in Moscow where she had another house, she still had this one, which she’d inherited from her family. Her estate here was actually the biggest of all three, but she hadn’t stayed here much until now. As soon as Alyosha came in, Madame Hohlakov hurried out to meet him in the hallway.
“Did you get my letter about the new miracle?” she asked, talking quickly and sounding pretty anxious.
“Yes.”
“Did you show it to everyone? He brought the son back to his mother!”
“He’s dying today,” Alyosha said quietly.

“I heard about it, I know, oh, I wish I could talk to you, to someone, about all of this. No, to you, to you! And I’m so sad I can’t see him! The whole town is buzzing, everyone’s waiting to see what happens. But now—did you know Katerina Ivanovna is here right now?”
“Oh, that’s perfect!” Alyosha said, excited. “Then I’ll get to see her here. She asked me yesterday to make sure I visited her today.”

“I know, I know everything. I heard exactly what happened yesterday—and how terribly that... person behaved. It’s tragic, and if I were in her place, I don’t know what I would have done. And your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch—what do you think of him?—my goodness! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I almost forgot—your brother is in there with her, not the awful one who made a scene yesterday, but the other, Ivan Fyodorovitch. He’s sitting with her, talking; they’re having a really serious conversation. If you only knew what they’re talking about—it’s horrible, I’m telling you, like something out of a nightmare. They’re ruining their lives for no reason anyone can understand. They both know it and almost seem to enjoy it. I’ve been waiting for you! I really needed to see you! It’s all too much for me. I’ll tell you everything soon, but first, there’s something even more important—I almost forgot. Tell me, why did Lise have a hysterical fit? As soon as she heard you were here, she started crying!”

“Mom, you’re the one being hysterical now, not me,” Lise’s voice sang from a tiny crack in the nearby door. She sounded like she wanted to laugh but was holding it back. Alyosha noticed the crack and guessed Lise was peeking out, but he couldn’t see her.

“No wonder, Lise, no wonder... your moods will make me hysterical too. She’s so sick, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she was up all night with a fever, moaning! I could barely wait for morning and for Dr. Herzenstube to come. He said he has no idea what’s wrong, that we just have to wait. Herzenstube always says he doesn’t know what’s wrong. As soon as you got close to the house, she screamed, had a hysterical fit, and insisted on being wheeled back into this room.”
“Mom, I didn’t even know he was here. I didn’t ask to be brought back just because of him.”
“That’s not true, Lise. Yulia ran to tell you that Alexey Fyodorovitch was coming. She was watching for him.”

“Oh, dear mom, that’s not very clever of you. But if you want to make up for it, you can tell our honored guest, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how silly he was to come visit us after what happened yesterday, when everyone is making fun of him.”
“Lise, that’s too much. I swear I’ll have to be strict with you. Who’s laughing at him? I’m so glad he came, I need him, I can’t do without him. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’m so upset!”
“But what’s wrong, mom, my dear?”

“Oh, your moods, Lise, your fidgeting, your sickness, that terrible night with the fever, and that never-ending Herzenstube, always the same! It’s everything, just everything... Even that miracle! Oh, how it’s shaken me, Alexey Fyodorovitch! And that drama in the drawing room, I can’t take it, I’m warning you. I just can’t. Maybe it’s all just a comedy, not a tragedy. Tell me, will Father Zossima live until tomorrow? Oh, God! What’s happening to me? Every time I close my eyes, it all seems silly, completely silly.”
“I’d really appreciate it,” Alyosha cut in suddenly, “if you could give me a clean cloth to wrap my finger. I hurt it, and it really hurts.”
Alyosha took off the bloody handkerchief from his bitten finger. The cloth was soaked with blood. Madame Hohlakov screamed and closed her eyes.
“Oh my goodness, what a terrible wound!”
As soon as Lise saw Alyosha’s finger through the door crack, she threw the door open wide.

“Come here,” she ordered sharply. “No more nonsense! Oh wow, why didn’t you say anything about this before? He could’ve bled to death, mom! How did you do it? Water, water! You have to wash it first, just hold it in cold water to stop the pain, and keep it there, keep it there... Quick, mom, get some water in a washbasin. But hurry up!” she finished nervously. She looked really scared by Alyosha’s wound.
“Shouldn’t we call Dr. Herzenstube?” Madame Hohlakov cried.

“Mom, you’ll be the death of me. If we call Herzenstube, he’ll just say he doesn’t know what’s wrong! Water, water! Mom, please go yourself and hurry Yulia—she’s always so slow and never comes quickly! Hurry up, mom, or I’ll die.”
“It’s not that bad,” Alyosha said, worried by how upset everyone was.
Yulia rushed in with a bowl of water, and Alyosha put his finger in it.

“Bring some lint, mom, please, and that antiseptic lotion for wounds—what’s it called? We have some. You know where it is, mom; it’s in your bedroom, in the right-hand cupboard. There’s a big bottle with the lint.”
“I’ll bring everything in a minute, Lise, just don’t scream or fuss. See how bravely Alexey Fyodorovitch is handling it. How did you get such a nasty cut, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Madame Hohlakov hurried out. That was exactly what Lise had been waiting for.
“First, tell me—how did you hurt yourself like this?” she asked Alyosha quickly. “And then I’ll talk to you about something else. Well?”
Knowing her mom wouldn’t be gone long, Alyosha quickly told Lise—in as few words as possible—about his strange meeting with the schoolboys. Lise put her hands together in surprise at his story.

“How can you, especially dressed like that, hang out with schoolboys?” she said angrily, as if she had the right to tell him what to do. “You’re just a boy yourself if you do that, a complete child! But you have to find out for me about that awful boy and tell me everything, because there’s something weird going on. Now for the second thing—but first: does the pain stop you from talking about totally unimportant things, but talking sensibly?”
“Of course not, and it doesn’t hurt much now.”

“That’s only because your finger is in the water. We’ll have to change it soon because it’ll get warm. Yulia, bring some ice from the cellar and another bowl of water. Now that she’s gone, I can talk—will you give me back the letter I sent you yesterday, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch? Quick, before mom comes back—I don’t want—”
“I don’t have the letter.”
“That’s not true, you do. I knew you’d say that. You have it in your pocket. I’ve been regretting that joke all night. Give me back the letter right now, give it to me.”
“I left it at home.”
“But you can’t think of me as a kid, a little girl, after that silly joke! I’m sorry I was so silly, but you have to bring me the letter, if you really don’t have it—bring it today, you have to.”
“I can’t today, because I’m going back to the monastery and I won’t be able to see you for the next couple of days—three or four maybe—because of Father Zossima—”
“Four days? That’s ridiculous! Tell me, did you laugh at me a lot?”
“I didn’t laugh at all.”
“Why not?”
“Because I believed everything you said.”
“You’re insulting me!”

“Not at all. As soon as I read it, I thought it would all happen just like you wrote. As soon as Father Zossima dies, I have to leave the monastery. Then I’ll go back to finish my studies, and when you’re old enough, we’ll get married. I’ll love you. I haven’t really thought about it, but I don’t think I could find a better wife than you, and Father Zossima said I should get married.”
“But I’m a cripple, stuck in a wheelchair,” Lise laughed, turning bright red.
“I’ll push you myself, but I’m sure you’ll be better by then.”
“But you’re crazy,” Lise said nervously, “to turn a joke into all this nonsense! Here comes mom, just in time, maybe. Mom, why are you always so slow? And here’s Yulia with the ice!”
“Oh, Lise, don’t scream, please don’t scream. That scream drives me... How can I help it when you moved the lint? I’ve been searching everywhere—I bet you did it on purpose.”
“How could I know he’d show up with a hurt finger? Otherwise maybe I would’ve done it on purpose. My sweet mom, you’re starting to say some really funny things.”

“Never mind if I’m funny, but you could show a little more sympathy for Alexey Fyodorovitch! Oh, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, what’s really upsetting me isn’t just Herzenstube, it’s everything together, it’s all just too much for me.”

“Enough about Herzenstube,” Lise said, laughing. “Hurry up with the lint and the lotion, mom. That’s just Goulard’s water, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I remember the name now, but it’s a great lotion. Mom, can you believe it—on his way here, he got into a fight with boys in the street, and one of them bit his finger. Isn’t he a child, just a kid himself? Is he ready to get married after that? Just imagine him married, mom. Wouldn’t that be funny? Wouldn’t it be awful?”
And Lise kept giggling her thin, nervous laugh, sneaking glances at Alyosha.
“But why married, Lise? Why are you talking about that? It’s not the right time—and maybe the boy had rabies.”
“Oh, mom! Like there are rabid boys!”

“Why not, Lise? Why act like I said something dumb? The boy could’ve been bitten by a rabid dog and then he’d go mad and bite anyone near him. You bandaged it so well, Alexey Fyodorovitch! I couldn’t have done it. Does it still hurt?”
“It’s not so bad now.”
“You’re not scared of water, are you?” Lise asked.

“Alright, that’s enough, Lise. Maybe I was a bit quick to say the boy had rabies, and you jumped on it. Katerina Ivanovna just found out you’re here, Alexey Fyodorovitch. She rushed to me, she’s desperate to see you, she really is!”
“Oh, mom, go to them yourself. He can’t go right now, he’s in too much pain.”
“Not at all, I can go,” Alyosha said.
“What! You’re leaving? Is that it?”
“Well, I’ll come back here to talk after I see them. But I really want to see Katerina Ivanovna now, because I need to get back to the monastery as soon as I can.”
“Mom, take him away quickly. Alexey Fyodorovitch, don’t bother coming back to see me—just go straight back to your monastery and good riddance. I want to sleep, I didn’t sleep at all last night.”
“Ah, Lise, you’re only joking, but I really wish you would sleep!” Madame Hohlakov cried.
“I don’t know what I did... I’ll stay another three minutes, five if you want,” Alyosha mumbled.
“Even five! Just take him away, mom, he’s a monster.”

“Lise, you’re being ridiculous. Come on, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let’s go—she’s too moody today. I’m afraid to cross her. Oh, the trouble with nervous girls! Maybe seeing you really will help her sleep. How quickly you’ve made her sleepy—it’s lucky!”
“Oh, mom, you say such sweet things! I have to kiss you for that, mom.”

“And I’ll kiss you too, Lise. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov said, lowering her voice like she was sharing a big secret. “I don’t want to give anything away, I don’t want to spoil the surprise, you’ll see for yourself what’s going on. It’s awful. It’s the strangest drama. She loves your brother Ivan and is doing everything she can to convince herself she loves your brother Dmitri. It’s terrible! I’ll go in with you, and if they don’t throw me out, I’ll stay until the end.”

In the drawing-room, the conversation had already ended. Katerina Ivanovna looked intense and determined, but also clearly upset. When Alyosha and Madame Hohlakov came in, Ivan Fyodorovitch was standing up, about to leave. Ivan looked pale, and Alyosha watched him with concern. This was the moment that might solve a confusing mystery that had been bothering Alyosha for a while. People had been hinting to him for the past month that his brother Ivan was in love with Katerina Ivanovna—and that Ivan even planned to “steal her away” from Dmitri. Alyosha had always thought that was ridiculous, even though it worried him. He cared about both his brothers and hated the idea of them fighting over the same woman. Just yesterday, Dmitri had told Alyosha straight out that he was glad Ivan was his rival, saying it actually helped him. Helped him do what—marry Grushenka? Alyosha thought that would be the worst outcome. Up until the night before, Alyosha had believed Katerina Ivanovna truly loved Dmitri, passionately and faithfully. He also thought she could never love someone like Ivan, and that she loved Dmitri for exactly who he was, no matter how strange that seemed.

But after the scene with Grushenka yesterday, Alyosha started thinking differently. The word “lacerating,” which Madame Hohlakov had just used, startled him, because he’d woken up at dawn yelling “Laceration, laceration!”—probably about his dream. He’d dreamed all night about what happened at Katerina Ivanovna’s the day before. Now, Madame Hohlakov’s blunt insistence that Katerina Ivanovna was really in love with Ivan—and only pretending to love Dmitri out of some twisted sense of duty or self-torture—got stuck in Alyosha’s mind. “Maybe she’s right,” he thought. But then, what did that mean for Ivan? Alyosha felt deep down that someone with Katerina Ivanovna’s personality would always want to control others, and she could only really control someone like Dmitri, not Ivan. Dmitri might eventually surrender to her, which Alyosha actually hoped for, but Ivan never would, and Alyosha doubted it would make Ivan happy anyway. As these messy thoughts whirled through his head while he entered the drawing-room, another idea hit him: “What if she doesn’t actually love either of them—not Ivan, not Dmitri?”

Alyosha felt embarrassed and guilty about thinking these things. “What do I know about love and women? How can I even judge something like this?” he scolded himself. But he couldn’t stop. He sensed that this rivalry was hugely important for his brothers’ futures, and that everything depended on how it played out.

“One reptile will eat the other,” Ivan had said angrily the day before, talking about their father and Dmitri. So Ivan thought of Dmitri as a reptile, maybe he’d felt that way for a long time—maybe ever since he met Katerina Ivanovna. Ivan hadn’t meant to say that out loud, but that only made it more important to Alyosha. If Ivan really felt this way, how could their family find peace? Wouldn’t it just lead to more hatred? And whose side was Alyosha supposed to take? What should he want for his brothers? He loved them both, but didn’t know what was best for either of them. He was lost in all this confusion, and it really hurt, because he wasn’t someone who could just sit by and do nothing. When Alyosha loved someone, he always tried to help. But to help, he needed to know what he was aiming for—what was truly best for each brother. Instead, all he saw was confusion and pain. It was “lacerating,” as Madame Hohlakov had said. And yet, he didn’t even understand what this “laceration” really meant. He felt completely lost in this emotional maze.

When Alyosha entered, Katerina Ivanovna quickly and excitedly asked Ivan to stay a little longer, saying, “Just a minute! Stay and hear the opinion of someone I trust completely.” She also asked Madame Hohlakov not to leave, then had Alyosha sit next to her, with Madame Hohlakov sitting across from Ivan.

“You’re all my friends here—the only friends I have in the world,” Katerina Ivanovna began, her voice shaking with real tears of pain. Alyosha immediately felt moved. “Alexey Fyodorovitch, you saw that terrible scene yesterday, and you saw what I did. Ivan Fyodorovitch, you weren’t there—he was. I don’t know what he thought of me yesterday. But I do know that if the same thing happened again—even right now—I would act the same as yesterday. The same feelings, the same words, the same actions. You remember what I did, Alexey Fyodorovitch; you even stopped me at one point…” As she said this, she blushed and her eyes sparkled. “I can’t stop thinking about it. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I don’t even know if I still love him. I feel sorry for him, which probably means I don’t love him. If I really loved him, maybe I wouldn’t pity him—I’d hate him instead.”
Her voice shook, and tears glistened in her eyes. Alyosha shivered inside. “She’s honest and sincere,” he thought. “She really doesn’t love Dmitri anymore.”
“That’s right, that’s right,” Madame Hohlakov said.

“Wait, my dear. I haven’t told you my main decision, the one I made during the night. Maybe it’s a terrible choice for me, but I know I’ll never change my mind—never. It will last my whole life. My dear, faithful, generous adviser—my only friend, Ivan Fyodorovitch—understands and approves of my decision. He knows what I’ve decided.”
“Yes, I approve,” Ivan said quietly but firmly.

“But I want Alyosha, too—oh, forgive me, Alexey Fyodorovitch, for calling you just Alyosha—I want Alexey Fyodorovitch to tell me what he thinks, right here in front of my two friends. I feel like your opinion, Alyosha, my dear brother (because you really are a dear brother to me),” she said with emotion, taking his cold hand in her warm one, “I feel like your answer will finally bring me peace, no matter how much I suffer. After you speak, I’ll be calm—I’ll accept whatever you say, I know it.”

“I’m not sure what you’re asking me,” Alyosha said, blushing. “I just know I care about you and right now I want you to be happy, even more than I want my own happiness! But I really don’t know anything about these things,” he added quickly.

“In things like this, Alexey Fyodorovitch, honor and duty are what matter most—and maybe something even higher than duty, though I can’t name it. I feel this powerful force inside me, and it makes me act. But I can put it simply: I’ve already decided, even if he marries that woman”—she said solemnly—“the woman I’ll never, ever forgive, even then, I won’t abandon him. From now on, I will never leave him!” she cried, almost hysterical. “But I won’t chase after him or bother him. No! I’ll move to another town—wherever you want—but I’ll keep watch over him my whole life. When he’s miserable with her, and he definitely will be soon, he can come to me and find a friend, a sister. Only a sister, of course, forever; but he’ll know that sister truly loves him and has given up her whole life for him. I’ll make sure of it. I’ll make him trust me completely, with no secrets,” she said, almost wild with emotion. “I’ll be like a god for him to pray to—and he owes me that, after betraying me and making me suffer so much yesterday. He’ll see that I’ll always be true to him, no matter how untrue he is to me. I’ll become nothing but a tool for his happiness, a machine for his happiness, my whole life—and he’ll know it every day! That’s my decision. Ivan Fyodorovitch completely agrees with me.”

She was out of breath. Maybe she’d meant to say all this in a calmer, more elegant way, but she spoke too fast and bluntly. Her words were full of raw emotion, and it showed she was still hurting from yesterday’s insult, and that her pride wanted payback. She realized this too—her face suddenly darkened and her eyes looked hard. Alyosha noticed instantly and felt sorry for her. Ivan made it worse by adding:

“I was just saying what I think,” Ivan said. “If anyone else said this, it would sound fake and over-the-top, but from you, it’s different. Any other woman would be wrong, but you are right. I can’t explain it, but you’re completely genuine, so you’re right.”
“But this is only for now. What does this moment even mean? Nothing except yesterday’s insult,” Madame Hohlakov cut in. She obviously hadn’t meant to interrupt but couldn’t help herself.

“Exactly, exactly,” Ivan said quickly, clearly annoyed she’d interrupted. “For anyone else, this would just be a reaction to yesterday, and it would pass. But with Katerina Ivanovna’s character, this moment will last her entire life. What would be just a promise for someone else is, for her, a never-ending, heavy, maybe even grim duty. She’ll keep going because she feels she must. Your life, Katerina Ivanovna, will now be spent worrying about your own feelings, your own heroism, and your own suffering. But in the end, that suffering will soften, and you’ll find peace in knowing you carried out your bold and proud plan. Yes, it’s proud, and maybe a little desperate, but it’s a victory for you. Knowing that will finally satisfy you and make you accept everything else.”
It was obvious Ivan was saying this with some bitterness, maybe even on purpose—he didn’t try to hide that he was being a little sarcastic.
“Oh, how wrong all of this is!” Madame Hohlakov burst out again.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you speak! I really want to know what you think!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, suddenly bursting into tears. Alyosha stood up from the sofa.
“It’s nothing, nothing!” she went on, crying. “I’m just upset—I didn’t sleep last night. But with friends like you and your brother, I still feel strong. I know you two will never leave me.”
“Unfortunately, I have to go back to Moscow—maybe tomorrow—and I’ll be gone for a long time. Sadly, I can’t avoid it,” Ivan said suddenly.

“Tomorrow—to Moscow!” Her face twisted for a second, but then she suddenly said, “But—actually, how lucky!” Her voice changed instantly. In a flash, she stopped crying. Alyosha was amazed to see her go from a hurt, weeping girl to a calm, even cheerful woman, as if something good had happened.

“Oh, not lucky that I’m losing you—of course not,” she quickly corrected herself, smiling in a polite, society way. “You’re such a good friend, of course I’m unhappy to lose you.” She hurried over to Ivan, grabbed his hands, and squeezed them. “But what’s lucky is that you’ll be in Moscow, so you can see Auntie and Agafya and tell them all about my terrible situation. You can be completely honest with Agafya, but please spare dear Auntie. You’ll know how to do it. I was miserable yesterday and this morning, trying to figure out how to write them that awful letter—because you can’t explain things like this in a letter. Now it’ll be easy, because you’ll see them and explain everything. Oh, I’m so glad! But I’m only glad about that, I promise. Nobody can replace you… I’ll go write the letter right away!” she finished, and started toward the door.
“And what about Alyosha and his opinion, which you were so desperate to hear?” Madame Hohlakov called out, her voice sharp and sarcastic.

“I didn’t forget!” Katerina Ivanovna said, stopping suddenly. “And why are you being so hostile right now?” she added, sounding hurt. “What I said, I meant—I need his opinion. Even more, I need his decision! Whatever he says, that’s what I’ll do. You can see how much his words matter to me, Alexey Fyodorovitch… But what’s wrong?”
“I can’t believe it. I just can’t understand!” Alyosha suddenly said in distress.
“What? What?”

“He’s going to Moscow, and you said you were glad. You did that on purpose! And then you tried to explain you’re only glad because he can help with your family, but that was acting too—like a scene in a play!”
“A play? What? What are you talking about?” Katerina Ivanovna cried, shocked and turning red.
“Even though you say you’re sad to lose a friend, you keep telling him right to his face that it’s good he’s going away,” Alyosha said, out of breath. He stayed standing at the table.
“What are you talking about? I don’t get it.”

“I don’t really get it myself… It just hit me, all at once. I know I’m not saying this right, but I have to say it anyway,” Alyosha continued, his voice shaking. “What I see is that maybe you don’t love Dmitri at all… maybe you never have. And Dmitri doesn’t love you either… he just respects you. I honestly don’t know how I have the nerve to say all this, but someone needs to tell the truth—because nobody else here will.”
“What truth?” Katerina Ivanovna cried, almost hysterical.

“I’ll tell you,” Alyosha went on, speaking so fast it was like jumping off a roof. “Call Dmitri; I’ll go get him—let him come here, take your hand, and take Ivan’s, and join your hands together. Because you’re torturing Ivan, just because you love him—and you’re torturing him, too, because you think you love Dmitri out of ‘self-laceration,’ but it’s not real love—it’s just something you convinced yourself of.”
Alyosha stopped talking and went silent.
“You… you… you’re a little religious idiot, that’s what you are!” Katerina Ivanovna snapped. Her face was pale, and her lips trembled with anger.
Ivan suddenly laughed and stood up, holding his hat.

“You’re wrong, Alyosha,” he said, showing an expression Alyosha had never seen before—honest and young, full of real, open feeling. “Katerina Ivanovna has never cared about me! She’s always known I loved her—even though I never said it out loud—but she didn’t care about me. I was never really her friend, not even for a moment; she’s too proud to need my friendship. She kept me close just to get back at Dmitri. She took out all the pain and insults Dmitri has given her on me. Even the very first time they met, she felt insulted, and it’s stuck with her ever since—that’s just the way she is! She’s talked to me about nothing but her love for him. I’m leaving now, but believe me, Katerina Ivanovna, you really do love him. And the more he hurts you, the more you love him—that’s your ‘laceration.’ You love him exactly as he is; you love him because he insults you. If he changed and became good, you’d stop loving him immediately. You need him so you can keep thinking about your own heroic loyalty, and so you can blame him for being unfaithful. And it all comes from your pride. There’s a lot of humiliation and self-doubt in it, but it’s still pride… I’m too young and I’ve loved you too much. I know I shouldn’t be saying this—that it would be more dignified to just leave quietly, and that would hurt you less. But I’m going far away and I’ll never come back… This is forever. I don’t want to be around this ‘laceration’ anymore… But I don’t know how to talk now. I’ve said it all. Goodbye, Katerina Ivanovna; you can’t be mad at me, because I’m suffering a hundred times more than you—just because I’ll never see you again. Goodbye! I don’t want your hand. You’ve hurt me too much for me to forgive you right now. I’ll forgive you someday, but not now. ‘Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht,’” he added with a forced smile, quoting Schiller, showing Alyosha he knew his German poetry by heart—which Alyosha would never have suspected. Ivan left the room without even saying goodbye to Madame Hohlakov. Alyosha wrung his hands.

“Ivan!” he cried desperately after him. “Come back, Ivan! No, nothing will make him come back now!” he said sadly. “But it’s my fault, my fault. I started it! Ivan spoke out of anger—he was wrong and unfair. He has to come back, he has to,” Alyosha kept repeating frantically.
Katerina Ivanovna suddenly left the room for the next one.
“You did nothing wrong. You acted beautifully, like an angel,” Madame Hohlakov whispered quickly and excitedly to Alyosha. “I’ll do everything I can to stop Ivan Fyodorovitch from leaving.”
She looked overjoyed, though Alyosha was deeply upset, but Katerina Ivanovna soon came back. She was holding two one-hundred rouble notes.

“I have a big favor to ask you, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said, sounding calm and even as if nothing had happened. “A week ago—yes, I think it was a week—Dmitri Fyodorovitch did something horrible and unfair. There’s a cheap tavern here, and in it he met a former army officer, that captain your father used to employ. Dmitri Fyodorovitch lost his temper, grabbed the captain by the beard, dragged him out into the street and along it, humiliating him. I heard his son, a little boy who goes to school here, saw it and ran after them, crying for his father, begging people to help, while everyone just laughed. I can’t think about that scene without getting angry… it’s just like Dmitri Fyodorovitch in his rage and wildness! I can’t even find the words for it. I found out the captain is very poor. His name is Snegiryov. He did something wrong in the army and was kicked out—I don’t know the details. Now he and his family are terribly poor, with sick children and, I think, a wife who isn’t well mentally. He’s been living here a long time. He used to work as a copying clerk, but now has no job. I thought maybe you—well, I thought—oh, I’m explaining this so badly!—I wanted to ask you, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, to go visit him, find some excuse to meet him—I mean the captain—oh, I can’t explain!—and gently, carefully (the way only you can do it),” she said, making Alyosha blush, “try to give him this money, these two hundred roubles. I’m sure he’ll accept it… I mean, persuade him to accept it. But it’s not meant as compensation, to keep him from suing or anything like that—it’s just a sign of sympathy, a wish to help him from me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s fiancée, not from Dmitri himself. I’d go myself, but you’ll handle it so much better. He lives on Lake Street, in a house owned by a woman named Kalmikov. Please, Alexey Fyodorovitch, do this for me—and now… now I’m tired. Goodbye!”

She quickly disappeared behind the curtain before Alyosha could say a word, though he wanted to apologize and blame himself, to say something—his heart was so full, he couldn’t stand to leave without saying it. But Madame Hohlakov took his hand and led him out. In the hall, she stopped him again.

“She’s proud, she’s fighting with herself, but she’s kind, charming, generous!” Madame Hohlakov whispered. “Oh, how I love her, especially at times like this! And I’m so happy about everything! Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, you didn’t know, but I must tell you—we, all of us—her aunts, myself, even Lise—have been hoping and praying for her to give up Dmitri (who doesn’t care about her) and marry Ivan Fyodorovitch, who’s such a wonderful, cultured young man and loves her more than anything. We’re all secretly plotting to make it happen. I’m even staying here for that reason.”
“But she was crying—she’s hurt again,” Alyosha said.
“Never trust a woman’s tears, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I’m never on the women’s side in these things. I always side with the men.”
“Mamma, you’re spoiling him!” Lise’s little voice called from behind a door.
“No, it’s my fault. I’m terribly to blame,” Alyosha repeated, hiding his face in his hands, feeling awful for his outburst.
“Not at all! You acted like an angel, a real angel. I’d say it a thousand times.”
“Mamma, how did he act like an angel?” called Lise’s voice again.
“I just suddenly thought,” Alyosha went on as if he hadn’t heard Lise, “that she loved Ivan, so I blurted out that stupid thing… What’s going to happen now?”
“To whom, to whom?” Lise cried. “Mamma, you’ll be the death of me! I ask and you don’t answer.”
Just then the maid rushed in.
“Katerina Ivanovna is unwell… She’s crying, struggling… hysterics.”
“What’s happening?” Lise cried, actually worried now. “Mamma, I’ll have hysterics myself—not her!”

“Lise, for heaven’s sake, don’t scream, don’t pester me. You’re too young to know everything grown-ups know. I’ll come tell you what you need to know. Oh, mercy! I’m coming, I’m coming… Hysterics are a good sign, Alexey Fyodorovitch; it’s a great thing she’s hysterical. That’s how it should be. I’m always against women’s tears and hysterics in these cases. Yulia, run and tell her I’m coming. As for Ivan Fyodorovitch leaving like that, it’s her own fault. But he won’t really go. Lise, don’t scream! Oh, it’s not you screaming, it’s me! Forgive your mother, but I’m delighted, delighted, delighted! Did you see how young Ivan Fyodorovitch looked just now, when he left? I always thought he was so serious and scholarly, but suddenly he was so open and full of feeling, just like you! And the way he quoted that German poem—it was just like you! But I have to go! Alexey Fyodorovitch, hurry and do what she asked, then come right back. Lise, do you need anything? Don’t keep Alexey Fyodorovitch waiting—he’ll come right back to you.”
Madame Hohlakov finally rushed off. Alyosha was about to open the door to see Lise before leaving.
“Don’t you dare!” Lise cried. “Not now! Talk through the door. I just want to know how you became an angel.”
“For doing something really dumb, Lise! Goodbye!”
“Don’t go away like that!” Lise started to say.
“Lise, I’m really upset! I’ll be back soon, but I’m very, very upset!”
And he hurried out of the room.

Alyosha really was upset—more than usual. He realized he’d acted foolishly by forcing himself into a situation he barely understood—a love affair. “What do I know about love? What could I possibly say?” he kept repeating to himself, his face burning red. “Being embarrassed is nothing; I deserve to feel ashamed. The real problem is, I probably just made things worse for everyone... And Father Zossima sent me to help them make peace. Is this what making peace looks like?” He remembered awkwardly trying to get them to shake hands, and cringed at the memory. “Even if I meant well, I need to be smarter next time,” he decided seriously. He didn’t even try to joke about it.

Because of what Katerina Ivanovna had asked, Alyosha headed to Lake Street. Dmitri lived nearby, just off that street. Alyosha decided he should check on Dmitri before visiting the captain, even though he had a strong feeling Dmitri would be avoiding him now. Still, he needed to find him. Time was slipping away, and Alyosha couldn’t stop thinking about his dying elder, Father Zossima, ever since he’d left the monastery.

Alyosha was especially curious about one part of Katerina Ivanovna’s request: she’d mentioned a captain’s son—a little boy who had run after his father, crying. Alyosha immediately thought this must be the same schoolboy who had bitten his finger the other day when Alyosha tried to ask what was wrong. Now Alyosha was almost sure of it, even if he couldn’t explain why. Thinking about this helped distract him from feeling guilty about the “mess” he’d made earlier; he decided he’d just do what he had to do now, no matter what happened. That thought made him feel better. As he walked toward Dmitri’s street, he realized he was hungry, so he took out the bread roll he’d brought from his father’s house and ate it, which made him feel stronger.

Dmitri wasn’t home. The people who owned the house—an old cabinet-maker, his son, and his wife—looked at Alyosha suspiciously. “He hasn’t slept here in three nights. Maybe he’s gone away,” the old man said, as if following instructions. When Alyosha asked if Dmitri might be at Grushenka’s or hiding at Foma’s (Alyosha asked on purpose, acting casual), the three of them looked worried. “They care about him and are trying to protect him,” Alyosha thought. “That’s good.”

Finally, Alyosha found the house on Lake Street. It was a run-down little place, leaning to one side, with three windows facing the street and a muddy yard with a lonely cow in the middle. He crossed the yard and went in through a door that led to a hallway. On the left lived the old woman who owned the house and her elderly daughter—both seemed hard of hearing. After Alyosha asked several times about the captain, one of them finally understood and pointed to a door across the hall. The captain’s room was really just a simple cottage room. Alyosha put his hand on the metal latch to open the door, but was surprised by how quiet it was inside. He remembered Katerina Ivanovna said the captain had a family. “Maybe they’re all asleep, or maybe they heard me and are waiting. I’d better knock first,” Alyosha thought, and knocked. There was a pause—maybe ten seconds—before someone answered.
“Who’s there?” shouted someone in a loud and angry voice.

Alyosha opened the door and stepped inside. It was a typical peasant room—big, but crowded with belongings and several people. On the left was a big Russian stove. A string hung across the room with rags drying on it. There was a bed against each wall, both covered in knitted blankets. The bed on the left had a stack of four pillows, each smaller than the one below. The other bed only had one tiny pillow. In the far corner, a curtain hung from a string, hiding a bed made up on a bench and a chair. In the middle window was a rough wooden table. The three windows, each made of four small, dirty greenish panes, were closed and let in very little light, making the room dim and stuffy. On the table was a frying pan with leftover eggs, a half-eaten piece of bread, and a small bottle with a little vodka left.

A thin, sickly-looking woman in a cotton dress sat by the bed on the left. Her face was yellow and her cheeks hollow, but what Alyosha noticed most was her proud and questioning eyes. While her husband spoke, her large brown eyes watched every word, both proud and curious. Standing by the window was a young girl with reddish hair, plain-looking but neat, who looked at Alyosha with a sort of scorn. By the other bed sat another girl, about twenty, who was hunchbacked and crippled—her legs were “withered,” as Alyosha heard later—and her crutches rested nearby. Despite her condition, she had beautiful, gentle eyes that looked at Alyosha calmly. At the table sat a man of about forty-five, thin and weak, with reddish hair and a wispy, scraggly beard. Alyosha thought he looked like “a wisp of tow”—the comparison popped into his mind and stuck. This was clearly the man who had yelled from inside. As Alyosha entered, he jumped up, wiped his mouth with a ragged napkin, and hurried over.
“It’s a monk come begging for the monastery. Great place to come!” the girl by the window said loudly. The man spun toward her and replied in a shaky, excited voice:
“No, Varvara, you’re wrong. Allow me to ask,” he turned to Alyosha, “what brings you to—our humble home?”

Alyosha studied him closely. He’d never seen him before. The man seemed nervous, twitchy, and irritable. He’d obviously been drinking, but wasn’t actually drunk. His face showed a strange mix of boldness and fear, like someone who’s been bossed around for a long time and is suddenly trying to stand up for himself—or like someone who wants to hit you but is scared you might hit back. His voice switched quickly from angry to nervous, sometimes even a little silly. When he asked about “our humble home,” he seemed to tremble all over, rolling his eyes and standing so close that Alyosha had to step back. He wore a shabby dark coat, patched and stained, and very old, checked pants that were so wrinkled and short he looked like he’d outgrown them.
“I’m Alexey Karamazov,” Alyosha began.
“I know that, sir,” the man snapped, trying to show he was already aware. “I’m Captain Snegiryov, but I’d still like to know exactly why you’ve—”
“Oh, it’s nothing urgent. I just wanted a word with you—if that’s okay.”

“If that’s the case, here’s a chair, sir. Please sit down. That’s what they always say in old plays, ‘please be seated,’” and with a quick gesture, he grabbed a rough, wooden chair and set it almost in the middle of the room for Alyosha. He took another chair for himself and sat down facing Alyosha, so close their knees nearly touched.

“Nikolay Ilyitch Snegiryov, sir. I used to be a captain in the Russian army. I lost my rank because of my own faults, but I’m still a captain. Though the way I talk now, you wouldn’t guess. Ever since I fell on hard times, I’ve started saying ‘sir’ to everyone. It’s something people do when they’ve slipped down in the world.”
“That’s very true,” Alyosha said, smiling. “But do you say it by habit, or do you mean to?”

“I swear, it just happens! I never said ‘sir’ in my life, but when I lost everything, I started saying it. It’s like some higher power makes you. You seem interested in the way things are nowadays, but I don’t see why you’d be curious about me, living here where there’s no way to be a good host.”
“I came—about that incident.”
“What incident?” the captain interrupted impatiently.
“About your run-in with my brother, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Alyosha blurted out, a little awkward.
“Which run-in, sir? Don’t tell me you mean that one? The one about my ‘wisp of tow’?” He scooted even closer, so their knees touched. His lips pressed into a thin line.
“What’s that, ‘wisp of tow’?” Alyosha muttered.

“He’s here to complain about me, father!” came a voice Alyosha recognized—the schoolboy’s—from behind the curtain. “I bit his finger just now.” The curtain was pulled aside, and Alyosha saw the boy who had attacked him, lying on a bed made up on a bench and chair in the corner under the religious icons. The boy was wrapped in his coat and an old quilt. He was clearly sick, his eyes burning with fever. He looked at Alyosha without fear, as if he knew he couldn’t be touched at home.
“What! Did he bite your finger?” The captain jumped up. “Was it your finger he bit?”

“Yes. He was throwing stones with other boys. There were six against him alone. I went up to him, and he threw a stone at me—then another one at my head. I asked what I’d done to him, and he ran at me and bit my finger hard. I still don’t know why.”
“I’ll beat him, sir, right now—this minute!” the captain jumped up.
“But I’m not complaining! I just wanted to let you know... I don’t want him punished. Besides, he looks sick.”

“You think I’d beat him? That I’d take my Ilusha and hit him in front of you just to make you happy? Would you like me to do it right now, sir?” the captain suddenly turned to Alyosha, looking like he might attack. “Sorry about your finger, sir. But instead of hitting Ilusha, should I cut off my own four fingers here, right in front of you, to make you feel better? Four fingers ought to be enough for your revenge, right? You wouldn’t want the fifth too?” He stopped, his voice catching. His whole face was twitching and tense; he looked wild, almost desperate.

“I think I understand now,” Alyosha said softly and sadly, still sitting. “Your boy is a good boy—he loves his dad, so he attacked me because I’m the brother of the man who hurt you... Now I get it.” He thought about it. “But my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch feels sorry for what happened, I know he does. If he can, he’ll come to you—or better yet, meet you where it happened—and apologize in front of everyone, if you want.”
“So after pulling out my beard, he’ll just say sorry? And he thinks that’s enough to make it right, does he?”
“No, it’s not like that at all! He’ll do whatever you want, however you want.”
“So if I asked him to go down on his knees in that tavern—the Metropolis—or in the marketplace, he’d do it?”
“Yes, he’d even kneel down if you asked.”

“You’ve really gotten to me, sir. You’ve touched my heart—made me want to cry. I’m very aware of your brother’s generosity. Let me introduce my family: my two daughters and my son—my kids. If I die, who’d take care of them? And while I’m alive, who else could care for a wreck like me but them? That’s something God gives even to guys like me—someone to love you, even if you don’t deserve it.”
“That’s so true!” Alyosha exclaimed.
“Oh, stop acting like an idiot! Some stranger comes in and you embarrass us!” the girl by the window snapped at her father, full of scorn.
“Wait a second, Varvara!” her father replied, sounding stern but looking at her with approval. “That’s just the way she is,” he explained to Alyosha.

“Or rather, for her, in the feminine: only someone special could win her favor. But now, let me introduce you to my wife, Arina Petrovna. She’s disabled, forty-three years old, and can barely move. She comes from humble roots. Arina Petrovna, look presentable. This is Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Stand up, Alexey Fyodorovitch.” He grabbed Alyosha’s hand and, surprisingly strong, pulled him up. “You must stand to be introduced to a lady. This isn’t the Karamazov, mama, who... well, never mind, but his brother, who’s full of good qualities. Come, Arina Petrovna, come, mama, let him kiss your hand first.”
He kissed his wife’s hand respectfully—even tenderly. The girl at the window turned her back, clearly annoyed. The woman’s proud, searching face suddenly looked warm and welcoming.
“Good morning! Sit down, Mr. Tchernomazov,” she said.
“Karamazov, mama, Karamazov. We’re from a humble family,” the captain whispered again.

“Well, Karamazov, or whatever you say, but I always think Tchernomazov... Sit. Why did he make you get up? He calls me crippled, but I’m not—just my legs are swollen like barrels, and the rest of me is shriveled. I used to be fat, but now it’s like I swallowed a needle.”
“We’re from a humble family,” the captain muttered again.
“Oh, father, father!” the hunchback girl suddenly said, hiding her eyes in her handkerchief.
“Buffoon!” the girl at the window blurted out.

“Heard our news?” the mother said, pointing at her daughters. “It’s like clouds coming over; the clouds pass, and music returns. When we traveled with the army, we had lots of guests. I’m not comparing you—everyone has their own taste. The deacon’s wife used to say, ‘Alexandr Alexandrovitch is a man with a noble heart, but Nastasya Petrovna is from the devil’s own family.’ ‘That’s your opinion,’ I told her, ‘but you’re a little spitfire.’ ‘And you need to be kept in your place,’ she said. ‘You black sword,’ I said, ‘who made you my teacher?’ ‘But my breath is fresh, and yours isn’t,’ she said. ‘Ask the officers if my breath is bad.’ Ever since then, I’ve thought about it. Not long ago, a general came by for Easter, and I asked him, ‘Your Excellency, can a lady’s breath really be bad?’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘you should open the window or door, the air isn’t fresh here.’ And everyone keeps on about it! What’s my breath to them? Dead people smell worse! ‘I won’t spoil the air,’ I said. ‘I’ll just get my slippers and leave.’ My darlings, don’t blame your mother! Nikolay Ilyitch, why can’t I make you happy? Only Ilusha comes home from school and loves me. Yesterday he brought me an apple. Forgive your own mother—a poor, lonely woman! Why does my breath bother you all?”
The poor, confused woman broke down in tears. The captain rushed to her side.

“Mama, mama, my dear, stop! You’re not alone. Everyone loves you, everyone adores you.” He kissed her hands again and gently stroked her face, wiping away her tears with a napkin. Alyosha thought he saw tears in the captain’s eyes, too. “See? Do you hear?” he turned to Alyosha, almost angrily, pointing at his wife.
“I see and hear,” Alyosha muttered.
“Father, father, how can you—when he’s here! Leave him alone!” cried the boy, sitting up in bed and glaring at his father with bright, feverish eyes.
“Stop your silly acting and showing off, it never leads anywhere!” Varvara shouted, stomping her foot angrily.

“You’re right to be angry this time, Varvara, and I’ll make it up to you. Come on, Alexey Fyodorovitch, put on your cap, and I’ll put on mine. We’ll go out. I want to talk to you seriously, but not in front of everyone. That girl there is Nina, my daughter—I forgot to introduce her. She’s like an angel who came down to earth... if you can understand.”
“Look, he’s shaking like he’s having a fit!” Varvara went on, annoyed.
“And she,” he pointed to Varvara, “who just called me a fool and stamped her foot, she’s an angel, too—and she has every right to call me that. Come on, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let’s finish up.”
Grabbing Alyosha’s hand, the captain pulled him out of the room and into the street.
“The air out here is fresh, but it’s nothing like that in my apartment. Let’s walk slowly, sir. I’m glad you’re interested in my story.”
“I actually have something really important to talk to you about too,” Alyosha (Alexey) said. “But I’m not sure how to start.”

“You must have a reason to talk to me,” the captain replied. “You wouldn’t just stop by for nothing. Unless you came to complain about the boy, which doesn’t seem likely. And speaking of him—I couldn’t explain before, but let me tell you what happened. My beard was thicker a week ago—the kids call it ‘tow,’ that’s their nickname for it. Anyway, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Dmitri) grabbed me by my beard for no reason, he was furious and just ran into me. He pulled me out of the tavern into the market. School had just let out, and Ilusha was with the other kids. As soon as Ilusha saw me, he ran up shouting, ‘Father! Father!’ He hugged me, tried to pull me away, and begged Dmitri, ‘Let go! Let go! That’s my father! Forgive him!’ He actually said, ‘forgive him.’ He grabbed Dmitri’s hand and kissed it. I’ll never forget his face at that moment, never.”
“I promise you,” Alyosha said passionately, “my brother will apologize—he’ll get down on his knees in the middle of the market if he has to. I’ll make sure of it, or he’s not my brother!”

“So it’s just your idea? Not his? You should have said so. Still, let me tell you what your brother actually did. He let go of me and said, ‘You’re an officer and so am I. If you want to challenge me, find a second and send me your challenge. I’ll answer it, even if you are a scoundrel!’ That was his ‘chivalry.’ I left with Ilusha, and that moment will be burned into Ilusha’s memory forever. But we’re not noblemen—we can’t pretend we are. You saw our house: three women—one is crippled and not right in the head, another is hunchbacked, and the third is too smart for her own good—a student who wants to go to Petersburg to fight for women’s rights. Ilusha’s only nine. I’m all they have, and if I die, what will become of them? Or if I challenge your brother and he only injures me, I’ll be useless and still need to eat. Who will feed us then? Should I make Ilusha beg in the streets? That’s what a duel would mean. It’s nonsense, nothing more.”
“He’ll apologize—he’ll bow at your feet in the middle of the market!” Alyosha repeated, his eyes shining.

“I thought about taking him to court,” the captain continued, “but what would I get? And then Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka) called me and shouted, ‘Don’t even think about it! If you do, I’ll tell everyone he beat you for being dishonest, and then you’ll be the one in trouble!’ I swear to God, I only did what she and Fyodor Pavlovitch told me. ‘And if you go forward, I’ll fire you, and you’ll never get another penny from me. I’ll talk to my merchant’—her old man—‘and he’ll fire you too!’ If he does, what can I do? Those two are all I’ve got. Fyodor Pavlovitch has stopped giving me work for another reason, and he wants to use some papers I signed to sue me. So I kept quiet, and you’ve seen how we live. But tell me: did Ilusha hurt your finger badly? I didn’t want to talk about it in front of everyone earlier.”

“Yes, it hurt a lot, and he was really angry. He was taking revenge on me as a Karamazov, I can see that now. But you should have seen him throwing rocks at the other boys! It’s dangerous. Someone could get seriously hurt.”
“That’s just what happened. He got hit by a stone today himself. Not on the head, but in the chest, just above his heart. He came home crying and now he’s sick.”
“And you know he starts the fights. He’s mad at them because of what happened to you. They say he stabbed a boy named Krassotkin with a penknife not long ago.”
“I’ve heard about that. It’s serious. Krassotkin’s family is important here, we might hear more about it.”
“I think you shouldn’t send him to school for a while,” Alyosha urged. “Let him calm down and get over his anger.”

“Anger! That’s exactly it. He’s just a little kid, but his anger is huge. You don’t know everything, sir. Ever since that happened, the other boys have teased him about my ‘tow’ beard. Schoolboys can be cruel—alone they’re angels, but together, they’re merciless. Their teasing brought out Ilusha’s spirit. A weaker boy would have just been ashamed of his father, but Ilusha stood up for me, for truth and justice. Only God knows what he felt when he kissed your brother’s hand and begged for forgiveness—that pain, only he and I know. Poor kids like us, we understand justice even at nine years old. How could the rich know? They never have to deal with this. That moment, when he kissed your brother’s hand, Ilusha understood what justice really is. It crushed him, sir.” The captain’s voice grew wild, and he smacked his right fist into his left palm as if to show how hard the truth hit Ilusha. “That same day, he got a fever and was delirious all night. He barely spoke to me, but he kept watching me from the corner of his eye, pretending to study. The next day I got drunk to forget my problems—yes, I admit it—and I barely remember anything. His mother started crying too—I love her very much. I spent my last coins just trying to forget. Don’t look down on me for that, sir; in Russia, the best men are often the biggest drinkers. I lay down and forgot everything about Ilusha, even though the boys were making fun of him all day at school. ‘Wisp of tow,’ they shouted, ‘your father was dragged out of the tavern by his beard, and you begged for forgiveness.’”

“On the third day, when Ilusha came home from school, he looked pale and miserable. I asked what was wrong, but he wouldn’t answer. There’s no way to talk in our house without his mother and sisters getting involved. The girls had already heard about everything the first day. Varvara started snapping, ‘You fools, can you ever act sensibly?’ I just agreed with her to keep the peace. That night, I took Ilusha for a walk, like we do every evening—always the same route, from our gate to the big stone down the road, by the field. It’s a lonely, beautiful place. We walked hand in hand. His fingers are always so thin and cold—he has chest problems, you know. ‘Father,’ he said. ‘What?’ I replied. His eyes were flashing. ‘Father, how could he treat you like that?’ ‘It’s done, Ilusha,’ I said. ‘Don’t forgive him, Father! Don’t forgive him! The kids at school say he paid you ten roubles for it.’ ‘No, Ilusha,’ I told him, ‘I would never take money for that.’ Then he started shaking, grabbed my hand, and kissed it again. ‘Father, challenge him to a duel! They say you’re a coward for not doing it, and that you took his money.’ ‘I can’t challenge him, Ilusha,’ I explained, and told him what I just told you. He listened. ‘Then don’t forgive him, Father! When I grow up, I’ll challenge him myself and kill him!’ His eyes were shining. Of course, as his father, I had to say something: ‘It’s a sin to kill, even in a duel.’ ‘Then when I grow up, I’ll knock him down, take away his sword, stand over him and say, “I could kill you, but I forgive you instead!”’ You see how his little mind was working, planning revenge all day and night.”

“But then he started coming home beaten up. I found out two days ago, and you’re right—I won’t send him back to that school. He’s been fighting the whole class by himself, filled with anger. I was worried about him, so we went for another walk. ‘Father, are rich people the strongest in the world?’ he asked. ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘no one’s stronger than the rich.’ ‘I’ll get rich then,’ he said. ‘I’ll become an officer and conquer everyone. The Tsar will reward me, and then no one will dare—’ Then he stopped, but his lips were still trembling. ‘Father, this is a terrible town.’ ‘Yes, Ilusha, it’s not a nice town.’ ‘Let’s move to a better one, where people don’t know us.’ ‘We will, Ilusha. I just need to save up.’ I was glad to distract him, and we started dreaming about moving, buying a horse and cart. ‘We’ll put your mother and sisters inside, cover them up, and walk beside them. You’ll get a turn riding now and then, but we have to take care of the horse. That’s how we’ll go.’ He loved the idea, especially about driving the horse. Russian boys love horses. We talked a long time. Thank God, he felt better for a while.”

“That was two nights ago, but last night everything changed. He went to school in the morning and came back looking even more upset. That evening I took him out for a walk again, but he wouldn’t talk. The wind was blowing, the sun had gone, and it felt like autumn. We were both sad. ‘So, my boy,’ I said, ‘should we get ready for our big trip?’ I hoped to remind him of our plans, but he didn’t answer; his fingers just trembled in my hand. I knew something new was wrong. When we reached the stone, I sat down. There were kites flying everywhere—thirty or more. I said, ‘Look, Ilusha, it’s time to fix our own kite. Where did you put it?’ He didn’t answer, just turned away. Suddenly, a gust of wind blew up the sand, and he threw his arms around my neck, holding on tight. You know how kids try to be tough, but when they break down, they cry so hard?
