He soaked my face with his tears, sobbing and shaking, clinging to me. ‘Father, dear father, how he insulted you!’ he kept crying. I cried too. We just sat there, holding each other. ‘Ilusha, my dear boy,’ I said. No one saw us but God. You should thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. But I won’t beat my son just to please you.”

The captain was back to his usual joking, resentful tone, but Alyosha could tell he actually trusted him. He wouldn’t have shared any of this with just anyone. This made Alyosha feel encouraged, even though he was nearly in tears.
“I’d really like to be friends with your boy!” Alyosha burst out. “If you could arrange it—”
“Of course, sir,” the captain muttered.

“Now, listen to something else,” Alyosha said, changing the subject. “I have a message for you. My brother Dmitri insulted his fiancée, too—a kind, good-hearted girl you’ve probably heard of. I have to tell you about what happened, because after hearing about your situation and what Dmitri did to you, she immediately sent me to help you—just now. But this help is only from her, not from Dmitri, or from me, or from anyone else—just her. She wants you to take this money from her, like from a sister to a brother in trouble. You’re both hurt by the same person. She thought of you only after she’d been hurt in the same cruel way. She told me to beg you to take these two hundred roubles from her, as from a sister. No one else will know, so no one can gossip about it. Here’s the money, and I swear you must take it, unless you want to believe everyone is your enemy! There are good people in the world. You have a big heart—you must see that,” Alyosha said, holding out two brand-new hundred-rouble notes.
They were standing by the big stone near the fence, alone. The captain stared at the money in disbelief. He hadn’t expected anything like this—not help, and definitely not such a big sum.
He took the notes and for a moment couldn’t even speak. His face changed completely.
“For me? That much—two hundred roubles? Good heavens! I haven’t seen so much money in four years! And she says she’s like a sister… Is this really true?”
“I swear everything I’ve told you is true,” Alyosha said.
The captain’s face turned bright red.

“Listen, my friend. If I take it, will you think I’m a scoundrel? Alexey Fyodorovitch, would you look down on me? No, seriously, listen. You’re asking me to take it, saying it’s from a sister, but deep down, won’t you still think less of me?”
“No, never! I swear it on my life! And no one will know but you, me, her, and one other lady—her close friend.”

“Forget the other lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, you have to understand what these two hundred roubles mean to me right now.” The captain was starting to sound almost wild with excitement. He was speaking so fast, as if he was afraid someone would stop him before he could finish.

“Besides being honestly earned from a ‘sister’ who deserves respect—do you know what this means? Now I can take care of mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel. Doctor Herzenstube came to see them out of kindness. He examined them for a whole hour and couldn’t figure it out, but he prescribed mineral water from the drugstore, said it would help, and ordered baths with medicine. The water costs thirty copecks a bottle—she’ll need forty bottles! I put the prescription under the icons, and there it sits. He said Nina needs hot baths, morning and night, but how can we do that in our place—no servants, no bath, barely any water? Nina is in pain all night, but she never complains so she won’t wake us up. We eat whatever we can get, and she only takes the leftovers, like she’s not worth eating. She thinks she’s a burden. We wait on her, but she hates it. She thinks she’s useless, but really, she keeps us all going with her gentle spirit. Without her, our home would be unbearable. Even Varvara is softer because of her. Don’t judge Varvara—she’s an angel too, she’s had a hard time. She came for the summer with sixteen roubles she earned teaching, planning to go back to Petersburg, but we spent her money just to survive, so now she can’t go back. She works like a slave for us, doing everything—cooking, cleaning, caring for mamma, who’s moody and not right in the head. Now, with this money, I can get a servant, buy medicine, send my student daughter to Petersburg, buy beef, feed everyone properly. It’s like a dream!”
Alyosha was thrilled that he could bring so much happiness, and that the captain was willing to accept it.

“Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait,” the captain said, talking even faster, caught up in a new fantasy. “Maybe Ilusha and I will really do what we dreamed of. We’ll buy a horse and cart—a black horse, he insists—and set off, just like we planned. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K. province, and I’ve heard he’d give me a job as a clerk if I went. So maybe I could. I’d put mamma and Nina in the cart, Ilusha would drive, and I’d walk. If I could just collect one debt that’s owed to me, I’d have enough to do it all!”

“You’d have enough!” Alyosha said happily. “Katerina Ivanovna will send you more if you need it. I have money too—take what you want, like from a brother or friend. You can pay it back later—(You’ll get rich, you’ll get rich!) And moving to another province is the best idea, especially for Ilusha. Go before winter, before it gets cold. Write to us when you get there, and we’ll always be like brothers. It’s not just a dream!”

Alyosha wanted to hug him, he was so happy. But when he looked at the captain, he stopped. The man was standing stiffly, neck out, lips trembling, pale and wild-eyed, like he was trying to say something but couldn’t get the words out. It was creepy.
“What’s wrong?” Alyosha asked, worried.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch... I... you...” the captain stammered, staring at him with a wild, desperate look, a weird smile on his lips. “I... you, sir... want to see a trick?” he whispered suddenly, his voice sure and quick.
“What trick?”
“A pretty trick,” the captain whispered, his mouth twisting to one side, one eye squinting, still staring at Alyosha.
“What’s wrong? What trick?” Alyosha cried, now really scared.

“Look!” the captain suddenly yelled. He held up the two banknotes he’d been clutching, then crumpled them up in his fist. “See? See?” he shouted, pale and furious. Suddenly, he threw the crushed notes down onto the sand. “Look there!” he yelled again, pointing.
Then, wild with anger, he started stomping on the money, gasping and shouting:
“That’s what I think of your money! That’s what I think of your money! That’s what I think of your money!”
Suddenly, he jumped back and stood tall in front of Alyosha, his whole body full of pride.

“Tell the people who sent you that the ‘wisp of tow’ doesn’t sell his honor!” he cried, raising his arm high. Then he turned and started to run away. But after five steps, he spun around and blew a kiss to Alyosha. He ran a few more steps, then turned again—this time with tears streaming down his face. In a choked, sobbing voice, he cried:
“What would I tell my son if I took money from you for our shame?”

He ran off without looking back. Alyosha watched him go, deeply upset. He realized that the captain hadn’t decided to throw away the money until the very last second. Alyosha knew he wouldn’t come back, and he wouldn’t call after him—he understood why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were dirty and crumpled from being stomped on, but otherwise fine, still crackling like new when he smoothed them out. He folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on how her mission had gone.

Madame Hohlakov was the first to greet Alyosha when he arrived. She looked nervous and upset—something big had happened. Katerina Ivanovna had stopped her hysterics only to faint, and then she got so weak that she was lying there with her eyes rolled back, talking nonsense. Now she had a high fever. They had sent for Dr. Herzenstube and the aunts. The aunts had already arrived, but Herzenstube hadn’t come yet. Everyone was waiting in Katerina Ivanovna’s room while she lay there unconscious. Madame Hohlakov was terrified that it might turn into brain fever.

Madame Hohlakov looked seriously worried. “This is serious, very serious,” she kept saying, acting like nothing in her life before had ever truly been serious. Alyosha listened anxiously and started to tell her what he had been through, but she cut him off right away. She didn’t have time to listen and asked him instead to go sit with Lise and wait for her there.

“Lise,” she whispered in Alyosha’s ear, “Lise really surprised me just now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch. She touched my heart, so I forgive her for everything. Just imagine, as soon as you left, she started feeling genuinely sorry for laughing at you today and yesterday—even though she was really just joking. She was so upset she was almost in tears, which amazed me. She’s never been that sorry for laughing at me; she usually just jokes about it. And she laughs at me all the time! But this time she meant it. She really cares what you think, Alexey Fyodorovitch, so please don’t be upset or take offense at her. I never get angry with her; she’s such a clever girl. Can you believe it? She just told me that you were her ‘best childhood friend’—just think of that—her very best! And what about me? Lise has strong feelings and memories, and sometimes she says these surprising, poetic things out of nowhere. Like, the other day she talked about a pine tree that used to stand in the garden when she was little—probably it’s still there, so she shouldn’t talk about it in the past. Pine trees don’t change fast, Alexey Fyodorovitch, not like people. She said, ‘Mama, I remember this pine tree like in a dream,’ but she said something really original about it that I can’t repeat or even remember now. Well, goodbye! I’m so anxious I think I might lose my mind. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ve lost my mind twice before in my life. Go to Lise and cheer her up, as you always do so well. Lise!” she called at her daughter’s door, “I’ve brought you Alexey Fyodorovitch, whom you insulted so much. He’s not angry at all, I promise; he’s just surprised you could even think that.”
“Thanks, Mama. Come in, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

Alyosha walked in. Lise looked embarrassed and blushed bright red. She was clearly ashamed about something, and, like people usually do in those situations, she immediately started talking about something else, as if it was the most interesting thing in the world.

“Mama just told me all about the two hundred roubles, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and how you took them to that poor officer ... and she told me the whole terrible story about how he was insulted ... you know, even though Mama gets things mixed up and jumps from one topic to another ... I actually cried when I heard it. Well, did you give him the money? And how is that poor man doing?”

“Actually, I didn’t give it to him, and it’s a long story,” said Alyosha, sounding as if he could only think about how sorry he was that he failed. But Lise could tell he was also avoiding the topic, just like she was.

Alyosha sat at the table and began to tell his story. As soon as he started, his embarrassment faded, and Lise was completely drawn in. He spoke with deep emotion, still under the effect of everything that had just happened, and explained everything in detail. Back in Moscow, he used to love telling Lise about things that happened to him, books he read, or memories from childhood. Sometimes they made up stories together—usually funny or happy ones. Now, for a moment, it felt like they were back in those old days, two years ago. Lise was deeply moved by his story. When Alyosha described Ilusha so warmly, and then explained how the poor man stomped on the money, Lise couldn’t help but clasp her hands and cry out:
“So you didn’t give him the money! You let him run off! Oh no, you should have chased after him!”
“No, Lise; it’s better that I didn’t go after him,” replied Alyosha, getting up and pacing around the room thoughtfully.
“How is it better? Now they have no food, and everything is hopeless for them, isn’t it?”

“Not hopeless—the two hundred roubles will still get to them. He’ll take the money tomorrow. I’m sure of it,” said Alyosha, walking back and forth, thinking hard. “You see, Lise,” he stopped and faced her, “I made a mistake, but even that is for the best.”
“What mistake? And why is it for the best?”

“I’ll explain. He’s a weak, nervous man who’s suffered a lot, but he’s very kind. I keep wondering why he got so offended all of a sudden, because right up to the last moment, he didn’t seem like he’d do something so dramatic as stomp on the money. But thinking about it, there was a lot that must have hurt his pride—it couldn’t have gone any other way for someone like him. First, he was embarrassed about how happy he was to get the money in front of me, and that he didn’t hide it. If he had acted less excited, or pretended to have mixed feelings like people usually do, he could have accepted it. But he was so genuinely thrilled, and that made it worse for him. Lise, he’s a good and honest man—that’s actually what made it so painful for him. As he talked, his voice was weak and shaky, and he spoke really fast, even laughing suddenly—or maybe he was crying, I think he was so happy he was crying. He talked about his daughters, and about jobs he might get in another town… but after opening up like that, he felt ashamed for showing me his feelings, so he started hating me right away. He’s one of those very sensitive people. What really upset him was that he accepted me as a friend too quickly. At first he was defensive, but as soon as he saw the money he kept hugging me and touching my hands. That must have been humiliating for him. And then I made a big mistake. I suddenly said that if he needed more money to move, we would give it to him—even from my own money. That really hit him. He thought, ‘Why does he think he can help me like this?’ You see, Lise, it’s hard for someone who’s been mistreated to have others act like his saviors. Father Zossima told me that once. I don’t know how to say it, but I’ve seen it too, and felt it myself. And the saddest thing is, even though he didn’t know he’d stomp on the money until the last second, I think he kind of sensed it might happen. That’s why he was so worked up. And even though it’s terrible, it’s actually for the best. In fact, I think nothing better could have happened.”
“Why? Why could nothing better have happened?” Lise asked, sounding amazed.

“Because if he’d taken the money, an hour after getting home he would have been crying out of shame. He might have come to me first thing tomorrow, thrown the money at me, and stomped on it just like he did today. But now he’s gone home proud and triumphant—even if he knows he’s ‘ruined himself.’ So now it’ll be much easier to get him to accept the money tomorrow, because he’s already claimed his honor and thrown the money away. He couldn’t have known I’d bring it to him again, but he’s still desperately in need. Tonight, he’ll be thinking about how much he’s lost, and by tomorrow morning he might even come ask me for forgiveness. That’s when I’ll show up and say, ‘You’re a proud man, you proved it, but now please take the money and forgive us!’ And he’ll take it!”
Alyosha was so happy as he said, “And then he’ll take it!” that Lise clapped her hands in delight.
“Oh, that’s true! I get it now. Alyosha, how do you know all this? You’re so young but you understand people’s hearts... I never would have figured that out.”
“The important thing now is to make him feel like he’s our equal, even though he’s taking money from us,” Alyosha went on, excited. “Actually, not just equal, but even higher than us.”
“‘Even higher’—that’s a nice way to say it, Alexey Fyodorovitch! But go on, go on!”
“You mean that’s not a real expression, ‘on a higher footing’? But it doesn’t matter, because—”

“Oh, no, it doesn’t matter at all. I’m sorry, Alyosha, really… You know, I hardly respected you until now—well, I did, but only as an equal. Now I’ll respect you even more. Please don’t be upset at my teasing,” she added, with real feeling. “I’m silly and childish, but you! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, isn’t there something kind of disrespectful in what we’re doing—analyzing him like this, as if we know better than he does, deciding he’ll definitely take the money?”

“No, Lise, it’s not disrespect,” Alyosha answered, as if he had already thought about it. “I was thinking about that on the way here. How could it be disrespect when we’re just like him? We’re no better. If we were in his place, we’d be the same. I don’t know about you, Lise, but I think my soul is pretty petty sometimes, while his is actually sensitive and good. No, I don’t look down on him. You know, my elder once told me to care for most people the way you would for children, and some like you would for sick people in a hospital.”
“Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let’s care for people like we would for the sick!”
“Let’s do that, Lise; I’m ready to try. Though honestly, I’m not always that patient myself. Sometimes I get annoyed or don’t notice things. You’re different.”
“Oh, I don’t believe that! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’m so happy!”
“I’m glad to hear it, Lise.”

“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you’re so good, but sometimes you’re kind of stiff… but then you’re really not. Go to the door, open it quietly, and see if Mama is listening,” Lise said in a nervous, hurried whisper.
Alyosha went, opened the door, and came back to report that nobody was listening.

“Come here, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Lise continued, blushing even more. “Give me your hand—okay, good. I have to confess something big: I didn’t write to you yesterday as a joke—it was serious,” and she covered her eyes with her hand, clearly embarrassed.
Suddenly she grabbed his hand and kissed it three times in a rush.
“Oh, Lise, that’s wonderful!” Alyosha exclaimed happily. “You know, I was absolutely sure you meant it.”
“Sure? Really?” She let go of his hand a little, but kept holding onto it, blushing and laughing a little. “I kiss your hand and you say, ‘What a good thing!’”
But her teasing wasn’t fair. Alyosha was just as moved as she was.
“I wish I could always make you happy, Lise, but I don’t really know how,” he mumbled, blushing, too.
“Alyosha, you’re so cold and awkward. See? He’s already decided to marry me—he’s sure I was serious. What a thing to say! That’s kind of rude, you know.”
“Why, was it wrong for me to be sure?” Alyosha asked, suddenly laughing.
“No, Alyosha, it was exactly right,” Lise said, looking at him with real affection and happiness.
Alyosha stood there, holding her hand. Then, all of a sudden, he bent down and kissed her on the lips.
“What are you doing?” Lise cried out. Alyosha was horribly embarrassed.
“Oh, sorry, maybe I shouldn’t have… Maybe I’m just stupid… You said I was cold, so I kissed you… But I can see it was dumb.”
Lise laughed and hid her face in her hands. “And in that outfit!” she said between giggles. But then she stopped laughing and suddenly looked serious, almost strict.

“Alyosha, we need to wait with the kissing. We’re not ready for that yet, and there’s a long time ahead of us,” she finished quickly. “Tell me instead, why would someone as smart and thoughtful as you choose a silly, sick girl like me? Oh, Alyosha, I’m so happy, but I don’t deserve you at all.”

“You do, Lise. I’ll be leaving the monastery for good in a few days. If I’m going to live in the world, I’ll have to get married, and he told me I should. Who could I marry better than you—and who else would even want me? I’ve been thinking about this. First, you’ve known me since we were kids, and you have so many good qualities I don’t have. You’re more cheerful than me, and you’re more innocent. I’ve already seen a lot of things… You don’t know, but I’m still a Karamazov. It doesn’t matter if you laugh and joke, even about me. Go ahead, I’m glad you do. You laugh like a child, but you think like someone who’s suffered a lot.”
“Like someone who’s suffered? How?”

“Yes, Lise, that question you just asked—about whether we were disrespectful by analyzing that poor man—that’s the kind of question someone who suffers asks. You see, I don’t know how to put it, but anyone who thinks about things like that is capable of deep feeling. You must have thought about a lot, even just sitting in your chair.”

“Alyosha, give me your hand. Why are you pulling it away?” Lise whispered, her voice weak with happiness. “Listen, Alyosha. What will you wear when you leave the monastery? What kind of suit? Don’t laugh or get mad, it’s very important to me.”
“I haven’t thought about it, Lise; I’ll wear whatever you want me to.”
“I want you to wear a dark blue velvet coat, a white vest, and a soft gray felt hat… Tell me, did you really believe I didn’t care for you when I said my letter didn’t mean anything?”
“No, I didn’t believe it.”
“Oh, you impossible person, you’ll never change.”
“You see, I knew you cared about me, but I pretended to believe you didn’t so it would be easier for you.”

“That makes it worse! Worse and better at the same time! Alyosha, I like you so much. Just before you came this morning, I tested my luck. I decided I’d ask for my letter, and if you calmly took it out and handed it to me (like I expected you would) it would mean you didn’t love me at all, that you felt nothing, and I’d be ruined. But you left the letter at home, and that made me happy. You left it behind on purpose so you wouldn’t have to give it back, because you knew I’d ask for it—right? Wasn’t that it?”
“Oh, Lise, not at all. I actually have the letter with me, right here in my pocket. Here it is.”
Alyosha pulled out the letter, laughing, and showed it to her from a distance.
“But I’m not giving it back. You can just look at it from here.”
“So you lied? You—a monk—lied?”

“I lied if you want to call it that,” Alyosha laughed, too. “I lied so I wouldn’t have to give you back the letter. It’s very precious to me,” he added, suddenly serious and blushing again. “It always will be, and I won’t give it to anyone!”
Lise looked at him with happiness. “Alyosha,” she whispered again, “look at the door. Is Mama listening?”
“Okay, Lise, I’ll look. But wouldn’t it be better not to? Why suspect your mother of something like that?”
“What’s so bad about it? If she wants to spy on her own daughter, that’s her right, not something mean!” Lise said, getting worked up. “If I ever have a daughter like me, I’ll definitely spy on her!”
“Really, Lise? That’s not right.”

“Oh, come on! What does meanness have to do with it? If she was listening to some boring conversation, it would be mean, but when her daughter is alone with a young man… Listen, Alyosha, you know I’m going to spy on you when we’re married, and I’ll open and read all your letters, so get used to it.”
“Well, if you say so…” Alyosha muttered, “but it’s still not right.”
“Oh, so judgmental! Alyosha, let’s not fight on our very first day. I’ll just tell you the truth. Of course, it’s wrong to spy, and you’re right and I’m not, but I’ll spy on you anyway.”
“Go ahead; you won’t find anything,” Alyosha laughed.
“And, Alyosha, will you let me have my way? We should decide that, too.”
“I’d be happy to, Lise, and I’m sure I will—except for the really important things. Even if you disagree, I’ll do what I have to in the most important matters.”

“That’s good; but I’ll tell you, I’m ready to give in to you not just in the most important things, but in everything. I could promise right now—to always give in, for my whole life!” Lise said with excitement. “And I’ll do it gladly! What’s more, I’ll swear never to spy on you, never to read your letters. Because you’re right, and I’m not. And even though I’ll be really tempted, I know I won’t do it if you think it’s dishonorable. You’re my conscience now… But, Alexey Fyodorovitch, why have you been so sad lately—yesterday and today? I know you have a lot of worries, but I feel like there’s something else, some secret sadness.”
“Yes, Lise, I have a secret sorrow, too,” Alyosha said sadly. “I can see you really love me, since you noticed.”
“What’s hurting you? Can you tell me?” Lise asked softly.
“I’ll tell you later, Lise—another time,” Alyosha said, looking uncomfortable. “You might not understand right now—and I might not be able to explain.”
“I know your brothers and your father are upsetting you, too.”
“Yes, my brothers, too,” Alyosha replied, thinking deeply.
“I don’t like your brother Ivan, Alyosha,” Lise said suddenly.
Alyosha was surprised by this, but didn’t answer.

“My brothers are destroying themselves,” he continued, “and my father too. And they’re hurting other people along the way. Father Païssy called it ‘the wild Karamazov energy’—a kind of raw, out-of-control force. I don’t even know if God’s spirit is guiding them. I just know that I’m a Karamazov, too… Me, a monk! Am I really a monk, Lise? You said I was.”
“Yes, I did.”
“And maybe I don’t even believe in God.”

“You don’t believe? What’s wrong?” Lise asked quietly and gently. But Alyosha didn’t answer. There was something too private and painful in what he’d just said, maybe even he didn’t understand it fully, but it was eating at him.

“And now, on top of everything, my friend—the best man I know—is dying, leaving this world! If you knew, Lise, how close I feel to him in my soul! After he’s gone, I’ll be alone… But I’ll come to you, Lise… We’ll be together in the future.”
“Yes, together! From now on, always together, our whole lives! Listen, kiss me, I give you permission.”
Alyosha kissed her.

“All right, now go. God be with you!” And she made the sign of the cross over him. “Hurry back to him while he’s still alive. I see I’ve kept you too long. I’ll pray for him and for you today. Alyosha, we’re going to be happy! Aren’t we? Will we be happy?”
“I believe we will, Lise.”

Alyosha decided it was better not to go in and see Madame Hohlakov, and was about to leave the house without saying goodbye. But as soon as he opened the door, he ran right into Madame Hohlakov. From her very first words, Alyosha could tell she’d been waiting for him on purpose.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, this is terrible. It’s all childish nonsense and ridiculous. I trust you’re not actually thinking—No, it’s just foolishness, all of it!” she said, launching at him right away.
“Just don’t tell her that,” Alyosha replied, “or she’ll be upset, and that would be bad for her right now.”
“Wise advice from a wise young man. Am I to understand you only agreed with her because you felt sorry for her being an invalid, and didn’t want to upset her by disagreeing?”
“No, not at all. I meant everything I said,” Alyosha insisted.
“It’s impossible to be serious about this, it’s just ridiculous. First of all, I’ll never let you visit us again, and I’ll take her away, you can count on that.”
“But why?” asked Alyosha. “It’s so far away. We might have to wait a year and a half.”

“Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that’s true, and in a year and a half you’ll have time to fight and break up a thousand times over. But I’m so upset! Even though it’s childish nonsense, it’s a big shock for me. I feel like Famusov in the last scene of ‘Woe from Wit.’ You’re Chatsky, she’s Sofia, and—can you believe it—I ran down the stairs to meet you, just like that scene. I heard everything; I almost fainted. So this explains her horrible night and her recent hysterics! It means love for her, but death for me as her mother. I might as well go to my grave now. And more seriously, what’s this letter she wrote? Let me see it right now, immediately!”
“No, that’s not necessary. Tell me, how is Katerina Ivanovna now? I need to know.”

“She’s still delirious, hasn’t woken up. The aunts are here, but all they do is sigh and act important. Herzenstube came, and he was so worried I thought he’d need a doctor himself. I had him taken home in my carriage. And on top of all that, there’s you and this letter! It’s true, nothing can happen for a year and a half. For the love of everything holy, for the sake of your dying elder, show me that letter, Alexey Fy

Alyosha knew he didn't have much time. Even while he was saying goodbye to Lise, he realized he had to come up with some way to find his brother Dmitri, who was clearly avoiding him. It was getting late—almost three o'clock. Every part of Alyosha wanted to return to the monastery to be with the dying Father Zossima, but seeing Dmitri felt even more important right now. With every hour, Alyosha felt more certain that something terrible was about to happen. He didn't know exactly what disaster was coming, or what he would say to Dmitri when it did. “Even if I miss being with my beloved elder when he dies, at least I won’t have to regret all my life that I could have stopped something bad and didn’t, just because I rushed home. If I do what I’m planning, I’ll be following his teachings.”

Alyosha decided to try to catch Dmitri by surprise. He’d climb over the fence, just like he did yesterday, sneak into the garden, and wait in the summer-house. If Dmitri wasn’t there, Alyosha wouldn’t let Foma or the women of the house know he was around; he’d just hide in the summer-house, even if it meant waiting until evening. If Dmitri was still watching for Grushenka like before, he’d probably come out to the summer-house. Alyosha didn’t think too much about the details—he just decided to go through with it, even if it meant not making it back to the monastery that day.

Everything went smoothly. Alyosha climbed over the fence at almost the same spot as before, and slipped into the summer-house without anyone seeing him. He didn’t want anyone to notice. The woman of the house, or Foma if he was there, might be loyal to Dmitri and follow his orders, so they could refuse to let Alyosha into the garden, or warn Dmitri that someone was looking for him.

The summer-house was empty. Alyosha sat down to wait. He looked around and noticed that the place felt much older and shabbier than it had yesterday. Even though the weather was just as nice, the summer-house seemed miserable now. There was a ring on the table—probably from someone spilling brandy the day before. His mind wandered with silly thoughts, like they always do when you’re stuck waiting and feeling tense. For example, he wondered why he sat in exactly the same spot as last time, instead of trying a different seat. After a while, the uncertainty and suspense made him feel really down. But he hadn’t been sitting there for more than fifteen minutes when he suddenly heard someone playing a guitar nearby. It sounded like people were sitting, or had just sat down, in the bushes less than twenty steps away. Alyosha suddenly remembered that when he left the summer-house yesterday, he noticed an old green bench among the bushes to the left, by the fence. The people must be sitting there now. But who were they?
Suddenly, a man’s voice started singing in a high, sugary voice, playing the guitar:

The singing stopped. The voice was definitely a servant’s, and the song sounded like something a servant would sing. Then a woman’s voice spoke up, trying to sound shy and sweet, but it was obviously put on:
“Why haven’t you visited us in so long, Pavel Fyodorovich? Why do you always look down on us?”

“Not at all,” a man’s voice replied politely, but with a proud tone, as if he was in control and the woman was the one making the move. “That must be Smerdyakov,” Alyosha thought, recognizing the voice. “And the woman must be the daughter of the house—the one who just came from Moscow, who wears that dress with a train and goes to Marfa for soup.”
“I really love poems of all kinds, as long as they rhyme,” the woman continued. “Why don’t you keep singing?”
The man started singing again:
“It was even better last time,” the woman said. “You sang ‘If my darling be in health’; it sounded sweeter. I guess you forgot today.”
“Poetry is nonsense,” Smerdyakov said sharply.
“Oh, I really like poetry,” said the woman.

“But when it comes to poetry, it’s just pointless,” Smerdyakov replied. “Think about it—who actually talks in rhymes? Even if the government made us all talk in rhyme, we wouldn’t have much to say, would we? Poetry is useless, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“You’re so smart! How did you get to understand things so deeply?” the woman said, sounding more and more flirty.

“I could've been even smarter. I could've learned a lot more, if my life hadn’t been so unlucky from the start. If someone insulted me about my background, I would have challenged him to a duel. In Moscow, people heard about me—thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch—and would tease me for being the son of a poor beggar with no father. Grigory Vassilyevitch thinks I shouldn’t complain about my birth, but honestly, I wish I’d never been born at all. People in the market, and even your mother, used to make fun of me for little things—like saying her hair was like a mat and she was just short of five feet, but using the word ‘wee bit’ instead of just ‘a little.’ She was trying to sound all emotional, like a peasant. But really, can a Russian peasant feel things the way an educated person does? He can’t, not really, not in his ignorance. Since I was a kid, I’ve hated that phrase ‘a wee bit’—it makes me so angry. I hate all of Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“If you’d been an army cadet or a young hussar, you wouldn’t say that. You’d grab your sword to defend Russia.”
“I don’t want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna. To be honest, I wish all soldiers were gone.”
“But if an enemy attacks, who will protect us?”

“We don’t need protection. Back in 1812, Napoleon invaded Russia, and honestly, it would have been better if he’d beaten us. A smarter country would have taken over a stupid one and made things better. We’d have had better laws and ways of living.”

“Are things really better in their country than here? I wouldn’t trade a certain stylish guy I know for three young Englishmen,” Marya Kondratyevna said in a soft, dreamy voice, probably giving him a flirty look.
“That’s up to you,” Smerdyakov replied.
“But you’re just like a foreigner—like a real gentleman from another country. I mean it, even though it makes me blush.”

“If you want to know, people here and there are just the same when it comes to being bad. They cheat too—only there the thieves wear fancy shoes, and here they roll in the dirt and don’t care. The Russian people need a good beating, just like Fyodor Pavlovitch said yesterday, even if he is crazy—and so are all his kids.”
“But you said yourself you really respect Ivan Fyodorovich.”

“He called me a stinking servant. He thinks I might act out. He’s wrong about that. If I had some money, I’d have left this place long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovich is worse than any servant in the way he acts, the way he thinks, and how poor he is. He can’t do anything, but everyone still respects him. I might just cook soup, but with some luck I could open a restaurant in Moscow—my cooking’s actually special, and only foreigners there can cook as well as I do. Dmitri Fyodorovich is broke, but if the richest count’s son challenged him, he’d fight him. But what makes him better than me? He’s dumber than I am. Look at all the money he’s wasted for nothing!”
“Duels must be amazing,” Marya Kondratyevna said suddenly.
“Why do you think so?”
“They must be scary and brave—especially when young officers shoot at each other over a girl. What a scene! Oh, if only girls could watch, I’d do anything to see one!”
“It sounds exciting when you’re shooting at someone, but when he’s aiming right at you, you probably feel pretty stupid. You’d want to run away, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“You wouldn’t actually run away, would you?” But Smerdyakov didn’t bother answering. After a moment, the guitar started up again, and he sang in the same high voice:

Then something unexpected happened: Alyosha suddenly sneezed. The two fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked toward them. He found Smerdyakov dressed up, wearing shiny boots, his hair slicked and maybe even curled. The guitar was lying on the bench. The woman was the daughter of the house, wearing a light blue dress with a two-yard-long train. She was young and might have been pretty if her face weren’t so round and covered in freckles.
“Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?” Alyosha asked, trying to sound calm.
Smerdyakov stood up slowly, and Marya Kondratyevna got up too.
“How should I know where Dmitri Fyodorovich is? I’m not his babysitter,” Smerdyakov answered coolly and smugly.
“I just wanted to know if you happened to know,” Alyosha explained.
“I don’t know where he is, and I don’t want to know.”
“But my brother told me you always keep him informed about what’s happening in the house, and you promised to let him know when Agrafena Alexandrovna comes.”
Smerdyakov gave him a long, calm look.
“And how did you get in this time, since the gate’s been locked for an hour?” he asked, staring at Alyosha.
“I came in from the back alley, over the fence, and straight to the summer-house. I hope you’ll forgive me,” he said to Marya Kondratyevna. “I was in a hurry to find my brother.”

“Oh, as if we’d be upset with you!” Marya Kondratyevna said, pleased by his apology. “Dmitri Fyodorovich comes to the summer-house that way all the time. We never know he’s here, but he’s sitting in the summer-house.”
“I really need to find him, or at least know where he is. Trust me, it’s for something very important.”
“He never tells us,” Marya Kondratyevna lisped.

“Even though I come here as a friend,” Smerdyakov spoke up again, “Dmitri Fyodorovich keeps bothering me with endless questions about his father—‘Any news? What’s happening in there? Who’s coming and going?’ He wants me to tell him more. He’s already threatened to kill me twice.”
“Threatened to kill you?” Alyosha said, surprised.

“Don’t you think he would, with that temper you saw yesterday? He said if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she stays the night, I’ll be the first to pay for it. I’m really scared of him, and if I weren’t even more scared of reporting him, I’d tell the police. Who knows what he might do!”
“He told him the other day, ‘I’ll crush you like spice in a mortar!’” Marya Kondratyevna added.
“Oh, if it’s just talk about pounding in a mortar, it’s probably just words,” Alyosha said. “If I could talk to him, I’d bring that up too.”

“Well, the only thing I can tell you,” Smerdyakov said, as if he’d decided to be more helpful, “is that I’m here as an old friend and neighbor, so of course I come by. But this morning, Ivan Fyodorovich sent me to your brother Dmitri’s place on Lake Street—not with a letter, just a message: he wanted Dmitri Fyodorovich to have dinner with him at the restaurant here in the market. I went, but Dmitri wasn’t home, even at eight in the morning. ‘He’s been here, but he’s gone now,’ is what his landlady said. It’s like they have some secret understanding. Maybe he’s at the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovich right now, because Ivan hasn’t been home for dinner, and Fyodor Pavlovitch ate alone an hour ago and then went to lie down. But please, I’m begging you—don’t tell anyone what I told you or mention me, or Dmitri would kill me for no reason.”
“Brother Ivan invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?” Alyosha repeated quickly.
“That’s right.”
“The Metropolis tavern in the market?”
“That’s the one.”
“That fits,” Alyosha said, now very excited. “Thank you, Smerdyakov. That’s really helpful. I’ll go there right away.”
“Don’t give me away,” Smerdyakov called after him.
“Don’t worry, I’ll just show up at the tavern like it’s a coincidence. You can relax.”
“Wait, I’ll open the gate for you,” called Marya Kondratyevna.
“No, it’s quicker this way—I’ll just climb the fence again.”

What he’d heard made Alyosha really anxious. He ran to the tavern. He couldn’t go inside wearing his monk’s robe, but he could at least ask at the door if his brothers were there and call them out. But just as he reached the tavern, a window opened and his brother Ivan called down to him.
“Alyosha, can you come up here? I’d really appreciate it.”
“Of course, but I’m not sure if I should in these clothes—”
“I’ve got a private room. Come up the steps; I’ll come down to meet you.”
A minute later, Alyosha was sitting next to his brother. Ivan was alone, eating dinner.

Ivan wasn’t in a private room, but behind a folding screen in the first room you entered, where a buffet lined the wall. Waiters rushed back and forth constantly. The only customer was an old retired soldier sipping tea in a corner. Even so, you could hear the normal racket from the other rooms in the tavern—people shouting for waiters, corks popping, billiard balls clacking, and the organ droning in the background. Alyosha (also called Alexey) knew Ivan didn’t usually come to this tavern—actually, he disliked taverns in general. So Alyosha figured Ivan must have come here only to meet Dmitri, like they’d planned. But Dmitri wasn’t there yet.
“Should I order you some fish, or soup, or something? You can’t just live on tea, right?” Ivan called out, sounding happy to see Alyosha. Ivan had already finished dinner and was drinking tea.
“I’ll take some soup, and then tea after. I’m hungry,” Alyosha said, grinning.
“And cherry jam? They have it here. Remember how you loved cherry jam when you were little?”
“You remember that? Yeah, I still like it—let’s get some jam too.”
Ivan called the waiter and ordered soup, jam, and tea.

“I remember everything about you, Alyosha. I remember you up until you were eleven—I was almost fifteen. There’s such a big difference between fifteen and eleven that brothers don’t really hang out together at those ages. I’m not even sure I was attached to you then. When I went off to Moscow, I didn’t think of you at all for years. Then, when you came to Moscow yourself, I think we only met once. Now I’ve been here over three months, and we’ve hardly talked. Tomorrow I’m leaving, and as I was sitting here thinking about how I could see you to say goodbye, you just happened to walk by.”
“So you really wanted to see me?”

“Definitely. I want us to finally get to know each other—and for you to know me. Then we can say goodbye. I think it’s always best to get to know someone right before you leave them. I’ve noticed the way you’ve been looking at me these past three months—you always look like you’re expecting something. Honestly, I couldn’t stand it. That’s why I’ve stayed away. But in the end, I started to respect you. The little man stands firm, I thought. And I’m not just joking. You really do stand firm, don’t you? I like people who stand by what they believe in, even if they’re little guys like you. After a while, your expectant look didn’t bother me anymore. In fact, I started to like it. You seem to love me, Alyosha. Why is that?”
“I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says you’re ‘a tomb.’ I say you’re a riddle. You’re still a mystery to me, but I think I figured something out about you this morning.”
“What’s that?” Ivan laughed.
“Promise you won’t get mad?” Alyosha laughed too.
“Well?”
“That you’re just like any other young guy of twenty-three. You’re young, fresh, and honestly, kind of naïve! Did I insult you terribly?”

“Not at all! Actually, that’s a funny coincidence,” Ivan said warmly, smiling. “Ever since that scene with her, I haven’t thought about anything except how green I am. And now, you bring it up like you read my mind. You know, I’ve been sitting here thinking: Even if I ever stopped believing in life, or lost faith in the woman I love, or thought everything in the world was just random, ugly chaos—even if I was crushed by how disappointing people can be—I’d still want to keep living. Once I’ve tasted life, I wouldn’t let go until I’d drunk it all. Maybe at thirty, I’ll finally put the cup down, even if I haven’t finished it, and just walk away—but until then, I know my youth will win out over every disappointment, every bit of disgust. I’ve wondered whether any kind of despair could kill this wild thirst for life in me, and I don’t think it can—not until I’m thirty, anyway. Some boring moralists (especially poets) say this thirst for life is a bad thing. And it’s true, the Karamazovs all have it—this hunger for life, no matter what. You probably have it, too. But why should it be bad? The force holding us to this world is still incredibly strong, Alyosha. I want to live, even if it doesn’t make sense. Even if I don’t believe in the order of the universe, I still love the sticky little leaves that come out in spring. I love the blue sky. I love some people, even if I don’t know why. I still value some great things people have done, even if I stopped truly believing in them a long time ago. Here comes your soup—eat it, it’s really good. They know how to make soup here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha. I’ll leave from here. And even though I know Europe is really just one big graveyard now, it’s a precious graveyard! Every stone there tells about how passionate and alive people used to be, how much they believed in what they were doing. When I get there, I know I’ll cry over those stones—not because I’m sad, but because I’ll be happy in that kind of emotion. I’ll soak my soul in it. I love sticky spring leaves, the blue sky—that’s it. It’s not about logic or reason—it’s loving with your insides, with your gut. You love the strength of being young. Do you get what I’m saying, Alyosha?” Ivan suddenly laughed.

“I understand it perfectly, Ivan. You said it so well—wanting to love with your insides, with your gut. I’m really glad you have this hunger for life,” Alyosha cried. “I think everyone should love life more than anything else.”
“Love life even more than its meaning?”

“Yes, absolutely. Love it, even if it doesn’t make sense—like you said, regardless of logic. That’s the only way you’ll ever understand the meaning of life. I’ve thought that for a long time. You’ve already done half the work, Ivan—you love life. Now you just have to do the second half, and you’ll be saved.”
“You’re trying to save me, but maybe I’m not lost! And what’s the second half?”
“You have to bring the dead back to life—maybe they’re not really dead after all. Come on, let’s have tea. I’m really glad we talked, Ivan.”
“I see you’re inspired. I love these kinds of declarations from beginners. You’re a steady guy, Alexey. Is it true you’re leaving the monastery?”
“Yes, my elder is sending me into the world.”

“So we’ll see each other in the real world, then. We’ll meet again before I’m thirty, when I’m supposed to start turning away from life’s cup. Father doesn’t want to give up his cup until he’s seventy—he even dreams of making it to eighty. He’s serious about it, even though he acts like a clown. He’s standing on solid ground, too—his own desires. Maybe after thirty, that’s all anyone stands on. But hanging on till seventy is gross—better to quit at thirty; at least you can pretend you still have a little self-respect. Have you seen Dmitri today?”
“No, but I did see Smerdyakov,” Alyosha said, and quickly told Ivan all about his meeting with Smerdyakov. Ivan listened carefully, asking questions.
“But he asked me not to tell Dmitri what he told me,” Alyosha added. Ivan frowned, thinking hard.
“Are you frowning because of Smerdyakov?” Alyosha asked.
“Yeah, it’s about him. Damn it, I really did want to see Dmitri, but now I don’t need to,” Ivan said, sounding reluctant.
“But are you really leaving so soon, brother?”
“Yes.”
“What about Dmitri and father? How’s it all going to end?” Alyosha asked, worried.

“You’re always stuck on that! What does it have to do with me? Am I supposed to be my brother Dmitri’s keeper?” Ivan snapped, annoyed, but then he suddenly gave a bitter smile. “That’s what Cain said about his murdered brother, isn’t it? Maybe that’s what you’re thinking right now? Well, whatever, I can’t stay here just to babysit them, can I? I’ve finished what I needed to do, and now I’m leaving. Do you really think I’m jealous of Dmitri, or that I’ve been trying to steal his beautiful Katerina Ivanovna these past three months? That’s nonsense. I had my own business. I finished it—you saw me finish it just now.”
“At Katerina Ivanovna’s place?”

“Yes, and now I’m finally free. And really, what does Dmitri have to do with it? He acts like there was some deal between us, but I never asked for that. He even officially handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. It’s all too ridiculous. Ah, Alyosha, if you only knew how light I feel now! I almost ordered champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Ugh! This has been dragging on for almost six months, and suddenly it’s just over. I wouldn’t have guessed even yesterday how easy it would be to end it if I really wanted to.”
“You’re talking about your love, Ivan?”

“If you want to call it that, yes. I fell in love with her, stressed myself out over her, and she stressed me out too. I looked after her... and then, suddenly, it’s gone! This morning I spoke with so much feeling, but after I left, I actually burst out laughing. Would you believe it? It’s true.”
“You seem really happy about it now,” Alyosha said, looking into Ivan’s face, which was suddenly brighter.

“But how was I supposed to know I didn’t care about her at all! Ha! It turns out I didn’t. And yet, she still attracts me. She was so charming just now when I made my speech! She still attracts me even now, but it’s so easy to walk away. Do you think I’m bragging?”
“No, but maybe it wasn’t really love.”

“Alyosha,” Ivan laughed, “don’t try to analyze love, it doesn’t suit you. You jumped right into the conversation this morning! I should have kissed you for that... But wow, she really tortured me! It was like sitting next to an open wound. She knew how much I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri,” Ivan insisted, almost cheerfully. “Her feelings for Dmitri were just her way of hurting herself. Everything I told her was true, but the sad part is, it might take her fifteen or twenty years to realize she doesn’t care for Dmitri and actually loves me, the one she torments. Or maybe she’ll never figure it out, even after today. Well, it’s better this way; I can just leave for good. By the way, do you know how she is now? What happened after I left?”
Alyosha told Ivan that Katerina Ivanovna had been hysterical and that, from what he’d heard, she was now unconscious and delirious.
“Isn’t Madame Hohlakov exaggerating?”
“I don’t think so.”
“I should find out. But nobody dies from hysterics. It’s just something women have for relief. I’m not going back to her. Why should I push myself in again?”
“But you told her she never loved you.”
“I said that on purpose. Alyosha, should I order some champagne? Let’s drink to my freedom. If only you knew how happy I am!”
“No, brother, let’s not drink,” Alyosha said suddenly. “Besides, I’m feeling kind of down.”
“Yeah, you’ve been down for a while. I’ve noticed.”
“So, you’re definitely leaving tomorrow morning?”

“Morning? I didn’t say I’d leave in the morning... but maybe it’ll be morning. You know, I ate here today just so I wouldn’t have to eat with the old man—I can’t stand him. If it were just about him, I would have left a long time ago. But why are you so worried about me leaving? We’ve got plenty of time before I go—almost an eternity!”
“If you’re leaving tomorrow, how can you call it an eternity?”

“But what does it matter to us?” Ivan laughed. “We still have time to talk, to get to the reason we came here. Why are you so surprised? Tell me, why did we meet here? To talk about my love for Katerina Ivanovna? About father and Dmitri? About traveling? About Russia’s problems? Or Napoleon? Is that it?”
“No.”

“Then you know why. For other people, it’s different, but for us, in our youth, we have to wrestle with the eternal questions first. That’s what matters to us. Young people in Russia talk about nothing but the big questions now, while the older folks are busy with practical stuff. Why have you been looking at me expectantly for three months? You want to ask, ‘What do you believe? Or do you believe in anything at all?’ Isn’t that right?”
“Maybe so,” Alyosha smiled. “You’re not making fun of me, are you, Ivan?”

“Me, making fun? I wouldn’t hurt my little brother who’s been watching me with such expectation for three months. Alyosha, look at me! I’m just as much a kid as you are, only not a beginner. And what do Russian boys do these days? Right here in this gross tavern, they meet up, sit in a corner—even if they’ve never met before and won’t see each other again for forty years—and what do they talk about? The eternal questions: does God exist, is there immortality? And if they don’t believe in God, they talk about socialism or anarchy or changing all of humanity—so it’s really just the same questions, flipped around. Tons of Russian boys do nothing but talk about these things! Isn’t that true?”
“Yes, for real Russians, questions about God and immortality—or the opposite—always come first, and that’s how it should be,” Alyosha said, still watching Ivan with his gentle, curious smile.

“Well, Alyosha, sometimes it’s pretty foolish to be Russian at all, but I can’t think of anything dumber than how Russian boys spend their time. Still, there’s one Russian boy named Alyosha I really like.”
“That was a nice way to put it!” Alyosha burst out laughing.
“So, tell me where to start—what’s your question? Want to talk about whether God exists?”
“Start wherever you want. Yesterday at father’s, you said God didn’t exist,” Alyosha said, looking at his brother closely.

“I said that yesterday just to mess with you—I saw your eyes light up. But now I’m serious, I really want to talk to you. I want us to be friends, Alyosha. I don’t have any friends and I want to try. Believe it or not,” Ivan laughed, “maybe I do believe in God. That surprises you, doesn’t it?”
“Yeah, if you’re not joking.”

“Joking? Yesterday, at the elder’s, they said I was joking, too. Listen, there was this old sinner in the 1700s who said, ‘If God didn’t exist, we’d have to invent Him.’ And humans really did invent God! What’s amazing isn’t that God exists, but that such a wild, vicious creature as man could come up with the idea that God is necessary. That’s so touching and wise, it actually makes humans look good. As for me, I stopped worrying about whether man created God or God created man. I’m not going to repeat all the theories Russian boys love to argue about—all of them borrowed from Europe anyway. What are we really after now? I’m trying to explain who I am, what I believe, what I hope for. That’s what you want, right? So, here it is: I accept God, simply. But listen: if God exists, and if He created the world, then He did it using the geometry of Euclid, and gave our minds the idea of just three dimensions. But there are scientists and philosophers—even some famous ones—who think maybe the universe isn’t just Euclid’s geometry; maybe two parallel lines, which never meet on earth, might meet somewhere in infinity. Since I can’t even understand that, how could I understand God? I admit I’m not equipped to answer these questions; I have an earthly mind. So I advise you not to worry about it either, Alyosha—especially about God’s existence or not. Our minds just aren’t made for those questions. So, I accept God and I’m glad about it. And I accept His wisdom and His purpose, even though they’re way beyond me. I believe in the hidden order and meaning of life. I believe in the eternal harmony everyone says we’ll be part of someday. I believe in the Word the universe is reaching for, the Word that ‘was with God’ and is God, and so on. There are all kinds of phrases for it. Sounds like I’m on the right track, right? But here’s the thing—would you believe it?—in the end, I don’t accept this world God made. I know it exists, but I don’t accept it. It’s not that I reject God, but I can’t and won’t accept the world He created. Let me explain: I believe, like a child, that all suffering will be healed; that all the crazy contradictions in life will disappear like a bad dream; that, in the end, something so great will happen that it will make up for all the pain, all the crimes, all the blood humans have shed. It will be enough to comfort and justify everything that’s happened. But even if that’s all true, I still don’t accept it. I won’t accept it. Even if parallel lines do meet and I see it myself, I’ll admit it, but I still won’t accept it. That’s the core of who I am, Alyosha. That’s my belief. I’m being serious. I started our talk in the dumbest way on purpose, but I wanted to confess all this to you, because I know that’s what you really want. You didn’t just want to talk about God, but to know what your brother lives by. So I’ve told you.”
Ivan finished his long speech with a lot more emotion than Alyosha expected.
“Why did you start ‘as stupidly as you could’?” Alyosha asked, looking dreamily at him.

“First, because that’s the Russian way. Russians always talk about these things in the dumbest way possible. Second, the dumber you are, the closer you are to reality. Stupidity is simple and honest—intelligence tries to hide and twist things. Intelligence is sneaky, but stupidity is real and direct. I brought our talk around to my despair, and the dumber I made it sound, the better for me.”
“Will you explain why you can’t accept the world?” Alyosha asked.

“Of course I will, it’s no secret. That’s what I was building up to. Little brother, I don’t want to mess you up or shake your faith. Maybe I want you to heal me,” Ivan said, suddenly smiling like a gentle child. Alyosha had never seen him smile like that before.

“I have to confess something to you,” Ivan began. “I’ve never understood how anyone could truly love their neighbors. In my opinion, it’s exactly the people closest to us who are hardest to love, while it’s much easier to love people from far away. I once read about a saint called John the Merciful, who took in a starving, freezing beggar. The beggar was horribly sick, his mouth was disgusting, but John hugged him and even breathed into his mouth. I think he only did that to punish himself, because he thought it was his duty as a Christian—not because he actually loved the man. For me, if you really want to love someone, it only works as long as they stay hidden, but as soon as you see their real face, the love disappears.”

“Father Zossima has talked about that before,” said Alyosha. “He said that sometimes it’s hard for people who haven’t practiced loving others to love the people they see face-to-face. But I still believe there’s a lot of love in people, even love like Christ had. I know that’s true, Ivan.”

“Well, I don’t know anything about that, and I can’t understand it. Most people probably feel the same as I do. Is that because people are bad, or is it just human nature? I think loving others like Christ did is a miracle—it’s impossible for us. Christ was God, but we’re not. Say I’m suffering really badly—no one else can ever truly know how much, because they aren’t me. And honestly, people rarely want to admit how much someone else is hurting. Why? Maybe because I smell bad, or my face is ugly, or I once stepped on their foot. And there are different kinds of suffering. If I’m starving, maybe someone will help me. But if I’m suffering for a higher reason—like for an idea—people almost never accept that, maybe because I don’t look like the kind of person they think should suffer for an idea. So they stop caring about me, and it’s not always out of cruelty. Beggars, especially if they try to be polite, should probably hide away and ask for help through the newspaper. It’s easy to love people in the abstract, or at a distance, but up close it’s nearly impossible. If beggars were like dancers in a ballet, wearing fancy rags and begging gracefully, maybe we’d enjoy looking at them, but we still wouldn’t love them. Anyway, that’s just my view. I wanted to talk about all human suffering, but let’s focus on the suffering of children. That narrows things down a lot, but it makes my point clearer. First, people can love children even when they’re dirty or ugly (though I don’t think children are ever truly ugly). Second, adults are harder to feel sorry for because they’ve already eaten the apple—they know good and evil, like gods. But children haven’t eaten anything; they’re innocent. I know you love children, Alyosha, and I do too. Even the cruelest people, like the Karamazovs, sometimes love little kids. Kids under seven are so different from adults, almost like a different species. I knew a criminal in prison who had killed whole families, including children, but he became strangely attached to kids while locked up. He’d watch them play and even became friends with one of them. Do you know why I’m telling you all this, Alyosha? My head hurts and I feel really sad.”
“You’re talking in a strange way,” Alyosha said worriedly. “It’s like you’re not really yourself.”

“Anyway, a Bulgarian I met in Moscow,” Ivan continued, ignoring Alyosha, “told me about horrible crimes by Turks and Circassians in Bulgaria. They were afraid the Slavs would rebel, so they burned villages, murdered people, and tortured women and children. They did things like nailing prisoners’ ears to fences and leaving them there overnight, then hanging them in the morning. People talk about ‘beastly’ cruelty, but that’s not fair to animals—a beast can’t be as cruel as a human. A tiger, for example, might bite or tear, but he wouldn’t think of nailing someone’s ears to a fence. The Turks even enjoyed torturing children—cutting unborn babies from their mothers and tossing infants in the air to catch them on bayonets, right in front of their mothers. Doing it in front of the mothers was the part they enjoyed most. Here’s another scene: picture a terrified mother holding her baby, surrounded by Turkish soldiers. They try to make the baby laugh, and when it does, one of them points a pistol at its face. The baby laughs and reaches for the gun, and the soldier shoots it in the face. Artistic, right? By the way, Turks are supposed to love sweets.”
“Ivan, what are you trying to say?” asked Alyosha.
“I think if the devil doesn’t exist, but humans made him up, then they made him in their own image.”
“Just like they did with God?” said Alyosha.

“‘You’re good with words,’ like Polonius says in Hamlet,” Ivan laughed. “You turned my words back at me. I’m glad you did. That would mean your God is just another version of man. You asked what I was getting at. Well, I like collecting stories like that. I even copy down certain stories from newspapers and books. The Turks are bad, but they’re foreigners. I have stories from right here at home that are even worse. You know, our thing is beating people—rods and whips. That’s a Russian tradition. We’d never nail someone’s ears to a fence, we’re Europeans after all. But the rod and the whip—we’ve always had those, and we’ll never lose them. In other countries, they don’t beat people much anymore, either because people are kinder now or the laws prevent it. But they have their own ways of cruelty, just as national as ours. I read a pamphlet, translated from French, about a murderer named Richard who was executed five years ago. He was twenty-three, grew up as an illegitimate child, given away to shepherds in Switzerland at age six. They treated him like an animal, barely fed or clothed him, made him work in the cold, beat him if he tried to eat pig food. He grew up wild, became a laborer in Geneva, then a thief, and finally killed an old man. He was caught, confessed, and sentenced to death. In prison, pastors and philanthropists taught him to read and write, told him about Jesus, and eventually he admitted his crime and ‘found God.’ Geneva was excited—everyone wanted to see the ‘new Richard,’ hugged him and called him brother. Richard cried all the time, saying, ‘This is my happiest day. I’m going to the Lord.’ They all followed him to the scaffold, cheering him on as he died. And then they cut off his head, as if it was some kind of loving act. That’s what they do there. Russians thought it was so moving, they translated the story and gave it out for free. But our specialty is different, maybe even worse: we want to hurt people just for the sake of it. There’s a poem by Nekrassov about a peasant beating a horse on its gentle eyes, just because it’s too weak to pull a heavy load. He gets carried away, beating harder and harder, even as the horse gasps for breath and trembles. It’s horrible—but it’s just a horse, and Tatars taught us to beat horses, leaving us the whip as a reminder. But people get beaten too. I know of a cultured man who, along with his wife, beat their seven-year-old daughter with a birch rod. The father was actually happy the rod had lots of twigs because it hurt more. Some people actually get excited from beating someone, and the more they do it, the worse it gets. The child screams, then can’t even scream, just gasps, ‘Daddy! Daddy!’ This case even went to court, and the lawyer defended the parents, saying it was just normal discipline. The jury agreed, and the public cheered. I wish I’d been there—I would’ve suggested we all pitch in for a gift for the father! What a lovely scene, right?”

“But I have even worse stories about children, Alyosha. I’ve collected a lot about Russian children. There was a girl of five whose parents—supposedly good, respectable people—hated her. This love of torturing children is something special in some people. They act kind and polite to everyone else, but they love tormenting children, even though they might claim to love kids. It’s the kids’ helplessness that makes it tempting—the innocence and trust of a child with nowhere to turn sets something evil off inside them. Every person has a demon inside—rage, twisted desires, wildness, even diseases caused by their own bad actions.”

“This poor five-year-old girl was tortured in every way by her educated parents. They beat her, kicked her for no reason, until her body was nothing but bruises. Then they got creative—they locked her all night in the freezing cold outhouse. Because she didn’t ask to go to the bathroom at night—though how could a little child be trained for that while asleep?—her mother smeared her face and stuffed her mouth with filth. And the mother could sleep with her child crying outside! Can you understand why a tiny innocent, who doesn’t even know what’s happening, would punch her own little chest in the dark and cold and pray her small, humble prayers to God for help? Do you get why this is allowed to happen? People say if things like this didn’t exist, people couldn’t tell good from evil. But why should knowing good and evil cost so much? The whole world’s knowledge isn’t worth just one of that little girl’s prayers to ‘dear, kind God.’ I don’t even care about adult suffering—they’ve eaten the apple, let them suffer. But these little ones! I know I’m making you feel awful, Alyosha, but I’ll stop if you want.”
“No, it’s okay. I want to feel it too,” Alyosha muttered.

“One more story, because it’s so strange and I just read it,” Ivan went on. “It was from the worst days of serfdom, in the early 1800s, before the people were freed. There was a general, a rich, powerful man who thought he could do whatever he wanted. He had hundreds of dogs and nearly a hundred boys to take care of them. One day, a peasant boy, only eight years old, accidentally hurt the general’s favorite dog. The general demanded to know who did it. When he found out, he had the boy locked up overnight. The next morning, the general gathered everyone for a hunt: all his servants, the dog-boys, and the boy’s mother. The boy was brought out, shivering with fear, and stripped naked. The general made the boy run, then set the dogs on him. The hounds tore the boy to pieces in front of his mother. Later, the general was declared insane and lost his land. So, what did he deserve? Should he be shot? What do you think, Alyosha?”
“He should be shot,” Alyosha said quietly, giving Ivan a pale, twisted smile.
“Bravo!” Ivan cried, pleased. “Even you say it. Some little devil does live in your heart, Alyosha Karamazov!”
“What I said was wrong, but—”

“That ‘but’ is the whole point!” Ivan interrupted. “Let me tell you, novice, that absurd things are actually necessary in this world. The world stands on absurdities. Maybe nothing would happen at all without them. We know what we know!”
“What do you know?”

“I understand nothing,” Ivan said, almost like he was feverish. “I don’t want to understand anything now. I want to stick to the facts. I decided a while ago not to try to understand. If I try, I’ll just start making excuses, and I want to stick to reality.”
“Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried, suddenly upset. “Will you finally say what you mean?”
“Of course, I will—that’s what I’ve been leading up to. You’re important to me, Alyosha. I don’t want to let you go, and I’m not giving you up to Father Zossima.”
For a minute, Ivan went quiet, and his face suddenly looked very sad.

“Listen! I focused on children to make my point clearer. I’m not even talking about all the other suffering in the world, though there’s plenty. I’ve narrowed it down on purpose. I know I’m just a lowly person, and I admit I can’t understand why the world is the way it is. People are probably to blame—they were given paradise, wanted freedom, and took it, even though it meant unhappiness. So maybe they don’t deserve pity. With my ordinary, logical mind, all I know is that suffering exists, and that no one is really guilty; things just happen, cause and effect. But that’s just logic, and I can’t accept it. What comfort is it to me that no one is really guilty, or that everything flows and balances out? I want justice, or else I’ll destroy myself. And I want justice now, on earth, something I can see—not someday in heaven. I want to see with my own eyes the lamb lying down with the lion, and the victim hugging their murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. Every religion is built on that hope, and I believe in it. But then there are the children—what am I supposed to do about them? That’s the question I can’t answer. There are lots of questions, but I picked children because their suffering can’t be explained away. Listen: if everyone has to suffer to create eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it? Why should they pay for harmony? Why should their suffering make the future better? I get that people are united in sin and punishment, but not children. If it’s true that kids have to pay for their fathers’ sins, that’s something I just can’t understand. Someone might joke that the child would have grown up to sin anyway, but he didn’t—he was torn apart by dogs at age eight. I’m not mocking, Alyosha! I know that when the whole universe comes together in one song of praise and everyone cries out, ‘You are just, O Lord, your ways are revealed,’—when the mother hugs the man who killed her child and all three cry, ‘You are just, O Lord!’—then everything will be explained. But I can’t accept that kind of harmony. While I’m alive, I choose to protect myself—I reject the whole idea. It’s not worth the tears of even one tortured child who cried to God in an outhouse. Those tears can’t be forgiven or made up for—they have to be paid for, or there’s no harmony. But how? How can you pay for them? By punishing the oppressors? What good is hell to the children who already suffered? And if there is hell, what happens to harmony? I want to forgive, to embrace, not to create more suffering. If the suffering of children is what’s needed for truth, I don’t want that truth. I don’t want the mother to forgive the man who threw her son to the dogs. She might forgive him for her own pain, but she can’t forgive him for her child’s suffering. Even if the child forgave, she still can’t. If that’s true, then what happens to harmony? Is there anyone in the world who has the right to forgive? I don’t want that kind of harmony. Out of love for humanity, I’d rather keep my anger and sadness, even if I’m wrong. The price is just too high. So I’m giving back my entrance ticket, and if I’m honest, that’s what I have to do. It’s not God I reject, Alyosha—I just respectfully return Him the ticket.”
“That’s rebellion,” Alyosha murmured, looking down.

“Rebellion? I’m sorry you call it that,” Ivan said seriously. “It’s hard to live in rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me honestly—say you could create a world where everyone ends up happy, but to do it, you had to torture one tiny child to death, like the baby beating its chest in the outhouse, and build that happiness on its suffering—would you agree to be the architect on those terms? Tell me the truth.”
“No, I wouldn’t agree,” Alyosha said softly.
“And do you think the people you’re building this world for would accept happiness based on the unpunished suffering of an innocent child? And if they did, could they really stay happy forever?”

“No, I can’t believe that,” said Alyosha suddenly, his eyes shining. “But, brother, you asked if there’s anyone in the world who could forgive—there is Someone. He can forgive everything, for everyone, because He gave His innocent blood for all of us. You forgot about Him. The whole hope is built on Him, and it’s to Him people cry, ‘You are just, O Lord, your ways are revealed!’ ”

“Ah, the one without sin, and His blood! No, I haven’t forgotten Him; honestly, I was waiting for you to bring Him up, since usually your side puts Him at the center. You know, Alyosha—don’t laugh—I made up a poem about a year ago. If you can spare another ten minutes, I’ll tell it to you.”
“You wrote a poem?”

“Oh, no, I didn’t actually write it,” Ivan laughed. “I’ve never written a poem in my life. But I made this one up in my head as a story in prose. I got really carried away. You’ll be the first person to hear it. Why shouldn’t an author want at least one listener?” Ivan smiled. “Do you want to hear it?”
“I’m listening,” said Alyosha.
“My story is called ‘The Grand Inquisitor.’ It’s a weird story, but I want to tell it to you.”

“Even this needs an introduction—a sort of story introduction,” Ivan laughed. “But I’m not very good at that. See, my story takes place in the 1500s, and back then, as you probably learned in school, it was pretty common in poetry for angels, saints, and even God to come down to earth. Not just in Dante—over in France, monks and church folks would put on plays where the Virgin Mary, the saints, angels, Jesus, and God himself would be characters onstage. It was all done simply, without any embarrassment. In Victor Hugo’s Notre Dame de Paris, there’s a scene where people watch a show at the Hôtel de Ville for the birth of the king’s son, where the Virgin Mary herself comes out and makes a judgment. Plays like that, often based on the Old Testament, were performed in Moscow too, up until Peter the Great’s time. Besides plays, there were all sorts of stories and songs about saints and angels helping out when needed. In monasteries, monks would translate, copy, or even write new poems like that—even when the Mongols ruled Russia. One poem, from the Greek, is called The Wanderings of Our Lady through Hell, and it’s as bold as Dante. Mary goes into hell, guided by the Archangel Michael, and sees all the different punishments. She’s horrified by the suffering, especially when she sees some sinners in a burning lake, sinking to the bottom so they can’t get out—those are ‘the ones God forgets.’ That’s a powerful image. Mary is so heartbroken she begs God to have mercy on everyone in hell, no matter what they did. She keeps pleading, even when God reminds her of Jesus’ suffering. She asks all the saints and angels to join her in her prayer. In the end, God agrees to give the sinners a break from their suffering every year from Good Friday to Trinity Day, and the people in hell thank Him for His justice. My poem would have been like that if I’d written it back then. In my story, He appears, but He doesn’t say anything—He just shows up and leaves. Fifteen centuries have passed since He promised to return in glory, since His prophet wrote, ‘Behold, I come quickly’; and even He said, ‘No one knows that day or hour, not even the Son, only the Father.’ But people are still waiting—still loving, still believing, maybe with even more faith, because it’s been so long since anyone’s seen a miracle from heaven.”

There was nothing left but faith in what people felt in their hearts. There were miracles in those days—saints healing the sick, and some holy people even claimed to have seen the Virgin Mary herself. But the devil didn’t rest, and people began to doubt if the miracles were real. Then, in northern Germany, a scary new heresy started. “A huge star, like a torch, fell on the water and made it bitter.” These heretics denied miracles and said they weren’t real. But the faithful just believed even more strongly. Humanity’s tears still reached out to Him, hoping, loving, praying to suffer and die for Him. For so many centuries, people had prayed, “Lord, please come soon,” and called out to Him, that in His mercy, He finally decided to come down to His servants. Before that, He had appeared to a few saints or hermits, as it’s written in their stories. Among us, Tyutchev once said—with all his heart—that
And that really was true, I promise you.

“So, He decided to appear for a moment to the people—the suffering, sinful people who still loved Him like children. My story happens in Spain, in Seville, during the worst time of the Inquisition, when heretics were burned at the stake every day ‘for the glory of God.’ Of course, this isn’t the final coming He promised, when He’ll return in full glory ‘like lightning flashing from east to west.’ No, He visits His children only briefly, right there where the flames are burning around the heretics. Out of mercy, He comes again in human form, just like when He walked among people fifteen centuries earlier. He comes down to the hot streets of Seville, where, the day before, almost a hundred heretics were burned in a grand ceremony by the cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, in front of the king, court, knights, other cardinals, noble ladies, and the whole city.”

“He arrives quietly, and yet, strangely, everyone recognizes Him right away. That could be one of the best parts of my story—why everyone knows it’s Him. People are drawn to Him—they gather around, follow Him, and He moves among them with a gentle smile full of compassion. There’s so much love in His heart, and His eyes shine with power and kindness, making everyone feel love in return. He blesses people, and just touching Him, or even His clothes, heals them. An old man in the crowd, blind from birth, shouts, ‘Lord, heal me so I can see You!’ and suddenly he can see. The crowd cries, weeps, and kisses the ground by His feet. Children throw flowers, sing, and shout hosannah. ‘It’s Him—it has to be Him!’ everyone says. He stops at the steps of Seville’s cathedral just as mourners are bringing a little white coffin. Inside is a seven-year-old girl, the only child of a well-known citizen, covered in flowers. ‘He’ll raise your child!’ the crowd shouts to the grieving mother. The priest looks confused and suspicious, but the mother drops to her knees at His feet, sobbing, ‘If it’s really You, please bring my child back!’ The procession stops, the coffin is laid at His feet. He looks kindly at the mother, and softly says, ‘Maiden, arise!’ The girl sits up in her coffin, smiling with big, surprised eyes, still holding the white roses in her hand.”
