“There are shouts, crying, and chaos among the people, and just then the cardinal—the Grand Inquisitor himself—walks by the cathedral. He’s almost ninety, tall and thin, with a wrinkled face and deep-set eyes that still have a spark in them. He isn’t dressed in his fancy red robes like the day before when he burned the heretics. Now he’s just in a simple, old monk’s robe. Behind him are his serious assistants, servants, and the ‘holy guard.’ He stops and watches the crowd from a distance. He sees everything—the coffin at His feet, the child coming back to life—and his face darkens. He frowns and his eyes flash with something dangerous. He points and signals the guards to arrest Him. The cardinal has so much power that the crowd immediately steps aside, and in total silence, the guards grab Him and take Him away. The crowd drops to the ground, bowing before the old Inquisitor. He silently blesses them and walks on. The guards take their prisoner to an old, dark, underground prison in the palace of the Holy Inquisition and lock Him inside. The day passes, and night falls over Seville—a hot, stifling night, with the smell of laurel and lemon trees in the air. Suddenly, in the darkness, the iron door creaks open, and the Grand Inquisitor comes in with a lantern. He’s alone. The door shuts behind him. He stands in the doorway, staring at His face for a minute or two. Finally, he walks up, sets the light on the table, and speaks.”

“‘Is it You? You?’ But since there’s no answer, he quickly adds, ‘Don’t answer. Be silent. What could You even say? I already know what You’d say. And You have no right to add anything to what You said before. Why have You come here to mess things up? Because that’s what You’re doing, and You know it. But do You know what will happen tomorrow? I don’t know who You are, and I don’t care if You’re really Him or just someone who looks like Him, but tomorrow, I’ll condemn You and burn You at the stake as the worst heretic of all. And the same people who kissed Your feet today, at the slightest signal from me, will be the first to light the fire under You. Do You know that? Yes, maybe You do,’ he added, still staring deep into the Prisoner’s eyes.”

“I don’t really get it, Ivan. What does that mean?” Alyosha, who’d been listening quietly, said, smiling. “Is this just some crazy fantasy? Or is it a misunderstanding by the old man—a sort of mix-up?”

“Take it as the last one,” Ivan laughed, “if you’re so stuck on realism that you can’t stand anything imaginative. If you want it to be a case of mistaken identity, fine. Sure,” he went on, still laughing, “the old man is ninety; he could be crazy, obsessed with his ideas. Maybe seeing the Prisoner just set him off. Maybe it’s all the wild thoughts of an old man, fired up by burning a hundred heretics the day before. But does it really matter to us if it’s mistaken identity or a wild fantasy? What matters is that the old man finally says out loud what he’s thought in secret for ninety years.”
“And the Prisoner stays silent too? Does He just look at him and say nothing?”

“He has to, no matter what,” Ivan laughed again. “The old man’s told Him He has no right to add anything new to what He already said. That’s a key part of Roman Catholicism, at least in my view. ‘You gave everything to the Pope,’ they say, ‘so everything’s in the Pope’s hands now, and there’s no need for You to come back at all. You shouldn’t interfere—not for now, anyway.’ They talk and write like that—the Jesuits, at least. I’ve read it myself in their books. ‘Do You have the right to reveal to us just one of the mysteries from Your world?’ my old man asks Him, and answers for Him: ‘No, You don’t. You can’t add to what’s already been said, and You can’t take away the freedom You valued so much when You were on earth. Anything new You reveal would be a miracle, and that would take away people’s freedom to believe. You said Yourself, “I will make you free.” But now look what Your “free” people have done,’ the old man adds, with a sad smile. ‘Yes, we’ve paid a high price for it,’ he continues, looking sternly at Him, ‘but we’ve finally finished the job in Your name. For fifteen centuries, we fought against Your freedom, and now it’s over—finished for good. Don’t You believe it’s really over? You look at me so gently, not even angry. But let me tell You: now, today, people are more convinced than ever that they’re completely free, but they’ve given up their freedom and laid it at our feet. And that’s our doing. Was this what You wanted? Was this Your idea of freedom?’”
“I still don’t get it,” Alyosha interrupted. “Is the old man being sarcastic? Is he joking?”

“Not at all! He actually thinks it’s a good thing that he and his Church have finally gotten rid of freedom so people can be happy. ‘Now,’ he says (he’s talking about the Inquisition, of course), ‘for the first time, it’s possible to make people happy. Man was made to rebel, so how can rebels ever be happy? You were warned,’ he says to Him. ‘You had plenty of warnings, but You ignored them; You turned down the only way people could be happy. But luckily, when You left, You gave the job to us. You promised, You gave us the right to bind and unbind, and now, of course, You can’t take it back. So why have You come to stop us?’”
“And what does he mean by ‘plenty of warnings’?” asked Alyosha.
“That’s actually the main part of what the old man has to say.

“‘The wise and fearsome spirit—the one who loves destruction and nothingness,’ the old man goes on, ‘the great spirit talked to You in the desert, and the stories say he “tempted” You. Isn’t that true? And honestly, could anything be truer than what he asked You in those three questions—what You rejected and what the stories call “the temptation”? If there’s ever been a real, unbelievable miracle, it happened that day. Just the fact those three questions were asked was a miracle. If you imagine, just for argument’s sake, that those three questions were lost and we had to make them up again, and we gathered all the wise people on earth—rulers, priests, scholars, philosophers, poets—and told them to invent three questions that would fit the moment and sum up all of human history, do you think all their wisdom together could come up with anything as deep or powerful as the actual three questions the spirit asked You in the desert? Just from those questions, you can see this isn’t ordinary human intelligence—it’s something absolute and eternal. In those three questions, all of humanity’s struggles are wrapped up and predicted. Back then, people couldn’t see it, because the future was unknown, but now, fifteen hundred years later, we see that everything in those three questions was exactly right, and has come true.”

“‘Judge for Yourself who was right—You or the one who questioned You back then. Remember the first question; basically, it meant: “You want to go into the world, offering people only freedom, but people are too simple and wild to understand it. They’re scared of it. Nothing is harder for people or for society than freedom. But see these stones in this empty desert? Turn them into bread, and people will follow You like sheep, grateful and obedient, but always scared You’ll take it away.” But You wouldn’t take away their freedom, and You refused, thinking, what is freedom worth if people only obey because You feed them? You replied that man doesn’t live by bread alone. But do You know that, because of that, the spirit of the world will rise up against You, and will win, and everyone will follow him, saying, “Who is as great as this beast? He gave us fire from heaven!” Do You know that, over the centuries, people will decide there is no such thing as crime, just hunger? “Feed people, then ask them to be good!”—that’s what they’ll write on their banners, and that’s how they’ll destroy Your church. Where Your church stood, they’ll build a new one—the tower of Babel all over again. It won’t be finished, but You could have stopped it and saved people so much suffering. After a thousand years of pain, they’ll come looking for us in the catacombs, saying, “Feed us, because those who promised us fire from heaven never delivered!” And then we’ll finish building their tower, because whoever feeds them, finishes it. Only we can feed them, pretending it’s in Your name. Oh, they can never feed themselves without us! No science will ever give them bread as long as they’re free. In the end, they’ll lay their freedom at our feet, saying, “Make us your slaves, just feed us.” They’ll realize that freedom and enough bread for everyone can’t exist together. They’ll see they can never really be free, because they are weak, mean, and rebellious. You promised them the bread of Heaven, but can that compare to real bread for weak, sinful people? And if thousands follow You for the bread of Heaven, what about the millions who can’t give up real bread for the sake of Heaven? Or do You care only about the strong few, while the millions must exist only for them? No, we care for the weak too. They’re sinners and rebels, but in the end, they’ll become obedient. They’ll look up to us like gods, because we’re willing to handle the burden of freedom for them. But we’ll say we’re Your servants, ruling them in Your name. We’ll lie, because we’ll never let You come back again. That lie will be our suffering, because we’ll have to keep lying.’”

“‘That’s what the first question in the desert meant, and that’s what You turned down because You valued freedom so much. But this question holds the secret of the world. If You had chosen “bread,” You would have given people what they wanted most: someone to worship. As long as people are free, they desperately search for someone or something to worship, and not just anything—they want something everyone can agree on. This need to worship together is the main misery of every person and all humanity. For the sake of common worship, people have killed each other. They’ve set up gods and said, “Get rid of your gods, worship ours, or we’ll kill you and your gods!” And it will always be like that, even if there are no more gods—people will still bow to new idols. You must have known this deep truth about people, but You refused the one sure way to make everyone bow to You—the way of “bread.” You gave it up for freedom and the bread of Heaven. Look what happened. You made freedom even bigger! Didn’t You realize people would rather have peace or even death than the burden of choosing between good and evil? Nothing is more tempting to people than giving up their freedom of conscience, but nothing causes them more pain. Instead of giving them a solid foundation to ease their conscience forever, You chose what’s mysterious and hard to understand, something people can’t handle. It’s almost as if You didn’t love them at all—even though You came to die for them! Instead of taking away people’s freedom, You made it even heavier—forever burdening people with spiritual struggles. You wanted people to love You freely, to follow You by their own choice. Instead of strict old rules, people now have to decide for themselves what’s good and evil, with only Your example to guide them. But didn’t You know they’d eventually reject even You and Your truth, if the burden of free choice was too much? In the end, they’ll say You don’t have the truth, because You’ve only made them suffer with so many problems and worries.’”

“‘So, really, You Yourself set up the destruction of Your own kingdom, and no one else is more to blame. But what were You offered? There are only three powers strong enough to control people’s conscience forever: miracle, mystery, and authority. You turned down all three and set the example for others to do the same. When the spirit took You to the top of the temple and said, “If You’re the Son of God, throw Yourself down, because it’s written: the angels will catch You, and that will prove who You are.” But You refused and wouldn’t throw Yourself down. Sure, You acted proudly, like God; but are people like You? Could You really believe for a second that regular people could handle such a test? Are people really able to reject miracles and, in their hardest moments, trust only their own hearts? Oh, You knew Your story would be written in books and handed down to the ends of the earth, and You hoped people would follow You without needing miracles. But You didn’t know that when people reject miracles, they also reject God. People want miracles more than they want God Himself. And if they don’t get real miracles, they’ll make up their own and worship magic or witchcraft, even if they’re rebellious or don’t believe. You didn’t come down from the Cross when people mocked You, shouting, “Come down and then we’ll believe You!” You didn’t do it, because You didn’t want to force people to believe with a miracle. You wanted faith that’s given freely, not the terrified faith of a slave. But You overestimated people, because they really are slaves, even if they rebel. Look around—fifteen centuries have gone by—who have You brought to Your side? I swear, people are weaker and meaner than You thought! Can they do what You did? By respecting them so much, You demanded too much from them—You, who loved them more than Yourself! If You’d respected them less, You’d have asked less from them. That would have been more loving, because their burden would be lighter. People are weak and mean. Even now, when they rebel against our power, it’s just childish pride. They’re like school kids locking the teacher out. But their fun won’t last; it will cost them. They’ll destroy churches and cover the earth with blood. But in the end, these foolish children will realize they’re helpless rebels, and they’ll cry that the One who made them rebels must be mocking them. They’ll say this in despair, and it’ll be a kind of blasphemy, which will only make them more miserable, because people can’t stand blasphemy, and in the end, it comes back to hurt them. So, thanks to You, people are left with confusion, unrest, and misery! The great prophet saw a vision of those who were saved in the end, twelve thousand from every tribe. But if there were so many, they must have been more like gods than people. They suffered in the desert, lived on locusts and roots, and carried Your cross—sure, You can be proud of those heroes who loved You freely. But remember, they were only a few thousand; what about the rest? How is it the fault of the weak that they can’t handle such heavy gifts? Did You only come for the chosen few? If so, it’s a mystery and we can’t understand. And if it’s a mystery, then we’re allowed to preach our own mystery—to teach people it’s not about love or free will, but about mystery and rule. That’s what we’ve done. We’ve fixed Your work and based it on miracle, mystery, and authority. And people were glad to be led like sheep, happy to have the painful gift of freedom taken away. Were we wrong to treat them this way? Tell me! Did we not love people, by accepting how weak they are and making their lives easier, even letting them sin sometimes if we say it’s okay? Why have You come now to mess things up? And why do You look at me so gently with those kind eyes? Be angry. I don’t want Your love—I don’t love You. And why should I hide anything from You? You know everything I could possibly say. Should I hide our secret from You? Maybe You want to hear it from me. Listen: we’re not working with You, but with him—that’s our secret. For eight centuries, we’ve been on his side, not Yours. Eight hundred years ago, we took from him what You refused—the last gift he offered You, when he showed You all the kingdoms of the world. We took Rome and the sword of Caesar, and declared ourselves rulers of the world, even if we haven’t finished the job yet. But whose fault is that? The work is just starting, but it’s begun. There’s still a long way to go, and the world will suffer, but we’ll win and become Caesars, and then we’ll design happiness for everyone. But You could have taken Caesar’s sword back then. Why did You turn it down? If You’d listened to that final suggestion from the spirit, You’d have given people everything they wanted: someone to worship, a keeper for their conscience, and a way to unite everyone. The longing for unity is the third and final ache for people. Humanity has always tried to organize a world state. Every big nation has wanted that, but the more advanced they were, the more miserable they were, because they felt the need for unity even more. Great conquerors like Tamerlane and Genghis Khan swept across the world trying to unite everyone, but even they were just showing the same instinct. If You had taken the world and Caesar’s purple robe, You would have created a world government and world peace. Who can rule people except the one who controls their conscience and their bread? We took Caesar’s sword, and by doing that, we rejected You and followed him. Oh, many ages of chaos and violence are coming—freedom and science will bring people to such misery that some will kill themselves, others will kill each other, and the rest will crawl to us, begging for help. They’ll say, “You alone have the truth, save us from ourselves!”’”

“‘When we give them bread, they’ll realize we’re just handing back what they made themselves, but they’ll be more grateful for getting it from our hands than for the bread itself! They’ll remember how, without us, their bread turned to stone, but with us, even stones turn into bread. They’ll finally know how good it feels to obey! And until they get that, they’ll be unhappy. Whose fault is it that they don’t know this? Who scattered the flock and sent it down strange roads? But the flock will come back and obey us for good. Then we’ll give them the quiet, simple happiness of weak creatures, just as they are. We’ll convince them not to be proud, because You made them proud by lifting them up. We’ll show them they’re weak, just helpless children, but that being a happy child is better than anything. They’ll cling to us, scared, like chicks to a mother hen. They’ll be amazed and even a little scared of us, proud that we’re so wise and powerful to control such a wild crowd. They’ll fear our anger, and quickly move from tears to laughter at our command. Yes, we’ll make them work, but in their free time, life will be like a children’s game, with songs and innocent dances. We’ll even let them sin—they’re weak and helpless—and they’ll love us for letting them. We’ll say every sin is forgiven if we allow it, because we love them, and any punishment we’ll accept ourselves. They’ll tell us all their secrets, and we’ll decide if they can be with their wives or girlfriends, or have kids—based on whether they’ve obeyed. They’ll gladly accept it. The deepest secrets of their hearts, everything—they’ll bring it to us, and we’ll have answers for it all. They’ll be happy to accept our answers, because it saves them from the agony of making choices. Everyone will be happy—except the hundred thousand who rule over them. Only we, who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There’ll be billions of happy little ones, and a hundred thousand suffering leaders who hold the knowledge of good and evil. They’ll die peacefully, believing in Your name, and beyond the grave, they’ll find only death. But we’ll keep the secret, and dangle the hope of heaven and eternity as a reward. If there is another world, it won’t be for people like them. The prophecy says You’ll return in victory, with Your chosen, the proud and strong, but we’ll say only they saved themselves, while we saved everyone. They say the evil woman sitting on the beast, holding the mystery, will be shamed, that the weak will rise and tear off her royal cloak and expose her. But I’ll stand and point to a billion happy children who never sinned. We, who took their sins so they could be happy, will stand before You and say, “Judge us if You can and dare.” Know that I don’t fear You. Know that I too have been in the desert, I too lived on roots and locusts, I too wanted to be among Your chosen, the strong and powerful, hoping to ‘make up the number.’ But I woke up and refused to serve a crazy dream. I went back and joined those who fixed Your work. I left the proud and sided with the humble, for their happiness. What I’m telling You will happen, and our rule will be built. Tomorrow, You’ll see that obedient flock who, at my signal, will rush to pile up the burning embers for Your fire. If anyone ever deserved our flames, it’s You. Tomorrow, I’ll burn You. Dixi.’”
Ivan stopped. He’d gotten really into it, speaking passionately, but when he finished, he suddenly smiled.
Alyosha had listened quietly; toward the end, he was clearly moved, and nearly interrupted a few times, but held back. Now his words came out in a rush.

“But...that’s ridiculous!” he burst out, his face red. “Your story praises Jesus, not blames Him—just like you said it would. And who’s going to believe you about freedom? Is that really the way to see it? That’s not how the Orthodox Church sees it...That’s Rome, and not even all of Rome—it’s wrong! Those are the worst Catholics, the Inquisitors, the Jesuits!... And there couldn’t be anyone like your Inquisitor. What are these sins they take on themselves for the happiness of mankind? Who are these keepers of the secret, taking on some curse for others? Have they ever been seen? We know the Jesuits—they have a bad reputation, but they’re not like that at all. They’re just the Pope’s army to rule the world someday, with the pope as emperor. That’s their dream, but there’s no secret, no deep sadness about it. It’s just a greedy desire for power and control, for making everyone into serfs and themselves the masters. That’s all it is. They might not even believe in God! Your suffering Inquisitor is just a fantasy.”

“Wait, wait,” Ivan laughed, “don’t get so worked up! Fantasy, you say—fine, let it be a fantasy! But let me ask: do you really think the Roman Catholic movement is nothing but greed for power and money? Is that what Father Païssy taught you?”
“No, no, actually, Father Païssy did say something a little like what you’re saying...but, of course, it’s not the same, not at all the same,” Alyosha quickly corrected himself.

“That’s a pretty big admission, even with your ‘not at all the same.’ Let me ask—why do you think the Jesuits and Inquisitors have only come together for power and money? Why couldn’t there be one among them, just one, who really suffers for humanity? Suppose there’s even one like my old Inquisitor, who lived in the desert, tried to conquer his own desires, and loved people all his life, but finally realized that most people can never be giants or complete the tower, that most people will never be able to use their freedom, and that God’s dream was wasted on them. Seeing all that, he went back and joined the ‘clever’ people. Couldn’t that happen?”

“Joined whom, what clever people?” Alyosha cried, totally caught up. “They’re not that clever, and they have no real secrets...Maybe it’s all just atheism, that’s their secret. Your Inquisitor doesn’t believe in God—that’s his secret!”

“And what if you’re right? You’ve finally guessed it. That’s the whole secret—it’s true! But isn’t that suffering, at least for someone like him, who spent his whole life in the desert but still couldn’t stop loving humanity? In his old age, he realizes that only the devil’s advice could ever help such weak, flawed creatures. So he decides to follow the devil’s plan—lie and trick people, lead them to destruction, but make them think they’re happy on the way. And the whole time, he does it in the name of the One he believed in all his life. Isn’t that tragic? If even one person like that led the whole movement—even if everyone else just wanted money and power—wouldn’t that be enough for a tragedy? More than that, one such person could shape the whole idea of the Roman Church, with all its armies and Jesuits, its highest ideals. I honestly believe there’s always been someone like that among the leaders. Who knows, maybe even among the Popes. Maybe there’s a group like that—old men who secretly agree to guard the mystery, to protect the weak and make them happy. I bet even among the Masons there’s something similar, and that’s why Catholics hate Masons so much—they see them as rivals. But I’m starting to sound like an author defending his story. Enough.”

“Maybe you’re a Mason yourself!” Alyosha suddenly burst out. “You don’t believe in God,” he said, sadly. He thought Ivan was looking at him with a mocking smile. “How does your story end?” he asked, looking down. “Or is that the ending?”

“I planned to end it like this: When the Inquisitor stops talking, he waits for the Prisoner to reply. The silence is heavy. He sees the Prisoner has listened closely, looking at him gently, clearly not planning to answer. The old man desperately wants Him to say something, even something harsh. But instead, He silently walks over and gently kisses the old man on his dry, aged lips. That’s all. The old man shudders. His lips move. He goes to the door, opens it, and says, ‘Go away, and don’t come back...never, never!’ Then he lets Him out into the dark streets. The Prisoner leaves.”
“And the old man?”
“The kiss stays in his heart, but the old man sticks to his beliefs.”
“And you—are you with him, too?” Alyosha asked sadly.
Ivan laughed.

“Come on, it’s all nonsense, Alyosha. It’s just a crazy story by a silly student who could never write poetry. Why are you taking it so seriously? You don’t really think I’m about to run off and join the Jesuits and help them ‘fix’ Jesus’ work? God, it’s none of my business. I told you, all I want is to live until I’m thirty, and then—I’ll throw the cup to the ground!”

“But what about the little sticky leaves, and the precious graves, and the blue sky, and the woman you love! How will you live, how will you love them?” Alyosha cried sadly. “With such a hell in your heart and mind, how can you? No, that’s why you’re leaving—to join them...if not, you’ll end up killing yourself, you can’t stand it!”
“There’s a kind of strength to endure anything,” Ivan said with a cold smile.
“What strength?”
“The strength of the Karamazovs—the strength of the Karamazov’s low instincts.”
“To sink into wild living, to smother your soul with corruption, right?”
“Maybe even that...but maybe I’ll hold out until I’m thirty, and then—”
“How will you escape it? What will save you? You can’t with your ideas.”
“In the Karamazov way, again.”
“‘Everything is allowed,’ you mean? Everything is allowed—is that it?”
Ivan frowned, and suddenly turned strangely pale.

“Ah, you’ve caught onto yesterday’s phrase, the one that annoyed Miüsov—and that Dmitri repeated so simply!” he smiled oddly. “Yes, if you want, ‘everything is allowed,’ since the words have been said. I won’t deny it. And Mitya’s version isn’t bad.”
Alyosha looked at him silently.

“I thought that by leaving, I’d still have you at least,” Ivan said suddenly, sounding unexpectedly emotional. “But now I see there’s no place for me even in your heart, my little hermit. I won’t give up the idea that ‘all is allowed’—so will you give up on me for that, yes?”
Alyosha got up, went over to him, and gently kissed him on the lips.
“That’s plagiarism!” Ivan cried, delighted. “You stole that from my story. Thank you, though. Get up, Alyosha, it’s time for both of us to go.”
They left, but paused at the entrance of the restaurant.

“Listen, Alyosha,” Ivan began seriously. “If I’m ever able to love the little sticky leaves, it’ll be because I remember you. Just knowing you’re here is enough for me not to lose my love for life—at least, not yet. Is that enough for you? Think of it as a declaration of love if you want. Now you go right and I’ll go left. And that’s enough—do you hear me? Even if I don’t leave tomorrow (though I probably will), and we see each other again, don’t ever bring up these topics again. I beg you. And about Dmitri, too—please, never talk to me about him again. It’s all exhausted, all been said enough, right? And I’ll promise you something in return: When I’m thirty, if I decide to ‘throw the cup to the ground,’ wherever I am—even if it’s in America—I’ll come back for one more talk with you. I promise. I want to see what you’ll be like then. It’s a real promise, you see. And we might not see each other for seven or ten years. Go now to your Pater Seraphicus, he’s dying. If he dies without you, you’ll blame me for keeping you. Goodbye, kiss me once more—there, now go.”

Ivan suddenly turned and walked away without looking back. It was just like how Dmitri had left Alyosha the day before, though the feeling was completely different. The strange similarity hit Alyosha hard as he stood there, sad and worried. He waited a little, watching his brother go. Suddenly he noticed that Ivan was swaying as he walked, and his right shoulder looked lower than his left. He’d never seen that before. Then Alyosha turned too, and almost ran to the monastery. It was nearly dark, and he felt a little scared; something new was growing inside him that he couldn’t explain. The wind was blowing again, just like the night before, and the old pines whispered darkly as he entered the woods by the hermitage. He nearly ran. “Pater Seraphicus—where did he get that name? Where from?” Alyosha wondered. “Ivan, poor Ivan, when will I see you again?... Here’s the hermitage. Yes, that’s him, Pater Seraphicus—he’ll save me—from Ivan and forever!”

Later, Alyosha would sometimes wonder how, after leaving Ivan, he could have completely forgotten about his brother Dmitri, even though that morning he’d promised himself he would find Dmitri and not give up, even if it meant not getting back to the monastery that night.

After saying goodbye to Alyosha, Ivan started walking back to his father Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. But as he got closer, he felt an unbearable sadness that just kept getting worse with every step. It wasn’t surprising for Ivan to feel down—he’d been depressed before. What was weird was that he couldn’t figure out why he felt this way. He was leaving behind everything that had brought him there and was about to start a new life, alone again, with big—maybe too big—hopes and dreams about the future. But if you’d asked him to explain exactly what he hoped for, or even what he wanted, he couldn’t have told you.

Still, even though he was definitely nervous about what the future might bring, that wasn’t what was really bothering him. “Do I just hate going back to my father’s house?” he wondered. “Maybe—I can’t stand the place, and even though this is the last time I’ll ever walk through that awful door, I still hate it.” But no, that wasn’t quite it either. “Is it because I said goodbye to Alyosha and had that long conversation with him? I’ve kept quiet for years and hardly talked to anyone, and then suddenly I start pouring out nonsense like that.” It could have been embarrassment from talking so much, especially in front of someone like Alyosha, who he’d really hoped to impress. That was probably part of it, but he knew it wasn’t the main thing. “I feel sick with depression, but I can’t even say what I want. Maybe it’s better not to think about it.”

Ivan tried not to think, but that didn’t help. What made the sadness so annoying was that it felt like it came from something outside of him. It was like when something gets in your line of sight and bugs you, even if you’re busy and don’t notice it right away. Eventually, it starts to bother you so much that you have to find and remove the thing—like a handkerchief left on the floor or a book out of place.
Ivan was in a bad mood by the time he got home, but when he was about fifteen steps from the garden gate, he suddenly realized what was actually bothering him.

Sitting on a bench near the gate was Smerdyakov, the valet. The moment Ivan saw him, he knew Smerdyakov was what was weighing on his mind—he felt a sudden rush of disgust. Everything became clear. Earlier, when Alyosha had told him about meeting Smerdyakov, Ivan had felt a flash of anger and dread, but then he’d forgotten about it during their talk. Now, alone on his way home, the feeling came back stronger. “How can someone as pathetic as him bother me so much?” Ivan thought, annoyed.

Lately, Ivan had started to really dislike Smerdyakov—almost to the point of hatred, especially in the last few days. When Ivan first came to the area, he’d actually been interested in Smerdyakov and thought he was an unusual guy. He encouraged Smerdyakov to talk, though he noticed the man’s mind was restless and hard to follow. They discussed big questions, like how there could be light on the first day of creation if the sun and stars weren’t made until the fourth day. But Ivan realized Smerdyakov didn’t really care about those questions. Instead, Smerdyakov showed off his pride and seemed to have his feelings hurt easily, and Ivan started to dislike him for that. Later, after Grushenka arrived and all the drama with Dmitri started, Smerdyakov would get excited talking about it, but Ivan could never tell what he really wanted. Smerdyakov asked lots of indirect, planned questions, but never explained himself, and he’d always go silent at the most important moment or change the subject. What really made Ivan dislike him most, though, was the creepy sense that Smerdyakov thought they shared some secret, like there was some special understanding between them. He was always respectful, but acted like they were in on something together—something no one else understood. Ivan hadn’t realized at first why Smerdyakov bothered him so much, but lately he’d figured it out.

Feeling disgusted and annoyed, Ivan tried to walk through the gate without looking at or talking to Smerdyakov. But Smerdyakov stood up from the bench, and Ivan knew instantly he wanted to talk. Ivan looked at him and stopped walking, and the fact that he stopped—when he’d just been planning to walk right past—made him even angrier. He stared at Smerdyakov’s sickly, pale face and the little curls combed over his forehead. Smerdyakov winked and grinned, as if saying, “Where are you going? We both know we have something to say to each other.”
Ivan trembled. He wanted to say, “Get lost, you idiot, what do I care about you?” but to his surprise, he heard himself softly ask, “Is my father still asleep, or is he awake?”

He was shocked to hear how gentle and quiet his own question was, and even more surprised when he sat down on the bench. For a second, he even felt a little scared—he remembered that later. Smerdyakov stood facing him, hands behind his back, looking serious and almost bossy.

“His honor is still asleep,” Smerdyakov said slowly and clearly (as if saying, “You spoke first, not me”). Then he added, after a pause, lowering his eyes and fiddling with his shiny boot, “I’m surprised at you, sir.”
“Why are you surprised?” Ivan snapped, trying hard to control himself, but suddenly realizing with disgust that he was actually really curious and couldn’t leave without finding out more.
“Why don’t you go to Tchermashnya, sir?” Smerdyakov asked, raising his eyes and giving Ivan a sly, familiar smile. His winking left eye seemed to say, “If you’re smart, you’ll know why I’m smiling.”
“Why should I go to Tchermashnya?” Ivan asked, confused.
Smerdyakov didn’t answer right away.
“Your father’s really been asking you to go,” he said finally, slowly, almost like it didn’t matter. It sounded like he was just saying it to say something.
“For God’s sake! Just say what you mean!” Ivan finally yelled, going from quiet to angry in a second.
Smerdyakov straightened up but still looked calm, with the same little smile.
“Nothing really—just making conversation.”

There was another long pause. Neither spoke for almost a minute. Ivan knew he should get up and show he was angry, and Smerdyakov seemed to be waiting to see if he'd do it. Finally, Ivan started to stand. Smerdyakov jumped at the chance.
“I’m in a terrible spot, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don’t know how to get out of it,” he said, speaking clearly and firmly, sighing at the end. Ivan sat back down.

“They’re both completely crazy—just like little kids,” Smerdyakov continued. “I’m talking about your father and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Fyodor Pavlovitch will wake up soon and start bugging me every minute: ‘Has she come? Why hasn’t she come?’ He’ll do that all night and even after midnight. And if Grushenka (Agrafena Alexandrovna) doesn’t show up—she might not come at all—he’ll start up again in the morning: ‘Why hasn’t she come? When will she come?’—and somehow it’s always my fault. Dmitri’s no better. As soon as it gets dark, or even before, your brother shows up with his gun: ‘Watch out, you crook, you soup-maker. If you miss her and don’t tell me she’s been here, I’ll kill you right now.’ Then, in the morning, he’s back at it: ‘Why hasn’t she come? Will she come soon?’ And of course, it’s my fault again. They get angrier and angrier every day. Sometimes I think I’ll just end it all. I can’t rely on either of them, sir.”
“So why did you get involved? Why did you start spying for Dmitri Fyodorovitch?” Ivan asked, irritated.

“How could I avoid it? Actually, I haven’t really meddled at all, if you want the truth. I kept quiet at first, but Dmitri picked me to be his servant. Since then, he’s only had one thing to say: ‘I’ll kill you if you miss her.’ I’m sure I’m going to have a long fit tomorrow.”
“What do you mean, ‘a long fit’?”

“A fit that lasts a long time—hours, or even a day or two. Once it lasted three days. I fell out of the attic that time. The shaking stopped and started again, and for three days I couldn’t think straight. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Dr. Herzenstube, who put ice on my head and tried some other remedy... I could have died then.”
“But people say you can’t predict when an epileptic fit will come. Why do you say you’ll have one tomorrow?” Ivan asked, his curiosity mixed with annoyance.
“That’s true. You can’t know in advance.”
“Besides, that time you fell from the attic.”
“I go up to the attic every day. I could fall again tomorrow. Or I could fall down the cellar steps. I have to go into the cellar every day, too.”
Ivan stared at him for a long moment.
“You’re talking nonsense, and I don’t really get you,” Ivan said quietly, but there was a threat in his voice. “Are you planning to fake a fit for three days, is that it?”
Smerdyakov, still staring at the ground and playing with his toe, shifted his feet, grinned, and said:

“If I could fake a fit—and it wouldn’t be hard for someone used to them—I’d have every right to do it to save my own life. Even if Grushenka comes while I’m ‘sick,’ your father couldn’t blame me for not telling him. He’d be too embarrassed.”
“For God’s sake!” Ivan shouted, his face twisting in anger. “Why are you always so terrified for your life? Dmitri’s threats are just words. He won’t kill you—it’s not you he’s after!”
“He’d kill me first, like a bug. Even worse, I’m afraid people will think I helped him if he does something crazy to your father.”
“Why would anyone think you helped?”
“Because I told him the secret signals your father and I use.”
“What signals? Who did you tell? Just say it clearly!”

“I’ll admit it,” Smerdyakov said in his usual slow, formal way. “I’m in on a secret with Fyodor Pavlovitch. For the past several days, he’s been locking himself in his room as soon as evening comes. Lately, you’ve been going upstairs early, and yesterday you didn’t come down at all, so maybe you don’t realize how careful he’s gotten. Even Grigory can’t get in unless Fyodor hears his voice. But Grigory doesn’t come anymore—I’m the only one serving him now, ever since things got crazy with Grushenka. At night, I’m ordered to leave and go to the lodge; I don’t sleep until midnight, just walk around the yard, waiting for Grushenka to show up. For days, he’s been obsessed, convinced she’ll sneak in late at night. He told me, ‘Watch for her until midnight or later. If she comes, run and knock on my door or window—knock twice, then three times quickly. Then I’ll know it’s her and let you in quietly.’ He also gave me a different signal in case something unexpected happens: two knocks, then a louder one after a pause. That means something urgent. If Grushenka can’t come herself and sends a message, that’s how I tell him. Also, if Dmitri (Mitya) shows up, I need to warn him—if Dmitri turns up while Grushenka is there, I must knock three times. So, five knocks mean Grushenka has arrived, three mean ‘something important.’ Only Fyodor Pavlovitch and I know these signals, so he’ll open the door without hesitation or calling out. Well, now Dmitri knows the signals too.”
“How does he know? Did you tell him? How could you?”

“I was scared. How could I not tell him? Dmitri kept demanding, ‘You’re hiding something from me! I’ll break your legs!’ So I told him the signals to prove I wasn’t hiding anything and that I was loyal.”
“If you think he’ll use the signals to break in, don’t let him in.”
“But if I’m having a fit, how can I stop him, even if I wanted to? He’s desperate.”
“Oh, come on! How can you be so sure you’ll have a fit? Are you messing with me?”
“I wouldn’t dare joke about this. I really feel a fit coming on. I have a bad feeling. Just being scared could bring it on.”
“If you’re sick, Grigory can keep watch. Warn Grigory—he’d never let Dmitri in.”

“I’d never dare tell Grigory about the signals without my master’s permission. Plus, Grigory’s been sick since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna is going to give him her special medicine tomorrow. She has this secret remedy made from some herb. She rubs it all over his back until it’s red and swollen, then gives him the rest to drink with a prayer. She always saves a little for herself, too. They never drink alcohol, so they fall asleep fast and sleep really deeply. When Grigory wakes up, he’s fine, but Marfa gets a headache. So if Marfa gives him the remedy tomorrow, they’ll both be asleep and won’t hear anything or stop Dmitri. They’ll sleep right through it.”

“What a mess! And it’s all happening at the same time, like it’s planned. You’ll have a fit, and they’ll both be knocked out,” Ivan said. “Are you setting this up on purpose?” he suddenly asked, frowning.
“Why would I? It all depends on what Dmitri decides to do. If he has something planned, he’ll do it. If not, I’m not the one pushing him toward his father.”

“But why would he go to our father in secret, especially if, as you say, Grushenka isn’t coming? You said yourself she’s not coming, and I’ve always thought this whole thing was just my father’s imagination, and she won’t come. Why would Dmitri break in if she’s not there? Tell me what you’re thinking!”

“You know why he’ll come. Why does it matter what I think? If anything, he’ll come because he’s angry or suspicious about my illness, just like he barged in yesterday to check if she’d snuck in. Plus, he knows Fyodor Pavlovitch has a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied with ribbon and sealed three times. It says, ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come,’ then later he added, ‘for my little chicken.’ Who knows what that could lead to?”

“That’s nonsense!” Ivan shouted, almost out of control. “Dmitri won’t break in to steal money and kill my father for it. He might have killed him over Grushenka, like a wild animal, but he wouldn’t steal.”

“He really needs money now, more than ever, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You don’t know how desperate he is,” Smerdyakov answered, calm and clear. “He considers those three thousand roubles his own—he told me so himself: ‘My father owes me exactly three thousand.’ And besides, think about it, Ivan Fyodorovitch. If Agrafena Alexandrovna wants to, she could make Fyodor Pavlovitch marry her. I know I said she wouldn’t come, but maybe she’s aiming higher—she might want to be the lady of the house. Samsonov, her merchant friend, teased her about it, saying it wouldn’t be a bad move. She’s smart—she wouldn’t marry a broke man like Dmitri. If she marries Fyodor Pavlovitch, then after your father dies, neither Dmitri, you, nor Alyosha would get anything—she’d get all the money. But if your father dies now, there would be about forty thousand roubles for Dmitri, even though Fyodor hates him, because he hasn’t made a will. Dmitri knows this.”
Ivan shuddered and his face suddenly turned red.
“Then why did you suggest I go to Tchermashnya? What are you getting at? If I leave, you see what could happen here.” Ivan was breathing hard.
“Exactly,” Smerdyakov said softly, watching Ivan closely.
“What do you mean, ‘exactly’?” Ivan demanded, his eyes flashing, barely keeping his temper in check.

“I only said it because I feel sorry for you. If I were you, I’d just give up and leave, rather than stay in this mess,” Smerdyakov replied, looking completely honest and meeting Ivan’s angry stare. They were both silent.

“You’re a complete idiot—and worse, a real scoundrel,” Ivan suddenly burst out, standing up. He was about to walk away, but stopped and turned back to Smerdyakov. Something strange happened—Ivan clenched his fists, bit his lip, and for a second looked like he might attack Smerdyakov, who flinched and shrank back. But Ivan stopped himself, turned silently and confused, and headed toward the gate.
“I’m leaving for Moscow tomorrow, if you care. Early in the morning. That’s all!” he suddenly shouted angrily, and later wondered why he’d bothered to tell Smerdyakov at all.
“That’s the smartest thing you could do,” Smerdyakov replied, like he’d been expecting it. “But you can always be sent a telegram from Moscow if anything happens here.”
Ivan stopped again and turned quickly to Smerdyakov. But now Smerdyakov looked different—all his casual friendliness was gone. His face was tense, expectant, but also nervous and kind of scared.
Ivan could see in Smerdyakov’s eyes that he was waiting for him to say something more, like, “Don’t you have something else to add?”
“And couldn’t I be sent for from Tchermashnya, too, if something happened?” Ivan suddenly shouted, for some reason raising his voice.
“From Tchermashnya, too...you could be sent for,” Smerdyakov muttered in almost a whisper, looking uneasy but staring into Ivan’s eyes.
“Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is closer. So is it just to save me travel money, or to keep me from going so far, that you keep pushing Tchermashnya?”

“Exactly...” Smerdyakov said in a shaky voice, giving Ivan a creepy smile and starting to back away. But to his surprise, Ivan suddenly laughed and walked through the gate, still laughing. Anyone who saw him would know he wasn’t laughing out of happiness, and Ivan himself couldn’t have explained how he felt. He moved and walked like someone wound up and close to losing control.

Ivan stormed into the drawing-room, clearly upset and nervous. As soon as he saw Fyodor Pavlovitch (his father), he waved his hands and yelled, “I’m going upstairs to my room, not to see you. Good-bye!” Without even glancing at his father, he hurried past. Maybe he hated his father too much at that moment to even look at him, but this open rudeness caught Fyodor Pavlovitch by surprise. The old man had actually come into the drawing-room on purpose to talk to Ivan. When Ivan ignored him like that, Fyodor Pavlovitch just stood there, silent and sarcastic, watching his son head up the stairs until he disappeared.
Right away, Fyodor Pavlovitch turned to Smerdyakov, who was following Ivan, and asked, “What’s wrong with him?”
Smerdyakov, the valet, just mumbled, “He’s angry about something. Who knows?”
“Bah! Let him be angry then. Bring in the samovar and get moving. Be quick! Any news?”

Fyodor Pavlovitch then started bombarding Smerdyakov with the same questions Smerdyakov had just complained about to Ivan—all about the expected visitor. We’ll skip those questions here. About half an hour later, the house was locked up, and the old man wandered through the rooms in a kind of wild anticipation, listening for the five knocks they had agreed on. Every so often, he’d peek out into the darkness, but saw nothing.

Meanwhile, Ivan was still wide awake, deep in restless thought. He stayed up until two in the morning. We won’t get into the details of what he was thinking now—his inner world is complicated and its turn will come later. Honestly, it would be hard to describe anyway, because his thoughts weren’t clear, just a blur of intense, nervous energy. He knew he felt lost and irritated, with all kinds of odd and even disturbing urges. For example, after midnight, he suddenly had a strong urge to go downstairs, open the door, and go beat up Smerdyakov. If you’d asked him why, he couldn’t have given a clear answer—maybe just that he hated Smerdyakov for insulting him worse than anyone else ever had. At other times that night, Ivan was struck by a strange, humiliating fear that made him feel physically paralyzed. His head hurt, and he felt dizzy. Anger was boiling inside him, as if he wanted to take revenge on someone. He even found himself angry at Alyosha, thinking about their recent conversation. Sometimes he hated himself too. Strangely, he almost forgot about Katerina Ivanovna, which surprised him later, especially since he remembered that when he had bravely told her he’d leave for Moscow the next day, some voice inside him whispered, “That’s a lie—you’re not going, and leaving won’t be as easy as you say.”

Much later, Ivan would remember that night with disgust—how he suddenly got up from the sofa, snuck out of his room as if he were afraid of being caught, and stood silently on the staircase listening to Fyodor Pavlovitch moving around downstairs. He stayed there for about five minutes, holding his breath, heart pounding, overwhelmed by a weird curiosity. He couldn’t even say why he was doing it. Later, he would call this his “worst action,” something he was deeply ashamed of. At that moment, he didn’t hate Fyodor Pavlovitch—he was just intensely curious about what his father was doing down there. He imagined his father peeking out of the dark windows, stopping in the middle of the room, listening for someone to knock. Ivan went onto the stairs twice that night just to listen like this.

By about two in the morning, when everything was quiet and even Fyodor Pavlovitch had gone to bed, Ivan finally got into bed himself, determined to fall asleep right away because he was exhausted. He did fall asleep instantly, sleeping deeply without dreams, but woke up early—at seven o’clock, with the sun already up. He was surprised to feel so energetic. He jumped out of bed, dressed quickly, dragged his trunk out, and started packing right away. His laundry had come back the day before, and Ivan actually smiled at how perfectly everything was falling into place for his sudden departure. It really was sudden, too. Even though he’d said yesterday (to Katerina Ivanovna, Alyosha, and Smerdyakov) that he was leaving the next day, he realized he hadn’t actually planned to leave when he went to bed. He hadn’t expected that the first thing he’d do in the morning was start packing. When he was done, it was about nine o’clock. Marfa Ignatyevna came in, as usual, and asked, “Where would you like your tea, sir? In your room or downstairs?” Ivan looked almost cheerful, but there was something rushed and distracted about him. He greeted his father politely and even asked about his health, but didn’t wait for the answer. Then he announced he’d be leaving in an hour, going back to Moscow for good, and asked for horses. His father didn’t seem surprised at all, and didn’t even bother to act sad about Ivan leaving. Instead, he suddenly remembered some business he needed to take care of.

“Why didn’t you tell me yesterday?” Fyodor Pavlovitch said. “Never mind, we’ll manage. Do me a favor, my boy. On your way, stop by Tchermashnya. It’s just a left turn from the station at Volovya—only twelve more versts and you’re there.”
“Sorry, I can’t,” Ivan replied. “It’s eighty versts to the railway, and the train for Moscow leaves at seven tonight. I’ll barely make it as it is.”

“You could catch the train tomorrow or the next day,” Fyodor Pavlovitch insisted. “Just turn off to Tchermashnya today. It won’t delay you much, and it would be a big help to your father! If I didn’t have things keeping me here, I’d have gone myself ages ago—I’ve got urgent business there. Listen, I have two small woods there. The Maslovs, a merchant and his son, are offering eight thousand for the timber. But last year, I almost sold it for twelve thousand. No one around here will pay more, since the Maslovs have a monopoly and everyone else is afraid to bid against them. But the priest at Ilyinskoe wrote me last Thursday saying a merchant named Gorstkin, whom I know, has arrived. He’s not from around here, so he’s not scared of the Maslovs. He says he’ll give eleven thousand for the woods. But he’ll only be here a week, the priest says, so you have to go right away and make the deal.”
“Why not just write to the priest? He can make the deal,” Ivan suggested.

“The priest isn’t good at business,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said. “I’d trust him with twenty thousand and not even need a receipt, but he’s clueless about deals—a child could fool him. And yet, he’s a smart, educated man! This Gorstkin looks like a peasant in his blue jacket, but he’s a real trickster. He’s a liar—he once told me his wife died and he’d remarried, but it was all a lie. His wife’s still alive and beats him up twice a week! So you need to find out if he’s lying or telling the truth about wanting to buy the woods for eleven thousand.”
“I’m no good at that kind of thing,” Ivan said. “I don’t have an eye for deals either.”

“Wait, listen!” his father said eagerly. “You’ll manage because I’ll tell you how to spot the truth with Gorstkin. I’ve done business with him for years. Watch his beard—he’s got a thin, reddish beard. If his beard shakes while he’s talking and he gets annoyed, then he’s serious and wants to do business. But if he strokes his beard with his left hand and grins, he’s trying to cheat you. Don’t bother watching his eyes—he’s too sly. Just watch the beard! I’ll give you a note for him. He’s called Gorstkin, but his real name is Lyagavy. Don’t call him Lyagavy or he’ll get offended. If you strike a deal and it seems real, send me a note right away—just write, ‘He’s not lying.’ Hold out for eleven thousand. If you have to, you can go as low as ten, but not less. Just think—the difference between eight and eleven thousand is huge! I really need the money. Once you say it’s serious, I’ll get there and seal the deal myself. But what’s the point of my rushing there if it’s just the priest’s fantasy? So, will you go?”
“I really can’t spare the time. Sorry,” Ivan said.

“Come on, do your father a favor. I’ll remember it. You have no heart, any of you. What’s a day or two—are you running off to Venice? Venice will still be there! I’d send Alyosha, but he’s useless for this. I’m asking you because you’re smart. You don’t know much about timber, but you can tell if someone’s serious. Just watch his beard—if it shakes, he’s in earnest.”
Ivan gave a bitter smile. “So you’re forcing me to go to that damn Tchermashnya yourself, then?”
Fyodor Pavlovitch either didn’t notice or pretended not to notice Ivan’s bitterness, but he did see the smile.
“So you’ll go, then? I’ll write the note right now.”
“I’m not sure yet. I’ll decide on the way.”

“Don’t be ridiculous—decide now! Please, settle it! If you finish the deal, send me a note through the priest and he’ll get it to me right away. I won’t hold you up any longer. You can go to Venice after. The priest will give you horses back to Volovya station.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch was thrilled. He wrote the note and called for the horses. They brought in a light meal and some brandy. Usually, when he was happy, Fyodor Pavlovitch would talk a lot, but today he seemed to hold back. He didn’t mention Dmitri at all, and didn’t seem to care about Ivan leaving. Ivan noticed this, thinking, “He must be bored with me.” When he walked his son out to the steps, Fyodor Pavlovitch started to fuss. He wanted to kiss Ivan goodbye, but Ivan quickly stuck out his hand, clearly dodging the kiss. Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed and stopped himself.
“Well, good luck! Good luck!” he called from the steps. “Come visit again sometime, all right? I’ll always be glad to see you. Well, may God go with you!”
Ivan got into the carriage.
“Goodbye, Ivan! Don’t be too hard on me!” his father called out one last time.
The whole household came out to say goodbye—Smerdyakov, Marfa, and Grigory. Ivan gave each of them ten roubles. As Ivan was getting settled in the carriage, Smerdyakov rushed up to arrange the rug.

Ivan suddenly blurted out, “You see... I’m going to Tchermashnya.” Just like the day before, the words seemed to come out on their own, and he laughed a strange, nervous laugh. He remembered it long afterward.
“So it’s true what they say—it’s always worth talking to a smart man,” Smerdyakov replied, looking at Ivan with special meaning in his eyes.

The carriage took off. Ivan’s mind was still a mess, but he stared eagerly at the fields, hills, trees, and a flock of geese flying high in the clear sky. Suddenly, he felt a wave of happiness. He tried talking to the driver and was strangely interested in the peasant’s answer, but realized a moment later that he hadn’t actually listened. He fell silent, and just being quiet felt nice. The air was cool and fresh, the sky bright. He thought about Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna, but just smiled and let the thoughts drift away. “There’s plenty of time for them,” he thought. They reached the station quickly, changed horses, and sped to Volovya. “Why is it worth talking to a smart man? What did Smerdyakov mean by that?” The question suddenly made him feel anxious. “And why did I tell him I was going to Tchermashnya?” They arrived at Volovya station. Ivan got out, and the drivers gathered around to discuss the price for the twelve versts to Tchermashnya. Ivan told them to get the horses ready. He stepped into the station house, looked around, glanced at the overseer’s wife, and suddenly turned back to the door.
“I’m not going to Tchermashnya. Is it too late to make the seven o’clock train, guys?”
“We’ll just make it. Want us to get the carriage ready?”
“Right away. Are any of you going to town tomorrow?”
“Sure thing. Mitri here will.”
“Mitri, could you do me a favor? Go to my father—Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov—and tell him I didn’t go to Tchermashnya. Can you do that?”
“Of course! I’ve known Fyodor Pavlovitch for years.”
Ivan laughed. “Here’s something for you, since he probably won’t give you anything.”
“You can count on that,” Mitri laughed too. “Thank you, sir. I’ll be sure to tell him.”

At seven o’clock, Ivan boarded the train for Moscow. “Goodbye to the past. I’m done with the old world forever, and I hope I never hear about it again. Here’s to a new life, new places, and no looking back!” But instead of feeling excited, Ivan was filled with a deep sadness and heartache like he’d never felt before. He spent the whole night thinking. The train sped on, and only at dawn, as they neared Moscow, did Ivan snap out of his thoughts.
“I’m a scoundrel,” he whispered to himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was happy after seeing his son off. For the next two hours, he felt almost cheerful and sat drinking brandy. But suddenly, something happened that upset the whole house and completely ruined his mood. Smerdyakov went down to the cellar and fell from the top of the steps. Luckily, Marfa Ignatyevna was in the yard and heard his scream—she knew that scream well, it was the sound Smerdyakov made when he had an epileptic fit. No one knew if the fit hit him on the stairs and caused the fall, or if the fall itself triggered the fit (Smerdyakov was known to be prone to them). They found him at the bottom of the stairs, writhing and foaming at the mouth. At first, they thought he must have broken an arm or leg, but “God protected him,” as Marfa said—he wasn’t hurt. It was hard to get him out of the cellar, but with help from the neighbors, they managed. Fyodor Pavlovitch was there the whole time, clearly worried. Smerdyakov didn’t wake up—the convulsions stopped for a while, then started again. Everyone figured it was like last year, when he’d fallen from the attic. They remembered putting ice on his head then, and since there was still ice in the cellar, Marfa brought some up. That evening, Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Doctor Herzenstube, an old, careful doctor. After examining Smerdyakov, the doctor said it had been a very bad fit and could have serious effects, but he didn’t fully understand it yet. By tomorrow morning, if Smerdyakov wasn’t better, he’d try something else. They moved Smerdyakov to a room in the lodge, next to where Grigory and Marfa slept.

That day, Fyodor Pavlovitch had one problem after another. Marfa cooked dinner, but compared to Smerdyakov’s, her soup was like dishwater and the chicken was so tough he couldn’t chew it. When he complained (fairly), Marfa said the chicken was old to begin with and she’d never been trained as a cook. That evening, there was more bad news—Grigory, who had been sick for three days, was now bedridden with back pain. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his tea early and locked himself up in the house, feeling nervous and on edge. He was expecting Grushenka to visit him that evening—almost certain of it. Smerdyakov had promised that morning that she’d definitely come. The old man’s heart raced with excitement. He paced through the empty rooms, listening. He had to be ready—Dmitri might be waiting for her somewhere outside, and when she knocked on the window (Smerdyakov had told her exactly how and where to knock), Fyodor Pavlovitch would need to open the door immediately, so she wouldn’t get scared and run away. He had a lot on his mind, but never had he felt such wild, hopeful excitement. This time, he was almost sure—she would really come!

When Alyosha entered his elder’s room, his heart was pounding with worry. He had expected to find Father Zossima weak, maybe even unconscious or dying. But what he saw surprised him: Father Zossima was sitting up in his chair, looking tired but cheerful, and talking quietly with a group of visitors. He had only gotten out of bed about fifteen minutes before Alyosha arrived. The visitors had actually come earlier and waited for him to wake up, because Father Païssy was sure that “the teacher will get up and, as he promised this morning, speak with those he loves one more time.” Father Païssy trusted Father Zossima’s promises completely—if Zossima had promised to say goodbye, Païssy would believe it even if Zossima stopped breathing. That morning, as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him, “I won’t die before I get to talk with you and see your face again.” The monks gathered around him had all been his close friends for years. There were four: Father Iosif; Father Païssy; Father Mihaïl, who was in charge of the hermitage and was a serious, strong-willed man who tried to hide his gentle side; and Father Anfim, a very old, quiet monk from a poor background. Father Anfim could barely read and rarely spoke, as if he was always a little scared of something too big to understand. Father Zossima was very fond of him and always treated him with respect, even though they hardly spoke, even when they traveled across Russia together forty years ago, begging for their poor monastery.

Everyone was crowded into the small bedroom—there was barely room for the four monks and Porfiry, the novice, to sit on chairs brought in from the other room. It was getting dark, but the room was lit by lamps and candles burning in front of the icons.
When Father Zossima saw Alyosha standing awkwardly in the doorway, he smiled warmly and held out his hand to him.
“Welcome, my quiet one, welcome, my dear. I knew you would come.”
Alyosha walked over, bowed low to the ground in front of his elder, and burst into tears. His heart was overflowing, and he almost started sobbing.

“Come now, don’t cry for me yet,” Father Zossima said with a smile, putting his right hand on Alyosha’s head. “See, I’m sitting up and talking. Maybe I’ll live another twenty years, just like that kind woman from Vishegorye wished yesterday, with her little daughter Lizaveta in her arms. God bless the mother and the little Lizaveta,” he said, making the sign of the cross. “Porfiry, did you give her offering where I told you?”

He meant the sixty copecks that the cheerful woman had brought the day before, asking that it be given “to someone poorer than me.” These kinds of gifts, earned by hard work, were often given as acts of repentance. Father Zossima had sent Porfiry just the night before to a widow whose house had burned down, leaving her and her children to beg for help. Porfiry quickly answered that he’d given the money, just as instructed, “from an unknown benefactress.”

“Stand up, my dear boy,” the elder continued to Alyosha. “Let me have a look at you. Have you been home and seen your brother?” Alyosha thought it was strange that he asked so directly about just one brother—but which one? Maybe Zossima had sent him out for that brother’s sake both yesterday and today.
“I saw one of my brothers,” Alyosha replied.
“I mean the older one, the one I bowed to.”
“I only saw him yesterday, and couldn’t find him today,” said Alyosha.

“Go and find him quickly. Go again tomorrow—don’t wait, drop everything and hurry. Maybe you can still stop something terrible from happening. Yesterday I bowed down before the great suffering he’s about to face.”
Father Zossima suddenly grew silent and thoughtful. His words were strange. Father Iosif, who had seen Zossima bow the day before, exchanged a look with Father Païssy. Alyosha couldn’t help asking:
“Father and teacher,” he said, his voice full of emotion, “your words are too mysterious... What suffering is waiting for him?”

“Don’t ask. Yesterday I felt like I saw something awful—like his whole future was in his eyes. There was a look in his eyes that filled me with horror, like he was heading toward disaster. Only once or twice before in my life have I seen that look, and every time, what I feared came true. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face might help him. But everything, all our fates, come from God. ‘Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings much fruit.’ Remember that. You, Alexey, I’ve often blessed you in my heart for your face, know that,” the elder added, smiling gently. “I believe you’ll leave these walls, but live as a monk in the world. You’ll have many enemies, but even they will love you. Life will bring you a lot of trouble, but you’ll find happiness in it, and you’ll help others find joy too—and that’s what matters most. That’s who you are. Fathers and teachers,” he said, turning to the others with a gentle smile, “I’ve never told even him why Alexey is so dear to me. I’ll tell you now. His face has always reminded me of something from my own life, and seems almost like a prophecy. When I was a child, I had an older brother who died at seventeen, right in front of me. Later, I came to believe that his life was a sign from God for me—if he hadn’t come into my life, I might never have become a monk or chosen this path. He appeared to me at the start of my life, and now, at the end, it’s like he’s come back in Alexey. It’s amazing, fathers and teachers, that Alexey, who only slightly resembles him in looks, feels so much like him in spirit that many times I felt as if he was my brother come back to me, to remind and inspire me. I even wondered at myself for thinking such strange things. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” he asked the novice. “Sometimes I’ve seen you look sad because I love Alexey more than you. Now you know why, but I love you too, and I’ve felt bad for making you sad. I’d like to tell you all about my brother, because no one in my life was more important or precious. My heart is full of tenderness, and right now it’s like my whole life is happening all over again.”

I should mention here that this final conversation between Father Zossima and his friends on his last day was partly written down. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov (Alyosha) wrote it from memory, some time after Zossima died. But it’s not clear if Alyosha only wrote what was said that night, or if he added parts from earlier talks too. In his version, Father Zossima’s story flows without interruption, like he’s telling his life story all at once, but other people say the conversation that night was more back-and-forth. The visitors didn’t interrupt much, but they did talk a bit themselves. Besides, Father Zossima was sometimes out of breath, his voice would fail, and he’d have to lie down to rest, though he didn’t fall asleep and his friends didn’t leave. A couple of times, Father Païssy stopped the conversation to read from the Gospel. Also, no one thought Zossima would die that night, because after his long sleep during the day, he seemed to have a sudden burst of energy. It was like a last wave of love that gave him strength—but only for a little while, because he died soon after. But more about that later. For now, I’ll stick to what Alexey wrote—it’s shorter and less tiring, even though he probably mixed in things from earlier conversations.
Notes on the Life of the late Elder and Monk Zossima, written down from his own words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.
Biographical Notes
(a) Father Zossima’s Brother

Dear fathers and teachers, I was born in a far-off northern province, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman, but he wasn’t rich or important. He died when I was only two, so I don’t remember him. He left my mother a small wooden house and enough money for her and her children to live comfortably. There were two of us, my older brother Markel and me. He was eight years older, had a quick temper, but was kind and never made fun of people. He was very quiet at home with our mother, me, and the servants. He did well in school, but didn’t fit in with the other boys, though he never fought with them, at least that’s what my mother said. Six months before he died, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile, a scholar from Moscow who lived alone in our town because of his “freethinking.” The exile liked Markel and invited him over, so my brother spent many evenings with him that winter, until the exile was allowed to return to Petersburg, thanks to his powerful friends.

Lent began, and Markel refused to fast. He was rude about it and laughed, saying, “That’s all nonsense, and there’s no God,” which shocked my mother, the servants, and even me—I was only nine, but I was horrified to hear such things. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of them, our lame old cook Afimya, for sixty paper rubles, and hiring a free servant instead.

In the sixth week of Lent, my brother, who had always been weak and looked sickly, fell ill. He was tall but thin, with a gentle face. Maybe he caught a cold, but the doctor soon whispered to my mother that it was advanced tuberculosis and he wouldn’t live through the spring. My mother started to cry, but tried to hide her worry from my brother. She begged him to go to church, to confess, and take communion while he still could walk. This made him angry, and he said something disrespectful about the church. Still, he became thoughtful, realizing he was really sick and that’s why Mom was begging him to confess. He had known he wasn’t healthy for a long time, and even a year before, he had calmly told us at dinner, “I won’t be with you long, I might not live another year,” which now seemed like he’d predicted his own death.

Three days went by, and Holy Week began. On Tuesday morning, my brother started going to church. “I’m only doing this for you, Mother, to make you happy,” he said. My mother wept with both happiness and sadness. She thought, “His end must be near if he’s changed this much.” But he couldn’t go to church for long—soon he was too sick to leave his bed, so he had to confess and take communion at home.

That year, Easter came late, and the days were bright, beautiful, and full of spring scents. My brother coughed all night and slept badly, but every morning he got dressed and tried to sit up in an armchair. That’s how I remember him: gentle, smiling, his face glowing with happiness even though he was very sick. Something amazing happened to him—his spirit seemed to change completely. Our old nurse would come in and say, “Let me light the lamp in front of the holy image, my dear.” Before, he would have stopped her and blown it out.
“Light it, light it, dear. I was wrong to stop you. When you light the lamp, you’re praying, and when I see you do it, I’m praying too. So we’re both praying to the same God.”

Those words sounded strange to us, and my mother would go to her room and cry. But when she went to see him, she wiped her tears and tried to look cheerful. “Mother, don’t cry, darling,” he’d say. “I have a long life ahead, a long time to be happy with you, and life is good and joyful.”
“Oh, my dear boy, how can you talk about joy when you lie awake every night coughing so much?”
“Don’t cry, mother,” he’d answer. “Life is paradise, and we’re all in paradise, but we don’t see it. If we did, we’d have heaven on earth right now.”

Everyone was amazed by what he said—he spoke so strangely and with such certainty. We were all touched and cried. Friends came to see him. “Dear ones,” he’d say, “what did I ever do to make you love me? How can you love someone like me, and how did I not realize it before?”
When the servants came in, he’d say over and over, “Kind people, why are you doing so much for me? Do I deserve it? If God let me live, I’d serve you, because everyone should serve each other.”
Mother would shake her head when she heard that. “My darling, it’s your illness making you talk like that.”

“Mother, darling,” he’d say, “there have to be servants and masters, but if so, I want to be the servant of my servants, just as they are to me. And another thing, mother—every one of us has sinned against everyone else, and I more than anyone.”

Mother even smiled through her tears. “How could you have sinned against everyone, more than anyone? Only criminals have done that. What sin could you have committed, that you think you’re worse than all?”

“Mother, my little heart,” he said (he had started using these sweet words), “my joy, believe me: everyone is really responsible for everyone else and for everything. I don’t know how to explain it, but I feel it deeply. How did we live before, getting angry and not knowing this?”
So each day he became kinder, happier, and more loving. When the doctor, an old German named Eisenschmidt, came:
“Well, doctor, do I have another day in this world?” my brother would ask, joking.
“You’ll live many more days,” the doctor would say, “and months and years too.”

“Months and years!” he’d exclaim. “Why count the days? One day is enough to know real happiness. Why do we argue, try to show off, and hold grudges? Let’s go outside, walk and play, love each other, and be grateful for life.”
“Your son can’t last long,” the doctor told my mother at the door. “The disease is affecting his brain.”

His room looked out on our shady garden, with old trees budding and the first birds of spring singing at the windows. Watching them, he suddenly started asking their forgiveness too: “Birds of heaven, happy birds, forgive me, for I have sinned against you too.” None of us understood that then, but he cried tears of happiness. “Yes,” he said, “God’s glory was all around me—birds, trees, grass, the sky—but I lived in shame and didn’t notice the beauty.”
“You take too many sins on yourself,” Mother would say, crying.

“Mother, it’s for joy, not sadness, that I’m crying. I can’t explain it, but I want to humble myself before them, because I don’t know how to love them enough. If I’ve sinned against everyone, they all forgive me too, and that’s heaven. Aren’t I in heaven now?”

There was a lot more I can’t remember. I remember one evening, the sun was setting and the whole room was filled with light. I went in when no one else was there. He motioned for me to come closer. He put his hands on my shoulders and looked at me with so much love, but said nothing for a minute.
“Well,” he said, “run and play now—enjoy life for me too.”

I went out and ran to play. Many times since, I’ve remembered—sometimes with tears—how he told me to enjoy life for him. There were many other amazing things he said, though we didn’t understand at the time. He died three weeks after Easter. He was conscious but couldn’t talk, but he was still happy, his eyes shining as he looked for us, smiling and beckoning. Even people in the town talked about his death. I was impressed, but not too much—after all, I was just a child—but the feeling never left my heart, waiting to wake up again when the time was right. And that’s exactly what happened.
(b) The Holy Scriptures in Father Zossima’s Life

After that, I was left with only my mother. Her friends advised her to send me to Petersburg, like other parents did. “You only have one son left and enough money, and you’ll ruin his future if you keep him here,” they said. They suggested I should go to the Cadet Corps in Petersburg, and then maybe join the Imperial Guard. Mother hesitated for a long time—it was hard to send away her only child—but finally decided it was for my good, though she cried a lot. She brought me to Petersburg and enrolled me in the Cadet Corps, and I never saw her again, because she died three years later. She spent those years mourning for both her sons.

The only things I took from my childhood home were precious memories, because nothing is more valuable than the memories of childhood in your first home—especially if there was any love or peace at all. Even a difficult home can leave good memories, if your heart knows how to find them. Among my memories, I especially remember the Bible, which I loved reading as a child. I had a book called A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament, filled with pictures, and I learned to read with it. I still have it on my shelf as a treasure from the past. Even before I could read, I remember being moved at age eight, when my mother took me alone to mass (I don’t remember where my brother was) on the Monday before Easter. It was a beautiful day, and I still see in my mind the incense floating upward, mixing with the sunlight in the church. I was deeply moved, and for the first time I felt God’s word planted in me. I watched a youth carry a huge book to the center of the church, open it, and begin to read—and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something I heard in church. It was the story of Job, a righteous and wealthy man whose children feasted and whom he loved. The devil came before God and challenged Him, and God allowed the devil to take everything from Job. Job lost his children and his wealth, but fell to the ground and cried, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I’ll return. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord forever.”

Fathers and teachers, forgive me if I cry now—my childhood comes back to me, and I feel as I did at eight years old, full of awe and wonder. The camels in the story amazed me, and the idea of Satan talking to God, and God letting His servant suffer.
