Yet Job said, “Blessed be Your name even though You punish me.” The singing in the church, the incense, the prayers—all of it has stayed with me. Even now, I can’t read that story without tears. There’s so much mystery in it! Later, I heard people mock the story, saying, “How could God let the devil destroy His best servant, just to make a point?” But that’s the whole point: it’s a mystery, where the temporary and the eternal come together. God looks at Job and praises His creation, and Job, by praising God through his suffering, helps everyone for all time. The Bible is an amazing book, full of wisdom for every age. It has answers for everything, and so many mysteries! God restores Job, gives him more children and happiness. But how could he love the new children after losing his first ones? Yet he could. The great mystery of life is that old grief turns into gentle, peaceful joy. Growing older, I love the setting sun even more than the rising, because it brings soft memories and a sense of forgiveness. My life is ending, but every day I feel closer to a new, unknown life, and it fills me with happiness and tears of joy.

Friends and teachers, I’ve heard many times lately that priests, especially those in villages, complain about their low pay and hard lives. They say they can’t teach the Bible to their people because they’re too poor, and if Lutherans or non-believers come to lead the people away, they let it happen because they have so little. May God help them, because their complaint is fair. But honestly, some of the blame is ours. Even if he’s busy, a priest can find an hour a week to remember God. He doesn’t work all year. He can gather people, at least the children at first, into his own cottage and read to them from the Bible. He doesn’t need to speak grandly—just read kindly, stopping now and then to explain. The people will understand, especially the children. Read them about Abraham and Sarah, about Isaac, about Jacob’s dream, about Joseph’s brothers selling him, and how Joseph forgave them. Tell them about old Jacob’s prophecy that from his family would come the Messiah.

Fathers and teachers, please forgive me for talking about things you know so much better than I do. I just love the Bible so much. Let the priest love it too, and his listeners will feel it. Even a tiny seed planted in a peasant’s heart will never die. You don’t need big explanations—they’ll understand. Try reading about Esther, or Jonah and the whale, or Jesus’ parables—especially from Luke—and the story of Saul turning into St. Paul. Tell them about saints like Alexey, the man of God, or Mary of Egypt. Just give them one hour a week, even if you’re poor, and you’ll see how grateful people are. They’ll help their priest and respect him even more, making his life better. It’s so simple that people might laugh at me for saying it, but it’s true! If someone doesn’t believe in God, they won’t believe in God’s people either. But if they do believe, they’ll see God’s holiness, even if they didn’t before. Only the people, with their future spiritual power, can bring back those who have lost their faith and connection.
What good are Christ’s words if we don’t set an example? People are lost without God’s word—their souls are thirsty for it and for goodness.

When I was young, nearly forty years ago, I traveled all over Russia with Father Anfim, collecting donations for our monastery. Once, we spent the night with some fishermen by a big river. A good-looking eighteen-year-old peasant stayed with us; he had to get up early to help pull a merchant’s barge. I noticed his clear, kind eyes, staring into the night. It was a warm, quiet July night, and everything was calm and peaceful. Only he and I were awake, and we talked about the beauty and mystery of the world. Every blade of grass and every animal follows its own path, showing God’s mystery. I saw the boy’s heart was touched. He told me he loved being in the forest and listening to the birds. He was a bird-catcher, knew every bird’s song, and could imitate them. “There’s nothing better than being in the forest,” he said, “though everything is good.”

“You’re right,” I told him. “Everything is good and beautiful because it’s all true. Look at the horse, or the gentle ox that works for man. See their kind faces, their trust, their beauty. It’s touching to know they are sinless, while only people sin. Christ has been with them before us.”
The boy asked, “Why is Christ with them too?”

“He must be,” I answered, “because the Word is for all. Every creature, every leaf, is reaching for the Word, praising God, and crying out to Christ, without even knowing it. Even the fierce bear, wandering in the forest, is innocent in its way.” I told him a story about a bear coming to a saint living in a tiny hut in the woods. The saint felt sorry for the bear, gave it bread, and said, ‘Go on, Christ be with you.’ The bear left without hurting anyone. The boy was delighted by that. “How wonderful that even the bear was gentle, and Christ was with him too!” he said. He sat quietly, thinking. I knew he understood. He fell asleep beside me, peaceful and innocent. God bless the young! I prayed for him that night: Lord, bring peace and light to Your people!
(c) Memories from Father Zossima’s Youth: The Duel

I spent almost eight years at the military cadet school in Petersburg, and during that time, the memories from my childhood grew faint, even though I didn’t forget anything. I learned so many new habits and opinions that I became cruel and ridiculous—almost wild. I did pick up the manners of polite society and learned to speak French.

But all of us, including me, thought of the soldiers under our command as nothing more than animals. I was probably the worst of the group because I was so sensitive and quick to pick up on things. By the time we graduated as officers, we were ready to die for the regiment’s honor, but none of us really knew what honor meant. If anyone had actually understood it, he would have been mocked. We almost bragged about our drinking, wild parties, and bad behavior. I’m not saying we were bad people deep down—my friends were good guys—but we acted terribly, and I was the worst. It was even easier for me to go wild because I had just inherited my own money, so I threw myself into a life of partying and did everything reckless that young men do.

I liked reading, but strangely, the Bible was the only book I never opened during that time, even though I always carried it with me. I was never separated from it; it was like I was saving it for some special time in the future, though I didn’t realize it then.

After four years of that lifestyle, my regiment was sent to the town of K. The people there were welcoming, wealthy, and loved to host parties. Since I was outgoing and known to have money, I was warmly received everywhere. Then something happened that changed everything.

I fell for a beautiful and smart young woman with a strong character. Her family was respected and influential. They were always kind to me, and I thought she liked me back. My heart raced at the thought she might love me, too. Looking back, I realize I probably wasn’t really in love with her—I just admired her intelligence and goodness. Still, I didn’t propose to her because I didn’t want to give up my fun, free life as a bachelor with money in my pocket. I hinted at my feelings, but kept putting off doing anything serious. Suddenly, our regiment was sent away for two months.

When I got back, I found out she had already married a rich landowner from the area. He was a nice man, still young but older than me, connected to high society in Petersburg, and much better educated than I was. The news hit me so hard I could barely think straight. The worst part was that I found out they had been engaged for a long time, and I had even met him at her house, but I was too full of myself to notice. Everyone else knew about it except me. I was furious. I remembered all the times I was about to declare my love to her, and since she hadn’t stopped me, I convinced myself she had been making fun of me the whole time. Later I understood she had never laughed at me—she would always change the subject or joke around to avoid any romantic talk—but at that moment, I couldn’t think clearly. I was obsessed with getting revenge. It’s strange, because anger didn’t come naturally to me and I usually couldn’t stay mad for long, so I had to work myself up on purpose, and I ended up acting completely ridiculous and disgusting.

I waited for a chance and finally managed to insult my “rival” in front of a big group of people. I made fun of his opinion about an important public event (this was in 1826). People said my insult was clever and hit home. I pushed him to demand an explanation, and I was so rude that he eventually agreed to a duel, even though he was older, more important, and higher in rank. I later found out he accepted out of jealousy—he’d been jealous of me even before they were married, and now he was afraid that if he let me insult him without fighting back, his wife might lose respect for him. I quickly found a friend from my regiment to be my “second.” Even though duels were supposed to be illegal and punished harshly, fighting duels was still a trend among officers—sometimes society clings to dangerous traditions for a long time.

It was late June, and the duel was set for seven o’clock the next morning on the edge of town. That evening, I came home in an angry, violent mood and lost my temper with my servant, Afanasy. I hit him twice in the face, so hard that he bled. He hadn’t worked for me long, and I had hit him before, but never so cruelly. Even though it’s been forty years, I still remember it with shame and pain. I went to bed and slept for about three hours. When I woke up at dawn, I got up, went to the window, and opened it. The sun was rising, the garden looked beautiful, and birds were singing.

“What’s wrong with me?” I thought. “Why do I feel so dirty and ashamed? Is it because I’m about to fight a duel and maybe kill someone? No, that’s not it. Am I afraid of dying? No, that’s not it either.” Suddenly it hit me: it was because I had beaten Afanasy the night before! I remembered every detail—how he stood there, arms stiff at his sides, head up, eyes straight ahead, taking the blows without defending himself. That’s what I had done to another human being! It felt like a knife went through my heart. I stood there stunned while the sun shone, the trees rustled, and the birds sang God’s praises. I hid my face in my hands, fell on my bed, and sobbed. Then I remembered my brother Markel on his deathbed, saying to his servants, “My dear ones, why do you wait on me, why do you love me, am I even worth it?”

“Am I worth it?” I thought. “Why should another person, made in God’s image just like me, serve me?” For the first time in my life, that question hit me hard. My brother had said, “Mother, my heart, we’re each responsible to everyone for everything, but people don’t realize it. If they did, the world would be paradise.”

“God, is that true?” I thought through my tears. “Maybe I really am more responsible for everything than anyone else—maybe I’m the biggest sinner of all.” Suddenly I saw the truth—that I was about to kill a good, smart, noble man who had never wronged me. And by doing that, I’d also be ruining his wife’s happiness for the rest of her life. I lay there with my face in the pillow, not caring how much time passed. Suddenly my second, the ensign, came in with the pistols.
“Ah,” he said, “it’s good you’re up. Time to go, let’s get moving!”
I was at a loss and rushed around, unsure what to do, but we went out to the carriage.
“Wait here a minute,” I told him. “I’ll be right back, I forgot my wallet.”
I ran back alone to Afanasy’s little room.
“Afanasy,” I said, “yesterday I hit you in the face—please forgive me.”
He jumped as if scared and stared at me. I realized that wasn’t enough, so right then and there, still in my officer’s uniform, I dropped to my knees at his feet and bowed my head to the floor.
“Forgive me,” I repeated.
He was completely stunned.
“Your honor ... sir, what are you doing? Am I worth it?”
Then he burst into tears like I had, covered his face, turned to the window, and shook with sobs. I ran out to my friend and jumped into the carriage.
“Ready!” I shouted. “Ever seen a real winner? Here’s one!”
I was overjoyed, laughing and talking the whole way—I don’t even remember what about.
My friend looked at me. “Wow, you’re brave,” he said. “You’ll bring honor to the uniform, I can tell.”

We got to the site and found them waiting. We stood twelve paces apart. He had the first shot. I stood cheerfully, looking him straight in the eyes, not flinching at all—I looked at him with kindness, because I knew what I was going to do. His bullet grazed my cheek and ear.
“Thank God, no one’s dead!” I cried, then threw my own pistol far into the woods. “That’s where you belong!” I shouted.
I turned to my opponent.
“Please forgive me, sir. I insulted you for no reason and made you shoot at me. I’m ten times worse than you, maybe more. Tell that to the person who means the most to you.”
As soon as I said that, all three of them started yelling at me.
“Honestly,” my opponent snapped, “if you didn’t want to fight, why didn’t you just leave me alone?”
“Yesterday I was a fool. Today I know better,” I said, still cheerful.
“I believe you about yesterday,” he replied, “but I’m not sure about today.”
“Well said!” I clapped my hands. “You’re right, I deserve that.”
“Are you going to shoot or not?” he asked.
“No, I’m not. If you want, shoot at me again, but it’s better if you don’t.”
The seconds—especially my friend—were shouting, “How can you embarrass the regiment like this, standing here apologizing in a duel! If I’d known you’d do this...”
I stood facing them all, not laughing anymore.
“Gentlemen,” I said, “is it really so strange these days for someone to admit their mistake and say sorry in public?”
“But not during a duel!” my friend shouted again.

“That’s what’s so strange,” I replied. “I should have admitted my fault as soon as I got here, before a shot was fired, before dragging him into deadly sin. But our lives have become so twisted that it’s almost impossible to do that. Only after facing his shot at twelve paces would my words mean anything—if I’d spoken up sooner, he’d have said, ‘He’s just a coward, afraid of the pistols—no point listening to him.’ Gentlemen,” I suddenly said, “look around at God’s gifts: the clear sky, fresh air, soft grass, the birds—nature is beautiful and pure, but we are sinful and foolish. We don’t understand that life is heaven, and if we did, it would become heaven instantly—we’d hug each other and cry.”
I wanted to say more but couldn’t; my voice broke from the joy and sweetness of it all, and I felt happier than ever before.
“All this is very wise and inspiring,” said my opponent, “and you’re certainly an unusual person.”
“Go ahead and laugh,” I told him, laughing too, “but you’ll agree with me someday.”
“Actually, I agree with you now,” he said. “Want to shake hands? I really believe you’re sincere.”
“No, not now—later, when I’ve become better and earned your respect. Then shake my hand and it’ll be real.”
We went home, my friend scolding me all the way while I hugged him. My fellow officers found out immediately and gathered to judge me that same day.
“He’s disgraced the uniform,” some said. “He should resign.”
Some stuck up for me: “He stood his ground and took the shot.”
“Yeah, but he was scared of the second shot and begged for forgiveness,” said others.
“If he was scared of being shot, he would have fired his own pistol first before asking forgiveness. Instead, he threw it away loaded. No, there’s something different about this—something new.”

I liked listening to them. “My friends,” I said, “don’t worry about me resigning—I already have. I turned in my resignation this morning, and as soon as I’m officially discharged, I’ll join a monastery. That’s why I’m leaving the regiment.”
When I said that, everyone burst out laughing.
“You should have told us that first—now it all makes sense! You can’t judge a monk.”

They couldn’t stop laughing, but it wasn’t mean—it was friendly and good-natured. Suddenly everyone was nice to me, even the ones who had been harshest. During the month before my discharge came through, they were extra kind. “Ah, you monk,” they’d say, and everyone had something nice to say. They tried to talk me out of it and even felt sorry for me: “What are you doing to yourself?”
“No,” others would say, “he’s brave—he took the shot and could have shot back, but he had a dream he’d become a monk, that’s why he did it.”

The same thing happened with people in town. Before, they’d been polite but not especially interested, but now everyone noticed me and invited me over. They laughed at me, but they liked me. Even though everyone talked about our duel, the authorities ignored it—my opponent was related to the general, no one was injured, and I had quit the army. They treated it as a joke. I started to speak openly and fearlessly, not caring if people laughed, because it was always friendly laughter. These talks often happened in the evening in the company of ladies, and they made the men listen, too.
“But how can I be responsible for everyone?” people would laugh. “How could I be responsible for you?”

“You don’t realize it,” I’d say, “because the world has been going about things differently for so long. We treat lies as truth and expect others to do the same. I’ve finally acted honestly for once, and you all think I’m crazy. Even though you’re nice to me, you’re all laughing.”

“But how can we help liking you?” said my hostess, laughing. The room was full. Suddenly, the young woman who was the reason for the duel, the one I’d once hoped to marry, stood up. I hadn’t even noticed her come in. She walked over to me and held out her hand.
“Let me tell you,” she said, “I’m the first not to laugh at you. On the contrary, I thank you with tears and respect you for what you did.”

Her husband came over, too, and then everyone gathered around me, almost hugging and kissing me. My heart was full of joy, but I especially noticed a middle-aged man who came up as well. I already knew his name, but had never actually met him until that night.
(d) The Mysterious Visitor

This man had been an important official in town for a long time—well-respected, wealthy, and known for his charity. He gave generously to the orphanage and almshouse, and secretly helped others, too—people only found out after he died. He was about fifty, looked stern, and didn’t talk much. He’d been married ten years, and his young wife had given him three children. The next evening, while I was alone in my room, he suddenly walked in.

By the way, I wasn’t living in my old place anymore. After resigning, I moved into rooms owned by an old widow whose servant took care of me. I went there because after the duel, I’d sent Afanasy back to the regiment—I was too ashamed to face him after our last meeting. That’s how easily people can feel embarrassed by doing the right thing.
“I’ve listened to you speak at different houses these last few days,” my visitor said, “and I wanted to meet you in person so we could talk more privately. Would you allow me that?”

“Of course, it’s an honor,” I replied, though I was a bit nervous. He made a strong impression on me right away. Other people had listened to me with interest, but no one had come to see me so seriously and intensely. Now he was sitting in my own room.
“You seem very strong-willed,” he said, “since you stood up for the truth even when you risked everyone’s contempt.”
“You’re probably giving me too much credit,” I answered.

“Not at all,” he said. “What you did is harder than you think, and that’s why I came to see you. Tell me, if you don’t mind, what exactly did you feel when you decided to ask for forgiveness at the duel? I’m not asking just to be nosy—there’s a personal reason, which maybe I’ll explain if we get to know each other better.”
As he talked, I looked him straight in the face and suddenly felt I could trust him completely. I was also very curious, because I sensed he was hiding something important.

“You want to know what I felt when I apologized at the duel,” I said, “but maybe it’s better if I tell you everything from the start—things I haven’t told anyone else.” I told him what had happened with Afanasy and how I had bowed down at his feet. “So you see,” I finished, “that by the time of the duel, I’d already started down that path, and once I took the first step, it wasn’t hard to keep going—it actually made me happy.”
I liked the way he listened to me. “That’s very interesting,” he said. “I’ll come see you again and again.”

And that’s what he did—he visited me nearly every evening. We could have become close friends if only he’d talked about himself, but he almost never did. He always asked about me instead. Still, I really liked him and spoke openly about my feelings, thinking, “Why should I need to know his secrets if I can already tell he’s a good man?” Even though he was older and serious, he treated me as an equal, and I learned a lot from him—he was very wise.

“I’ve been thinking for a long time that life is heaven,” he told me suddenly. Then he added, “Actually, I think about nothing else.” He looked at me and smiled. “I believe it even more than you do—I’ll tell you why someday.”
I listened and thought he clearly wanted to tell me something important.
“Heaven is hidden inside each of us,” he continued. “It’s inside me right now, and if I really want to, I can make it appear—tomorrow, and forever.”
I looked at him—he was speaking with real passion and staring at me as if waiting for a response.

“And you were completely right that we’re all responsible for everyone else’s actions, not just our own. It’s amazing you understood that so quickly. Once people accept that, the Kingdom of Heaven won’t just be a dream—it’ll be real.”
“But when?” I asked him sadly. “When will that actually happen? Will it ever happen, or is it just a fantasy?”

“You don’t believe it,” he said. “You preach it, but you don’t really believe. Believe me, this dream will come true—but not right away. Everything has its own time. It’s a spiritual process. To change the world, people need to change inside, become different. Until we really treat each other like brothers, brotherhood won’t exist. No scientific theory or shared interest will make people treat each other fairly—everyone will think they deserve more and complain or fight. You ask when it’ll happen—it will, but first comes an age of isolation.”
“What do you mean by isolation?” I asked.

“I mean the way everyone tries to keep to themselves these days—especially now, though it hasn’t reached its worst yet. Everyone wants to make the most of life for themselves, but all they get is loneliness. People split into little groups, stick to their own routines, and keep their distance. Each person keeps to himself, hides what he has, and ends up pushing others away. He saves up money and thinks, ‘Now I’m strong and safe,’ but doesn’t see he’s only making himself weaker. He’s learned to rely on no one but himself, to cut himself off from others, and he’s afraid to lose his money and privileges. These days, people don’t understand that true safety comes from sticking together, not from going it alone. But this kind of selfishness has to end sometime. One day, people will realize how strange it is that they’ve been so separated. Then, the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky.... Until then, we have to keep the idea alive, even if just one person does it, even if he looks crazy. He has to set an example, to help others out of their loneliness, so the great idea doesn’t die.”

Night after night, we had these deep, passionate talks. I stopped visiting people in town so much—my popularity was fading anyway, though people still liked me and treated me well. I started to admire my mysterious visitor, not just for his mind, but because I could tell he was planning something big in his heart. Maybe he liked that I didn’t pry into his secret, but I began to notice that he seemed like he wanted to tell me something. This grew more obvious about a month after he started visiting.
“You know,” he said to me one day, “people in town are curious about why I visit you so often. But let them wonder—it’ll all come out soon.”

Sometimes he’d get extremely nervous and leave suddenly. Other times, he’d stare at me intensely, and I’d think, “He’s about to say something important,” but then he’d change the subject. He also complained about headaches often.
Then one day, after he’d been speaking passionately for a long time, I saw him go pale, his face twitching, and he stared hard at me.
“What’s wrong?” I asked. “Are you feeling sick?” He had just said he had a headache.
“I ... you know ... I murdered someone.”
He said this and gave a pale smile. I thought, “Why is he smiling?” before I could even process the words. I went pale, too.
“What are you saying?” I cried out.
“You see,” he said, still pale and smiling, “it took everything just to say that first word. Now that I’ve said it, I’ll keep going.”

For a while I didn’t believe him, and not even then. But after he visited me for three days and told me everything, I realized he was telling the truth, and it shocked and saddened me. His crime was truly terrible.

Fourteen years earlier, he had killed the widow of a wealthy landowner—a young, beautiful woman who owned a house in our town. He fell deeply in love with her, confessed his feelings, and tried to get her to marry him. But she loved another—a high-ranking officer who was away at war but was coming back soon. She rejected him and told him not to come anymore. After he stopped visiting, he used his knowledge of her house to sneak in at night through the garden and the roof, risking being caught. But sometimes bold crimes succeed where cautious ones don’t.

He entered through the attic window and climbed down a ladder, hoping the door at the bottom would be left unlocked, as it sometimes was. It was. He crept in the dark to her bedroom, where a lamp was burning. Both her maids had gone to a birthday party nearby without permission. The other servants were sleeping in the servants’ quarters or kitchen downstairs. He was overwhelmed when he saw her sleeping, and then jealousy and anger took over. Like a man possessed, he stabbed her in the heart. She didn’t even cry out. Then, to make it look like the servants did it, he stole her purse and some things from her chest, taking only money and leaving more valuable items. He also took a few things as keepsakes. When he was done, he left the way he had come.

The next day, and ever after, no one suspected him. No one knew he’d loved her—he was always quiet and had no close friends. People thought he was just a casual acquaintance, and he hadn’t visited her for two weeks. One of her serfs, Pyotr, was immediately suspected. She’d made it clear that she planned to send Pyotr as a conscript because he had no family and was badly behaved. People had heard him threaten her while drunk. Two days before the murder, he had run away and spent the night somewhere in town. The day after the murder, he was found on the road out of town, drunk, with a knife in his pocket and blood on his hand. He claimed it was a nosebleed, but no one believed him. The maids admitted they’d gone to a party and left the door open. Everything pointed to the innocent servant.

He was arrested and put on trial, but a week later he got sick with a fever and died in the hospital without ever regaining consciousness. That was the end of it—everyone, including the judges and townspeople, believed the servant was guilty. Then the real punishment began.

My mysterious visitor—now my friend—told me that at first, he didn’t feel guilty at all. He was miserable, but not because of the murder—only because he regretted killing the woman he loved. He hardly even thought about the innocent blood he’d spilled. The idea that she might have married someone else was unbearable, so for a long time, he told himself he had no choice.

He worried when the servant was arrested, but the man’s illness and death soon made him feel safe. He thought the fever wasn’t caused by the arrest, but by the man getting drunk and sleeping outside on cold ground. The theft didn’t bother him much either—he told himself he only did it to divert suspicion. The stolen money wasn’t much, and soon after, he donated it (and more) to the almshouse, to calm his conscience. For a while, that actually worked. He threw himself into his work, volunteering for tough assignments for two years, and almost forgot what he’d done. When memories came up, he tried to push them aside. He got very involved in charity, helped set up institutions in town and in both Moscow and Petersburg, and was elected to several charity societies.

Eventually, though, he started thinking about the past, and it was too much for him. He fell in love again and got married, hoping that loving his wife and children would help him forget his loneliness and guilt. But the opposite happened. Even in the first month of marriage, he was bothered by the thought, “My wife loves me—but what if she knew?” When she announced she was pregnant, he felt guilty. “I’m giving life, but I’ve taken life.” When the children were born, he thought, “How can I talk to them about goodness? I’ve spilled blood.” He longed to hug them, but felt unworthy when he looked at their innocent faces.

He started being haunted by the blood of his victim and the life he’d destroyed. Nightmares began. But he was tough—he tried to bear it, thinking, “I’ll make up for it by suffering in silence.” But that only made it worse.

People respected him for his charity, though they were a little afraid of his gloomy, stern manner. But the more they respected him, the more unbearable it became. He even thought about killing himself. Then another idea took hold—one he first thought impossible, but that eventually he couldn’t stop thinking about: publicly confessing to the murder. For three years, this idea followed him in different forms. Finally, he was convinced that if he confessed, his soul would be healed and he’d be at peace. But the thought also terrified him—how could he possibly go through with it? Then he saw what happened at my duel.
“Watching you, I made up my mind.”
I looked at him.
“Is it possible,” I cried, “that something so small pushed you to such a big decision?”
“I’ve been thinking about it for three years,” he answered. “Your story was just the last straw. Watching you, I felt ashamed of myself and jealous.” He said this almost angrily.
“But no one will believe you,” I said. “It’s been fourteen years.”
“I have proof. Strong proof. I’ll show them.”
I burst into tears and hugged him.

“Tell me one thing,” he said—as if his whole decision depended on me—“my wife, my children! My wife may die of grief, and even though my kids won’t lose their status, they’ll still be known as a criminal’s children, forever! What kind of memory will I leave them with?”
I said nothing.
“And leaving them, never seeing them again? It’s forever, you know—forever!”
I sat there, saying a silent prayer. At last I got up, feeling afraid.
“Well?” He looked at me.
“Go,” I said. “Confess. Everything else passes away, but the truth remains. When your children grow up, they’ll understand how brave your decision was.”

He left looking as if he’d finally made up his mind. But for more than two weeks, he kept coming to see me every evening, still getting ready, still unable to actually do it. It broke my heart. Sometimes he’d come determined and say passionately:

“I know it’ll be heaven for me, real heaven, as soon as I confess. For fourteen years I’ve been in hell. I want to suffer. I’ll take my punishment and start living. You can go through life doing wrong, but there’s no going back. Now I don’t dare love my neighbor or even my own children. Maybe my children will understand someday what my punishment cost me and won’t hate me! God isn’t in strength but in truth.”
“Everyone will understand your sacrifice,” I told him. “Maybe not right away, but later. You served a higher truth.”
He would leave comforted, but the next day come back looking pale and bitter.

“Every time I come, you look at me like you’re thinking, ‘He still hasn’t confessed!’ Wait, don’t judge me too harshly. It’s not as easy as you think. Maybe I won’t do it at all. You’re not going to report me, are you?”
Far from being nosy, I was actually afraid to look at him. I was sick with worry and couldn’t sleep.

“I just came from my wife,” he said. “Do you even understand what it means to have a wife? When I left, my kids called, ‘Bye, Dad! Come back soon and read with us!’ You don’t understand that! No one learns wisdom from someone else’s pain.”
His eyes were shining, his lips twitching. Suddenly he slammed his fist on the table—the first time he’d ever done anything like that, since he was usually so gentle.

“But do I have to?” he shouted. “Does it have to be done? No one else was punished—no one was sent to Siberia, the servant died of fever. I’ve suffered for the blood I shed. And no one will believe me or my proof. Do I really have to confess? I’m willing to suffer forever if it means sparing my wife and kids. Is it right to destroy them along with me? Are we making a mistake? Will people see it as right, will they respect it?”

“Wow,” I thought, “he’s still worried about what other people think at a time like this!” I felt so sorry for him that I would have shared his fate if it would have helped. I realized what a huge, terrifying decision this was.
“Decide for me!” he cried again.
“Go and confess,” I whispered. My voice almost gave out, but I said it firmly. I picked up the New Testament on the table (in Russian) and showed him John 12:24:
“Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
I had just been reading that verse when he came in. He read it.
“That’s true,” he said, but he smiled bitterly. “There are some terrifying things in these books. It’s easy to throw them at someone. And who wrote them anyway? Were they really written by people?”
“The Holy Spirit wrote them,” I said.
“Easy for you to say,” he replied, this time almost hating me.
I took the book again, opened it to Hebrews 10:31, and showed him. He read:
“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
He read it and threw the book down, trembling all over.

“That’s a terrifying verse,” he said. “You really know how to pick them.” He stood up. “Well, goodbye—maybe I won’t come again.... We’ll meet in heaven. So I’ve spent fourteen years in ‘the hands of the living God’—that’s what those years really were. Tomorrow I’ll beg those hands to let me go.”
I wanted to hug him, but I didn’t dare—his face was twisted and dark. He left.

“God help him,” I thought. “What is he about to face?” I dropped to my knees in front of the icon and prayed for him, crying to the Holy Mother of God. I prayed for half an hour—it was late, around midnight. Suddenly, the door opened and he came back in. I was surprised.
“Where have you been?” I asked.
“I think I forgot something...my handkerchief, maybe.... Even if I didn’t, let me stay a little longer.”
He sat down. I stood near him.
“Sit down, too,” he said.
I sat. We were silent for two minutes. He stared at me and suddenly smiled—I remember that. Then he stood up, hugged me tightly, and kissed me.
“Remember,” he said, “how I came back to you a second time. Do you hear me? Remember it!”
And he left.
“Tomorrow,” I thought.

And that’s what happened. I didn’t know it was his birthday the next day—I hadn’t been out in days, so I hadn’t heard. He always held a big party then, and everyone in town went. This time was no different. After dinner, he walked to the center of the room with a paper in his hand—a confession to the chief of his department, who was there. He read it out loud to everyone. It explained the crime in every detail.
“I separate myself from people as a monster. God has found me,” he finished. “I want to suffer for my sin!”

Then he laid out the things he’d kept for fourteen years to prove his guilt: jewelry he’d stolen from the murdered woman, a cross and locket from her neck (the locket had her fiancé’s picture), her notebook, and two letters—one from her fiancé saying he’d be home soon, and her unfinished reply. He’d taken those letters—why? Why keep them as evidence for fourteen years instead of destroying them?

Here’s what happened: everyone was shocked and horrified, but no one believed him—they thought he was insane, though they listened closely. A few days later, everyone in the town agreed he was crazy. The legal system couldn’t ignore it, but they dropped the case. Even though the jewelry and letters made them think, they decided that she might have given him those things as a friend or for safekeeping. Still, I later heard her friends and family confirmed the items were real and belonged to her. But in the end, nothing came of it.

Five days later, everyone heard he was sick and possibly dying. They said his heart was failing, but his wife also asked doctors to check his mental health, and they said he was insane. I told no one, though people came to question me. When I wanted to visit him, his wife especially wouldn’t let me.

“You caused his illness,” she said. “He was always gloomy, but this last year he was especially upset and did strange things, and now you’ve ruined him. Your preaching brought him to this—he spent the last month always with you.”

Not only his wife but the whole town blamed me. “It’s your fault,” they said. I stayed quiet and was actually glad, because I saw God’s mercy to a man who’d turned against himself and punished himself. I never believed he was insane.
They finally let me see him—he insisted on saying goodbye. When I arrived, I could see he was dying—weak, yellow, shaking, struggling to breathe—but his face was full of gentle happiness.
“It’s done!” he said. “I’ve wanted to see you for so long—why didn’t you come?”
I didn’t tell him they wouldn’t let me.

“God is calling me now. I know I’m dying, but for the first time in years I feel joy and peace. Heaven entered my heart as soon as I did what I had to do. Now I can love my children and kiss them. No one, not even my wife or the judges, believes me. My children will never believe it either—God has shown them mercy. I’ll die, and my name will be clean for them. Now I feel God close—I’m as happy as if I were in Heaven. I’ve done my duty.”
He couldn’t talk much—he was short of breath, but squeezed my hand and looked at me with love. We didn’t speak long—his wife kept checking in. But he had time to whisper:
“Remember how I came back to you that second time, at midnight? I told you to remember. Do you know why I came back? I came to kill you!”
I was shocked.

“I left you and wandered in the dark streets, torn inside. Suddenly, I hated you so much I could hardly stand it. I thought, ‘Now he’s the only one who knows and judges me. I can’t avoid my punishment tomorrow, because he knows everything.’ It wasn’t that I thought you’d betray me—I never even considered that—but I couldn’t bear the idea of you being alive and knowing everything, judging me. I hated you as if you were to blame for it all. I came back, remembering you had a knife on your table. I sat down and asked you to sit, and for a whole minute I thought about it. If I’d killed you, that murder would have ruined me even if I hadn’t confessed the other. But I didn’t care about that then. I just hated you and wanted to take it out on you for everything. God stopped me. But let me tell you, you were never closer to death.”

A week later, he died. The whole town came to his funeral. The chief priest gave a moving speech. Everyone mourned his early death. But after the funeral, the whole town turned against me—people even refused to see me. Some, at first only a few but then more, started to believe his story and came to question me, because people love to see the downfall of good men. But I said nothing, and soon after, I left the town. Five months later, by God’s grace, I entered the safe and blessed path I walk now, and I still pray for the soul of Mihail, who suffered so much.
(e) The Russian Monk and What He Might Mean

Fathers and teachers, what does it mean to be a monk? These days, when people talk about monks, some make fun of them, and others use the word as an insult. This disrespect is only getting worse. Yes, sadly, it’s true that there are many lazy, greedy, and even rude monks. Educated people point at them and say, “You’re just lazy beggars, living off everyone else, doing nothing useful.” But they ignore or forget about the many gentle and humble monks who just want to pray alone in peace. If I said that Russia’s salvation might come from these quiet monks, people would be shocked! But it’s possible. In their silent lives, these monks keep Christ’s image pure and beautiful, holding on to God’s truth from the days of the Apostles and martyrs. When the right moment comes, they’ll remind the world of that truth. That’s a big idea. Like a new star rising in the East.

That’s how I see monks—am I wrong, or just too hopeful? Look at the people who think they’re better than the faithful—hasn’t God’s image and truth been twisted in them? They rely on science, but science only explains what we can see and touch. It ignores the spiritual world—the best part of being human—and even rejects it with pride and anger. Today’s world shouts about freedom, but what do we actually see? Only more slavery and self-destruction! The world says:

“You have desires, so go ahead and satisfy them. You deserve just as much as the richest and most powerful. Don’t hold back, and even create new desires for yourself.” That’s what the world now teaches. They call it freedom. But what actually happens when everyone tries to satisfy every desire? The rich become alone and empty inside, and the poor grow jealous and angry, even turning to violence, because they’re told they have rights but not given any way to meet their needs. People claim the world is becoming more united, with new technology and shared ideas.

But don’t believe this so-called unity. When people think freedom means having and chasing every desire, they actually damage themselves. They fill their lives with pointless cravings, bad habits, and silly dreams. Life becomes all about showing off and competing. Things like big dinners, fancy visits, high status, and having servants are seen as must-haves, even worth dying for. Some people even kill themselves when they can’t keep up. The poor, meanwhile, drown their pain and jealousy in alcohol, but soon that might not be enough—they may turn to violence. Is this real freedom? I knew a so-called “freedom fighter” who almost betrayed his cause in prison just for a little tobacco! Yet he claimed to be fighting for humanity.

Can someone like that really help anyone? What can he achieve? Maybe something quick, but he won’t last. No wonder, instead of finding freedom, people end up as slaves—slaves to their own desires. Instead of brotherly love and unity, there’s more division and loneliness, just as a wise teacher once told me when I was young. That’s why the idea of truly serving others, of real brotherhood, is fading away. Some even mock it. But how can a person escape their own habits? When you’re chained to satisfying endless desires, you’re cut off from others. People have more things than ever, but less joy.

The monastic life is the opposite. People laugh at obedience, fasting, and prayer, but these are the real path to freedom. By letting go of extra desires, controlling my wild will, and learning obedience with God’s help, I find freedom in my spirit—and real joy. Who is more likely to come up with great ideas and serve them: the rich man in his loneliness, or the monk who’s freed himself from material things and habits? Monks are criticized for their solitude: “You’ve locked yourself away for your own salvation and forgotten about helping others!” But let’s see who really cares more for brotherhood. It’s not us monks who are isolated—it’s the rest of the world, even if they don’t realize it. In the past, leaders came from among us, so why not again? The humble monks will rise up to work for the greater good. Russia’s salvation will come from the people, and the Russian monk has always stood with the people. We are only alone if the people are alone. The people share our faith, and an atheist reformer will never succeed in Russia, even if he means well. Remember that! The people will face atheists and stay true to their faith. Take care of the peasant and his heart. Quietly help him learn. That’s your duty as monks—the peasant has God in his heart.
(f) Of Masters and Servants, and Whether They Can Be Spiritual Brothers

Of course, I don’t pretend peasants are perfect. Sin is spreading fast among them, starting from above and moving down. The spirit of isolation is creeping into the people as well. Loan sharks and greedy people are appearing. Merchants are obsessed with status and try to look cultured, even though they really aren’t, and they’re embarrassed by their own traditions and even by their faith. They try to mix with nobles, but they’re just peasants who have lost their way. Many peasants are ruined by drinking and can’t quit. This leads to terrible cruelty towards their wives and even their kids—almost always because of alcohol. I’ve seen little kids, only nine years old, sick and twisted from working all day in dirty, noisy factories, learning bad language and drinking. Is that what a child’s heart needs? He needs sunshine, play, good examples, and at least a little love. This must stop, monks—no more hurting children! Stand up and speak out—hurry!

But God will save Russia, because even though the peasants are sinful and can’t give up their vices, they know these sins are cursed by God and that what they do is wrong. So our people still believe in goodness, have faith, and shed tears of devotion.

It’s different with the upper classes. They want to build justice only on reason, leaving out Christ, and they openly say there’s no such thing as crime or sin anymore. That makes sense—if there’s no God, what does “crime” even mean? In Europe, the people are rising up against the rich, and their leaders encourage violence, telling them their anger is righteous. But their anger is cursed, because it’s cruel. Still, God will save Russia, just as He has before. Salvation will come from the people, from their faith and humility.

Fathers and teachers, protect the faith of the people and this won’t just be a dream. I’ve always been amazed by the dignity of our people—their real, honest sense of worth. I’ve seen it myself, even among the poorest and most sinful peasants. They’re not servile, and even after two hundred years of being serfs, they carry themselves freely, but without arrogance or resentment. They seem to say, “You’re rich, talented, and clever—good for you, God bless you. I respect you, but I know I’m a person too. By respecting you without jealousy, I prove I have dignity.”

Even if they don’t say this out loud (because they may not know how), that’s how they act. I’ve seen it, I know it. And believe it or not, the poorer the Russian peasant, the more you can see this calm goodness—because the rich peasants are usually more corrupted, often because we haven’t cared enough. But God will save His people; Russia is great in her humility. I dream of a future I can almost see: even the most corrupt rich person will one day be ashamed of his wealth before the poor, and the poor, seeing his humility, will respond with kindness and understanding. I believe it will happen; we’re moving towards it. Real equality is found only in the spiritual dignity of a person, and only here will people understand that. If we were all brothers, we’d have true brotherhood. But until then, no one will agree on dividing wealth. We keep the image of Christ, and it will shine for the world like a diamond. So let it be!

Fathers and teachers, let me tell you something that touched me deeply. On my travels, I met my old army orderly, Afanasy, in the town of K. I hadn’t seen him in eight years. He spotted me in the market, and when he realized who I was, he ran up and was overjoyed! He almost jumped on me: “Master, is that you? Is it really you?” He took me home with him.

He wasn’t in the army anymore—he was married with two little kids. He and his wife made a living selling vegetables at the market. Their room was poor, but bright and clean. He made me sit down, put on the samovar for tea, called his wife as if my visit was a huge celebration, and brought me his children: “Bless them, Father.”

“Should I bless them? I’m just a humble monk. But I’ll pray for them. And for you, Afanasy Pavlovitch, I’ve prayed for you every day since that day, because you’re the reason my life changed,” I told him, and explained as best I could. He just stared at me, amazed that his old officer was now a monk, and it brought tears to his eyes.
“Why are you crying?” I asked him. “You should be happy for me, my friend, because my path is a joyful one.”
He didn’t say much, but he kept sighing and looking at me with gentle concern.
“What happened to your fortune?” he asked.
“I gave it to the monastery,” I said. “We share everything.”

After tea, as I was about to leave, he brought out half a rouble to give to the monastery, and I saw him slip another half-rouble into my hand for my travels: “Take this, Father, it might help you on the road.”

I accepted his half-rouble, bowed to him and his wife, and left rejoicing. As I walked away, I thought, “Here we are, both of us—he at home, me on the road—both sighing and shaking our heads, but also smiling with joy in our hearts, remembering how God brought us together.”

I never saw him again. Once, I was his master and he was my servant, but when we hugged goodbye with full hearts, there was a real human bond between us. I’ve thought about it a lot, and now I wonder: Isn’t it possible that this kind of true, simple unity could one day exist everywhere among the Russian people? I believe it will, and the time is coming soon.

About servants in general, I’ll add this: When I was young, I often got mad at servants—maybe the cook made something too hot, or my orderly didn’t brush my clothes well enough. But what changed my thinking was something my dear brother said when we were kids: “Do I really deserve to have someone serve me, to order him around in his poverty and ignorance?” I was surprised that such a simple, obvious thought wasn’t more common.

There will always be servants in the world, but act so that your servant is freer in spirit than if he weren’t a servant at all. Why can’t I serve my servant, and let him see it—without pride on my part or suspicion on his? Why shouldn’t my servant be like family, so I can welcome him into my home and be glad to do it? Even now, it’s possible, and it will lead to a future where people don’t want servants for themselves, or want to turn others into servants, but want, with all their hearts, to serve everyone else, as the Gospel teaches.

Is it really just a dream that, in the end, people will find joy only in acts of kindness and mercy—not in cruel pleasures, overeating, showing off, boasting, and jealousy? I truly believe it’s not a dream, and that time is coming. People laugh and ask, “When will that happen? Does it even look possible?” But with Christ’s help, we’ll make it real. So many ideas in history seemed impossible just ten years before they happened! But when the time was right, they spread across the earth. It will be the same with us—our people will shine, and everyone will say, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.”

And to those who scoff at our hope: If you think our dream is foolish, when will you build your perfect world using only your own reason, without Christ? Even among themselves, only the most naive really believe they’re getting close to unity. In truth, their dreams are wilder than ours. They want justice, but without Christ, they’ll just end up shedding blood—because violence leads to more violence, and those who live by the sword die by it. Without Christ’s promise, people would destroy each other until only two were left—and even those last two would kill each other out of pride. But Christ promised the days would be shortened for the sake of the humble and gentle.

After my duel, when I was still an officer, I once talked about servants in society. People were shocked: “What, are we supposed to let our servants sit on the sofa and offer them tea?” I answered, “Why not, at least sometimes?” Everyone laughed. Their question was silly, and my answer wasn’t clear, but there was some truth in it.
(g) On Prayer, Love, and Our Connection to Other Worlds

Young man, don’t forget to pray. Every time you pray sincerely, you’ll feel something new, and it will give you fresh courage. You’ll see that prayer teaches you. Try to remember every day, and whenever you can, to say: “Lord, have mercy on everyone who stands before You today.” Every hour, thousands of people die, and their souls stand before God. Many die alone, sad, and forgotten. But maybe, because you prayed for them, your prayer will reach God, even though you never knew each other. Imagine how comforting it would be, for a soul standing before God, to know that someone prayed for them! God, who loves more than any of us, will look kindly on both of you, and may even forgive them because of your prayer.

Brothers, don’t be afraid of people’s sins. Love people even when they sin—that’s the closest we can come to God’s own love, and it’s the greatest kind of love on earth. Love everything God made, every grain of sand. Love every leaf, every ray of sunlight. Love animals, love plants, love everything. If you love everything, you’ll start to see God’s mystery in everything, and you’ll understand more every day. Eventually, you’ll come to love the whole world. Love animals—God gave them simple thoughts and pure happiness. Don’t harm them or take away their joy. Don’t think you’re better than animals; they don’t sin, but we humans often spoil the earth and leave a mess behind us. Love children most of all—they are innocent, like angels, and help soften our hearts. Woe to anyone who hurts a child! Father Anfim taught me to love children; he’d spend the little money we got on sweets for them, and he couldn’t walk past a child without feeling moved. That’s just how he was.

Sometimes you wonder, especially when you see people sin, whether you should use force or gentle love. Always choose humble love. If you make that your rule, you could change the whole world. Humble love is incredibly strong—stronger than anything else.

Every day, every hour, even every minute, watch yourself—see what kind of example you’re setting. Maybe you walk past a child, angry and saying something mean. You might not even notice the child, but he saw you, and your bad example could stick in his heart. You’ll never know, but you may have planted a seed of evil, just because you didn’t show careful, active kindness. Brothers, love is a teacher, but you have to learn it—it’s hard work and takes time. We must love not just for a moment, but forever. Anyone can love just for a while, even bad people.

My brother once asked birds to forgive him. That sounds silly, but it’s actually right; everything is connected, like an ocean—one touch can cause waves far away. If you ask birds for forgiveness, maybe they’ll be a little happier around you, and so will children and animals, if you become a better person. It’s all like an ocean. Then, filled with love, you might find yourself praying for the birds too, asking them to forgive you. Treasure this feeling, even if others think it makes no sense.

My friends, pray for happiness! Be as joyful as children or birds. Don’t let people’s sin make you lose hope in your work. Don’t say, “Sin and evil are too strong, and we are too weak and alone.” Don’t give in to that sadness! There’s only one way to be saved: take responsibility for all the world’s sins. It’s true—if you really do this, you’ll see that you are to blame for everyone and everything. But if you blame others for your own laziness and weakness, you’ll end up proud and angry at God.

About Satan’s pride: it’s hard for us to really understand it, so it’s easy to make mistakes and even to share in it, thinking we’re doing something great. Many of our strongest feelings are beyond our understanding here on earth. But don’t let that confuse you or use it as an excuse. God will only judge us for what we can understand, not for what we can’t. Later, we’ll see everything clearly, and then we won’t argue about it. Here on earth, we’re a bit lost, and without the image of Christ to guide us, we’d be completely lost, like people before the flood. Much is hidden from us, but to make up for it, we’re given a deep feeling that connects us to the other world, the higher world. Our thoughts and feelings have their roots in other worlds. That’s why philosophers say we can’t fully grasp reality here.

God took seeds from different worlds and planted them on this earth, and everything grew as it could. But things only stay alive if they keep feeling their connection to those mysterious worlds. If you lose that feeling, the heavenly part of you dies. Life becomes dull or even hateful. That’s what I believe.
(h) Can We Judge Others? Faith to the End

Remember, you can’t judge anyone else. No one can fairly judge a criminal until he realizes that he is just as guilty as the person before him—maybe even more responsible for the crime. When you understand that, you’re ready to be a judge. It may sound crazy, but it’s true. If I had been truly good, maybe there wouldn’t be a criminal standing before me. If you can take the criminal’s guilt upon yourself and suffer for him, do it, and let him go. Even if the law makes you a judge, try to act in this spirit—he’ll feel your kindness and judge himself even more harshly. If, after your kindness, he just laughs at you, don’t be discouraged. It just means he’s not ready yet, but his time will come. If not him, someone else will understand and change, and the truth will be fulfilled. Believe this without doubt; that’s where the hope and faith of the saints lies.

Never stop working. If, as you go to sleep, you remember you forgot to do something important, get up and do it. If people around you are mean and cold and won’t listen, humble yourself before them and ask forgiveness—because you’re to blame for their unwillingness to listen. If you can’t talk to them, serve them silently and humbly, never losing hope. If everyone abandons you and even forces you out, fall to the ground, kiss it, and water it with your tears; it will still bring fruit, even if no one sees or hears you. Keep believing, even if everyone else goes astray and you’re the only one faithful. Offer your praise to God even then. And if there are two of you together, that’s already a whole world—a world of living love. Hug each other and praise God, because even if you’re only two, God’s truth has been fulfilled.
If you sin and are crushed by guilt, rejoice for others—rejoice for those who are righteous. If you’ve sinned, be glad that someone else is good.

If other people’s evil makes you angry and want revenge, avoid that feeling at all costs. Instead, seek suffering for yourself, as if you were guilty of that evil. Accept it, bear it, and you’ll find comfort, understanding that you, too, are responsible. Maybe you could have been a light to those people, and you weren’t. If you had been, maybe they wouldn’t have sinned. If your light shone but people still weren’t saved, don’t lose faith—your light will last even after you die. The good person dies, but his light remains. People are often saved after their savior dies. They reject their prophets, but honor their martyrs later. You’re working for everyone, for the future. Don’t look for rewards—your reward is the spiritual joy given only to the righteous. Don’t fear the powerful, but stay wise and calm. Know the right time for things. When you’re alone, pray. Love to throw yourself on the earth and kiss it. Love all people, love everything. Seek that joy and ecstasy. Water the earth with your tears of happiness—don’t be ashamed, treasure it, because it’s God’s gift to you, and it’s rare.
(i) Of Hell and Hell Fire, a Mystic Reflection

Fathers and teachers, I’ve wondered: what is hell? I believe it’s the suffering of not being able to love. Once, in eternity, a spiritual being came to earth and was given the chance to say, “I am, and I love.” Just once, he was given the moment to live out real love. That’s why he was given life and time. But if he wasted that gift, didn’t value it, even made fun of love—then, after death, he sees the joy of heaven and realizes what he missed. That’s his torment: to be near God and those who loved, but having never loved himself. He realizes, “Now I see, and I want to love, but too late—my earthly life is over, there’s nothing I can sacrifice anymore. Abraham won’t come even with a drop of water to cool my burning thirst for love, because that’s only given on earth. Now there’s a gulf between life and this existence.”

Some talk about hell fire as if it’s real flames. I don’t go into that mystery. But I think if it were just physical fire, people in hell might actually be glad for it, because it would distract them from the worse pain inside. The real torment is spiritual, and it can’t be taken away. Even if the righteous in heaven forgave them and called them up in love, it might only make their suffering worse, because it would make them long even more for love they can never return. But maybe, in accepting the love of the righteous and realizing they can’t return it, they’ll find a little comfort—becoming humble and a bit closer to real love. I’m sorry I can’t say this more clearly. But woe to those who kill themselves! I believe no one is more miserable than they are. The Church says not to pray for them, but I secretly pray for them anyway. Love can never be wrong in Christ’s eyes. I’ve always prayed for them, and I still do.

Some people stay proud and angry even in hell, even though they know the truth. Some give themselves completely to Satan’s pride. For them, hell is something they choose—they’re tortured by their own choices, feeding on their bitterness but never satisfied. They refuse forgiveness, curse God, and want Him to disappear. They burn with anger forever, longing for death, but never finding it.

Here Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov’s manuscript ends. It’s unfinished and in pieces. For example, it only covers the early part of Father Zossima’s life. His teachings and opinions are just bits and pieces from different times. His last words aren’t separated from the rest, but you can get a sense of them from what’s in Alexey’s manuscript.

Father Zossima’s death was sudden. Though everyone around him knew he was dying, it was hard to believe the end would come so fast. In fact, his friends thought he seemed better that last night, cheerful and talkative, and believed he’d get at least a little better. Even five minutes before he died, no one expected it. Suddenly, he felt a sharp pain in his chest, turned pale, and held his hands over his heart. Everyone jumped up to help. But even in pain, he smiled at them, sank from his chair to his knees, bowed to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as if in joyful prayer, quietly and happily gave his soul to God.

News of his death spread quickly through the hermitage and to the monastery. His closest friends and those with official duties began to prepare his body in the old way, and all the monks gathered in the church. Before dawn, news reached the town. By morning, everyone was talking about it, and crowds came from the town to the monastery. But the next book will talk more about this. I’ll just add: before a day had passed, something so unexpected and strange happened that it shocked the monks and townspeople alike—and even today, people in town still remember that day of suspense.

Father Zossima's body was prepared for burial following the usual monastery rituals. As everyone knows, when a monk or hermit dies, their body isn’t washed. The Church’s rules say: “If a monk dies, the monk assigned must wipe the body with warm water, first making the sign of the cross with a sponge on the forehead, chest, hands, feet, and knees—and that’s enough.” Father Païssy did all this, then dressed Father Zossima in his monk’s robes and wrapped him in his cloak, which was cut a bit so it could be folded around him like a cross. On his head, he placed a hood with an eight-pointed cross, and covered his face with black gauze. An icon of the Savior was put in his hands. Early in the morning, the body was placed in the coffin that had been made ahead of time. The coffin was left all day in the elder’s cell, in the bigger room where he used to meet visitors and other monks. Since Father Zossima was a strict priest and monk, the Gospel—not the Psalms—had to be read over him, and only by monks who were priests. Father Iosif began reading as soon as the requiem service ended. Father Païssy wanted to read the Gospel all day and night for his friend, but for now, he and the Father Superintendent were busy, because something strange and restless was happening among the monks, the guests from the monastery lodgings, and the crowds coming from town. As time passed, the excitement grew. Both the Superintendent and Father Païssy worked hard to calm everyone down.

Once it was fully daylight, people from the town began bringing their sick relatives—mostly children—to the hermitage. It was as if they had all waited for this moment, believing that the remains of the dead elder had the power to heal, and that miracles would happen if they just believed strongly enough. Only then did it become obvious how much everyone in town had thought of Father Zossima as a real saint while he was alive. And it wasn’t just poor people; there were people from all walks of life coming.

The rush and obvious impatience of the believers bothered Father Païssy. He had expected something like this, but the real thing was much more intense than he imagined. When he saw any monks acting too excited, he scolded them. “Expecting a miracle right away shows a lightness that might be okay for ordinary people, but is wrong for us monks,” he told them.

But hardly anyone listened, and this worried Father Païssy. Secretly, though, he had to admit that deep down, he had almost the same hopes as the others, even though he was annoyed by their impatience, which he saw as shallow and vain. Yet it especially bothered him to see certain people in the crowd—people whose presence made him uneasy. In Father Zossima’s cell, he spotted Rakitin and the monk from Obdorsk, who was still staying in the monastery, and he felt a sudden distrust towards both of them, though he might have felt the same about others too.

The monk from Obdorsk stood out as the most restless and nosy person in the crowd. He was everywhere, asking questions, listening in, and whispering with a secretive, mysterious look on his face. He seemed very impatient, even irritated.

As for Rakitin, it turned out he had come so early to the hermitage because Madame Hohlakov had asked him to. As soon as this kind but rather silly woman woke up and heard that Father Zossima had died, she became so curious that she sent Rakitin to the hermitage to watch closely and write her letters every half-hour telling her “everything that happens.” She thought Rakitin was a very religious young man. Rakitin was especially good at pretending to be whatever people wanted if he thought it could help him.

The day was bright and clear, and many visitors wandered among the graves that surrounded the church and were scattered around the hermitage. As he walked, Father Païssy realized he hadn’t seen Alyosha (Alexey), Father Zossima’s favorite, since the night before. As soon as he thought of him, he spotted Alyosha sitting in the farthest corner of the garden, on the tomb of a monk who had been famous for his holiness long ago. Alyosha had his back to the hermitage and his face to the wall, as if he was hiding. When Father Païssy came closer, he saw Alyosha was crying hard, his face buried in his hands, his whole body shaking with sobs. Father Païssy stood by him for a while.

“That’s enough, dear boy, enough,” he finally said gently. “Why are you crying? You should rejoice, not weep. Don’t you know this is the greatest day for him? Just think where he is now, at this very moment!”
Alyosha looked up, his face swollen from crying like a little kid’s, but he turned away again without saying a word and hid his face in his hands.
“Maybe it’s for the best,” Father Païssy said thoughtfully. “Cry if you need to—Christ sent you those tears.”

“Your tears are just easing your soul and will eventually make your heart feel lighter,” he thought to himself as he walked away, thinking kindly of Alyosha. But he hurried off, because he felt he might start crying too if he stayed.

Time passed; the monastery services and prayers for the dead went on as usual. Father Païssy took over reading the Gospel from Father Iosif by the coffin. But before three in the afternoon, something happened—something I hinted at before. It was so unexpected and so opposite to what everyone hoped for, that even now, people in the town and nearby remember it in detail. I have to admit, I almost hate remembering it, because it caused such silly excitement and was such a shock to many, even though it was really just a normal thing. I would have left it out if it didn’t have such a huge effect on Alyosha, the main character—this was a turning point for him, a moment that shook his faith but eventually made him stronger and gave his life new direction.

Back to the story: before dawn, when Father Zossima’s body was put in the coffin and moved into the main room, some people around the coffin suggested opening the windows. But no one really responded, and most people ignored the idea. Some may have noticed it but thought it was silly—even insulting—to worry about the body of such a saint decaying. They expected something completely different.

But after noon, people began silently noticing something. At first, no one wanted to say anything, but by three o’clock, it became so obvious that the news spread quickly among the monks and visitors. It soon reached the whole monastery, and then the town—surprising everyone, both believers and nonbelievers. The nonbelievers were happy, but some of the believers seemed even happier, because, as Father Zossima once said, “People love to see the righteous fall.”

The truth is, a smell of decay started coming from the coffin. It got stronger, and by three o’clock, you couldn’t miss it. Nothing like this had ever happened in the history of the monastery, and no one could remember such a scandal. Even years later, sensible monks were shocked when they thought about how big a fuss was made. In the past, other very holy monks had died—old men everyone respected—and their bodies also decayed naturally, but it had never caused a scandal or even much discussion. Of course, there were stories of some saints whose bodies didn’t decay and whose relics were preserved. The monks treasured these stories, seeing them as miracles and a sign that greater glory would come from their tombs one day.

One of these special memories was of an old monk named Job, who died seventy years ago at the age of 105. He was famous for his strict fasting and silence, and his grave was shown to visitors with special respect and mysterious hints that great things might happen there. (That was the very grave where Father Païssy found Alyosha sitting earlier.) There was also Father Varsonofy, who had only recently died and was the elder before Father Zossima. Pilgrims thought he was a kind of “holy fool” and revered him. The tradition said that both of these monks looked as if they were alive when they were buried, with no sign of decay, and some people even claimed their bodies gave off a sweet smell.

But even with these uplifting memories, it’s hard to explain the silly, mean-spirited behavior that happened around Father Zossima’s coffin. In my opinion, there were a few causes. One was the deep dislike some monks felt toward the whole idea of elders, which they saw as a bad new custom. Even more important was jealousy of Father Zossima’s saintliness, which was so widely accepted that no one dared question it while he was alive. He had won over many people by his kindness, not by miracles, and had gathered a lot of loving followers. But because of that, he had also attracted jealous and bitter enemies, both in the monastery and outside. He never hurt anyone, but people asked, “Why do they think he’s so holy?” And that question led some to hate him intensely. That’s why some were actually happy about the quick smell of decay, even though he hadn’t been dead a whole day. On the other hand, some of his followers were deeply embarrassed and hurt by what happened. Here’s how it all unfolded.

As soon as signs of decay appeared, the monks’ true feelings showed in the way they acted. They would go into the cell, stay a short time, then hurry out to tell others waiting outside. Some shook their heads sadly, but others clearly enjoyed spreading the news, their eyes shining with mean satisfaction. No one scolded them or told them off, which was strange, because most of the monks had loved Father Zossima. But for the moment, it seemed like the minority was in control.

Soon, educated visitors from outside came in to see for themselves. Few peasants went in, though there were crowds at the gates. After three o’clock, even more people from town showed up, probably drawn by the shocking news. Some who hadn’t planned to visit came anyway, including some important people. Outwardly, things were still calm, and Father Païssy kept reading the Gospel out loud by the coffin, pretending not to notice what was happening, though he knew something was wrong. Finally, the whispers—which grew louder and more confident—reached him. “It shows God’s judgment isn’t like man’s,” he heard someone say. The first to say this out loud was an elderly town official known for his piety, but he was just repeating what the monks had been whispering for a while. The most troubling thing was how happy some people seemed about it, as if they had the right to feel that way. Soon, even the outward calm started to break down.
“How could this happen?” some monks said, pretending to be sad. “He was thin, hardly any flesh—what was there to rot?”

“It must be a sign from heaven,” others said quickly, and this idea caught on right away. They pointed out that if the decay were normal, like with every dead sinner, it would have shown up later, after at least twenty-four hours. But this early decay was “more than natural,” so it had to be God’s sign. This seemed undeniable to many.

Gentle Father Iosif, the librarian and a favorite of Father Zossima’s, tried to answer the critics by saying, “This isn’t believed the same way everywhere. The idea that saints’ bodies don’t decay isn’t an official teaching of the Orthodox Church—just a tradition. Even in very Orthodox places, like Mount Athos, they aren’t shocked by the smell of decay. There, the real sign of sainthood isn’t whether the body decays, but the color of the bones after many years in the ground. If the bones are yellow like wax, it’s a sign the Lord has glorified the saint; if they’re black, it means God hasn’t given them that special honor. That’s what they believe in Athos, where Orthodox teaching has stayed pure.” That was how Father Iosif ended his explanation.

But his gentle words didn’t change anyone’s mind—in fact, some mocked him. “That’s just book-learning and new ideas, no use listening to it,” the monks said. “We stick to the old ways; there are too many changes these days—are we supposed to follow every one?” others added.
“We’ve had just as many holy fathers as they have. They live among the Turks and have forgotten everything. Their religion is already impure—and they don’t even have bells,” said the most sarcastic.

Father Iosif walked away, even sadder now, because he hadn’t been very confident in his argument in the first place. He saw with worry that things were getting out of control, and that people were starting to act out. Before long, all the sensible monks were silent, just like Father Iosif. Everyone who loved the elder and believed in the idea of elders suddenly felt completely crushed and looked at each other nervously. The monks who disliked the idea of elders, thinking it was just a new fad, now stood tall. “There was no smell of decay from Father Varsonofy, only a sweet scent,” they said meanly. “But he got that honor because he was truly holy, not because he was an elder.”

Then came a wave of criticism and even blame directed at Father Zossima. “His teachings were wrong; he said life was joyful instead of full of suffering,” said some who weren’t thinking clearly. “He went along with trendy ideas; he didn’t believe in real fire in hell,” others added. “He wasn’t strict enough—he let himself have sweets, drank tea with cherry jam sent by ladies. Should a strict monk drink tea?” whispered some of the jealous ones. “He was proud,” the nastiest said; “he acted like a saint and accepted it when people knelt before him.” “He misused confession,” some of the harshest opponents of elders whispered. Even some of the oldest, strictest monks—real ascetics—who had kept quiet while Zossima was alive, now spoke up. This was serious, because their words influenced the younger monks with shaky beliefs. The monk from Obdorsk listened carefully, sighing and nodding. “Yes, clearly Father Ferapont was right with his judgment yesterday,” he said, and just then, Father Ferapont himself appeared, as if to stir things up even more.

As I’ve mentioned, Father Ferapont rarely left his little wooden hut by the beehives. He was hardly ever seen at church, but people let this slide because they thought he was a bit crazy, and didn’t make him follow all the usual rules. Honestly, they didn’t have much choice. It would have looked bad to force such a holy man, who prayed day and night (even falling asleep on his knees), to follow the normal schedule. If anyone had tried, the monks would have said, “He’s holier than we are and follows a tougher rule. If he doesn’t come to church, it’s because he knows when he should.” To avoid people complaining, they let Father Ferapont do as he pleased.

Everyone knew that Father Ferapont especially disliked Father Zossima. Now, the news had reached him in his hut that “God’s judgment is not like man’s,” and that something had happened that was “beyond nature.” It’s likely the monk from Obdorsk, who had visited Ferapont the night before and left terrified, was one of the first to tell him.

As I said earlier, even though Father Païssy was standing firm, reading the Gospel over the coffin, and couldn’t see or hear what was happening outside, he could sense most of it, because he knew the people around him well.
