He wasn’t shaken; he waited calmly to see what would happen next, watching closely for the outcome.

Suddenly, a loud commotion broke out in the hallway, completely ignoring the usual rules. The door flew open and Father Ferapont appeared in the doorway. Behind him was a crowd of monks and townspeople. They didn’t go into the cell, but stood at the bottom of the steps, waiting to see what Ferapont would do or say. Even though they were bold, they still felt a bit intimidated, knowing he wouldn’t have come for nothing. Standing in the doorway, Father Ferapont lifted his arms, and the curious monk from Obdorsk peeked in under his arm. He was the only one who couldn’t resist following Ferapont up the steps. The rest stepped back, startled as the door crashed open. Raising his hands, Father Ferapont suddenly shouted:

“I cast out, I cast out!” and, turning to each of the four walls and corners of the cell, he made the sign of the cross in every direction. Everyone there knew what he was doing—he always did this to drive out evil spirits wherever he went, and he wouldn’t sit or talk until he had done so.
“Satan, get out! Satan, get out!” he repeated as he made the sign of the cross. “I cast out, I cast out!” he shouted again.

He was dressed in a rough robe tied with a rope. His bare, gray-haired chest showed under his simple shirt, and his feet were bare. As he waved his arms, you could hear the heavy iron chains he wore under his robe clanking.
Father Païssy stopped reading, stepped forward, and faced him, waiting.
“Why have you come, respected Father? Why are you breaking the peace? Why are you disturbing the flock?” he asked, looking at him sternly.

“Why have I come? You ask why? What is your faith?” Father Ferapont shouted wildly. “I’ve come to drive out your visitors—the unclean devils. I’ve come to see how many have gathered here while I was gone. I want to sweep them out with a broom.”
“You cast out evil, but maybe you’re serving it yourself,” Father Païssy replied bravely. “And who can say ‘I am holy’? Can you, Father?”

“I’m not holy, I’m unclean. I don’t sit in a fancy chair and let people bow to me like an idol,” Father Ferapont thundered. “People are ruining the true faith now. The dead man—your saint,” he said to the crowd, pointing at the coffin, “didn’t believe in devils. He gave out medicine to drive them away. So now devils are everywhere, like spiders. And now he’s begun to stink. That’s a clear sign from God.”

What he meant was this: once, a monk had been haunted by dreams—and later, waking visions—of evil spirits. When terrified, he told Father Zossima, who advised constant prayer and strict fasting. When that didn’t help, Zossima suggested that, along with prayer and fasting, he take a specific medicine. Many people were shocked by this advice, and especially Ferapont, who was quick to criticize.

“Go away, Father!” Father Païssy said firmly. “It’s not for man to judge, but for God. Maybe this is a sign none of us can understand. Go, Father, and don’t trouble the others!” he repeated forcefully.

“He didn’t keep the fasts properly, and now this sign has come. It’s clear, and it’s a sin to hide it,” Ferapont ranted, his zeal getting the better of him. “He loved sweet things, ladies brought them to him, he drank tea, he loved his stomach and had proud thoughts. And for that, he’s been shamed....”
“You talk carelessly, Father.” Now Father Païssy raised his voice, too. “I admire your fasting, but you speak as thoughtlessly as a child. Go, Father, I order you!” he finished loudly.

“I’ll go,” said Ferapont, a little surprised, but still just as bitter. “You smart people! You look down on my simplicity. I came here knowing little, and here I’ve forgotten even that. God has protected me from your cleverness.”
Father Païssy stood over him, waiting firmly. Father Ferapont paused, then suddenly rested his cheek on his hand and spoke in a singsong voice, looking at the coffin:

“Tomorrow they’ll sing ‘Our Helper and Defender’ for him—a grand song. For me, when I die, all they’ll sing is ‘What earthly joy’—just a little hymn,” he added sadly. “You’re all proud here; this is a proud place!” he suddenly shouted, waving his hand as if he’d lost control, and hurried down the steps. The crowd below wavered; some followed him, others stayed behind because the cell was still open. Father Païssy followed Ferapont out and watched him. But the old fanatic wasn’t finished. About twenty steps away, he turned to the setting sun, raised both arms, and suddenly collapsed to the ground with a loud cry.

“My God has conquered! Christ has conquered the setting sun!” he screamed, reaching for the sun and then falling face down on the ground, sobbing like a child, shaking and spreading his arms out. Everyone rushed to him; people cried out, some sobbed with sympathy—a kind of wild excitement swept through them all.
“He’s the real saint! He’s the holy man!” some people shouted, losing their fear. “He should be an elder!” others added viciously.

“He would never be an elder... he’d refuse... he wouldn’t take part in that nonsense,” other voices chimed in. Who knows how far they would have gone, but just then the bell rang, calling everyone to the service. They all crossed themselves quickly. Father Ferapont also got up, crossed himself, and walked back to his hut without looking back, still muttering nonsense. A few followed him, but most hurried to the service. Father Païssy let Father Iosif take over reading and went down. The wild shouts of the fanatics didn’t affect him, but his heart suddenly felt heavy for a special reason. He stopped and wondered, “Why am I so sad?” Then he realized, to his surprise, that it was for a small, specific reason. In the crowd at the entrance, he had noticed Alyosha, and he realized that seeing the boy had given him a sudden pang. “Does that boy mean so much to me now?” he wondered.

At that moment, Alyosha passed by, hurrying away—not toward the church. Their eyes met, but Alyosha quickly looked away and dropped his gaze, and from that look alone, Father Païssy could tell something huge was changing inside him.
“Have you fallen into doubt, too?” Father Païssy called out. “Are you joining those with little faith?” he added sadly.
Alyosha stopped and looked vaguely at Father Païssy, but then looked away again. He stood sideways, not facing Païssy, who watched him closely.
“Where are you going? The bell is calling for the service,” Païssy asked, but again Alyosha didn’t answer.
“Are you leaving the hermitage? Without asking for permission or a blessing?”

Alyosha suddenly gave a twisted smile and shot a strange, very strange look at Father Païssy—the man his beloved elder had put him in the care of on his deathbed. Then, still silent, Alyosha waved his hand, not even bothering to be respectful, and hurried away toward the gates, leaving the hermitage behind.
“You’ll come back,” Father Païssy murmured, watching him go with sad surprise.

Father Païssy (Father P) wasn’t wrong when he guessed that his “dear boy” Alyosha would come back. Maybe he even understood Alyosha’s true feelings better than anyone else. But honestly, it’s hard for me to fully explain what Alyosha was going through right then. When Father Païssy had asked him, “Are you losing your faith too?” I could easily answer for Alyosha: “No, he’s not losing his faith. In fact, he has too much faith.” That’s really what his problem was—his faith was so strong, it made his pain even worse. And the pain was real. Even a long time after, Alyosha remembered that day as one of the worst and most heartbreaking of his life. If you’re wondering, “Was all this suffering really just because his elder’s body started to decay too soon instead of performing miracles?” I have to say, “Yes, that’s exactly it.” But please don’t be quick to laugh at Alyosha’s pure heart. I’m not here to make excuses for him because of his age or inexperience. Actually, I respect his heart. Sure, a more cautious, less passionate teenager might not have gone through what Alyosha did. But sometimes, especially when you’re young, it’s better to be swept away by real feelings than to be cold and sensible all the time. A young person who’s always practical is, in my opinion, not really living.
“But,” reasonable people might say, “not every young person can believe in such superstitions. Your hero isn’t exactly a role model.”
My answer is the same: “Yes! Alyosha had faith—a strong, holy faith. But I’m still not going to apologize for him.”

Even though I said I wouldn’t explain or defend Alyosha, I realize I need to, so you’ll understand the story. The truth is, it wasn’t about miracles for Alyosha. He wasn’t sitting around waiting for something magical to happen. He didn’t need some miracle to prove his beliefs. What really mattered to him was his beloved elder—the holy man he looked up to more than anyone else. All the love in Alyosha’s heart had focused, maybe too much, on this one person. His elder had become his hero and his ideal. On that awful day, Alyosha even forgot about his brother Dmitri, even though he’d been worried about him before, and he forgot about the money he was supposed to give Ilusha’s father. But it wasn’t miracles he needed; it was “higher justice,” because in his mind, something deeply unfair had happened. Maybe he expected justice to come through miracles from his elder’s body, but everyone at the monastery felt the same way, even smart people like Father Païssy. Alyosha just dreamed like everyone else, because a year at the monastery had made him expect it. Still, what he really wanted was justice—not just miracles.

Now, the man Alyosha thought deserved more glory than anyone in the world was suddenly being shamed and dishonored! Why? Who decided this? Who had the right to judge him? These questions tore at Alyosha’s innocent heart. He couldn’t stand the idea that the holiest of men was being mocked by a crowd so much less worthy than him. Even if there were no miracles, why did his elder have to be humiliated like this, and why the strange, early decay, as the meaner monks said? Why did people, especially Father Ferapont and his supporters, celebrate it as a “sign from heaven”? Where was God’s hand in all this? Why did God seem to look away “at the most important moment” (at least, that’s how Alyosha saw it), like He was letting things happen according to cold, uncaring nature?

That’s why Alyosha’s heart was breaking. The worst of it was that the person he loved most in the world was being shamed. Maybe Alyosha’s complaints were childish or unreasonable, but honestly, I’m glad he let his feelings take over at that moment. Sensible people always come back to reason eventually, but if love isn’t strong in a boy’s heart at a time like this, when will it ever be? But there was also something else on Alyosha’s mind, something left over from his talk with Ivan. That conversation kept coming back to him now, bothering him. It didn’t shake the core of his faith—he still loved and believed in God, even if he was upset with Him. But the doubts and dark thoughts Ivan had shared started to rise up in Alyosha’s mind, and he couldn’t ignore them.

It was getting dark when Rakitin, coming through the pine trees from the hermitage to the monastery, noticed Alyosha lying face-down on the ground under a tree. He wasn’t moving and looked like he was asleep. Rakitin went over and called his name.
“You here, Alexey? Don’t tell me—” Rakitin started to say, but stopped himself. He was about to ask, “Don’t tell me you’ve ended up like this?”
Alyosha didn’t look at him, but he moved a little, so Rakitin knew he’d heard him.
“What’s wrong?” Rakitin asked, but his surprise faded, and he started to smirk in a mocking way.
“I’ve been looking for you for two hours. You just disappeared. What are you doing here? What kind of nonsense is this? At least look at me…”
Alyosha lifted his head, sat up, and leaned against the tree. He wasn’t crying, but his face showed pain and irritation. He still didn’t look at Rakitin—he stared off to the side.
“You know, you look completely different. None of your usual kindness. Are you mad at someone? Did someone hurt you?”
“Leave me alone,” Alyosha said suddenly, making a tired gesture with his hand, still not looking at him.

“Wow! So that’s how it is! You can yell at people like the rest of us after all. So much for being a saint. I have to say, Alyosha, you’ve surprised me. I don’t get surprised much around here. I always thought you were the sensible one….”
Alyosha finally glanced at Rakitin, but it was a blank look, like he barely understood what he was saying.
“Are you really this upset just because your old man started to smell? Did you honestly think he’d work miracles?” Rakitin said, truly surprised.
“I believed, I still believe, I want to believe, and I will believe—what more do you want?” Alyosha snapped, irritated.

“Nothing, man. Seriously! Even a thirteen-year-old wouldn’t believe that stuff now. But whatever. So now you’re mad at God, rebelling against Him because He didn’t hand out medals or make your elder a saint? You guys are something else!”
Alyosha stared at Rakitin for a while, his eyes half-closed. There was a sudden glint in his eyes—but it wasn’t anger at Rakitin.
“I’m not rebelling against God. I just ‘don’t accept His world,’” Alyosha said, forcing a smile.
“What do you mean, you don’t accept the world?” Rakitin thought about it for a second. “What kind of nonsense is that?”
Alyosha didn’t answer.
“Alright, enough of this. Let’s be practical. Have you eaten anything today?”
“I don’t remember… I think I have.”

“You need some food, judging by your face. You look awful. I heard you didn’t sleep at all either, with that meeting last night and everything that happened after. You’ve probably had nothing but a bit of holy bread. I’ve got some sausage in my pocket—from town, just in case. But you probably won’t eat sausage, will you…?”
“Give me some.”

“Whoa! You’re really going for it! This is like a mini-rebellion! Well, might as well make the most of it. Come on over to my place… I could use a shot of vodka myself—I’m dead tired. But vodka’s too much for you, right? Or do you want some?”
“Give me some vodka too.”
“Whoa! You’re full of surprises, brother!” Rakitin looked at him in shock. “Well, sausage or vodka, this is too good to pass up. Let’s go.”
Alyosha stood up without saying anything and followed Rakitin.
“If your brother Ivan could see you now—he’d be shocked! By the way, Ivan left for Moscow this morning. Did you know?”

“Yeah,” Alyosha answered without much interest, and suddenly he thought of his brother Dmitri. But the thought faded quickly, even though it reminded him of something urgent he was supposed to do—some duty he couldn’t put off. Even that didn’t really affect him and disappeared from his mind right away. Much later, Alyosha would remember this moment.

“Your brother Ivan once called me a ‘liberal idiot with no talent.’ And you once told me I was ‘dishonorable.’ Well, I’d like to see what your talent and honor do for you now,” Rakitin muttered to himself under his breath.

“Hey, listen,” he said out loud, “let’s take the path past the monastery and head straight to town. By the way, I should stop at Madame Hohlakov’s. You won’t believe it, but I wrote her all about what happened, and she wrote back instantly—in pencil! (She loves writing notes.) She said, ‘I never expected such behavior from a man as respected as Father Zossima.’ She actually called it ‘behavior.’ She’s angry, too. You guys are something! Wait!” he suddenly stopped, grabbing Alyosha’s shoulder to stop him, too.

“You know, Alyosha,” he peered closely at him, clearly thinking of something new and not sure how to say it. He was smiling on the outside, but he was nervous about bringing it up, because Alyosha’s mood was so strange and unexpected. “Alyosha, you know where we should go?” he finally said, sounding both sneaky and unsure.
“I don’t care… wherever you want.”
“Let’s go see Grushenka, okay? Will you come?” Rakitin finally said, almost trembling with excitement.
“Let’s go to Grushenka,” Alyosha answered calmly, right away. Rakitin was so shocked by Alyosha’s quick and calm answer that he almost jumped back.
“Wow! Seriously!” Rakitin said in amazement, but he grabbed Alyosha’s arm tight and led him down the path, worried he might change his mind.
They walked in silence. Rakitin was honestly afraid to say anything.

“She’ll be so happy—so excited!” he mumbled, but then fell silent again. Actually, Rakitin wasn’t doing this for Grushenka’s sake. He was practical and never did anything unless it would benefit him. He had two reasons: first, he wanted to see the “good guy” Alyosha fall—from saint to sinner—which he was already imagining with glee; and second, he was hoping for some kind of reward for himself, but more about that later.
“So the moment of truth has come,” Rakitin thought to himself, feeling mean satisfaction. “And we’re going to catch it right as it happens, which is exactly what I want.”

Grushenka lived in the busiest part of town, near the cathedral square, in a small wooden cottage in the yard of the widow Morozov’s house. The main house was big, old, made of stone, and pretty ugly. The widow lived quietly with her two old, unmarried nieces. She didn’t really need to rent out the cottage, but everyone knew she took in Grushenka four years ago only to please her relative, the merchant Samsonov, who looked after Grushenka. People said the jealous old man wanted the widow to keep a close eye on Grushenka’s behavior. But it turned out she didn’t need much watching, and soon the widow hardly ever saw Grushenka, never bothering her at all. It had been four years since Samsonov brought Grushenka, then a shy, delicate, sad girl of eighteen, from the main city. Not much was known about her past, even though by now, Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka) was well-known and many people were curious about her. There were rumors that, at seventeen, she had been betrayed and abandoned by an officer who later married someone else, leaving her poor and disgraced. But people also said that, even though Samsonov had rescued her from poverty, Grushenka actually came from a good family and was the daughter of a church deacon or something like that.

Over those four years, the sad, sensitive orphan turned into a plump, rosy Russian beauty—confident, bold, and even a little arrogant. She was smart with money, careful, and managed to build up a small fortune by any means she could. Everyone agreed on one thing: Grushenka wasn’t easy to approach, and in all those years, besides Samsonov, no man could say he’d won her over. Lots had tried, especially recently, but she always turned them down, sometimes making their failed attempts look ridiculous. People also said she was getting into “speculation” lately and was really good at it—so good that some compared her to a clever moneylender. It wasn’t that she loaned money, but she and old Karamazov had bought up worthless debts for almost nothing and somehow managed to make money off them.

Samsonov, the old widower who took care of Grushenka, was rich, stingy, and mean. He bossed his grown sons around, but after getting sick and losing the use of his swollen legs, he started depending a lot on Grushenka, even though he’d first kept her on a tight budget, jokingly called “Lenten fare.” Grushenka, however, managed to get her freedom while still making Samsonov totally trust her. The old man, who had been harsh and greedy all his life, became so attached to her that he couldn’t live without her, especially in the last two years. Still, he never gave her much money, and even if she’d threatened to leave, he wouldn’t have changed his mind. In the end, he did give her a small sum, and people were surprised when they found out.

“You’re a smart girl,” he told her when he gave her eight thousand roubles. “You can look after yourself, but remember, except for your yearly allowance, you’re getting nothing more from me as long as I live. I won’t leave you anything in my will either.”

And he kept his promise: when he died, he left everything to his sons, whom he had always treated like servants. Grushenka wasn’t even mentioned in his will. Everyone found this out later. Still, Samsonov had helped her with advice, showing her how to grow her money and giving her ideas for business.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had first met Grushenka over a business deal, fell head over heels for her, old Samsonov (even though he was seriously ill) thought it was hilarious. Interestingly, Grushenka was always open and honest with Samsonov—he seemed to be the only person she trusted that way. But recently, when Dmitri (Mitya) also started chasing her, the old man stopped laughing and gave her some serious advice.

“If you have to choose between the father or the son, pick the old man—just make sure he’ll marry you and give you money first. But don’t mess around with the son. You won’t get anything good from that.”
Those were the exact words of the old man, who knew he was dying—and, in fact, he died five months later.

I should mention that, even though everyone in town knew about the weird rivalry between father and son Karamazov, both after Grushenka, hardly anyone really knew what Grushenka thought of either of them. Even her two servants (as they later testified in court after something terrible happened) said she only let Dmitri see her because “he threatened to kill her.” Her servants were an almost deaf, sick old cook from Grushenka’s childhood home, and the cook’s clever granddaughter, who worked as her maid. Grushenka lived simply, not in luxury. Her cottage had three rooms, furnished with old-fashioned mahogany furniture that belonged to the landlady.

It was already dark when Rakitin and Alyosha came to Grushenka’s rooms, but no lights were on yet. Grushenka was lying on a big, uncomfortable sofa in the living room, with two white pillows from her bed under her head. She was stretched out on her back, not moving, her hands behind her head. She was dressed up, expecting someone, in a black silk dress with a pretty lace scarf over her hair and a lace shawl pinned with a big gold brooch. She definitely looked like she was waiting for someone, lying there looking impatient and tired, her face pale, lips and eyes hot, tapping the sofa with her foot. When Rakitin and Alyosha entered, she got a little excited. They heard her jump up from the sofa and call out, scared, “Who’s there?” But her maid met them at the door and called back to her.
“It’s not him, it’s just other visitors.”
“What’s going on?” Rakitin muttered, leading Alyosha into the living room.

Grushenka was standing by the sofa, still looking nervous. A thick strand of her dark brown hair had slipped out from under her scarf and hung over her shoulder, but she didn’t fix it until she’d looked closely at her visitors and recognized them.
“Oh, it’s you, Rakitin? You really scared me. Who did you bring with you? Oh my gosh, you brought him!” she cried, realizing it was Alyosha.
“Can you ask for some candles?” Rakitin said, acting like he was at home and could give orders.

“Candles... of course, candles. Fenya, bring them a candle. Well, you sure picked a time to bring him!” she said, nodding at Alyosha. She turned to the mirror and quickly fixed her hair with both hands, looking annoyed.
“What, I didn’t make you happy?” Rakitin asked, sounding a little hurt.

“You just startled me, that’s all,” Grushenka said, smiling at Alyosha. “Don’t be afraid of me, Alyosha, I’m actually really happy to see you, even though you surprised me. But Rakitin, you scared me—I thought it was Mitya breaking in. I tricked him earlier: I got him to promise to believe what I said, and then I lied. I told him I’d be at old man Kuzma Kuzmitch’s house all evening, helping him count money. I do spend one evening a week there, going over his accounts. We lock ourselves in and I keep track while he counts with his beads. I’m the only one he trusts. Mitya thinks I’m still there, but I came back and have been hiding here, waiting for news. How did Fenya let you in? Fenya, run to the gate and check if Mitya is around! Maybe he’s hiding, spying on me. I’m really scared.”
“There’s no one there, Agrafena Alexandrovna, I just checked. I keep peeking through the crack in the gate—I’m scared myself.”

“Are the shutters closed, Fenya? We should draw the curtains, too—that’s better!” Grushenka pulled the heavy curtains herself. “If he sees a light, he’ll rush in. I’m really afraid of your brother Mitya today, Alyosha.”
Even though she sounded scared, Grushenka’s voice was full of excitement and happiness.
“Why are you so afraid of Mitya today?” Rakitin asked. “I thought you could handle him, like he was nothing.”

“I told you, I’m waiting for some news, really important news, and I don’t want Mitya here at all. And I can tell he didn’t believe I’d stay at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. He’s probably hiding behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house right now, spying on me. If he’s there, he won’t come here—so that’s good! But I really did go to Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. Mitya took me there. I told him I’d be there until midnight and asked him to come pick me up. He left, I sat with Kuzma for ten minutes, then ran back here. Ugh, I was so scared of bumping into Mitya.”
“And why are you all dressed up? That’s a weird scarf you’re wearing!”
“You’re the weird one, Rakitin! I told you, I’m expecting a message. If it comes, I’m leaving, I’ll run off and you won’t see me again. That’s why I’m dressed up, to be ready.”
“And where will you go?”
“If you know too much, you’ll get old too soon.”
“Wow, you’re in a great mood! I’ve never seen you like this. You look like you’re going to a ball.” Rakitin looked her over.
“Shows how much you know about balls.”
“And you do?”

“I’ve seen one. Kuzma Kuzmitch’s son got married two years ago, and I watched from the balcony. Anyway, do you think I want to talk to you when someone special like this is here?” She looked at Alyosha. “Alyosha, I can’t believe you’re here! Honestly, I never thought you’d visit me. I’m so glad you’re here, even if the timing is weird. Sit on the sofa, right here, my bright young moon. I can hardly believe it... Oh, Rakitin, I wish you’d brought him yesterday or the day before! But maybe it’s best he came now, at just this moment.”

She sat down next to Alyosha on the sofa, looking at him with real happiness. She wasn’t faking—her eyes sparkled, her lips smiled, and it was a warm, genuine smile. Alyosha hadn’t expected her to look at him with such kindness. Until the day before, he’d hardly met her and had thought she was scary, especially after the mean trick she’d played on Katerina Ivanovna. But now, even though he was still sad himself, Alyosha couldn’t help but notice how different and much nicer Grushenka seemed. She wasn’t acting sweet or seductive now—she was just simple, friendly, and excited.
“Wow, everything’s happening today!” she kept chattering. “And I don’t even know why I’m so happy to see you, Alyosha! I just am!”
“Come on, you must know why,” Rakitin said, grinning. “You kept asking me to bring him, so you must have had a reason.”

“I did have a reason once, but that’s over now. Right now, I just want everyone to be happy. Rakitin, why are you just standing there? Oh, you’ve already sat down? I knew you couldn’t go long without looking after yourself.” She laughed. “Look, Alyosha, he’s pretending to be offended that I didn’t ask him to sit first. Rakitin is so sensitive! Don’t be mad, Rakitin, I’m in a good mood today. Why are you so sad, Alyosha? Are you scared of me?” She peeked into his eyes, teasing.
“He’s sad because he didn’t get promoted,” Rakitin joked loudly.
“What promotion?”
“His elder died.”

“What? You’re just saying nonsense to be mean. Be quiet! Alyosha, can I sit on your knee like this?” Suddenly, she jumped onto Alyosha’s knee, laughing and hugging him like a kitten. “Will you let me? If it bothers you, I’ll get off.”

Alyosha didn’t say anything. He sat still, hearing her say, “If you tell me, I’ll get off,” but he didn’t answer. He didn’t feel anything bad in his heart, nothing like what Rakitin, watching from his corner, might think. His own sadness was so strong that it covered up any other feelings. Even so, he felt a surprising new feeling—this “dreadful” woman didn’t scare him at all now. In fact, sitting on his knee and holding him, she made him feel curious and warmly interested, not afraid. That surprised him.
“That’s enough silly talk,” Rakitin cut in. “Why don’t you give us some champagne? You owe me, remember!”

“I do! Alyosha, I promised him champagne if he brought you. I’ll have some too! Fenya, bring the bottle Mitya left! Hurry up! I’m stingy, but I’ll open a bottle for you, Alyosha—not for Rakitin, he’s a fungus, but you’re a falcon! My heart is in a strange mood tonight, so let’s drink!”
“So what’s going on with you? What’s this message you’re waiting for, or is it a secret?” Rakitin asked, pretending he didn’t care about her insults.

“Oh, it’s not a secret, and you know it, Rakitin,” Grushenka said, suddenly sounding worried as she turned her head to Rakitin, though she still had her arm around Alyosha. “My officer is coming, Rakitin. My officer is coming.”
“I heard he was coming, but is he really that close?”
“He’s at Mokroe now; he’s sending a messenger from there. He wrote me a letter today. I’m expecting the messenger any minute.”
“No way! Why’s he at Mokroe?”
“That’s a long story. I’ve told you enough.”
“Mitya will do something crazy now, I bet! Does he know, or not?”

“Does he know? Of course not. If he did, there’d be a murder. But I’m not scared of his knife now. Don’t remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, Rakitin. He’s already hurt me enough. I want to think about Alyosha here. Alyosha... smile at me. There! He’s smiling—he’s so kind to me! Alyosha, I was sure you were angry at me for what happened the other day with that young lady. I was awful, but maybe it’s good it happened. It was terrible, but also maybe a good thing.” Grushenka smiled in a dreamy way, with a little bitterness. “Mitya told me she screamed that I ‘ought to be beaten.’ I was really mean to her. She tried to win me over with chocolate... No, it’s better it ended that way.” She smiled again. “But I’m still afraid you’re mad at me.”
“That’s actually true,” Rakitin said, surprised. “Alyosha, she’s really scared of a gentle guy like you.”
“He’s a chicken to you, Rakitin, because you don’t have a conscience! But I love him with all my soul, that’s why! Alyosha, do you believe I love you with all my soul?”
“Oh, you shameless woman! She’s confessing her love, Alexey!”
“So what? I love him!”
“What about your officer? And that big message from Mokroe?”
“That’s different.”
“Typical woman logic!”

“Don’t make me mad, Rakitin,” Grushenka said seriously. “This is different. I love Alyosha in a different way. It’s true, Alyosha, I had sneaky plans for you before. I’m terrible sometimes. But other times, I’ve thought of you as my conscience. I used to think, ‘Someone like him must hate someone like me.’ I thought that all the way home the other day. I’ve thought about you that way for a long time, and Mitya knows it. Sometimes I look at you and feel totally ashamed of myself. I can’t even remember when I started thinking about you like that...”
Fenya came in carrying a tray with an uncorked bottle and three glasses of champagne.

“Here’s the champagne!” Rakitin called out. “You’re all worked up, Agrafena Alexandrovna—after a glass of this, you’ll probably start dancing. Ugh, they can’t even serve it right,” he added, looking at the bottle. “The old woman poured it in the kitchen and brought it in warm, with no cork. Oh well, I’ll have some anyway.”
He went to the table, took a glass, drank it in one gulp, and poured himself another.

“You don’t get champagne every day,” he said, licking his lips. “Come on, Alyosha, let’s see what you can do! What should we drink to? The gates of heaven? Take a glass, Grushenka, you drink to the gates of heaven, too.”
“What gates of heaven?”
She took a glass, Alyosha took his, tasted a little, and set it down.
“No, I think I’d better not,” he said gently.
“And you made such a big deal!” Rakitin teased.
“Well, then I won’t either,” Grushenka said. “I really don’t want any. You can drink the whole bottle, Rakitin. If Alyosha has some, I will.”
“How sweet,” Rakitin said sarcastically. “And she’s sitting on his knee! He’s got something to be sad about, but what’s your excuse? He’s upset with God and ready to eat sausage...”
“What do you mean?”
“His elder died today—Father Zossima, the saint.”

“So Father Zossima is dead!” Grushenka gasped. She made the sign of the cross. “Oh no, what am I doing, sitting on his knee at a time like this?” She jumped up, looking upset, and sat back down on the sofa.
Alyosha gave her a long, thoughtful look, and a light seemed to shine in his face.

“Rakitin,” he said suddenly, loudly and firmly, “don’t mock me for being upset with God. I don’t want to be angry with you, so you should try to be kinder. I’ve lost a treasure you’ve never had, and you can’t judge me right now. You should look at her—see how she feels sorry for me? I came here looking for someone bad because I felt bad myself, and I found a true sister, a treasure—a loving heart. She just had pity on me... Agrafena Alexandrovna, I mean you. You pulled me out of the darkness.”
Alyosha’s lips trembled and he caught his breath.
“So she saved you, huh?” Rakitin said, laughing meanly. “And she wanted to trap you, did you realize that?”

“Wait, Rakitin!” Grushenka jumped up. “Stop, both of you. I’ll tell you everything now. Alyosha, your words make me ashamed because I’m bad, not good—that’s the truth. And you, Rakitin, stop lying. I did want to trap him, but now it’s different. Don’t say anything else, Rakitin.”
Grushenka said all this with deep emotion.
“They’re both crazy,” Rakitin said, looking at them like they were nuts. “It feels like a madhouse—they’ll both be crying any minute.”
“I will cry, yes, I will,” Grushenka said. “He called me his sister, and I’ll never forget that. Let me tell you, Rakitin, even though I’m bad, I once gave away an onion.”
“An onion? You really are crazy.”

Rakitin was amazed by how intense they were. He felt annoyed and left out, though maybe he should have realized both of them were going through something you don’t experience often in your life. But Rakitin, even though he was sensitive about himself, was kind of clueless about other people’s feelings—probably because he was young and selfish.

“Look, Alyosha,” Grushenka turned to him, laughing nervously. “I bragged to Rakitin about giving away an onion, but I’ll tell you the story—it's not to brag, it’s just a good story. My cook Matryona, who’s still with me, used to tell it to me when I was a kid. Once, there was a really mean peasant woman who died and hadn’t done a single good thing. The devils grabbed her and threw her into the lake of fire. Her guardian angel tried to think of any good deed she’d done, and finally remembered she once pulled up an onion and gave it to a beggar woman. God said, ‘Take that onion, hold it out to her, and if you can pull her out, she can come to heaven. If the onion breaks, she stays.’ The angel gave her the onion in the lake and started to pull her out. Other sinners grabbed her, trying to get out, too, but she kicked at them, saying, ‘It’s my onion, not yours!’ The onion broke, and she fell back into the fire. The angel cried and left. So that’s the story, Alyosha—I know it by heart because I feel like I’m that woman. I told Rakitin I gave away an onion, but really, that’s the only good thing I’ve done. So don’t praise me, Alyosha, don’t think I’m good—I’m bad, and you make me ashamed when you say nice things. Oh, I’ll confess everything. I even paid Rakitin twenty-five roubles to bring you to me. Wait, Rakitin!”
She hurried to the table, opened a drawer, pulled out her purse, and took out a twenty-five rouble note.
“What nonsense! What nonsense!” Rakitin protested, embarrassed.
“Take it, Rakitin, I owe it to you. Don’t act like you wouldn’t take it—you asked for it yourself.” She tossed him the money.
“Like I’d refuse,” Rakitin said, pretending not to care but clearly embarrassed. “That’ll come in handy; fools are there for smart people to use.”
“Now be quiet, Rakitin, what I’m about to say isn’t for you. Sit in the corner and don’t interrupt. You don’t even like us, so just hush.”

“Why should I like you?” Rakitin snapped, showing his bad mood. He put the money in his pocket, feeling awkward about Alyosha seeing it. He’d hoped to be paid later, privately, but now he was annoyed. Until now, he’d tried not to argue too much with Grushenka so he could get what he wanted, but now he was angry too.
“People only love others for a reason, but what have either of you done for me?”
“You should love people for no reason, like Alyosha does.”
“How does he love you? What’s he done that’s such a big deal?”
Grushenka stood in the middle of the room, speaking passionately, her voice shaky.

“Shut up, Rakitin, you know nothing about us! And don’t talk to me like that again. How dare you? Sit over there and stay quiet like a servant! Now, Alyosha, I’ll tell you the whole truth, so you see what a jerk I am. I wanted to ruin you, Alyosha—truly. I wanted to so badly that I paid Rakitin to bring you. Why? You didn’t know anything, but I saw you turn away from me, drop your eyes when you passed me. I’ve watched you a hundred times before today; your face haunted me. ‘He despises me,’ I thought, ‘he won’t even look at me.’ I was so hurt, I wondered why I was scared of a boy. So I decided I’d trap you and laugh at you. I was full of anger. You should know, no one dares even think of coming near me with bad intentions—except for old Kuzma, who I was basically sold to, thanks to the devil. But no one else. Still, I thought, ‘I’ll trap him and laugh at him.’ That’s how mean I am—and you call me your sister! Now the man who wronged me is back, and I’m waiting for a message from him. Five years ago, when Kuzma brought me here, I hid away, crying all night, thinking, ‘Where is he now? Laughing at me with someone else?’ If I could just see him again, I’d pay him back! At night, I’d cry into my pillow and stew in my anger. ‘I’ll pay him back!’ Sometimes I’d realize I wouldn’t do anything, and he’d forgotten me or was laughing, and I’d fall to the floor, crying until morning. I’d get up full of rage, ready to fight the world. Then I started saving money, got tough, put on weight—got “wiser,” maybe? But at night, I still sometimes cry and get angry just like before. Then, a month ago, a letter came—he was coming, he was a widower, he wanted to see me. I couldn’t breathe, then thought, ‘If he whistles, will I crawl back like a beaten dog?’ Could I really be that weak? Would I run to him or not? I was so angry with myself all month, worse than ever. Do you get it now, Alyosha? I played with Mitya just to stop myself running to the other one. Hush, Rakitin, this isn’t for you. Before you came, I was lying here, deciding my whole future, and you can never know what was in my heart. Yes—tell your young lady not to be angry with me for the other day. No one knows what I’m going through, no one will ever know. Maybe I’ll take a knife with me today—I can’t decide...”
At this dramatic moment, Grushenka broke down, covered her face, and sobbed like a child into the pillows.
Alyosha stood up and went over to Rakitin.
“Misha,” he said, “don’t be angry. She hurt your feelings, but don’t be angry. You heard what she said? People can only take so much—you have to have compassion.”

Alyosha said this from the heart. He felt he had to speak, so he turned to Rakitin. If Rakitin hadn’t been there, Alyosha would’ve just spoken to the air. But Rakitin looked at him with sarcasm, and Alyosha stopped short.
“You’re just repeating what your elder taught you, Alexey, man of God,” Rakitin said with a mean smile.

“Don’t laugh, Rakitin, don’t joke about the dead—he was better than anyone!” Alyosha said, his voice shaking. “I’m not judging you—I’m the lowest of the low. I came here wanting to ruin myself, thinking ‘What does it matter?’ out of cowardice. But she, after five years of pain, hears one kind word and forgives everything, even the man who wronged her, and runs to meet him—she won’t take a knife, she’ll forgive. I’m not like that. I don’t know if you are, Misha, but I’m not. It’s a lesson for me—she’s more loving than we are. Have you ever heard her talk about this before? No, or you’d have understood her. And the lady insulted the other day should forgive her too! She will, once she knows. There’s still a treasure in this soul—we should be gentle with her...”
Alyosha stopped, catching his breath. Even Rakitin, annoyed as he was, looked at him in surprise. He’d never heard Alyosha talk like that before.
“You’re her defender now, huh? Are you in love with her, Alyosha? Agrafena Alexandrovna, our monk is in love with you—you’ve got a new fan!” Rakitin said, laughing rudely.
Grushenka lifted her head from the pillow and looked at Alyosha with a soft, tearful smile.

“Don’t mind him, Alyosha, my angel; you see what he’s like—he’s not worth talking to. Mihail Osipovitch,” she said to Rakitin, “I was going to apologize for being rude, but now I don’t want to. Alyosha, come here, sit with me.” She beckoned with a happy smile. “That’s right, sit here. Tell me,” she grabbed his hand and smiled into his face, “do I love that man or not? The one who hurt me—do I love him? Before you came, I was lying here in the dark, asking my heart. You decide for me, Alyosha. Should I forgive him or not?”
“But you’ve already forgiven him,” Alyosha said, smiling.

“Yes, I really have forgiven him,” Grushenka said thoughtfully. “What a weak heart! Such a weak heart!” She grabbed a glass, drank it in one gulp, raised it and threw it on the floor. It broke loudly. A mean little smile appeared on her face.

“Or maybe I haven’t forgiven him,” she said, sounding almost threatening, looking down. “Maybe my heart’s only getting ready to forgive. I’ll struggle with it. You know, Alyosha, I’ve learned to love my tears these last five years. Maybe I just love my anger, not him...”
“Well, I wouldn’t want to be that guy,” Rakitin muttered.
“Well, you won’t be, Rakitin! You can shine my shoes, that’s all you’ll ever get. You’ll never get a woman like me—and maybe he won’t either...”
“Oh yeah? Then why are you so dressed up?” Rakitin sneered.

“Don’t tease me about dressing up, Rakitin. You don’t know what’s in my heart! If I want, I’ll rip all this off right now,” she cried, her voice loud. “You don’t know why I’m dressed up! Maybe I’ll see him and say, ‘Have you ever seen me like this?’ He left me a skinny, sick kid at seventeen. I’ll sit by him, dazzle him, and say, ‘See what I am now? Well, that’s enough for you! There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip!’ Maybe that’s why I dressed up.” Grushenka finished with a bitter laugh. “I’m angry and stubborn, Alyosha. I’ll rip off my fancy clothes, ruin my looks, mess up my face, and become a beggar if I feel like it! You think I wouldn’t dare? I would! I could do it right now—don’t push me! I’ll send him away, too. He’ll never see me again!”
She screamed the last words, then broke down crying again, hiding her face in the pillows.
Rakitin stood up.
“It’s time to go,” he said. “It’s late—we’ll be locked out of the monastery.”
Grushenka jumped up.
“You’re not leaving, are you, Alyosha?” she cried, sad. “How can you do this to me? You’ve stirred up all my feelings, made me suffer, and now you’ll leave me to face the night alone!”
“He can hardly spend the night here! But if he wants to, let him! I’ll go alone,” Rakitin sneered.
“Shut up, you snake!” Grushenka yelled at him. “You never said anything to me like he just did.”
“What did he say that was so special?” Rakitin grumbled.

“I can’t explain it—I don’t know. I don’t know what he said, but it went straight to my heart. He’s the first, the only one who’s ever really pitied me, that’s what it is. Why didn’t you come sooner, you angel?” She dropped to her knees before Alyosha, almost in a frenzy. “I’ve waited all my life for someone like you—to forgive me. I always believed, no matter how awful I am, someone would love me for real, not in a shameful way!”
“What did I do for you?” Alyosha asked gently, bending down and taking her hands. “I only gave you an onion, just a tiny little onion, that’s all!”
He was close to tears himself. Just then, there was a loud noise in the hall—someone came in. Grushenka jumped up, looking really scared. Fenya burst in, excited and out of breath:

“Mistress, mistress, a messenger just came!” she cried, thrilled. “A carriage from Mokroe for you—Timofey the driver, with three horses—they’re putting in fresh horses right now. Here’s a letter, mistress!”
She waved a letter in the air as she spoke. Grushenka grabbed it and read it by candlelight. It was just a note, a few lines. She read it in a second.
“He’s sent for me!” she cried, her face pale and twisted, with a strange smile. “He whistles! Crawl back, little dog!”
But she only stood frozen for a second; suddenly, her cheeks filled with color.

“I’m going!” she shouted. “Five years of my life! Good-bye, Alyosha, my fate is decided. Go, all of you, don’t let me see you again! Grushenka is running off to a new life! Don’t hold anything against me, Rakitin. Maybe I’m going to my death—ugh, I feel drunk!”
She ran out of the room and into her bedroom.
“Well, she’s not thinking about us now,” Rakitin grumbled. “Let’s go, or we’ll hear more of her yelling. I’m sick of all these tears and drama.”

Alyosha let himself be led outside. In the yard, a covered cart waited. Horses were being switched out, men ran around with lanterns, and three fresh horses were being brought in through the gate. As Alyosha and Rakitin reached the steps, Grushenka’s bedroom window suddenly opened and she called out to Alyosha:

“Alyosha, tell your brother Mitya not to hate me, even though I’ve brought him pain. Tell him, from me: ‘Grushenka has gone to a scoundrel, not to you, noble heart.’ Also, tell him Grushenka loved him for only one hour, just a single hour—so let him remember that hour forever. Tell him, ‘Grushenka says so!’ ”
Her voice was full of sobs. The window slammed shut.
“Ha!” Rakitin laughed. “She ruins your brother Mitya and then tells him to remember it forever! How savage!”

Alyosha didn’t reply. He walked quickly beside Rakitin, deep in thought, barely even noticing where he was going. Rakitin felt a pang—it hadn’t turned out how he’d hoped by bringing Alyosha and Grushenka together.

“That officer of hers is a Pole,” he started again, trying to keep his cool, “and he’s not really an officer anymore. He worked customs in Siberia, somewhere near China, just a poor little Pole who lost his job. Now he’s heard Grushenka has money, so he’s shown up again—that’s the real story.”
Again, Alyosha didn’t seem to hear. Rakitin couldn’t hold back.
“So, you saved the sinner, huh?” he said nastily. “Did you turn the Magdalene into a saint? Driven out all her demons? See, miracles do happen after all!”
“Stop, Rakitin,” Alyosha said quietly, his heart aching.
“So now you hate me over those twenty-five roubles? You think I sold my friend? But you’re not Jesus, and I’m not Judas.”
“Oh, Rakitin, I’d forgotten about it until you brought it up,” Alyosha cried.
That was the last straw for Rakitin.
“Curse all of you!” he shouted. “Why did I even bother with you? I don’t want to know you anymore. Go on your way!”
And he turned suddenly into another street, leaving Alyosha alone in the dark. Alyosha walked out of town, across the fields, back to the monastery.

It was very late, at least by monastery standards, when Alyosha (also called Alexey) finally returned to the hermitage. The door-keeper let him in through a special side entrance. It was already nine o’clock—the time when everyone was supposed to be resting after such a stressful day. Alyosha quietly opened the door and stepped into Father Zossima’s cell, where the elder’s coffin now stood. The cell was almost empty; only Father Païssy was there, sitting alone and reading the Gospel over the coffin. In the next room, the young novice Porfiry, exhausted from last night’s long talk and today’s events, was fast asleep on the floor. Although Father Païssy heard Alyosha come in, he didn’t even look up. Alyosha turned right, knelt down in the corner, and began to pray.

Alyosha’s heart was overflowing, but his feelings were all mixed up. It wasn’t just one emotion—his thoughts and feelings kept chasing each other, changing from one to another. Still, there was a kind of sweetness inside him, and, strangely, Alyosha wasn’t surprised by it. He saw the coffin again, with the body of the person he loved so much hidden inside, but the sharp pain and tears from earlier that morning were gone. As soon as he entered, he knelt by the coffin like it was a holy place, but this time, joy was shining inside him. The room’s only window was open, letting in cool, fresh air. “They must have opened the window because of the smell,” Alyosha thought. But even the thought of decay, which had seemed so horrible and embarrassing a few hours ago, didn’t bother him now. He began to pray quietly, but soon realized he was doing it almost automatically. Bits of thought flickered through his mind like shooting stars—here for a second, then gone, replaced by new ones. Yet, deep down, he felt a sense of wholeness and comfort, and he knew it. Sometimes he prayed with all his heart, wanting to pour out his love and gratitude…

But as soon as he started praying, his mind would wander to something else, and he’d forget both his prayer and whatever interrupted it. He tried to listen to what Father Païssy was reading, but he was so tired that he started to drift off to sleep.
“And on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee,” read Father Païssy. “And Jesus’ mother was there; and Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding.”

“A wedding? What’s that?... A wedding!” Alyosha’s thoughts spun in his head. “There’s happiness for her, too… She’s gone to the celebration… No, she didn’t take the knife… That was just a dramatic way of speaking… Well, dramatic words should be forgiven—people need them. Without them, sorrow would be too much to bear. Rakitin has gone off to sulk in the back alley. As long as Rakitin focuses on his anger, he’ll always end up in the back alley… But the main road… The main road is wide and straight and clear as crystal, with the sun shining at the end… Ah! What’s being read now?”
“And when they ran out of wine, Jesus’ mother said to him, ‘They have no wine,’” Alyosha heard.

“Ah, yes, I love this part and didn’t want to miss it. It’s the wedding in Cana, the first miracle… Ah, that miracle! That sweet miracle! Jesus didn’t come for people’s sadness, but their happiness. His first miracle was to help people enjoy themselves… ‘If you love people, you love their happiness, too’… He always used to say that—it was one of his main ideas… ‘There’s no living without joy,’ Mitya (Dmitri) says… Yes, Mitya… ‘Everything true and good is always full of forgiveness,’ he used to say that, too…”
“Jesus said to her, ‘Woman, what does this have to do with me and you? My hour hasn’t come yet.’”
“His mother said to the servants, ‘Do whatever he tells you.’”

“Do it… Happiness, the happiness of some poor, really poor people… Of course they were poor—they didn’t even have enough wine for a wedding… Historians say that the people who lived around Lake Gennesaret then were the poorest you can imagine… and another great heart, His Mother, knew that He didn’t just come to make a huge sacrifice. She knew His heart was open even to the simple fun of ordinary and unimportant people, who had kindly invited Him to their little wedding. ‘My hour hasn’t come yet,’ He said, probably with a gentle smile (He must have smiled at her). Was it really just to make more wine at poor weddings that He came to earth? And yet He did as she asked… Ah, he’s reading again…”
“Jesus said to them, ‘Fill the water jars with water.’ And they filled them to the top.”
“Then he said, ‘Now draw some out and take it to the man in charge of the feast.’ And they did.”
“When the man in charge tasted the water that had become wine, he didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who got the water knew). The man in charge called the groom over,”
“And said to him, ‘Everyone serves the best wine first, and when people have had plenty, then the cheaper wine. But you’ve saved the best wine until now.’”

“But what’s this? Why does the room seem to be getting bigger?... Oh, yes… It’s the wedding, the celebration… yes, of course. Here are the guests, the young couple, the happy crowd and… Where’s the wise man in charge of the feast? But who is that? Who? The walls are fading away again… Who’s getting up from the big table? What! He’s here, too? But he’s in the coffin… but he’s here, too. He’s standing up, he sees me, he’s coming toward me… God!”

Yes, he was coming up to Alyosha—it was him, the small, thin old man, his face covered in little wrinkles, smiling softly and joyfully. There was no coffin now, and he was dressed just as he’d been yesterday when everyone gathered around him. His face was uncovered, his eyes were shining. How could this be? He, too, had been invited to the feast. He, too, was at the wedding in Cana…
“Yes, my dear, I’ve been invited, too—called and welcomed,” Alyosha heard a gentle voice say above him. “Why are you hiding here, out of sight? Come and join us.”
It was his voice—the voice of Father Zossima. And it had to be him, since he was calling Alyosha!
The elder took Alyosha’s hand and helped him up from his knees.

“We are celebrating,” the thin old man said. “We’re drinking the new wine, the wine of great new joy. Do you see how many guests are here? Here are the bride and groom, and the wise man in charge of the feast, tasting the new wine. Why are you surprised to see me? I gave an onion to a beggar, so I’m here, too. And many here have only given a single onion—just one small thing. What do our good deeds amount to? And you, my gentle one, my kind boy—you also knew how to give an onion to a hungry woman today. Start your work, dear one, start it, gentle one!... Do you see our Sun? Do you see Him?”
“I’m afraid… I don’t dare look,” Alyosha whispered.

“Don’t be afraid of Him. He’s awe-inspiring in His greatness, amazing in His glory, but endlessly merciful. Out of love, He became like us, and He celebrates with us. He’s turning water into wine so the guests’ happiness won’t end. He’s always waiting for new guests, always calling more, forever and ever… Look, they’re bringing more wine. Do you see them bringing the jars?”
Something warmed Alyosha’s heart, filling it so much it hurt, and tears of joy rose up in him. He stretched out his hands, cried out, and woke up.

The coffin was there again, the window open, and Father Païssy’s gentle, steady reading from the Gospel. But Alyosha wasn’t listening anymore. Strangely, he’d fallen asleep on his knees, but now he found himself standing, and suddenly, almost as if pushed, he quickly took three strong steps right up to the coffin. His shoulder brushed against Father Païssy, but he didn’t even notice. Father Païssy looked up from his book for a moment, but then looked away, sensing something unusual was happening to Alyosha. Alyosha stared for half a minute at the coffin, at the still, hidden body with the icon on its chest and the cap with the eight-pointed cross on its head. He had just been hearing that voice, and it still echoed in his ears. He listened, hoping for more words, but suddenly he turned sharply and walked out of the cell.

He didn’t stop on the steps either, but hurried down; his heart, overflowing with happiness, longed for freedom and open space. The sky above was full of soft, shining stars, stretching endlessly. The Milky Way ran across the sky in two pale streams. The night was fresh and perfectly still. The white towers and golden domes of the cathedral stood out against the deep-blue sky. The bright autumn flowers in beds around the house slept quietly until morning. The silence of earth seemed to blend into the silence of the sky. The mystery of the earth and the stars felt like one great mystery.

Alyosha stood, gazed up, and suddenly threw himself down onto the ground. He didn’t know why he hugged the earth. He couldn’t have explained why he wanted so badly to kiss it, to kiss all of it. But he kissed it, crying, sobbing, and soaking the ground with his tears, promising with all his heart to love it forever. “Water the earth with the tears of your joy and love those tears,” echoed inside him.
What was he crying for?

Oh! In his happiness, he was crying for everything—even for those stars shining at him from the endless sky, and “he wasn’t ashamed of his joy.” It felt like there were invisible threads from all those countless worlds of God, connecting his soul to them, and he trembled all over, “in contact with other worlds.” He wanted to forgive everyone for everything, and to ask forgiveness himself. Not just for him, but for all people, for everything. “And others are praying for me too,” echoed again inside him. But every second, he felt more and more clearly that something strong and steady—like the sky above him—had entered his soul. It was as if a new idea had taken charge of his mind, for his whole life, forever. He had fallen to the ground a weak boy, but now he stood up a determined champion, and he knew it, right there in that moment of joy. Alyosha would never, ever forget that moment as long as he lived.
“Someone visited my soul in that hour,” he used to say afterwards, sure that it was true.
Within three days, he left the monastery, just as his elder had told him to do—to “live in the world.”

Dmitri (Mitya), to whom Grushenka had given her last goodbye before leaving to start a new life, had no idea what had happened to her. Right then, he was caught up in a feverish, restless state. For the past two days, he'd been so anxious and worked up that, as he later said, he might have made himself seriously ill. Alyosha couldn't find him the morning before, and Ivan had missed him at the tavern that day, too. The people where Dmitri was staying were told by him to keep his whereabouts secret.

Dmitri had spent those two days running all over town, “fighting with his fate and trying to save himself,” as he described it later. He even left town for a few hours on urgent business, even though he hated leaving Grushenka out of his sight. All these details would be explained later with proof, but for now, we’ll focus on the most important things that happened in those two horrible days right before the disaster that changed everything for Dmitri.

Even though Grushenka really had loved Dmitri for a brief time, she still hurt him cruelly at times. The worst part was, he never knew what she was going to do next. He couldn't win her over by force or by being kind—she wouldn't give in, and if he tried, she’d just get mad and leave him. He also guessed, quite rightly, that Grushenka was struggling inside herself, unable to make up her mind about something big. He could tell that sometimes she must hate him and his strong feelings for her. Maybe that was true, but Dmitri didn’t know what was really troubling her. For him, the whole problem centered on the fight between himself and his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Here’s an important fact: Dmitri truly believed that Fyodor Pavlovitch would ask Grushenka to marry him—or maybe already had—and he never thought for a second that his father was just trying to get her for three thousand roubles. Dmitri figured this out from knowing Grushenka’s character. That’s why he sometimes thought Grushenka’s nervousness was because she couldn’t decide which of them would be better for her.

Oddly, Dmitri never thought about the return of the “officer”—the man from Grushenka’s past who had caused her so much pain and whose arrival she was dreading and hoping for. Lately, Grushenka hadn’t mentioned him much, but Dmitri knew she’d gotten a letter from that man a month ago—she’d even shown it to him in a moment of anger. Dmitri, though, didn’t take the letter seriously at all, which surprised her. Maybe, since he was so weighed down by his own battle with his father, he just couldn’t imagine any worse threat. Plus, the “officer’s” letter was vague and dramatic, not definite about coming back. Grushenka had hidden the last lines of the letter from Dmitri, where the officer talked more clearly about returning. Dmitri did remember that when he saw the letter, he thought Grushenka looked proud and even a little disgusted by it. She never told him anything else about her old lover, so Dmitri slowly forgot all about the officer.

Dmitri felt that, no matter what happened later, he first had to face his final showdown with Fyodor Pavlovitch. He was waiting for Grushenka to make her choice, always thinking she’d decide suddenly, in the heat of the moment. He imagined her saying, “Take me, I’m yours forever,” and then it would all be settled. He’d grab her and run away with her—far away, maybe to the farthest part of Russia or even the whole world. There, they’d get married and start a new life in secret, so no one would know where they were. Then, everything would be different.

Dmitri dreamed constantly of this new and “good” life (“it has to be good,” he thought). He longed for a fresh start. The filthy, miserable life he’d gotten himself into disgusted him, and like a lot of people in his situation, he thought moving somewhere else would solve everything. If only he could get away from this cursed place and these people, he’d become a new man, following a better path. That’s what he believed and desperately wanted.

But all this depended on Grushenka picking him. There was another, more awful possibility: what if she suddenly said, “Go away. I’ve just agreed to marry Fyodor Pavlovitch. I don’t want you anymore.” What would Dmitri do then? He had no idea. To be fair, until the very end, he didn’t make any plans for what he’d do if that happened—he hadn’t plotted any crime. He was just watching, hoping, and getting ready for his best chance. He tried to ignore any other outcomes. But even if he got his wish, another big, nearly impossible problem was waiting for him.

If Grushenka said, “I’m yours; take me away,” how could he actually do it? Where would he get the money? By this time, his father Fyodor Pavlovitch had stopped giving him any money at all, even though he’d supported Dmitri for years. Grushenka had money, but Dmitri felt a huge pride about this—he wanted to take her away and start their new life using his own money, not hers. The idea of using her money disgusted him. Maybe this was because he secretly felt guilty about the money he’d taken from Katerina Ivanovna. “I’ve been a jerk to one woman, and I’ll just be a jerk to another,” he thought. “And once Grushenka finds out, she’ll never love someone like that.”
So where was he supposed to get the money he needed? Without it, everything would fall apart, and it would all be his fault—just because he didn’t have the cash. “Oh, the shame!” he thought.

To get ahead of the story: maybe Dmitri did know where he could get the money—he might have even known exactly where it was. But to actually take it, and have the right to take it, he first had to pay back the three thousand roubles he owed Katerina Ivanovna. If he didn’t, “I’m nothing but a thief, a scoundrel, and I don’t want to start a new life like that,” he decided. So he made up his mind to do whatever it took to pay Katerina Ivanovna back first. He only became totally sure of this after his last talk with Alyosha, two days before, when Grushenka had insulted Katerina Ivanovna and Dmitri admitted to Alyosha that he was a scoundrel. After that, he felt he’d rather rob or even kill someone than not pay Katya back. “Better everyone thinks I’m a robber or murderer and I end up in Siberia, than for Katya to say I tricked her and used her money to run off with Grushenka! I can’t do that!” Dmitri thought, grinding his teeth. But still, he kept struggling on...

Oddly, even though it seemed impossible for him to get that much money with nothing to his name, Dmitri still kept hoping something would turn up. He believed the three thousand roubles would just appear somehow, as if from nowhere. That’s how it often is for people like Dmitri, who’ve only ever had money dropped in their laps and never had to work for it. After his talk with Alyosha, his mind filled up with wild, unrealistic ideas. That’s how he first came up with a completely crazy scheme. Maybe people like him, in tough situations, always come up with the most unrealistic plans first—and they actually seem possible to them.

Dmitri suddenly decided to go to Samsonov, the merchant who had been Grushenka’s “protector,” and propose a business deal to get all the money he needed. He was sure his idea would work, and only wondered how Samsonov would react. Dmitri had seen the merchant around but had never actually spoken to him before. Still, for some reason, Dmitri believed that the old, dying man might want Grushenka to have a good life and marry a dependable man. Maybe he’d even prefer Dmitri to Fyodor Pavlovitch as a match for Grushenka. Dmitri had heard something along these lines—from gossip or maybe from something Grushenka said.

Some people might think Dmitri was being rude or insensitive, expecting to get help like this and to “take” his bride from her old protector. But Dmitri saw Grushenka’s past as over and done with. He looked at her past with sympathy and was determined that if she chose him, they’d both start fresh, forgiving each other for everything. As for Kuzma Samsonov, Dmitri saw him as just a part of Grushenka’s past—someone she never really loved and who now hardly mattered at all. Besides, everyone knew that Samsonov was now just a sick old man, more like a father figure to Grushenka than anything else.

Dmitri was pretty naïve about all this. Despite his wild side, he was simple-hearted in many ways. He truly believed that, since Samsonov was close to dying, he would feel bad about his past with Grushenka and want to help her now more than anyone else.

After talking with Alyosha at the crossroads, Dmitri barely slept, and by ten the next morning, he was at Samsonov’s house, asking the servant to announce him. The house was big and gloomy, with two floors and lots of people living there—Samsonov’s two married sons and their families, his old sister, and his unmarried daughter all lived downstairs. Two of his clerks lived in the lodge, and one had a large family, too. The lower floor and lodge were crowded, but Samsonov kept the whole upper floor to himself, not even letting his daughter live there, even though she took care of him.

The upper floor had big, old-fashioned rooms, lined with heavy mahogany chairs, glass chandeliers, and dark mirrors. But they were hardly ever used; Samsonov stayed in a small back bedroom, where an old woman and a young boy took care of him. Because of his swollen legs, he could barely walk, and only occasionally was helped up to walk a little. He was grumpy and hardly ever spoke to even the old woman who cared for him.

When the servant told Samsonov that “the captain” (Dmitri) had arrived, he immediately refused to see him. But Dmitri wouldn’t give up and sent his name up again. Samsonov questioned the boy who brought the message: What did the visitor look like? Was he drunk? Was he going to cause trouble? The answer: he was sober, but wouldn’t leave. Again, Samsonov refused to see him. Dmitri, expecting this, wrote on a piece of paper: “On most important business closely concerning Agrafena Alexandrovna,” and had it sent to the old man.

After thinking it over, Samsonov told the boy to show Dmitri into the drawing room, and sent the old woman to call his younger son upstairs. This younger son was huge and strong, clean-shaven, and wore modern clothes, while his father still wore the old Russian long coat and beard. The whole family was afraid of the father. Samsonov wanted his son there not because he was scared of Dmitri, but in case anything happened, he’d have a witness. Supported by his son and the boy, Samsonov finally waddled into the drawing room. He must have been pretty curious. The room where Dmitri waited was huge and depressing, with two rows of windows, marble walls, a gallery, and three giant chandeliers.

Dmitri was sitting on a little chair near the entrance, anxiously waiting. When the old man appeared on the other side of the room, Dmitri jumped up and walked quickly to meet him. Dmitri was dressed neatly in a buttoned-up coat, with a round hat and black gloves, just like at the family meeting with his father and brothers. The old man waited, standing tall and serious, and Dmitri could tell he was being sized up. Dmitri was struck by Samsonov’s swollen face and thick, hanging lower lip. Samsonov silently bowed, pointed to a low chair for Dmitri, and, leaning on his son, lowered himself onto the sofa, groaning with effort. Dmitri, seeing how hard this was for the old man, felt instantly awkward and small for having bothered him.
“What do you want from me, sir?” the old man said in a slow, clear, stern, but polite voice once he was seated.

Dmitri jumped, then sat back down, and started talking fast, waving his arms and sounding desperate. He looked like someone at the end of his rope, grabbing at any hope. Samsonov probably saw this instantly, though his face stayed cold and unmoved.

“Honorable sir, Kuzma Kuzmitch,” Dmitri began nervously, “I’m sure you’ve heard about my fights with my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, who cheated me out of my inheritance from my mother... everyone in town talks about it... maybe you heard from Grushenka—sorry, Agrafena Alexandrovna, who I respect very much...”

Dmitri broke down after his first sentence. We won’t repeat every word, but here’s what he meant: Three months ago, he said, he “on purpose” went to a lawyer in the main city—“a famous lawyer, Kuzma Kuzmitch, Pavel Pavlovitch Korneplodov. Maybe you’ve heard of him? Brilliant man... he knows you, too... spoke very highly of you...” Dmitri stumbled again, but kept pushing ahead, skipping over the awkward parts.

Korneplodov, after looking into everything (Dmitri vaguely referred to some documents), told him he could sue over the village of Tchermashnya, which should have come to Dmitri from his mother, and maybe force his father to pay up. “It wasn’t all hopeless—justice might still win.” Dmitri thought he could get six or seven thousand roubles extra from his father, since the village was worth at least twenty-five thousand—maybe even thirty. But his father only gave him seventeen thousand. Dmitri had dropped the whole thing for a while, since he didn’t know the law, but when he got here, he was shocked by a new claim against him. (Here, Dmitri lost his train of thought again.) “So, honorable Kuzma Kuzmitch, would you take over my claims against my father and pay me just three thousand roubles now? You can’t lose—on my honor! In fact, you could make six or seven thousand instead of just three if it works out.” Most of all, Dmitri wanted this settled today.

“We could do it with a notary or however it’s done... I’ll give you all the documents, sign whatever you want... we can make the deal right away—maybe even this morning. You could give me the three thousand, since you’re the richest man in town, and you’d be saving me... really saving me, for a good reason. I have the highest respect for a certain person, whom you care for like a father. I wouldn’t have come otherwise. It’s really a fight between three people, a matter of fate—a real tragedy, Kuzma Kuzmitch! But since you’ve stepped back, it’s just between two of us now. I may not be explaining it well, but you get it—I can see you understand, and if you don’t, I’m finished... so you see!”
Dmitri ended his nervous, rambling speech with “so you see!” He jumped out of his seat, waiting for an answer to his clumsy proposal. Right then, he realized that his whole plan sounded ridiculous.

“Strange! On my way here, it all seemed to make sense, but now it’s just nonsense,” Dmitri thought, suddenly despairing. While Dmitri was talking, Samsonov had just sat and stared at him coldly. After a moment, the old man finally spoke, in a firm, icy voice:
“Sorry, but we don’t do that kind of business.”
Dmitri suddenly felt his legs go weak.
“What am I supposed to do now, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” he said with a pale smile. “I guess that’s it for me—what do you think?”
“Excuse me…”
Dmitri stood there, unmoving, staring. He noticed a change in the old man’s face and jumped.
“You see, sir, business like that isn’t our thing,” the old man said slowly. “There’s the court and the lawyers—that’s a nightmare. But if you want, there’s someone else you could try.”
“Really? Who? You’re saving me, Kuzma Kuzmitch!” Dmitri said hopefully.

“He doesn’t live here, and he’s not in town right now. He’s a peasant who works in timber—his name is Lyagavy. He’s been arguing with Fyodor Pavlovitch for a year about buying your forest at Tchermashnya. They can’t agree on a price, maybe you’ve heard? He’s back now, staying with the priest in Ilyinskoe, about twelve versts from Volovya station. He wrote to me about the forest, asking for advice. Fyodor Pavlovitch is planning to go see him. So if you go see Lyagavy first and make him the offer you just made me, he might—”
“That’s a great idea!” Dmitri broke in excitedly. “He’s perfect—he’s haggling over it, and here he could get all the documents straight away! Ha ha!”
Dmitri suddenly burst out with his quick, awkward laugh, which startled Samsonov.
“How can I thank you, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” Dmitri said, almost gushing.
“Don’t mention it,” Samsonov replied, nodding.
“You don’t know—you’ve saved me. I felt something told me to come to you. Now, off to the priest!”
“No need to thank me.”
“I’ll hurry and get there. I hope I haven’t worn you out. I’ll never forget this—a true Russian thanks you, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a real R-r-russian!”
“Of course!”
Dmitri tried to shake the old man’s hand, but saw a cruel look in Samsonov’s eye. Dmitri pulled back, then scolded himself for being suspicious.
“It’s just because he’s tired,” Dmitri thought.

“For her sake! For her sake, Kuzma Kuzmitch! You understand it’s for her,” Dmitri shouted, his voice echoing. He bowed, turned sharply, and hurried out the door without looking back. He was shaking with happiness.

“Everything was about to fall apart, and my guardian angel saved me,” Dmitri thought. And if a businessman as serious as Samsonov (so dignified!) suggested this, then it had to be a good idea. He’d go right away. “I’ll be back tonight and it’ll all be done. Could the old man have been making fun of me?” Dmitri wondered as he rushed home. But he couldn’t believe someone like Samsonov would joke about business, especially about Lyagavy (what a name!). Or—maybe the old man was just laughing at him.

Sadly, the second option was true. Much later, after everything had happened, Samsonov himself admitted, laughing, that he had tricked “the captain.” He was a cold, mean, sarcastic man who could hold a serious grudge. Maybe it was Dmitri’s desperate face, or the ridiculous idea that Samsonov would fall for his wild scheme, or maybe jealousy over Grushenka—who knows? But the moment Dmitri stood there, desperate and begging, Samsonov decided to make a joke out of him. After Dmitri left, the old man, furious, told his son to make sure that beggar never set foot in the house again—or else he’d—

He didn’t finish his threat. Even his son, who’d seen his father angry before, was scared. For an hour after Dmitri left, Samsonov shook with rage, and by that evening, he was feeling worse and called for the doctor.

Mitya (Dmitri) knew he had to travel fast, but he didn't have money for horses. All he had left was forty kopecks, after all those years of living well! At home, though, he still had an old silver watch that didn't work anymore. He grabbed it and rushed to a Jewish watchmaker in the town square. The watchmaker gave him six roubles for it.

"I didn't expect that!" Mitya shouted, thrilled. (He was still really hyped up.) He grabbed the six roubles and hurried home. Once there, he borrowed three more roubles from the people he lived with. They liked Mitya so much that they happily gave him the money, even though it was all they had. In his excitement, Mitya told them right away that everything would be decided for him that day. He frantically explained his plan with Samsonov, how Samsonov had answered, and what he hoped for in the future. The people he lived with already knew a lot about his secrets, so they saw him as a friendly gentleman, not stuck-up, almost like family. With nine roubles collected, Mitya sent for posting-horses to take him to Volovya station. That’s why people later remembered, and could prove, that “at midday, the day before everything happened, Mitya was broke, sold his watch for money, and borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in front of witnesses.”
I mention this detail because it will be important later on.

Even though Mitya was excited and hopeful that he’d finally fix all his problems, he got nervous as he got close to Volovya station. He kept worrying about what Grushenka might do while he was gone. What if she decided to go visit Fyodor Pavlovitch (his father) today? That’s why he had sneaked out without telling her, and he’d asked his landlady not to tell anyone where he’d gone if they came asking.

“I have to— I absolutely have to get back tonight,” he kept repeating as the cart rattled along. “And I’ll probably have to bring this Lyagavy guy back with me... to finish the paperwork.” That’s what Mitya was hoping for, his heart pounding. But, unfortunately, things weren’t going to work out the way he dreamed.

First, he was late because the shortcut from Volovya station turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve (so it was way longer than he’d thought). Then, when he got to Ilyinskoe, the priest wasn’t home; he’d gone to a village nearby. Mitya went off to find him, using the same tired horses, and by then it was almost dark.

The priest was a shy, friendly-looking little man. He told Mitya right away that, although Lyagavy had been staying with him before, he was now at Suhoy Possyolok, spending the night in the forester’s cottage because he was buying timber there, too. Mitya begged him to take him there immediately—“to save me, please!”—and after hesitating, the priest agreed. He was clearly curious. He thought they should go on foot, since it was “not much more” than a verst away. Mitya agreed, and started off in huge steps, so the priest almost had to run to keep up. The priest was careful and not very old.

Right away, Mitya started telling the priest all about his plans, nervously asking for advice about how to handle Lyagavy, and talking nonstop. The priest listened but didn’t say much. He mostly answered, “I don’t know. I can’t say. How could I know?” and similar things. When Mitya started talking about his fight with his father over his inheritance, the priest seemed worried, since he depended on Fyodor Pavlovitch in some way.
