Still, he asked, confused, why Mitya kept calling the peasant-trader “Lyagavy,” and explained that, even though that was his real name, everyone called him Gorstkin. If he was called Lyagavy to his face, he’d be really offended and wouldn’t listen to anything Mitya had to say.

Mitya was surprised and told the priest that Samsonov had called him Lyagavy. Once the priest heard that, he dropped the subject, even though he probably should have wondered if Samsonov was making fun of Mitya by sending him to the peasant and calling him by a name that would annoy him. But Mitya didn’t have time to think about little things like that. He hurried along, only realizing when they got to Suhoy Possyolok that they’d walked at least three versts, not one or even one and a half. That annoyed him, but he kept it together.

They went inside the hut. The forester lived in one half, and Gorstkin (Lyagavy) was staying in the better room on the other side of the hall. They went in and lit a cheap candle. The hut was super hot. On the table, there was a samovar that had gone out, a tray with cups, an empty rum bottle, a partly full vodka bottle, and some half-eaten bread crusts. Gorstkin himself was stretched out on the bench, using his coat as a pillow, snoring loudly. Mitya didn’t know what to do.

“I have to wake him up. This is too important. I came in such a rush. I need to get back tonight,” he said, upset. But the priest and the forester just stood there, saying nothing. Mitya tried to wake the man himself—he really tried—but the man wouldn’t wake up.

“He’s drunk,” Mitya decided. “Oh no! What am I supposed to do?” He started tugging at the man’s arms and legs, shaking his head, even trying to sit him up. But no matter how hard he tried, the drunk man just grunted, mumbled nonsense, and cursed in a slurred way.
“You’d better wait a bit,” the priest finally said, “he’s clearly not in any shape to talk.”
“He’s been drinking all day,” the forester added.
“Oh, come on!” Mitya cried. “If you only knew how important this is to me, how desperate I am!”
“You’d better wait until morning,” the priest repeated.
“Until morning? No way! That’s impossible!”
In his frustration, Mitya almost tried to shake the man awake again, but quickly realized it wouldn’t work. The priest stayed silent, and the sleepy forester just looked grumpy.

“Real life creates such awful problems for people,” Mitya said, completely hopeless. Sweat was pouring down his face. The priest took the chance to explain that, even if they woke the man, he’d still be drunk and unable to talk seriously. “Your business is important,” he said, “so you should definitely wait till morning.” Mitya, totally defeated, agreed.

“Father, I’ll stay here with the light and grab the right moment as soon as he wakes up. I’ll pay you for the candle,” he said to the forester, “and for letting me sleep here. Just remember Dmitri Karamazov. But Father, I don’t know about you—where will you sleep?”
“No, I’m going home. I’ll take the forester’s horse and head back,” the priest said, pointing to the forester. “I’ll say goodbye now. I hope everything works out for you.”

So that’s what they decided. The priest rode off on the forester’s horse, glad to get away, but shaking his head and wondering if he should tell his patron, Fyodor Pavlovitch, about this strange event the next day—“or else he might hear about it, get angry, and stop helping me.”

The forester scratched himself and went to his own room without a word. Mitya sat on the bench, waiting for the “right moment,” as he called it. He felt weighed down by sadness, like a thick fog pressing on his soul. He sat and thought, but couldn’t figure anything out. The candle burned low, a cricket chirped, and it was unbearably stuffy in the hot room. Suddenly, he pictured the garden, the path behind it, the door to his father’s house mysteriously opening, and Grushenka running inside. He jumped up from the bench.

“This is a tragedy!” he said, grinding his teeth. He walked over to the sleeping man and stared at his face. He was a skinny, middle-aged peasant with a very long face, light-colored curly hair, and a thin reddish beard. He wore a blue cotton shirt and a black vest, with a silver watch chain sticking out. Mitya glared at his face with anger, and for some reason, the curly hair really got on his nerves.

What really stung was that, after leaving behind so much and making so many sacrifices, Mitya was now completely worn out and stuck with urgent business, forced to wait on this idiot—his whole future depending on him—while the guy just snored like nothing was wrong, as if he’d come from another planet.

“Oh, the irony!” Mitya shouted, losing his temper. He tried to wake the drunk peasant again, shaking and pulling him, even hitting him a little. But after five minutes of useless effort, he went back to the bench, completely helpless, and sat down.

“Stupid! This is so stupid!” Mitya yelled. “And it’s so unfair!” he added, for no clear reason. His head started pounding. He wondered if he should just give up and leave. “No, I’ll wait till tomorrow. I’ll stay, that’s what I came for. Besides, I can’t leave now anyway—how would I even get out of here? This is so ridiculous!”

But his headache just got worse. He sat there, not moving, and without realizing it, he dozed off and fell asleep sitting up. He must have slept for two hours or more. He woke up because his head hurt so much he felt like screaming. His temples were pounding and the top of his head ached. It took a long time for him to fully wake up and remember where he was.

Finally, he realized that the room was filled with fumes from the stove—charcoal smoke—and he could have suffocated. The drunken peasant was still snoring. The candle was almost out. Mitya shouted and stumbled into the forester’s room across the hall. The forester woke up right away, but when he heard about the fumes, he didn’t care much, though he did go to check on it.
“But he could be dead! What am I supposed to do then?” Mitya cried, panicking.

They opened all the doors, a window, and the chimney. Mitya brought a bucket of water from the hallway. First, he splashed his own head, then found a rag, soaked it, and put it on Lyagavy’s head. The forester still acted like it was no big deal and, when he opened the window, just grumbled:
“It’ll be fine now.”

He went back to sleep, leaving Mitya a lantern. Mitya spent half an hour fussing over the drunk peasant, wetting his head, and promised himself he wouldn’t sleep at all that night. But he was so exhausted that, when he sat down to rest for a minute, he ended up lying down and sleeping like a rock.

When Mitya finally woke up, it was really late—about nine in the morning. Sunlight filled the little windows. The curly-haired peasant was sitting on the bench with his coat on. There was another samovar and another bottle in front of him. Yesterday’s bottle was empty, and the new one was already more than half gone. Mitya jumped up and instantly realized the awful peasant was drunk again—hopelessly drunk. He stared at him in shock. The peasant watched him with a sly, almost mocking look, as if he thought he was better than Mitya. Mitya rushed over to him.
“Excuse me, but... you probably heard from the forester who I am. I’m Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, son of old Karamazov, the one whose woodland you’re buying.”
“That’s a lie,” the peasant said, cool and confident.
“A lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“I don’t know any Fyodor Pavlovitch,” the peasant slurred.

“You’re making a deal with him for the woodland! Wake up—get it together! Father Pavel from Ilyinskoe brought me here. You wrote to Samsonov, and Samsonov sent me to you,” Mitya said, almost out of breath.
“You’re lying,” Lyagavy blurted again. Mitya’s legs felt weak.
“Please! This isn’t a joke. Maybe you’re drunk, but you can talk and understand... unless... I just don’t get it!”
“You’re a painter!” the peasant said.
“Please, I’m Karamazov—Dmitri Karamazov. I want to make you an offer, a really good offer about the woodland!”
The peasant stroked his beard, acting important.
“No, you took the job and made a mess of it. You’re a cheat!”
“You’re wrong!” Mitya cried, wringing his hands in frustration. The peasant kept stroking his beard and then squinted his eyes slyly.
“No, you show me the law that lets people cheat. Did you hear me? You’re a crook! Do you get that?”

Mitya stepped back, gloomy, and suddenly it was like something hit him on the head, as he described later. Suddenly, everything made sense—“a light turned on and I understood it all.” He stood there, shocked at how someone like him, who thought he was smart, could get himself into such a mess, chasing after this Lyagavy, fussing over him, even wetting his head for almost a whole day.
“This man is dead drunk, and he’ll just keep drinking for a week. What’s the point of staying? What if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? What if she—? Oh God, what have I done?”

The peasant just sat grinning. At another time, Mitya might have been furious enough to hurt him, but now he just felt weak, like a child. He quietly got his overcoat, put it on, and left the hut. The forester wasn’t in the next room—no one was there. Mitya took fifty kopecks in small coins out of his pocket and left it on the table to pay for the night, the candle, and all the trouble. When he stepped outside, he saw nothing but forest everywhere. He wandered off, not even knowing which way to go. The evening before, he’d hurried there with the priest and hadn’t paid attention to the road. He felt no anger— not even toward Samsonov. He just wandered along a narrow forest path, dazed and lost, barely able to walk. Somehow, he made it out of the woods and saw harvested fields stretching as far as he could see.
“What despair! What a dead, empty world!” he muttered as he kept walking.

He was saved when he met an old merchant traveling across the country in a hired carriage. When Mitya caught up to him, he asked for directions, and it turned out the merchant was also going to Volovya. After talking it over, Mitya got a ride in the carriage. Three hours later, they arrived. At Volovya, Mitya quickly ordered posting-horses to take him to town, and suddenly realized he was starving. While the horses were being readied, someone made him an omelet. He devoured it, ate a big chunk of bread, some sausage, and drank three glasses of vodka. After eating, he felt a little better, his spirits rising. He raced toward the town, urging the driver to hurry, and suddenly made a new, “final” plan to get that “cursed money” before evening. “And to think a person’s whole life can be ruined over a measly three thousand roubles!” he said bitterly. “I’ll settle it today.” If it weren’t for the constant worry about Grushenka—what might have happened to her—he might have felt almost happy again. But the thought of her stabbed at his heart every second, like a knife.
At last, they reached town, and Mitya headed straight for Grushenka.

This was the visit from Mitya (Dmitri) that Grushenka had told Rakitin about, the one that frightened her so much. She was waiting for the “message” and felt relieved that Mitya hadn't come to see her that day or the day before. She hoped, “please God, he won’t come before I leave,” but then he suddenly showed up. We already know the rest. To get rid of him quickly, she suggested they walk together to see Samsonov, where she said she absolutely had to go to “settle his accounts.” Mitya went with her right away, and then she said goodbye at the gate, making him promise to come back at midnight to take her home. Mitya was happy with this deal—if Grushenka was at Samsonov’s, she couldn’t be at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. “Unless she’s lying,” he thought. But from how she acted, he believed she was telling the truth.

Mitya was the kind of jealous man who, when his beloved woman isn’t around, immediately imagines all sorts of awful things she might be doing, and how she might be cheating on him. But even when he’s heartbroken and sure she’s betrayed him, the moment he sees her happy, smiling, and loving face, all his doubts disappear. He instantly feels ashamed of being jealous and blames himself.
After leaving Grushenka at the gate, Mitya rushed home. He still had so much to do that day! But at least the heavy feeling on his chest was gone for now.
“Now I just need to hurry up and find out from Smerdyakov if anything happened there last night—if, by any chance, she went to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s...ugh!” he thought.
But before he even reached his lodgings, jealousy started boiling up inside him again.

Jealousy! “Othello wasn’t jealous, he was trustful,” Pushkin once said. That one line shows just how smart our famous poet was. Othello’s world fell apart because his perfect image of love was ruined, but he didn’t start spying or sneaking around. He trusted his wife—he had to be pushed and manipulated a lot before he even started to suspect anything. Real jealousy isn’t like that. The real jealous person can sink to such shameful, awful things without even feeling guilty. And it’s not just bad people who get jealous—sometimes, people with really good hearts do the worst things, like hiding under tables, paying shady people for information, or spying and eavesdropping.

Othello couldn’t even bring himself to believe someone could be unfaithful—not that he couldn’t forgive it, just that he couldn’t believe it—his heart was as innocent as a child’s. But real jealousy is different. It’s hard to imagine what a jealous person can decide to accept or forgive. The jealous are usually the quickest to forgive—women know this. A jealous man can forgive almost anything (though usually after a huge blow-up), even if he’s seen clear evidence of cheating, if only he’s convinced it’s really the “last time,” and that his rival will disappear forever, or that he’ll take the woman away where nobody else can get her. Of course, the peace only lasts an hour. Even if the rival disappears, he’ll imagine another one and get jealous all over again. You might wonder what kind of love needs so much guarding—is it even real love? But jealous people never get that. And even the most noble-hearted of them, hiding in closets and spying, don’t feel guilty in the moment, even though they know how low they’ve sunk.

When Mitya saw Grushenka, all his jealousy vanished, and for a moment he felt trusting and generous, and actually despised himself for his bad feelings. That just showed that his love for her was more than just physical attraction, not just about “the curve of her body” like he once told Alyosha. But as soon as Grushenka left, he started suspecting her of all sorts of sneaky things, and felt no guilt about it.

So jealousy took over him again. He had to hurry. First, he needed to get at least a little money as a loan. The nine roubles he’d gotten earlier were almost all gone from his recent trip. And as everyone knows, you can’t do anything without money. While riding in the cart, he had thought about where to get a loan. He had a pair of really nice dueling pistols that he hadn’t pawned yet because they meant a lot to him.

At the “Metropolis” tavern, he had met a young official who loved collecting weapons. This guy bought pistols, revolvers, daggers, hung them on his wall, and showed them off. He was proud of them and knew everything about how they worked. Mitya went straight to him and offered to pawn his pistols for ten roubles. The official was thrilled and tried to get Mitya to sell them instead, but Mitya refused. So the man gave him ten roubles as a loan, saying he wouldn’t take any interest. They parted as friends.

Mitya was in a big hurry; he rushed toward Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house by the back way, heading for the arbor to find Smerdyakov as soon as possible. This proves that three or four hours before a certain event (which will be described later), Mitya was completely broke and had to pawn something valuable just to get ten roubles—though three hours later, he somehow had thousands. But I’m getting ahead of myself. From Marya Kondratyevna (the woman who lived near Fyodor Pavlovitch), he heard the troubling news that Smerdyakov was sick. She told him about Smerdyakov’s fall in the cellar, his seizure, the doctor’s visit, and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s concern. Mitya also heard with interest that his brother Ivan had left for Moscow that morning.

“Then he must have passed through Volovya before me,” Dmitri thought, but he was much more worried about Smerdyakov. “Now what? Who’ll watch for me? Who’ll bring me news?” he wondered. He started questioning the women, trying to find out if they’d seen anything the night before. They got what he was asking and reassured him—no one had been there. Ivan Fyodorovitch had stayed the night; everything was normal. Mitya got thoughtful. He knew he’d have to keep watch himself today, but where? Here or at Samsonov’s gate? He decided he’d have to keep an eye on both places, and meanwhile...well, meanwhile he had to carry out the new plan he’d made on his way back. He was sure it would work, but he couldn’t wait. Mitya decided to spend just one hour on this plan: “In an hour I’ll know everything and settle everything, then I’ll go to Samsonov’s, check if Grushenka’s there, and come back here till eleven, then back to Samsonov’s to take her home.” That was his decision.

He rushed home, washed up, combed his hair, changed his clothes, and went to see Madame Hohlakov. He was counting on her—he had decided to ask her to lend him three thousand roubles. For some reason, he felt sure she wouldn’t say no. You might wonder why, if he was so sure, he hadn’t gone to her first instead of trying Samsonov—a man he barely knew and wasn’t comfortable talking to.

But the truth was, he didn’t know Madame Hohlakov very well, and hadn’t seen her in the last month. He also knew she couldn’t stand him. She’d disliked him from the start because he was engaged to Katerina Ivanovna, while for some reason she was determined that Katerina should dump him and marry the “charming, refined” Ivan, who had such good manners. She hated Mitya’s manners. Mitya actually laughed at her and once called her lively but uncultured. But that morning, while riding in the cart, he got a brilliant idea: “If she wants so badly for me not to marry Katerina Ivanovna (and I know she’s obsessed with it), why wouldn’t she lend me three thousand roubles to help me leave Katya and get away for good? These spoiled rich women will pay anything to get what they want. Besides, she’s rich,” Mitya reasoned.

His “plan” was the same as before: offer his rights to Tchermashnya, but not to make a profit for himself like he’d tried with Samsonov—just as security for the loan. Thinking about this new idea got Mitya all excited, but that was always the case with him and his wild plans. He’d throw himself into every idea with passion. But as he went up the steps to Madame Hohlakov’s house, he suddenly felt a chill of fear. He realized, for sure, that this was his last hope. If this failed, he had nothing left but to “rob and kill someone for the three thousand.” It was 7:30 when he rang the bell.

At first, things seemed to go his way. As soon as they announced him, he was taken in right away. “It’s like she was expecting me,” thought Mitya. And as soon as he was shown into the drawing room, Madame Hohlakov herself hurried in and said right away that she’d been expecting him.

“I was expecting you! I really was! Even though I had no reason to think you’d visit me, and you know that yourself. Still, I expected you. You might be surprised, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but I was sure all morning you’d come.”
“That really is amazing, madam,” Mitya said, flopping into a chair, “but I came to you about something very important...something that means everything to me, madam...and I need to—”

“I know you came on urgent business, Dmitri Fyodorovitch; it’s not just a feeling, and not some miracle (have you heard about Father Zossima?). This is just logical: after everything that’s happened with Katerina Ivanovna, you couldn’t help but come to me. It’s basic math.”
“It’s just real life, madam, that’s all. But please let me explain—”
“Real life, indeed, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m all about realism these days. I’ve had enough of miracles. Did you hear that Father Zossima died?”
“No, madam, this is the first I’ve heard of it.” Mitya was a little surprised. He thought of Alyosha.
“Last night, and just imagine—”

“Madam,” said Mitya, “I can’t think of anything right now except that I’m in a desperate situation, and if you don’t help me, everything will fall apart—me most of all. Sorry to put it so simply, but I’m really desperate—”

“I know, I know you’re desperate. You couldn’t help but be. And whatever you tell me, I already know. I’ve been thinking about your destiny for a long time, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I’m watching over it and studying it...Oh, believe me, I’m an expert at reading souls.”

“Madam, if you’re an expert, then I’m definitely a very experienced patient,” said Mitya, trying to be polite, “and I hope that since you’re watching over my fate, you’ll help me in my ruin. At least let me explain my plan and what I’m hoping for...I came, madam—”

“Don’t explain now. That’s not important. And as for helping you, you’re not the first. You probably heard of my cousin, Madame Belmesov. Her husband was broke, ‘had come to grief,’ as you so nicely put it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I told him to try horse-breeding, and now he’s doing well. Do you know anything about horse-breeding?”

“Not a thing, madam; oh, not a thing!” cried Mitya, getting impatient and almost jumping out of his chair. “I beg you, madam, just give me two minutes to explain everything, my whole plan for why I came. I’m in a huge hurry,” Mitya said desperately, afraid she’d start talking again and trying to cut her off. “I came in total despair, to beg you for a loan of three thousand, but with really safe security, the best guarantees! Just let me explain—”

“You must tell me all that later!” Madame Hohlakov insisted, raising her hand for silence. “And whatever you say, I already know. You’re asking for three thousand, but I can give you even more—a lot more. I’ll save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you have to listen to me.”
Mitya jumped up again.
“Madam, will you really do that?” he cried, deeply moved. “Oh God, you’ve saved me! You’ve saved a man from a bullet, from a violent death. I’ll be forever grateful—”
“I’ll give you more, much more than three thousand!” Madame Hohlakov said, smiling brightly at Mitya’s excitement.
“Much more? But I don’t need that much. I just need the three thousand, and I can give you great security for it. I even have a plan—”

“Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it’s settled.” Madame Hohlakov cut him off, proud to be generous. “I promised to save you, and I will. I’ll save you like I did Belmesov. What do you think about gold-mines, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
“Gold-mines, madam? I’ve never thought about them at all.”

“But I’ve thought about them for you. Over and over. I’ve watched you walk by a hundred times in the last month and thought: that’s a man of energy who belongs at the gold-mines. I’ve studied your walk and decided: that’s a man who will find gold.”
“From my walk, madam?” Mitya said, smiling.

“Yes, from your walk! Surely you agree that you can tell a person’s character by their walk, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Science says so. I believe in science and realism now. After everything with Father Zossima, I’ve decided to focus on practical things. I’m cured—‘That’s enough!’ as Turgenev says.”
“But, madam, the three thousand you so kindly promised—”

“It’s yours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov interrupted. “The money is as good as in your pocket—not three thousand, but three million, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, in no time. I’m giving you the idea: you’ll find gold-mines, make millions, come back a hero, and lead us to better things. Why leave it all to the Jews? You’ll start new institutions, help the poor, and they’ll bless you. This is the age of railways—you’ll become famous and important to the Department of Finance. The rouble’s value keeps me awake at night, Dmitri Fyodorovitch; people don’t know that side of me—”

“Madam, madam!” Dmitri interrupted, starting to worry. “I might really take your wise advice, madam...I might go to the gold-mines...I’ll come see you about it again...but right now, that three thousand you so kindly...oh, that would set me free, and if you could today...I don’t have a minute to lose—”
“Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, enough!” Madame Hohlakov said firmly. “The question is, will you go to the gold-mines or not; have you made up your mind? Yes or no?”
“I will go, madam, later...I’ll go wherever you want...but now—”
“Wait!” Madame Hohlakov cried, jumping up and rushing to a fancy desk with lots of little drawers. She started pulling them open, searching for something in a panic.
“The three thousand,” thought Mitya, his heart pounding. “And right away—no papers or signatures—that’s how real generosity works! She’d be great if only she didn’t talk so much.”
“Here!” Madame Hohlakov shouted, running back to Mitya, “here it is!”
It was a tiny silver icon on a cord, the kind people sometimes wear under their shirt with a cross.
“This is from Kiev, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” she said seriously, “from the relics of Saint Varvara. Let me put it on you myself and dedicate you to a new life, a new future.”
She actually put the cord around his neck and started arranging it. Mitya, really embarrassed, bent down to help her, and finally got it under his tie and collar, against his chest.
“Now you can go,” Madame Hohlakov said, sitting back in her chair triumphantly.

“Madam, I’m so touched. I don’t know how to thank you for such kindness, but...If only you knew how precious time is to me. That money, the debt I’ll owe you for your generosity...Oh, madam, since you’re so kind, so generous,” Mitya burst out, “let me confess to you—even though you probably already know—that I love someone here...I’ve been unfaithful to Katya—Katerina Ivanovna, I mean...I’ve treated her horribly, but I fell in love with another woman here—a woman you probably despise, but I can’t leave her. That’s why I need the three thousand now—”

“Leave everything, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov cut in firmly. “Leave it all, especially women. The gold-mines are your destiny, and there’s no room for women there. Later, when you return rich and famous, you’ll find the girl of your dreams in high society. She’ll be modern and educated. By then, women’s rights will have advanced, and the new woman will have arrived.”
“Madam, that’s not the point at all...” Mitya pleaded, clasping his hands.

“Yes, it is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it’s exactly what you need, even if you don’t realize it. I’m not against the women’s movement—far from it. The progress and even political freedom of women is my dream. I have a daughter myself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch—people don’t know that about me. I wrote a letter about it to the author Shtchedrin, who’s taught me so much about women’s roles. Last year I sent him an anonymous note: ‘I kiss and embrace you, my teacher, for the modern woman. Don’t stop.’ I signed it ‘A Mother.’ I almost wrote ‘A contemporary Mother,’ but I kept it simple—there’s more beauty in that. Besides, ‘contemporary’ might have reminded him of the magazine ‘The Contemporary,’ which was censored...Good Heavens, what’s wrong?”
“Madam!” Mitya cried, standing up and clasping his hands desperately. “You’ll make me cry if you keep delaying what you promised—”
“Oh, do cry, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it’s a noble emotion! Such a path is ahead of you! Tears will heal your heart, and you’ll return to me from Siberia just to share your joy—”
“But please!” Mitya shouted suddenly. “One last time, I beg you—can I have the money today? If not, when can I get it?”
“What money, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
“The three thousand you promised me...that you so generously—”
“Three thousand? Roubles? Oh no, I don’t have three thousand,” Madame Hohlakov said with calm surprise. Mitya was stunned.
“But you just said...you said it was as good as in my hands—”
“Oh, you misunderstood me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I was talking about the gold-mines. It’s true I promised you more, infinitely more, but I meant the gold-mines.”
“But the money? The three thousand?” Mitya asked, awkwardly.

“Oh, if you meant money, I don’t have any. Not a penny, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m fighting with my steward about it, and I just borrowed five hundred roubles from Miüsov myself. No, I have no money. And honestly, if I did, I wouldn’t give it to you. I never lend money—it ruins friendships. And especially not to you, because I like you and want to save you. All you need is the gold-mines, the gold-mines, the gold-mines!”
“Oh, damn it!” Mitya shouted, slamming his fist on the table.
“Aie! Aie!” screamed Madame Hohlakov, running to the other end of the room.

Mitya spat on the floor, stormed out of the room, through the house, and into the dark street. He walked like he was possessed, beating his chest right where he’d hit himself two days before in front of Alyosha, the last time they saw each other. What those hits meant, and why he did it, was a secret he hadn’t told anyone—not even Alyosha. But for Mitya, it meant more than disgrace; it meant total ruin or even suicide. He had decided that if he couldn’t get the three thousand to pay his debt to Katerina Ivanovna and wipe away the shame on his heart, he would be lost. This will all be explained later, but now, with his last hope gone, this tough-looking man broke down and cried like a little kid a few steps from Madame Hohlakov’s house. He kept walking, wiping his tears away with his fist, not even knowing what he was doing. Suddenly, on the town square, he bumped into someone and heard an old woman cry out.
“Good Lord, you nearly killed me! Why don’t you look where you’re going, you rascal?”
“Why, it’s you!” Mitya shouted, realizing who it was even in the dark. It was Samsonov’s old servant—the one he’d noticed the day before.
“And who are you, young man?” the old woman said, her voice changing. “I can’t see you in the dark.”
“You live at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. You’re the servant there, right?”
“That’s right, sir. I was just running out to Prohoritch’s...But I don’t know you now.”
“Tell me, please, is Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka) there now?” Mitya asked, barely able to contain himself. “I saw her go into the house a little while ago.”
“She was there, sir. She stayed a bit, then left again.”
“What? Left?” Mitya cried. “When did she leave?”
“Why, right after she came. She just stayed for a minute, told Kuzma Kuzmitch something funny, and ran off.”
“You’re lying, you old devil!” Mitya yelled.
“Aie! Aie!” shrieked the old woman, but Mitya was already gone.
He ran as fast as he could to Grushenka’s house. At that very moment, Grushenka herself was leaving for Mokroe. It was less than fifteen minutes since she’d gone.
Fenya was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother, the old cook Matryona, when “the captain” burst in. Fenya screamed when she saw him.
“You scream?” Mitya roared. “Where is she?”
But before the terrified Fenya could answer, he collapsed at her feet.
“Fenya, for God’s sake, tell me—where is she?”
“I don’t know, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I swear I don’t know! You could kill me and I couldn’t tell you,” Fenya promised desperately. “You just left with her yourself—”
“She came back!”
“She didn’t, I swear to God she didn’t!”
“You’re lying!” Mitya shouted. “Your fear tells me where she is.”

He rushed out. Fenya, scared, was just glad he’d left so quickly—otherwise, she might not have gotten off so easily. But as he ran, Mitya did something that shocked both Fenya and old Matryona. On the table was a brass mortar with a small pestle, a short brass stick about six inches long. Mitya, already with one hand on the door, snatched up the pestle with his other hand and stuffed it in his pocket.
“Oh, Lord! He’s going to kill someone!” Fenya cried, throwing up her hands.

Where was he running? “Where else could Grushenka be except at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house?” Dmitri (Mitya) thought. “She must have gone straight there from Samsonov’s place—that’s obvious now. The whole scheme, the whole trick, is clear.” His mind was spinning with these thoughts. He didn’t bother going to Marya Kondratyevna’s house. “There’s no point... I can’t let anyone get suspicious... If I go, they’ll tell everyone right away. Marya Kondratyevna is definitely in on this, and Smerdyakov too—they’ve all been bribed!”

Mitya quickly came up with a new plan: instead of heading straight for Fyodor Pavlovitch’s place, he took a long detour around the house. He crossed the lane, ran down Dmitrovsky Street, crossed the small bridge, and finally reached the quiet, empty alley behind the house. On one side was a neighbor’s kitchen garden with a low fence; on the other, the tall, sturdy fence that went all the way around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. He picked a spot that he remembered—according to stories, Lizaveta had once climbed over here. “If she could do it,” he thought, “so can I.” He jumped, grabbed the top of the fence, pulled himself up, and sat on it. From there, he could see the garden bathhouse, and through the trees, the lighted windows of the house.

“Yes, the old man’s bedroom is lit up. She’s there!” he told himself, then jumped down into the garden. Even though he knew Grigory was sick—and probably Smerdyakov too, so there shouldn’t be anyone to hear him—he instinctively hid in the shadows and listened. Everything was completely silent around him, so quiet it seemed like the world was holding its breath.

“And nothing but whispering silence,” a line of poetry popped into his head. “I hope no one heard me jump the fence. I doubt it.” He waited a minute, then walked softly over the grass, keeping away from the trees and bushes. He moved slowly, sneaking with each step, listening to the sound of his own feet. It took him five minutes to get close to the lit window. He remembered that there were thick, tall elder and whitebeam bushes right under it. He also checked that the garden door on the left side of the house was closed, just like he’d hoped. Finally, he reached the bushes and crouched down behind them, holding his breath. “I’ll wait a bit,” he thought, “in case anyone heard my steps and is listening... I just need to make sure I don’t sneeze or cough.”

He waited for two minutes. His heart was pounding so hard it felt like he could barely breathe. “No, I can’t stand this anymore,” he thought. He was hidden in the shadow of the bush, but the light from the window shone on the front of it.

“Those whitebeam berries are so red,” he whispered for no reason. Quietly, step by step, he moved closer to the window and stretched up on tiptoe. He could see straight into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s bedroom. The room wasn’t big, and a red screen divided it in two—Fyodor Pavlovitch called it “Chinese.” The word “Chinese” popped into Mitya’s mind, and he thought, “She’s probably behind that screen—Grushenka.” He started watching Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was wearing a new striped silk robe Mitya had never seen before, tied with a silk cord with tassels. Under the robe was a crisp white shirt with gold studs. On his head was the same red bandage Alyosha had seen earlier.
“He’s really dressed up,” thought Mitya.

His father stood near the window, deep in thought. Suddenly, Fyodor Pavlovitch jerked his head up, listened for a second, and, hearing nothing, walked over to the table, poured himself half a glass of brandy, and drank it quickly. He let out a deep sigh, paused, then wandered over to the mirror on the wall. With his right hand, he lifted the red bandage on his forehead a little and started examining the bruises and cuts that still hadn’t healed.
“He’s alone,” Mitya thought. “He’s probably alone.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch walked away from the mirror, suddenly turned toward the window, and looked out. Mitya instantly ducked back into the shadows.

“Maybe she’s hiding behind the screen. Maybe she’s asleep by now,” Mitya thought, his heart aching. Fyodor Pavlovitch moved away from the window. “He’s looking for her outside, so she’s not there. Why would he stare into the darkness otherwise? He’s losing his patience.” Mitya slipped back to the window and started watching again. The old man sat down at the table, looking disappointed. After a while, he put his elbow on the table and leaned his cheek on his hand. Mitya watched him closely.
“He’s alone, he’s alone!” Mitya repeated to himself. “If she were here, his face would look different.”

Strangely, Mitya suddenly felt annoyed that Grushenka wasn’t there. “It’s not that she isn’t here,” he told himself, “it’s that I can’t be sure one way or another.” He remembered later that his thoughts were unusually clear at that moment—he noticed every detail and missed nothing. But the uncertainty, not knowing what to do, was making him miserable. “Is she here or not?” That angry doubt filled him, and suddenly, making up his mind, he reached out and softly tapped on the window frame. He knocked using the secret signal Fyodor Pavlovitch had worked out with Smerdyakov—two slow knocks, then three quick ones—the code for “Grushenka is here!”
The old man jumped, jerked his head up, and quickly ran to the window. Mitya melted back into the shadows. Fyodor Pavlovitch opened the window and stuck his whole head out.
“Grushenka, is that you? Is it you?” he whispered shakily. “Where are you, my angel, where are you?” He was trembling with excitement and out of breath.
“He’s alone,” Mitya decided for sure.
“Where are you?” the old man called again. He leaned farther out the window, looking all around. “Come here, I have a little present for you. Come, I’ll show you...”
“He means the three thousand,” thought Mitya.
“But where are you? Are you at the door? I’ll open it right away.”

The old man was practically climbing out the window, staring toward the right, where the door to the garden was, trying to see through the darkness. In another second, he would have run out to open the door without even waiting for Grushenka to answer.

Mitya watched from the side, not moving. He hated the old man’s profile—his sagging Adam’s apple, his hooked nose, his lips twisted in greedy excitement—all lit up by the lamp shining from the left. Suddenly, a wave of hatred and anger crashed over Mitya: “There he is, my rival, the man who’s made my life miserable!” It was that uncontrollable, furious rage he’d talked about with Alyosha four days earlier in the gazebo. Back then, Alyosha had asked, “How can you say you’ll kill our father?” and Mitya replied, “I don’t know, maybe I will, maybe I won’t. I’m scared he’ll just disgust me so much in the moment. I hate his double chin, his nose, his eyes, his nasty grin. I feel sick just looking at him. That’s what I’m afraid of, that it’ll be too much.” Now that feeling was almost unbearable. Out of control, Mitya suddenly pulled the brass pestle from his pocket.

“God was watching me then,” Mitya would later say. At that exact moment, Grigory woke up in his sickbed. Earlier that night, he’d gone through the treatment Smerdyakov had described to Ivan—he rubbed himself with vodka mixed with a super strong secret herbal brew, then drank the leftovers while his wife Marfa Ignatyevna said a special prayer over him. Afterward, he’d gone to bed. Marfa tried the drink too, but since she wasn’t used to alcohol, she slept like a rock beside him.

But Grigory woke up suddenly in the night. After a moment, even though his back hurt badly, he sat up. He thought about it, then got up and dressed quickly. Maybe he felt guilty for sleeping when the house was in danger. Smerdyakov, worn out from his seizure, was motionless in the next room. Marfa didn’t move—“the drink was too much for her,” Grigory thought, and groaned as he went outside. He probably just meant to check things from the steps since he could barely walk from the pain in his back and leg. But suddenly, he remembered he’d forgotten to lock the little garden gate that evening. Grigory was a stickler for routines and habits. Limping and wincing with pain, he went to check the gate. Sure enough, it was wide open. He stepped into the garden out of habit. Maybe he heard something or saw a shadow, and when he looked left, he spotted his master’s window open—no one was looking out just then.
“Why is it open? It’s not summer,” Grigory thought. And at that exact moment, he saw something strange in the garden. About forty steps away, a person was running in the dark—a shadow moving quickly.

“Good Lord!” Grigory cried out, shocked, and forgot all about his pain as he rushed to cut off the running figure. He took a shortcut—he knew the garden better than anyone. The figure ran toward the bathhouse, darted behind it, and headed for the garden fence. Grigory chased after him, not losing sight for a second. He reached the fence just as the man was climbing over. Grigory shouted, threw himself at him, and grabbed his leg with both hands.
His gut feeling had been right. He recognized him—it was him, the “monster,” the “parricide.”
“Parricide!” the old man screamed so loudly the whole neighborhood could hear. But he didn’t get to yell anything else—he suddenly collapsed as if he’d been struck by lightning.

Mitya jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. He still had the brass pestle in his hands, and he automatically tossed it into the grass. It landed just a couple steps from Grigory, not hidden but right on the path where anyone could see it. For a few moments, he stared at Grigory lying there. The old man’s head was bleeding heavily. Mitya reached out and touched it, trying to figure out if he’d smashed Grigory’s skull or just knocked him out. But there was so much blood—soon, Mitya’s hands were covered in it. He remembered later that he pulled out his clean white handkerchief—the one he’d brought for visiting Madame Hohlakov—and pressed it to Grigory’s head, trying uselessly to wipe the blood from his face and temples. The handkerchief was instantly soaked.

“Wait, what am I doing?” Mitya thought, snapping back to his senses. “If I broke his skull, how can I tell now? And what does it matter?” he added hopelessly. “If I killed him, I killed him... It’s over for you, old man—so you’ll just have to stay there!” he said out loud. He turned to the fence, jumped over it into the lane, and took off running—the bloody handkerchief balled up in his right fist. As he ran, he stuffed it into his back coat pocket. He sprinted, and a few people who saw him running in the dark streets later remembered seeing someone tearing through the night. He raced back to the widow Morozov’s house.

Right after Mitya had left earlier that evening, Fenya had rushed to the main porter, Nazar Ivanovitch, and begged him, for the love of God, “don’t let the captain in again tonight or tomorrow.” Nazar Ivanovitch promised, but then his mistress called for him, so he told his nephew—a twenty-year-old who’d just come from the country—to take his place. But he forgot to warn him about “the captain.” When Mitya came running up to the gate, he knocked. The young man recognized him immediately—Mitya had tipped him before. He opened the gate and cheerfully told him, “Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t home right now, you know.”
“Where is she, Prohor?” Mitya asked, stopping in his tracks.
“She left about two hours ago with Timofey. They went to Mokroe.”
“What for?” Mitya cried out.
“I don’t know. To see some officer. Someone invited her and sent horses to pick her up.”
Mitya didn’t say anything else—he just ran like a madman to Fenya.

She was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother, both of them getting ready for bed. They hadn’t locked the doors because they trusted Nazar Ivanovitch to keep them safe. Suddenly, Mitya burst in, rushed straight at Fenya, and grabbed her by the throat.
“Tell me right now! Where is she? Who is she with at Mokroe?” he yelled, furious.
Both women screamed in terror.
“Aie! I’ll tell you, I’ll tell you everything, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, please, I won’t keep anything secret,” Fenya stammered, shaking with fear. “She’s gone to Mokroe, to meet her officer.”
“What officer?” Mitya shouted.
“Her officer—the same one from before, the one who left her five years ago,” Fenya blurted out as quickly as she could.

Mitya let go of her throat and stood in front of her, pale as a ghost, unable to say a word. But his eyes showed that he understood everything instantly—he got the whole picture. Fenya was still in shock, unable to tell if he understood or not, frozen where she sat on the trunk, hands up as if to protect herself, shaking all over. Her eyes were wide and locked on him. To make things worse, both of Mitya’s hands were smeared with blood. On the way there, he must have wiped his sweaty forehead with them, so now there were bloody streaks on his face too. Fenya was about to have a breakdown. The old cook had jumped up and stared at Mitya, completely terrified.

Mitya stood there for a moment, then sat down heavily on a chair next to Fenya. He didn’t seem to be thinking—he just looked shocked and numb. Still, everything was crystal clear: that officer—he knew about him, he’d heard about the letter from Grushenka herself a month ago. So for a whole month, this had been happening behind his back, and he never even suspected! How could he have forgotten this officer? That question haunted him, making him feel cold with fear.

Then, all at once, Mitya’s manner changed—he spoke gently to Fenya, like a kind child, as if he had forgotten how scary he’d just been. He started asking Fenya questions—very precise questions, even though his hands were still bloody and Fenya stared at them in horror. Fenya, desperate to help, answered everything quickly and truthfully. She explained every detail: how Rakitin and Alyosha (Alexey) had visited, how she herself had kept watch, how her mistress had left, and how she’d called out the window to Alyosha to tell Mitya, “Remember forever how she loved you for just one hour.”
Listening to that message, Mitya suddenly smiled, and his pale face turned a bit red. At the same time, Fenya asked him, not afraid anymore:
“Look at your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They’re covered in blood!”
“Yeah,” Mitya replied absently. He glanced at his hands, but forgot all about them and Fenya’s question right away.

He fell silent again. Twenty minutes had passed since he had run in. His first wave of horror faded, but it was clear he had made up his mind about something. He stood up suddenly, smiling like he was lost in a dream.
“What happened to you, sir?” Fenya asked, pointing at his hands again. She spoke with sympathy, feeling close to him now in his pain. Mitya looked again at his hands.

“That’s blood, Fenya,” he said, his expression strange. “That’s human blood. God, why was it shed? But... Fenya... imagine a fence here,” he said, as if giving her a riddle, “a tall, scary fence. But tomorrow at dawn, when the sun rises, Mitya will jump over that fence... You don’t get what fence I mean, Fenya, but don’t worry—you’ll know tomorrow, and you’ll understand. Now, goodbye. I won’t stand in her way. I know how to step aside. Live, my joy... you loved me for an hour, remember me—Mityenka Karamazov—forever. She used to call me Mityenka, remember?”
With that, he suddenly left the kitchen. Fenya was almost more scared by his sudden exit than when he’d attacked her.

Just ten minutes later, Dmitri went to see Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, the young official he’d pawned his pistols to. It was about 8:30 p.m.; Pyotr Ilyitch had finished his tea and was putting on his coat to go to the “Metropolis” to play billiards. Mitya caught him at the door.
When Pyotr Ilyitch saw Mitya’s face smeared with blood, he cried out in shock.
“Good heavens! What happened to you?”
“I’ve come for my pistols,” said Mitya, “and I brought your money. Thanks a lot. I’m in a hurry, Pyotr Ilyitch, please be quick.”

Pyotr Ilyitch grew even more surprised when he saw the bundle of banknotes in Mitya’s hand—he was holding the money out in the open, the way no one ever carries money, even on the street. The servant boy who met Mitya in the hall later said he came in with the money out like that, so he must have walked through the street like that too. The notes were all colorful hundred-rouble bills, and Mitya’s bloody fingers were gripping them.

Later, when Pyotr Ilyitch was asked about the money, he said it was hard to guess how much, but maybe two or three thousand roubles—a huge, thick stack. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he said later, “seemed totally out of it—not drunk, but distracted and lost in thought, like he was searching for something and couldn’t decide what to do. He was in a huge rush, answered strangely, and sometimes seemed even cheerful.”
“But what happened to you? What’s wrong?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked, staring at Mitya. “You’re covered in blood! Did you fall? Look at yourself!”
He took Mitya by the arm and led him to the mirror.
When Mitya saw his own bloody face, he jumped and frowned angrily.

“Damn it! That’s all I needed,” he muttered, quickly switching the money to his left hand and pulling a handkerchief from his pocket. But the handkerchief was soaked with blood too—it was the one he’d used to wipe Grigory’s face. It was stiff and balled up, impossible to open. Mitya threw it angrily on the floor.
“Oh, damn!” he said. “Don’t you have some rag or something... so I can wipe my face?”
“So you’re just stained, not hurt? You should wash up,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. “Here, use this washstand. I’ll pour you some water.”
“A washstand? Fine, but where do I put this?”
He looked at his bundle of bills in confusion, silently asking Pyotr Ilyitch what to do with them.
“Put them in your pocket, or on the table. No one will take them.”

“In my pocket? Yeah, all right... But look, that can wait,” Mitya suddenly said, snapping out of his daze. “Let’s sort out the pistols first. Give them back to me. Here’s your money—I really need them, and I have no time to waste.”
He handed the top bill from the stack to Pyotr Ilyitch.
“I don’t have enough change. Do you have anything smaller?”
“No,” said Mitya, glancing at the bills and flipping through a few.
“No, they’re all the same,” he said, looking to Pyotr Ilyitch for help.
“How did you get so rich?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked. “Wait, I’ll send my boy to Plotnikov’s—they close late—he can try to get change. Misha!” he called.

“To Plotnikov’s—great idea!” Mitya said, like he just thought of something. “Misha,” he said to the boy, “run to Plotnikov’s and tell them Dmitri Fyodorovitch sends his regards and will be there soon. Tell them to have three dozen bottles of champagne ready, packed like before for Mokroe. I took four dozen last time,” he added to Pyotr Ilyitch, “they know what I want. Misha, wait—also tell them to include cheese, pies, smoked fish, ham, caviar—everything, up to a hundred roubles, or a hundred and twenty, like last time. And dessert: sweets, pears, a watermelon—no, just one—and chocolate, candy, toffee, fondants—everything I ordered before, three hundred roubles’ worth, with the champagne. Same as last time. And, Misha—is your name Misha?” He checked with Pyotr Ilyitch.
“Hold on,” Pyotr Ilyitch broke in, watching Mitya worriedly, “you’d better go yourself and explain. He’ll just mess it up.”

“He will, I can tell! Misha, I was about to kiss you for helping. If you get it right, ten roubles for you. Hurry! Champagne is the most important! And brandy, red and white wine, everything I got last time—they know.”
“But listen!” Pyotr Ilyitch interrupted, a little impatient. “Let him just change the money and tell them not to close. You can go and explain the rest. Give him your bill. Go, Misha! Quick!”
Pyotr Ilyitch seemed eager to get Misha out of there, since the boy just stood staring at Mitya’s bloody face and trembling fingers, totally confused and scared.
“Now come wash up,” Pyotr Ilyitch said sternly. “Put the money down or in your pocket. All right, come on. But take off your coat.”
As he helped Mitya take off his coat, he shouted again:
“Look, your coat’s covered in blood too!”

“That? It’s just a little on the sleeve. That’s where the handkerchief was. I must have sat on it at Fenya’s and the blood soaked through,” Mitya explained almost like a little kid. Pyotr Ilyitch frowned at him.
“Well, you must have gotten into trouble—fighting with someone,” he muttered.

They started to wash up. Pyotr Ilyitch held the jug and poured water. Mitya hurried, barely soaping his trembling hands, but Pyotr Ilyitch made him do it thoroughly. It was clear Pyotr Ilyitch was starting to take charge of things. He was a young man with a strong character.
“Look, your nails aren’t clean. Now wash your face—here, on your temples, by your ear. Are you really going out in that shirt? And look, your right cuff is all bloody.”
“Yeah, it’s all bloody,” Mitya said, checking his sleeve.
“Then change your shirt.”
“No time. Look, I’ll just turn up the wrist. You won’t see it under the coat. See?” Mitya said, as he dried off and put his coat back on.

“Now tell me, what did you get into? Fighting again? In the tavern? Did you beat up that captain again?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked, almost like a parent. “Who did you beat up this time—or did you kill someone, maybe?”
“Nonsense,” Mitya said.
“Why ‘nonsense’?”
“Don’t worry,” said Mitya, suddenly laughing. “I just knocked over an old woman in the market.”
“Knocked over? An old woman?”
“An old man!” Mitya shouted, laughing and staring right at Pyotr Ilyitch, almost shouting in his face.
“Geez—an old woman, an old man—did you kill someone?”

“We made up. We fought, and then made up. In a place I know. We’re friends now. What a fool. He’s forgiven me—he must have by now. If he got up, maybe he wouldn’t forgive me.” Mitya suddenly winked. “But whatever, Pyotr Ilyitch, forget him! I don’t want to talk about him now!” he said, firmly.

“Why do you always pick fights with everyone? Just like you did with that captain, all over nothing. Fighting, and now you’re going off on a spree—typical you! Three dozen champagne bottles—what do you even need them for?”
“Bravo! Now give me the pistols. I really don’t have time. I’d like to chat, but not now. And there’s no point, it’s too late. Where’s my money? Where did I put it?” he said, searching his pockets.

“You put it on the table yourself. Here it is. Did you forget? Money’s like water to you. Here are your pistols. Funny—you pawned them for ten roubles at six o’clock, now you’ve got thousands. Two or three, I’d say.”
“Three, you bet!” Mitya laughed, stuffing the money into his pants pocket.
“You’ll lose it that way. Did you find a gold mine?”

“Gold mines? The mines?” Mitya yelled, then burst out laughing. “Want to go to the mines, Perhotin? There’s a lady who’ll give you three thousand roubles if you go—she did it for me. She loves gold mines. Do you know Madame Hohlakov?”
“I don’t know her, but I’ve heard of her. Did she really give you three thousand? Really?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked, suspicious.
“Tomorrow, as soon as the sun rises, as soon as Apollo flies up, you go to her—Madame Hohlakov—and ask if she gave me three thousand. See for yourself.”

“I don’t know what’s going on between you, but since you say it so surely, I guess she did. You’ve got the money, but instead of running off to Siberia you’re spending it all. Where are you really headed now?”
“To Mokroe.”
“To Mokroe? But it’s night!”
“Once the lad had all, now the lad has nothing,” Mitya suddenly cried.
“Nothing? But you’ve got all those thousands!”
“I’m not talking about money. Forget money! I mean women.”
“I agree with Ulysses. That’s what he says.”
“I don’t get you!”
“Am I drunk?”
“Not drunk—worse.”
“I’m drunk in spirit, Pyotr Ilyitch, drunk in spirit! But enough of that.”
“What are you doing, loading the pistol?”
“Yeah, I’m loading it.”
Mitya opened the pistol case, poured in powder, and packed it down. Then he picked up the bullet, and before loading it, he held it up to the candle, studying it.
“Why are you looking at the bullet?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked, curious but uneasy.
“Oh, just wondering. If you were planning to shoot yourself with that bullet, would you want to look at it first?”
“Why would anyone do that?”

“Well, it’s about to go into my brain, so it’s interesting to see what it looks like. But that’s just silly—a passing thought. Okay, that’s done,” he said, packing the bullet in with the ramrod. “Pyotr Ilyitch, my friend, it’s all nonsense—if only you knew! Give me a piece of paper.”
“Here’s some.”
“No, a clean one. Writing paper. Good.”

Taking a pen, Mitya quickly wrote two lines, folded the paper, and put it in his vest pocket. He locked the pistols in their case and held it in his hand. Then he gave Pyotr Ilyitch a slow, thoughtful smile.
“Now, let’s go.”
“Go where? Wait a minute... Are you thinking of shooting yourself?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked, worried.
“I was just joking about the bullet! I want to live. I love life, trust me. I love the golden sun and its warmth. Pyotr Ilyitch, do you know how to step aside?”
“What do you mean by ‘stepping aside’?”

“Letting someone else through. Letting someone I care about—and someone I hate—go ahead. Letting the one I hate become someone I care about. That’s what ‘stepping aside’ means. Telling them: God bless you, go on, while I—”
“While you—?”
“That’s enough. Let’s go.”
“Seriously, I’ll tell someone to keep you from going there,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. “Why are you going to Mokroe now?”
“There’s a woman there. That’s all you need to know. Mind your own business.”
“Listen, even though you’re wild, I’ve always liked you... I’m worried.”
“Thanks, man. Yeah, I’m wild. Wild! That’s what I always say—wild! Oh, here’s Misha! I almost forgot him.”

Misha rushed in with a handful of change, saying everyone at Plotnikov’s was busy: “They’re packing the bottles, the fish, the tea; it’ll all be ready soon.” Mitya grabbed ten roubles and handed them to Pyotr Ilyitch, then gave another ten-rouble note to Misha.

“Don’t you dare!” Pyotr Ilyitch shouted. “I won’t have it in my house—it’s a bad habit. Put your money away. Save it for tomorrow—you’ll probably be asking me to lend you ten roubles again. Why do you keep stuffing the bills in your side pocket? You’ll lose them!”
“Hey, let’s go to Mokroe together.”
“Why? What for?”
“Let’s open a bottle right now and drink to life! I want to drink, especially with you. We’ve never done that, have we?”
“Fine, we can go to the ‘Metropolis.’ I was going anyway.”
“No time for that. Let’s drink at Plotnikov’s, in the back room. Want to hear a riddle?”
“Go ahead.”
Mitya pulled out the paper he’d written on, unfolded it, and showed it. In big letters, it said: “I punish myself for my whole life, my whole life I punish!”
“I’ll definitely tell someone. I’ll go right now,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, after reading it.
“You won’t have time, my friend. Come have a drink. Move!”

Plotnikov’s shop was on the corner, just a couple doors from Pyotr Ilyitch’s. It was the biggest grocery store in town and not a bad one, owned by rich merchants. They sold everything you could get in a big city—groceries, bottled wines, fruit, cigars, tea, coffee, sugar, and more. Even though the area had gotten poorer and trade was down, the grocery stores kept booming, with plenty of shoppers.

Everyone in the shop was waiting for Mitya. They remembered how, a few weeks ago, he’d come in and bought hundreds of roubles’ worth of wine and food, paying cash—no way would they have given him credit. He had a big stack of hundred-rouble bills then, too, and just flung them around, not caring what he bought or how much. People in town joked that he’d spent three thousand roubles in one night with Grushenka at Mokroe, and came back broke. He’d even picked up a group of gypsies, who partied with him for days, drinking expensive wine and eating fancy food. They liked to laugh about how he gave champagne to dirty-handed peasants and fed village women sweets and pies. But laughing at Mitya’s face was risky—still, people joked behind his back, especially about how all he got from Grushenka was permission to kiss her foot.

By the time Mitya and Pyotr Ilyitch got to the shop, a cart with three horses was waiting for Mitya at the door, driven by Andrey. Inside, they’d nearly finished packing one box of food, just waiting for Mitya to arrive so they could nail it shut and load it. Pyotr Ilyitch was amazed.
“How’d this cart get here so fast?” he asked Mitya.
“I saw Andrey on my way to you and told him to come straight here. We can’t waste time. Last time I went with Timofey, but he’s already gone ahead with her. Are we going to be late, Andrey?”

“They’ll only get there maybe an hour before us, probably less. I know how fast Timofey drives. He can’t keep up with us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. No way. They won’t be an hour ahead!” said Andrey, the tall, red-haired driver in a long coat.
“Fifty roubles for vodka if we’re only an hour behind them.”
“I guarantee it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They won’t be half an hour ahead, let alone an hour.”
Mitya rushed around giving orders, but he was oddly scattered—starting sentences and forgetting what he was saying. Pyotr Ilyitch had to step in to help.
“Four hundred roubles’ worth, not less! Just like last time,” Mitya ordered. “Four dozen bottles of champagne—not one less.”
“Why do you need so much? What’s it for? Wait a minute!” Pyotr Ilyitch cried. “What’s in this box? There can’t be four hundred roubles’ worth here.”

The shop assistants politely explained that the first box just had a few bottles of champagne and some treats like candy and toffee. The rest would be packed and sent in another cart, just like last time, arriving about an hour after Mitya.
“Not more than an hour! And add more toffee and fondants—the girls love them,” Mitya insisted.

“The fondants are set. But why four dozen champagne? One’s enough,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, annoyed. He started haggling, demanded an itemized bill, and managed to save a hundred roubles. In the end, they agreed to send only three hundred roubles’ worth.
“Fine, do what you want!” Pyotr Ilyitch said. “It’s your money—waste it if you want.”
“Come on, you penny-pincher, don’t be mad,” Mitya said, pulling him into a back room. “They’ll bring us a bottle here. Let’s try it. Pyotr Ilyitch, you’re a good guy, I like you.”
Mitya sat on a wicker chair at a little table with a dirty napkin. Pyotr Ilyitch sat across from him. Soon, champagne arrived, and someone suggested oysters. “Top quality, just in.”
“Forget oysters. I don’t eat them. We don’t need anything else,” Pyotr Ilyitch snapped.
“No time for oysters,” Mitya agreed. “And I’m not hungry. You know, friend,” he said seriously, “I never liked all this chaos.”
“Who does? Three dozen bottles of champagne for peasants—no wonder I’m annoyed!”

“That’s not what I mean. I mean the chaos inside me. I have no order in my life, no higher purpose. But... it’s too late to worry now. My whole life’s been a mess, and now it’s time to fix it. Is that a pun?”
“You’re raving, not making puns.”
“That line came from my heart once—it’s not a poem, it’s a tear. I wrote it myself... not while I was pulling the captain’s beard, though.”
“Why mention him now?”
“Why? Just being silly. Everything ends, everything’s made equal. That’s all there is to it.”
“You know, I keep thinking about your pistols.”

“That’s silly too! Drink and stop worrying. I love life. I’ve loved it too much, too much for my own good. Let’s drink to life! Why am I so happy with myself? I’m a scoundrel, but I’m pleased with myself. And yet it bugs me that I’m a scoundrel, but still pleased. I bless creation. I could bless God and everything right now, but... I have to get rid of one nasty bug so it doesn’t ruin things for others. Let’s drink to life, my brother. What’s more precious than life? Nothing! To life, and to a queen of queens!”
“Let’s drink to life and your queen, too, if that’s what you want.”
They each drank a glass. Even though Mitya seemed excited and talkative, he was also weighed down by some deep anxiety.
“Misha... here’s your Misha! Misha, come here, boy, drink this glass to the golden-haired sun of tomorrow’s morning...”
“Why are you giving him that?” Pyotr Ilyitch snapped.
“Yes, yes, let me! I want to!”
“Ech!”
Misha drank, bowed, and ran out.

“He’ll remember this someday,” Mitya said. “Woman—I love women! What is a woman? The queen of the world! My heart is sad, Pyotr Ilyitch. Remember Hamlet? ‘I am very sorry, good Horatio! Alas, poor Yorick!’ Maybe that’s me—Yorick now, and a skull later.”
Pyotr Ilyitch listened in silence. Mitya, too, was quiet for a bit.
“Whose dog is that?” he asked the shop clerk, noticing a little lap dog with dark eyes in the corner.
“It’s Varvara Alexyevna’s, the boss’s. She brought it and forgot it here. We need to take it back to her,” the clerk replied.
“I saw one like it in the regiment,” Mitya murmured dreamily, “but that one’s back leg was broken... By the way, Pyotr Ilyitch, have you ever stolen anything?”
“What kind of question is that?”
“Oh, nothing. I mean, stolen from someone’s pocket—not government money, everyone steals that, even you, probably...”
“Go to hell.”
“I mean taking money from another person’s pocket, or purse?”
“I stole twenty copecks from my mother when I was nine. I took it off the table secretly and held it tight in my hand.”
“And then what?”
“Nothing. I kept it three days, then felt ashamed, confessed, and gave it back.”
“And then?”
“Of course I got whipped. But why are you asking? Did you steal something?”
“I did,” Mitya said, winking.
“What did you steal?” asked Pyotr Ilyitch.
“I stole twenty copecks from my mother when I was nine, and gave it back three days later.”
As he said this, Mitya stood up suddenly.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, are you coming now?” called Andrey from the shop door.

“Ready? Coming! Just a few last words—Andrey, a glass of vodka before we go! Give him some brandy too! Put that box—the one with the pistols—under my seat. Goodbye, Pyotr Ilyitch, don’t think badly of me.”
“But you’re coming back tomorrow?”
“Of course.”
“Will you pay the bill now?” the clerk called, jumping forward.
“Oh, right, the bill. Of course.”

He pulled out the bundle of bills, picked out three hundred roubles, tossed them on the counter, and hurried out of the shop. Everyone followed, bowing and wishing him luck. Andrey, coughing from the brandy, jumped up on the box. But as Mitya was about to climb on, he suddenly saw Fenya in front of him. She ran up, panting, hands clasped, and fell at his feet.

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, please, don’t hurt my mistress. I’m the one who told you everything. And don’t kill him—he came first, he’s hers! He’ll marry Agrafena Alexandrovna now—that’s why he came back from Siberia. Please, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, don’t take a life!”

“So that’s it, huh? Off to make trouble,” muttered Pyotr Ilyitch. “Now I get it, clear as day. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, give me those pistols if you want to act like a real man!” he shouted. “Do you hear, Dmitri?”

“The pistols? Wait, brother—I’ll throw them in a pond on the road,” Mitya answered. “Fenya, get up—don’t kneel. Mitya won’t hurt anyone, the fool won’t hurt anyone again. But Fenya,” he yelled as he took his seat, “I hurt you just now, forgive me, have pity on me, forgive a scoundrel... but even if you don’t, it doesn’t matter. It’s all the same now. Andrey, go, full speed!”
Andrey whipped the horses, and the bells began to ring.
“Goodbye, Pyotr Ilyitch! My last tear is for you!...”

“He’s not drunk, but he talks like a madman,” Pyotr Ilyitch thought as he watched him go. He thought about staying to watch the rest of the provisions get packed, knowing they’d cheat Mitya, but suddenly got annoyed with himself and went to the tavern to play billiards.

“He’s an idiot, though a good guy,” he muttered. “I’ve heard about that officer, Grushenka’s old flame. Well, if he’s back... Those pistols! Damn! I’m not his babysitter! Let them do what they want. It’ll all amount to nothing—they’re just a bunch of brawlers. They’ll drink, fight, make up. Nothing real will happen. What does he mean by ‘stepping aside, punishing myself’? He’s said stuff like that a thousand times, drunk, in the taverns. But now he’s not drunk. ‘Drunk in spirit’—they love dramatic words, those guys. Am I his nurse? He must have been fighting—his face was covered in blood. With who? I’ll find out at the Metropolis. And his handkerchief, soaked in blood—it’s still on my floor. Ugh!”

He got to the tavern in a bad mood and started a billiards game. Playing cheered him. He played a second game, and then started telling someone that Dmitri Karamazov came into money again—about three thousand roubles—and went off to spend it with Grushenka at Mokroe. This news caught everyone’s attention, and they talked about it seriously, not joking. They stopped playing.
“Three thousand? How could he get three thousand?”
People asked questions. The story about Madame Hohlakov’s “gift” sounded suspicious to them.
“Didn’t he rob his old father? That’s the real question.”
“Three thousand! Something’s fishy about it.”
“He said right here he’d kill his father—we all heard him. And he talked about three thousand then too...”
Pyotr Ilyitch listened. Suddenly, he got short and distant in his answers. He didn’t mention the blood on Mitya’s face and hands, even though he’d meant to at first.

They started a third game, and gradually people stopped talking about Mitya. But by the end, Pyotr Ilyitch didn’t feel like playing anymore. He put down his cue and, without eating supper as planned, left the tavern. When he got to the market, he stopped, confused with himself. He realized he wanted to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house to see if anything had happened. “Am I really going to wake everyone up and make a fuss over some stupid nonsense?” he thought. “Ugh, is it my job to look after them?”

In a foul mood, he headed home, then suddenly remembered Fenya. “Damn, I should have questioned her,” he thought, annoyed. “I could have found out everything.” The urge to talk to her got so strong that halfway home, he turned around and went to Grushenka’s house. At the gate, he knocked. The sound in the quiet night sobered him a little and made him feel awkward. No one answered—everyone inside was asleep.
“Now I’m just making a scene,” he thought, feeling uncomfortable. But instead of leaving, he started pounding on the gate even louder, making a racket in the street.
“Not coming? Well, I’ll wake them up, I will!” he muttered after each knock, angry at himself, but knocking even harder.

Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya) was racing down the road. It was just over twenty versts to Mokroe, but Andrey’s three horses were running so fast that they could get there in just over an hour. The rush of the ride made Mitya feel alive again. The air was cool and fresh, and the sky was full of bright stars. It was the very same night—and maybe even the same hour—that Alyosha had thrown himself to the ground and promised to love the world forever.

Mitya’s mind was a storm of confusion, but even though a million things were making his heart ache, right now he wanted only one thing: to see her, his “queen,” one last time. Whatever else he was feeling, his heart was steady and clear about that. You might not believe it, but this jealous lover wasn’t even a little bit jealous of the new rival who had suddenly appeared. If it had been anyone else, Mitya would’ve instantly gotten jealous, maybe even violent. But flying through the night, he felt no anger, no resentment toward the man who had been her first love... though, of course, he hadn’t seen him yet.

“There’s no point arguing,” Mitya thought to himself. “She has the right. He has the right. This was her first love, and she hasn’t forgotten him after five years. So she’s only truly loved him for those five years. Where does that leave me? What right do I have? Step aside, Mitya, and make way! Who am I now? Now it’s all over, even without that officer—even if he hadn’t shown up, it would still be over…”

That’s about how he would have put his feelings into words, if he could think straight. But he wasn’t thinking clearly at all. His plan had appeared instantly, the moment Fenya told him the news—it came from pure emotion, not reason. Still, even with this resolve, his mind was in chaos. He just couldn’t find peace. The past, all the pain he’d left behind, still tortured him. It felt strange to realize that he had already written his own “death sentence” on paper: “I punish myself.” The note was right there in his pocket, ready. His pistol was loaded. He’d even decided exactly how he would meet the sunrise—the “golden-haired Phoebus”—the next morning.

But he just couldn’t let go of the past, the pain was still there. It sank into his heart with a kind of despair. At one point, he even felt like telling Andrey to stop, to jump out of the cart, grab his gun, and end everything right then and there. But that feeling passed as quickly as it came. The horses kept racing, eating up the distance, and as they got closer to their destination, his thoughts filled more and more with her, pushing away all the dark images that had haunted him. Oh, how he wanted to see her—even for a second, even from far away!

“She’s with him now,” Mitya thought. “Now I’ll see what she looks like beside him, her first love—and that’s all I want.” Never before had this woman, who had changed his life so much, made him feel such love, such a strange and powerful feeling that even surprised him. It was so tender it felt almost holy, as if he wanted to disappear for her sake. “I’ll disappear!” he told himself, almost overwhelmed by emotion.

They’d been riding hard for almost an hour. Mitya stayed quiet, and though Andrey was normally a chatty guy, he didn’t say a word either. He just kept urging his three skinny but lively bay horses on. Suddenly, Mitya shouted in a panic:
“Andrey! What if they’re asleep?”
This new thought hit him like a punch. He’d never thought of it before.
“They might be in bed already, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Andrey replied.

Mitya frowned, like the thought hurt him. Yes, really... here he was, racing there with all these feelings, but maybe they were all just sleeping... maybe she was asleep right now, too. He felt a flash of angry frustration.
“Drive on, Andrey! Faster! Hurry up!” Mitya yelled, almost losing control.
“But maybe they’re not in bed,” Andrey said after a pause. “Timofey said there’s a whole bunch of people there—”
“At the station?”
“No, not the post station, but at Plastunov’s inn. They rent out horses there, too.”
“I know the place. But you’re saying there’s a lot of people? Who? Who are they?” Mitya asked, suddenly worried by this unexpected news.
“Well, Timofey said they’re all gentlefolk. Two from our town—don’t know their names. There are two others, strangers, maybe more. I didn’t ask for details. They’re playing cards, Timofey said.”
“Cards?”
“Yeah, so maybe they’re not in bed if they’re playing cards. It’s probably not later than eleven.”
“Faster, Andrey! Hurry!” Mitya shouted, nervous again.
“Can I ask you something, sir?” Andrey said after a minute. “I’m just afraid you’ll get mad.”
“What is it?”
“Well, just now Fenya begged you not to hurt her mistress—and someone else, too... So you see, sir, it’s me taking you there... Forgive me, sir, I just feel guilty... Maybe I shouldn’t say anything—”
Suddenly, Mitya grabbed Andrey by the shoulders from behind.
“Are you a driver?” he asked, desperate.
“Yes, sir.”

“Then you know you have to make way for others. What would you think of a driver who never let anyone pass, just barreled ahead and ran people over? No, a driver can’t run people down. You can’t mess up people’s lives. But if you have messed up someone’s life—punish yourself. If you’ve ruined even one life—punish yourself and go away.”
These words burst out of Mitya almost like he was losing control. Andrey was surprised, but kept the conversation going.

“You’re right, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You shouldn’t crush or hurt anyone—or any creature. Every creature’s made by God. Take horses, for example: some drivers just whip them and force them to go, no matter what.”

“To hell?” Mitya interrupted, with a short, sharp laugh. “Andrey, you simple soul,” he said, grabbing his shoulders again, “tell me: will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell or not? What do you think?”

“I don’t know, sir. It depends on you, because you see... When the Son of God was nailed to the cross and died, He went straight down to hell and let all the suffering sinners free. The devil moaned, thinking he wouldn’t get any more sinners in hell. But God said to him, ‘Don’t worry—you’ll still get all the powerful of the earth, the rulers, the chief judges, the rich men, and hell will be as full as ever until I return.’ That’s what He said…”
“A peasant story! Not bad! Whip up the left horse, Andrey!”

“So, you see, sir, that’s who hell is for,” Andrey said, whipping up the horse. “But you’re like a child... that’s how we think of you. And even if you’re quick-tempered, God will forgive you for your kind heart.”
“And you, Andrey, do you forgive me?”
“Forgive you for what, sir? You’ve never done me any harm.”
“No, I mean for everyone—for all of them. You’re the only one here on this road—will you forgive me for everything? Speak, simple-hearted peasant!”
“Oh sir, you’re scaring me. Your talk is so strange.”
But Mitya didn’t hear. He was praying to himself, muttering frantically.

“Lord, take me in, with all my sins, and don’t judge me. Let me pass by Your judgment... don’t judge me, because I’ve judged myself, don’t judge me, because I love You, Lord. I’m a wretch, but I love You. If You send me to hell, I’ll love You even there, and I’ll shout from there that I love You forever... But let me love to the end... Just five more hours, till the first light of Your day... because I love the queen of my soul... I love her and I can’t stop loving her. You see my whole heart... I’ll ride up, I’ll fall before her and say, ‘You’re right to move on and leave me. Goodbye, and don’t worry about your victim... never trouble yourself about me!’”
“Mokroe!” Andrey cried, pointing his whip ahead.

In the pale darkness, a big black cluster of buildings appeared out in the open plain. The village of Mokroe had two thousand people, but at this hour they were all asleep, except for a few places where lights still glimmered.
“Keep going, Andrey, I’m coming!” Mitya said feverishly.
“They’re not asleep,” Andrey pointed with his whip at the Plastunovs’ inn at the edge of the village. All six windows facing the street were brightly lit.
“They’re not asleep,” Mitya repeated with joy. “Faster, Andrey! Gallop! Pull up fast! Ring the bells! Let everyone know I’m here. I’m coming! I’m coming, too!”
Andrey forced his tired horses into a last sprint, and pulled up with a flourish at the big front steps, the horses panting and steaming.
Mitya jumped out of the cart just as the innkeeper, heading to bed, peeked out from the steps, curious about the late arrival.
“Trifon Borissovitch, is that you?”
The innkeeper leaned down, stared hard, rushed down the steps, and hurried up to Mitya with eager respect.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, sir! Is it really you again?”

Trifon Borissovitch was a stocky, healthy man, not too tall, with a round face. He usually acted tough, especially with the peasants, but could instantly become polite and fawning if he thought it’d help him.
