He wore traditional Russian clothes—a shirt buttoned on the side, and a full-skirted coat. He’d saved up a lot of money, but always dreamed of having more. Most of the local peasants owed him money, and he bought and rented land from nearby landowners, making the peasants work it to pay off debts they could never escape. He was a widower with four grown daughters. One was already a widow and lived at the inn with her two kids, working like a maid. Another was married to a low-level official, and you could see a photo of this man in uniform on the wall. The two youngest daughters wore fancy blue or green dresses for church or visits, but the next morning they’d be up at dawn, sweeping rooms, emptying slops, and cleaning after guests.

Even though he was rich, Trifon Borissovitch loved getting extra money out of drunk guests. He remembered how, just a month ago, he’d made two or three hundred roubles out of Dmitri in one night, when Mitya had come with Grushenka. So now, when he saw Mitya drive up, he greeted him with extra enthusiasm, already smelling money.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, here you are again!”
“Hang on, Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya said, “first things first—where is she?”
“Agrafena Alexandrovna?” The innkeeper got it right away, looking closely at Mitya. “She’s here, too…”
“With who? Who’s with her?”

“Some strangers. One’s an official, a Pole I think, judging by his accent. He sent the horses for her from here; and there’s another with him, a friend or maybe just a travel companion, hard to say. They’re both dressed in civilian clothes.”
“So, are they having a party? Do they have money?”
“Not much of a party, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Nothing special.”
“Nothing special? And who else is there?”

“Two gentlemen from town. They came back from Tcherny and are staying here. One’s a young man, related to Mr. Miüsov, I think, but I forgot his name... and you probably know the other, Maximov. He says he’s been on a pilgrimage to the monastery in town. He’s traveling with the young Miüsov relation.”
“That’s all?”
“Yes.”
“Wait, listen, Trifon Borissovitch. Tell me the main thing: what about her? How is she?”
“Oh, she’s just arrived. She’s sitting with them.”
“Is she happy? Is she laughing?”
“No, she’s not laughing much. She seems kind of bored. She’s combing the young man’s hair.”
“The Pole—the officer?”
“No, he’s not young, and he’s not an officer. Not him, sir. It’s the young man who’s Mr. Miüsov’s relation... I forgot his name.”
“Kalganov.”
“That’s it, Kalganov!”
“Okay. I’ll see for myself. Are they playing cards?”
“They were playing, but not anymore. They’ve been drinking tea. The official asked for liqueurs.”
“Wait, Trifon Borissovitch, wait, my good man, I’ll see for myself. Now, one more question: are the gypsies here?”
“You can’t have gypsies now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The police sent them away. But there are some Jewish musicians in the village, they play cymbals and fiddle. I can send for them. They’ll come.”
“Send for them. Definitely send for them!” Mitya cried. “And get the girls together like last time—Marya especially, Stepanida, and Arina. Two hundred roubles for a chorus!”

“Oh, for that kind of money I could wake up the whole village, even if they’re asleep now. Are these peasants or girls worth such generosity, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Spending that much on such roughness! What’s the point of giving a peasant a cigar? And the girls aren’t anything special, either. Besides, my daughters will sing for you for free, let alone for a sum like that. They just went to bed, but I’ll wake them up and get them singing. You gave the peasants champagne the other day, too, ha!”

Even though Trifon Borissovitch pretended to care, the last time Mitya was here he’d hidden away half a dozen bottles of champagne for himself, and pocketed a hundred-rouble note he found under the table.
“Trifon Borissovitch, I blew through more than a thousand last time I was here. Remember?”
“You sure did. I remember. You must have left three thousand behind.”
“Well, I’m here to do it again, you see?”
He pulled out a thick roll of cash and waved it in front of the innkeeper.

“Now, listen up. In an hour, bring up the wine, snacks, pies, and sweets—bring everything at once. That box Andrey has is to come up right now, too. Open it and serve champagne right away. And the girls—I need the girls, Marya especially.”
He turned to the cart and took out the box of pistols.
“Here, Andrey, let’s settle up. Here’s fifteen roubles for the drive, and fifty for vodka—for your quickness, for your loyalty... Remember Karamazov!”
“I’m scared, sir,” Andrey stammered. “Give me five extra roubles, but no more. Trifon Borissovitch, you heard me. Sorry for my foolish words...”

“What are you afraid of?” Mitya asked, looking him over. “Well, go to the devil, then!” he shouted, throwing him five roubles. “Now, Trifon Borissovitch, take me in quietly so I can get a look at them without being seen. Where are they? In the blue room?”

Trifon Borissovitch glanced nervously at Mitya, but did what he asked right away. He led Mitya inside to a big room next to where the visitors were, took away the light, and quietly put Mitya in a dark corner where he could watch them without being seen. But Mitya didn’t watch long—he couldn’t really see the company, he only saw her, and his heart beat so hard that everything went black before his eyes.

She was sitting sideways to the table in a low chair, and next to her on the sofa was the young, handsome Kalganov. She was holding his hand and seemed to be laughing, but he looked annoyed and wasn’t looking at her. He was loudly saying something to Maximov, who sat across the table from Grushenka. Maximov was laughing hard about something. On the sofa was another stranger, and on a chair next to the sofa sat yet another. The man on the sofa was leaning back, smoking a pipe—a short, stout man with a broad face, who seemed grumpy. The other stranger was super tall, but Mitya couldn’t see much else. He could barely breathe. He couldn’t take it any longer, so he put the pistol case on a chest, and with his heart pounding
Mitya walked quickly across the room, his long legs closing the distance in big, fast steps.

“Everyone,” he said loudly, his voice nearly a shout, but he kept tripping over his words, “I'm—I'm all right! Don't worry about me!” He turned suddenly to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair next to Kalganov and was holding his hand tightly. “I'm coming too. I’m staying here till morning. Is that okay, everyone? Can I stay just for tonight, in this same room, one last time?”
He finished speaking and looked at the chubby little man with a pipe sitting on the sofa. The man took the pipe out of his mouth and said sternly:
“Sir, we’re here for a private gathering. There are other rooms you could use.”
“Wait, is that you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? What are you talking about?” Kalganov suddenly responded. “Sit down with us. How are you?”
“I’m so happy to see you, my dear friend. I’ve always thought a lot of you,” Mitya said excitedly, reaching out his hand across the table.
“Hey! You’re squeezing my hand too hard—you’ve nearly broken my fingers!” Kalganov laughed.

“He always squeezes like that, always,” Grushenka said with a nervous but playful smile. She seemed relieved by the look on Mitya’s face, as if she realized he wasn’t going to cause a scene. Still, she watched him closely, curious and a bit uneasy, surprised he’d show up and act like this at such a tense moment.
“Good evening,” Maximov said kindly from the left. Mitya hurried over to greet him, too.

“Good evening! You’re here as well? I’m so happy to see you!” Mitya said, addressing the Polish man with the pipe, clearly thinking he was the main person in the room. “I rushed over... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour, in this room... the room where I, too, adored... my queen. Forgive me, sir,” he cried out, almost wild, “I promised myself—oh, don’t worry, it’s my last night! Let’s drink to friendship. The wine will be here soon—I brought it.” (He pulled out a bunch of money.) “Let’s have music, singing, a party, just like before. But the unneeded worm will crawl away and be gone. I want to celebrate tonight, my last night, as a happy day.”

He was almost choking on his words. He wanted to say so much, but only strange outbursts came out. The Polish man stared at him, glancing at the money in his hand, then at Grushenka, clearly confused.
“If my sovereign lady allows—” he began.

“What does ‘sovereign’ mean? Do you mean ‘queen’?” Grushenka interrupted, starting to giggle. “You’re so funny the way you talk. Sit down, Mitya. What are you saying? Please don’t scare us. You aren’t going to, right? If not, I’m glad you’re here...”
“Me, scare you?” Mitya cried, throwing up his hands. “Go ahead, don’t mind me—I won’t get in your way!”
Then, to everyone’s surprise—including his own—he dropped into a chair and started crying, turning his face to the wall and hugging the back of the chair as if it were a person.

“Come on, what’s with you?” Grushenka scolded. “That’s just how he is—he starts talking, and I can never figure out what he means. He’s cried like this before, and now he’s doing it again. It’s embarrassing! Why are you crying? You don’t even have a reason!” she added, her words sharp but mysterious.
“I... I’m not crying... Well, good evening!” He spun around in his chair and suddenly laughed, not his usual harsh laugh, but a shaky, quiet, nervous one.

“There you go again... Come on, cheer up!” Grushenka said, trying to comfort him. “I’m really glad you came, Mitya, I really am! I want him to stay with us,” she said, looking at everyone, but especially at the man on the sofa. “I mean it! And if he leaves, I’ll leave, too!” Her eyes flashed.
“What my queen commands is law!” the Polish man declared, gallantly kissing Grushenka’s hand. “I invite you, sir, to join us,” he added politely to Mitya.
Mitya seemed about to make another big speech but couldn’t get the words out.
“Let’s drink, sir!” he blurted out instead. Everyone laughed.

“Oh my gosh, I thought he was going to start up again!” Grushenka said, a bit nervously. “Listen, Mitya, don’t act crazy. But I’m glad you brought champagne—I want some, and I don’t like sweet drinks. And best of all, you’re here. We were so bored before... You’re here to party again, right? But put your money away. Where’d you get so much?”

Mitya had been holding the crumpled wad of bills the whole time, and everyone—especially the two Polish men—kept staring at it. Flustered, he shoved it into his pocket and blushed. Just then, the innkeeper brought in a bottle of champagne and glasses. Mitya grabbed the bottle, but he was so confused he didn’t know what to do next. Kalganov took it and poured the drinks.

“Another bottle!” Mitya shouted to the innkeeper, and, forgetting to toast with the Polish man he’d invited to drink, he gulped down his glass before anyone else. Suddenly, his whole face changed—the serious, upset look he’d come in with disappeared and was replaced by something almost childlike. He seemed softer, shy and happy, with a nervous laugh, grinning like a dog who did something bad but was forgiven. He looked around at everyone with a big, goofy smile, happy just to be there. He scooted closer to Grushenka, laughing, and started to figure out who the two Poles were, though he hadn’t formed any clear opinions yet.

The Polish man on the sofa stood out to Mitya with his fancy manners, strong accent, and especially his pipe. “Well, whatever, at least he’s smoking a pipe,” Mitya thought. The man’s pudgy, middle-aged face, tiny nose, and silly, pointed, dyed mustache didn’t bother Mitya at all. He didn’t even notice the man’s ridiculous Siberian wig with its goofy hair hanging over his temples. “If he wears a wig, it must be fine,” Mitya thought, still in a blissful mood. The other, younger Pole was tall and looked around the room with a kind of arrogance, but the only thing Mitya noticed was how huge he was—“He must be six foot three,” Mitya guessed. He figured the big Pole was the little Pole’s friend or bodyguard, but that seemed totally normal to Mitya. He was feeling so humble and content, he didn’t feel competitive at all.

Grushenka’s mysterious words and her mood totally went over Mitya’s head. All he could feel, with a pounding heart, was that she was being kind to him, that she’d forgiven him, and wanted him to sit by her. He was thrilled just watching her drink her champagne. The silent, awkward group did start to bother him, though, and he looked around expectantly.
“Why are we just sitting here, guys? Why doesn’t anyone do anything?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
“He’s been talking nonsense, and we were all laughing,” Kalganov said suddenly, as if reading Mitya’s mind, and pointed at Maximov.
Mitya immediately looked at Kalganov, then at Maximov.
“He’s talking nonsense?” Mitya repeated, breaking into his odd, wooden laugh, suddenly delighted—“ha ha!”
“Yeah. He keeps saying all our army officers in the 1820s married Polish women. Isn’t that ridiculous?”
“Polish women?” Mitya repeated, completely delighted.

Kalganov knew how Mitya felt about Grushenka, and had guessed something about the Pole, but he didn’t really care about that. What interested him was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by accident, and this was his first time meeting the Poles at the inn. He already knew Grushenka from before, but she hadn’t liked him much then. Tonight, though, she was being really friendly to him—at least before Mitya showed up. But he didn’t seem to react either way. Kalganov was a young guy, maybe twenty, dressed really nicely, with a handsome, fair face and thick blond hair. His eyes were pale blue, intelligent, and sometimes even deep for his age, though he could act and talk like a kid and didn’t mind it. He was often stubborn and moody, sometimes dreamy and distracted, other times excited—for no real reason.

“Just picture it—he’s been hanging out with me for four days now,” Kalganov continued, talking slowly and lazily, but not in a fake way. “Ever since your brother pushed him off the carriage and sent him flying. That made me interested in him, so I took him out to the country, but he keeps talking such nonsense I’m embarrassed to be seen with him. I’m bringing him back.”
“The gentleman hasn’t seen real Polish ladies, and says things that aren’t true,” the Polish man with the pipe told Maximov.
He actually spoke Russian pretty well, much better than he pretended. But when he used Russian, he’d always twist the words to sound more Polish.
“But I was married to a Polish woman myself,” Maximov giggled.
“But were you in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you an officer?” Kalganov jumped in.
“Was he a cavalry officer? Ha ha!” Mitya said, excited, looking from one person to the next as if expecting a surprise.

“No, see,” Maximov explained to him. “What I mean is that those pretty Polish ladies... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlan soldiers... when a lady dances with a Uhlan, she jumps on his knee like a little kitten... a little white kitten... and her parents watch and don’t mind at all. They don’t mind... and the next day the Uhlan comes and proposes to her. That’s how it goes... he proposes, he he!” Maximov finished, giggling.
“The man is a scoundrel!” the tall Pole suddenly growled, crossing his legs. Mitya noticed his giant, greasy boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles looked kind of shabby.
“Now he’s calling names! What’s he so mad about?” Grushenka said, getting annoyed.
“Madam Agrippina, what the gentleman saw in Poland were servant girls, not ladies from good families,” the Polish man with the pipe said to Grushenka.
“You can bet on that,” the tall Pole snapped with contempt.
“What now! Let him talk! People talk, why stop them? It keeps things lively,” Grushenka said, sounding grumpy.
“I’m not stopping anyone, madam,” said the man in the wig, giving Grushenka a long look, and then went back to puffing his pipe in silence.

“No, no. The Polish gentleman is right,” Kalganov piped up, getting excited, like it was a big deal. “He’s never even been to Poland, so how can he talk about it? I suppose you weren’t married in Poland, were you?”

“No, in the Province of Smolensk. But a Uhlan brought her and her family to Russia before that. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a nice guy. At first, he meant to marry her himself, but he didn’t because she turned out to be lame.”
“So you married a lame woman?” Kalganov shouted.
“Yes. They tricked me a little and hid it. I thought she was hopping just for fun.”
“She was so happy she was going to marry you!” Kalganov yelled, laughing like a kid.

“Yes, she was happy. But it turned out for a different reason. After we got married, that very evening, she confessed and asked me to forgive her. ‘When I was a child, I jumped over a puddle and hurt my leg,’ she said. He he!”
Kalganov burst out laughing, nearly falling off the sofa. Grushenka laughed too. Mitya was on top of the world.
“Believe it or not, that’s true—he’s not lying now,” Kalganov told Mitya. “And you know, he’s been married twice; this is about his first wife. But his second wife ran away, and she’s still alive.”
“Really?” Mitya said, staring at Maximov in shock.

“Yes, she ran away. It happened to me,” Maximov admitted, “with a Frenchman. Worse, she had already taken all my money. ‘You’re educated,’ she said. ‘You can always make a living.’ That’s how she settled things. A wise old bishop once told me: ‘One wife was lame, but the other was too quick on her feet.’ He he!”

“Listen, listen!” Kalganov said, barely able to contain himself. “If he’s lying—and he does a lot—it’s just to entertain us. No harm in that, right? You know, I kind of like him. He’s pretty low, but that’s just how he is. And get this—he claims that Gogol wrote Dead Souls about him. You remember the landowner called Maximov in it, who gets beaten by Nozdryov? He says he was that Maximov! Now, does that make any sense? Tchitchikov traveled in the early 1820s, so the dates don’t fit. He couldn’t have been beaten then, could he?”
It was hard to tell why Kalganov was so worked up, but he really was. Mitya just went along.
“Well, but what if they did beat him!” Mitya laughed.
“It’s not exactly that they beat me, but what I mean is—” Maximov tried to explain.
“What do you mean? Either they beat you or they didn’t.”
“What time is it, sir?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, looking bored. The other man shrugged—neither had a watch.

“Why shouldn’t people talk? Just because you’re bored, does that mean no one else can talk?” Grushenka snapped at him. Suddenly something seemed to dawn on Mitya. This time, the Pole answered with obvious irritation.
“Madam, I didn’t object. I said nothing.”
“All right then. Come on, tell us your story,” Grushenka urged Maximov. “Why is everyone so quiet?”

“There’s nothing to tell, it’s all silly,” Maximov said right away, clearly enjoying the attention, his voice a bit high-pitched. “Besides, Gogol gave everyone in Dead Souls names that mean something. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov’s real name was Shkvornev. Fenardi was really called Fenardi, only he was Russian, not Italian, and Mademoiselle Fenardi was a pretty girl with sparkly tights and a short skirt, and she’d spin around and around—not for four hours, but just four minutes—and she enchanted everyone...”
“But what did they beat you for?” Kalganov demanded.
“For Piron!” Maximov answered.
“Who’s Piron?” Mitya asked.

“The famous French writer, Piron. We were all drinking at a fair, a big group. They’d invited me, and I started quoting jokes. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a weird outfit!’ and Boileau says he’s going to a masquerade, meaning the baths, he he! They got offended, so I quickly told another joke, a really sarcastic one, that every educated person knows:

That made them even madder, and they started yelling at me. To smooth things over, I told a story about Piron, how he wasn’t accepted into the French Academy, so he wrote his own epitaph to get revenge:
They grabbed me and beat me up.”
“But why? Why?”
“Because I was educated. People can beat a man up for anything,” Maximov finished, acting wise.
“Ugh, that’s enough! That’s all dumb, I don’t want to listen anymore. I thought it would be funny,” Grushenka interrupted suddenly.
Mitya snapped to attention and stopped laughing. The tall Pole stood up with a bored, stuck-up look, and started pacing around the room, hands behind his back.
“He can’t sit still,” Grushenka said, glaring at him. Mitya started to feel uneasy. He noticed the Pole on the sofa was scowling at him, too.
“Sir!” Mitya called. “Let’s drink! And the other gentleman, too! Let’s drink.”
In a flash, he grabbed three glasses and filled them with champagne.
“To Poland, gentlemen! I drink to Poland!” Mitya shouted.
“I would be honored, sir,” said the Pole on the sofa, acting grand and polite, taking his glass.
“And the other gentleman, what’s his name? Drink up, my good man, take your glass!” Mitya encouraged.
“Pan Vrublevsky,” the Pole on the sofa said.
Pan Vrublevsky staggered over to the table.
“To Poland, gentlemen!” Mitya shouted, raising his glass. “Hurrah!”
All three drank. Mitya grabbed the bottle and poured three more glasses.
“Now to Russia, gentlemen, and let’s all be friends!”
“Pour some for us,” Grushenka said. “I’ll drink to Russia, too!”
“Me too,” said Kalganov.
“And I’d like to, too... to Russia, the old grandmother!” Maximov giggled.
“Everyone, everyone!” Mitya cheered. “Trifon Borissovitch, more bottles!”
The innkeeper brought the other three bottles Mitya had brought and put them on the table. Mitya filled everyone’s glasses.
“To Russia! Hurrah!” he yelled again. Everyone drank except the Poles. Grushenka finished her glass in one gulp. The Poles didn’t touch theirs.
“What’s this, gentlemen?” Mitya cried. “Aren’t you going to drink it?”
Pan Vrublevsky picked up his glass, raised it, and said loudly:
“To Russia as she was before 1772.”
“That’s better!” the other Pole said, and they both finished their glasses.
“You guys are fools,” Mitya suddenly blurted out.
“Sir!” both Poles shouted, turning on Mitya angrily, like a pair of fighting cocks. Pan Vrublevsky was especially furious.
“You can’t help loving your own country!” he yelled.
“Quiet! No fighting! I won’t allow it!” Grushenka shouted, stomping her foot. Her face was flushed, her eyes shining. The champagne was clearly having an effect. Mitya was terrified.
“Gentlemen, forgive me! It’s my fault, I’m sorry. Vrublevsky, sir, I apologize.”
“Shut up, you! Sit down, you idiot!” Grushenka snapped, really annoyed.
Everyone sat down. The room went silent as they looked at each other.
“Gentlemen, it’s all my fault,” Mitya started again, not really understanding Grushenka’s words. “Come on, why are we just sitting here? What should we do for fun?”
“Ugh, it’s not fun at all,” Kalganov mumbled lazily.
“Let’s play faro again, like before,” Maximov giggled suddenly.
“Faro? Awesome!” Mitya cried. “If only the gentlemen—”
“It’s late, gentlemen,” the Pole on the sofa said, like he didn’t really want to.
“That’s right,” Pan Vrublevsky agreed.
“Late? What do you mean, ‘late’?” Grushenka asked.
“Late, madam. I mean it’s getting late,” the Pole on the sofa said.

“It’s always late with them. They never want to do anything!” Grushenka nearly yelled. “They’re boring, so they want everyone else to be bored. Before you came, Mitya, they just sat there and turned up their noses at me.”
“My goddess!” the Pole on the sofa declared, “You’re angry with me, that’s why I’m gloomy. But I’m ready, gentlemen,” he added, turning to Mitya.
“Let’s begin, sir,” Mitya agreed, pulling out his money and laying two huge bills on the table. “I want to lose a lot to you. Take the cards. Be the banker.”
“We’ll get the landlord to bring us cards, sir,” the little Pole said, very serious.
“That’s the best way,” Pan Vrublevsky agreed.
“From the landlord? Fine, I get it. Hey, cards!” Mitya called out.

The landlord brought in a new, unopened pack, and let Mitya know the girls were getting ready and the musicians would be there soon, but the food hadn’t arrived yet. Mitya jumped up and ran to the next room to give orders, but only three girls were there and Marya hadn’t come yet. He wasn’t sure what to do or why he’d run out. He just told them to take out the presents for the girls—the sweets and candy—and called out, “And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey! I was rude to Andrey!”
Suddenly, Maximov, who had followed him, tapped Mitya on the shoulder.
“Give me five roubles,” he whispered. “I want to play faro too, he he!”
“Great! Awesome! Take ten, here!”
He took out his money and handed Maximov a ten-rouble note. “If you lose that, come back for more.”

“Awesome,” Maximov whispered, grinning, and hurried back. Mitya returned, apologizing for the wait. The Poles were already sitting, opening the pack, and seemed much friendlier. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and looked very serious as he prepared to deal.
“Take your places, gentlemen,” Pan Vrublevsky said.
“No, I’m done playing,” Kalganov said. “I already lost fifty roubles to them.”
“The gentleman had no luck, maybe he’ll have better luck now,” the Pole on the sofa said, glancing at Kalganov.
“How much is in the bank? To match?” asked Mitya.
“As you like, sir—maybe a hundred, maybe two hundred, whatever you want to bet.”
“A million!” Mitya laughed.
“Have you heard of Pan Podvysotsky, Captain?” the Pole asked.
“Who’s Podvysotsky?”

“In Warsaw there was a bank you could bet against. Podvysotsky came, saw a thousand gold pieces, and bet against the bank. The banker said, ‘Are you putting up gold, or are we trusting your word?’ ‘My word,’ Podvysotsky said. ‘Even better.’ The banker rolled the dice. Podvysotsky won. ‘Take it, sir,’ the banker said, handing him a million. ‘I didn’t know there was a million in the bank,’ Podvysotsky said. ‘You gave your word, we gave ours.’ Podvysotsky took the million.”
“That can’t be true,” Kalganov said.
“Sir, in polite society you don’t say things like that,” the Pole replied.

“As if a Polish gambler would just hand over a million!” Mitya cried, but stopped himself. “Sorry, sir, my fault again, of course he would—for honor, for Polish honor. See, I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I bet ten roubles, the jack leads.”

“And I’ll put a rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little lady, he he!” Maximov giggled, pulling out his queen and, trying to hide it, quickly crossed himself under the table. Mitya won. Maximov’s rouble won, too.
“A corner!” Mitya shouted.
“I’ll bet another rouble, a single bet,” Maximov said, overjoyed at winning.
“Lost!” Mitya shouted. “Double on the seven!”
The seven lost, too.
“Stop!” Kalganov suddenly yelled.
“Double! Double!” Mitya doubled his bets, but each time he did, the Poles beat him. The rouble bets kept winning.
“Double again!” Mitya shouted, getting worked up.
“You’ve lost two hundred, sir. Want to bet another hundred?” the Pole on the sofa asked.
“What? Two hundred already? Then another two hundred! All doubles!”
Mitya was about to slap two hundred roubles on the queen, but Kalganov stopped him with his hand.
“That’s enough!” Kalganov shouted.
“What’s wrong?” Mitya asked, surprised.
“That’s enough! I don’t want you to play anymore. Stop!”
“Why?”
“Because I said so. Come on, let’s go. That’s why. I won’t let you keep gambling.”
Mitya stared at him, confused.
“Give it up, Mitya. He might be right. You’ve lost enough,” Grushenka said with an odd tone. Both Poles stood up, looking very insulted.
“Are you kidding, sir?” the short man said, glaring at Kalganov.
“How dare you!” Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov.
“Don’t shout like that,” Grushenka scolded. “You two turkeys!”
Mitya looked at everyone, but then something in Grushenka’s face caught his attention, and at that moment a strange new idea flashed into his mind.
“Madam Agrippina,” the little Pole began, red with anger, but Mitya suddenly walked up to him and clapped him on the shoulder.
“My good man, I need two words with you.”
“What do you want?”
“In the next room. I have something nice—very nice—to tell you. You’ll like it.”
The little Pole looked startled and a little nervous, but agreed—as long as Pan Vrublevsky came too.
“The bodyguard? Bring him, I want him there! Let’s go, gentlemen!” Mitya said. “March!”
“Where are you going?” Grushenka asked, anxious.
“We’ll be back in a minute,” Mitya said.
He looked bold now, his eyes shining with confidence. He looked totally different from when he’d come in an hour ago.

He led the Poles into the bedroom on the right, not the big room where the girls were gathering and the table was set. The bedroom had trunks and packages, and two big beds piled high with cotton pillows. There was a lit candle on a small table in the corner. The little Pole and Mitya sat at the table, facing each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood behind. Both Poles looked serious but curious.
“What do you want from me, sir?” the little Pole lisped.
“Here’s the deal, sir, I won’t keep you long. Take this money.” He pulled out his notes. “How about three thousand? Take it and leave.”
The Pole stared at Mitya, searching his face.
“Three thousand, sir?” He glanced at Vrublevsky.

“Three thousand, gentlemen, three! Listen, sir, you seem smart. Take three thousand and get out of here, and take Vrublevsky with you—do you hear me? Right away, this minute, and never come back. Understand? Never. Here’s the door. Got a coat? I’ll bring it. The horses will be ready soon, and then—goodbye, sir!”
Mitya waited confidently for an answer, sure of himself. The Pole’s face suddenly grew determined.
“And the money, sir?”
“The money? I’ll give you five hundred roubles right now for the trip, and the rest—two thousand five hundred—tomorrow, in town. I swear I’ll get it, whatever it takes!” Mitya said desperately.
The Poles looked at each other again. The short man’s face got even colder.

“Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, right now, cash!” Mitya added, sensing something was wrong. “What’s the matter, sir? Don’t you trust me? I can’t give you all three thousand right now. If I did, you might come back for her tomorrow. Anyway, I don’t have it with me. It’s at home, in town,” Mitya mumbled, losing confidence with every word. “I swear, the money’s there, hidden.”
Suddenly, the little Pole’s face filled with pride.
“What’s this?” he asked sarcastically. “Shame on you!” And he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
“You’re doing this, sir,” Mitya said, realizing sadly it was hopeless, “because you want to get more out of Grushenka? You’re just a couple of chickens, that’s what!”

“This is an insult!” The little Pole turned bright red and stormed out, as if he couldn’t stand to hear another word. Vrublevsky followed, and Mitya, embarrassed and upset, came after. He was scared of Grushenka, worried the Pole would start yelling. And he did—the Pole walked dramatically into the room and threw himself in front of Grushenka.
“Madam Agrippina, I have been mortally insulted!” he exclaimed. But Grushenka lost her patience, as if he’d hurt her deeply.
“Speak Russian! Speak Russian!” she shouted. “Not another word of Polish! You used to speak Russian. You can’t have forgotten it in five years.”
She was red with anger.
“Madam Agrippina—”
“My name is Agrafena, Grushenka! Speak Russian or I won’t listen!”
The Pole, offended, tried to speak in broken Russian:
“Madam Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to leave it all behind—”
“Forgive? You came here to forgive me?” Grushenka cut him off, jumping to her feet.
“Exactly, madam. I’m not a coward, I’m a generous man. But I was shocked by your lovers. Pan Mitya offered me three thousand in the other room to leave. I spit in his face.”
“What? He offered you money for me?” Grushenka screamed. “Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”
“Sir, sir!” Mitya shouted. “She’s pure and innocent, and I’ve never been her lover! That’s a lie...”

“How dare you defend me to him?” Grushenka yelled. “It wasn’t goodness that kept me pure, and it wasn’t because I was scared of Kuzma. It was so I could hold my head up and tell him he’s a scoundrel. And he really refused the money?”
“He took it! He took it!” Mitya cried. “He just wanted all three thousand at once, but I could only give him seven hundred up front.”
“I get it: he heard I had money and came to marry me!”
“Madam Agrippina!” the little Pole cried. “I’m a knight, a nobleman—not a scoundrel! I came to marry you, and I find you are different, rebellious, and shameless.”

“Oh, get out of here! I’ll have them throw you out and you’ll be gone,” Grushenka shouted, furious. “I’ve been a fool, miserable for five years—not because of him, but because of my own anger. And he’s not even the same person! Is this what he looked like? It could be his father! Where did you get that wig? He was a falcon, and this is a goose. He used to laugh and sing for me... And I’ve been crying for five years, what an idiot I am, so weak and pathetic!”
She sank into her chair, hiding her face in her hands. Right then, the chorus of girls in the next room started singing a wild dance song.
“This is like Sodom!” Vrublevsky suddenly yelled. “Landlord, throw out these shameless women!”
The landlord, who’d been peeking in, curious about the shouting and guessing there was trouble, walked in.
“What are you yelling for? You trying to lose your voice?” he snapped at Vrublevsky, surprisingly rude.
“Animal!” Pan Vrublevsky bellowed.
“Animal? What kind of cards were you playing with? I gave you a pack and you hid it. You used marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for cheating—it’s the same as using fake money...”
He walked over to the sofa, stuck his hand between the back and the cushion, and pulled out an unopened pack of cards.
“Here’s my pack, unopened!”
He held it up so everyone could see. “I saw him hide my pack and put in his own—you’re a cheat, not a gentleman!”
“And I saw him switch a card twice!” Kalganov yelled.
“How shameful! How shameful!” Grushenka exclaimed, blushing with real embarrassment. “Oh, how far he’s fallen!”
“I thought so too!” said Mitya. But before he finished, Vrublevsky, face red and furious, shook his fist at Grushenka and shouted:
“You low harlot!”
What happened next was like a wild party, open to everyone. Grushenka was the first to call for wine.
“I want to drink! I want to get really drunk, just like last time. Do you remember, Mitya? Do you remember how we became friends here before?”
Mitya was almost out of his mind with excitement, feeling that happiness was finally within his reach. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her side.

“Go have fun! Tell them to dance, to celebrate—let the whole house dance, just like last time!” she shouted, full of energy. Mitya rushed to do as she said. The singers were waiting in the next room because the room they’d been in was too small. It was split in half by cotton curtains, and behind them was a big bed with a fluffy mattress and a pile of pillows. There were beds in the other rooms for guests, too. Grushenka sat right by the door, and Mitya brought her a comfy chair. She had sat in the same spot watching the dancing and singing the last time they’d partied here. All the same girls had been there before, along with a Jewish band playing fiddles and zithers. Finally, the cart had come with wine and food.

Mitya bustled around, greeting people as more and more neighbors—peasants and their wives—came to see the fun, hoping for another amazing party like the one a month ago. Mitya recognized many of them, hugging everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured wine for everyone who wanted some. The girls especially wanted champagne, while the men liked rum, brandy, and especially hot punch. Mitya ordered chocolate for the girls and had three samovars going all night so there would always be tea and punch for anyone who wanted some.

The whole thing quickly became a wild mess, but Mitya loved it—even the crazier it got, the happier he seemed. If the peasants had asked for money right then, he probably would have handed out all he had. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hanging around Mitya, trying to protect him. Trifon gave up on going to bed that night, but didn’t drink much—just one glass of punch—and kept an eye on Mitya’s spending. He politely but firmly stopped Mitya from giving away cigars, wine, and especially money to the peasants, like he had the last time. Trifon was also annoyed that the peasant girls were drinking liqueur and eating sweets.
“They’re a lousy bunch, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Trifon muttered. “I’d give each of them a kick, and they’d think it was an honor—that’s all they’re worth!”

Mitya suddenly remembered Andrey, and ordered some punch to be taken out to him. “I was rude to him earlier,” he said, his voice soft and regretful. Kalganov didn’t want to drink at first and didn’t care for the girls’ singing, but after a couple glasses of champagne, he cheered up a lot, wandering around, laughing, and praising everything. Maximov, completely drunk, stuck right by his side. Grushenka was starting to get tipsy, too. She pointed to Kalganov and said to Mitya:
“What a sweet, charming boy he is!”

Mitya was thrilled and ran over to hug and kiss Kalganov and Maximov. He was full of hope! Grushenka hadn’t said anything clear yet, and seemed to avoid talking about it, but she kept giving him loving and passionate looks. Suddenly, she grabbed his hand and pulled him close. She was sitting in the low chair by the door.
“How did you show up just now, huh? Did you walk right in? I was scared! So you wanted to hand me over to him, did you? Did you really mean it?”
“I didn’t want to ruin your happiness,” Mitya said, blissful but nervous. But she didn’t wait for him to finish.
“Well, go have fun...” she told him again. “Don’t cry, I’ll call you back soon.”
He’d run off, and she’d listen to the singing and watch the dancing, but her eyes always followed him around the room. After a little while, she’d call him back, and he’d run to her again.
“Come, sit with me. Tell me, how did you hear about me coming here yesterday? Who told you first?”
Mitya started telling her everything, but his words came out jumbled and rushed. He kept frowning and stopping mid-sentence.
“Why are you frowning?” she asked.
“It’s nothing... I left a man sick back there. I’d give ten years of my life if only he’d be okay.”

“Don’t worry about him if he’s sick. So you were going to shoot yourself tomorrow? What a silly boy! Why? I like crazy guys like you,” she said, her words a little slurred. “You’d do anything for me, huh? Did you really mean to shoot yourself tomorrow, you fool? No, wait. Tomorrow I might have something to tell you... Not today, but tomorrow. Do you want it to be today? No, not today. Go on, go have fun now.”
Once, though, she called him back, looking confused and worried.

“Why are you sad? I can tell you’re sad... yeah, I see it,” she said, staring into his eyes. “Even though you’re hugging the peasants and shouting, I can tell. But don’t be sad. I’m happy—so you be happy too... I love someone here—guess who it is. Oh look, my boy’s fallen asleep; poor thing, he’s drunk.”

She was talking about Kalganov. He really was drunk, asleep on the sofa. But it wasn’t just the alcohol—he was suddenly down, or as he said, “bored.” The girls’ songs, which were getting cruder as everyone drank more, made him feel even worse. The dancing was just as bad. Two girls dressed up as bears, and a lively girl named Stepanida played their keeper, waving a stick around and pretending to train them.
“Move it, Marya, or you’ll get the stick!”
The “bears” ended up rolling around on the floor in a really embarrassing way, making everyone burst out laughing.
“Let them be! Let them have fun,” said Grushenka, her face glowing with excitement. “When people finally get a chance to have fun, why shouldn’t they enjoy themselves?”
Kalganov looked like he’d just rolled in the mud.
“This is just gross, all this peasant nonsense,” he muttered as he walked away. “It’s the kind of thing they do in the summer when it stays light all night.”
He especially hated one new song the girls sang, with a bouncy dance tune. It was about a gentleman trying to win the girls’ love:
But the girls didn’t love the gentleman:
Then a gypsy tried his luck:
But they didn’t love the gypsy either:
Lots of other men tried too, including a soldier:
But the soldier got rejected in two rude lines, sung so openly that the crowd went wild. The song ended with a merchant:
And it turned out the girls loved him because:
Kalganov was actually angry.
“That’s just a new song from yesterday,” he said out loud. “Who writes this stuff for them? They might as well have had a railway worker or a Jew try his luck—they would have been the favorites!”
Almost as if he’d been personally insulted, he announced that he was bored, sat on the sofa, and fell asleep right away. His cute little face looked pale as it sank onto the cushion.
“Look how cute he is,” said Grushenka, bringing Mitya over. “I was just combing his hair—it’s so soft and thick...”
She bent down and kissed his forehead. Kalganov opened his eyes at once, stood up, and asked anxiously where Maximov was.
“So that’s who you want,” Grushenka laughed. “Stay with me a moment. Mitya, go find his Maximov.”

Maximov was having too much fun with the girls to leave, only running away now and then to grab another glass of liqueur. He’d had two cups of chocolate, his face was red, his nose was bright, and his eyes were watery and goofy. He ran up, saying he was going to dance the “sabotière.”
“I learned all those fancy dances when I was a kid...”
“Go with him, Mitya. I’ll watch from here and see how he dances,” said Grushenka.

“No, no, I’m coming to watch too,” said Kalganov, ignoring Grushenka’s offer to stay with him. They all went to watch. Maximov did his dance, but no one liked it except Mitya. It was just hopping and kicking, and every time he hopped, Maximov slapped the bottom of his foot. Kalganov wasn’t impressed, but Mitya gave Maximov a kiss.
“Thanks. Are you tired? What do you want? Want some sweets? Or a cigar?”
“A cigarette.”
“Want a drink?”
“I’ll take a liqueur... Got any chocolates?”
“Yeah, there’s a bunch on the table. Pick one, my friend!”
“I like the ones with vanilla... for old men. He he!”
“Nope, we don’t have any of your special kind.”
Maximov leaned in to whisper to Mitya, “That girl, little Marya—he he! Maybe you could help me get to know her?”
“So that’s what you’re up to! No, that won’t work, brother.”
“I wouldn’t hurt anyone,” Maximov said sadly.
“Oh, fine, fine. They’re just here to sing and dance, you know. But hold on... Eat, drink, and have fun for now. Want some money?”
“Maybe later,” Maximov grinned.
“Alright, alright...”

Mitya’s head was on fire. He went out onto the wooden balcony that ran around the building, looking down into the courtyard. The cool air cleared his mind a little. Standing alone in the shadows, he grabbed his head with both hands. Suddenly, his scattered thoughts snapped into focus, all his feelings coming together in one terrible moment. “If I’m going to kill myself, why not now?” he thought. “Why not grab the pistols, bring them here, and end it in this dark, messy corner?” He stood there, frozen. Just a few hours earlier, when he’d rushed here, he’d been running from disgrace, from the theft he’d committed, and from the blood—oh, the blood! But it had felt easier then, because he’d lost her for good. She was gone, so his death felt necessary, even right. What did he have left to live for?

But now? Was it the same? One nightmare, at least, was over—the first, rightful lover, that haunting figure, was gone for good, locked away and never coming back. Grushenka was ashamed, and he could see in her eyes who she really loved. Now he had everything he needed to be happy... but he still couldn’t imagine going on. “Oh God! Bring back the man I hit at the fence! Let me be spared this horror! Lord, you’ve done miracles for worse sinners than me! But what if the old man is still alive? If he is, I’ll wipe away my shame, return the stolen money, and make it right—nothing left but the guilt in my heart forever. But no, no, that’s just wishful thinking! Oh, damn it!”

Still, there was a tiny bit of hope in all the darkness. He jumped up and ran back to the room—to Grushenka, his queen forever! Wasn’t one moment of her love worth all the rest of his life, even in disgrace? The thought burned in his chest. “To her, only her, for one night, for one hour, for even a moment!” As he turned from the balcony, he bumped into Trifon Borissovitch, the landlord, who looked worried and stressed.
“What is it, Trifon Borissovitch? Are you looking for me?”
“No, sir,” the landlord said, looking uncomfortable. “Why would I be looking for you? Where have you been?”
“Why do you look so serious? You’re not mad at me, are you? Don’t worry, you’ll get to bed soon. What time is it?”
“It’s nearly three o’clock. Past three, actually.”
“We’ll stop soon, I promise.”
“Don’t worry about it; keep having fun as long as you want...”

“What’s up with him?” Mitya wondered for a second, then hurried back to the party room. But Grushenka wasn’t there. She wasn’t in the blue room either—only Kalganov was there, asleep on the sofa. Mitya peeked behind the curtains and saw Grushenka in the corner, sitting on a trunk, her head and arms on the bed, crying hard and trying not to make a sound. When she saw Mitya, she waved him over and grabbed his hand tightly.

“Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. I really did—these last five years! Did I love him or just my own anger? No, it was him! It’s a lie that it was just anger. Mitya, I was only seventeen then. He was so nice to me, so cheerful—he’d sing to me... or at least that’s how it seemed to a silly girl like me. But now, oh God, he’s changed. Even his face is different—I wouldn’t have recognized him. I rode here with Timofey, thinking about what I’d say, how we’d look at each other. My heart was pounding, and then it was like he dumped a bucket of dirty water on me. He talked to me like a teacher, so stiff and serious. I couldn’t say a word. At first I thought he was just embarrassed in front of his fancy friend. I just stared at him, wondering why I couldn’t talk. Maybe his wife changed him—he dumped me to marry her. Oh, it’s so shameful! Mitya, I’m ashamed—ashamed for my whole life. Curse it, curse those five years!”
She started crying again, but still clung to Mitya’s hand.
“Mitya, please, stay. Don’t go. I want to ask you something,” she whispered, lifting her tear-streaked face. “Tell me, who is it I love? I love one man here. Who is he? You have to tell me.”
A smile broke through her tear-swollen face, and her eyes sparkled in the half-dark.

“A falcon flew in, and my heart dropped—‘Fool, that’s the man you love!’ That’s what my heart said right away. You came in, and everything lit up. I wondered what you were scared of—because you were scared, you couldn’t speak. You weren’t scared of them; you’re not afraid of anyone. It was me you were scared of. Fenya told you, you silly, how I told Alyosha out the window that I’d loved Mitya for one hour and was going to love someone else now. Mitya, how could I ever think I could love anyone after you? Do you forgive me, Mitya? Do you? Do you love me?” She jumped up, grabbing his shoulders. Mitya, in total joy, stared into her eyes, her face, her smile—and then wrapped her up in his arms and kissed her.

“Will you forgive me for teasing you? I did it out of spite. I made everyone miserable on purpose—even made the old man crazy... Remember how you broke the wine glass at my house? I remembered that and did the same today, drinking to my ‘rotten heart.’ Mitya, my falcon, why don’t you kiss me? You kissed me once, and now you just watch and listen. Why listen? Kiss me, kiss me like you mean it! If you love me, then love me! I’ll be your slave now, your slave for life. It feels good to be a slave. Kiss me! Hit me, treat me however you want... I deserve it. But wait, not now...” She suddenly pushed him away. “Go, Mitya. I’ll come have some wine—I want to get drunk and dance. I have to, I have to!” She ran off behind the curtain. Mitya followed, still feeling stunned.

“Whatever happens now, even just one minute with her is worth the whole world,” he thought. Grushenka really did gulp down a glass of champagne in one go and got instantly drunk. She sat back in her chair, smiling blissfully. Her cheeks were red, her lips hot, her eyes shining with passion. Even Kalganov felt something in his heart and went over to her.
“Did you feel me kiss you when you were asleep?” she slurred. “I’m drunk now, that’s why... Aren’t you drunk? And why isn’t Mitya drinking? Why not, Mitya? I’m drunk, and you’re not...”
“I am drunk! I’m drunk on you... and now I’ll be drunk on wine too.”

He drank another glass, and—much to his surprise—that was it. He was completely drunk. Suddenly, everything spun around him, like he was dreaming. He walked, laughed, talked to everyone, but didn’t know what he was doing. Only one burning feeling stayed—the “red-hot coal in his heart,” as he later called it. He went to Grushenka, sat by her, watched her, listened to her. She became very talkative, calling people over, waving at the different girls. When a girl came up, she’d either kiss her or make the sign of the cross over her. She was close to tears. She found Maximov, the “little old man,” hilarious. He kept running up to kiss her hands, each finger, and finally danced again, singing an old song. He put extra energy into dancing to the chorus.

“Give him something, Mitya,” Grushenka said. “Give him a present—he’s poor, you know. Oh, the poor people! Mitya, I’m going to join a convent. No, really, Alyosha said something today that I’ll remember forever. But today, let’s dance. Tomorrow, the convent—today, we dance! I want to have fun, and why not? God will forgive us. If I were God, I’d forgive everyone: ‘Dear sinners, you’re all forgiven from now on.’ I’m going to ask forgiveness: ‘Forgive me, everyone, I’m just a silly girl.’ I’m a beast, but I want to pray. I gave a little onion. I want to pray, even if I’ve been bad. Mitya, let them dance, don’t stop them. The whole world is good—everyone, even the worst. The world is a good place, even if we’re bad sometimes. We’re good and bad, good and bad. Come, tell me, I’ve got a question: Why am I so good? You know I am. I’m very good... So why am I so good?”

Grushenka kept rambling on, getting more and more drunk. At last, she said she was going to dance too. She got up, wobbling. “Mitya, don’t give me any more wine—even if I ask. Wine doesn’t bring peace. Everything’s spinning—the stove, the room, everything. I want to dance. Let everyone see how I dance...”

She meant it. She took a white handkerchief from her pocket, holding one corner in her right hand, ready for the dance. Mitya ran around, getting everyone ready. The girls got quiet, waiting for the signal to start singing. Maximov, hearing Grushenka wanted to dance, squealed with delight and skipped around in front of her, humming.
But Grushenka waved her handkerchief at him and shooed him away.
“Shh! Mitya, why don’t they come? Everyone should watch. Call in the ones who were locked in, too. Why did you lock them up? Tell them I’m going to dance. Let them see too.”
Mitya swaggered up to the locked door and started banging on it for the Poles.
“Hey, you—Podvysotskys! Come on, she’s going to dance. She’s calling you.”
“Lajdak!” one of the Poles shouted back.
“You’re a lajdak yourself! You’re a little scoundrel, that’s what you are.”
“Stop making fun of Poland,” said Kalganov seriously. He was drunk too.
“Calm down, boy! If I call him a scoundrel, that doesn’t mean I mean all of Poland. One jerk doesn’t represent a country. Relax, pretty boy—have some candy.”

“Oh, what guys! Aren’t they men too? Why won’t they make friends?” said Grushenka, then moved forward to dance. The girls started singing “Ah, my porch, my new porch!” Grushenka threw her head back, half-opened her lips, smiled, waved her handkerchief, but suddenly staggered and stopped in the middle of the room, looking confused.
“I’m weak...” she said in a tired voice. “Sorry... I’m too weak, I can’t... I’m sorry.”
She bowed to the singers, then bowed to everyone else.
“I’m sorry... Forgive me...”
“She’s been drinking. The pretty lady’s been drinking,” people whispered.
“She’s had too much,” Maximov told the girls, giggling.
“Mitya, take me away... help me,” said Grushenka weakly. Mitya ran to her, scooped her up, and carried her through the curtains.

“Well, I’ll go now,” thought Kalganov, and left the blue room, closing the doors behind him. But the party in the big room kept going, louder than ever. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her.
“Don’t touch me,” she begged. “Don’t touch me until I’m really yours... I told you I’m yours, but not yet. Please, not with them here, not while they’re close by. He’s here. It’s awful here...”
“I’ll do as you say! I won’t even think about it. I adore you!” Mitya whispered. “Yes, it’s horrible here, just awful.”
Still holding her, he knelt down by the bed.

“I know you’re a wild man, but you’re generous,” Grushenka said with difficulty. “It has to be honorable... it will be from now on. Let’s be honest, let’s be good—not animals, but good. Take me away, far away, do you hear? Not here, but far, far away...”
“Yes, yes, that’s how it has to be!” said Mitya, hugging her. “I’ll take you away, we’ll escape... Oh, I’d give my whole life just to know about that blood!”
“What blood?” Grushenka asked, confused.
“Nothing,” Mitya muttered. “Grusha, you want to be honest, but I’m a thief. I stole money from Katya... Such shame!”

“From Katya, that young lady? No, you didn’t steal. Give it back to her, take it from me... Why make a fuss? Now everything I have is yours. Money doesn’t matter—we’ll just waste it anyway. But let’s go work the land. I want to dig with my own hands. We have to work, you hear? Alyosha said so. I won’t be your mistress—I’ll be faithful, I’ll be your slave, I’ll work for you. We’ll go see the young lady and beg her to forgive us, then we’ll leave. And if she won’t forgive us, we’ll leave anyway. Take her money and love me... Don’t love her... If you do, I’ll strangle her... I’ll poke out both her eyes with a needle...”
“I love you. Only you. I’ll love you in Siberia...”

“Why Siberia? Okay, Siberia, if you want. I don’t care... we’ll work. There’s snow in Siberia... I love driving in the snow... and we’ll need bells... Do you hear a bell? Where’s that bell? People are coming... Now it’s stopped.”

She closed her eyes, worn out, and dozed off for a second. There really had been a bell ringing, but now it was silent. Mitya let his head rest on her chest. He didn’t notice the bell had stopped, or that the songs and shouts had faded to total silence. Grushenka opened her eyes.

“What’s wrong? Was I asleep? Yes... a bell... I dreamed I was riding through the snow with bells, and I dozed off. I was with someone I loved—with you. I was holding you, kissing you, snuggling close. I was cold, and the snow sparkled... You know how snow shines at night in the moonlight? It felt like I wasn’t on earth. I woke up, and my dear one is here. How sweet...”

“I’m right here,” Mitya whispered, kissing her dress, her chest, her hands. Suddenly, something strange struck him: Grushenka was staring straight ahead, not at him, but over his head, with a strange, almost scared look on her face.
“Mitya, who’s that watching us?” she whispered.
Mitya turned and saw that someone had pulled back the curtains and was watching. It wasn’t just one person, either.
He jumped up and walked quickly toward the intruders.
“Come here, come over here,” said a voice—calm but commanding.

Mitya stepped through the curtain and froze. The room was packed with people—but not the same ones from before. He shivered. He recognized them all at once. The tall, chubby old man in an overcoat and cap was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. The thin, stylish man with shiny shoes was the deputy prosecutor—Mitya remembered he had a fancy watch. The young man with glasses—Mitya couldn’t remember his name but knew he was the investigating lawyer, just recently arrived. There was also the police inspector, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who Mitya knew well. There were guys with brass badges, and two peasants. At the door stood Kalganov and Trifon Borissovitch...
“Gentlemen! What’s going on, gentlemen?” Mitya started, but suddenly, almost without realizing it, he shouted at the top of his lungs:
“I un—der—stand!”
The young man with glasses stepped forward, speaking formally but quickly:
“We need you to... In short, please come this way, over to the sofa. You need to give us an explanation right now.”
“The old man!” Mitya yelled in panic. “The old man and his blood!... I understand!”
He almost collapsed onto a chair, as if he’d been cut down.
“You understand? He understands! Monster! Parricide! Your father’s blood cries out against you!” the old police captain suddenly roared at Mitya.
He was shaking, red-faced, completely out of control.
“This is impossible!” the young lawyer cried. “Mihail Makarovitch, you can’t! Please let me speak. I never expected this from you...”
“This is madness, gentlemen, absolute madness!” shouted the captain of police. “Look at him: drunk at this hour, with a loose woman, his father’s blood on his hands... It’s madness!”
“Please, Mihail Makarovitch, control yourself,” the prosecutor whispered quickly to the police captain. “Or I’ll have to—”
But the young lawyer interrupted, turning to Mitya and speaking in a loud, steady, official voice:
“Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, it’s my duty to inform you that you are accused of murdering your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, tonight...”
He said more, and the prosecutor added something too, but even though Mitya heard them, he couldn’t understand. He just stared at them all, wild-eyed.

Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who we last saw banging on the locked gates of the widow Morozov’s house, eventually made enough noise that someone heard him. Fenya, still shaken from her scare two hours earlier and too worked up to sleep, almost had a panic attack when she heard the angry knocking. Even though she’d watched Pyotr Ilyitch leave earlier, she was sure it must be Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya)—no one else would knock so furiously. She ran to the house-porter, who was already awake and heading for the gate, begging him not to open it. But after talking to Pyotr Ilyitch and finding out he needed to see Fenya on “important business,” the porter finally let him in. In the kitchen, Fenya insisted the porter stay with her because she was so nervous. Pyotr Ilyitch started questioning Fenya and quickly learned something crucial: when Dmitri had run out to look for Grushenka, he’d grabbed a heavy pestle from the mortar, and when he came back, he didn’t have it—and his hands were stained with blood.

“The blood was just pouring off him, it was dripping!” Fenya kept saying, though this was mostly her scared imagination exaggerating things. Still, Pyotr Ilyitch himself had seen Dmitri’s hands covered in blood and had even helped wash them. The big question Pyotr Ilyitch needed to answer wasn’t how wet the blood was, but where Dmitri had gone with the pestle—or more specifically, had he gone to his father Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, and how could he be sure? Pyotr Ilyitch kept coming back to this question. Even though he didn’t get a clear answer, he left with the strong feeling that Dmitri must have gone to his father’s, which meant something bad probably happened there.

“And when he came back,” Fenya continued, getting more and more upset, “I told him everything, then I asked, ‘Why do you have blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?’ and he said it was human blood, that he’d just killed someone. He confessed it all to me, then suddenly ran off like a crazy person. I sat there thinking, Where’s he going now, all wild like that? He’ll go to Mokroe and kill my mistress! I rushed out to stop him from hurting her. I was running to his place, but glanced at Plotnikov’s shop and saw him leaving—there was no blood on his hands then.” (Fenya remembered this detail clearly.) Fenya’s old grandmother backed up her story as best as she could. After a few more questions, Pyotr Ilyitch left the house, feeling even more worried than before.

The simplest thing for Pyotr Ilyitch to do would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house to see if anything had happened, and only go to the police captain after he knew for sure. But it was a dark night, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s gates were strong, and he’d have to knock loudly again. Pyotr Ilyitch barely knew Fyodor Pavlovitch, and if he woke him up for nothing, Fyodor Pavlovitch would probably laugh about it all over town—telling everyone that some stranger, Perhotin, barged in at midnight to check if he’d been murdered. That would be embarrassing, and Pyotr Ilyitch hated scandals more than anything.

Still, the feeling that something was wrong was so strong that, even though he cursed himself for it, Pyotr Ilyitch went out again—not to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, but to Madame Hohlakov’s. He decided: if she denied giving Dmitri three thousand roubles, he’d go straight to the police captain; but if she admitted it, he’d just go home and wait until morning.

Of course, it was probably even more awkward to visit a high-class lady he didn’t know, at eleven at night, maybe even waking her up, just to ask a weird question, than to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s. But that’s how it goes sometimes—especially in stressful situations—even the calmest, most logical people make odd choices. Pyotr Ilyitch definitely wasn’t calm now. He would always remember how a strange anxiety took over, growing until it drove him on, no matter how much he scolded himself. Still, as he hurried along, he kept thinking, “I have to get to the bottom of this, I will!” and he stuck to his plan.

It was exactly eleven o’clock when he got to Madame Hohlakov’s house. He was let into the yard right away, but when he asked if the lady was still awake, the porter just shrugged and said she was usually in bed by now.
“Ask up at the top of the stairs. If she wants to see you, she will. If not, she won’t.”

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but things didn’t get any easier. The footman didn’t want to take his name in, but eventually called for a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch politely but firmly asked her to tell her mistress that an official named Perhotin, who lived in town, had come on a very important matter—and that if it weren’t so serious, he wouldn’t have bothered her. “Please, tell her exactly that, in those words,” he insisted.

The maid left, and Pyotr Ilyitch waited in the hallway. Madame Hohlakov was already in her bedroom, not yet asleep but feeling unsettled since Mitya’s visit. She had a feeling she’d get a bad headache, as she always did after such excitement. The news of a strange late-night visitor annoyed her, but she was also very curious about this “official from town.” Still, she said she didn’t want to see him. But Pyotr Ilyitch was stubborn. He begged the maid to go back with another message, this time asking her to use these exact words:
“He says he’s come on extremely important business, and that Madame Hohlakov might regret it later if she doesn’t see him now.”
“I just jumped in headfirst,” he later said about it.

The maid, now totally puzzled, went to deliver the message again. This time Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought for a minute, asked what the visitor looked like, and learned he was “well dressed, young, and very polite.” (It’s worth noting that Pyotr Ilyitch was a good-looking young man, and he knew it.) Madame Hohlakov decided to see him. She was in her dressing gown and slippers, but threw a black shawl around her shoulders. “The official” was shown into the drawing-room—the very room where Mitya had been earlier. Madame Hohlakov came in with a serious, questioning look and, without inviting him to sit, immediately asked:
“What do you want?”
“I’m sorry to bother you, madam, but it’s about our mutual acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov,” Perhotin began.
But he barely got the name out before Madame Hohlakov’s face twisted in anger. She practically screamed, cutting him off:

“How much longer do I have to deal with that horrible man?” she shouted. “How dare you, sir? How could you force your way into a stranger’s house at this hour—to talk about a man who came to this very room just three hours ago, tried to murder me, and stomped out like no decent person ever would? I’ll report you! I won’t let this go. Please leave immediately. I’m a mother, I—I—”
“Murder! So he tried to kill you too?”
“Why, has he killed someone else?” Madame Hohlakov asked, suddenly worried.

“If you’d just listen for a moment, madam, I’ll explain everything in a couple of words,” said Perhotin firmly. “At five o’clock today, Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know he had no money. But at nine o’clock, he came to see me with a huge bundle of hundred-rouble notes—about two or three thousand roubles. His hands and face were covered with blood, and he looked like a madman. When I asked where he got the money, he said you gave him three thousand roubles to go to the gold-mines.”
Madame Hohlakov’s face became deeply troubled and excited.
“Oh my God! He must have killed his old father!” she cried, wringing her hands. “I never gave him any money, never! Please, go—don’t say another word! Save the old man—hurry to his father—go now!”
“Excuse me, madam, so you definitely didn’t give him any money? You’re sure you didn’t?”

“No, I didn’t, I didn’t! I refused because he wouldn’t use it well. He stormed out in a rage, almost attacked me, but I dodged him. And to be honest, since I want to tell you everything now, he actually spat at me! Can you believe it? But why are we standing? Oh, sit down!”
“Excuse me, I—”
“Or better yet, go, go, you have to go save the poor old man from being murdered!”
“But what if he’s already killed him?”
“Oh dear, yes! Then what do we do? What do you think we should do?”

By now she had made Pyotr Ilyitch sit down, and she sat facing him. Pyotr Ilyitch quickly but clearly told her what had happened—at least the part he’d seen himself. He described his visit to Fenya and told her about the missing pestle. These details had a huge effect on Madame Hohlakov, who kept shrieking and hiding her face in her hands.

“Would you believe it, I saw this coming! I have a special gift—whatever I imagine seems to happen. And I’ve always thought, looking at that horrible man, he’ll end up killing me. And now it’s happened—well, if he didn’t kill me but killed his own father instead, it must be God’s will that saved me. Maybe he was ashamed to murder me because, right here, I put the holy icon from Saint Varvara’s relics around his neck. I was so close to death then—I went right up to him, and he let me put it on! You know, Pyotr Ilyitch (that is your name, right?), I don’t really believe in miracles, but this icon, and now this real miracle—it convinces me! Have you heard of Father Zossima? But I’m rambling...and to think, even with the icon on his neck, he spat at me. He only spat, didn’t kill me, and ran away! But what should we do now? What do you think?”
Pyotr Ilyitch stood up and said he was going straight to the police captain to report everything and let him handle it.
“Oh, he’s wonderful, just wonderful! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he’s the right person. How sensible you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! I would never have thought of that in your place!”
“Especially since I know the police captain very well too,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, still standing and clearly eager to escape from the emotional lady, who wouldn’t let him say goodbye and leave.

“And be sure, be sure,” she chattered on, “to come back and tell me what you find out—what happens—how they’ll put him on trial—and what he’s sentenced to... Tell me, we don’t have the death penalty, do we? Still, come back, even if it’s three in the morning, four, half past four—tell them to wake me, shake me if I don’t get up. But really, I won’t sleep! Wait, maybe I should come with you?”
“N-no. But if you could write a quick note saying, in your own handwriting, that you didn’t give Dmitri Fyodorovitch any money, that might help—just in case.”
“Of course!” Madame Hohlakov jumped up, delighted, and went to her desk. “You know, I’m so impressed—your quick thinking, your good sense! Are you working here in town? I’m glad you’re working here!”
Still talking, she scribbled the following on half a sheet of notepaper:

I have never, ever lent that poor man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, after all, he is unfortunate), three thousand roubles today. I have never given him money, never! I swear by all that’s holy!
K. Hohlakov.
“Here’s the note!” she said quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. “Go save him. You’re doing something good!”
She made the sign of the cross three times over him and hurried out to walk him to the hallway.

“I’m so grateful to you! You can’t imagine how thankful I am that you came to me first. How have I never met you before? Please, visit me in the future. How wonderful that you’re living here—so precise, so sensible! They must appreciate you, they must! If there’s anything I can do, just ask... Oh, I love young people! The younger generation is the hope of our country... now go, go!”

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already rushed out, or she never would have let him leave so quickly. Still, Madame Hohlakov had actually made a rather good impression on him and that softened his worries about being dragged into such a mess. People have different tastes, after all. “She’s not so old at all,” he thought, pleased. “I’d have taken her for her daughter.”

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was completely charmed by the young man. “Such sense! Such precision! And so young! People say young people today are useless, but here’s proof they’re wrong!” So she forgot all about the “terrible business,” and only as she was getting into bed did she suddenly remember “how close she’d been to death,” and cry out, “Oh, it’s awful, just awful!”
But she immediately fell into a deep, peaceful sleep.

I wouldn’t have gone into all these small details, except that this strange meeting between the young official and the not-so-old widow actually ended up being the beginning of Pyotr Ilyitch’s whole career. To this day, people in our town remember his story with amazement, and I might talk more about it when I finish telling the full story of the Brothers Karamazov.

Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, used to be a lieutenant-colonel before he retired. He was a widower and a really good man. He’d only moved to our town three years ago, but everyone respected him, mostly because he was so good at bringing people together. He always had guests over—he couldn’t stand eating alone. He threw dinners for all sorts of reasons, even for the smallest things. The food wasn’t fancy, but there was always plenty, and his fish pies were especially good. As for the wine, he made up for its cheapness by making sure there was lots of it.

When guests arrived, the first room they entered was a nice billiards room, with black-framed pictures of English racehorses on the walls (because every bachelor’s billiards room had to have those). There was card-playing at his house every night, even if it was just one table. But every now and then, the whole town—mothers, daughters, and young men—would show up at his place for a dance. Even though Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, he wasn’t alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, along with her two grown daughters, who had finished school. They were pretty and lively, and even though everyone knew they wouldn’t get a dowry, all the fashionable young men still wanted to visit their grandfather’s house.

Mihail Makarovitch wasn’t exactly a top-notch worker, but he did his job as well as most. To be honest, he wasn’t very well-educated. He didn’t always understand how far his authority went, and sometimes made big mistakes interpreting new laws and reforms. It wasn’t that he was dumb—he just didn’t pay enough attention and rushed through things.

“I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian,” he used to joke about himself. He didn’t really understand the big changes that came with freeing the serfs, and just picked things up as he went along, learning from experience. Even though he owned land himself, he was still figuring things out. Pyotr Ilyitch knew he’d probably meet some of Mihail Makarovitch’s guests there that evening, but wasn’t sure exactly who would be there. As it turned out, the prosecutor and Varvinsky—the district doctor, a young guy who had just moved to town after getting his medical degree in Petersburg—were playing cards at the police captain’s house. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor (technically the deputy prosecutor, but everyone just called him “the prosecutor”), was a strange man, about thirty-five, who looked a bit sickly and was married to a large, childless woman. He was smart and kind, but also vain and easily annoyed. The problem was, he thought a little too highly of himself, which made him seem uneasy all the time. He liked to think of himself as a deep thinker and was especially interested in psychology, especially when it came to criminals. He felt like he’d been overlooked at work and that people didn’t appreciate him, and sometimes, when he was in a bad mood, he’d threaten to quit and become a criminal lawyer instead. The sudden Karamazov case really shook him up: “Everyone in Russia will be talking about this!” But I’m getting ahead of myself.

Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the young investigating lawyer who had only arrived from Petersburg two months ago, was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. Later, people would talk about how strange it was that all these important men had gathered at the police captain’s house on the night of “the crime.” But really, it just happened naturally, without anyone planning it.

Ippolit Kirillovitch’s wife had been moaning with toothache for two days, so he left home to get away from her groaning. The doctor couldn’t imagine spending an evening anywhere but at the card table. Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov had been planning for three days to drop by the police captain’s house that evening, hoping to surprise the oldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, by showing that he knew her secret—it was her birthday, and she was trying to hide it to avoid having to throw a dance. He looked forward to teasing her about her age and how she was keeping it a secret, and maybe even telling everyone. The ladies called him “the naughty man” because he was so good at these kinds of jokes, and he seemed to love the nickname. Even so, he was polite, from a good family, and although he liked to have fun, he never crossed the line. He was short and delicate-looking, and always wore a bunch of big, shiny rings on his slender, pale fingers. When doing his job, though, he became very serious, as if he knew how important it was. He was especially good at questioning peasant criminals—he might not make them respect him, but he always left them amazed.

Pyotr Ilyitch was shocked when he walked into the police captain’s house. He could tell right away that everyone already knew. They had all stopped playing cards and were standing up, talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and hurried in, looking serious and ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch was greeted with the jaw-dropping news that old Fyodor Pavlovitch had really been murdered that evening in his own house—killed and robbed. The news had just reached them in the following way.

Marfa Ignatyevna, Grigory’s wife, had been sleeping deeply after taking some medicine, since she’d been knocked out near the fence earlier. But suddenly, she woke up—probably because of a terrifying scream from Smerdyakov, who was in the next room, unconscious. He always screamed like that before his epileptic fits, and it always scared Marfa. She never got used to it. She jumped up, half-asleep, and ran to Smerdyakov’s room, but it was dark and she could only hear him gasping and struggling. Marfa screamed, too, and was about to call for her husband, but then realized he wasn’t in bed beside her. She went back to the bed, feeling around, but it was really empty. He must have gone out—but where? She hurried to the steps and called for him, but got no answer. Instead, she heard groaning far off in the garden, in the dark. She listened more closely. The groans came again, definitely from the garden.
“Dear God! Just like what happened with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” she thought, panicked. She nervously went down the steps and saw that the gate to the garden was open.
“He must be out there, poor thing,” she thought. She went to the gate and suddenly heard Grigory calling her name—“Marfa! Marfa!”—in a weak, painful, awful voice.

“God, protect us from evil!” Marfa whispered, and ran toward the sound of his voice. That’s how she found Grigory—not by the fence where he was knocked down, but about twenty paces away. Later, people learned that he had crawled there after waking up, probably taking a long time and passing out several times. She saw right away that he was covered in blood and screamed as loud as she could. Grigory was muttering, not making much sense:
“He killed...murdered his father...Why are you screaming, fool?...Run...get someone...”

But Marfa kept screaming, and when she saw her master’s window open with a candle burning, she ran over and called Fyodor Pavlovitch. But when she peeked through the window, she saw a horrifying sight. Her master was lying flat on his back, not moving, on the floor. His light-colored robe and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table made the blood and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s dead face look even more terrifying. Terrified, Marfa dashed away from the window, ran out of the garden, unlocked the big gate, and ran as fast as she could to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Both Marya and her daughter were sleeping, but woke up when Marfa started screaming and banging on the shutters. Somehow, through her shrieks, Marfa managed to explain what had happened and begged for help. It turned out that Foma, who had come back from his travels, was spending the night there. They woke him up right away and all three rushed to the crime scene. On the way, Marya remembered hearing a terrible scream from their garden around eight o’clock—probably Grigory’s shout of “Parricide!” when he grabbed Mitya’s leg.

“Someone screamed and then it was quiet,” Marya Kondratyevna explained as they ran. When they got to where Grigory was lying, the two women and Foma carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was still having a seizure: he was twisting around, his eyes squinting, and foam coming out of his mouth. They put water mixed with vinegar on Grigory’s forehead, and it revived him right away. The first thing he asked was:
“Is the master dead?”

Then Foma and the women ran to the house and saw that not only the window, but also the door to the garden was wide open—even though for the past week, Fyodor Pavlovitch had locked himself in every night and wouldn’t let even Grigory in for anything.
