Seeing the door open, they were too scared to go inside, afraid something might happen. When they got back to Grigory, he told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and told everyone at the police captain’s house what had happened. She arrived just five minutes before Pyotr Ilyitch, so his story matched exactly with hers, proving the theory about who the criminal was—a theory he hadn’t wanted to believe until then.

They decided to act quickly. The town’s deputy police inspector was told to take four witnesses and go into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house to start an official investigation, following all the usual rules (which I won't go into here). The district doctor was eager to help, so he joined the police captain, the prosecutor, and the investigating lawyer.

To put it simply, Fyodor Pavlovitch was found dead, his skull smashed in. But with what? Most likely the same thing that was used to hit Grigory. They found the weapon right away—Grigory, who was getting medical help, described in a weak, shaky voice how he’d been attacked. They searched by the fence with a lantern and found the brass pestle lying in plain sight on the garden path. The room where Fyodor Pavlovitch was found wasn’t messy or disturbed. But by the bed, behind a screen, they found a big thick envelope on the floor. It said: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” Below, Fyodor Pavlovitch had added: “For my little chicken.” There were three red wax seals on the envelope, but it had been ripped open and was empty—the money was gone. They also found a piece of narrow pink ribbon that had been tied around the envelope.

One detail Pyotr Ilyitch shared really shook the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer: his idea that Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya) would shoot himself before morning. Mitya had told Ilyitch he was going to do it, had taken his pistols, loaded them in front of him, written a letter and put it in his pocket, and so on. When Pyotr Ilyitch, still not wanting to believe it, threatened to tell someone to stop the suicide, Mitya just grinned and said, “You’ll be too late.” So they realized they had to hurry to Mokroe to catch the criminal before he killed himself.
“That makes sense, that makes sense!” the prosecutor said, very excited. “That’s just how crazy guys like that act: ‘I’ll kill myself tomorrow, so tonight I’ll party like there’s no tomorrow!’ ”
The story of how Mitya bought wine and food made the prosecutor even more suspicious.

“Remember that guy who killed the merchant Olsufyev, gentlemen? He stole fifteen hundred, went straight to get his hair done, and then, without even hiding the money, carried it almost out in the open and went off to the girls.”

Still, they were all delayed by the investigation, the search, and all the official paperwork at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. It all took time, so two hours before they were ready, they sent the rural police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov (who had come to town the day before for his pay), ahead to Mokroe. He was told not to raise any alarm when he got there, but to keep a close eye on the “criminal” until the rest arrived, and to get witnesses and police officers ready for the arrest. Mavriky did exactly as he was told, staying undercover and only letting his old friend, Trifon Borissovitch, know what was going on. He spoke to Trifon just before Mitya met the landlord out on the balcony in the dark, and noticed right away that Trifon seemed different. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew they were being watched. Trifon also took the box with the pistols and hid it somewhere. Only after four o’clock, almost sunrise, did all the officials—the police captain, prosecutor, and investigating lawyer—arrive in two carriages, each pulled by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house to do an autopsy on the body the next day, but he was especially interested in Smerdyakov’s condition.

“Such strong, non-stop epileptic fits, going on for twenty-four hours, are really rare and interesting for science,” he told his friends with excitement. As they left, they jokingly congratulated him on his “find.” The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer both remembered the doctor saying that Smerdyakov would not survive the night.
Now that I’ve explained all that (which I think was necessary), let’s go back to the moment in our story where we left off.
Mitya sat there, looking wildly at everyone around him, not understanding what they were saying. Suddenly, he jumped up, threw his hands in the air, and shouted:
"I'm not guilty! I didn't spill that blood! I didn't kill my father... I wanted to kill him, yes. But I didn't do it. Not me."
But before he could say more, Grushenka rushed out from behind the curtain and threw herself at the police captain's feet.

"It's my fault! All mine! I'm wicked!" she cried, sobbing hard, reaching her clasped hands out to them. "He did it because of me. I tortured him, I drove him to it. I made that poor old man suffer too, and that's why all this happened! It's my fault, all mine!"

"Yes, it's your fault! You're the real criminal! You devil! You harlot! It's mostly your fault!" yelled the police captain, shaking his fist at her. But the prosecutor quickly stopped him, grabbing his arm.
"This isn't how things should be done, Mihail Makarovitch!" he cried. "You're messing up the investigation... You're ruining the case..." He sounded like he could barely breathe.
"We have to do things the right way! The right way!" shouted Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking scared too. "Otherwise, we can't continue!"
"Judge us together!" Grushenka screamed, still kneeling. "Punish us both. I'll go with him, even if it's to my death!"

"Grusha, my love, my heart, my angel!" Mitya dropped to his knees beside her, hugging her tightly. "Don't believe her," he begged. "She's not guilty of anything, of anyone's blood, of anything at all!"

Later, Mitya remembered being dragged away from Grushenka by a bunch of men, while she was led out. When he came to his senses, he was sitting at the table. Behind and beside him stood men with metal badges. Across from him sat Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, who kept trying to get Mitya to drink some water from a glass on the table.

"It'll help you feel better, it'll calm you. Don't be scared," Parfenovitch said kindly. Mitya remembered later how he suddenly got obsessed with the lawyer's big rings—one had a purple amethyst, the other a sparkling yellow stone. Even during the worst moments of questioning, those rings totally distracted him, and he couldn't stop staring at them. To Mitya's left, where Maximov had sat earlier, now sat the prosecutor. To his right, where Grushenka had been, was a young man with rosy cheeks wearing a shabby hunting jacket, with ink and paper in front of him—this was the secretary the lawyer had brought. The police captain now stood by the window at the far end, next to Kalganov who was sitting there.
"Drink some water," the lawyer said softly for at least the tenth time.
"I've drunk it, gentlemen, I have... but... come on, gentlemen, punish me, decide what happens to me!" Mitya cried, staring with wide, wild eyes at the lawyer.
"So you really claim you're not guilty of killing your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch?" the lawyer asked, still gentle but firm.

"I'm not guilty. I'm guilty for hurting another old man, but not my father. And I feel terrible about it! I killed, yes, I knocked down the old man... But it's so hard to be blamed for another, even worse murder, one I didn't do... It's a horrible accusation, gentlemen, a huge blow. But if I didn't kill my father, then who did? Who could have done it? It's unbelievable, impossible."
"Yes, who could have killed him?" the lawyer began, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glanced at him and spoke to Mitya.
"You don't need to worry about the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He's alive, he's recovering. Even though you hurt him badly—he and you both said that—the doctor thinks he will survive."

"Alive? He's alive?" Mitya cried, throwing up his hands. His face lit up. "Lord, thank you for this miracle! I'm a sinner, and you saved me! That's the answer to my prayers. I've been praying all night." He quickly crossed himself three times, almost out of breath.
"From Grigory, we've gotten important evidence about you, so—" the prosecutor started, but Mitya suddenly jumped to his feet.
"Wait, gentlemen, please, just one minute; let me run to her—"
"You can't, not now!" Nikolay Parfenovitch almost screamed, jumping up too. The men with metal badges grabbed Mitya, but he sat down on his own.

"Gentlemen, that's a shame! I just wanted to see her for a minute—to tell her that the guilt I felt is gone, the blood isn't on my heart anymore, and I'm not a murderer now! Gentlemen, she's my fiancée!" he said, looking around at everyone with shining eyes. "Oh, thank you, gentlemen! In just a minute, you've given me new life, a new heart! That old man used to carry me as a child, you know. He washed me in the tub when I was three and abandoned by everyone—he was like a father to me!"
"So you—" the lawyer began.

"Please, gentlemen, just one more minute," Mitya interrupted, putting his elbows on the table and covering his face with his hands. "Let me think, let me breathe. All this is so overwhelming, so hard. I'm not a drum, gentlemen!"
"Drink some more water," Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.

Mitya lowered his hands and laughed. His eyes were clear and confident. He seemed like a different person, suddenly back to his old self, as if they were all just old friends at a party the day before, when nothing bad had happened. For the record, when Mitya first arrived in town, the police captain had welcomed him warmly, but lately, especially in the last month, Mitya hardly visited, and when they ran into each other, the captain just frowned and nodded politely. Mitya didn't know the prosecutor as well, though sometimes he visited the prosecutor's nervous wife, not sure why, and she always welcomed him and seemed to like him for some reason. Mitya had only met the lawyer twice, both times they talked about women.

"You're a skilled lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch," Mitya said, laughing, "but I can help you out now. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new person, and please don't mind if I talk to you so directly. Honestly, I'm a bit drunk, too. I think we've met before, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my cousin Miüsov's house. Gentlemen, I know I'm not your equal, I know why I'm here. There's a horrible suspicion over me... if Grigory has testified... but let's get down to business. I'm ready, we can finish this right now! Listen, since I know I'm innocent, we can solve this in a minute. Can't we? Right?"
Mitya talked a lot, and fast, sounding nervous but friendly, as if these men were his closest pals.
"So, for now, we'll write down that you completely deny the charge against you," Nikolay Parfenovitch said seriously, then leaned down and whispered to the secretary what to write.

"Write it? You want to write that? Sure, write it. I agree, gentlemen, but... wait, write this too. I'm guilty of acting wild, of hurting an old man. And there's something else I'm guilty of, deep in my heart—but you don't need to write that," he said suddenly to the secretary. "That's my private life, gentlemen, that's just me. But about murdering my father—I'm not guilty. That's just crazy, a wild idea! I'll prove it to you, you'll see... You'll laugh at yourselves for even suspecting me!"

"Calm down, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the lawyer said, trying to keep things steady. "Before we go on, I want to confirm something: you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and argued with him a lot. Just a little while ago, you said you wanted to kill him: 'I didn't kill him,' you said, 'but I wanted to.'"
"Did I say that? Oh, maybe I did, gentlemen! Yes, sadly, I did want to kill him... I wanted to, more than once... sadly, sadly!"
"You wanted to. Can you explain exactly why you hated your father so much?"

"What is there to explain, gentlemen?" Mitya shrugged, looking down. "I've never hidden my feelings. Everyone in town knows—everyone at the tavern knows. Just recently I said so in Father Zossima's cell... And that same night, I beat my father. I almost killed him, and I swore I'd come back and finish the job, with people watching... oh, a thousand witnesses! I've been shouting it for a month, anyone can tell you! The facts are clear, but feelings, gentlemen, feelings are different. See, gentlemen," Mitya frowned, "I don't think you have any right to question me about my feelings. I know it's your job, but that's private. Still... since I've never hidden my feelings, not even in the tavern, I won't keep it secret now. I know there are terrible things against me. I told everyone I'd kill him, and now suddenly he's dead. So of course you'll think it's me! Ha! I get it, gentlemen, I really do. Even I can't believe it—if I didn't do it, then who could have? That's what it comes down to, right? If not me, then who? I want to know, I demand to know!" he burst out. "Where was he killed? How? With what? Tell me," he asked, looking at the lawyers.
"We found him in his study, on his back on the floor, with his head smashed in," said the prosecutor.
"That's terrible!" Mitya shuddered, put his elbows on the table, and hid his face in his hand.
"Let's go on," Nikolay Parfenovitch said. "So, what made you hate your father? I think you told people it was because you were jealous?"
"Well, yes, jealousy. But it wasn't just that."
"Arguments about money?"
"Yes, about money too."
"There was a fight over three thousand roubles, right? You said it was your inheritance?"

"Three thousand! No, more, more," Mitya said, getting worked up. "More than six thousand, maybe more than ten. I told everyone, yelled it at them. But I finally decided to call it three thousand, because I desperately needed that much... So I thought the bundle of notes under his pillow—meant for Grushenka—was really mine. Yes, gentlemen, I thought it was mine, my own money..."
The prosecutor glanced at the lawyer and even managed to wink.
"We'll come back to that," the lawyer said quickly. "Let us just make a note: you considered that money your own?"

"Write it down, of course. I know that makes me look bad, but I'm not afraid of facts, even if they're against me. Listen, gentlemen, you think I'm someone I'm not," he said, suddenly sounding sad. "You're dealing with a man of honor, a man who always wanted to be honorable, even if I've done plenty of bad things. That's what's made my life miserable—I wanted to be an honorable man, like Diogenes with his lantern searching for an honest man, but all my life I've done stupid, disgusting things—well, maybe just me, not everyone else. Sorry, that's a mistake—just me. My head hurts..." He winced. "You see, I couldn't stand the way he looked, always so rude, disrespectful, mocking, crushing everything sacred. He disgusted me. But now that he's dead, I feel different."
"How do you mean?"
"I don't mean I feel differently, just that I wish I hadn't hated him so much."
"You feel sorry?"
"No, not sorry, don't write that. I'm not so great myself, not handsome, so I shouldn't have found him so disgusting. That's what I mean. Write that down if you want."
As he said this, Mitya looked really sad. The more they questioned him, the more depressed he became.

Just then, something else unexpected happened. Even though Grushenka had been taken away, she wasn't far off—just in the next room after the blue room where they were questioning Mitya. It was a small room with one window, right after the big room where the party had been earlier. She was sitting there with no one but Maximov, who was terrified and clung to her for comfort. A peasant with a metal badge stood at the door. Grushenka was crying, and suddenly, her grief overwhelmed her. She jumped up, threw her arms in the air, and with a loud wail, ran out of the room to Mitya—so quickly that nobody could stop her. Mitya heard her cry, trembled, and ran to her, shouting, without knowing what he was doing. But they weren't allowed to meet; people grabbed them both. It took three or four men to hold Mitya back. She was held too, and he saw her reach for him, crying out as they took her away. When it was over, Mitya found himself back in his seat, facing the lawyer, and shouted:
"What do you want with her? Why are you torturing her? She hasn't done anything, nothing!"
The lawyers tried to calm him down. About ten minutes went by like this. Finally, Mihail Makarovitch, who had been gone, came rushing in and spoke loudly to the prosecutor:
"She's taken downstairs. Can I say something to this poor man, gentlemen? Right here, in front of you?"
"Go ahead, Mihail Makarovitch," the lawyer said. "We have no problem with it in this case."

"Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my friend," the police captain began, and his face was warm, almost fatherly toward Mitya. "I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself and left her with the landlord's daughters, and that old Maximov is with her. I calmed her down, do you hear? I told her you need to clear yourself, so she shouldn't upset you or you'll say the wrong thing. I talked to her and she understood. She's a smart girl, a good girl—she wanted to kiss my old hands, begging me to help you. She sent me herself, to tell you not to worry about her. Now I must go and tell her that you're calm and not worried about her. So you must be calm, understand? I was unfair to her; she's a good Christian, gentlemen, a gentle soul, not to blame for anything. So what should I tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you stay calm or not?"
The police captain said a lot that wasn't exactly proper, but he was really touched by Grushenka's suffering. Tears filled his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

"Forgive me, gentlemen, please, let me, let me!" he cried. "You have the heart of an angel, Mihail Makarovitch. Thank you for helping her. I will be calm, I'll even be cheerful. Tell her, please, that I'm cheerful, that I'll be laughing soon, knowing she has someone like you to protect her. I'll get through all this soon, and as soon as I'm free, I'll be with her, just wait. Gentlemen," he said to the lawyers, "now I'll tell you everything, I'll open my whole soul. We'll finish this quickly, and even laugh about it! But gentlemen, that woman means everything to me. Let me say that. I see you're honorable men. She's my light, my angel, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, 'I'll go to death with you'? And what have I—just a poor nobody—done for her? Why does she love me so much? How can someone like me deserve that? And how she begged you for me, just now!... and yet she's proud and hasn't done anything wrong! How could I not love her, how could I not run to her like I did? Forgive me, gentlemen! But now, now I'm okay."

He dropped back in his chair, covered his face, and sobbed—but now they were happy tears. He quickly pulled himself together. The old police captain looked pleased, and so did the lawyers. They felt the questioning was moving in a new direction. When the captain left, Mitya was almost cheerful.

"Now, gentlemen, I'm all yours. If it weren't for all these little details, we'd figure everything out in a minute. But let's trust each other—me in you, you in me—or we'll never finish. It's for your good, too. Let's get to the point, gentlemen, and stop poking around in my soul. Just ask me about the real facts and I'll answer right away. Forget the details!"
That's how Mitya spoke. The questioning started again.

"You have no idea how much it helps us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, that you’re willing to answer our questions," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, looking excited and genuinely pleased. His big, light gray, nearsighted eyes shone as he took off his glasses for a moment. "And you’re absolutely right about the need for trust—without it, it’s almost impossible to get anywhere in cases like this, especially if the person suspected really wants to defend himself. We’ll do everything we can on our side, and you can see how we’re handling things. Do you agree, Ippolit Kirillovitch?" he asked, turning to the prosecutor.
"Absolutely," replied the prosecutor, though his tone was much cooler than Nikolay Parfenovitch’s enthusiasm.

Just so you know, Nikolay Parfenovitch was new to town, but right from the start, he had a lot of respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, and had become almost his best friend. Nikolay was pretty much the only one who totally believed in Ippolit Kirillovitch’s amazing skills as a psychologist and speaker, as well as his sense of justice. He’d even heard about him back in St. Petersburg. Meanwhile, Ippolit Kirillovitch actually liked Nikolay Parfenovitch more than anyone else in the world. On their way to Mokroe, they had talked things over and agreed on how to handle this case. Now, sitting together at the table, Nikolay Parfenovitch carefully watched every little sign from his senior partner—a word, a look, or even a wink.
"Gentlemen, just let me tell my story without interrupting me with little questions, and I’ll tell you everything right away," Mitya said, fired up.

"Perfect! Thank you. But before we listen to your story, can I ask you about something else that’s important to us? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday at around five o’clock by pawning your pistols to your friend, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin."
"I pawned them, gentlemen. I pawned them for ten roubles. That’s all there is to it. As soon as I got back to town, I pawned them."
"So, you got back to town? Does that mean you were out of town before?"
"Yes, I took a trip about forty versts out of town. Didn’t you know?"
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch exchanged a look.

"Maybe it would help if you started from the beginning—just tell us everything you did yesterday, starting from the morning. For example, can you explain why you left town, when you left, and when you came back—all the details?"

"You should have asked me like that from the start," Mitya said, laughing out loud. "And if you want, I can start even earlier—the morning of the day before. Then you’ll see exactly how, why, and where I went. The day before yesterday, I went to a local merchant named Samsonov to try to borrow three thousand roubles, using solid security. It was really urgent, gentlemen, a sudden emergency."
"Excuse me for interrupting," the prosecutor said politely. "Why did you need exactly three thousand roubles so urgently?"

"Oh, gentlemen, there’s no need to get into all the little details—how, when, why, and why that exact amount instead of something else. That would take three whole books, and you’d want an ending, too!"
Mitya said all this with a friendly, but impatient tone, like someone who really wants to tell the truth and means well.

"Gentlemen!" he quickly corrected himself, "please don’t get annoyed with me for being restless—I apologize again. Believe me, I really respect you and understand what’s going on. Don’t think I’m drunk—I’m completely sober now. And honestly, being drunk wouldn’t make a difference for me. There’s a saying about me: ‘When he’s sober, he’s a fool; when he’s drunk, he’s wise.’ Ha! But I see now isn’t the right time for jokes—not until we’ve cleared things up. I have my own dignity to keep, too. I know I’m basically in the position of a criminal now, not on equal terms with you, and it’s your job to watch me. I can’t expect you to pat me on the back for what I did to Grigory—you can’t go around cracking old men’s heads and get away with it. I guess you’ll lock me up for six months, maybe a year, in a correctional house. I don’t know what the usual punishment is—but it won’t take away my rank, right? So you see, I know the difference between us. But you’ve got to admit, you’d confuse even God with all these questions. ‘How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?’ If you keep this up, I’ll get mixed up, and you’ll write it all down against me. What’s the point? Even if I’m talking nonsense now, let me finish—and you, being honorable and classy men, will forgive me! Please just drop this usual method—starting with tiny things, like how I got up, what I ate for breakfast, how I spat, and where, and then suddenly hitting me with, ‘Who did you murder? Who did you rob?’ Ha! That’s your usual trick. It might fool peasants, but not me. I know the game—I’ve been in the service, too. Ha ha ha! You’re not mad, are you? You forgive my cheekiness?" he added, looking at them with an almost surprising friendliness. "It’s just Mitya Karamazov, you know, so you can let it go. It’d be unforgivable in a sensible man, but you can forgive Mitya. Ha ha!"
Nikolay Parfenovitch listened and laughed too. The prosecutor didn’t laugh, but watched Mitya closely, as if he didn’t want to miss a single word or even the tiniest movement in his face.

"That’s how we’ve treated you from the start," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still smiling. "We haven’t tried to trip you up by asking how you got up or what you had for breakfast. We’ve started with the really important questions."

"I know. I noticed and appreciated it, and I’m even more thankful for your kindness now—it’s amazing, and shows your good hearts. The three of us are gentlemen here, so let’s have real trust between educated, honorable people, who all share a sense of pride and honor. For now, let me think of you as my best friends, especially at this moment when my honor is under attack. That’s okay with you, right?"
"On the contrary! You said it perfectly, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch replied with serious approval.
"And enough with all those little questions, gentlemen, those tricky ones!" Mitya burst out enthusiastically. "Otherwise, there’s no telling where we’ll end up! Right?"
"I’ll take your good advice," the prosecutor said, turning to Mitya. "But I still need to ask: it’s really important for us to know exactly why you needed that specific amount—three thousand."
"Why I needed it? Oh, for different things… Well, it was to pay a debt."
"A debt to whom?"

"That I absolutely refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I can’t, or am scared, or because it would hurt me. It’s actually a small, unimportant thing—but I won’t say, out of principle. That’s my private life, and I won’t let anyone poke into it. That’s my rule. Your question doesn’t matter for the case, and anything not about the case is my own business. I wanted to pay a debt of honor, but I’m not telling you to whom."
"Let me make a note of that," the prosecutor said.
"Go ahead. Write down that I refuse to say, and that I think it would be dishonorable to answer. You can write it—you’ve got nothing better to do!"

"Let me remind you, sir," the prosecutor said, in a serious, formal tone, "that you have every right not to answer our questions, and we can’t force you if you don’t want to. That’s your choice. But we have to let you know that by refusing to answer, you might be hurting your own case. Now, please continue."
"Gentlemen, I’m not angry… I…" Mitya muttered, sounding a bit unsettled. "Well, you see, about Samsonov, the man I went to…"

I won’t repeat what you already know. Mitya was super eager not to leave out a single detail, but he also wanted to get it over with quickly. As he spoke, they wrote everything down, which meant they kept stopping him. Mitya didn’t like this, but he put up with it—sometimes getting annoyed, though still trying to stay friendly. Every now and then, he’d blurt out, "Gentlemen, this is enough to make even an angel lose his patience!" or, "Gentlemen, it’s no use making me angry."

Even when he complained, he stayed mostly friendly for a while. He told them how Samsonov had tricked him two days ago (and by now, Mitya knew he’d been fooled). Selling his watch for six roubles to get money for the trip was new to the lawyers—they got very interested, and to Mitya’s annoyance, wrote it down as more proof that he was broke at the time. Bit by bit, Mitya started to get grumpy. Then, after describing his trip to see Lyagavy, spending the night in a hot, stuffy hut, and so on, he got to returning to town. Here, without much prompting, he gave a detailed account of his intense jealousy over Grushenka.

They listened in total silence. They asked a lot about how he’d hidden in Marya Kondratyevna’s house behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden to spy on Grushenka, and about Smerdyakov bringing him information. They were especially interested in this and made careful notes. Mitya talked passionately and at length about his jealousy, and even though he was embarrassed to reveal such private feelings to "the public," he forced himself to be honest. The cold, serious way the investigating lawyer—and especially the prosecutor—stared at him as he talked eventually made him feel pretty uncomfortable.

"That kid, Nikolay Parfenovitch, the one I was joking with about women a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor—they’re not worth telling this to," he thought sadly. "It’s humiliating. ‘Be patient, humble, hold your peace.’" He ended his thoughts with that line, but pulled himself together and kept going. When he got to the part about visiting Madame Hohlakov, he cheered up and even wanted to share a funny story about her that had nothing to do with the case. But the investigating lawyer stopped him and politely suggested he stick to "more important matters." Finally, when he described his despair and explained how, after leaving Madame Hohlakov’s, he thought, "I’ll get three thousand even if I have to kill someone," they stopped him again and wrote down that he had "intended to murder someone." Mitya let them write it without arguing. He finally got to the point where he found out Grushenka had tricked him and had come back from Samsonov’s right after he left, even though she’d said she’d stay till midnight.

"If I didn’t kill Fenya then, gentlemen, it was only because I didn’t have time," he suddenly blurted out at that point. They carefully wrote that down, too. Mitya waited gloomily, and was just starting to tell how he rushed into his father’s garden when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him, opened a big folder that was on the sofa, and took out the brass pestle.
"Do you recognize this?" he asked, showing it to Mitya.
"Oh, yeah," Mitya said with a gloomy laugh. "Of course I recognize it. Let me see it... Oh, forget it!"
"You forgot to mention this," the investigating lawyer pointed out.
"Come on, I wouldn’t have hidden it from you. Do you really think I could have managed without it? I just forgot."
"Please tell us exactly how you ended up taking it with you."
"Of course, gentlemen."
Then Mitya explained how he grabbed the pestle and ran off.
"But what was your reason for taking a weapon like that?"
"Reason? No real reason. I just picked it up and ran."
"Why, if you had no reason?"
Mitya’s temper flared. He stared hard at "the boy" and gave a dark, angry smile. He felt more and more embarrassed for sharing so much about his jealousy with "people like them."
"Forget the pestle!" he suddenly burst out.
"But still—"
"Oh, to keep off dogs... Or because it was dark... In case something happened."
"But have you ever taken a weapon with you before, since you’re afraid of the dark?"
"Ugh! I can’t talk to you at all, gentlemen!" Mitya shouted, totally frustrated. He turned to the secretary, his face red with anger, and said quickly, his voice shaking with rage:

"Write this down—right now—‘I grabbed the pestle to go and kill my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, by hitting him on the head with it!’ There! Happy now? Does that make you feel better?" he demanded, glaring at the lawyers.

"We understand perfectly that you just said that out of frustration with us and our questions, which you think are pointless, though they’re actually important," the prosecutor answered, sounding dry.

"Honestly, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle... Why do people grab things in moments like that? I don’t know why. I just grabbed it and ran, that’s all. Let’s move on, or I swear I won’t say another word."

He sat with his elbows on the table, his head in his hand, turned sideways to them and staring at the wall, trying to keep from feeling sick. He really wanted to get up and shout that he wouldn’t say another word, "even if you hang me for it."

"You see, gentlemen," he said at last, barely able to keep himself together, "when I listen to you, I keep thinking of this dream I have... It’s a dream that comes to me a lot—always the same. Someone is chasing me, someone I’m really scared of... hunting me at night, in the dark... I hide somewhere, behind a door or in a cupboard, hiding in a pathetic way, and the worst part is, he always knows where I’m hiding, but pretends not to, just to drag out my fear and enjoy it... That’s exactly what you’re doing now. It feels just like that!"
"Is that really what you dream about?" asked the prosecutor.
"Yeah, it is. Don’t you want to write that down, too?" Mitya said with a twisted smile.
"No, there’s no need to write that. But you do have strange dreams."
"This isn’t about dreams now, gentlemen—this is real! I’m the wolf and you’re the hunters. Well, go ahead and hunt me down!"
"You shouldn’t compare things like that..." Nikolay Parfenovitch said softly.

"No, I’m not wrong, not at all!" Mitya snapped again, even though getting angry seemed to cheer him up. He actually grew kinder with each word. "You might not trust a criminal or someone being questioned, but an honorable man, someone who follows his heart (and I say that boldly!)—no! You can’t doubt that. You have no right. But—"
"So, should I keep going?" he finished, sounding gloomy.
"If you’d be so kind," Nikolay Parfenovitch answered.

Even though Mitya (Dmitri) spoke in a grumpy way, it was clear he was trying harder than ever not to leave out a single detail of his story. He told the lawyers how he jumped over the fence into his father's garden, how he went up to the window, and described everything that happened under the window. He explained, clearly and exactly, how he felt while he was in the garden, desperate to know if Grushenka was with his father or not. But strangely, the lawyers now listened with stiff seriousness, looking at him coldly and barely asking any questions. Mitya couldn’t read anything from their faces.
“They’re mad at me, or insulted,” he thought. “Well, forget them!”

When he described how he finally decided to give the “signal” to his father that Grushenka had come, so his father would open the window, the lawyers didn’t react at all to the word “signal.” It was like they didn’t understand what he meant, and Mitya noticed this. When he got to the part where, seeing his father’s face at the window, his hatred boiled over and he pulled out the pestle from his pocket, he suddenly stopped talking on purpose. He just stared at the wall, aware the lawyers were staring at him.
“Well?” said the investigating lawyer. “You took out the weapon and... what happened next?”
“Then? Why, then I killed him... hit him on the head and smashed his skull... That’s what you want me to say, right? That’s your story!”
His eyes suddenly lit up with anger. All the frustration he’d kept inside exploded out with incredible force.
“Our story?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. “Well—what’s your story, then?”
Mitya dropped his eyes and sat in silence for a long time.

“My story, gentlemen? Well, here it is,” he started quietly. “Maybe someone’s prayers saved me, or my mother prayed to God, or maybe an angel stopped me—I don’t know. But the evil in me lost. I ran away from the window and headed for the fence. My father saw me for the first time then, got scared, yelled, and jumped back from the window. I remember that clearly. I ran across the garden to the fence... and that’s where Grigory caught me when I was sitting on top of it.”
At that moment, Mitya finally looked up at his listeners. They seemed to be watching him calmly, without any emotion. Suddenly, a wave of anger hit Mitya.
“You’re laughing at me right now, aren’t you, gentlemen!” he burst out.
“Why do you think that?” asked Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“Because you don’t believe a word I’m saying! I get it—I’ve reached the crucial part. My father’s lying there with his head smashed, and after I tell you how I wanted to kill him, and how I grabbed the pestle, suddenly I say I ran away from the window. It sounds like a made-up story! Like poetry! Who would believe me just because I say so? Ha! You’re mocking me, gentlemen!”
He spun around in his chair so hard that it creaked.
“Did you notice,” the prosecutor suddenly asked, as if ignoring Mitya’s outburst, “when you ran from the window, whether the door to the garden was open?”
“No, it wasn’t open.”
“It wasn’t?”
“It was closed. Who could have opened it? Oh, the door. Wait a second,” he said, suddenly thinking of something.
“Did you find the door open?”
“Yes, it was open.”
“But who could’ve opened it if you didn’t open it yourselves?” Mitya said, truly surprised.

“The door was open, and your father’s killer definitely went in that way, and after the murder, left through the same door,” the prosecutor said slowly, as if carving each word into stone. “That’s perfectly clear. The murder happened inside the room, not through the window; that’s obvious from the investigation, the way the body was found, and everything else. There’s no doubt about it.”
Mitya was completely stunned.

“But that’s impossible!” he cried, totally confused. “I... I didn’t go inside... I swear, the door was closed the entire time I was in the garden, and when I ran out. I only stood at the window and saw him through it. That’s all, I swear. Even if I didn’t remember, it wouldn’t matter. Only Smerdyakov, me, and the dead man knew about the signals. And my father wouldn’t have opened the door to anyone without the signals.”

“Signals? What signals?” asked the prosecutor, suddenly very eager and nervous. He lost all his calm and seriousness, and asked almost like he was afraid Mitya wouldn’t answer. He seemed to think this was a huge clue he’d missed before.

“So you didn’t know!” Mitya winked at him with a nasty, mocking smile. “What if I don’t tell you? Who else could you ask? No one knew about the signals except my father, Smerdyakov, and me. That’s it. God knew too, but He’s not talking. It’s a big deal, isn’t it? Who knows what you’ll guess now. Ha! Don’t worry, gentlemen, I’ll tell you. You probably have some silly theory. You don’t know who you’re dealing with! I’m a prisoner who tells the truth, even if it hurts me! Yes, because I’m an honest man, and you—aren’t.”

The prosecutor just swallowed this, too eager to care. He was shaking with impatience. Mitya then told them in detail about the secret signals Fyodor Pavlovitch had invented for Smerdyakov. He explained exactly what each tap on the window meant, even tapping them out on the table. When Nikolay Parfenovitch asked if Mitya had tapped the signal “Grushenka has come” to his father, Mitya said yes, that’s exactly what he’d tapped.
“So now you can build your big theory,” Mitya sneered, turning away from them in disgust.
“So no one knew about the signals except your dead father, you, and Smerdyakov the servant? No one else?” asked Nikolay Parfenovitch again.
“Right. Smerdyakov and God. Write down about God. You’ll need Him yourselves.”
Of course, they’d already started writing it all down. But while they did, the prosecutor suddenly seemed to get a new idea:
“But if Smerdyakov also knew the signals, and you totally deny killing your father, maybe it was Smerdyakov who gave the signal, got your father to open up, and then... committed the murder?”
Mitya turned and stared at him with a look of deep sarcasm and hatred. He stared so long that the prosecutor blinked.

“You think you’re clever,” Mitya finally said. “You think I’ll jump on your idea and shout, ‘Aha! It was Smerdyakov—he’s the killer.’ Isn’t that what you were hoping? Admit it, and I’ll keep talking.”
But the prosecutor didn’t admit anything. He just waited.
“You’re wrong. I’m not going to say ‘It was Smerdyakov,’” said Mitya.
“So you don’t even suspect him?”
“Do you suspect him?”
“He’s a suspect, too.”
Mitya stared at the floor.

“Seriously,” he said gloomily. “Listen. From the beginning, almost from the moment I ran out from behind the curtain, I’ve had Smerdyakov on my mind. I’ve been sitting here, yelling that I’m innocent, but thinking ‘Smerdyakov!’ I can’t get him out of my head. In fact, just now, I thought of Smerdyakov again—but only for a second. Almost at once I thought, ‘No, it’s not Smerdyakov.’ It’s just not him, gentlemen.”
“Then is there anyone else you suspect?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked carefully.
“I have no idea who it could be, whether it was Heaven or the devil, but... not Smerdyakov,” Mitya said firmly.
“But why are you so sure it’s not him?”

“It’s just what I feel—my gut tells me. Because Smerdyakov is the weakest, most cowardly person you’ll ever meet. He’s not just a coward—he’s cowardice in human form. He’s always been terrified of me, even though I never laid a hand on him. He’s literally begged at my feet, crying and begging me not to scare him. I even offered him money. He’s a total weakling—sickly, epileptic, not very smart—a little kid could beat him up. He doesn’t care about money; he wouldn’t accept my gifts. And what reason would he have to kill my father? Honestly, he might even be my father’s son—his illegitimate son. Did you know that?”
“We’ve heard that rumor. But you’re your father’s son, too, and you told everyone you wanted to murder him.”

“That’s a low blow! I’m not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn’t it rotten to say that right to my face? It’s mean, because I told you that myself. I didn’t just want to kill him; I might have done it. And I even told you, straight up, that I almost did. But you see, I didn’t do it; my guardian angel stopped me—that’s what you’re missing. That’s why it’s so unfair. Because I didn’t kill him, I didn’t! Do you hear me—I did not kill him.”
He was almost choking with emotion. He hadn’t been this upset during the whole interrogation so far.
“And what has Smerdyakov told you, gentlemen?” he suddenly asked after a pause. “Can I ask that?”

“You can ask anything,” the prosecutor answered coldly, “anything about the case, and we have to answer you. We found Smerdyakov, the servant you’re asking about, lying unconscious in his bed, in a very bad epileptic fit, which had happened maybe ten times. The doctor said he might not survive the night.”
“Well, if that’s true, then the devil must have killed him,” Mitya suddenly blurted out, as if he’d been debating in his head whether Smerdyakov did it or not.
“We’ll come back to this later,” Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. “Now, would you like to continue your statement?”

Mitya asked for a break. They politely agreed. After resting, he continued his story, but he was obviously depressed, drained, and shaken. To make it worse, the prosecutor kept interrupting him with annoying questions about “minor details.” As soon as Mitya described how he was sitting on the wall when he hit Grigory on the head with the pestle, and how the old man had grabbed his leg, the prosecutor interrupted to ask exactly how he was sitting on the wall. Mitya was surprised.
“Oh, I was sitting like this—straddling the wall, one leg on each side.”
“And the pestle?”
“The pestle was in my hand.”
“Not in your pocket? Are you sure? Did you hit him hard?”
“It must have been a hard blow. But why do you ask?”
“Would you mind sitting on the chair like you were on the wall, and showing us how you moved your arm and in what direction?”
“Are you making fun of me?” Mitya asked, glaring, but the lawyer didn’t flinch.
Mitya turned quickly, sat astride the chair, and swung his arm.
“This is how I hit him! That’s how I knocked him down! What else do you need?”
“Thank you. Now, can you explain why you jumped down—what were you trying to do?”
“Oh, whatever!... I jumped down to look at the guy I’d hit... I don’t even know why!”
“Even though you were so worked up and ready to run?”
“Yes, even though I was worked up and running away.”
“Did you want to help him?”
“Help!... Maybe I did want to help him... I don’t remember.”
“You don’t remember? Then you didn’t really know what you were doing?”
“No, I remember everything—every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and wiped his face with my handkerchief.”
“We’ve seen your handkerchief. Did you hope to bring him back to consciousness?”
“I don’t know if I hoped that. I just wanted to see if he was alive or not.”
“Ah! So you wanted to be sure? And then?”
“I’m not a doctor. I couldn’t tell. I ran away thinking I’d killed him. Now it turns out he’s alive.”
“Good,” said the prosecutor. “That’s all I wanted. Please continue.”

Unfortunately, it never crossed Mitya’s mind to tell them—even though he remembered—that he’d jumped back out of pity, and even said a few words to the unconscious Grigory: “You’ve had bad luck, old man—nothing can be done about it. You’ll have to stay there.”

The prosecutor could only draw one conclusion: that Mitya had jumped back “at such a moment and in such excitement just to make sure the only witness to his crime was dead; so he must have been a strong, cold-blooded, and clever person, even in such a situation,” and so on. The prosecutor felt satisfied: “I pushed him with these little questions, and he said more than he planned to.”
With effort, Mitya kept going. But this time, Nikolay Parfenovitch stopped him right away.
“How did you end up running to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands and even your face covered in blood?”
“I didn’t notice the blood at all,” Mitya answered.
“That’s believable. It happens sometimes,” the prosecutor said, exchanging a look with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“I just didn’t notice. You’re right about that, prosecutor,” Mitya agreed suddenly.

Next, Mitya told how he suddenly decided to “step aside” and let Grushenka be happy. But he couldn’t bring himself to open up to the lawyers like before or talk about “the queen of his soul.” He hated talking about her in front of these cold men who “latched onto him like bugs.” So, when they kept asking, he answered briefly and gruffly:

“Well, I decided to kill myself. What else was there for me to live for? That question was staring me in the face. Her first real lover had come back—the guy who’d hurt her but now came back after five years to make it right by marrying her. So I knew it was over for me. And behind me was disgrace and Grigory’s blood. What did I have left? So I went to get back the pistols I’d pawned, to load them and shoot myself tomorrow.”
“And you had a big party the night before?”

“Yeah, a big party the night before. Damn it, gentlemen! Hurry up and finish this. I planned to shoot myself just past the village, at five in the morning. I even had a note in my pocket already. I wrote it at Perhotin’s when I loaded the pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! I’m not telling you this for you,” he added with contempt. He took the letter from his pocket and tossed it on the table. The lawyers read it with curiosity and, as usual, added it to the case files.
“And you didn’t even think of washing your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t worried about looking suspicious?”

“What suspicion? Suspicious or not, I would’ve rushed here anyway and shot myself at five, and you wouldn’t have been able to stop me. If my father hadn’t been killed, you’d never have found out, and wouldn’t have come here so fast. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. The devil killed my father, and the devil helped you find out so quickly. How did you get here so fast? It’s unreal, like a dream!”
“Mr. Perhotin told us that when you came to him, you had in your hands... your bloody hands... your money... a stack of hundred-rouble notes, and his servant boy saw it, too.”
“That’s true, gentlemen. I remember it now.”
“There’s one question. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began gently, “where did you suddenly get so much money, since it looks like you hadn’t been home?”
The prosecutor frowned at the directness of the question but didn’t stop Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“No, I didn’t go home,” Mitya answered calmly, looking at the floor.
“Let me repeat my question,” Nikolay Parfenovitch continued, carefully. “How did you get that much money so fast, when, by your own confession, at five o’clock the same day you—”

“I needed ten roubles, so I pawned my pistols at Perhotin’s, then went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on, and so on,” Mitya interrupted sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I needed the money and suddenly ended up with thousands, right? You’re both worried now, thinking, ‘What if he won’t say where he got it?’ That’s exactly what’s happening. I’m not telling you, gentlemen. You guessed right. You’ll never know,” Mitya said, each word sharp and determined. The lawyers fell silent for a moment.
“You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it’s extremely important for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch softly.
“I understand. But I still won’t tell you.”
The prosecutor also reminded him that he could refuse to answer if he thought it was for his own good, but that silence could hurt him, especially in such a serious case—
“Yeah, yeah, I’ve heard that speech before,” Mitya interrupted again. “I know how important it is, and this is the main issue, but I still won’t say.”
“It’s your choice, not ours. You’re only hurting yourself,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said nervously.

“You see, gentlemen, seriously now,” Mitya lifted his eyes and looked them in the face, “I figured from the start we’d clash over this point. At first, when I began talking, everything seemed far away and unclear, so I assumed we could trust each other. Now I see that was impossible—we were bound to hit this cursed obstacle. And now we have! It’s hopeless and that’s that! But I don’t blame you. You can’t just take my word for it. I get that.”
He sank back into gloomy silence.
“Couldn’t you, without actually telling us the main thing, at least give us a hint about your reasons? What could make you stay silent, when it’s so dangerous for you?”
Mitya gave a sad, almost dreamy, smile.

“I’m actually nicer than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you why, and give you a hint, even though you don’t deserve it. I won’t answer because it would ruin my honor. Telling you where I got the money would disgrace me even worse than being accused of killing and robbing my father, if I’d done those things. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, because it would be shameful. What, are you going to write that down?”
“Yes, we’ll write it,” Nikolay Parfenovitch lisped.

“You shouldn’t write about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you that because I’m kind. I didn’t have to. I gave you that as a gift, but you grab it right away. Oh well, write what you want,” he finished, disgusted. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still hold my head high.”
“And can’t you tell us what kind of disgrace it is?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked.
The prosecutor frowned even more.
“No, no, that’s it, I’m done. Don’t bother. I’ve dirtied myself enough with your questions already. You’re not worth it... No one is... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not saying any more.”
He said this so firmly that Nikolay Parfenovitch didn’t push further, but Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes showed he wasn’t giving up hope.
“Can you at least tell us how much money you had when you went to Perhotin’s—exactly how many roubles?”
“I can’t tell you that.”
“You told Perhotin, I think, that you’d gotten three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”
“Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I’m not saying how much I had.”
“Will you please tell us how you got here and what you’ve done since arriving?”
“Oh! You could ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you if you want.”

He told them, but we won’t repeat his story. He spoke dryly and without much detail. He didn’t mention his love for Grushenka at all, and just said he stopped planning to shoot himself because of “new developments.” He didn’t explain why, and this time the lawyers didn’t push him. It was clear this wasn’t an important point for them.

“We’ll check all that. We’ll come back to it during the witness questioning, which of course you’ll attend,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch at the end. “And now, please lay out everything you have with you, especially any money.”

“My money, gentlemen? Of course. I get that it’s necessary. Honestly, I’m surprised you didn’t ask sooner. It’s true I couldn’t run away—I’ve been sitting here in plain sight. Here’s my money—count it—take it. That’s everything, I think.”
He emptied all his pockets—even the small change, two twenty-copeck coins from his vest. They counted it: eight hundred thirty-six roubles and forty copecks.
“And that’s all?” asked the lawyer.
“Yes.”
“You said earlier you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs'. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then...”
Nikolay Parfenovitch added it all up. Mitya helped him, and together they remembered every bit. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly totaled it.
“With this eight hundred, you must have had about fifteen hundred at first?”
“I guess so,” Mitya snapped.
“How come everyone else says it was much more?”
“Let them say whatever they want.”
“But you said it yourself.”
“Yeah, I did.”
“We’ll compare this with what other people say later. Don’t worry about your money. It will be kept safe and given back if it’s proven to be yours. Now, then...”
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly stood up and told Mitya firmly that it was his duty to do a very thorough search “of your clothes and everything else...”
“Sure, gentlemen. I’ll empty all my pockets if you want.”
And he really did start pulling everything out of his pockets.
“You’ll also have to take off your clothes.”
“What! Undress? Ugh! Seriously? Can’t you just search me as I am?”
“That’s impossible, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You have to take off your clothes.”
“Fine, if you say so,” Mitya answered gloomily. “But not here—behind the curtains, okay? Who’s going to search them?”
“Behind the curtains, of course.”
Nikolay Parfenov

What happened next to Mitya (Dmitri) was something he never could have imagined. Not even a minute before did he think anyone would treat him this way—him, Mitya Karamazov! The worst part was how humiliating it felt, and the people around him seemed cold and almost mocking. It wasn’t just that he was told to take off his coat—they ordered him to undress further. Mitya got the message: this wasn’t a polite request, it was a command. Out of pride, and maybe anger, he obeyed silently. A few peasants stood with the lawyers, staying on their side of the curtain. “They must be here to use force if I resist,” Mitya thought, “or maybe there’s another reason.”

“Well, do I have to take off my shirt too?” Mitya snapped, but Nikolay Parfenovitch didn’t answer. He and the prosecutor were busy inspecting Mitya’s coat, pants, vest, and cap, clearly very interested in what they might find. “They’re not even pretending to be polite,” Mitya thought. “They don’t care about respect at all.”
“I’m asking you again—do I have to take off my shirt or not?” Mitya said, his voice even sharper and more annoyed.
“Don’t worry about it. We’ll tell you what to do,” Nikolay Parfenovitch replied, sounding so firm and bossy that it made Mitya even angrier.

Meanwhile, the two lawyers were whispering to each other. They found a huge dried bloodstain on the back left side of Mitya’s coat, and there were blood spots on his pants too. In front of the peasants, Nikolay Parfenovitch ran his fingers along the collar, cuffs, and seams of both the coat and pants, clearly searching for something—probably money. He didn’t even try to hide his suspicion that Mitya might have sewn money into his clothes.

“He’s treating me like a thief, not an officer,” Mitya muttered under his breath. The lawyers talked openly about their suspicions. The secretary, who was also behind the curtain, bustled around and pointed out Mitya’s cap for Nikolay Parfenovitch to check.

“Remember Gridyenko, the office clerk?” the secretary said. “Last summer, he said he lost the office’s wages after getting drunk. And where did they find the money? Sewn up in his cap’s lining—rolled-up notes hidden in the seams.”
Both lawyers remembered Gridyenko’s trick and put aside Mitya’s cap, deciding they’d need to search all his clothes even more carefully later.
Suddenly, Nikolay Parfenovitch noticed the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was turned in and covered with blood. “Excuse me, but what’s this—blood?” he asked.
“Yes,” Mitya answered quickly.
“Where did the blood come from? And why is the cuff turned in?” Nikolay Parfenovitch pressed him.
Mitya explained that he’d gotten blood on his sleeve while helping Grigory, and he had turned the cuff inside when washing his hands at Perhotin’s house.
“You’ll need to take your shirt off too. That’s important evidence,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said.
Mitya’s face turned red and he burst out in anger.
“What, do you want me completely naked?” he yelled.
“Don’t worry. We’ll handle it. For now, take off your socks too,” Nikolay Parfenovitch instructed.
“Are you serious? Is that really necessary?” Mitya’s eyes flashed with frustration.
“We’re not joking,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said sternly.

“Fine, if I have to,” Mitya muttered. He sat on the bed and took off his socks, feeling horribly awkward. Everyone else was dressed, but he was nearly naked. Strangely, being undressed in front of them made him feel guilty and ashamed, almost as if he really were less than they were and deserved their scorn.

“It’s not so bad if everyone’s undressed, but being the only one—while everyone stares—it’s humiliating,” Mitya kept thinking to himself. “It’s like one of my nightmares.” He hated taking off his socks, which were filthy, as were his underwear, and now everyone could see. Even worse, he was very self-conscious about his feet—he’d always thought his big toes were ugly, especially the right one, with its thick, crooked nail. Now everyone would see it. This shame made him act rougher on purpose. He yanked off his shirt himself.
“Anything else you want to see? If you’re not too ashamed,” he said sarcastically.
“No, that’s all for now.”
“So am I supposed to sit here naked?” Mitya growled.
“Yes, for now, that’s just how it is. Sit down and wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed. I’ll sort things out,” Nikolay Parfenovitch replied.

All Mitya’s clothes were shown to the witnesses. They wrote up a report, and finally Nikolay Parfenovitch left, with the clothes carried out after him. The prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, left too. Mitya was left alone with the peasants, who just stared at him in silence. He wrapped himself in the quilt but felt cold—his bare feet stuck out, and he couldn’t cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch was gone for what felt like forever. “He treats me like I’m a puppy,” Mitya thought, grinding his teeth. “That miserable prosecutor left too—he probably can’t stand to see me naked, thinks I’m disgusting.”
Mitya expected his clothes would be searched and then returned. But he was furious when Nikolay Parfenovitch came back with totally different clothes, which a peasant brought in behind him.

“Here’s some clothes for you,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said casually, looking pleased with himself. “Mr. Kalganov kindly let us use these for the emergency, and there’s a clean shirt too. Luckily he had them in his trunk. You can keep your own socks and underwear.”
Mitya exploded with anger.
“I’m not wearing someone else’s clothes!” he shouted, furious. “Give me my own!”
“That’s impossible,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said.
“Give me my clothes! Forget Kalganov and his stupid clothes!”

It took a long time to calm Mitya down. But eventually, they managed to convince him. They explained that his clothes, since they were bloody, had to be kept as evidence, and they weren’t even allowed to give them back, considering the possible outcome of the case. Finally, Mitya understood. He fell silent and dressed quickly. As he put on the new clothes, he grumbled that they were much nicer than his old ones, and he hated “benefiting from the change.” The coat, though, was “ridiculously tight. Am I supposed to look like a clown for your entertainment?”
They told him he was overreacting, that Kalganov was only a little taller, so maybe the pants were a bit long. But the coat was really tight in the shoulders.
“For crying out loud! I can barely button it,” Mitya grumbled. “Tell Kalganov from me that I never asked for his clothes, and it’s not my fault I look like a clown.”
“He gets it, and he’s sorry... I mean, not sorry to help, just sorry about the situation,” Nikolay Parfenovitch mumbled.
“To heck with his sympathy! So what now? Do I just keep sitting here?”

They told him to go back to the “other room.” Mitya stomped in, angry and trying not to make eye contact with anyone. Wearing someone else’s clothes, he felt humiliated, even in front of the peasants and Trifon Borissovitch, whose face popped up in the doorway for a moment and then disappeared. “He just came to see me dressed up like this,” Mitya thought. He sat down on the same chair as before, feeling like he was in a nightmare and maybe losing his mind.

“Well, what’s next? Are you going to flog me? Is that all that’s left for you?” he said through clenched teeth, talking to the prosecutor. He refused to look at Nikolay Parfenovitch, as if he didn’t even deserve to be spoken to.
“He even checked my socks, turning them inside out so everyone could see how dirty they were—the scoundrel!” Mitya thought.
“Now we have to question the witnesses,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, as if answering Mitya’s question.
“Yes,” the prosecutor said thoughtfully, lost in his own thoughts.

“We’ve done all we could for you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch continued, “but since you absolutely refuse to tell us where you got the money that was found on you, we are, at this moment—”
“What’s the stone in your ring?” Mitya suddenly interrupted, as if waking up from a daydream. He pointed at one of the big rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s right hand.
“Ring?” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, surprised.
“Yes, that one on your middle finger, with the little veins in it. What kind of stone is that?” Mitya asked, sounding almost like a cranky kid.
“That’s a smoky topaz,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, smiling. “Would you like to see it? I’ll take it off—”

“No, don’t take it off!” Mitya suddenly snapped, angry at himself. “Don’t take it off—there’s no need. Damn it! Gentlemen, you’ve dirtied my soul! Do you really think I would hide the truth from you if I had actually killed my father? That I’d lie and cover things up? No, that’s not who Dmitri Karamazov is. If I were guilty, I wouldn’t have waited for you to come, or even for sunrise, as I first planned. I would have killed myself already— I know that about myself now. I’ve learned more about myself in this one cursed night than in twenty years! And look at me now, sitting here talking to you—do you think I could act this way if I’d really murdered my father? When just thinking I might have accidentally killed Grigory has tortured me all night—not just because I’m afraid of punishment! The shame of it! And you expect me to be honest with people like you, who don’t believe in anything, who just mock and doubt? You want me to confess to something else shameful, even if it would help my case? No, I’d rather go to Siberia! The man who opened the door to my father and went in—he killed and robbed him. Who was he? I’ve racked my brain and can’t figure it out. But I can tell you one thing: it was not Dmitri Karamazov. That’s all I can say, and it’s enough. Leave me alone. Exile me, punish me, but stop bothering me. I won’t say anything else. Call your witnesses!”
Mitya said this in a burst, as if he meant to stay silent from now on. The prosecutor watched him the whole time, and when Mitya finished, he replied in the calmest, most ordinary voice:

“About the open door you just mentioned—we should tell you about a very important piece of evidence that Grigory, the old man you injured, gave us. After he recovered, he told us clearly that when he came out to the steps and heard a noise in the garden, he decided to enter through the little gate, which was open. Before he saw you running from the open window where you saw your father, he glanced left and saw the door standing wide open—the same door you claimed was closed the whole time you were in the garden. I should tell you, Grigory insists that you must have run from that door, though he didn’t see you do it—he only saw you later, running in the garden toward the fence.”
Mitya jumped up from his chair halfway through this explanation.
“That’s a lie!” he yelled, exploding with anger. “He couldn’t have seen the door open, because it was shut. He’s lying!”
“I have to repeat, he’s very confident in his statement. He hasn’t changed his story, no matter how many times we’ve questioned him.”
“Yes, I personally questioned him several times,” Nikolay Parfenovitch added.

“It’s a lie! Either he’s trying to frame me or he’s lost his mind,” Mitya kept shouting. “He’s just rambling from blood loss and his injury. He imagined it. He must have been confused when he woke up. He’s not thinking straight.”
“But he noticed the open door before he was injured, as soon as he entered the garden from the lodge,” the prosecutor pointed out.
“But it’s not true! It’s impossible! He’s lying about me out of spite…. He couldn’t have seen that. I didn’t come out the door,” Mitya gasped.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and said seriously,
“Show him the evidence.”
“Do you recognize this object?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked.
He placed a large, thick official envelope on the table, sealed in three places. It was empty and had one end slit open. Mitya stared at it with wide eyes.

“That... that must be my father’s envelope, the one with the three thousand roubles. And if it says, let me see, ‘For my little chicken’—yes! Three thousand!” he shouted. “See? Three thousand, do you see?”
“Yes, we see. But there was no money in it. It was empty and lying on the floor by the bed, behind the screen,” the prosecutor said.
For a few seconds, Mitya just stood there, shocked.

“Gentlemen, it was Smerdyakov!” he suddenly screamed at the top of his lungs. “He’s the one who killed him! He’s the one who robbed him! No one else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It was Smerdyakov, that’s obvious now!”
“But you knew about the envelope too, and that it was under the pillow.”

“I never knew that! I never saw it. This is the first time I’ve even looked at it. I only heard about it from Smerdyakov. He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it. I didn’t know—” Mitya was out of breath.
“But you told us yourself the envelope was under your father’s pillow. You specifically said that, so you must have known.”
“We have it written down,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed.

“That’s ridiculous! I had no idea it was under the pillow. Maybe it wasn’t even there at all. I just guessed it! What does Smerdyakov say? Did you ask him where it was? That’s the real question. And I ended up lying against myself— I told you without thinking that it was under the pillow, and now you— You know how people say the wrong thing sometimes. Only Smerdyakov knew, no one else. He didn’t even tell me! But he’s the one—he did it, I’m sure. He murdered him, it’s clear as day,” Mitya ranted, becoming more and more frantic, stumbling over his words, and getting even more upset. “You have to arrest him now. He must have killed him while I was running away and Grigory was unconscious, that’s obvious. He gave the signal, and father let him in—no one else knew the signal, and without it, father never would have opened the door.”
“But you’re forgetting something,” the prosecutor said, still calm but sounding a bit proud. “If the door was already open when you were in the garden, there was no need for a signal.”
“The door... the door,” Mitya muttered, staring silently at the prosecutor. He slumped back into his chair. No one said a word.
“Yes, the door! This is a nightmare. God is against me!” he cried, staring ahead in disbelief.

“So you see,” the prosecutor continued, now sounding grand, “you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On one hand, we have the evidence of the open door you ran from, which puts you in a terrible position. On the other, there’s your strange and stubborn silence about where you got the money that suddenly appeared, when just three hours before, you pawned your pistols for ten roubles! Given all these facts, what are we supposed to believe? Don’t accuse us of being cold, cynical people who can’t believe in your good intentions. Try to see things from our point of view.”
Mitya was visibly shaken. He turned pale.
“Fine!” he suddenly shouted. “I’ll tell you my secret. I’ll tell you where I got the money! I’ll reveal my shame, so I won’t have to blame myself or you later.”
“And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, almost sounding hopeful, “a full and honest confession could really help you later. It could—”
But the prosecutor nudged him under the table, and he stopped talking. Mitya, though, hadn’t even noticed.
“Gentlemen,” Dmitri (Mitya) began, still visibly shaken, “I have to confess everything: that money was mine.” The lawyers’ faces fell. This was not what they had expected at all.
“What do you mean?” Nikolay Parfenovitch stammered. “But at five o’clock that day, you admitted—”

“Forget about five o’clock and my earlier confession! That doesn’t matter now. The money was mine—well, not really mine, I stole it… It was fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it with me the whole time, every minute…”
“But where did you get it?”
“I took it from around my own neck, gentlemen. Right here, sewn into a rag. I’d been wearing it around my neck for a month. I’m ashamed to admit it!”
“And who did you… take it from?”
“You mean, who did I steal it from? Let’s say it plainly. Yes, I basically stole it. If you want to say ‘took,’ fine, but I see it as stealing. And last night I finally stole it for good.”
“Last night? But you said you got it a month ago…?”

“Yes, but not from my father. Don’t worry, I didn’t take it from him. I stole it from her. Let me explain without interruptions, because this is hard for me. A month ago, Katerina Ivanovna—my former fiancée—sent for me. You know her, right?”
“Yes, of course.”
“I know you do. She’s a truly noble person. But she’s hated me for a long time, and for good reason!”
“Katerina Ivanovna!” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, surprised. The prosecutor looked astonished too.

“Please, don’t say her name like that! I’m a jerk for bringing her into this. I knew she hated me, even from the very first time we met at my place… But that’s not important now. The point is, she sent for me a month ago and gave me three thousand roubles to send to her sister and another relative in Moscow—though she could have sent it herself! It was right when I had just fallen for someone else—her, Grushenka—she’s downstairs now. I took Grushenka here to Mokroe and blew half the three thousand in two days, but I kept the other half with me. I kept that fifteen hundred sewn up around my neck, like a locket, but yesterday I took it off and spent it. The eight hundred roubles you have now, Nikolay Parfenovitch, is what’s left from the fifteen hundred I had yesterday.”
“Wait a second. That can’t be right. When you were here a month ago, you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred—everyone knows that.”
“Who actually knows? Who counted the money? Did I let anyone count it?”
“But you told everyone yourself that you spent exactly three thousand.”

“Yeah, I did. I told the whole town, and everyone here at Mokroe thought it was three thousand. But I didn’t spend all of it—just fifteen hundred. I sewed up the other fifteen hundred. That’s where the money came from yesterday.”
“This is almost unbelievable,” Nikolay Parfenovitch muttered.
“Let me ask,” the prosecutor finally said, “did you tell anyone else about this? That you had fifteen hundred left a month ago?”
“I didn’t tell anyone.”
“Really? Absolutely no one?”
“No one at all.”

“Why keep it such a secret? What was your reason? You finally told us this secret you call ‘disgraceful,’ but really—well, at least in my view—taking three thousand roubles that belonged to someone else, and only for a while, is reckless but not as shameful as you think. Even if it was really wrong, many people already guessed this past month that you’d spent Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand. I heard the rumor myself. Mihail Makarovitch heard it too, so it wasn’t just a rumor but something everyone was saying. There are even hints that you told someone yourself it was Katerina Ivanovna’s money. So it’s very odd that you kept the fifteen hundred such a secret, and that it upset you so much. You even yelled that you’d rather go to Siberia than admit it…”
The prosecutor stopped. He was irritated, and didn’t hide his annoyance. He spoke in a rushed, jumbled way, not picking his words.
“It’s not the fifteen hundred that’s shameful,” said Mitya firmly, “it’s that I kept it separate from the rest of the three thousand.”

“Why?” the prosecutor asked, annoyed. “What’s so shameful about putting aside half of what you took? Taking the three thousand is the big issue. Why did you split it up? What was your goal? Can you explain?”
“Oh, gentlemen, that’s the whole point!” Mitya cried. “I put it aside because I was being sneaky. Saving some for later, that’s what’s really shameful. I’ve been disgusted with myself for a month.”
“That doesn’t make sense.”

“I’m surprised at you. But I’ll try to explain. Maybe it really doesn’t make sense to you. Listen. I’m trusted with three thousand roubles, and I blow it all on a wild spree. The next morning, I go to her and say, ‘Katya, I wasted your three thousand.’ That’s bad, right? It’s cowardly and selfish, but at least I’m not a thief—I just lost it. Now, another option: I spend only fifteen hundred, half of it, and the next day, I give the rest back—‘Katya, take this fifteen hundred. I’m a jerk, but at least I’m giving some back. Keep it away from me so I don’t waste it, too.’ I’d still be a jerk, but not a thief, because I brought back what was left. She’d see I was trying to make up for it. So, I’d be selfish, but not a full-on thief. You see the difference?”
“I get that there’s a difference,” said the prosecutor coldly. “But it’s odd you think it’s so important.”

“Yes, it matters to me! Anyone can be a jerk sometimes, but not everyone’s a thief. It takes something worse to be a thief. I can’t explain it well, but I believe a thief is lower than a scoundrel. Look, I carried that money for a month. I kept thinking I might give it back, so I wasn’t totally a thief yet. But every day I didn’t give it back, I hated myself. Is that right? Do you get it?”

“No, that’s not right, and I can see why you feel that way,” the prosecutor answered carefully. “But let’s move on. You still haven’t told us why you split the money, spending half and hiding the other. What were you planning to do with the fifteen hundred you hid? I need you to answer that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, of course!” Mitya cried, smacking his forehead. “Sorry, I’m dragging this out and not explaining the main thing. The real reason is the shameful part! It was all about my father. He was always after Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka), and I was jealous. I thought maybe she was choosing between us. So I kept thinking, what if she suddenly picks me and says, ‘I love you, let’s run away together.’ But I only had forty copecks—how could I take her anywhere? I thought she wanted money, and that she’d never forgive me for being poor. So I counted out half that three thousand, hid it, and then got drunk on the rest. That was the selfish part. Now do you get it?”
Both lawyers burst out laughing.
“Honestly, I’d say it was smart and even responsible not to waste it all,” chuckled Nikolay Parfenovitch. “So what’s the big deal?”

“The big deal is that I stole it! You’re scaring me by not understanding! Every day I had that fifteen hundred around my neck, I kept telling myself, ‘You’re a thief!’ That’s why I was angry all month, why I fought in the tavern, why I fought with my father. Because I felt like a thief. I couldn’t even tell my brother Alyosha about it—I felt like a pickpocket. But at the same time, every hour, I thought, ‘Maybe I’m not a thief if I give it back.’ And yesterday, I finally tore the money off my neck, right before going to Perhotin’s from Fenya’s. Until then, I just couldn’t do it. And as soon as I spent it, I became a full-on thief, for the rest of my life. Why? Because now I couldn’t go to Katya and say, ‘I’m a jerk, but not a thief.’ Do you understand now?”
“What made you decide to do it yesterday?” Nikolay Parfenovitch interrupted.

“Why? That’s a silly question. Because I’d decided to kill myself at five in the morning, at dawn. I thought it didn’t matter anymore if I died a thief or an honest man. But now I see it does matter. What tortured me most last night wasn’t that I’d killed the old servant, or that I was facing Siberia when my love was finally working out. Yes, that was hard, but not like the horrible feeling that I’d finally spent that hidden money and become a real thief! I swear, gentlemen, I learned a lot last night. It’s not just impossible to live as a jerk, but even to die as one. You have to die honest.”
Mitya looked pale. His face was drawn and tired, even though he was still full of energy.

“I’m starting to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said quietly, almost kindly. “But honestly, I think this is just your nerves. Why didn’t you just go and give the fifteen hundred back to the woman who trusted you? And if things were really so bad for you, why not explain everything to her and ask her to lend you the money you needed? She would have given it to you, especially if you gave her some sort of guarantee, maybe even the security you tried to give to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. You still think that security is worth something, right?”
Mitya’s face turned red.
“Do you really think I’m that much of a scoundrel? You can’t be serious!” he said angrily, looking the prosecutor straight in the eye.
“I promise you, I’m serious. Why do you think I’m not?”

“That would have been disgusting! You’re torturing me! Fine, I’ll admit everything, even the worst thoughts. You’ll see how low people’s minds can go. I actually did think of that plan—the one you just mentioned, prosecutor! I almost went to Katya to tell her what I’d done and ask her for money so I could run off with the other woman, Grushenka, who hated her. Can you imagine? Are you crazy?”
“I’m not crazy, but I suppose I didn’t think about how jealous she’d feel… maybe there really was some jealousy involved,” said the prosecutor, smiling a little.

“That would have been so horrible!” Mitya slammed his fist on the table. “So dirty! Yes, she might have given me the money, just to get revenge, to show how much she looked down on me—she’s got a fiery temper. And I would have taken it, too, just to betray her! Oh, God! I’m yelling because this thought just came to me a couple days ago, that night with Lyagavy and then all day yesterday, until… until that happened…”
“Until what happened?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, but Mitya didn’t hear him.

“I’ve made a terrible confession,” Mitya said, gloomy now. “You should appreciate that—and respect it.
