If you don’t, if it means nothing to you, then you clearly have no respect for me, and I’ll die of shame for telling you! Oh, I’ll shoot myself! I can see you don’t believe me. What, you want to write that down, too?” he cried, upset.

“Yes, what you just said,” Nikolay Parfenovitch replied, surprised. “That up to the last hour, you were thinking of begging Katerina Ivanovna for that money. That’s very important for us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, for the whole case—and especially for you.”
“Have a heart, gentlemen!” Mitya threw up his hands. “Don’t write that down, at least—not that! I’ve just opened up my soul to you, and now you’re poking at my wounds… Oh, God!”
In despair, he covered his face with his hands.

“Don’t worry, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said. “Everything we write down will be read back to you, and you can change what you don’t agree with. But now, let me ask you one more time: are you sure absolutely no one knew about the money you sewed up? It’s hard to believe.”
“No one, no one! I told you already! Leave me alone!”

“Alright, but we’ll get to the bottom of it. Meanwhile, remember: we have maybe a dozen witnesses who say you yourself told everyone you spent three thousand here—not fifteen hundred. And when you got the money yesterday, you made people think you’d brought three thousand with you.”
“You’ve got not dozens, but hundreds of witnesses! Two hundred! Thousands! Everyone’s heard it!” Mitya shouted.
“See, everyone says so. And ‘everyone’ means something.”
“It means nothing. I talked nonsense, and people repeated it.”
“But why did you ‘talk nonsense,’ as you put it?”

“Who knows? Maybe to brag about spending so much… Or to forget about the money hidden around my neck… Yeah, that was it… Ugh, how many times will you ask me that? I lied, and that was that. Why do people lie?”
“That’s a tough question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said seriously. “Tell me, was that ‘amulet’ on your neck a big thing?”
“No, not big.”
“How big, exactly?”
“About as big as a folded hundred-rouble note.”
“You should show us what’s left of it. You must have it somewhere.”
“Oh, come on! I don’t know where it is.”
“But wait: where and when did you take it off your neck? You said you didn’t go home.”
“When I was going from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s, I tore it off on my way and took out the money.”
“In the dark?”
“Why would I need a light? I did it with my fingers in a minute.”
“No scissors, in the street?”
“In the market-place, I think. Why would I need scissors? It was just an old rag. I ripped it off in a second.”
“Where did you put it after?”
“I dropped it there.”
“Where exactly?”
“In the market-place! Who knows where exactly? Why do you need to know?”
“That’s really important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It could be proof for you. Don’t you see that? Who helped you sew it up a month ago?”
“No one helped. I did it myself.”
“You can sew?”
“A soldier has to know how to sew. It wasn’t hard.”
“Where’d you get the rag you used to sew the money in?”
“Are you making fun of me?”
“Not at all. We’re not in the mood for jokes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“I don’t remember where I got the rag—somewhere, I guess.”
“You’d think you’d remember.”
“Honestly, I don’t. Maybe I tore a piece off my shirt.”
“That’s interesting. We could check your place tomorrow for a shirt or something with a piece missing. What kind of rag was it, cloth or linen?”
“Who knows? Wait… I think I didn’t tear it off anything. It was calico… I think I sewed it up in my landlady’s old cap.”
“In your landlady’s cap?”
“Yes. I took it from her.”
“How?”

“I remember once grabbing a cap just for a rag, maybe to wipe my pen. I didn’t ask because it was worthless. I tore it up and sewed the notes inside. I think it was that rag. It was old and washed a hundred times.”
“Are you sure about that now?”
“I’m not sure. I think it was the cap. But honestly, what does it matter?”
“Then your landlady should remember it’s missing?”
“No, she wouldn’t notice. It was just an old rag. Not even worth a penny.”
“Where did you get the needle and thread?”
“I’m done. I’m not saying anything else. That’s enough!” Mitya snapped, finally losing his temper.
“It’s odd you don’t remember at all where you threw the pieces in the market.”

“Tell them to sweep the marketplace tomorrow—maybe you’ll find it,” Mitya sneered. “Enough, gentlemen, enough!” he said, sounding exhausted. “I see you don’t believe me—not for a second. It’s my own fault. Why did I lower myself by confessing to you? This is just a joke to you. I can see it in your eyes. You led me into this, prosecutor. Go ahead, celebrate if you want… Curse you, torturers!”

He dropped his head and hid his face in his hands. The lawyers were silent. After a minute, Mitya looked up with a blank, hopeless expression. He sat there, mute, almost unaware of what was happening. Meanwhile, the lawyers had to carry on—they had to start questioning the witnesses. It was already eight in the morning. The lights had been out for a while. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who had been coming and going during the questioning, had now both left again. The lawyers themselves looked exhausted. The weather was miserable—the sky gray, and rain pouring down. Mitya stared blankly out the window.
“Can I look out the window?” he suddenly asked Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Of course, go ahead,” Nikolay answered.

Mitya got up and walked to the window. Rain hammered the greenish glass. He could see the muddy road below, and farther off, a row of shabby, black huts, looking even worse in the rain. Mitya thought of “Phoebus the golden-haired,” and how he’d planned to shoot himself at dawn. “Maybe it would be better on a morning like this,” he thought with a faint smile, and, lowering his hand, turned back to his “torturers.”

“Gentlemen,” he burst out, “I know I’m doomed! But what about her? Please, tell me about her. She doesn’t have to go down with me, does she? She’s innocent, you know! She was out of her mind last night when she said, ‘It’s all my fault!’ She didn’t do anything! I’ve been so worried about her all night while sitting here… Can’t you, won’t you tell me what will happen to her?”

“You don’t need to worry, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor replied quickly. “So far, we have no reason to involve the lady you care about. I hope it stays that way as the case goes on. We’ll do everything we can for her. You really don’t need to worry.”
“Thank you, gentlemen. I knew you were honest, decent people, despite everything. That’s a weight off my mind. Well, what now? I’m ready.”
“We need to hurry. We have to start questioning witnesses in your presence—so—”
“Shouldn’t we have some tea first?” Nikolay Parfenovitch cut in. “I think we’ve earned it!”

They decided that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had probably gone to get some), they’d have a glass and then get back to work, saving a proper breakfast for later. The tea was ready and soon brought up. At first, Mitya refused the glass Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered, but then he asked for it and drank it eagerly. He looked completely exhausted. With his strength, you’d think even a wild night wouldn’t wear him down, but he felt so weak he could barely hold his head up. Everything around him seemed to be spinning. “Any more of this and I’ll start losing my mind,” he thought to himself.

The questioning of the witnesses began. But from here on, we won’t go into as much detail as before. So, we won’t describe how Nikolay Parfenovitch reminded every witness to tell the truth and that they’d have to swear to it later, or how each person had to sign their statement, and so on. What mattered most in the questioning was the issue of the three thousand roubles: did Mitya spend three thousand or only fifteen hundred at Mokroe the first time, a month ago? And did he spend three thousand or fifteen hundred yesterday? Sadly for Mitya, every witness spoke against him. None helped his case, and some even brought up new, damaging information that contradicted Mitya’s own story.

The first witness was Trifon Borissovitch. He wasn’t nervous at all in front of the lawyers. In fact, he acted angry at Mitya, which made him seem honest and respectable. He spoke carefully, only answering when asked, and never rushed. He was certain that Mitya had spent at least three thousand roubles a month ago. Trifon said everyone in the area would say they heard Mitya mention “three thousand.” “He threw away so much money just on the gypsy girls! Probably a thousand on them alone.”
Mitya muttered gloomily, “I don’t think I gave them even five hundred. I wish I’d counted, but I was drunk…”
Mitya sat sideways, his back to the curtains. He listened with a tired, sad look, as if he wanted to say:
“Say whatever you want. It doesn’t matter anymore.”

“It was more than a thousand, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Trifon insisted. “You were throwing it around, and they just grabbed it. The gypsies were a crooked bunch—they steal horses! They’ve been chased away now, but if they were here, they’d tell you how much they got. I saw the money in your hands myself—didn’t count it, you wouldn’t let me, but by the look of it, it was way more than fifteen hundred. We know what money looks like. We can tell.”
As for the money spent yesterday, Trifon said that Mitya himself told him when he arrived that he had brought three thousand.
“Come on, Trifon Borissovitch,” said Mitya. “Did I really say I’d brought three thousand? I don’t think I was that sure.”

“You did say it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it in front of Andrey. Andrey is still here—call him! And when you were buying drinks for the singers in the hall, you shouted you’d leave your ‘sixth thousand’ here—that means, with what you spent before. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing right next to you. Maybe he remembers.”
The “sixth thousand” comment really caught the lawyers’ attention. They liked this way of adding it up: three thousand before, three thousand now—that makes six. It seemed clear to them.

They called all the witnesses Trifon suggested: Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver all backed up what Trifon said. They especially wrote down what Andrey said about his talk with Mitya on the road: “ ‘Where am I going, Andrey?’ Mitya asked, ‘To heaven or hell, will I be forgiven or not?’ ”
Ippolit Kirillovitch, who was interested in people’s minds, listened with a sly smile and finally said these questions about Mitya’s fate should be “added to the case.”

When Kalganov was called in, he came unwillingly, looking annoyed, and acted like he didn’t even know the lawyers, though he saw them every day. He started by saying, “I know nothing about it and don’t want to.” But he had heard about the “sixth thousand,” and admitted he was nearby when it was said. He claimed he didn’t know how much money Mitya had. He said the Poles had cheated at cards. Asked again and again, he said that after the Poles were thrown out, things got better between Mitya and Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka), and that she said she loved him. He spoke about Grushenka with respect, like she was a lady from high society, and never called her by her nickname. Even though Kalganov clearly hated giving evidence, Ippolit Kirillovitch made him talk for a long time and got all the details of Mitya’s “romance” that night. Mitya never interrupted. Finally, they let Kalganov go, and he left, obviously angry.

The Poles were questioned next. Even though they’d gone to bed, they hadn’t slept and got dressed quickly when the police arrived, knowing they’d be called in. They answered with dignity, though they seemed a bit nervous. The little Pole turned out to be a retired official, Pan Mussyalovitch, who used to work as a vet in Siberia. Pan Vrublevsky was an uncertified dentist. Even though Nikolay Parfenovitch asked them questions, they answered Mihail Makarovitch instead, mistaking him for the boss, and called him “Pan Colonel” every time. Only after Mihail Makarovitch told them several times did they realize they should speak to Nikolay Parfenovitch. They could speak Russian pretty well, except with an accent. Pan Mussyalovitch spoke proudly about his relationship with Grushenka, which made Mitya angry, and he shouted that he wouldn’t let that “scoundrel” talk like that in front of him. Pan Mussyalovitch pointed out the insult and wanted it written down. Mitya was furious.
“He is a scoundrel! A scoundrel! Write that down. And write down that even with the official record, I still say he’s a scoundrel!” Mitya yelled.

Nikolay Parfenovitch did write this down, but he handled things carefully. After scolding Mitya, he quickly moved on from the romantic stuff to the important things. The lawyers were especially interested in one thing the Poles said: that Mitya tried to pay off Pan Mussyalovitch in that very room, offering him three thousand roubles to give up his claim, with seven hundred right then and the rest—two thousand three hundred—the next day in town. Mitya had sworn he didn’t have all the money at Mokroe, but that it was in town. Mitya insisted angrily that he never promised to pay the rest for sure. But Pan Vrublevsky confirmed the story, and after thinking, Mitya frowned and admitted that maybe he had said it, since he was excited at the time.

The prosecutor jumped on this. It seemed to prove that maybe some of the three thousand Mitya got was hidden in town, or even somewhere at Mokroe. This would explain why they only found eight hundred roubles on him—a detail that, until now, had been the only thing helping Mitya’s case. Now even this was against him. When the prosecutor asked where Mitya would get the rest of the money, since he had denied having more than fifteen hundred, Mitya said he planned to offer the “little guy” not cash, but legal rights to the village of Tchermashnya, which he had already tried to give to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor just smiled at this “innocent trick.”
“And you really think he’d accept legal rights instead of two thousand three hundred in cash?”

“He definitely would,” Mitya answered passionately. “He could have gotten not just two thousand, but four or six from it! He’d have his lawyers—both Poles and Jews—work on it, and could take not just three thousand, but maybe the whole property from my father.”

All of Pan Mussyalovitch’s statement was written down carefully. Then the Poles were let go. The card cheating was barely mentioned—Nikolay Parfenovitch was happy enough with their evidence and didn’t want to bother them with small details. Besides, it was just a silly, drunken fight. There had been enough drinking and trouble that night. So, the Poles kept the two hundred roubles.

Next was old Maximov. He came in nervously, looking messy and sad. He’d spent all this time downstairs with Grushenka, just sitting by her and sometimes crying and wiping his eyes with a blue checkered handkerchief. Grushenka had even tried to comfort him. Maximov quickly admitted he’d done wrong, that he’d borrowed “ten roubles because I was poor,” from Mitya, and was ready to pay it back. Asked directly if he saw how much money Mitya had, since he’d taken a note from him, Maximov insisted there was twenty thousand.
“Have you ever seen twenty thousand before?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, smiling.

“Sure, not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged our little place. She only let me see it from a distance, showing off. It was a thick bundle, all colorful notes. Mitya’s money looked the same—rainbow-colored.”

Maximov wasn’t kept long. Finally, it was Grushenka’s turn. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed worried about how her appearance might affect Mitya and whispered a warning to him, but Mitya nodded silently to show he wouldn’t cause trouble. Mihail Makarovitch himself brought Grushenka in. She entered with a serious, almost calm face, and sat quietly, wrapping herself tightly in her fancy black shawl. She was very pale, shivering with a slight fever—the first sign of the long sickness she would have after that night. Her serious air, honest look, and calm manners made a great impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little enchanted. Later, he admitted he only then realized “how beautiful she was,” since he’d always thought of her as just a “local floozy” before. “She acts like a real lady,” he said excitedly to some women later, but they were shocked and called him “naughty,” which secretly pleased him.

As she entered, Grushenka glanced at Mitya just for a second—he looked at her nervously, but her face calmed him right away. After the usual questions and warnings, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, very politely, what kind of relationship she had with Mitya. Grushenka answered firmly and calmly:

“He was just someone I knew. He visited me as a friend in the last month.” When asked more, she answered honestly that, while she sometimes found him attractive, she didn’t love him; she had won his heart and his father’s, “just to be mean.” She knew Mitya was jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and everyone else, but that just amused her. She never planned to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch—she was just joking. “I wasn’t thinking about either of them for the last month. I was waiting for another man who had hurt me. But I don’t think you need to ask about that, and I don’t need to answer—it’s my business.”

Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly took her hint, dropped the “romantic” questions, and got to the main point: the three thousand roubles. Grushenka confirmed that three thousand were definitely spent during the first party at Mokroe, and though she hadn’t counted it herself, she’d heard Mitya say it.
“Did he tell you this alone, or in front of others, or did you just overhear him say it?” the prosecutor asked.
Grushenka said she’d heard him say it both in front of others and when they were alone.
“Did he say it to you alone once, or several times?” the prosecutor continued. Grushenka answered that he’d told her several times.
Ippolit Kirillovitch was very pleased with this answer. As they kept questioning, they found out Grushenka also knew where the money came from—Mitya got it from Katerina Ivanovna.
“And did you ever hear that the money spent a month ago was less than three thousand, and that Mitya had kept half for himself?”
“No, I never heard that,” Grushenka replied.
In fact, Mitya often told her he had no money at all.
“He was always hoping to get some from his father,” Grushenka finished.
“Did he ever say, even as a joke or when he was upset,” Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly asked, “that he wanted to hurt or kill his father?”
“Oh, he did say that,” Grushenka sighed.
“Once or several times?”
“Several times, but always when he was angry.”
“Did you ever believe he would actually do it?”
“No, I never believed it,” she said firmly. “I trusted his good heart.”
“Gentlemen, please,” Mitya suddenly said, “let me say one word to Agrafena Alexandrovna, here with you all.”
“Go ahead,” Nikolay Parfenovitch agreed.
“Agrafena Alexandrovna!” Mitya stood up. “Trust God and trust me. I did not kill my father!”

After saying that, Mitya sat down. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself in front of the icon. “Thank you, Lord,” she said emotionally, and still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:
“Believe what he just said! I know him. He might joke or be stubborn, but he would never lie against his conscience. He’s telling the truth, I’m sure of it.”
“Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you’ve given me hope again,” Mitya said, his voice shaking.

As for the money spent yesterday, Grushenka said she didn’t know the amount but heard Mitya tell several people he had three thousand with him. When asked where he got it, she said he told her he “stole” it from Katerina Ivanovna, and she told him he hadn’t really stolen it and must pay it back the next day. When the prosecutor asked whether the money he said he stole from Katerina Ivanovna was what he spent yesterday or a month ago, she said he meant the money spent a month ago—that’s how she understood him.
Grushenka was finally allowed to leave. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly told her she could return to town right away, and if she wanted any help—like horses or an escort—he would be happy to—
“Thank you very much,” Grushenka said, bowing. “I’m going back to town with this old gentleman, and if it’s okay, I’ll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

She left. Mitya was calm and even seemed happier, but only for a moment. He felt weaker and weaker, as if something weighed him down. His eyes were heavy with exhaustion. The witness questioning was finally over. They started reviewing the written statements. Mitya got up, moved to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a chest covered with a rug, and fell asleep instantly.
He had a strange dream, totally out of place for where he was and what was happening.

He was traveling somewhere out on the steppe, where he had been stationed long ago. A peasant was driving him in a cart with two horses, through snow and cold rain. Mitya was freezing—it was early November, and big, wet flakes of snow were falling, melting as soon as they hit the ground. The peasant, who had a light-colored long beard and looked about fifty, wore a gray smock. Not far away was a village with black huts, half of them burnt down, just charred beams sticking up. As they entered, peasant women stood along the road, a long row of them, all thin, tired, with brownish faces. One at the edge was tall and bony, looked forty but could have been twenty, with a thin face. She held a wailing baby, and her breasts were so empty there was no milk. The baby cried and cried, stretching out its little bare arms, fists blue from the cold.
“Why are they crying? Why are they crying?” Mitya asked as they sped by.
“It’s the baby,” the driver said. “The baby is weeping.”
Mitya noticed the peasant used the word “babe,” and it touched him. The way the man said it sounded even more caring.
“But why is it crying?” Mitya asked again. “Why are its arms bare? Why don’t they wrap it up?”
“The baby’s cold. Its little clothes are frozen and don’t keep it warm.”
“But why? Why?” Mitya kept on, confused.
“Because they’re poor. Their house burned down. They have no bread. They’re begging because they lost everything.”

“No, no,” Mitya still didn’t get it. “Tell me, why are those poor mothers standing there? Why are people poor? Why is the baby poor? Why is the steppe so empty? Why don’t they hold each other and kiss? Why don’t they sing with joy? Why are they so dark and miserable? Why don’t they feed the baby?”

He felt that even if his questions made no sense, he had to ask them. He felt a powerful wave of pity rising inside him, stronger than ever before. He wanted to cry, to help them all, so the baby would stop weeping, so the dried-up mother would smile, so no one would cry again, ever. He wanted to do it right now, with all the wildness of the Karamazovs.

“And I’m coming with you. I won’t leave you now, not ever. I’m coming with you,” he suddenly heard Grushenka’s loving voice beside him. His heart filled with hope, and he reached for the light, longing to live, to keep going, to hurry forward into the new, inviting light—right now!

“What? Where?” he said, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest like he’d just woken from a dream, smiling. Nikolay Parfenovitch stood over him, saying he should listen to the protocol being read and sign it. Mitya realized he’d been asleep for an hour or more, but he didn’t really listen—he suddenly noticed there was a pillow under his head, which hadn’t been there when he first lay down, so tired.
“Who put this pillow under my head? Who was so kind?” he cried out, his voice full of grateful tears, as if someone had done him a huge favor.

He never found out who did it—maybe one of the peasants or Nikolay Parfenovitch’s secretary—someone had felt sorry for him and given him a pillow. But Mitya’s whole heart was trembling with emotion. He went to the table and said he’d sign whatever they wanted.
“I had a good dream, gentlemen,” he said in an odd voice, but with a new light of happiness in his face.

When the official papers were signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned to Mitya (Dmitri) with a serious look and read out the “Committal.” It explained that on a certain date, in a certain place, the investigator from the local court had questioned Dmitri, who was accused of several crimes (each charge was listed in detail). Since Dmitri hadn’t confessed or provided a real defense, and since the witnesses and the facts seemed to point against him, the law said he should be locked up to keep him from escaping before his trial. This decision would be shared with both Dmitri and the deputy prosecutor.

In other words, Mitya was told that he was now officially a prisoner. He’d be taken straight to town and locked in a place that wouldn’t be pleasant at all. Mitya listened carefully, then just shrugged.
“Well, gentlemen, I don’t blame you. I’m ready. I get it—you don’t have any other choice.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch told him gently that he’d be escorted right away by Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, the rural police officer who happened to be there.
“Wait,” Mitya suddenly cut in, unable to hold back his feelings anymore. He turned to everyone in the room and spoke out:

“Gentlemen, we’re all cruel, we’re all a little monstrous. We make people cry—children, mothers, everyone. But let’s be honest, I’m the worst of all! I’ve promised to be better, but I keep doing the same awful things. Now I realize that guys like me need something huge to snap them out of it, something like fate grabbing them and forcing them to stop. I never would’ve changed on my own! But now, fate has struck. I accept the pain of being accused and shamed in public. I want to suffer, because maybe suffering will make me better. Maybe I’ll be purified, gentlemen. But listen, one last time: I’m not guilty of my father’s murder. I accept my punishment, not because I killed him, but because I wanted to—and maybe I could have. Still, I’m going to fight you on this. I warn you. I’ll fight all the way, and then God will decide. Goodbye, gentlemen. Please don’t be mad at me for yelling during the questioning. I was still such a fool then. In a minute I’ll be a prisoner, but right now, for the last time as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. As I say goodbye to you, I say it to all people.”
His voice shook as he reached out his hand, but Nikolay Parfenovitch, who was closest, quickly hid his hands behind his back, almost nervously. Mitya noticed right away and dropped his hand.

“The investigation isn’t over yet,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, sounding a bit awkward and embarrassed. “We’ll continue in town, and of course, I hope you succeed... in your defense. Honestly, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I’ve always thought of you as more unlucky than truly bad. I think everyone here would agree—you’re basically an honorable young man, but you’ve gotten carried away by your passions a bit too much...”

By the end of his speech, Nikolay Parfenovitch, though a small man, seemed almost grand. Mitya thought that in another minute this “boy” would take him aside to talk about girls again. It was strange, but even on the way to prison, weird and random thoughts can pop into your head.
“Gentlemen, you’re kind, you’re good people. May I see her—just to say goodbye one last time?” Mitya asked.
“Of course, but considering... well, now it’s only possible if we’re present—”
“Oh, well. If that’s how it has to be, so be it!”
Grushenka was brought in. The goodbye was short, with only a few words, and it didn’t really satisfy Nikolay Parfenovitch. Grushenka bowed deeply to Mitya.
“I told you I’m yours, and I will be. I’ll follow you forever, no matter where they send you. Goodbye. You’re innocent, even if you’ve messed up your own life.”
Her lips trembled and tears rolled down her cheeks.
“Forgive me, Grusha, for loving you, for ruining your life with my love.”

Mitya wanted to say more, but stopped himself and left the room. Immediately, he was surrounded by guards watching his every move. At the bottom of the steps—where, just yesterday, he had arrived in a rush with Andrey’s three horses—two carts were waiting. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a stocky, wrinkled man, seemed upset about something unexpected and was yelling angrily. He told Mitya to get in the cart, sounding extra grumpy.

“He looked so different when I was buying him drinks at the tavern,” thought Mitya as he climbed in. At the gates, a crowd of peasants, women, and drivers had gathered. Trifon Borissovitch came down the steps too. Everyone stared at Mitya.
“Forgive me as I leave, good people!” Mitya suddenly shouted from the cart.
“Forgive us too!” he heard a couple of people call back.
“Goodbye to you, too, Trifon Borissovitch!”

But Trifon Borissovitch didn’t even look around. Maybe he was just too busy. He was yelling and running around, trying to sort something out. The second cart, which two policemen were supposed to ride in with Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, wasn’t ready yet. The peasant driver was arguing that it wasn’t his turn, but Akim’s. But no one could find Akim. They ran off to look for him while the first peasant begged them to wait.

“See how our peasants are, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch? They have no shame!” said Trifon Borissovitch. “Akim gave you twenty-five copecks two days ago. You drank it all, and now you complain. I’m amazed at your patience with our lowly peasants, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, that’s all I can say.”
“But why do we even need a second cart?” Mitya asked. “Let’s just go in this one, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. I won’t cause trouble, I won’t run away from you, man. Why do we need an escort?”

“I’d appreciate it if you learned how to talk to me properly,” snapped Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, clearly enjoying the chance to be angry. “I’m not ‘man’ to you, and you can keep your advice to yourself!”
Mitya went quiet, blushing all over. Suddenly, he felt very cold. The rain had stopped, but the sky was still gray and windy, and the cold wind hit him right in the face.
“I’m catching a chill,” thought Mitya, shivering.
Finally, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch climbed into the cart with a heavy thud, accidentally squishing Mitya into the corner. The officer was clearly grumpy and really didn’t like having this job.
“Goodbye, Trifon Borissovitch!” Mitya shouted again, but this time, he felt it wasn’t out of kindness—it was because he was upset.
Trifon Borissovitch stood tall, hands behind his back, staring at Mitya with a stern and angry face. He didn’t reply.
Suddenly, Mitya heard Kalganov’s voice: “Goodbye, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, goodbye!” Kalganov had run out, no cap on, and hurried to the cart, reaching out his hand to Mitya.
Mitya quickly grabbed and squeezed his hand.
“Goodbye, my friend! I’ll never forget your kindness,” he said warmly.
But the cart started moving, and their hands separated. The bell rang, and Mitya was taken away.

Kalganov ran back inside, sat in a corner, put his head in his hands, and started to cry. He sat there for a long time, crying like a little boy, even though he was twenty. Deep down, he almost definitely believed Mitya was guilty.
“What kind of people are these? How can people be like this?” he muttered, lost in sadness, nearly in despair. Right then, he didn’t want to keep living.
“Is it worth it? Is it worth it?” Kalganov said, broken-hearted.

It was early November. There had been a hard frost—about eleven degrees on the Réaumur scale—but there wasn’t any real snow, just a light dusting that had fallen overnight. A sharp, dry wind was blowing the powdery snow through the gloomy streets of our town, especially around the market square. The morning was gray and dull, but the snow had stopped falling.

Not far from the market, right next to Plotnikov's shop, there was a small, very tidy house. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, the widow of a provincial secretary who had died fourteen years before. She was still a good-looking woman of thirty-two and lived quietly on her own savings in her neat house. She kept to herself, but she was gentle and fairly cheerful. When her husband died, she was only eighteen, married for just a year, and had just given birth to their son. From that day on, she put all her energy into raising her beloved Kolya. Even though she loved him deeply for fourteen years, Kolya had given her more worry than happiness. She was always terrified he’d get sick, catch a cold, get into trouble, or hurt himself climbing somewhere he shouldn’t. When Kolya started school, she began studying all his subjects so she could help him with his homework. She hurried to meet his teachers and even tried to befriend his classmates and their parents, hoping it would keep them from teasing or bullying Kolya. But she went so far that the other boys started picking on him for being such a “mama’s boy.”

But Kolya could stand up for himself. He was a determined kid—people at school said he was “super strong,” and he really was. He was quick, stubborn, bold, and always looking for adventure. He was smart, and some people said he could even beat their teacher, Dardanelov, at math and history. Even though he sometimes acted superior, he was still a good friend and wasn’t stuck-up. He accepted the respect of his classmates but treated them well. He knew how far he could go and never crossed the line with teachers—he didn’t mess around so much that he’d get in big trouble. But he loved causing a stir, not just for mischief’s sake, but because he wanted to stand out and be noticed. He was very vain. He even managed to make his mother do whatever he wanted; he practically ruled the house. She always gave in to him, and her biggest fear was that he didn’t really love her. She was always worried Kolya was “cold” to her and would sometimes burst into tears, accusing him of not caring. Kolya hated this, and the more she demanded affection, the more he seemed to avoid it—not on purpose, but just because that was his personality. His mother was wrong; he really did love her. He just didn’t like what he called “mushy stuff.”

There was a bookcase in the house with a few books that had belonged to his father. Kolya loved to read and had read several of them on his own. His mother didn’t mind, but she was sometimes surprised to see him reading for hours instead of going out to play. Because of this, Kolya ended up reading some books that weren’t really meant for a boy his age.

Even though Kolya usually knew when to stop with his tricks, lately he’d started pulling pranks that really scared his mother. There was nothing truly bad or mean about them, but they were wild and reckless.

That July, during summer break, Kolya and his mother visited a distant relative who lived about forty-five miles away. Her husband worked at the train station—the same one Ivan Fyodorovich Karamazov would leave from to go to Moscow a month later. Kolya immediately got interested in everything about the trains, hoping he could impress his school friends when he got back. There were other boys around, some living at the station, some nearby, about six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, with two from Kolya’s own town. They played together, and on the fourth or fifth day, the boys made a crazy bet. Kolya, who was almost the youngest and kind of looked down on by the older boys, wanted to prove himself, so he bet two rubles that he would lie down between the rails at night and let the eleven o’clock train pass right over him—without moving. They checked first and thought it was possible to lie flat enough that the train wouldn’t hit you, but it was still a terrifying idea. Kolya insisted he could do it. At first, the others laughed and called him a liar and a show-off, but that just made him want to prove them wrong. What bothered him most was that the older boys treated him like a little kid, and he couldn’t stand that.

So, they decided to do it that night, half a mile from the station to make sure the train would be moving at full speed. The boys gathered. It was pitch black—no moon at all. When the time came, Kolya lay down between the rails, while the others waited hidden in the bushes, their hearts pounding with nervous excitement that soon turned to fear and regret. Finally, they heard the train coming from the station, the rails shaking. Two red lights appeared in the darkness, and the huge train roared closer.

“Run! Get off the tracks!” the boys shouted from the bushes, terrified. But it was too late—the train sped by. The boys dashed over to Kolya. He was lying there, not moving. They pulled at him and tried to get him up. Suddenly, he stood up and walked away without saying a word. Later, he explained that he’d pretended to be out cold just to scare them, but he eventually admitted to his mother that he had really fainted from fear. That night, Kolya earned a reputation as a “daredevil” for good. He went back to the house as pale as a ghost. The next day, he had a mild fever, but he was in a great mood and proud of himself. People didn’t hear about the stunt right away, but after they returned to town, the story got around the school and even reached the teachers. Kolya’s mother begged the teachers to forgive him, and in the end, Dardanelov, a respected teacher, spoke up for him, so the whole thing was quietly ignored.

Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been secretly in love with Madame Krassotkin for years. About a year before, trembling with nerves, he had asked her to marry him, but she gently refused, feeling it would be a betrayal of her son—even though Dardanelov had reason to believe she didn’t actually dislike him. Kolya’s crazy stunt broke the ice a little, and because Dardanelov helped him, Madame Krassotkin gave him a small hint of hope—not much, but enough to make the shy and proper Dardanelov happy for now. He liked Kolya, though he thought it was beneath him to try to win the boy over, and was always strict with him at school. Kolya, in turn, kept a respectful distance. He did his work well and was second best in class, but he was reserved with Dardanelov. Everyone at school believed Kolya was so good at history that he could even “beat” Dardanelov. Once, Kolya asked him, “Who founded Troy?” Dardanelov gave a vague answer about old legends and migrations, but couldn’t name the people who actually founded Troy, and seemed to think the question was silly. The kids all thought this meant Dardanelov didn’t know the answer. Kolya had read about Troy’s founders in a book called Smaragdov from his father’s collection. Soon, all the boys got interested in the question, but Kolya wouldn’t tell his secret, and his reputation for being super smart stayed strong.

After the train incident, Kolya started acting differently toward his mother. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) found out what her son had done, she was so horrified she nearly lost her mind. She had terrible hysterical fits that lasted for days. Kolya, finally scared by her reaction, promised on his honor never to do anything like that again. He swore on his knees, in front of a holy icon, and by the memory of his father, just as his mother asked. The “tough” Kolya broke down in tears like a little kid. All day, mother and son kept hugging and crying. The next day, Kolya went back to acting “unfeeling,” but he was now quieter, more serious, and thoughtful.

Six weeks later, he got caught up in another mess—a silly one this time—that even brought his name to the Justice of the Peace, but he wasn’t the ringleader, just involved by accident. (That story comes later.) His mother kept worrying, but Dardanelov’s hopes for romance grew with every scare. Kolya knew exactly how Dardanelov felt about his mother and, of course, secretly looked down on him for it. In the past, he’d even hinted to his mother that he knew what Dardanelov was after. But after the train incident, Kolya stopped making sly comments or acting rude, and started speaking more respectfully about Dardanelov in front of his mother—a change that she noticed and deeply appreciated. Still, if anyone mentioned Dardanelov while Kolya was in the room, she would blush bright pink. At those moments, Kolya would either stare angrily out the window, fuss with his boots, or yell for “Perezvon,” the big, scruffy dog he’d found a month earlier and secretly kept at home, never showing him to any of his friends. Kolya bossed the dog around, teaching him tricks until the poor animal howled when Kolya was away, and went wild with happiness when Kolya came home—spinning, begging, playing dead, and doing all the tricks, not just on command, but out of pure excitement and love for his boy.

Oh, and I almost forgot: Kolya Krassotkin was the boy who got stabbed with a penknife by Captain Snegiryov’s son, Ilusha—the same Ilusha who had stood up for his father when the other boys teased him and called him “wisp of tow.”

On that cold, snowy, and windy November day, Kolya Krassotkin was at home. It was Sunday, so there was no school. The clock had just struck eleven, and Kolya really wanted to go out on what he called “very important business.” But he was stuck at home in charge, because all the adults were gone due to something unusual that had happened. Madame Krassotkin had rented out two small rooms (separated from the rest of the house by a hallway) to a doctor’s wife and her two young kids. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna and was a close friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had left a year ago, first going to Orenburg and then to Tashkent, and she hadn’t heard from him in six months. If it wasn’t for Madame Krassotkin’s friendship, which helped her feel a little better, the poor lady probably would have cried herself away by now. And then, to make things worse, her only servant, Katerina, suddenly announced the night before that she was about to have a baby—something nobody had noticed could happen so soon. The doctor’s wife was shocked, but quickly decided to take Katerina to a place in town run by a midwife for situations like this. She cared a lot about her servant, so she did this right away and stayed there to help. By the next morning, Madame Krassotkin was busy too, trying to help and ask others for assistance.

So now, both women were out of the house, and the Krassotkins’ servant, Agafya, had gone to the market. That left Kolya in charge for a while, especially to look after “the kids”—the doctor’s wife’s son and daughter—who were alone. Kolya wasn’t worried about taking care of the house. Plus, he had Perezvon, his dog, who was ordered to stay very still under the bench in the hall. Every time Kolya walked by, Perezvon would wag his tail and thump it on the floor, hoping Kolya would whistle and let him out, but Kolya just gave him a serious look and the dog would go quiet again. The only thing Kolya didn’t like was having to watch “the kids.” He thought Katerina’s surprise pregnancy was ridiculous, but he actually really liked the two “kiddies” and had already brought them a picture book. Nastya, the older girl who was eight, could read, and Kostya, her seven-year-old brother, liked when she read to him. Kolya could have played more exciting games with them—like playing soldiers or hide and seek—like he’d done before. In fact, someone at school once said Kolya even played “horses” with the little lodgers, pretending to be a horse himself! But Kolya had defended himself, saying it would be embarrassing to play like that with kids his own age, but it was fine for the younger ones because he liked them, and nobody could judge him for that. The two kids adored Kolya.

But today, Kolya wasn’t in the mood to play games. He had something important and secret to do. Time kept passing, but Agafya still hadn’t come back from the market. He’d already crossed the hall a few times, opened the door to the lodgers’ room, and checked on the kids, who were sitting with their book just like he’d told them. Every time he opened the door, they smiled at him, hoping he’d come in and do something fun, but Kolya was too preoccupied and didn’t go in.

When it finally struck eleven, Kolya decided that if “that useless” Agafya didn’t come back in ten minutes, he would just go out anyway, after making the kids promise to be brave and not get into trouble or cry while he was gone. With this plan, he put on his thick winter coat with a fur collar, swung his satchel over his shoulder, and totally ignored his mother’s usual advice to wear galoshes in the cold—he looked at them with disgust and went out in just his boots. Perezvon saw him getting ready and started thumping his tail on the floor, trembling with excitement and even whining a little. But Kolya, seeing how worked up Perezvon was, decided it was undisciplined and made him wait another minute before finally whistling for him. The dog shot out from under the bench and raced ahead, thrilled.

Kolya opened the door to check on the kids. They were still sitting at the table, not reading but arguing about something. The two often debated big questions about life, and Nastya, being older, usually won. If Kostya disagreed, he’d appeal to Kolya, whose opinion they both trusted completely. This time, their argument caught Kolya’s attention, and he paused in the hallway to listen. The kids noticed and started arguing even more energetically, hoping to impress him.
“I’ll never, ever believe,” Nastya chattered, “that old women find babies in the cabbage patch. It’s winter now—there aren’t even any cabbages! So how could the old woman bring Katerina a baby?”
Kolya quietly whistled to himself.
“Or maybe they do bring babies from somewhere,” Nastya went on, “but only to people who are married.”
Kostya stared at Nastya, thinking hard.
“Nastya, you’re being silly!” he finally said, calmly. “How could Katerina have a baby if she isn’t married?”
Nastya got annoyed.
“You don’t know anything,” she snapped. “Maybe she does have a husband, but he’s in prison, so now she’s having a baby.”
“But is her husband in prison?” Kostya asked, very seriously.

Nastya suddenly changed her mind and interrupted, “Or, you know what? She doesn’t have a husband—you’re right. But she wants to get married, and she’s thought about it so much that now she’s got...not a husband, but a baby.”
“Well, maybe,” Kostya agreed, giving up. “But you didn’t say that before, so how was I supposed to know?”
“All right, kids,” Kolya said as he came into the room. “You two are something else, you know.”
“And Perezvon’s with you!” Kostya grinned and started snapping his fingers, calling Perezvon over.
“I’m in a tough spot, kids,” Kolya said seriously. “I think Agafya must have broken her leg or something—she still isn’t back. I have to go out. Will you let me?”
The kids looked at each other, worried. They smiled nervously, but it was clear they weren’t sure what Kolya wanted from them.
“You won’t be naughty while I’m gone, right? No climbing up on cupboards and breaking your legs? You won’t get scared and cry?”
The kids looked very sad at this.
“But I could show you something as a reward—a little copper cannon that really fires with real gunpowder.”
Instantly, both kids brightened up. “Show us the cannon!” Kostya said, grinning.
Kolya reached into his satchel, pulled out a tiny bronze cannon, and set it on the table.
“Of course you want to see it! Look, it’s even got wheels,” he said, rolling the toy along the table. “And it can really fire. You just load it with shot and fire away.”
“Could it kill someone?” Nastya asked.

“It could,” Kolya said, “as long as you aim it at someone.” He explained where to put the powder and the shot, showed them the little hole for lighting it, and warned them it would kick when it fired.
The kids listened, fascinated. The idea that the cannon would kick especially amazed them.
“Do you have any powder?” Nastya asked.
“Yes, I do.”
“Show us the powder, too!” she begged, smiling.

Kolya dug into his satchel again and pulled out a little flask with real gunpowder. He even had some shot wrapped up in paper. He uncorked the flask and poured a little powder into his palm for them to see.
“You have to be careful with fire, or it’ll blow up and kill us all,” Kolya said dramatically.
The kids stared at the powder, half-scared but thrilled. But Kostya was even more interested in the shot.
“Does the shot burn?” he asked.
“No, it doesn’t.”
“Can I have some shot?” he pleaded.
“Sure, you can have a little,” Kolya said. “But don’t show it to your mom till I get back. She’ll think it’s gunpowder, freak out, and punish you.”
“Mother never punishes us,” Nastya answered right away.
“I know, I just said that to finish the sentence. And don’t ever trick your mom—except this once, until I come back. So, kids, can I go out now? You won’t cry when I’m gone?”
“We will cry,” Kostya said softly, already close to tears.
“We’ll cry, we’ll definitely cry,” Nastya added quickly, sounding scared.
“Oh, kids, your age is full of danger!” Kolya said dramatically. “Looks like I’ll have to stay with you for who knows how long. And time is ticking away, oh no!”
“Make Perezvon pretend he’s dead!” Kostya begged.
“I guess we’ll have to use Perezvon,” Kolya said. “Come here, Perezvon.” He started giving the dog commands, and Perezvon did all his tricks.

Perezvon was a scruffy, medium-sized dog with a kind of grayish-lilac fur. He was blind in his right eye and had a torn left ear. He whined, jumped, walked on his hind legs, and even lay on his back with his paws in the air, playing dead. While he was doing his dead-dog trick, the door opened and Agafya—the Krassotkin’s servant, a plump woman of about forty with smallpox scars—came in with a bag of groceries from the market. She stood there, holding her bag, watching the dog. Even though Kolya had been so eager for her to come back, he didn’t stop the show. Once Perezvon had pretended to be dead for the usual amount of time, Kolya finally whistled, and the dog jumped up, excited to have finished his job.
“Would you look at that! A dog!” Agafya said, making a wise-sounding comment.
“Why are you late, woman?” Kolya demanded, pretending to be strict.
“Woman, huh? Watch it, you brat,” Agafya shot back.
“Brat?”

“Yeah, brat. What’s it to you if I’m late? If I am, I’ve got a good reason,” Agafya grumbled as she started putting things away in the kitchen. She didn’t sound angry at all—she actually seemed to enjoy joking around with Kolya.
“Listen, you silly woman,” Kolya said, getting up from the sofa. “Can you swear by all that’s sacred to you—and more—that you’ll watch over the kids super carefully while I’m gone? I have to go out.”
“What do I need to swear for?” Agafya laughed. “I’ll look after them without all that.”
“No, you have to swear on your eternal soul. Otherwise, I’m not going.”
“Well, then don’t go. What do I care? It’s cold outside—stay home.”

“Kids,” Kolya said, turning to them, “this woman will stay with you till I get back, or until your mom comes—she should have been back by now anyway. She’ll give you lunch too. You’ll feed them, right, Agafya?”
“Of course I will.”

“Goodbye, chickens. Now I can leave with peace of mind. And you, grandma,” Kolya added quietly as he passed Agafya, “please don’t tell the kids any of your old-woman stories about Katerina. Come on, Perezvon!”
“Get out of here!” Agafya snapped, actually annoyed this time. “Ridiculous boy! You need a good spanking for saying things like that!”

But Kolya didn’t pay any attention to her. At last, he was able to leave. As he walked out the gate, he looked around, shrugged his shoulders, and said, “It’s freezing.” He kept walking straight down the street, then turned right toward the market. When he reached the second-to-last house before the market, he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle from his pocket, and blew it as loudly as he could, like he was sending a signal. He didn’t have to wait long—after about a minute, a rosy-cheeked boy about eleven years old ran out to meet him. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two grades below Kolya Krassotkin), whose father was a well-off official. Smurov’s parents apparently didn’t want him hanging out with Kolya, since Kolya was known for being a seriously naughty kid, so Smurov was clearly sneaking out to meet him. If you remember, Smurov was one of the group of boys who, two months earlier, threw stones at Ilusha. He was also the one who told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
“I’ve been waiting for you for an hour, Krassotkin,” Smurov said flatly, and the two boys walked together toward the market.
“I’m late,” Kolya replied. “I got held up by something. Are you going to get in trouble for coming with me?”
“Come on, I never get in trouble! Did you bring Perezvon?”
“Yes.”
“You’re taking him, too?”
“Yes.”
“Oh! If only it was Zhutchka!”
“That’s impossible. Zhutchka doesn’t exist anymore. She’s lost and gone forever.”

“Wait, what if we did this?” Smurov suddenly stopped walking. “See, Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-colored dog, like Perezvon. Couldn’t you tell Ilusha this is Zhutchka? Maybe he’d believe you.”
“Don’t lie, even for a good reason. That’s important. And I hope you haven’t told anyone I’m coming.”

“No way! I know what I’m doing. But Perezvon won’t really cheer him up,” Smurov sighed. “You know his dad, the captain—‘the wisp of tow’—said he’d bring a real mastiff puppy with a black nose today. He thinks that’ll make Ilusha feel better, but I doubt it.”
“How is Ilusha?”

“Oh, he’s bad, really bad! I think he’s got consumption. He’s awake, but his breathing is terrible. The other day, he asked to put his boots on so he could be led around the room. He tried to walk, but he couldn’t stand up. ‘I told you before, father,’ he said, ‘those boots are useless. I never walked right in them.’ He thought his boots made him stumble, but really, it’s just weakness. He probably won’t live another week. Dr. Herzenstube is taking care of him. Now they have money again—lots of it.”
“They’re cheats.”
“Who are cheats?”

“Doctors and all those fakes, both as a group and as individuals. I don’t trust medicine. It’s pointless. I’m going to study all that someday. But what’s up with all that sentimental stuff at their place? It seems like the whole class is there every day.”
“It’s not the whole class—only ten of us go every day. That’s all.”
“What I don’t get is why Alexey Karamazov is so involved. His brother’s about to go on trial for a huge crime, and yet he spends so much time with you all, doing sentimental stuff with kids.”
“It’s not sentimental. You’re going now yourself to make up with Ilusha.”
“Make up with him? That’s a dumb way to put it. And anyway, nobody gets to question my actions.”
“Ilusha will be so happy to see you! He has no idea you’re coming. But why? Why wouldn’t you come before?” Smurov suddenly asked, sounding emotional.

“That’s my business, not yours,” Kolya said. “I’m going because I want to, but Alexey Karamazov made all of you go—that’s different. And for your information, I might not be making up at all. That phrase is stupid.”

“It’s not Karamazov’s doing at all. We started visiting Ilusha ourselves. Sure, we first went with Karamazov, but there wasn’t anything silly. First one went, then another. Ilusha’s dad was so glad to see us. You know he’ll lose his mind if Ilusha dies. He knows Ilusha is dying. He’s so happy we made up with Ilusha. Ilusha just asks about you sometimes, that’s all. If his son dies, his dad will go crazy or kill himself. You remember how he acted before. He’s actually a decent guy. We messed up. It’s all because of that murderer who beat him up back then.”
“Karamazov is still a mystery to me. I could’ve gotten to know him before, but I like to keep my pride sometimes. Plus, I have a theory about him I need to test out.”

Kolya fell silent in a dignified way. Smurov didn’t say anything either. Smurov, of course, really looked up to Kolya Krassotkin and never thought of himself as Kolya’s equal. Now he was fascinated that Kolya said he was “going of himself” to see Ilusha. Smurov guessed there must be a secret reason Kolya suddenly decided to go that day. They crossed the market, which was packed with wagons from the countryside and a ton of live chickens. The market women were selling bread rolls, fabrics, thread, and other stuff in their booths. These Sunday markets were called “fairs” in town, and there were lots of them every year.
Perezvon ran around full of energy, sniffing this way and that. Whenever he met another dog, they sniffed each other all over, just like dogs always do.
“I love watching scenes like this, Smurov,” Kolya said suddenly. “Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It must be a law of nature.”
“Yeah, it’s a funny habit.”

“No, it’s not funny. You’re wrong. Nothing in nature is really funny, even if people think it is because of their own opinions. If dogs could think and judge us, they’d probably find way more things about humans funny, especially the way we act with each other. Actually, I’m sure we’re even sillier. That’s Rakitin’s idea—really smart. I’m a Socialist, Smurov.”
“What’s a Socialist?” Smurov asked.

“It’s when everyone is equal, everyone shares everything, there’s no marriage, and everyone can have whatever religion or laws they want, and stuff like that. You’re not old enough to get it yet. It’s cold, though.”
“Yeah, it’s twelve degrees below zero. My dad checked the thermometer earlier.”

“You notice, Smurov, that in the middle of winter, when it’s fifteen or eighteen degrees below zero, we don’t feel as cold as we do now, at the start of winter, when it suddenly drops to twelve below, especially when there’s not much snow. That’s because people aren’t used to it yet. Habit is everything for humans—everything, even in how we act in society and politics. Habit is what makes people do things. What a strange-looking peasant!”

Kolya pointed to a tall peasant with a friendly face, wearing a long sheepskin coat, standing next to his wagon. He was clapping his hands together in big leather mittens to warm them. His long blond beard was covered with frost.
“That peasant’s beard is frozen!” Kolya yelled loudly as he passed by, trying to get a reaction.
“Lots of people’s beards are frozen,” the peasant answered calmly and wisely.
“Don’t tease him,” Smurov said.
“It’s fine, he won’t get mad. He’s a good guy. Bye, Matvey!”
“Good-bye.”
“Is your name Matvey?”
“Yeah. Didn’t you know?”
“No, I just guessed.”
“Really! You’re a schoolboy, I bet?”
“Yes.”
“Do you get whipped at school?”
“Not much—sometimes.”
“Does it hurt?”
“Well, yeah, it does.”
“Wow, what a life!” The peasant sighed deeply.
“Bye, Matvey.”
“Bye. You’re a nice kid, you are.”
The boys kept walking.
“That was a nice peasant,” Kolya said to Smurov. “I like talking to peasants, and I always try to be fair to them.”
“Why did you lie and say we get beaten?” Smurov asked.
“I had to say that to make him happy.”
“What do you mean?”

“See, Smurov, I don’t like being asked the same thing twice. People should get it the first time. Some things just can’t be explained. Peasants think schoolboys get whipped, and they have to be. If I told him we don’t, he’d be disappointed. But you don’t get that. You have to know how to talk to peasants.”
“Just don’t mess with them, okay, or you’ll get in trouble again like you did with that goose.”
“So you’re scared?”
“Don’t laugh, Kolya. Of course I’m scared. My dad would be furious. I’m strictly not allowed to go out with you.”
“Relax, nothing’s going to happen this time. Hey, Natasha!” he shouted to a market woman in one of the stalls.
“Call me Natasha! Really! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged market woman yelled back.
“I’m glad it’s Marya. Bye!”
“Oh, you little rascal! A kid like you, acting like that!”
“I’m in a hurry. Can’t stop now. You can tell me next Sunday,” Kolya said, waving at her like she had teased him instead of the other way around.
“I have nothing to tell you next Sunday. You’re the one bothering me, you cheeky little monkey! I didn’t say anything,” Marya shouted. “Someone should give you a whipping, you little brat!”

The other market women around her burst out laughing. Suddenly, a man came rushing out from the shop arcade nearby, looking really angry. He was young, not from town, with dark, curly hair and a long, pale face marked with smallpox scars. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap—he looked like a merchant’s clerk. He was really worked up, shaking his fist at Kolya.
“I know you!” he yelled, furious. “I know you!”
Kolya stared at him. He couldn’t remember ever fighting with this guy, but he’d been in so many arguments on the street he couldn’t keep track.
“You do?” he answered, sounding sarcastic.
“I know you! I know you!” the man repeated, acting like an idiot.
“Good for you. Anyway, I have to go. Bye!”
“You’re up to your tricks again, aren’t you?” the man shouted. “You’re up to your tricks! I know you are!”
“That’s not your problem, man, if I’m up to my tricks,” Kolya said, stopping and staring him down.
“Not my problem?”
“No, it’s not your problem.”
“Then whose is it? Whose?”
“It’s Trifon Nikititch’s problem, not yours.”
“Who’s Trifon Nikititch?” the guy asked, staring at Kolya like he was totally confused, but still angry.
Kolya looked him over carefully.
“Have you ever been to the Church of the Ascension?” he suddenly demanded, sounding very serious.
“What Church of the Ascension? Why? No, I haven’t,” the man said, now a little thrown off.
“Do you know Sabaneyev?” Kolya asked, sounding even more serious.
“Who’s Sabaneyev? No, I don’t know him.”
“Then go to hell,” Kolya said, ending the conversation. He quickly turned right and walked away, acting like he was too good to waste time with someone who didn’t even know Sabaneyev.
“Wait, hey! Who’s Sabaneyev?” the man finally snapped out of his confusion, just as mad as before. “What did he say?” He turned to the market women, looking clueless.
The women laughed.
“You never know what that kid’s up to,” one of them said.
“Which Sabaneyev is he talking about?” the man asked again, still furious, waving his fist.
“It must be the Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that’s probably it,” one of the women guessed.
The man just stared at her, wide-eyed.
“But his name wasn’t Trifon. It was Kuzma, not Trifon. But the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can’t be the same,” another woman said.
“It’s not Trifon and not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov,” a third woman chimed in, who’d been quietly listening until now. “Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”
“Definitely, it’s Tchizhov,” a fourth woman agreed.
The confused young man looked from one woman to another, totally lost.
“What did he want, what did he want, ladies?” he cried, almost desperate. “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ he says. Who the heck is Sabaneyev?”
“You’re clueless. I’m telling you, it’s not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that’s who!” one woman said firmly.
“Which Tchizhov? Who is that? Tell me if you know.”
“That tall, whiny guy who used to sit here in the market in the summer.”
“And what’s your Tchizhov got to do with me, ladies, huh?”
“How should I know what he has to do with you?” another answered. “You should know why you want him if you’re making such a fuss. He talked to you, not us, you dummy. Don’t you really know him?”
“Know who?”
“Tchizhov.”
“To hell with Tchizhov and you, too! I’ll beat him up, I swear. He was making fun of me!”
“You’ll beat up Tchizhov? More likely he’ll beat you up! You’re a fool, that’s what you are.”
“Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you mean old woman! I’ll beat up that kid. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

The women burst out laughing. But by then, Kolya was already far away, walking along with a proud look. Smurov walked next to him, glancing back at the shouting group. He was excited too, although still a bit nervous about getting in trouble with Kolya.
“Who’s Sabaneyev, anyway?” he asked Kolya, guessing what the answer would be.

“How should I know? Now those people will argue about it all day. I like messing with idiots in every group. Here’s another dummy, that peasant over there. You know, they say ‘no one is dumber than a dumb Frenchman,’ but a dumb Russian shows it right in his face. Can’t you see it all over that peasant’s face that he’s a fool?”
“Leave him alone, Kolya. Let’s just go.”
“Nothing can stop me now that I’m on a roll. Hey, good morning, peasant!”
A tough-looking peasant with a round, simple face and a grey beard, walking by, looked up at the boy. He seemed a little drunk.
“Good morning, unless you’re making fun of me,” he said carefully.
“And what if I am?” Kolya laughed.
“Well, a joke’s a joke. Go ahead and laugh. I don’t care. There’s no harm in a joke.”
“Sorry, man, I was just joking.”
“Well, God forgives you.”
“You forgive me too?”
“Of course I do. Move along.”
“You seem like a smart peasant.”
“Smarter than you,” the peasant shot back, serious as ever.
“I doubt it,” Kolya said, caught off guard.
“It’s true, though.”
“Maybe.”
“It is, kid.”
“Bye, peasant!”
“Bye!”
“There are all kinds of peasants,” Kolya told Smurov after a short pause. “How was I supposed to know I’d find a clever one? I’m always ready to admit it

Kolya leaned against the fence, trying to look as cool and grown-up as possible while he waited for Alyosha to show up. He’d wanted to meet Alyosha for a long time—he’d heard a lot about him from the other boys—but he always pretended not to care and even criticized Alyosha when people talked about him. Secretly, though, Kolya was really curious and wanted to get to know him. There was something about Alyosha that just seemed likable. Kolya wanted to make a good impression and show that he wasn’t just a little kid. “If I act too much like a thirteen-year-old, he’ll just think I’m a kid, like the others. I wonder what he thinks of the other boys—maybe I’ll ask him when I know him better. Too bad I’m so short. Tuzikov is younger than me but half a head taller. At least I have a smart-looking face, even if I’m ugly. But I have to be careful not to act too friendly at first, or he’ll think I’m too eager. Ugh, that would be embarrassing if he thought that!”

Kolya had all these thoughts racing through his head as he did his best to seem independent and mature. What really bothered him was being short; he didn’t worry so much about his “ugly” face. Last year, he’d made a mark on the wall at home to keep track of his height, and every two months he measured himself, hoping he’d grown. But he grew slowly, and that sometimes made him really upset. In reality, his face wasn’t ugly at all—it was actually kind of nice, with pale, freckled skin and lively gray eyes that always seemed full of energy. He had high cheekbones, small and very red lips, and a little nose that turned up. “I’ve got a pug nose, a real pug nose,” he would mutter to himself in the mirror, then walk away annoyed. Sometimes he even wondered if his face was smart-looking at all. But it’s not like he was always worried about his looks or his height. Even if looking in the mirror made him feel bad for a minute, he usually forgot about it and got caught up in his thoughts and real life, as he liked to put it.

Alyosha came out quickly and walked straight toward Kolya, looking honestly happy to see him. Kolya noticed this and felt pleased—“Is he really that glad to see me?” he wondered. By the way, Alyosha looked very different now than before. He wasn’t wearing his monk’s robe anymore; now he had on a nice coat and a soft hat, and his hair was cut short. It really suited him, and he looked pretty good. His face was always kind and cheerful, but there was also a calmness about him. Kolya was surprised that Alyosha came out without even putting on an overcoat, like he was in a hurry. Alyosha reached out to shake Kolya’s hand right away.
“You’re finally here! We’ve all been so anxious to see you!” Alyosha said warmly.
“There were reasons for my delay—you’ll hear about them soon. Still, I’m glad to meet you. I’ve been hoping for a chance and heard a lot about you,” Kolya said, a little out of breath.
“We would have met eventually. I’ve heard plenty about you, too, but you sure took your time coming here,” said Alyosha.
“So, how are things going?” Kolya asked.
“Ilusha is very sick. He’s definitely dying,” Alyosha replied quietly.
“That’s terrible! You have to admit, doctors are useless, Karamazov,” Kolya burst out, upset.

“Ilusha talks about you a lot—really, a lot—even when he’s half-asleep or confused. It’s obvious you meant a lot to him… before the thing with the knife happened. There’s something else, too… By the way, is that your dog?” Alyosha asked, looking at the dog beside Kolya.
“Yeah, his name’s Perezvon,” Kolya answered.
“Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha looked at Kolya with pity. “So she’s really gone forever?”

“I know everyone wishes it was Zhutchka. I’ve heard all about that,” Kolya replied, smiling mysteriously. “Listen, Karamazov, I’ll tell you the whole story. That’s actually why I wanted you to come outside—to explain everything before we go in,” he said, getting excited. “So, here’s what happened: Ilusha joined the prep class last spring. You know what that class is like—a bunch of little kids. They started picking on Ilusha right away. I’m two grades above them, so I just watched from a distance. Ilusha was small and weak, but he wouldn’t give in—he fought back and was really proud, with fire in his eyes. I like kids like that. So the others teased him even more. The worst part was, his clothes were terrible at the time—pants too short, holes in his boots. They made fun of him for it. That made me mad, so I stood up for him and really let the others have it. I even fought them, but they all like me anyway. You know, Karamazov, I’ve always liked little kids. I’ve even got two baby chickens at home right now—that’s what made me late today. Anyway, after I defended Ilusha, the others stopped beating him up, and I sort of took him under my wing. He was a proud kid, but he got really devoted to me—he’d do anything I asked, almost like I was God or something, and he always tried to copy me. During breaks, he’d run right to me, and we’d hang out, even on Sundays. Some people laugh when older kids make friends with younger ones, but that’s just a dumb rule. If I want to help him grow and develop, why not? You do the same thing, Karamazov—you help all the younger boys, and I really admire that about you. But then I noticed something: Ilusha started getting kind of soft, almost sentimental, and I honestly hate that sort of thing. He was full of contradictions—proud, but also really attached to me, but then sometimes he’d argue or get mad at me just because I wasn’t very warm with him. So, to toughen him up, the more tender he acted, the colder I acted in return. That was my plan—to shape his character, make him tougher… you probably get it. Then, for three days, he seemed really down, but not because of me being cold. It was something else, something more serious. I asked around and found out he’d met Smerdyakov, who used to be your father’s servant before he died. Smerdyakov taught Ilusha a mean trick: stick a pin in a piece of bread and throw it to a hungry dog, just to see what happens. So they did it to Zhutchka, the shaggy dog everyone’s been talking about. The owners never fed her, so she was always starving. (Do you like dogs barking all the time, Karamazov? I can’t stand it.) Anyway, Zhutchka ate the bread, then started squealing and spinning in circles before running away. That’s what Ilusha told me, and he was really upset about it—hugging me and crying that the dog ran away squealing. You could tell he felt horrible. I decided to teach him a lesson. I acted even more upset than I was and told him, ‘You did a rotten thing. You’re a scoundrel. I won’t tell on you, but I’m not going to talk to you anymore for now. I’ll let you know through Smurov—he’s the boy who came with me—if I’ll ever be friends with you again or if I’m done with you forever.’ Ilusha was crushed. Honestly, I might have gone too far, but it seemed like the right thing to do at the time. A couple days later, I sent Smurov to tell him I wouldn’t talk to him again. That’s what we call it when two kids stop being friends. Secretly, I just meant to ignore him for a few days and then, if he seemed sorry, I’d forgive him. But guess what happened? When Smurov gave him the message, Ilusha’s eyes flashed. He said, ‘Tell Krassotkin I’ll throw bread with pins to all the dogs—all of them!’ So he was acting out. I decided to ignore him and act sarcastic whenever I saw him. And right then, that whole thing with his father happened—you remember? He was already really wound up. The other boys saw that I’d dropped him, so they started bullying him, calling him names like ‘wisp of tow.’ He got into fights with them, and I think they beat him up badly once. One day he attacked them all outside school. I was nearby, watching. I swear, I didn’t laugh—I actually felt really sorry for him and was about to help. But he saw me, and for some reason, he pulled out a penknife and stabbed me in the thigh. I didn’t move—I can be brave, you know—and just looked at him as if to say, ‘So this is how you treat me? Go ahead, do it again if you want.’ But he didn’t—he broke down, dropped the knife, started crying, and ran away. I never told on him and made sure the other boys didn’t, either, so the teachers wouldn’t find out. I didn’t even tell my mom until my leg had healed, and it was only a scratch anyway. Then I heard he’d thrown stones and even bitten your finger that same day—but now you can see what state he was in! I should have come to make up with him when he got sick, and I regret not doing it. But I had my reasons. So now you know everything… I probably acted stupidly.”

“Oh, that’s such a shame,” Alyosha said, truly moved. “If I’d only known how things were between you two, I would have come to you earlier and begged you to visit him with me. You wouldn’t believe it, but when he was feverish, he talked about you in his delirium. I didn’t realize how much you meant to him! And you really haven’t found that dog? His father and the boys have searched the whole town. Since he’s been sick, I’ve heard him cry three times, ‘It’s because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I’m ill. God is punishing me.’ He can’t get over it. If we could prove the dog was alive, I honestly think the happiness might cure him. We’re all counting on you.”
“Tell me, why did everyone expect me to find the dog?” Kolya asked, really curious. “Why me, instead of anyone else?”

“There was a rumor that you were looking for the dog and would bring it if you found it. Smurov said something like that. We’ve all been trying to convince Ilusha that the dog is alive and has been seen around. The boys even brought him a live rabbit, but he just gave a small smile and asked us to let it go free in the fields, so we did. His father just got him a mastiff puppy, hoping it would make him feel better, but I think it only upsets him more.”
“What kind of man is Ilusha’s father, anyway? I know him, but what do you think—is he just a clown or a joke?”

“No, not at all. Some people have deep feelings but have been beaten down by life. Acting silly is their way of being bitter and making fun of people they’re too scared to be honest with, because they’ve been bullied and embarrassed for years. Trust me, Krassotkin, sometimes that kind of joking is actually really sad. Now, his whole life is focused on Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he’ll either go insane with grief or kill himself. I’m almost sure of it when I look at him,” Alyosha said quietly.
“I get what you mean, Karamazov. You really understand people,” Kolya said, with feeling.
“And as soon as I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing back Zhutchka,” Alyosha told him.

“Wait, Karamazov, maybe we’ll find Zhutchka yet. But this is Perezvon. I’ll take him in, and maybe he’ll cheer Ilusha up more than the mastiff puppy. Just wait a second, Karamazov, you’ll see something soon. But hey, I’m keeping you out here!” Kolya suddenly cried. “You’re not even wearing an overcoat in this freezing cold. I’m so selfish. Really, we’re all selfish, Karamazov!”
“Don’t worry about it; it is cold, but I don’t get sick easily. Let’s go in, though. Oh, and by the way, what’s your full name? I know you’re called Kolya, but what’s the rest?”
“Nikolay—Ivanovitch Krassotkin. Or, as the official papers say, ‘Krassotkin son.’” Kolya laughed for some reason, then added seriously, “But honestly, I hate the name Nikolay.”
“Why’s that?” Alyosha asked.
“It’s just so boring and common.”
“You’re thirteen, right?” Alyosha asked.

“No, I’ll be fourteen soon—in two weeks. I’ll admit something to you, Karamazov, just because it’s our first meeting and I want you to understand my personality. I hate being asked how old I am. Even worse, there’s a nasty rumor about me that I played robbers with the prep kids last week. It’s true I played with them, but it’s a total lie to say I did it for fun. I have reason to think you’ve heard the story. But I only did it for the little kids, because they couldn’t figure out what to play on their own. There are always dumb stories like that. This is a terrible town for gossip.”
“But even if you did play for your own fun, what’s so bad about that?” Alyosha asked.
“Come on, you really think I’d play for my own amusement? You don’t play horses, do you?” Kolya said, frowning.

“But look at it this way,” Alyosha said, smiling. “Adults go to the theater to watch plays about heroes—sometimes there are robbers and battles, too. Isn’t that basically the same thing as kids playing games? Sure, it’s different, but playing soldiers or robbers is just kids acting out their own shows. It comes from a creative instinct, and sometimes their games are even better than real plays. The only difference is that in the theater you watch others act, but in games, you get to be the actor yourself. That’s only natural.”

“You think so? Is that really your opinion?” Kolya looked at Alyosha closely. “You know, that’s actually an interesting way to see it. I’ll have to think more about it when I go home. Honestly, I thought I might learn something from you today. I came to learn from you, Karamazov,” Kolya said, his voice full of honest emotion.
“And I from you,” Alyosha replied, smiling and squeezing Kolya’s hand.
Kolya was really pleased with Alyosha. What he liked most was that Alyosha treated him like an equal and spoke to him just like he would to an adult.
“I’ll show you something soon, Karamazov—it’s like our own play,” Kolya said, laughing nervously. “That’s why I came.”
“Let’s stop by the people’s house on the left first. All the boys leave their coats there, since the other room is small and hot,” Alyosha suggested.

“Oh, I’m just staying for a minute. I’ll keep my coat on. Perezvon will stay here in the hallway and play dead. Ici, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! See, he’s dead. I’ll go in first to check things out, then I’ll whistle for him when I’m ready, and you’ll see—he’ll rush in like a maniac. Just make sure Smurov opens the door at the right moment. I’ll arrange everything, and you’ll see something cool.”

The room where Captain Snegiryov’s family lived was already known to the reader. Right now, it was crowded with visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha, and although they all—like Smurov—acted as if Alyosha hadn’t brought them together or helped them make peace with Ilusha, that’s exactly what had happened. Alyosha’s way had been to bring the boys to Ilusha one at a time, acting casual and never making it awkward or sentimental. This meant a lot to Ilusha while he was sick.
