He was deeply touched by the kindness shown by these boys who used to be his enemies. Only Krassotkin (Kolya) was missing, and Ilusha’s heart ached because of it. The memory that hurt most was when he had stabbed Krassotkin, his only real friend and protector. Clever Smurov, who was the first to reconcile with Ilusha, thought this was the main reason. But whenever Smurov tried to hint to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to see him, Kolya would cut him off, telling Smurov, “Tell Karamazov I know what I’m doing. I don’t need advice. If I want to see Ilusha, I’ll go when I want—I have my reasons.”

That was two weeks before this Sunday. That’s why Alyosha hadn’t seen Kolya, even though he wanted to. Instead, he sent Smurov to talk to Kolya twice more. Both times, Kolya just snapped at him and told Alyosha to stop bothering him, saying that if Alyosha kept it up, he’d never go to see Ilusha at all. Even up to the day before, Smurov had no idea Kolya actually planned to visit Ilusha that morning. It was only the night before, as they were saying goodbye, that Kolya suddenly told Smurov to wait for him at home the next morning, so they could go to the Snegiryovs’ together—but he warned Smurov not to tell anyone, since he wanted the visit to seem like a surprise. Smurov did as he was told. Smurov’s hope that Kolya would bring back the lost dog came from something Kolya had said: “They must be idiots if they can’t find the dog, if it’s still alive.” When Smurov nervously guessed out loud if Kolya might bring the dog back, Kolya blew up in anger: “I’m not dumb enough to search the whole town for someone else’s dog when I have my own! And besides, how could a dog be alive after swallowing a pin? That’s just silly, soft-hearted stuff!”

For the last two weeks, Ilusha hadn’t left the little bed beneath the religious icons in the corner. He hadn’t gone to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He got sick that same day, though for a month afterwards he could sometimes get up and walk around the room or hallway. But lately, he had grown so weak that he needed his father’s help to move at all. His father was desperately worried about him. He even quit drinking and was practically losing his mind with fear that his son might die. Often, after helping Ilusha walk around and then putting him back in bed, the captain would rush to a dark corner in the hallway, lean his head against the wall, and cry as hard as he could—trying to muffle his sobs so Ilusha wouldn’t hear.

When he came back, the captain would usually try to cheer Ilusha up by telling stories or funny jokes, or by acting out silly characters or imitating animal noises. But Ilusha didn’t really like seeing his father act like a clown. Even though the boy tried to hide it, it hurt him to see that other people didn’t respect his father, and he couldn’t stop thinking about the “wisp of tow” and that “terrible day.”

Ilusha’s gentle, disabled sister Nina didn’t like their father’s goofiness either (their other sister, Varvara, had left for university in Petersburg). But their half-mad mother actually enjoyed the captain’s clowning—she laughed loudly whenever he did something silly. It was the only thing that made her happy; the rest of the time she just complained that everyone ignored her, didn’t respect her, and so on. But lately, she had changed completely. She kept looking over at Ilusha’s bed and seemed deep in thought. She was quieter, and if she cried, she tried to do it quietly. The captain noticed the change, feeling sad and confused. At first, the boys’ visits annoyed her, but eventually their noisy games and stories cheered her up, and she came to like them so much that she would have missed them if they stopped coming. When they told stories or played games, she laughed and clapped, and even called some of the boys over to kiss them—especially Smurov, whom she liked best.

As for the captain, having the boys in his room to keep Ilusha company filled him with joy from the very start. He even hoped that being less lonely would help Ilusha feel better and recover more quickly. Even though he was worried about Ilusha, up until recently he hadn’t really doubted that his son would get well.

The captain treated Ilusha’s friends like honored guests, doing everything for them. He even let them ride on his back, but Ilusha didn’t enjoy that game, so they stopped. The captain bought them little treats like gingerbread and nuts, made them tea, and cut sandwiches for them. It’s important to note that he had plenty of money at this time. He had taken the two hundred rubles from Katerina Ivanovna, just like Alyosha had predicted he would. Later, Katerina Ivanovna learned more about their situation and Ilusha’s illness, visited the family herself, and managed to charm the half-mad mother. Since then, Katerina Ivanovna had been extremely generous in helping them, and the captain, scared that his son might die, put his pride aside and accepted her help.

During this time, Doctor Herzenstube—who Katerina Ivanovna had called—came every other day, but his visits didn’t help much, and he gave Ilusha a lot of medicine. On this Sunday morning, though, a new doctor was expected. He was famous in Moscow, and Katerina Ivanovna had paid a lot to bring him—not just for Ilusha, but for another reason that would be explained later. Since he was coming, she asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain was told to expect him. The captain had no idea Kolya Krassotkin would be visiting, though he’d long wished Kolya would come, since Ilusha missed him badly.

When Kolya Krassotkin opened the door and came in, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha’s bed, looking at a tiny mastiff puppy that had been born just the day before. The captain had ordered it a week earlier, hoping it would cheer Ilusha up, since he was still sad about losing his old dog, Zhutchka. Three days before, Ilusha had heard he’d be getting a puppy—not just any puppy, but a purebred mastiff (which was a big deal). He tried to act happy about it out of politeness, but his father and the boys could tell the puppy only made him think about the beloved dog he’d lost. The little puppy lay beside him, moving weakly, and Ilusha stroked it with his thin, pale hand, giving a sad smile. He liked the puppy, but it wasn’t Zhutchka. If only he could have both Zhutchka and the puppy, then he’d be truly happy.
“Krassotkin!” one of the boys suddenly shouted, spotting him first as he walked in.
Kolya’s entrance caused a stir; the boys moved to either side of the bed so Kolya could see Ilusha clearly. The captain hurried over to greet him.
“Please come in—you’re very welcome!” the captain said quickly. “Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin is here to see you!”

Kolya shook the captain’s hand quickly, showing he knew how to act politely. He turned first to the captain’s wife, who was sitting in her armchair in a bad mood, complaining that the boys were blocking her view of Ilusha’s bed and the new puppy. Kolya bowed to her very politely, scraping his foot on the floor, and then gave a similar bow to Nina, since she was the only other lady present. This made a very good impression on the captain’s wife, who wasn’t quite in her right mind.
“See, you can tell right away he’s a well-raised young man,” she said out loud, throwing up her hands. “Our other visitors just rush in one after the other.”
“What do you mean, ‘one after the other,’ Mama? How do they come in?” the captain asked gently, though a little worried about her.
“They come in riding on each other's shoulders in the hallway, then barge in that way, bothering a respectable family! Strange visitors!”
“But who came in like that, Mama?”
“That boy came in riding on the other’s back, and this one was on another’s shoulders.”

By now, Kolya was already at Ilusha’s bedside. The sick boy turned even paler. He sat up in bed and stared at Kolya. Kolya hadn’t seen his friend for two months, and the sight shocked him. He hadn’t expected Ilusha to look so thin and sickly, with a yellow face, huge feverish eyes, and skinny little hands. He noticed Ilusha’s hard, fast breathing and dry lips. Kolya stepped closer, held out his hand, and, nearly overwhelmed, said:

“Hey, old friend… how are you?” But his voice broke, and he couldn’t sound casual. His face twitched and his mouth quivered. Ilusha gave him a small, pitiful smile, but couldn’t say a word. Kolya was moved to reach out and gently run his hand over Ilusha’s hair.
“It’s okay,” he whispered softly, trying to comfort him—or maybe just because he didn’t know what else to say. They sat in silence for a minute.
“So, you have a new puppy?” Kolya suddenly said, trying to sound uninterested.
“Yes…” Ilusha whispered, struggling to breathe.

“A black nose—that means he’ll be fierce, a good watchdog,” Kolya said in a serious, matter-of-fact way, as if all he cared about was the puppy and its nose. But in reality, he was fighting hard not to burst into tears, and even then, he could barely keep it together. “Once he grows up, you’ll have to keep him on a chain, I bet.”
“He’ll be a big dog!” one of the boys shouted.
“Of course he will!” “A mastiff!” “Huge!” “As big as a calf!” several boys yelled.

“As big as a real calf!” the captain chimed in. “I got a really fierce one on purpose. His parents are huge and mean, they stand this high off the floor… Sit here, on Ilusha’s bed, or on the bench. You’re very welcome—we’ve been wanting you to visit for a long time. You were so kind to come with Alexey Fyodorovich (Alyosha)?”
Kolya sat down on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha’s feet. Even though he might have planned out an easy conversation on his way there, now he was completely at a loss for words.

“No, I came with Perezvon. That’s my dog now—his name’s Perezvon. It’s a Slavic name. He’s outside… If I whistle, he’ll come in. I brought a dog to show you,” he said, suddenly talking straight to Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old friend?” he suddenly blurted out.

Ilusha’s face trembled. He looked at Kolya with pain in his eyes. Alyosha, standing at the door, frowned and motioned for Kolya to stop talking about Zhutchka, but Kolya ignored him or pretended not to notice.
“Where… is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked, his voice shaky.
“Well, buddy, your Zhutchka is lost and gone for good,” Kolya answered.
Ilusha didn’t say anything, but kept staring at Kolya. Alyosha caught Kolya’s eye and motioned again for him to stop, but Kolya looked away, pretending he hadn’t seen.

“She must have run away and died somewhere. After eating something like that, she must be dead,” Kolya said, sounding heartless even though he was a little out of breath. “But I’ve got a dog—Perezvon, a Slavic name. I brought him to show you.”
“I don’t want him!” Ilusha suddenly said.

“No, really, you have to see him—he’ll make you laugh. I brought him just for you… He’s the same kind of shaggy dog. May I bring my dog in, madam?” he asked Madame Snegiryov, his voice strangely excited.
“I don’t want him, I don’t want him!” Ilusha cried, his voice breaking and his eyes full of hurt.

“You’d better wait,” the captain started to say, getting up from the chest he had just sat on. “Maybe another time…” he muttered. But Kolya couldn’t wait. He quickly shouted to Smurov, “Open the door!” and as soon as Smurov did, Kolya blew his whistle. Perezvon ran into the room at full speed.

“Jump, Perezvon! Beg! Beg!” Kolya shouted, jumping up. The dog stood up on his hind legs by Ilusha’s bed. What happened next surprised everyone: Ilusha jerked forward, bent over Perezvon, and stared at him, barely able to breathe.
“It’s… Zhutchka!” Ilusha suddenly cried out, his voice full of both joy and pain.
“And who did you think it was?” Kolya shouted, now grinning with happiness. He bent down, grabbed the dog, and lifted him up to Ilusha.

“Look, buddy, see—the dog’s blind in one eye and his left ear is torn, just like you described. That’s how I found him. I found him right away. He didn’t belong to anyone!” Kolya explained, turning quickly to the captain, his wife, Alyosha, and then Ilusha again. “He used to live in the Fedotovs’ backyard. Even though he stayed there, they never fed him—he was a stray who ran off from the village. I found him. See? He couldn’t have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he would have died for sure! So he must have spit it out, since he’s alive. You didn’t see him do it, but the pin pricked his tongue—that’s why he squealed and ran away. Dogs’ mouths are really sensitive—even more than people’s!” Kolya cried, his face glowing with joy. Ilusha was too stunned to speak. He stared at Kolya, white as a sheet, eyes wide, mouth open. If Kolya had known how dangerous this might be for Ilusha’s health, he never would have pulled this trick, but he had no idea. Only Alyosha seemed to realize the risk. The captain, for his part, acted like a little kid.
“Zhutchka! It’s Zhutchka!” he shouted with delight. “Ilusha, it’s your Zhutchka! Mama, look—it’s Zhutchka!” He was close to tears.
“And I never guessed!” Smurov cried, disappointed. “Bravo, Krassotkin! I told you he’d find the dog, and he did!”
“He did!” another boy echoed, excited.
“Krassotkin’s the best!” a third called out.
“He’s the best! He’s the best!” the others shouted, clapping their hands.

“Wait, wait!” Kolya tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I’ll tell you how it all happened—that’s the best part. I found the dog, took him home, and hid him right away. I didn’t show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov knew for the last two weeks, but I told him the dog was named Perezvon, so he didn’t guess. Meanwhile, I taught the dog all kinds of tricks. You should see what he can do!” Kolya said, excitedly. “I trained him so I could bring you a smart, well-behaved dog, old friend, and say, ‘Look how awesome your Zhutchka is now!’ Do you have any meat? He’ll show you a trick that will make you laugh so hard. Any meat?”

The captain ran across the hall to the landlady’s kitchen. Not wanting to waste time, Kolya hurriedly shouted to Perezvon, “Dead!” and the dog immediately rolled over on his back with his paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same pained smile as before, but the person who loved the performance most was “mama.” She laughed at the dog, snapping her fingers and calling, “Perezvon, Perezvon!”

“Nothing will make him get up, nothing!” Kolya said proudly. “He won’t move no matter how much you yell, but if I call him, he’ll jump up right away. Ici, Perezvon!” The dog leaped up, running around and whining with excitement. The captain hurried back with a piece of cooked beef.

“Is it hot?” Kolya asked, businesslike, taking the meat. “Dogs don’t like hot food. No, it’s fine. Look, everyone—look, Ilusha. Hey, old friend, why aren’t you looking? He won’t even look at him, now that I brought him.”

The new trick was to make the dog stand perfectly still with his nose out, while Kolya put the tempting piece of meat right on his nose. The poor dog had to stay frozen like that, sometimes for up to half an hour, until his master gave the signal. But Kolya only made Perezvon wait a few seconds this time.
“Paid for!” Kolya yelled, and the meat instantly disappeared from the dog’s nose into his mouth. Everyone cheered and acted amazed.
“Did you really stay away all this time just to train the dog?” Alyosha asked, sounding a bit reproachful.
“Just for that,” Kolya replied honestly. “I wanted to show him off when he was at his best.”
“Perezvon! Perezvon!” Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and calling the dog.

“What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! Ici, Perezvon!” Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon jumped up beside Ilusha. The boy hugged the dog’s head, and Perezvon immediately licked his cheek. Ilusha snuggled close, stretched out in bed, and hid his face in the dog’s shaggy fur.
“Dear, dear!” the captain kept exclaiming. Kolya sat back down on the edge of the bed.
“Ilusha, I can show you another trick. I brought you a little cannon. Remember I told you about it before, and you said you wanted to see it? Well, here it is.”

Kolya quickly pulled a small bronze cannon out of his bag. He hurried because he was so happy himself. Normally, he would have waited until the excitement over Perezvon died down, but now he rushed on, thinking, “Everyone’s happy now, so here’s something to make it even better!” He was thrilled.

“I’ve wanted this for a while; it’s for you, old friend. It used to belong to Morozov, but he didn’t need it—he got it from his brother. I traded a book for it from my father’s bookshelf—A Kinsman of Mahomet or Salutary Folly, some scandalous book from Moscow, written a hundred years ago, before there was any censorship. And Morozov likes that kind of thing, so he was happy. . .”

Kolya held up the cannon for everyone to see and admire. Ilusha sat up, still hugging the dog, and stared at the toy in delight. The excitement grew even more when Kolya announced he had gunpowder, too, and that they could fire the cannon right away—“if it won’t scare the ladies.” “Mama” immediately wanted to inspect the toy and was given it. She was very pleased with the little cannon on wheels and rolled it back and forth on her lap. She quickly agreed to let them fire it, not really knowing what she was saying yes to. Kolya showed the powder and shot. The captain, being a former soldier, agreed to load it, but asked that they wait to use the shot until another time. They set the cannon on the floor, aimed at an empty part of the room, put a tiny bit of powder in, and touched it with a match. There was a huge bang. Mama jumped, but then laughed happily. The boys were speechless with excitement. The captain was even more delighted, watching Ilusha. Kolya picked up the cannon and gave it, along with the powder and shot, to Ilusha.
“I got it for you, for you! I’ve been saving it for you for a long time,” Kolya repeated, gleeful.
“Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!” Mama begged like a little kid, her face showing real fear that she wouldn’t get it. Kolya felt awkward. The captain shuffled nervously.

“Mama, mama,” he said, hurrying to her, “the cannon is yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it’s a gift for him. But it’s really as good as yours—Ilusha will always let you play with it—so it belongs to both of you, to both of you.”
“No, I don’t want to share it. I want it all to myself, not Ilusha’s,” Mama insisted, close to tears.

“Take it, mother—here, keep it!” Ilusha cried. “Krassotkin, can I give it to my mother?” he asked, looking at Kolya with pleading eyes, as if he was afraid Kolya might be offended if he gave away the present.
“Of course you can,” Kolya agreed warmly. He took the cannon from Ilusha and handed it to Mama with a polite bow. She was so touched, she started crying.
“Ilusha, darling, you’re the one who loves his mama!” she said fondly, and immediately began rolling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
“Mama, let me kiss your hand,” the captain said, rushing over and kissing her hand.
“And I’ve never met such a charming boy as this nice young man,” Mama said gratefully, pointing to Kolya.

“And I’ll bring you as much gunpowder as you want, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov figured out the recipe—twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten parts sulfur, and six parts birch charcoal. You mix it together with water and push it through a sieve—that’s how you make it.”
“Smurov told me about your powder, but my father says it’s not real gunpowder,” Ilusha said.
“Not real?” Kolya blushed. “Well, it burns. I don’t know, honestly.”
“No, I didn’t mean that,” the captain added, looking guilty. “I just said that real gunpowder isn’t made exactly like that, but it doesn’t matter—it still works.”

“I don’t know, you know better than me. We lit some in a cold cream jar, and it burned great—burned all up, just a little ash left. But that was just the paste, and if you push it through the sieve… but you know best, I’m not sure. And did you hear Bulkin’s dad beat him because of our powder?” he asked Ilusha.
“Yes,” Ilusha replied, listening to Kolya with huge interest and happiness.

“We’d made a whole bottle of it, and he kept it under his bed. His dad found it, said it might explode, and beat him right away. He wanted to complain about me to the teachers. Now Bulkin isn’t allowed to hang out with me, and neither is Smurov. I’ve got a bad reputation with everyone. They say I’m a ‘bad influence,’” Kolya said, a little proudly. “It all started with what happened at the railroad tracks.”
“Ah, we heard about that, too,” the captain cried. “How did you lie still on the tracks? Weren’t you scared, lying there with the train coming? Weren’t you afraid?”
The captain was clearly trying to flatter Kolya.

“No, not really,” Kolya replied, acting casual. “But what really wrecked my reputation here was that stupid goose,” he said, turning back to Ilusha. Even though he tried to seem relaxed, he still couldn’t control his excitement and kept slipping out of the calm tone he wanted.
“Oh! I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, his face lighting up. “They told me, but I didn’t get it. Did they really take you to court?”

“The whole thing was stupid and pointless—they made a big deal out of nothing, like always,” Kolya answered, trying to sound casual. “I was walking through the marketplace one day, just as they brought in the geese. I stopped to look at them. Suddenly, a guy who’s now an errand boy at Plotnikov’s looked at me and said, ‘Why are you staring at the geese?’ I looked back at him—he’s a dumb, moon-faced guy of about twenty. I’m always on the peasant’s side, you know—I like talking to them. We’ve fallen behind the peasants, that’s a fact. Are you laughing, Karamazov?”
“No, of course not. I’m listening,” said Alyosha, looking friendly, which reassured Kolya right away.

“My theory is simple, Karamazov. I believe in the people and always give them credit, but I don’t believe in spoiling them—that’s non-negotiable. But anyway, about the goose. So I told the guy, ‘I’m wondering what the goose is thinking about.’ He looked at me, all confused, and asked, ‘What does the goose think about?’ I pointed at a cart full of oats. ‘The oats are falling out of the sack, and the goose is sticking its neck under the wheel to eat them—see?’ ‘Yeah, I see,’ he said. ‘Well,’ I said, ‘if the cart moves just a little, will it break the goose’s neck or not?’ ‘Of course it will!’ he said, grinning. ‘Let’s try it, then,’ I said. ‘Let’s,’ he agreed. It didn’t take long to set up: he held the bridle, and I stood to guide the goose. The owner wasn’t paying attention, so the goose put its head under the wheel for the oats. I winked at the guy, he tugged the bridle, and—crack! The goose’s neck broke. And just then, all the peasants saw us and started yelling, ‘You did that on purpose!’ ‘No, not on purpose!’ ‘Yes, you did!’ They shouted, ‘Take him to the judge!’ They brought me, too. ‘You were there, you helped, everyone knows you!’ And for some reason, everyone in the market really does know me,” Kolya added, sounding proud. “We all went to the judge, and they brought the goose. The guy was crying, really bawling, and the farmer kept yelling that you could kill as many geese as you wanted that way. There were witnesses. The judge settled it quickly: the farmer got a ruble, the guy got the goose, and he was warned not to do it again. The guy kept crying and blamed me, saying, ‘He made me do it!’ I answered calmly that I hadn’t told him to do it, I was just talking in general. The judge smiled, then got annoyed with himself for smiling. ‘I’ll tell your teachers so you won’t waste time on these ideas instead of studying.’ But he never did. Still, everyone heard about it, and my teachers found out—especially Kolbasnikov, who was really shocked. But Dardanelov defended me. Kolbasnikov is mad at everyone now—did you know he just got married? Got a thousand-ruble dowry, but his bride is super ugly. The third-years wrote a poem about it:
And so on—it’s really funny, I’ll bring it for you next time. I have nothing against Dardanelov; he’s a smart man and I respect people like that. It’s not just because he defended me.”
“But you beat him in an argument about the founders of Troy!” Smurov suddenly added, clearly proud of Kolya, especially after the goose story.
“Did you really beat him?” the captain asked, sounding impressed. “About who founded Troy? We heard about it—Ilusha told me.”
“He knows everything, father! He just pretends not to, but he’s top in every subject,” Ilusha added, looking at Kolya with total happiness.
Ilusha beamed at Kolya with pure joy.

“Oh, the Troy thing doesn’t matter—trivial question,” Kolya said, acting humble but proud. By now, he’d mostly recovered his dignity, but he was still a little nervous. He realized he’d gotten too excited, especially talking about the goose, and Alyosha had looked serious the whole time and not said a word. Kolya started to worry that Alyosha was silent because he looked down on him, thinking he was just showing off. If that’s what Alyosha thought, Kolya would—
“I consider it a trivial matter,” Kolya said again, this time more confidently.
“And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who hadn’t spoken before, surprising everyone. He was shy, about eleven, and his name was Kartashov. He sat near the door. Kolya looked at him in surprise.

The truth was, at school, the question of who founded Troy was a big secret. The answer could only be found in a book called Smaragdov, and only Kolya had that book. Once, when Kolya wasn’t around, Kartashov peeked at Smaragdov and found the answer. He’d wanted to show he knew, but was always afraid Kolya would embarrass him. But now, he couldn’t hold back anymore—he had wanted to for weeks.

“Okay, so who did found it?” Kolya asked, looking at him with a mix of pride and arrogance. He could tell that Kartashov really knew the answer, and Kolya quickly decided how to react. It was a little uncomfortable for everyone.

“Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius, and Tros,” Kartashov blurted out, and immediately turned bright red. The boys stared at him for a whole minute, then turned to look at Kolya, who just stared back at Kartashov, acting cool.
“But what does it even mean to ‘found’ a city?” he finally said. “Did they each lay a brick, or what?”
The other boys laughed. Kartashov turned even redder and looked close to tears. Kolya let him squirm for a minute.

“Before you talk about history, you should first know what you’re talking about,” Kolya scolded him, sharp and serious. “But I don’t care much about these old stories or about history in general,” he added, now talking to everyone.
“History?” the captain asked, a little nervous.

“Yes, history! It’s just the story of all the dumb things people have done, that’s all. The only subjects I respect are math and science,” Kolya said, still showing off. He glanced at Alyosha—whose opinion he cared about most. But Alyosha was still silent and serious. If Alyosha had said anything, Kolya would have stopped, but Alyosha’s silence (maybe he was judging him?) finally got on Kolya’s nerves.
“The classical languages, too… they’re just crazy. Isn’t that right, Karamazov?”
“I don’t agree,” Alyosha said, giving a little smile.

“Studying classics, in my opinion, is just a way for the authorities to control us—that’s the only reason it’s in our schools,” Kolya said, getting more worked up. “Latin and Greek were added just to make school more boring and to dull our minds. It was bad enough before, but they wanted to make it worse. So they thought of Greek and Latin. That’s what I think, and I hope I never change my mind.” Kolya’s cheeks were flushed.
“That’s true,” Smurov chimed in, sounding completely convinced. He’d been listening closely.
“But he’s first in Latin himself!” one of the boys suddenly pointed out.
“Yeah, Dad, he’s first in Latin, even though he says that!” Ilusha echoed.

“So what?” Kolya defended himself, even though he liked the compliment. “I’m working hard at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mom I’d pass my exams. I think whatever you do, you should do well. But deep down, I totally hate the classics and think it’s all fake… Don’t you agree, Karamazov?”
“Why call it ‘fake’?” Alyosha asked, smiling again.

“Well, all the classical authors have already been translated into every language, so it’s not like you need Latin to read them. That means they only make us learn Latin to control us and make us dull. What else can you call it but a fake?”
“Who taught you all that?” Alyosha asked, finally sounding surprised.
“I can think for myself—I don’t need to be taught. But what I just said about the classics being translated, our teacher, Kolbasnikov, said it to the whole third class.”
“The doctor’s here!” Nina exclaimed, who had been quiet until then.

A carriage from Madame Hohlakov pulled up outside. The captain, who had been waiting for the doctor all morning, rushed out to meet him. “Mama” straightened up and tried to look dignified. Alyosha went to fix Ilusha’s pillows. Nina, sitting in her chair, watched nervously as Alyosha tidied the bed. The boys quickly said goodbye. Some promised to come again that evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped off the bed.
“I’m not leaving, I’m not leaving,” Kolya quickly told Ilusha. “I’ll wait in the hallway and come back after the doctor’s gone—I’ll bring Perezvon too.”

But now the doctor had already come in—a serious-looking man with long, dark sideburns and a shiny shaved chin, wearing a big fur coat. When he crossed the doorway, he froze, surprised; maybe he thought he’d come to the wrong place. “What is this? Where am I?” he muttered, not taking off his coat or hat. The crowded, poor room, with laundry hanging in the corner, confused him. The captain bowed low, almost doubled over.
“It’s here, sir, here, sir,” he stammered, “you’re in the right place, you were coming to us…”
“Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor asked loudly, trying to sound important. “Mr. Snegiryov—are you him?”
“That’s me, sir!”
“Ah!”

The doctor looked around the room with a disgusted expression again, then took off his coat, showing off a fancy medal on his chest. The captain caught his fur coat in the air, and the doctor took off his cap.
“Where is the patient?” he asked, in a very official tone.
“What do you think the doctor’s going to say to him?” Kolya asked quickly. “He’s got such a gross face, hasn’t he? I just can’t stand anything to do with medicine!”
“Ilusha is dying. I’m pretty sure of it,” Alyosha answered sadly.
“Doctors are such fakes! Medicine is just a scam. But still, I’m glad we’ve finally met, Karamazov. I’ve wanted to meet you for ages. It’s just a shame it had to happen like this.”
Kolya really wanted to say something even kinder or more heartfelt, but he felt awkward. Alyosha noticed and smiled, then squeezed his hand.

“I’ve respected you for a long time—you’re such a rare person,” Kolya mumbled, sounding uncertain. “I heard you’re a mystic and spent time in the monastery. I know you’re into all that, but…it doesn’t bother me. Being out in the real world will fix you, though. People like you always change when they see real life.”
“What do you mean, mystic? Fix me of what?” Alyosha looked surprised.
“Oh, you know—God and all that stuff.”
“Wait, do you not believe in God?”

“I don’t really have a problem with God. Of course, God is just a theory, but…I admit He’s necessary…for the universe to make sense, and all that. And if there wasn’t a God, we’d have to make one up anyway.” Kolya started blushing. He suddenly thought Alyosha might believe he was just trying to act smart and show he was grown up. “I’m not showing off for him!” Kolya thought, feeling annoyed with himself.

“Honestly, I hate talking about this kind of stuff,” he said, sounding final. “A person who doesn’t believe in God can still love people, right? Voltaire didn’t believe in God and he loved humanity, didn’t he?” (Kolya thought, “There I go again.”)

“Voltaire did believe in God—just not very much, I think. And he didn’t really love people that much either,” Alyosha replied quietly and kindly, as if he was talking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was struck by how Alyosha didn’t try to push his point, almost as if he was leaving the decision up to Kolya.
“Have you read Voltaire?” Alyosha asked.
“Not really…well, I read Candide, but in a weird old Russian translation.” (Kolya thought again, “There I go again!”)
“And did you actually understand it?”

“Oh, yeah, I got it…well…why wouldn’t I understand it? There’s a lot of nasty stuff in it, of course. But I understand it’s a book with a philosophy, trying to make a point…” Kolya was getting confused now. Suddenly, for no reason, he announced, “I’m a Socialist, Karamazov, a total Socialist.”
“A Socialist?” Alyosha laughed. “But when did you have time for that? I thought you were only thirteen?”
Kolya winced.
“First of all, I’m not thirteen—I’ll be fourteen in two weeks,” he said, blushing and angry. “Second, what does age have to do with anything? What matters is what I believe, not how old I am, right?”
“When you’re older, you’ll see how much age affects what you believe. Honestly, I wondered if these were even your own ideas,” Alyosha said calmly, but Kolya interrupted, fired up:
“Come on—you just want obedience and mysticism. You have to admit, Christianity’s really just helped rich people keep everyone else under their control, right?”
“Oh, I know where you got that! Someone told you that, I’ll bet!” Alyosha cried.

“Why do you think someone told me? I can think for myself. I’m not against Christ, if that’s what you mean. He was a really kind person, and if He was around today, He’d be with the revolutionaries, probably leading them. No doubt about it.”
“Where did you get that from? Who told you that nonsense?” Alyosha demanded.
“Okay, fine! I’ve talked a lot with Mr. Rakitin, but…they say old Byelinsky said that too.”
“Byelinsky? I don’t remember that. I don’t think he wrote that anywhere.”
“Maybe he didn’t write it, but people say he said it. I heard that from a…well, never mind.”
“Have you read Byelinsky?”
“Well, not all of him…but I read the part about Tatyana, about why she didn’t run off with Onyegin.”
“Didn’t run off with Onyegin? Seriously—do you even understand that already?”

“Why, do you think I’m like little Smurov?” Kolya said, grinning, but annoyed. “But don’t think I’m some crazy revolutionary. I argue with Mr. Rakitin plenty. And even though I brought up Tatyana, I’m not for women’s rights or anything. I actually think women should obey, like Napoleon said, ‘les femmes tricottent.’” Kolya smiled for some reason. “At least on that, I agree with that so-called great man. And I think leaving Russia for America is cowardly and stupid. Why go to America when we can help people here? Especially now—there’s so much we could do. That’s what I told them.”
“What do you mean? Told who? Did someone suggest you go to America?”

“Honestly, they tried to get me to, but I refused. Just between us, Karamazov—not a word to anyone, okay? I don’t want to get mixed up with the secret police or get sent to the Chain bridge for lessons.”

“Remember? It’s great. Why are you laughing? You don’t think I’m making this up, do you?” (Kolya worried suddenly, “What if he finds out all I’ve read is just that one issue of The Bell from my dad’s bookshelf?”)
“No, I’m not laughing and I’d never think you’re lying. Honestly, it’s all pretty believable. But tell me, have you read Pushkin—Onyegin, for example? You mentioned Tatyana just now.”
“No, I haven’t read it yet, but I want to. I’m open-minded, Karamazov. Why do you ask?”
“Oh, no reason.”
“Tell me, Karamazov, do you secretly think I’m ridiculous?” Kolya blurted out, standing up straight like he was at attention. “Please tell me honestly.”

“You think I look down on you?” Alyosha looked at him, puzzled. “Why would I? I’m just sad that someone as interesting as you is getting caught up in all this silly nonsense before you’ve even really lived.”
“Don’t worry about me,” Kolya interrupted, trying to sound confident. “But it’s true, I’m stupidly sensitive. You smiled before, and I thought you were—”

“Oh, my smile meant something else. I’ll tell you why. Not long ago, I read what a German wrote about Russian students these days: ‘Show a Russian schoolboy a map of the stars he knows nothing about, and next day he’ll bring it back with corrections!’ The German meant Russian schoolboys have no real knowledge, just endless arrogance.”

“That’s so true,” Kolya suddenly laughed. “Exactly! Good for the German! But he missed the good part, you know? Sure, there’s arrogance, but it comes from being young—that can be fixed. But we also get independent thinking early, real courage to believe things for ourselves, not just follow the rules like those sausage-making Germans. But yeah, the German was right. Still, Germans should be strangled, even though they’re so good at science and learning.”
“Strangled? Why?” Alyosha grinned.

“Okay, maybe I’m talking nonsense. I’m really childish sometimes. When I’m excited, I just start rambling. But anyway, we’re sitting here talking, and that doctor’s been in there forever. Maybe he’s checking on the mother and poor Nina, too. I liked Nina. As I was leaving, she whispered, ‘Why didn’t you come sooner?’ She sounded so sad. I think she’s really sweet and pitiful.”

“Yes, yes! You’ll visit more and see what she’s like. It would be great for you to know people like them. You’d learn a lot—things you can’t learn any other way,” Alyosha said warmly. “That would help you more than anything else.”
“Oh, I feel so guilty for not coming sooner!” Kolya burst out in frustration.
“Yeah, it’s a shame. You saw how happy Ilusha was to see you. He’s been waiting and worrying about you coming.”

“Don’t remind me! That makes it worse! But I deserve it. What stopped me was my pride, my selfishness, and my stubbornness. I’ve always struggled with it, but I can’t get rid of it. I see that now. I’m a jerk in so many ways, Karamazov!”
“No, you’re a wonderful person, even if you’re a bit twisted by all this,” Alyosha said warmly. “I totally get why you’ve had such an effect on that sensitive, generous boy.”
“And you say that to me!” Kolya cried. “Would you believe it—I kept thinking you looked down on me! If only you knew how much I care about your opinion!”
“Are you really that sensitive? At your age? Honestly, when you were telling your story just now, I thought you must be sensitive.”

“You guessed? You’re really sharp! I bet you thought that when I was talking about the goose. That’s exactly when I thought you were judging me for showing off, and for a second I kind of hated you for it, so I started acting like an idiot. Then I thought, just now, when I said if there were no God we’d have to invent Him, that I was just trying to sound clever, since I got that from a book. But I swear I wasn’t showing off—at least, not on purpose. Maybe just because I was so happy? Yes, probably because I was happy…but it’s embarrassing to get so gushy just because you’re pleased. Anyway, I’m sure now you don’t look down on me—it was all in my head. Oh, Karamazov, I’m really unhappy. Sometimes I think everyone is laughing at me, the whole world, and then I feel like smashing the whole system.”
“And you drive everyone around you crazy,” Alyosha smiled.
“Yes, I drive everyone crazy, especially my mom. Karamazov, just tell me—am I being really ridiculous right now?”

“Don’t worry about that—don’t even think of it!” Alyosha said. “And what does ridiculous even mean? Isn’t everyone always being or seeming ridiculous? Besides, most smart people now are terrified of looking ridiculous, and that just makes them miserable. The weird thing is that you’re feeling this so early—I’ve noticed it in you, and not just you. Even kids now feel it. It’s almost like a sickness. Vanity is like the devil for your whole generation—it’s everywhere,” Alyosha finished seriously, without the smile Kolya expected. “You’re like everyone else,” Alyosha said, “that is, like a lot of people. But you don’t have to be like everyone else.”
“Even if everyone is like that?”

“Yes, even then. You be the one who’s different. You’re already not like everyone else—you’re not afraid to admit when you’re wrong or even when you’re being silly. Who does that nowadays? No one. People don’t even think about criticizing themselves anymore. Don’t be like everyone else, even if you’re the only one.”
“That’s awesome! I knew you’d understand. You really know how to make someone feel better. I’ve wanted to meet you for so long, Karamazov! Did you really think about me, too? You said you did?”
“Yeah, I’d heard about you and thought about you, too…and even if part of you just wants praise, that’s okay.”
“You know, Karamazov, this whole conversation has felt like a love confession,” Kolya said, blushing. “That’s not stupid, is it?”
“Not at all, and even if it was, it wouldn’t matter, because it’s a good thing.” Alyosha smiled brightly.
“But you know, Karamazov, you have to admit you’re a little embarrassed too…I can see it in your eyes,” Kolya said, grinning slyly.
“Why would I be embarrassed?”
“Well, you’re blushing!”
“You made me blush,” Alyosha laughed, and he really did blush. “Well, maybe I am a little embarrassed—I don’t even know why,” he said, almost mumbling.
“Oh, I love you and admire you so much right now, just because you’re a bit embarrassed! You’re just like me,” Kolya cried, completely excited. His face was glowing and his eyes were shining.
“You know, Kolya, you’re probably going to have a tough life,” Alyosha said suddenly.
“I know, I know. How do you always know everything ahead of time?” Kolya agreed right away.
“But you’ll still love life, overall.”

“Exactly! You’re a prophet. We’re going to get along great, Karamazov! What makes me happiest is that you treat me like an equal. But we’re not equals—you’re better. Still, we’ll get along. All last month, I kept thinking, ‘Either we’ll be friends forever, or we’ll be enemies for life!’”
“And of course, thinking that, you were already liking me,” Alyosha laughed.
“I was! I’ve been loving and dreaming about meeting you. And how do you know everything ahead of time? Oh, here’s the doctor—look at his face! What’s he going to tell us?”

The doctor came out of the room again, bundled up in his fur coat and with his hat still on. He looked almost angry and disgusted, like he was afraid he might get dirty just being there. He glanced quickly around the hallway, giving Alyosha and Kolya a harsh look. Alyosha waved at the coachman from the door, and the carriage that had brought the doctor pulled up. The captain rushed out after the doctor, bowing and apologizing, hoping to get a final word in. The poor man looked completely crushed, his eyes full of fear.

“Your Excellency, your Excellency... is it really possible?” he started, but he couldn’t finish and just clasped his hands in despair. Still, he stared at the doctor, hoping he might say something to change the boy’s fate.
“I can’t do anything. I’m not God!” the doctor replied, brushing him off but still sounding important.
“Doctor... your Excellency... will it be soon? Very soon?”
“You have to be ready for anything,” the doctor said sharply and seriously, looking down and getting ready to leave for the carriage.
“Your Excellency, for Christ’s sake!” the terrified captain stopped him again. “Your Excellency! But is there nothing, absolutely nothing that can save him now?”

“It’s out of my hands now,” the doctor said impatiently, “but... hmmm!” He suddenly paused. “If you could, for example... send... your patient... immediately, without any delay”—the words “immediately, without any delay” came out so sternly that the captain jumped—“to Syracuse, the new, healthy climate might possibly help—”
“To Syracuse!” the captain blurted out, not understanding.
“Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya explained quickly. The doctor glanced at him.
“Sicily! Your Excellency,” the captain stammered, “but you saw”—he waved his hands at the poor surroundings—“my wife and family?”

“No, no, Sicily is not the place for your family. The family should go to the Caucasus in early spring... your daughter must go to the Caucasus, and your wife... after some time at the Caucasus mineral baths for her rheumatism... she should be sent straight to Paris to the mental specialist Lepelletier; I could give you a note to him, and then... maybe there could be a change—”
“Doctor, doctor! But look!” The captain spread his hands again in despair, showing off the bare wooden walls of the hallway.
“Well, that’s not my problem,” the doctor grinned. “I’ve only told you the answer from medical science about possible treatments. As for the rest, unfortunately—”

“Don’t worry, apothecary, my dog won’t bite you,” Kolya said loudly, noticing the doctor glancing uneasily at Perezvon, who was standing in the doorway. There was anger in Kolya’s voice. He used the word “apothecary” instead of doctor on purpose, and later explained he did it “to insult him.”
“What’s that?” The doctor jerked his head up, surprised by Kolya. “Who is this?” he asked Alyosha, as if for an explanation.
“I’m Perezvon’s owner, don’t worry about me,” Kolya replied sharply.
“Perezvon?” the doctor repeated, confused.
“He hears the bell, but doesn’t know where it’s coming from. Goodbye, we’ll meet in Syracuse.”
“Who is this? Who is this?” The doctor suddenly got furious.

“He’s just a schoolboy, doctor, a mischievous kid; don’t pay attention to him,” Alyosha said, frowning and speaking quickly. “Kolya, be quiet!” he shouted at Krassotkin. “Ignore him, doctor,” he said again, sounding a bit annoyed.
“He needs a beating, a good beating!” the doctor yelled in a fury.
“And you know, apothecary, my Perezvon might bite!” Kolya replied, turning pale, his voice shaking but his eyes blazing. “Here, Perezvon!”
“Kolya, if you say one more word, I won’t have anything to do with you,” Alyosha said firmly.
“There’s only one person in the world who can order Nikolay Krassotkin around—this man,” Kolya pointed to Alyosha. “I listen to him. Goodbye!”

He stepped forward, opened the door, and quickly went into the inner room. Perezvon rushed in after him. The doctor stood frozen for five seconds, staring at Alyosha in disbelief; then, muttering a curse, he hurried out to the carriage, repeating out loud, “This is... this is... I don’t know what this is!” The captain ran forward to help him into the carriage. Alyosha followed Kolya into the room. Kolya was already by Ilusha’s bedside. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later, the captain came back too.

“Father, father, come... we...” Ilusha gasped, extremely excited, but couldn’t finish. He threw his thin arms around his father and Kolya, hugging them both as tightly as he could. The captain suddenly started shaking with silent sobs, and Kolya’s lips and chin trembled.
“Father, father! I feel so sorry for you!” Ilusha moaned sadly.
“Ilusha... darling... the doctor said... you’ll be all right... we’ll be happy... the doctor...” the captain started.
“Oh, father! I know what the new doctor told you about me... I saw!” cried Ilusha, and again he hugged them both with all his strength, hiding his face on his father’s shoulder.
“Father, don’t cry, and when I die, find a good boy, another one... pick one of them, a good one, call him Ilusha and love him instead of me...”
“Stop it, old man, you’ll get better,” Krassotkin burst out suddenly, his voice sounding almost angry.

“But don’t ever forget me, father,” Ilusha continued, “come visit my grave... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to go walking, and come there with Krassotkin in the evening... and with Perezvon... I’ll be waiting for you there.... Father, father!”
His voice broke. All three were silent, still hugging each other. Nina was quietly crying in her chair, and when she saw everyone else crying, “mamma” started crying too.
“Ilusha! Ilusha!” she cried.
Krassotkin suddenly pulled himself out of Ilusha’s hug.

“Goodbye, old man, my mom expects me home for dinner,” he said quickly. “Too bad I didn’t tell her I’d be late! She’ll be super worried.... But after dinner I’ll come back and stay with you all afternoon and evening, and I’ll tell you all sorts of stories. And I’ll bring Perezvon, but right now I’ll take him with me, because he’ll start howling if I leave and bother you. Goodbye!”
And he ran out into the hallway. He tried not to cry, but once he was in the hall, he burst into tears. Alyosha found him crying.
“Kolya, you have to promise to come back, or Ilusha will be really let down,” Alyosha said seriously.
“I will! Oh, I wish I hadn’t waited so long to visit him!” Kolya muttered through his tears, not caring anymore if anyone saw him crying.
Just then the captain dashed out of the room and quickly shut the door behind him. His face looked wild, his lips shaking. He stood in front of the two and threw up his arms.

“I don’t want a good boy! I don’t want any other boy!” he whispered wildly, clenching his teeth. “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my tongue—” He broke off with a sob and dropped to his knees by the wooden bench. Pressing his fists to his head, he started sobbing, making weird whimpering noises, trying his hardest not to let anyone in the room hear him.
Kolya ran out into the street.
“Bye, Karamazov! Are you going to come yourself?” he called sharply and angrily to Alyosha.
“I’ll definitely come this evening.”
“What did he mean about Jerusalem?... What was that supposed to mean?”
“It’s from the Bible. ‘If I forget you, Jerusalem’—it means, if I forget what’s most precious to me, if anything else becomes more important, then may—”
“I get it, that’s enough! Make sure you come! Here, Perezvon!” he shouted fiercely to his dog, and then walked quickly home.

Alyosha walked across Cathedral Square to the widow Morozov’s house to visit Grushenka, who had sent her maid Fenya to him with an urgent message that morning, begging him to come right away. When Alyosha questioned Fenya, he learned that her mistress had been especially upset since yesterday. In the two months since Mitya’s (Dmitri’s) arrest, Alyosha had often visited the widow Morozov’s house, both because he wanted to and to deliver messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya’s arrest, Grushenka became very sick and stayed ill for almost five weeks, spending a whole week unconscious. She looked different now—thinner, with a slightly yellowish face, though she had been well enough to leave the house for the last two weeks. To Alyosha, though, her face seemed even more beautiful than before, and he enjoyed meeting her eyes when he visited. There was now a new sense of strength and determination in her expression, as if she had changed on the inside. A small vertical wrinkle between her brows made her pretty face look serious, even strict, at first glance. There was hardly any sign left of her old playful ways.

Alyosha found it strange that, even after everything Grushenka had gone through—her fiancé arrested for a terrible crime just after they got engaged, her own illness, and the threat of Mitya being found guilty—she hadn’t lost her youthful spirit. There was a gentle glow in her eyes, which used to be proud, though sometimes they still flashed with jealousy, especially when she thought about Katerina Ivanovna. Grushenka had even talked about Katerina in her feverish delirium. Alyosha knew Grushenka was extremely jealous of her. Yet Katerina Ivanovna hadn’t visited Mitya in prison, even though she could have whenever she wanted. This whole situation was a tough puzzle for Alyosha, because he was the only one Grushenka opened up to and always asked for advice. Sometimes, he just didn’t know what to say.

Worried, Alyosha walked into Grushenka’s apartment. She was home, having just returned from visiting Mitya half an hour ago. The way she jumped up quickly from her chair to greet him made it clear she’d been waiting for him impatiently. On the table, a game of cards was laid out, and on the leather sofa across the room, Maximov was lying half-sitting, dressed in a robe and a cotton nightcap. He looked sick and weak, but was smiling happily. When the old, homeless Maximov had returned with Grushenka from Mokroe two months ago, he had simply stayed with her. He’d arrived soaked and frightened, sat on the sofa, and looked at her with a shy, hopeful smile. Grushenka, who was heartbroken and feverish, almost forgot he was there during her first half hour home. But then she noticed him, laughed a little, and told Fenya to get him something to eat. That day he barely moved from the sofa. When night came and the shutters were closed, Fenya asked her mistress:
“Is the gentleman going to stay the night, mistress?”
“Yes; make him a bed on the sofa,” Grushenka answered.
After asking him more questions, Grushenka learned that Maximov had nowhere to go, and that “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me directly that he wouldn’t take me in again and gave me five roubles.”

“Well, God bless you, you’d better stay then,” Grushenka decided, even though she was grieving, and gave him a kind smile. The old man was so touched that he almost cried. And so the poor wanderer stayed on with her ever since. Even when Grushenka was ill, Maximov didn’t leave. Fenya and her grandmother, the cook, didn’t kick him out either, but kept giving him meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka got used to him, and after her visits to Mitya in prison (which she started before she was really well), she would sit and chat with “Maximushka” about little things to distract herself from her sadness. The old man turned out to be a good storyteller, and she ended up needing his company. Grushenka barely saw anyone else except Alyosha, who didn’t come every day and never stayed long. Her former rich lover was seriously ill at this time—“on his last legs,” as people in town said—and he actually died a week after Mitya’s trial. Three weeks before his death, feeling the end was near, he finally made his sons, their wives, and children come to him and told them not to leave again. From then on, he told his servants not to let Grushenka in and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness and tells you to forget him.” Still, Grushenka sent someone almost every day to ask how he was.

“You’re here at last!” Grushenka cried, dropping her cards and greeting Alyosha happily. “Maximushka was scaring me, saying maybe you wouldn’t come. Oh, I need you so much! Sit down at the table. What do you want—coffee?”
“Yes, please,” said Alyosha, sitting down. “I’m really hungry.”

“Good! Fenya, Fenya, coffee!” Grushenka called. “It’s been ready for ages. And bring some little pies, make sure they’re hot. You know, we had a whole argument about those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and guess what—he threw them back at me, refused to eat them. He even flung one on the floor and stomped on it. So I said, ‘I’ll leave them with the guard; if you don’t eat them before evening, it means your nasty temper is all you need!’ Then I left. We had another fight, can you believe it? Every time I go, we argue.”
Grushenka said all this in one breath, obviously upset. Maximov, feeling nervous, just smiled and stared at the floor.
“What did you argue about this time?” Alyosha asked.

“I didn’t see it coming at all. Would you believe, he’s jealous of the Pole now. ‘Why are you keeping him?’ he said. ‘So you’re supporting him now.’ He’s jealous all the time, even while eating and sleeping! Last week, he even got jealous of Kuzma.”
“But he knew about the Pole before?”

“Yes, he’s always known about him, but today he suddenly started scolding me about it. I’m too embarrassed to repeat what he said. Silly man! Rakitin went in just as I was leaving. Maybe Rakitin is making him worse. What do you think?” she added carelessly.
“He loves you, that’s why—he loves you so much. And now he’s especially anxious.”

“He has every reason, with the trial tomorrow. And I went to talk to him about it, because I’m terrified about what will happen. You say he’s worried, but I’m even more worried! And he talks about the Pole! He’s ridiculous! At least he’s not jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was terribly jealous of me, too,” Maximov chimed in.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka laughed in spite of herself. “Who could she be jealous of?”
“Of the servant girls.”

“Stop it, Maximushka, I’m not in the mood for jokes right now; I’m angry. And don’t stare at the pies. I’m not giving you any; they’re not good for you. And no vodka, either. I have to take care of him, just like I run a charity house,” she said with a laugh.
“I don’t deserve your kindness. I’m a useless person,” Maximov said, his voice trembling. “You’d be better off being kind to someone more useful than me.”

“Oh, everyone’s useful, Maximushka. Who knows who’s most useful? If only that Pole didn’t exist, Alyosha. Now he’s decided to get sick today, too. I went to see him as well. I’ll send him some pies, just because of this. I wasn’t planning to, but since Mitya accused me, I will! Oh, here’s Fenya with a letter! Yes, it’s from the Poles—begging again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch had really sent a very long, dramatic letter asking her to lend him three roubles. Inside was a signed receipt promising to pay her back in three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Grushenka had received lots of letters like this from her ex-lover while she was recovering. But she knew that both Poles had come to ask about her during her illness. The first letter was long, written on large paper with a big family crest on the seal. It was so confusing and full of fancy words that Grushenka gave up reading halfway through, unable to understand it. She couldn’t bother with letters at that time. The next day came another letter from Pan Mussyalovitch, asking for a loan of two thousand roubles for a short time. Grushenka ignored that one, too. More letters followed, one every day—just as fancy, but each time the amount he asked for got smaller: from a hundred roubles, to twenty-five, to ten, and finally, both Poles wrote begging for just one rouble, including a receipt signed by them both.

After that, Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them and went to their place at dusk. She found both Poles nearly starving, with no food or fuel, no cigarettes, and owing money to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they’d taken from Mitya at Mokroe were gone. But Grushenka was surprised that they still put on airs, acting very formal and giving pompous speeches. She just laughed and gave her old admirer ten roubles, then told Mitya about it, laughing again. He wasn’t jealous at all. But after that, the Poles wouldn’t leave Grushenka alone and started asking her for money every day, and she kept sending them small amounts. And today, suddenly, Mitya had gotten extremely jealous about it.

“Like an idiot, I stopped by the Pole’s for a minute on my way to see Mitya, since he’s sick too, my Pole,” Grushenka continued nervously. “I even laughed and told Mitya about it. ‘Imagine,’ I said, ‘the Pole thought he could win me over by singing his old songs on the guitar—he thought I’d be so touched I’d marry him!’ Mitya jumped up and started swearing. So, I’ll send them the pies! Fenya, is it that little girl they sent? Give her three roubles and pack up a dozen pies in paper for her to take. And you, Alyosha, make sure to tell Mitya I really did send the pies.”
“I wouldn’t tell him for anything,” Alyosha said, smiling.
“Oh! You think it upsets him. He’s being jealous on purpose. He doesn’t really care,” Grushenka said bitterly.
“On purpose?” Alyosha asked.

“You’re so clueless, Alyosha. You know nothing, for all your smarts. I’m not offended that he’s jealous of a girl like me. I’d be offended if he weren’t jealous. That’s how I am. I’m not upset by jealousy—I can be jealous, too. What upsets me is that he doesn’t really love me. I’m telling you, he’s just pretending to be jealous now. Am I blind? Don’t I see? He started talking to me about that woman, Katerina, saying she did this and that—ordered a doctor from Moscow for him, got the best lawyer. So he must love her, if he praises her in front of me! He’s treated me badly, so now he blames me, to make it look like I’m the one in the wrong. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can’t be blamed for Katerina’—that’s what he means. He wants to blame everything on me. He attacked me on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I’ll—”
Grushenka couldn’t finish what she wanted to say. She buried her face in a handkerchief and sobbed hard.
“He doesn’t love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said seriously.

“Well, I’ll find out soon enough if he does or not,” Grushenka replied, sounding angry as she wiped her tears. Her face, which a moment ago was gentle and calm, now looked sullen and bitter, and Alyosha felt sad to see the change.

“Enough of this nonsense,” she said suddenly. “That’s not why I sent for you. Alyosha, dear, tomorrow—what’s going to happen tomorrow? That’s what I’m worried about! And it’s only me who’s worried! I look at everyone and no one else seems to care. Are you even thinking about it? Tomorrow’s his trial, you know. Tell me, how will it go? You know it’s the valet—the valet killed him! Oh God! Can they really punish Mitya instead of the valet, and no one will speak up for him? They haven’t even bothered with the valet, have they?”
“He’s been questioned a lot,” Alyosha said thoughtfully, “but everyone decided it wasn’t him. Now he’s very sick. He’s been sick ever since the attack. Really sick,” Alyosha added.
“Oh dear! Couldn’t you go to the lawyer yourself and tell him everything? They say he was brought from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

“We paid that three thousand together—Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna, and me—but Katerina paid two thousand of her own money for the doctor from Moscow. The lawyer, Fetyukovitch, would have charged more, but the case is famous all over Russia; it’s in all the newspapers. Fetyukovitch agreed to come mostly for the publicity, because the case is so well-known. I saw him yesterday.”
“Well? Did you talk to him?” Grushenka asked eagerly.
“He listened but didn’t say anything. He told me he’d already made up his mind. But he promised to think about what I said.”
“Think about it! Oh, they’re all cheats! They’ll ruin him. And why did she send for the doctor?”
“As an expert. They want to argue that Mitya’s insane and killed his father without knowing what he was doing,” Alyosha said gently, smiling. “But Mitya won’t agree to that.”

“That would be true if he had killed him!” Grushenka cried. “He really was crazy then, and it was my fault, the wretch that I am! But of course, he didn’t do it—he didn’t! And everyone’s against him, the whole town. Even Fenya’s testimony made him look guilty. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern—people had heard him say so before! They’re all, all against him.”
“Yes, the evidence against him is pretty overwhelming,” Alyosha said grimly.
“And Grigory—Grigory Vassilyevitch—keeps insisting the door was open, swears he saw it, and won’t budge. I went to talk to him myself. He’s rude, too.”
“Yes, that’s probably the strongest evidence against Mitya,” Alyosha said.

“And as for Mitya being insane, he really seems like it lately,” Grushenka said, her voice anxious and secretive. “Alyosha, I’ve wanted to talk to you about this for a while. I see him every day and I just can’t figure him out. Do you know what he’s always talking about? He goes on and on, and I can’t make sense of it. At first I thought he was talking about something smart that I just couldn’t understand. But then he started talking about a baby—some child. ‘Why is the baby poor?’ he said. ‘It’s for that baby I’m going to Siberia now. I’m not a murderer, but I have to go to Siberia!’ What did he mean? What baby? I had no idea, but I cried when he said it, because he said it so sweetly. He cried, too, and kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha? What is this baby?”
“It must be Rakitin—he’s been visiting Mitya lately,” Alyosha said with a smile, “although ... that doesn’t really sound like Rakitin. I didn’t see Mitya yesterday. I’ll go today.”
“No, it’s not Rakitin; it’s his brother Ivan Fyodorovitch upsetting him. Ivan’s visits are what’s doing it,” Grushenka said, but then suddenly stopped. Alyosha stared at her, surprised.
“Ivan’s going? He’s been to see Mitya? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn’t visited even once.”

“There, there! I’m such a blabbermouth!” Grushenka said, embarrassed and suddenly blushing. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I’ve said this much, I’ll tell you everything—the truth is, Ivan’s been to see him twice; first, right after he arrived from Moscow, before I got sick, and second, a week ago. He made Mitya promise not to tell you, or anyone else. He came in secret.”
Alyosha sat deep in thought, clearly affected by this news.

“Ivan doesn’t talk to me about Mitya’s case,” he said slowly. “He’s barely said anything to me these past two months. And when I go see him, he seems annoyed by my visits, so I haven’t been to see him for the last three weeks. Hmm... if he was there a week ago... there really has been a change in Mitya this week.”

“There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They have a secret, a real secret! Mitya told me himself there was a secret, and it’s bothering him so much he can’t rest. Before that, he was cheerful—and really, he’s mostly cheerful now—but when he shakes his head like that and paces the room, pulling at his hair on the right side, I know something’s really bothering him... I know! He was cheerful before, and even now, he’s cheerful today.”
“But you said he was worried.”

“Yes, he’s worried, but he’s also cheerful. He’ll be cranky for a minute, then happy, then cranky again. You know, Alyosha, I’m always amazed by him—with all this hanging over him, sometimes he laughs at the silliest things, just like a little kid.”
“And did he really tell you not to tell me about Ivan? Did he actually say, ‘Don’t tell him’?”

“Yes, he told me, ‘Don’t tell him.’ You’re the one Mitya’s most afraid of. Because it’s a secret—he told me so. Alyosha, please, go see him and find out what the secret is, then come tell me,” Grushenka begged, suddenly desperate. “Set my mind at ease—let me know the worst. That’s why I sent for you.”
“You think it’s about you? If it were, he wouldn’t have told you there was a secret.”
“I don’t know. Maybe he wants to tell me but doesn’t dare. He’s warning me: there’s a secret, he says, but he won’t say what it is.”
“What do you think it is?”

“What do I think? I think it’s the end for me. The three of them have been plotting to get rid of me—Katerina’s involved, it all comes from her. She’s this and that, which means I’m not. He tells me that ahead of time, as a warning. He’s planning to dump me, that’s the whole secret. They’ve planned it together—Mitya, Katerina, and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I’ve been wanting to ask you for a while. A week ago, Mitya suddenly told me that Ivan’s in love with Katerina, because he goes to see her a lot. Did he tell me the truth or not? Tell me honestly—tell me the worst.”
“I won’t lie to you. I don’t think Ivan is in love with Katerina Ivanovna.”

“Ah, that’s what I thought! He’s lying to me, the shameless cheat! That’s what it is! And he just tried to be jealous of me, so he could blame everything on me later. He’s so bad at hiding what he’s up to—so obvious! But I’ll show him, I’ll show him! ‘You think I did it,’ he said. He said that to me, to me! He blamed me for that! God forgive him! Just wait, I’ll make life hard for Katerina at the trial! I’ll say what I know then... I’ll tell everything!”
And again, she broke down in tears.

“Here’s what I can tell you for sure, Grushenka,” Alyosha said, getting up. “First, he loves you—loves you more than anyone in the world, and only you, believe me. I know it. Second, I don’t want to force his secret out of him, but if he tells me on his own today, I’ll tell him straight out that I promised to tell you. Then I’ll come back and tell you. But... I really think Katerina Ivanovna isn’t involved, and the secret is about something else. I’m sure of it. It doesn’t seem likely it’s about Kater

The first thing Alyosha had to do was visit Madame Hohlakov's house, and he rushed there, wanting to get it over with quickly so he wouldn’t be late meeting Mitya (Dmitri). Madame Hohlakov had been a bit sick for the past three weeks—her foot had swollen up for some reason. She wasn’t stuck in bed, but she spent all day lounging on her couch in her personal sitting room, dressed up in fancy but proper loungewear. Alyosha once noticed, with a bit of innocent amusement, that even though Madame Hohlakov was supposed to be sick, she’d started dressing up more—adding bows, ribbons, and colorful robes. He had a hunch about why, but tried not to think about it. Over the last two months, the young official Perhotin had begun visiting her regularly.

Alyosha hadn’t visited for four days, and he wanted to go straight to Lise (Liza), since she’d sent her maid to ask him to come about something “very important,” which, for some personal reasons, really interested Alyosha. But while the maid went to let Lise know he was there, Madame Hohlakov heard about his arrival and immediately sent someone to ask him to come see her “for just a minute.” Alyosha realized it was best to go to the mother first, or else she’d keep interrupting his visit with Lise. Madame Hohlakov was lying on her couch, dressed up especially nicely, and she was clearly very nervous and excited. She welcomed Alyosha with loud, happy exclamations.

“It’s been ages, ages, simply forever since I saw you! It’s been a whole week—just imagine! Oh wait, you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You’ve come to see Lise. I bet you were hoping to sneak into her room without me noticing. Dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if you only knew how worried I am about her! But that’s for later, even though it’s the most important thing. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust you completely with my Lise. After Father Zossima died—may God rest his soul!” (She crossed herself.) “I see you as a monk, even though you look wonderful in your new suit. Where did you find such a good tailor around here? No, no, that’s not the main thing—later for that. And forgive me if I sometimes call you Alyosha; an old lady like me can get away with that,” she smiled playfully. “But that’s for later, too. The important thing is that I don’t forget what’s important. You must remind me if I get off track. Just say, ‘the important thing?’ if I start babbling. Oh! How am I supposed to know what’s most important now? Ever since Lise took back her promise—her silly promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch—to marry you, you’ve realized, of course, it was just the playful idea of a sick kid stuck in her chair—thank goodness, she can walk now! That new doctor Katya brought from Moscow for your poor brother, who tomorrow—But why talk about tomorrow? I feel like dying just thinking about tomorrow. Dying of curiosity... That doctor was here yesterday and saw Lise... I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that’s not the point, again, not the point. See, I’m mixing everything up. I’m in such a rush. Why am I in a rush? I don’t know. It’s terrible how I can’t seem to understand anything anymore. Everything’s all tangled up. I’m afraid I’m boring you so much you’ll just jump up and leave, and then I won’t get to see you at all. Goodness! Why are we sitting here and there’s no coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!”
Alyosha quickly thanked her and said that he’d just had coffee already.
“Where?”
“At Agrafena Alexandrovna’s.”

“At... at that woman’s house? Oh, she’s ruined everyone. Not that I know much about it. They say she’s turned into a saint, but it’s a bit late for that. She should’ve done it sooner. What good is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I have so much to tell you I’m afraid I’ll tell you nothing at all. This terrible trial... I’m definitely going, I’m making arrangements. I’ll be carried there in my chair; anyway, I can sit up. I’ll have people with me. And, you know, I’m a witness. How will I speak, what will I say? I have no idea. I’ll have to take an oath, right?”
“Yes, but I don’t think you’ll actually be able to go.”

“I can sit up. Oh, you’re distracting me! This trial, this awful crime, and then they’re all going to Siberia, some are getting married, and it’s all happening so fast, everything’s changing, and then—nothing. Everyone gets old and has death waiting for them. Well, so be it! I’m tired. This Katya, such a lovely person, has disappointed all my hopes. Now she’s going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother will follow her and live in the closest town, and they’ll all just make each other miserable. It’s enough to drive me crazy. But worst of all—the gossip. The whole story has been repeated a million times in all the Moscow and Petersburg newspapers. Oh! Would you believe it, there’s a paragraph that calls me ‘a dear friend’ of your brother’s—ugh, I can’t even say the word. Just imagine, just imagine!”
“That’s impossible! Where was the paragraph? What did it say?”

“I’ll show you in a second. I got the newspaper and read it yesterday. Here, in the Petersburg paper called Gossip. It started publishing this year. I really like gossip, so I subscribed, and now it’s come back to bite me—this is what gossip does! Here it is, right here, read this part.”
She handed Alyosha a newspaper page that had been under her pillow.

She wasn’t exactly upset—she seemed overwhelmed, and maybe everything really was tangled up in her mind. The article was very typical, and must have shocked her, but luckily, she couldn’t focus on any one thing for long, so she might just forget about the newspaper in a minute.

Alyosha knew the story about his brother’s terrible case had spread all over Russia. And, wow, he’d read some wild rumors about his brother, about the Karamazovs, and even about himself in the past two months! One paper even claimed he’d joined a monastery and become a monk, horrified by his brother’s crime. Another paper said he and Father Zossima had robbed the monastery and run away. The article in Gossip was under the headline “The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk” (which, unfortunately, was the real name of their little town—I’d tried to keep it secret until now). The article was short and didn’t mention Madame Hohlakov by name. In fact, no names were used. It just said that the criminal, whose upcoming trial was causing such a stir—a retired army captain, a lazy show-off, and a bully—was always getting into romantic trouble and was especially popular with certain ladies “who were lonely and bored.” One such lady, a sad widow who tried to look young even though she had an adult daughter, was so taken with him that only two hours before the crime, she offered him three thousand roubles, if he would run away with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, hoping to escape punishment, chose to murder his father to get the three thousand instead of going off to Siberia with the “middle-aged charms” of his lonely lady. The article ended with a passionate rant about how evil parricide was, and about the now-abolished system of serfdom. Alyosha read it curiously, then folded the paper and handed it back to Madame Hohlakov.

“Well, that’s obviously me,” she rushed on. “Of course they mean me. It was just over an hour before that I suggested the gold mines to him, and here they write about ‘middle-aged charms’ like that’s why I did it! He wrote that out of spite! May God forgive him for the ‘middle-aged charms’—I forgive him! You know who it is, don’t you? It’s your friend Rakitin.”
“Maybe,” Alyosha said, “though I haven’t heard anything about it.”
“It’s him, it’s definitely him! No ‘maybe’ about it. You know I kicked him out of the house... You know that story, right?”
“I know you asked him not to visit anymore, but I haven’t heard why—from you, at least.”
“Ah, so you heard from him! He probably talks badly about me, right? Says terrible things?”
“Yes, he does—but honestly, he says bad things about everyone. I still don’t know why you broke off with him, and he never told me either. I hardly see him now. We’re not really friends.”

“Well, I’ll tell you the whole story. It can’t be helped—I have to confess, even though maybe I was a tiny bit to blame. Just a little, so small it hardly counts. You see, my dear boy”—Madame Hohlakov suddenly looked playful, with a mysterious smile—“I think... Forgive me, Alyosha. I’m like a mother to you... No, no, actually, it feels like you’re my father—saying ‘mother’ isn’t quite right. It’s more like I’m confessing to Father Zossima! I called you a monk just now. Well, that silly young man, your friend Rakitin (bless him, I can’t stay mad at him. I’m annoyed, but only a little), that immature boy, would you believe, seems to have fallen in love with me. I only noticed it later. At first—a month ago—he just started coming over more, almost every day, though we already knew each other. I didn’t realize at first... and then it suddenly hit me, and I started noticing things. You remember, two months ago, that polite, wonderful young man, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who works here, started visiting regularly. You’ve met him here lots of times yourself. He’s a really good, serious young man, isn’t he? He comes once every three days, not every day (although I’d love to see him every day), and he’s always dressed so well. I love young people, Alyosha, especially talented, modest ones like you, and he’s almost as smart as a politician—he talks so well, and I’ll definitely try to get him promoted. He’s a future diplomat. On that awful night, he almost saved my life by coming over. But your friend Rakitin comes in old boots and always stretches his feet out on the carpet... He started hinting at his feelings, and one day, as he was leaving, he squeezed my hand really hard. My foot started swelling right after that. He’d met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe, he’s always grumbling and making fun of him for no reason. I just watched them and laughed to myself. Anyway, I was sitting here alone—actually, I was stuck here. So, I was lying here, and suddenly Rakitin comes in, and would you believe it, he brought me a poem he wrote about my bad foot! He wrote about my foot in a poem. Wait, how did it go?

It started something like that. I can never remember poetry. I have it here somewhere; I’ll show you later. But it’s a cute poem—really nice, and not just about my foot; it had some good message, too, but I forgot what it was. Honestly, it was just the kind of thing you’d put in an autograph album. So of course, I thanked him, and he was clearly flattered. I’d barely finished thanking him when Pyotr Ilyitch came in, and Rakitin suddenly looked very angry. I could see Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, since Rakitin clearly wanted to say something after giving me his poem. I had a feeling about it, but Pyotr Ilyitch came in. I showed him the poem without saying who wrote it. But I’m sure he guessed, even though he denies it. Pyotr Ilyitch started laughing and criticizing the poem right away. ‘Awful doggerel,’ he said, ‘must be some theology student’s work,’ and he said it so strongly!
