Instead of laughing it off, your friend got mad. ‘Goodness!’ I thought, ‘they’re going to start a fight.’ ‘I wrote it,’ he said. ‘I wrote it as a joke. I think writing poetry is beneath me... But it’s good poetry. They want to put up a statue to Pushkin for writing about women’s feet, but I wrote with a moral purpose, and you,’ he said, ‘support serfdom. You aren’t humane,’ he said, ‘you aren’t modern, you don’t care about progress, you’re just a government official,’ he said, ‘and you take bribes.’ Then I started screaming and begging them to stop. And you know, Pyotr Ilyitch is no coward. He immediately switched to a very polite tone, looked at Rakitin sarcastically, listened, and apologized. ‘I had no idea,’ he said, ‘I wouldn’t have said that if I’d known. I’d have praised it. Poets are all so touchy,’ he said. Basically, he made fun of Rakitin but in the most polite way. Later, he explained to me that it was all sarcastic. I thought he was being serious. The whole time I was here, just like I am now, I wondered, ‘Should I throw Rakitin out for yelling so rudely at a guest in my house?’ I actually lay here, closed my eyes, and thought, ‘Should I make a big scene or not?’ I kept worrying and my heart started pounding, and I just couldn’t decide. One part of me said, ‘Say something,’ and another said, ‘No, be quiet.’ And as soon as the second voice said that, I cried out and fainted. Of course, that caused a fuss. I got up and told Rakitin, ‘It hurts me to say this, but I don’t want to see you at my house anymore.’ So I kicked him out. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I know I did wrong. I was pretending. I wasn’t really mad at him at all; I just suddenly thought it would make for a dramatic scene... But honestly, it was natural enough—I really cried for several days, and then out of nowhere, one afternoon, I forgot all about it. So it’s been two weeks since he’s been here, and I kept wondering if he’d come back. I even wondered yesterday. Then suddenly, last night, this Gossip article came out. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have. He went home, wrote it right away, sent it in, and they published it. That’s two weeks ago, you see. But, Alyosha, it’s awful how I keep talking and never get to what I really want to say. Words just come pouring out!”
“It’s really important that I get to see my brother today,” Alyosha said hesitantly.
“Of course, of course! You’re bringing me back to the point. Tell me, what’s an aberration?”
“What kind of aberration?” Alyosha asked, confused.
“In law. An ‘aberration’ where anything you do is forgiven. Whatever you do, you’re found not guilty right away.”
“What do you mean?”

“I’ll explain. This Katya... She’s such a lovely person, I just never know who she’s in love with. She was here recently and I couldn’t get anything out of her. She’ll only talk to me about my health now, nothing else, and she’s so formal with me, too. I just told myself, ‘Fine, whatever...’ Oh yes, I was talking about aberration. This doctor has come—you know, the one who can spot mad people. You asked for him. No, it wasn’t you, it was Katya. She arranged everything. Anyway, sometimes a person can be perfectly sane and suddenly have an ‘aberration.’ They might know what they’re doing and still be in a state of aberration. And there’s no doubt Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. They figured out what aberration was as soon as they reformed the law courts. It’s all thanks to the new law courts. The doctor came here and asked me about that night, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?’ he asked. He must’ve been in a state of aberration. He came in yelling, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!’ and then went out and did the murder. ‘I don’t want to murder him,’ he said, and then suddenly he went and murdered him. That’s why they’ll acquit him, because he fought against it, but still did it.”
“But he didn’t murder him,” Alyosha interrupted sharply. He was feeling more and more anxious and impatient.
“Yes, I know, it was that old man Grigory who killed him.”
“Grigory?” Alyosha exclaimed.
“Yes, yes, Grigory. He was lying there after Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocked him down, then got up, saw the door open, went in, and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“But why, why?”

“He was suffering from aberration. When he woke up from the blow Dmitri gave him, he was in a state of aberration, so he killed Fyodor Pavlovitch. If he says he didn’t, maybe he just doesn’t remember. But really, it would be better if Dmitri Fyodorovitch did it. That’s how it must have been, even though I’m saying it was Grigory. It was certainly Dmitri, and that’s better, much better! Not better that a son kills his father—I’m not saying that’s right. Children should honor their parents. But if it was Dmitri, you’d have nothing to be sad about, because he did it without realizing, or, rather, he was conscious but didn’t know what he was doing. Let them declare him innocent—that’s humane and shows how great the new law courts are. I didn’t know about this before, but apparently it’s been this way for a while. When I heard it yesterday, I was so amazed I wanted to send for you right away. And if he’s found not guilty, bring him straight from court to dinner with me. I’ll have a party and we’ll drink to the new law courts. I don’t think he’d be dangerous. Besides, I’ll invite a lot of people so if he does anything, he can be taken out. Maybe he could become a judge in another town—people who’ve been through hard times make the best judges. And, besides, who isn’t in a state of aberration these days? You, me, all of us are a bit crazy, and there are so many examples—I read about a guy just sitting, singing a song, then something annoys him, he grabs a gun and shoots someone, and no one blames him. I just read that, and all the doctors say it’s true. The doctors agree with anything. My Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday and the day before, and today I realized it’s all because of aberration. Oh, Lise upsets me so much—I think she’s gone a little mad. Why did she send for you? Did she call for you, or did you come yourself?”
“Yes, she sent for me, and I’m just about to go to her.” Alyosha stood up, determined.

“Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, maybe that’s the most important thing,” Madame Hohlakov suddenly burst into tears. “God knows I trust you with my whole heart when it comes to Lise, and I don’t mind her calling you secretly, without telling me. But forgive me, I can’t trust my daughter so easily with your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, even though I still think he’s a true gentleman. But imagine, he visited Lise and I didn’t know anything about it!”
“What? How? When?” Alyosha was very surprised. He was still standing, listening.

“I’ll tell you; maybe that’s the real reason I asked you to come—I don’t even know anymore. Ivan Fyodorovitch has visited me twice since he came back from Moscow. The first time, he came just as a friend; the second time, Katya was here and he came because he heard she was here. I didn’t expect him to come much, since he has so much to do, you know, with this whole case and your father’s terrible death. But then I suddenly found out he came again—not to see me, but to see Lise. That was six days ago. He came, stayed five minutes, and left. I didn’t hear about it until three days later, from Glafira, so it was a big shock. I called Lise right away. She laughed. ‘He thought you were asleep,’ she said, ‘and came to ask how you were doing.’ I’m sure that’s how it happened. But Lise, oh, Lise! She upsets me so much! Would you believe, one night, four days ago, just after you saw her and left, she had a fit—screaming, crying, hysterical! Why don’t I ever have hysterics? Then, the next day, another fit, and the same on the third day, and yesterday too, and then yesterday that ‘aberration.’ She suddenly yelled, ‘I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch. I demand you never let him come to the house again.’ I was stunned by those words and answered, ‘What reason could I have not to see such a fine young man, so smart and so unlucky?’—since all this trouble is a misfortune, isn’t it? She just burst out laughing, so rudely. Well, I was glad; I thought I’d cheered her up and the fits would stop, especially since I wanted to stop seeing Ivan Fyodorovitch anyway because of his strange visits behind my back, and I meant to ask him about it. But early this morning Lise woke up and got angry with Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her in the face. That’s awful; I’m always polite to my servants. Then, an hour later, she was hugging Yulia’s feet and kissing them. She sent me a message saying she wouldn’t come see me anymore, ever. When I forced myself to go to her, she ran to kiss me, crying, and then as she kissed me, she pushed me out of the room without saying a word, so I couldn’t find out what was wrong. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’m counting on you, my whole life is in your hands. Please, I beg you, go to Lise and find out everything from her—as only you can—and then come back and tell me, her mother, because if this goes on, it will be the death of me, I swear, or else I’ll just have to run away. I can’t take it anymore. I have patience, but I might lose it, and then... then something terrible will happen. Oh dear! Finally, Pyotr Ilyitch!” cried Madame Hohlakov, brightening as Perhotin came in. “You’re late! Well, sit down, tell us, what does the lawyer say? Where are you going, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
“To Lise.”
“Oh, yes. You won’t forget, will you, what I asked? It’s a matter of life and death!”
“Of course I won’t forget, if I can... but I’m really late,” Alyosha muttered, hurrying away.
“No, you have to come back, don’t say ‘if you can.’ I’ll die if you don’t,” Madame Hohlakov called after him, but

When Alyosha walked in to see Lise, he found her half-lying in the special chair she used when she couldn’t walk. She didn’t move to greet him; her sharp eyes just stared straight at his face. Her eyes looked feverish, and her face was pale and almost yellow. Alyosha was shocked at how much she’d changed in just three days—she looked skinnier. She didn’t reach out her hand, so Alyosha gently touched her thin fingers, which lay still on her dress, and then sat down across from her quietly.
“I know you’re in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said abruptly. “And my mother’s kept you here forever. She’s probably been telling you all about me and Yulia.”
“How do you know that?” Alyosha asked.
“I was listening in. Why are you staring at me? I want to listen, so I do—there’s nothing wrong with that. I’m not sorry.”
“Are you upset about something?”

“No, actually, I’m really happy. I’ve just been thinking for the thirtieth time how glad I am that I turned you down and won’t be your wife. You’re not meant to be a husband. If I married you and gave you a note to deliver to the man I loved after you, you’d take it for me, deliver it, and even bring back his answer. Even if you were forty, you’d still be running my love letters.”
Suddenly, she laughed.
“There’s something mean about you, but you’re also really honest,” Alyosha said, smiling at her.

“I’m honest because I’m not embarrassed around you. I don’t even want to be embarrassed in front of you—just you. Alyosha, why don’t I respect you? I’m really fond of you, but I don’t respect you. If I did, I wouldn’t talk to you like this, would I?”
“No.”
“But do you really think I’m not ashamed with you?”
“No, I don’t think so.”
Lise laughed again, a little nervously, and started talking quickly.
“I sent your brother, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, some candy in prison. Alyosha, you know, you’re actually pretty cute! I’ll love you so much just because you made it so easy for me not to love you.”
“So why did you ask me to come today, Lise?”
“I wanted to tell you about something I keep wishing for. I want someone to torture me—marry me, then hurt me, cheat on me, and leave me. I don’t want to be happy.”
“You’re in love with chaos?”

“Yes, I want chaos. I keep wanting to set our house on fire. I imagine sneaking up and starting a fire secretly—no one knows. They’ll try to put it out, but it’ll keep burning. And I’ll just watch and say nothing. Ugh, it’s so silly! I’m just so bored!”
She waved her hand in disgust.
“It’s your rich, easy life,” Alyosha said softly.
“So, is it better to be poor?”
“Yes, it is.”

“That’s what your monk taught you. But it’s not true. I’d rather be rich while everyone else is poor, eating sweets and drinking cream and not sharing any. Ugh, don’t talk, don’t say anything,” she interrupted, waving her hand at him, even though Alyosha hadn’t said a word. “You’ve told me all that before—I know it by heart. It’s boring. If I ever become poor, I’ll probably kill someone. Even if I’m rich, I might do it—why not? But you know what? I’d like to work in the fields, cutting rye. I’ll marry you, and you’ll become a real peasant. We’ll keep a young colt, okay? Do you know Kalganov?”
“Yes.”

“He’s always wandering around, daydreaming. He says, ‘Why live in real life? Dreaming is better. You can dream about the best things, but real life is boring.’ Still, he’ll get married soon. He’s already been flirting with me. Can you spin a top?”
“Yes.”
“Well, he’s just like a top: he needs to be wound up and then spun, and then whipped and whipped again. If I marry him, I’ll keep him spinning forever. Are you embarrassed to be with me?”
“No.”
“You’re really annoyed because I don’t talk about holy stuff. I don’t want to be holy. What happens to people in the next world if they do the worst sin? You must know that.”
“God will judge you,” Alyosha said, watching her closely.
“That’s exactly what I want. I’d walk up, they’d judge me, and I’d just burst out laughing in their faces. I’d really love to set fire to our house, Alyosha—don’t you believe me?”
“Why not? There are kids as young as twelve who get the urge to set things on fire, and sometimes they actually do it. It’s like a sickness.”
“That’s not it, not at all. Maybe there are kids like that, but that’s not what I mean.”
“You’re confusing evil with good; it’s just a phase, maybe because you’re not well.”
“You do look down on me! But it’s not about sickness. I just don’t want to do good—I want to do bad things.”
“Why do bad things?”

“So everything would fall apart. Oh, wouldn’t it be great if everything was destroyed! Sometimes I want to do tons of evil things for a long time in secret, and then suddenly everyone would find out. They’d all stand around pointing at me, and I’d just look at them. That would be so amazing. Why do you think that would feel so good, Alyosha?”
“I don’t know. Maybe it’s just the urge to destroy something good—or like you said, to set something on fire. People feel that sometimes.”
“I don’t just say it—I’ll actually do it.”
“I believe you.”
“Oh, I love you for believing me. And you’re not lying at all. But maybe you think I’m saying this just to annoy you?”
“No, I don’t think that... although maybe that’s a small part of it.”
“A little, yes. But I can never lie to you,” she said, her eyes burning strangely.
What stood out to Alyosha most was how serious she was. Her face had no trace of humor, even though she used to find something funny even when she was being “serious.”
“There are times when people actually love doing bad things,” Alyosha said thoughtfully.
“Yes, yes! That’s exactly what I think. People love evil, all of them, all the time—not just sometimes. It’s like everyone secretly agreed to pretend they hate evil, but actually, they all love it.”
“Are you still reading those awful books?”
“Yes, I am. My mom reads them and hides them under her pillow, and I steal them from her.”
“Aren’t you ashamed you’re hurting yourself?”

“I want to hurt myself. There’s a boy here who lay down between train tracks as the train came. Lucky boy! Listen, your brother is on trial now for killing his father, and everyone loves that he killed his father.”
“Loves that he killed his father?”
“Yes, loves it! They all say it’s terrible, but deep down they love it. I know I do.”
“There’s some truth to what you say about people,” Alyosha said quietly.

“Oh, what a thing for you to say!” Lise squealed with delight. “And you’re a monk, too! You don’t know how much I respect you, Alyosha, for never lying. Oh, let me tell you a weird dream I have. Sometimes I dream about devils. It’s night, I’m in my room with a candle, and suddenly there are devils everywhere, in the corners, under the table, behind the doors. They want to grab me. They’re just about to, but then I make the sign of the cross and they pull back. They don’t leave, though—they wait in the corners and by the doors. Then I suddenly really want to curse God out loud, so I do, and the devils rush back, all excited, and grab me again. I cross myself, and they retreat again. It’s freaky, but kind of fun—it takes my breath away.”
“I’ve had the same dream,” Alyosha said suddenly.
“Really?” Lise said, surprised. “Wait, Alyosha, don’t laugh—that’s a big deal. Can two different people really have the same dream?”
“Looks like they can.”

“Alyosha, I’m telling you, it’s really important,” Lise said, sounding overly amazed. “Not the dream itself, but the fact that you had the same dream as me. You never lie to me, so don’t lie now. Is it true? Are you laughing at me?”
“It’s true.”
Lise seemed really struck by this, and sat silently for about half a minute.
“Alyosha, come see me more often,” she suddenly pleaded.
“I’ll always come see you, as long as I live,” Alyosha replied firmly.

“You’re the only person I can talk to,” Lise went on. “I talk to no one but you and myself. Only you, in the whole world. And I talk to you more easily than I do to myself. I’m not ashamed with you—not at all. Alyosha, why is that? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter, the Jews steal a child and kill it?”
“I don’t know.”

“There’s a book here about a trial of a Jew who supposedly took a four-year-old child, cut off all his fingers, nailed him to a wall, and crucified him. When he was on trial, he said the kid died pretty quickly—in four hours. That was ‘quick’! He said the child kept moaning, and he stood there watching. Isn’t that nice?”
“Nice?”
“Nice. Sometimes I imagine it was me who crucified the child. He’d be hanging there, crying, and I’d just sit there eating pineapple compote. I really love pineapple compote. Do you like it?”
Alyosha just stared at her in silence. Her pale, yellowish face twisted suddenly, and her eyes seemed to burn.

“You know, when I read about that Jew, I cried all night. I kept picturing the poor child crying and moaning (a four-year-old understands, you know), and all the while I couldn’t stop thinking about pineapple compote. In the morning I wrote a letter to someone and begged them to come see me. He came, and I told him everything about the child and the pineapple compote. All of it, and said it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice, then got up and left. He was only here for five minutes. Did he hate me? Tell me, Alyosha, did he hate me or not?” She sat up on the couch, her eyes blazing.
“Tell me,” Alyosha said anxiously, “did you send for that person?”
“Yes, I did.”
“Did you write him a letter?”
“Yes.”
“Just to ask him about that, about the child?”
“No, not about that. But when he came, I asked him about it first thing. He answered, laughed, and left.”
“That person behaved honorably,” Alyosha said quietly.
“Did he hate me? Was he laughing at me?”
“No, maybe he believes in the pineapple compote himself. He’s very sick right now too, Lise.”
“Yes, he does believe in it,” Lise said, her eyes burning.
“He doesn’t look down on anyone,” Alyosha continued. “But he doesn’t trust anyone, either. And if you don’t trust people, then you do kind of look down on them.”
“So he despises me, too?”
“You, too.”
“Good,” Lise said through clenched teeth. “When he left laughing, I thought it was great to be hated. The child with his fingers cut off is great, and being hated is great...”
And she let out a wild, feverish laugh right in Alyosha’s face.

“You know, Alyosha, you know, I wish—Alyosha, save me!” Suddenly she jumped up, rushed to him, and grabbed him with both hands. “Save me!” she almost cried. “Is there anyone else in the world I could tell what I’ve told you? I told you the truth, all of it. I’m going to kill myself because I hate everything—I can’t stand living because I hate everything! I hate it all, everything! Alyosha, why don’t you love me, not even a little?” she finished, almost frantic.
“But I do love you!” Alyosha said warmly.
“And will you cry for me—will you?”
“Yes.”
“Not because I won’t be your wife, but just cry for me?”
“Yes.”

“Thank you! All I want is your tears. Everyone else can punish me and walk all over me—everyone, I don’t care who. Because I don’t love anyone. Do you hear me? Not anyone! In fact, I hate them! Go, Alyosha, you need to see your brother.” She suddenly pulled away from him.
“How can I leave you like this?” Alyosha said, nearly panicked.
“Go to your brother, or the prison will close. Go, take your hat. Tell Mitya I send my love—go, go!”

And she almost shoved Alyosha out the door. He looked back at her, surprised and hurt, when he suddenly noticed a tiny, tightly folded letter in his right hand, sealed. He glanced at it and immediately saw the address: “To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov.” He looked quickly at Lise. Her face looked almost threatening.
“Give it to him—you have to give it to him!” she demanded, trembling and out of control. “Today, right now, or I’ll poison myself! That’s why I asked you here.”

Then she slammed the door hard. He heard the bolt slide shut. Alyosha put the letter in his pocket and went straight downstairs, totally forgetting about Madame Hohlakov. As soon as Alyosha left, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a little, stuck her finger in the crack, and slammed it as hard as she could, crushing her finger. Ten seconds later, she let her finger go, walked slowly back to her chair, sat up straight, and stared at her bruised finger and the blood under her nail. Her lips trembled as she whispered quickly to herself:
“I’m a wretch, a wretch, a wretch, a wretch!”

It was getting pretty late (November days end early) when Alyosha (Alexey) arrived at the prison gate. The sun was almost gone. But Alyosha knew he’d have no trouble getting inside. In our small town, everything worked pretty much like everywhere else—at first, when the investigation was new, only family and a few others were allowed to visit Mitya (Dmitri), and even they had to jump through a bunch of hoops. But after a while, even though the rules didn’t really change, they made exceptions for some people. That meant sometimes Mitya could have almost private, one-on-one visits.

Still, only a few people got this special treatment—Grushenka, Alyosha, and Rakitin. The police captain, Mihail Mihailovitch, had really warmed up to Grushenka. He’d felt bad about how he’d yelled at her at Mokroe, and once he found out the whole story, he totally changed his opinion. Strangely, even though the captain was sure Mitya was guilty, after he was locked up, he started to feel sorry for him. “Maybe he’s got a good heart,” the captain thought, “he just got messed up by drinking and wild living.” Now, instead of being horrified, he felt pity. As for Alyosha, the captain liked him a lot and had known him for years. Rakitin, who’d recently started coming to see Mitya all the time, was friends with the police captain’s daughters and always hung around their house. He also tutored at the prison superintendent’s house. The superintendent, though very strict about his job, was a kind old man. He liked talking to Alyosha—usually about religion—and respected Ivan Fyodorovitch’s opinions too, though he was a bit scared of Ivan’s intelligence (even though the old man thought of himself as a self-taught philosopher). Alyosha had a special pull for him. Lately, the superintendent had started reading the Apocryphal Gospels and always wanted to discuss them with Alyosha and the monks. So even if Alyosha arrived late, he just had to see the superintendent and everything would be fine. Everybody at the prison, even the lowliest guard, was used to seeing Alyosha. The sentry didn’t bother him as long as the bosses were okay with it.

Whenever Mitya got called from his cell, he’d go downstairs to the visitor’s room. As Alyosha came in, he saw Rakitin leaving. They were talking loudly, and Mitya was laughing hard as Rakitin left, while Rakitin looked annoyed. Rakitin didn’t like running into Alyosha, especially lately. He barely spoke to him and only gave a stiff nod. When he saw Alyosha come in now, he frowned and pretended to be busy buttoning his heavy, fur-lined coat, then started looking for his umbrella.
“I have to be careful not to forget my stuff,” Rakitin muttered, just to say something.
“Be careful you don’t take other people’s stuff by mistake,” Mitya joked, laughing at his own joke. Rakitin immediately got upset.
“You should give that advice to your own family—they’ve always been a bunch of tyrants—not to me!” Rakitin snapped, suddenly shaking with anger.

“What’s wrong? I was just kidding,” Mitya said. “Sheesh, they’re all like that,” he added to Alyosha, nodding toward Rakitin as he rushed out. “He was happy and laughing, and then suddenly he explodes. He didn’t even say hi to you. Are you two not talking anymore? Why are you so late? I haven’t just been waiting for you—I’ve been dying to see you all morning! But never mind, we’ll catch up now.”
“Why does he come here so much? You two aren’t even close, are you?” Alyosha asked, nodding toward the door Rakitin had just gone through.

“Close with Rakitin? No way—he’s a jerk. He thinks I’m trash. People like that can’t take a joke, that’s their problem. They’re all dry and boring, like these prison walls when I first got here. But he’s smart, I’ll give him that. Anyway, Alexey, it’s all over for me now.”
He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit next to him.
“Yeah, the trial’s tomorrow. Are you really that hopeless, brother?” Alyosha asked, feeling worried.

“What are you talking about?” Mitya replied, looking uncertain. “Oh, the trial! Up till now we’ve been talking about stuff that doesn’t really matter, and I haven’t told you the main thing. Yeah, the trial’s tomorrow, but that’s not what I meant when I said it’s all over for me. Why are you looking at me like that?”
“What do you mean, Mitya?”
“Ideas! It’s all ideas! Morals and stuff! What are morals, anyway?”
“Morals?” Alyosha repeated, puzzled.
“Yeah, is it a science or something?”
“Well, yeah, there is a science about it... but honestly, I don’t know how to explain it.”

“Rakitin knows. He knows everything, that jerk! He’s not going to be a monk—he wants to go to Petersburg and write fancy articles. Maybe he’ll actually make something of himself. Ugh! Those kinds of people are great at getting ahead. Forget morals—I’m finished, Alexey, totally finished! I love you more than anyone. It hurts my heart to look at you. Who was Karl Bernard?”
“Karl Bernard?” Alyosha was surprised again.
“No, not Karl. Wait, I messed up. Claude Bernard. Who was he? Some kind of scientist?”
“I think he was a scholar,” Alyosha answered, “but I honestly don’t know much about him. I’ve heard the name, but that’s it.”
“Well, forget him! I don’t know either,” Mitya grumbled. “Probably some kind of crook. They’re all crooks. And Rakitin will get ahead—he’s another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They’re everywhere.”
“But what’s really wrong?” Alyosha pressed.

“He wants to write an article about me—about my case—to kick off his writing career. That’s why he comes. He told me himself. He wants to prove some theory, like ‘He couldn’t help killing his father, his environment messed him up,’ and so on. He told me all about it. He says he’ll throw in some Socialism too. But whatever, let him write what he wants—I don’t care. He can’t stand Ivan, hates him. He’s not too fond of you, either. But I let him visit because he’s smart, even if he’s full of himself. I told him just now, ‘The Karamazovs aren’t scum, they’re thinkers. Russians are all thinkers. You’ve studied, but you’re not a thinker—you’re a jerk.’ He laughed, in a nasty way. And I told him, ‘De ideabus non est disputandum.’ Not bad, right? I can sound fancy too!” Mitya laughed suddenly.
“But why did you say it’s all over for you?” Alyosha interrupted.
“Why is it all over? Well... when you look at the big picture, I’m sad about losing God—that’s why.”
“What do you mean, ‘sad about losing God’?”

“Picture this: inside your brain, in the nerves, there are these tiny little tails—nerve endings, I guess—and when they start twitching... well, when I see something, those little tails twitch, and then an image pops up. Not right away—a second later. Then the image appears; it’s not really a ‘moment’—whatever, the point is, I see and then I think because of those tails, not because I have a soul or am made in God’s image. All that stuff is nonsense! Rakitin explained it to me yesterday, and it blew my mind. It’s amazing, Alyosha—science is amazing! A new kind of person is coming. But still, I’m sad about losing God.”
“Well, at least you’re sad about it,” Alyosha said.

“Sad about losing God? It’s all chemistry, brother, chemistry! You can’t fight it, Father Alyosha, you just have to make room for science. Rakitin really hates God, you know. That’s what bugs people like him, but they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Will you write about this in your articles?’ I asked him. ‘Well, if I did it openly, they wouldn’t publish it,’ he said, and laughed. ‘But what will happen to people without God or the afterlife?’ I asked. ‘Then everything’s allowed, they can do whatever they want!’ ‘Didn’t you know?’ he said, laughing. ‘A smart man can do whatever he wants. A smart guy knows how to handle himself, but you, you messed up—killed someone, and now you’re rotting in jail.’ He says that to my face! What a pig! I used to kick out people like that, but now I just listen. He does make some good points, though. He writes well. He read me something he wrote last week. I copied out three lines. Wait, here it is.”
Mitya quickly pulled a slip of paper from his pocket and read:
“‘To answer this question, you first have to put your personality in conflict with your reality.’ Do you get that?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha. He looked at Mitya with curiosity.

“I don’t get it either. It’s confusing but sounds smart. ‘Everyone writes like this now,’ he says. ‘It’s because of their surroundings.’ He writes poetry too, the scoundrel. He even wrote a poem about Madame Hohlakov’s foot. Ha ha!”
“I’ve heard about that,” said Alyosha.
“You have? But have you heard the poem?”
“No.”

“I’ve got it. I’ll read it to you. You don’t know—there’s a story behind it. He’s such a sneak! Three weeks ago he started teasing me, saying, ‘You got into trouble over three thousand rubles, but I’m going to get a hundred and fifty thousand. I’m going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.’ He said he was wooing Madame Hohlakov. She wasn’t very smart before, and now at forty she’s lost whatever she had. ‘But she’s so sentimental,’ he said. ‘That’s how I’ll get her. I’ll marry her, take her to Petersburg, and start a newspaper.’ He was drooling over the money, not the widow. And he convinced me! He came to see me every day: ‘She’s coming around,’ he’d say, all happy. Then suddenly, he gets thrown out of her house. Perhotin is winning now—good for him! I could kiss that old fool for kicking Rakitin out. And Rakitin had written this silly poem. ‘It’s the first time I’ve written poetry,’ he said, ‘but it’s to win her over, so it’s for a good cause. When I get her money, I’ll do great things for society.’ They always have an excuse for their bad behavior! ‘Anyway, it’s better than Pushkin’s poetry,’ he said, ‘since I managed to sneak in some talk about progress.’ I get what he means about Pushkin, if Pushkin just wrote about women’s feet. But Rakitin is so proud of his dumb poem! The ego on these guys! ‘On the recovery of the swollen foot of my beloved’—what a title! He really thinks he’s funny.”
“He’s a pig, a total pig, but he’s clever, I’ll give him that. And he did put in a ‘progressive’ idea. Boy, was he mad when she kicked him out! He was furious!”
“He’s already gotten his revenge,” said Alyosha. “He wrote a gossip piece about Madame Hohlakov.”
Alyosha quickly told Mitya about the gossip article.
“Of course that was him!” Mitya agreed, frowning. “That’s Rakitin! Those nasty little articles... I know all about them. They wrote terrible things about Grushenka, and about Katya too. Hmph.”
He paced the room, looking stressed.

“Brother, I can’t stay long,” Alyosha said after a pause. “Tomorrow is going to be a huge and terrible day for you—the day of God’s judgment... I’m shocked you’re wandering around, talking about all sorts of things...”

“Don’t be shocked by me,” Mitya broke in warmly. “Should I talk about that filthy dog? The murderer? We’ve talked about him enough. I don’t want to talk about that stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta anymore! God will deal with him, you’ll see. Hush!”
He rushed over to Alyosha and kissed him. His eyes were shining.

“Rakitin wouldn’t get this,” he said, almost in a trance, “but you—you’ll understand. That’s why I needed you so badly. There’s so much I’ve wanted to tell you during these two months in this place, but I never found the right time. Now I can’t wait anymore—I have to spill my heart. Brother, I feel like I’ve found a new person inside me these past two months. He was always there, hidden, but would never have come out if this disaster hadn’t happened. I’m afraid! But I don’t care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking rocks. That’s not what I’m afraid of. I’m afraid that this new person in me will disappear. Even in the mines, underground, I might find another person—another convict or murderer—and make friends with him, because even down there you can love and suffer and become human again. Maybe I could help someone else, bring their soul back from the dark, even turn a lost person into an angel or a hero! There are hundreds of them, and we’re all to blame for them. Why did I dream about that poor child at that moment? ‘Why is the child so poor?’ That was a sign to me. It’s for that child I’m going. We’re all responsible—for all the children, big and small. I’m going for everyone, because someone has to. I didn’t kill Father, but I have to go. I accept it. It all came to me here, in these peeling walls. There are so many like me, working underground with hammers. Sure, we’ll be in chains, but in our suffering, we’ll find joy again. God gives joy—that’s His gift. Ah, people should live in prayer! What would I be underground without God? Rakitin laughs, but if they banish God from the earth, we’ll hide Him underground. You can’t survive prison without God—it’s even harder than outside. And then we’ll sing a hymn to God from deep under the earth, and with Him there’s joy. Praise God and His joy! I love Him!”
Mitya was almost out of breath as he finished his passionate speech. He turned pale, his lips shook, and tears ran down his cheeks.

“Yes, there’s life—even underground,” he went on. “You wouldn’t believe how much I want to live now, Alexey, how thirsty I am for life and consciousness, all since I’ve been in here. Rakitin doesn’t get that—he only cares about buying a house and renting out apartments. But I’ve been longing for you. And suffering? I’m not afraid of it now, even if it’s endless. I’m not afraid anymore. Maybe I won’t even answer at the trial... And I feel so strong, I think I could handle anything, any pain, as long as I can keep saying to myself, ‘I exist.’ Even in torture—I exist. Alone on a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and even if I can’t see it, I know it’s there. There’s a whole life in just knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are killing me. To hell with them! Brother Ivan—”
“What about brother Ivan?” Alyosha interrupted, but Mitya didn’t hear.

“You see, I never had all these doubts before, but they were inside me. Maybe that’s why I drank and fought and got wild—to drown those doubts out. Ivan isn’t like Rakitin—he really has ideas. Ivan is like a riddle, always silent. The thing that really haunts me is God. That’s all that worries me. What if He doesn’t exist? What if Rakitin’s right, and people just invented God? Then man is the boss of the earth, the whole universe. That sounds amazing! But then how will people be good without God? That’s the real question. Who will people love then? Who will they thank? Who will they sing to? Rakitin laughs and says you can love humanity without God. But only a fool would say that. I just don’t get it. Life is easy for Rakitin. ‘You should worry about giving people more rights, or keeping meat prices low. That’s a better way to love humanity than philosophy,’ he says. I told him, ‘Well, without God, you’re more likely to raise meat prices just to make money.’ He got mad. But what is goodness? Is it the same for me as for a Chinese person? So is it all relative? Or not? That question has kept me up for two nights. It amazes me how people can live and never think about it. Vanity! Ivan has no God, just ideas. I don’t get him. But he’s silent. I think he’s a Freemason. I asked, but he won’t say. I wanted to know his innermost thoughts—he stayed silent. But once, he did say something.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha asked quickly.
“I said, ‘So everything is allowed, then?’ He frowned and said, ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our father, was a pig, but his ideas were right.’ That’s all he said. That’s even worse than Rakitin.”
“Yeah,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he here?”

“I’ll tell you about that later. I haven’t said anything to you about Ivan before. I was waiting until after the trial. When all this is over, I’ll tell you everything. We’ve got something huge going on... and you’ll be my judge. But not now; let’s not talk about it yet. You keep asking about tomorrow, about the trial, but honestly? I know nothing about it.”
“Have you talked to your lawyer?”

“What’s the point? I told him everything. He’s just a city guy—a Bernard! But he doesn’t believe me, not at all. Can you believe it—he thinks I did it! So I asked him, ‘Why are you defending me then?’ Forget them all! They even brought in a doctor to prove I’m insane. I won’t stand for that! Katerina Ivanovna wants to do her ‘duty’ to the end, no matter how hard it is!” Mitya gave a bitter smile. “She’s so cold! She knows I called her a woman of ‘great wrath’ at Mokroe, and someone told her. Now the evidence against me is piling up like sand. Grigory won’t back down. He’s honest, but a fool. Rakitin thinks a lot of honest people are just fools. Grigory is my enemy. Some people are better enemies than friends—like Katerina Ivanovna. I’m scared—really scared—she’ll tell everyone in court how she bowed to the ground after that four thousand rubles. She’ll pay it all back. I don’t want her sacrifice—they’ll just humiliate me in court. I don’t know how I’ll stand it. Go to her, Alyosha—ask her not to bring that up in court, could you? But whatever, it doesn’t matter! I’ll get through it. I don’t feel sorry for her—it’s her own fault. I’ll tell my own story, Alexey.” He gave another bitter smile. “But... but Grusha, Grusha! God, why does she have to suffer so much?” he suddenly cried, in tears. “Grusha’s killing me; just thinking about her is killing me. She was with me just now...”
“She told me you upset her a lot today.”
“I know. Stupid temper! I was jealous. I felt bad, I kissed her as she left. I didn’t ask her to forgive me.”
“Why not?” Alyosha exclaimed.
Suddenly Mitya laughed almost cheerfully.

“God save you, my dear boy, from ever asking a woman you love to forgive you. Especially if you really love her—no matter how much you mess up. Because women—who knows what to make of them! I know a thing or two about them, anyway. But if you admit you’re wrong to a woman and say, ‘I’m sorry, forgive me,’ she’ll hit you with a whole storm of complaints! She’ll never forgive you easily—she’ll bring up everything, even stuff that never happened, and only then forgive you. Even the nicest women do it. She’ll dig up every little thing and throw it at you. They’ll skin you alive, I tell you—every one of them, these angels we can’t live without! I’ll tell you straight, every decent man should be under some woman’s thumb. That’s how it should be—not just my opinion, but my feeling. A man should be generous, and there’s no shame in it! Not even for a hero or a Caesar! But still, never actually beg her pardon. Remember that from your brother Mitya, who’s ruined by women. No, I’ll make it up to Grusha some other way, without asking forgiveness. I adore her, Alexey, really adore her. But she doesn’t see it. No, she still thinks I don’t love her enough. And she tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! Before, it was just her beauty that drove me mad, but now I’ve taken her soul into mine, and through her I’ve become a man. Will they let us get married? If not, I’ll die of jealousy. I imagine things every day... What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha repeated everything Grushenka had told him that day. Mitya listened, asked him to repeat things, and seemed happy.

“So she’s not mad that I’m jealous?” he burst out. “She’s such a real woman! ‘I’ve got a fierce heart myself!’ Oh, I love women with fierce hearts, though I hate it when anyone is jealous of me. I can’t stand it. We’ll fight, but I’ll love her, love her deeply. Will they let us marry? Can convicts marry? That’s the big question. I can’t live without her...”
Mitya paced, frowning. It was almost dark now. Suddenly, he looked really worried.

“So she thinks there’s some secret, some plot against her, and that Katya is involved. No, Grushenka, you’re way off, that’s not it—not even close. Alyosha, my dear, okay, here it is—I’ll tell you our secret!”

He looked around, hurried over to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered as if it was a huge secret, though really no one could hear them—the old guard was dozing in the corner, and the soldiers outside couldn’t hear a thing.

“I’ll tell you our secret,” Mitya whispered quickly. “I meant to wait, because how can I decide anything without you? You’re everything to me. Even though I say Ivan’s smarter, you’re my angel. You’ll have the final say. Maybe you’re smarter than Ivan after all. It’s a question of conscience—a big one—and I can’t decide alone. I was waiting for you. But it’s still too soon to decide; we have to wait for the verdict. After that, you’ll decide my fate. I’ll tell you now, but don’t decide yet. I’ll just give you the idea, not the details, and you just listen—no questions, no reactions. Deal? But what am I going to do about your eyes? I’m scared your eyes will tell me your decision even if you don’t speak. Oh! I’m scared. Okay, Alyosha, listen! Ivan wants me to escape. I won’t tell you the details—it’s all planned. It could work. But don’t decide yet. I’d go to America with Grusha—you know I can’t live without her! What if they won’t let her come to Siberia? Do they let prisoners get married? Ivan says no. And without Grusha, what would I do underground? I’d just smash my head with the hammer! But then, what about my conscience? I’d be dodging my punishment. There’s a sign—I’m refusing the sign. I have a way out, but I’d be turning my back on it. Ivan says in America, if I’m free, I could do more good than in prison. But what about our hymn from underground? America is just empty dreams—and probably full of cheats too. I’d be running from my own cross! I’m telling you, Alexey, because you’re the only one who could understand. Nobody else. To others, it’s all nonsense, what I said about the hymn. They’d say I’m crazy. But I’m not. Ivan gets it—he understands about the hymn, but he doesn’t answer, doesn’t talk. He doesn’t believe in it. Don’t say anything, don’t even look at me—I can see you’ve already made up your mind. Please, don’t decide yet, give me a break! I can’t live without Grusha. Let’s wait until after the trial!”
Mitya ended, almost out of control. He grabbed Alyosha’s shoulders, staring into his brother’s eyes, desperate.
“They don’t let convicts marry, do they?” he asked for the third time, pleading.
Alyosha listened in shock, deeply moved.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan really pushing for this? Whose idea was it?”

“His. It’s all his idea, and he really wants it. At first, he didn’t visit me, then suddenly a week ago he came and brought it up right away. He’s really into it. He doesn’t ask, he orders me to escape. He thinks I’ll just do what he says, even though I’ve told him everything in my heart, including the hymn. He said he’d handle it; he’s figured everything out. But more on that later. It’s all about money—he’ll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. He says we can pull off a great escape for ten thousand.”
“And he told you not to tell me?” Alyosha asked again.
“He said not to tell anyone, especially not you. He’s afraid you’ll act as my conscience. Don’t let him know I told you. Don’t tell him, no matter what.”
“You’re right,” Alyosha said. “You can’t decide anything before the trial. After the trial, you’ll decide for yourself. That new man in you will decide.”
“A new man, or a Bernard who’ll decide like Bernard, because I think I’m just a worthless Bernard myself,” Mitya replied, with a bitter grin.
“But, brother, do you have no hope of being found innocent?”

Mitya shrugged nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, dear, you need to go,” he said suddenly. “The superintendent’s yelling in the yard. He’ll be here soon. We’re running late—this isn’t allowed. Hug me quick. Kiss me! Bless me, brother, for the cross I’ll have to carry tomorrow.”
They hugged and kissed.
“Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “suggested I escape—but of course, he thinks I did it.”
A sad smile appeared on his lips.
“Have you asked him if he believes it?” Alyosha asked.
“No, I haven’t. I wanted to, but I couldn’t. I didn’t have the guts. But I could tell from his eyes. Well, goodbye!”
They hugged quickly again, and Alyosha was about to leave when Mitya called him back.

“Stand facing me! That’s it!” He grabbed Alyosha’s shoulders again. Suddenly, his face went completely pale, so pale it was obvious even in the dim light. His lips trembled, and his eyes locked onto Alyosha.
“Alyosha, swear to me—tell me the absolute truth, like you’re standing before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you? Don’t lie!” he pleaded desperately.
Alyosha felt the world spinning and a sharp pain in his heart.
“Stop! What are you saying?” he stammered helplessly.
“The whole truth, don’t lie!” Mitya begged.
“I’ve never, not for a second, believed you were the murderer!” Alyosha burst out, his voice shaking, and he lifted his right hand as if calling God to witness.
Mitya’s whole face lit up with joy.

“Thank you,” he said slowly, like someone breathing again after fainting. “Now you’ve given me life again. Would you believe it, I was even afraid to ask you—yes, even you. Well, go! You’ve given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Go on, love Ivan!” were Mitya’s last words.

Alyosha left in tears. That Mitya could be so distrustful, so unsure even of him, Alyosha, suddenly showed Alyosha just how deep his brother’s hopelessness and pain went. He was overwhelmed by a wave of compassion, his heart aching. “Love Ivan!”—he remembered Mitya’s words. And he was on his way to see Ivan. He’d wanted to see Ivan all day. He was just as worried about Ivan as he was about Mitya—maybe even more now.

On his way to see Ivan, Alyosha (Alexey Fyodorovitch) had to pass by the house where Katerina Ivanovna was staying. He noticed the lights were on in her windows and suddenly decided to go in. He hadn’t seen Katerina Ivanovna in over a week, but it occurred to him that Ivan might be there now, especially since tomorrow was going to be such a difficult day. As he rang the bell and walked up the dimly lit stairs, he saw someone coming down. When they met, he realized it was his brother, Ivan. So Ivan had just been visiting Katerina Ivanovna.
“Oh, it’s just you,” Ivan said, sounding cold. “Well, goodbye! Are you going up to see her now?”
“Yes,” Alyosha replied.
“I wouldn’t if I were you,” Ivan said. “She’s upset, and you’ll only make her feel worse.”
Just then, a door upstairs flew open and someone shouted:
“No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, have you just come from him?”
“Yes, I was just with him,” Alyosha answered.
“Did he send me a message? Come upstairs, Alyosha! And Ivan Fyodorovitch, you have to come back too, do you hear me?”
Katya’s voice was so commanding that Ivan, after hesitating for a second, decided to turn around and go back upstairs with Alyosha.
“She was listening in,” Ivan muttered angrily to himself, but Alyosha caught what he said.
“Sorry, but I’m keeping my coat on,” Ivan said as they entered the living room. “I’m not going to sit down. I’ll only be here for a minute.”

“Sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Katerina Ivanovna said, though she stayed standing herself. She didn’t look much different than before, but there was something dangerous in her dark eyes. Later, Alyosha would remember thinking she looked especially beautiful at that moment.
“Did he ask you to tell me something?” she asked.

“Just one thing,” Alyosha replied, looking her right in the eyes. “He wants you to protect yourself and not say anything at the trial about what…” (Alyosha hesitated, feeling awkward) “…about what happened between you two when you first met, in that other town.”
“Oh! That I bowed down to the ground for that money?” She gave a bitter laugh. “So who is he really worried about—me or himself? He wants me to protect—who? Him or me? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!”
Alyosha watched her closely, trying to understand what she meant.
“Both you and him,” he said gently.
“Good to know,” she snapped back, almost meanly, and then suddenly blushed.
“You don’t know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said in a threatening way. “And I don’t know myself either. Maybe after my testimony tomorrow, you’ll want to stomp on me.”
“You’ll tell the truth at the trial,” Alyosha said. “That’s all that matters.”

“Women aren’t always honest,” she said harshly. “Just an hour ago, I was so disgusted by that monster, I was afraid to even touch him—he seemed like a snake. But no, he’s still a human being to me! But did he really do it? Is he the murderer?” she suddenly cried out, turning to Ivan in a burst of hysteria. Alyosha realized she had already asked Ivan this question, maybe just before he arrived—probably not for the first time, but for the hundredth. It seemed like their conversation always ended in an argument.

“I went to see Smerdyakov… It was you, you’re the one who convinced me that he killed his father. You’re the only one I believed!” she said, still talking to Ivan. Ivan gave her a tense, forced smile. Alyosha was surprised by how close and familiar they seemed.
“That’s enough,” Ivan interrupted, cutting off the conversation. “I’m leaving. I’ll come tomorrow.” He turned around and left the room, heading straight downstairs.
Katerina Ivanovna grabbed Alyosha’s hands with a forceful gesture.

“Go after him! Catch up to him! Don’t leave him alone, not for a minute!” she whispered urgently. “He’s losing his mind! Don’t you see he’s sick? The doctor told me he has a nervous fever. Go! Run after him!”
Alyosha jumped up and hurried after Ivan, who was only about fifty steps ahead.
“What do you want?” Ivan said sharply when he saw Alyosha running after him. “She sent you after me because she thinks I’m crazy. I know the whole routine,” he added irritably.
“She’s wrong, but she’s right that you’re sick,” Alyosha said. “I could see it in your face just now. You really look ill, Ivan.”
Ivan kept walking without stopping. Alyosha stayed by his side.
“Do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how people actually go insane?” Ivan asked, his voice suddenly calm and curious, with no hint of anger.
“No, I don’t. I guess there are lots of different ways to go mad.”
“But can a person realize it themselves, when they start losing their mind?”
“I don’t think people can see themselves clearly in that situation,” Alyosha answered, surprised.
Ivan was quiet for half a minute.
“If you want to talk to me, let’s change the subject,” he said suddenly.

“Oh, I almost forgot, I have a letter for you,” Alyosha said shyly, pulling Lise’s note from his pocket and handing it to Ivan. They were standing under a streetlamp. Ivan recognized the handwriting immediately.
“Ah, from that little demon!” he laughed meanly, and without even opening the envelope, tore it into pieces and let the wind blow them away.
“She’s not even sixteen yet, but already throwing herself at people,” he said with disgust, walking off again.
“What do you mean, throwing herself at people?” Alyosha cried.
“Like women who offer themselves for money, obviously.”

“How can you say that, Ivan? How can you?” Alyosha said, his voice hurt. “She’s just a child! You’re insulting a sick child! She’s very ill, maybe even on the edge of insanity herself… I was hoping you’d say something kind, something that might help her.”
“You won’t hear anything from me. If she’s a child, I’m not her babysitter. Drop it, Alexey. I’m not even thinking about her.”
They walked in silence for a moment.
“She’ll be praying all night now to the Mother of God, trying to figure out what to do tomorrow at the trial,” Ivan said suddenly, sharply.
“You mean Katerina Ivanovna?”

“Yes. She can’t decide whether to save Mitya or destroy him. She’ll pray for some sign from above because she can’t make up her own mind. She treats me like I’m her babysitter too, wants me to sing her lullabies.”
“Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother,” Alyosha said sadly.
“Maybe so, but I don’t really care that much about her.”
“She’s hurting. Why do you say things to her that give her hope?” Alyosha asked, gently scolding him. “I know you’ve led her to hope. Forgive me for saying this.”

“I can’t act the way I should with her—just end it straight out,” Ivan said, irritated. “I have to wait until the verdict about the murderer. If I break up with her now, she’ll get back at me by destroying that scoundrel tomorrow at the trial, since she hates him—she knows she does. It’s all lies, one lie after another! As long as I don’t break up with her, she keeps hoping, and she won’t ruin that monster because she knows I want him to be saved. If only they’d just give the verdict already!”
The words “murderer” and “monster” echoed painfully in Alyosha’s mind.
“But how could she ruin Mitya?” he asked, trying to figure out what Ivan meant. “What evidence could she give that would destroy Mitya?”
“You don’t know yet. She has a document, written by Mitya himself, that proves he killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“That’s impossible!” Alyosha cried out.
“Why is it impossible? I’ve read it myself.”
“There can’t be such a thing!” Alyosha insisted. “There can’t be, because he’s not the killer. He didn’t kill Father. He didn’t!”
Ivan suddenly stopped walking.
“Then who is the killer, according to you?” he asked, sounding cold and a bit smug.
“You know who it is,” Alyosha said quietly, his voice intense.
“Who? Are you talking about that story—the one about the crazy epileptic, Smerdyakov?”
Alyosha suddenly felt himself shaking all over.
“You know who I mean,” he forced out, barely able to breathe.
“Who? Who?” Ivan shouted, almost angrily. He suddenly lost all his self-control.
“I only know one thing,” Alyosha continued in a near-whisper, “you didn’t kill Father.”
“‘Not you’! What do you mean, ‘not you’?” Ivan was stunned.
“You didn’t kill Father. Not you!” Alyosha repeated firmly.
They stood in silence for half a minute.
“I know I didn’t. Are you crazy?” Ivan said, his face twisted in a pale, strange smile. He stared straight at Alyosha. They were standing under a streetlight again.
“No, Ivan. You’ve told yourself many times that you are the murderer.”
“When did I say that? I was in Moscow… When did I ever say that?” Ivan asked, suddenly unsure.

“You’ve told yourself, over and over, in your head, when you’ve been alone these past two terrible months,” Alyosha said, his voice soft and clear. But it was as if he wasn’t speaking for himself, but because something bigger was making him. “You’ve blamed yourself, confessed to yourself that you’re the murderer and no one else. But you’re wrong—you didn’t do it. You’re not the murderer. Do you hear me? It wasn’t you! God sent me to tell you this.”
They were both silent, staring into each other’s eyes, not moving for a long minute. Both were pale. Suddenly Ivan started trembling and grabbed Alyosha’s shoulder.
“You’ve been in my room!” he whispered harshly. “You were there at night, when he came… Admit it—have you seen him? Have you seen him?”
“Who do you mean—Mitya?” Alyosha asked, confused.
“Not him, curse that monster!” Ivan yelled, nearly out of control. “You know who visits me! How did you find out? Tell me!”
“Who are you talking about? I don’t know what you mean,” Alyosha stammered, getting worried.
“Yes, you do… Otherwise how could you—? There’s no way you don’t know.”
Suddenly Ivan seemed to stop himself. He stood still, thinking, with a strange grin twisting his mouth.

“Brother,” Alyosha said again, his voice shaking, “I had to tell you this because I know you’ll believe me. I’m telling you once and for all, it’s not you. Do you hear me? Once and for all! God put it in my heart to say this, even if it means you’ll hate me from now on.”
Ivan seemed to pull himself together.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” he said coldly, “I can’t stand prophets or epileptics—especially messengers from God—and you know that. I’m cutting off all contact with you starting now, probably forever. Please leave me here. This is your way home too. And don’t come see me today! You hear?”
He walked away quickly, not looking back.
“Brother!” Alyosha called after him. “If anything happens to you today, come to me first, before anyone else!”

But Ivan didn’t respond. Alyosha stood under the lamp at the crossroads, watching until Ivan disappeared into the darkness. Then Alyosha slowly walked home. Both brothers were staying in rented rooms; neither wanted to live in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s empty house. Alyosha rented a furnished room in a working family’s house. Ivan lived farther away, in a comfortable apartment attached to a fine house owned by a wealthy widow. His only helper was a deaf, stiff old woman who went to bed at six in the evening and woke up at six in the morning. Ivan didn’t care much about comfort lately and liked being alone. He did everything for himself in his one room and rarely went into the other rooms.

Ivan reached his building’s gate and put his hand on the bell, but suddenly stopped. He realized he was shaking all over with anger. Suddenly, he let go of the bell, cursed out loud, and walked away quickly in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a small, crooked wooden house, almost a shack, where Marya Kondratyevna—the woman who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen for soup, and to whom Smerdyakov once sang and played guitar—was now living with her mother. They had sold their old house and moved here. Smerdyakov, who was very sick—almost dying—had been staying with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch died. Ivan was heading there now, pulled by a sudden, unstoppable urge.

This was the third time Ivan had visited Smerdyakov since coming back from Moscow. The first visit was on the day he arrived; the second was two weeks later. After that, he stopped visiting, so it had been over a month since he’d seen Smerdyakov or heard much about him.

Ivan only came back five days after his father’s death, so he missed the funeral, which happened the day before he arrived. The delay was because Alyosha didn’t know Ivan’s address in Moscow, so he had to ask Katerina Ivanovna to send a telegram. She didn’t know it either, so she telegraphed her sister and aunt, hoping Ivan would visit them when he got to Moscow. But Ivan didn’t go to them until four days after arriving. Once he got the telegram, he rushed to their town. Alyosha was the first to meet him, and Ivan was surprised to find out that, unlike everyone else, Alyosha didn’t think Dmitri was guilty, but instead suspected Smerdyakov. After speaking with the police and hearing the details, Ivan was even more surprised by Alyosha’s opinion, thinking it was just brotherly loyalty to Dmitri.

By the way, Ivan’s feelings toward Dmitri were pretty negative. He mostly disliked him, sometimes felt sorry for him, but even that was mixed with contempt and even disgust. Dmitri’s personality and appearance were very off-putting to Ivan. Ivan was angry about Katerina Ivanovna’s love for Dmitri, but he still went to see Dmitri on his first day back. That meeting just made Ivan even more sure that Dmitri was guilty. Dmitri was agitated, nervous, and all over the place. He talked a lot, but his words didn’t make much sense. He kept accusing Smerdyakov and was obsessed with the three thousand roubles, insisting his father had “stolen” them from him.
“The money was mine, it was my money,” Mitya (Dmitri) kept repeating. “Even if I stole it, it would still be mine by right.”

Dmitri barely tried to argue against the evidence, and when he did, his explanations were rambling and confusing. He didn’t seem interested in defending himself to Ivan or anyone else. Instead, he was angry and scornful about the accusations, lashing out at everyone. He just laughed at Grigory’s story about the open door, saying “the devil opened it,” but couldn’t explain anything clearly. He even managed to insult Ivan, saying people who claimed “everything is allowed” had no right to question him. All in all, Dmitri wasn’t friendly with Ivan at all in that meeting. Right after seeing Dmitri, Ivan went to see Smerdyakov for the first time.

On the train from Moscow, Ivan kept thinking about Smerdyakov and their last conversation before Ivan left town. There were things that seemed suspicious and confusing. But when Ivan talked to the investigators, he didn’t mention that conversation—he wanted to see Smerdyakov first, who was in the hospital.

Doctor Herzenstube and Dr. Varvinsky, who Ivan met at the hospital, both insisted that Smerdyakov’s epileptic fit was real, and were surprised Ivan would even suggest he might have faked it. They said the attack was especially bad, with repeated seizures that put his life at risk, and only now could they be sure he’d survive. “But,” added Doctor Herzenstube, “his mind might be damaged for a long time, maybe forever.” When Ivan impatiently asked if Smerdyakov was now insane, they answered that he wasn’t fully mad, but he did have some problems. Ivan decided to see for himself.

At the hospital, Ivan was allowed to see Smerdyakov right away. Smerdyakov was lying on a small bed in a separate room. The only other patient was a dying tradesman, who wouldn’t overhear them. Smerdyakov gave Ivan an awkward grin, looking nervous at first—at least that’s how Ivan saw it—but soon seemed calm. Ivan could tell right away Smerdyakov was very sick: weak, talking slowly, looking thin and yellowish. During their twenty-minute talk, Smerdyakov kept complaining of headaches and pain everywhere. His pale, almost girlish face looked tiny, his hair was messy, and a little tuft stuck up in front. But there was a sly look in his squinting left eye—he was still the same Smerdyakov there. Ivan remembered how Smerdyakov liked talking to “clever men.” Ivan sat on a stool at the end of the bed. Smerdyakov moved painfully but didn’t say anything first; he didn’t even look very interested.
“Can you talk to me?” Ivan asked. “I won’t keep you long.”
“Of course I can,” Smerdyakov mumbled weakly. “Have you been back long?” he added, as if trying to make Ivan feel comfortable.
“I just arrived today... to see what a mess you’re in here.” Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why are you sighing? You knew this would happen,” Ivan blurted out.
Smerdyakov was silent for a while, not showing any emotion.
“How could I not know? It was obvious something would happen. But how could I know it would turn out like this?”
“What do you mean, ‘turn out’? Don’t dodge the question! You predicted you’d have a seizure—on the way down to the cellar, remember? You even said exactly where it would happen.”
“Did you mention that in your statement to the police?” Smerdyakov asked calmly.
Ivan suddenly felt annoyed.
“No, not yet, but I definitely will. You have a lot to explain, and I’m not going to let you play games with me!”
“Why would I play games with you, when I trust you completely, like God himself?” Smerdyakov answered with the same calmness, closing his eyes for a moment.

“First of all,” Ivan said, “I know you can’t predict epileptic fits. I asked the doctors—don’t try to fool me. You can’t know the exact day and hour. So how could you tell me in advance about the time and place, and about the cellar? How could you know you’d fall down the cellar stairs if you weren’t faking it?”

“I had to go to the cellar anyway—several times a day,” Smerdyakov said slowly. “A year ago, I fell from the attic in the same way. It’s true you can’t know exactly when a fit will happen, but you can sometimes sense it coming.”
“But you predicted the exact day and time!”
“About my epilepsy, you should ask the doctors here. They’ll tell you if it was real or fake; there’s nothing more for me to say.”
“But what about the cellar? How could you know it would happen there?”

“You just can’t get past that cellar, can you? When I was going down, I was terrified and worried. What scared me most was losing your support and being left alone. So I went down thinking, ‘It’ll hit me now, I’m about to fall—will I fall?’ That fear brought on the seizure. I told all this to Doctor Herzenstube and Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigator, and they wrote it down. And Dr. Varvinsky said it was my fear that triggered it. So they wrote that’s how it happened—just from my fear.”
When he finished, Smerdyakov took a deep, tired breath.
“So you told all that to the police?” Ivan asked, surprised. He had planned to threaten Smerdyakov by revealing their conversation, but Smerdyakov had already told them everything.
“What do I have to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole truth,” Smerdyakov said firmly.
“Did you tell them every word of our conversation at the gate?”
“Not every single word.”
“Did you tell them you can fake fits, like you bragged to me before?”
“No, I didn’t mention that.”
“Then tell me—why did you send me to Tchermashnya?”
“I was afraid you’d go to Moscow; Tchermashnya is closer anyway.”
“You’re lying; you were the one who suggested I leave. You told me to get out before trouble started.”

“That was just because I care about you and wanted to protect you, knowing there might be trouble at home. But I wanted to protect myself even more. That’s why I told you to get out of danger—hoping you’d realize there was trouble coming and stay home to protect your father.”
“You could have just said it straight, you idiot!” Ivan snapped.

“How could I have said it more directly? I was just scared, and you might have gotten angry. I was afraid Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and take the money, since he thought it belonged to him; but who could have guessed it would end in murder? I thought he’d just take the three thousand under the master’s mattress, and now you see, he’s killed him. How could you or I have known that?”
“But if you say it was impossible to guess, how was I supposed to guess and stay home? You’re contradicting yourself,” Ivan said, thinking it over.
“You could have guessed from me sending you to Tchermashnya instead of Moscow.”
“How would that make me guess?”
Smerdyakov seemed very tired, and went quiet for a minute.

“You could have guessed from me asking you not to go all the way to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya, which is closer. If Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew you weren’t far away, he might not act so boldly. And if something happened, you could come back quickly to help me—I warned you Grigory Vassilyevitch was sick, and I was worried about having a fit. And when I told you about the knocks—the secret way to get in to your father—and that Dmitri knew about them because of me, I thought you’d realize something was about to happen, and you’d stay instead of going away.”
“He’s explaining himself pretty clearly,” Ivan thought, “even if he mumbles. Where’s the mental problem Herzenstube mentioned?”
“You’re being sneaky with me, you jerk!” Ivan burst out.
“But I really thought you understood,” Smerdyakov replied simply.
“If I’d understood, I would have stayed,” Ivan said.
“Well, I thought you did understand, and that’s why you left in such a hurry—to get away and save yourself.”
“You think everyone’s as much of a coward as you?”
“Sorry, I thought you were like me.”

“Of course, I should have figured it out,” Ivan said, upset, “and I did suspect you were up to something... but you’re lying, you’re lying again,” he suddenly remembered. “Remember when you came up to the carriage and said, ‘It’s always worth talking to a clever man’? So you were glad I left, since you praised me?”
Smerdyakov sighed again and a bit of color came to his face.

“If I was happy,” he said, breathing hard, “it was just because you agreed not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya. It’s closer, after all. But when I said those words, I didn’t mean them as praise, but as a criticism. You didn’t get it.”
“Criticism for what?”
“For leaving your own father when you knew something bad might happen, and not protecting us. I could have been blamed for stealing the three thousand.”
“You jerk!” Ivan swore. “Wait, did you tell the police about the secret knocks?”
“I told them everything exactly as it happened.”
Ivan was surprised again.

“If I suspected anything then,” he went on, “it was just that you were up to something. Dmitri might kill him, but I didn’t think he’d steal. But I was ready to believe anything bad from you. You told me you could fake a fit. Why did you say that?”
“I was just bragging, honestly. I’ve never faked a fit in my life. I only said that to show off. I liked you back then and was being open with you.”
“My brother now says you’re the one who killed and robbed our father.”

“What else can he do?” Smerdyakov said with a bitter grin. “But who’s going to believe him with all the evidence against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the open door. What can he say to that? Anyway, he just wants to save himself.”
Smerdyakov stopped talking, then added after thinking for a second:

“And look—he’s trying to blame it on me, saying I did it. I’ve heard that already. But about me faking fits: if I planned to do something so bad, would I have told you beforehand that I could fake one? If I was planning murder, would I be stupid enough to give myself away to you, his son? That makes no sense. No one would do that. No one hears us now except God, and if you told the police about this, you’d actually be helping defend me—because who would plan a crime and then talk so openly about it? Anyone can see that.”

“Well,” Ivan said, getting up to end the talk, struck by Smerdyakov’s last argument. “I don’t suspect you at all—I think it’s silly to suspect you. In fact, thanks for putting my mind at ease. I’ll go now, but I’ll visit again. Take care. Do you need anything?”
“Thank you, but Marfa Ignatyevna takes care of me and brings me whatever I need. Good people visit me every day.”
“Goodbye. And I won’t mention your claim about faking fits—and you shouldn’t either,” Ivan said suddenly.
“I understand. And if you don’t talk about that, I won’t say anything about our conversation at the gate.”

After that, Ivan left. When he’d gone a dozen steps down the hall, he suddenly realized there was something insulting in Smerdyakov’s last words. For a moment, he almost turned back, but decided it was silly and left the hospital.

Mostly, Ivan just felt relieved that it was Mitya, not Smerdyakov, who had killed his father—even though maybe he should have felt the opposite. He didn’t want to think about why, and even found it disgusting to try to figure out his feelings. He just wanted to forget. Over the next few days, as he learned more about the evidence against Mitya, he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt. Even the testimony of people like Fenya and her mother seemed convincing. The statements from Perhotin, the people at the tavern, Plotnikov’s shop, and witnesses at Mokroe all seemed definite. The details were especially damaging. The secret knocks impressed the lawyers almost as much as Grigory’s story about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, told Ivan that Smerdyakov had been lying all night just on the other side of the wall from her. “He wasn’t three steps from our bed,” she said, and though she was a deep sleeper, she woke up several times and heard him moaning. “He was moaning constantly.”
When Ivan talked to Doctor Herzenstube and said he thought Smerdyakov wasn’t crazy, just sort of weak, the old doctor just gave a sly smile.

“Do you know how he spends his time now?” Herzenstube asked. “He’s memorizing lists of French words. He keeps an exercise book under his pillow with French words written out in Russian letters by someone—ha ha!”

Ivan decided to stop doubting. He couldn’t even think about Dmitri without disgust. But one thing was strange—Alyosha still insisted Dmitri wasn’t the killer and that “probably” Smerdyakov was. Ivan always valued Alyosha’s opinions, so that surprised him. Another strange thing was that Alyosha never tried to talk to Ivan about Mitya, only answering questions if Ivan brought it up. Ivan noticed that, too.

But at the time, Ivan was mostly caught up in something else. After coming back from Moscow, he threw himself into his wild, obsessive love for Katerina Ivanovna. This isn’t the place to tell the whole story, which would fill another book, but I can’t avoid mentioning it here. When Ivan told Alyosha, “I’m not interested in her,” it was a total lie—he actually loved her desperately, though sometimes he hated her enough to want to hurt her. Many things led to this. After everything with Mitya, Katerina turned to Ivan when he returned, hoping he could save her. She was hurt, insulted, and embarrassed. Here was the man she knew had loved her before (she knew it well), and she thought his heart and mind were better than hers. But even with all her feelings, Katerina, who was very proper, never gave in completely to Ivan, no matter how much he fascinated her. She still felt guilty for leaving Mitya, and during their many arguments, she told Ivan so directly. That’s what Ivan called “lies on top of lies.” There was plenty of dishonesty, and it made Ivan even angrier... But more on that another time.

For a while, Ivan almost forgot all about Smerdyakov. But two weeks after his first visit, he started getting the same strange thoughts as before. He kept asking himself: why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, did he sneak onto the stairs like a thief to listen to what his father was doing? Why did he remember that with such disgust? Why was he so depressed the next morning on his trip? Why, when he got to Moscow, did he think, “I’m a scoundrel”? Now, these thoughts were so overwhelming he almost forgot about Katerina Ivanovna. Just after realizing that, he bumped into Alyosha on the street and stopped him right away to ask:

“Do you remember when Dmitri rushed in after dinner and beat up father? And then I told you outside that I reserved ‘the right to desire’?... Tell me, did you think back then that I wanted father dead or not?”
“I did think so,” Alyosha answered quietly.

“And that’s true—it’s not just a guess. But did you also think I wanted ‘one reptile to eat another’—meaning Dmitri would kill father as soon as possible, and that I was even willing to help make it happen?”
Alyosha turned pale and stared silently at his brother’s face.
“Say something!” Ivan demanded. “I need to know what you really thought. I want the truth, just the truth!”
He took a deep breath, glaring at Alyosha, waiting for the answer.
“I’m sorry, but I did think that too, back then,” Alyosha whispered, not trying to soften it.

“Thanks,” Ivan snapped, and hurried away. After that, Alyosha noticed Ivan started avoiding him, even acting like he disliked him, so Alyosha stopped visiting. Right after that meeting, Ivan didn’t go home—he went straight back to see Smerdyakov.

By this time, Smerdyakov had been released from the hospital. Ivan knew where he was staying now—a run-down little wooden house that was split in half by a hallway. On one side lived Marya Kondratyevna (let’s call her Marya) and her mother, and on the other side, Smerdyakov. No one really knew what his relationship was with them, if he was a friend or just renting a room. Later, people guessed he was engaged to Marya and that he was staying there for free while they waited to get married. Both Marya and her mother respected Smerdyakov a lot and thought he was much better than them.

Ivan knocked on the door, and when it opened, he went straight into the hallway. Marya told him to go right to the nicer room on the left, which was Smerdyakov’s. The room was super hot because of the tile stove. The walls were covered with blue wallpaper, but it was old and peeling, and there were so many cockroaches crawling in the cracks that you could hear them rustling all the time. There wasn’t much furniture: just two benches along each wall and two chairs by the table. The wooden table had a pink-patterned cloth on it. There was a pot of geraniums in each of the two tiny windows. In one corner, there was a shelf with religious icons. On the table, there was a small, dented copper samovar and a tray with two cups, but the tea was already finished and the samovar was cold. Smerdyakov was sitting at the table, on a bench, staring at a notebook and writing slowly with a pen. There was a bottle of ink and a flat iron candlestick with a cheap candle. Ivan saw right away that Smerdyakov looked completely healthy again—he looked fresher, even a bit chubbier, and his hair stuck up in front but was slicked down on the sides. He wore a padded, multi-colored robe that was dirty and frayed. He even had glasses on, which Ivan had never seen him wear before. That little detail just made Ivan even angrier: “Someone like him, and he’s wearing glasses?”

Smerdyakov slowly looked up and stared at Ivan through his glasses, then took them off and got up from the bench—but not in a respectful way, more like he was lazy and only doing the bare minimum to be polite. Ivan noticed all of this instantly—especially the way Smerdyakov looked at him, with eyes that were mean, rude, and proud. His look seemed to say, "Why are you bothering me? We finished everything before—why are you back?" Ivan could barely keep his temper.
“It’s hot in here,” Ivan said, still standing, and started to unbutton his coat.
“Take off your coat,” Smerdyakov said, almost like it was a favor.
Ivan took off his coat and threw it on a bench, his hands shaking. He grabbed a chair, quickly moved it to the table, and sat down. Smerdyakov managed to sit back down on his bench before Ivan.
“First of all, are we alone?” Ivan asked, his voice sharp and impatient. “Can they hear us in the other room?”
“No one can hear anything. You saw for yourself—there’s a hallway between us.”
