“Listen, pal, what was that you mumbled when I left the hospital? You said that if I kept quiet about your fake fits, you wouldn’t tell the police all about our talk at the gate. What did you mean by ‘all’? Were you threatening me? Did we make some kind of deal? Do you think I’m scared of you?”

Ivan was furious as he spoke, making it clear he wasn’t going to play games and wanted everything out in the open. Smerdyakov’s eyes flashed with anger, and his left eye twitched, but he answered in his usual calm, slow way, like he was thinking, “You want honesty? Fine, I’ll give it to you.”

“I meant just this: you knew ahead of time about your own father’s murder, but you left him anyway. People might think you hated him—or even something worse. That’s what I promised not to tell the police.”
Smerdyakov spoke slowly and controlled himself, but his voice was firm, angry, and almost daring Ivan. He stared at Ivan boldly. For a moment, Ivan’s mind went blank.
“What? Are you crazy?” Ivan shouted.
“I’m totally sane,” Smerdyakov replied.
“You seriously think I knew about the murder?” Ivan cried, slamming his fist on the table. “And what did you mean by ‘something else’? Speak up, you scoundrel!”
Smerdyakov stayed silent, still staring at Ivan with that rude look.
“Talk, you filthy rat! What’s that ‘something else’ you meant?”
“By ‘something else,’ I meant that you probably really wanted your father dead, too.”

Ivan jumped up and hit Smerdyakov hard on the shoulder, making him crash into the wall. Instantly, Smerdyakov’s face was covered in tears. “It’s shameful to hit a sick man,” he whimpered, wiping his eyes with a filthy blue handkerchief, then quietly wept. A minute passed.
“That’s enough. Stop it,” Ivan ordered, sitting back down. “Don’t push me past my limit.”
Smerdyakov lowered his rag. Every wrinkle on his face showed how insulted he felt.
“So you thought, you rat, that I was planning, along with Dmitri, to kill my father?”
“I didn’t know what you were thinking,” Smerdyakov said bitterly. “That’s why I stopped you at the gate—to find out.”
“To find out what, exactly?”
“If you wanted your father dead or not.”
What drove Ivan crazy most was the rude, snotty tone Smerdyakov kept using.
“You killed him, didn’t you?” Ivan suddenly accused.
Smerdyakov sneered.
“You know perfectly well it wasn’t me who killed him. I figured a smart man like you wouldn’t even need to talk about it again.”
“Then why did you suspect me back then?”

“Like I said already, I was scared. I was so freaked out I suspected everyone. I tried to find out what you were thinking, too. I thought, if you wanted your father dead like your brother did, then it was probably a done deal, and I’d be crushed, too.”
“You didn’t say that two weeks ago.”
“I meant the same thing when I talked to you in the hospital. I thought you’d get it without me spelling it out, and that, being so smart, you wouldn’t want to talk about it openly.”
“Seriously? Come on, answer me. What did I ever do to make you think something that awful about me?”
“You couldn’t have done the killing yourself, and you didn’t want to, but you did want someone else to do it.”
“And he says it so calmly! Why would I have wanted that? What reason could I possibly have?”

“Why? The inheritance, of course,” Smerdyakov said sarcastically, almost with a grudge. “After your father died, each of you would get at least forty thousand, maybe more. But if Fyodor Pavlovitch married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka), she’d get all his money right after the wedding, because she’s smart. Then your father wouldn’t leave you a cent. And were they close to getting married? Absolutely—they were a finger-snap away. All she had to do was say the word and he’d be chasing her to the church.”
Ivan fought hard to control himself.
“Fine,” he said finally. “See, I haven’t jumped up, I haven’t hit you, I haven’t killed you. Go on. So, in your mind, I was planning for Dmitri to do it? I was counting on him?”

“How could you not count on him? If he killed your father, he’d lose his title, his property, and be sent into exile. So his share of the inheritance would go to you and your brother Alexey (Alyosha). You’d each get not forty, but sixty thousand. No question—you were counting on Dmitri.”
“You’re unbelievable! If I was counting on anyone, it would have been you, not Dmitri. I honestly did suspect you might do something evil… I remember feeling that way!”

“For a moment, I thought you were counting on me, too,” Smerdyakov said with a mean smirk. “That’s actually how you showed me what you were thinking. If you suspected me and still left, it was like you were saying, ‘You can kill my father, I won’t stop you!’”
“You snake! So that’s how you took it!”

“All because you went to Tchermashnya. You were planning to go to Moscow, and you refused every time your father begged you to go to Tchermashnya. Then, at a random word from me, you agreed! Why did you go? You had no reason—so if you went just because I suggested it, you must have expected something from me.”
“No, I swear I didn’t!” Ivan shouted, grinding his teeth.

“You didn’t? Then as your father’s son, you should have had me arrested or at least punched me right then for saying something like that. But you weren’t even mad. Instead, you listened and went along with my stupid suggestion and left, which made no sense. You should have stayed to protect your father. How could I not draw conclusions?”
Ivan just sat there, scowling, his fists clenched on his knees.

“Yeah, I do regret not punching you,” he said bitterly. “I couldn’t have had you arrested right then—who would have believed me, and what could I charge you with? But a punch in the face… Oh, I wish I’d thought of it. Even though hitting is illegal, I’d have smashed your ugly face.”
Smerdyakov looked at him almost as if he enjoyed it.

“Usually, people aren’t allowed to hit each other anymore, and most have stopped, but in special situations, people still get violent—everywhere, not just here, even in fancy places like France, just like in Adam and Eve’s days. And they’ll never stop. But you, even in a special case, didn’t dare.”
“Why are you learning French?” Ivan nodded at the notebook on the table.
“Why not? I want to get smarter—maybe one day I’ll get to go to those nice places in Europe.”

“Listen, monster,” Ivan’s eyes flashed and he started shaking. “I’m not scared of your accusations. Say whatever you want about me. If I don’t beat you to death, it’s only because I think you did it, and I’m going to bring you to justice. I’ll expose you.”
“I think you should keep quiet, since I’m totally innocent. Who would believe you, anyway? But if you start, I’ll tell everything, too, because I have to defend myself.”
“Do you think I’m scared of you now?”
“Maybe the court won’t believe what I just told you, but the public will, and then you’ll be ashamed.”
“So you’re saying, ‘It’s always worth talking to a smart guy,’ right?” Ivan snapped.
“Exactly. And you’d better be smart about this.”

Ivan stood up, shaking with anger, put on his coat, and left the cottage without another word or even looking at Smerdyakov. The cool night air hit him as he stepped outside. The moon was bright. Ivan’s mind was spinning with wild thoughts and feelings. “Should I go straight to the police and report Smerdyakov? But what proof do I have? He’s not really guilty, anyway. He’d just accuse me in return. And why did I go to Tchermashnya in the first place? Why? Why?” Ivan wondered. “Yes, I was expecting something… and he’s right.” He remembered, for the hundredth time, how he’d listened on the stairs that last night in his father’s house, but now that memory hurt so much he felt frozen in place, like he’d been stabbed. “I did expect it! I wanted the murder. Did I want it? Did I? I have to kill Smerdyakov! If I can’t kill him now, life isn’t worth living!”

Ivan didn’t go home. Instead, he went straight to Katerina Ivanovna’s and scared her with how wild he looked. He seemed out of his mind. He told her every detail of his conversation with Smerdyakov, word for word. She tried to calm him down, but it didn’t work; he kept pacing the room and talking in a strange, scattered way. Finally, he sat down, put his elbows on the table, buried his head in his hands, and said something strange: “If Smerdyakov is the murderer, not Dmitri, then I share the guilt, because I encouraged him. Maybe I did, maybe I didn’t. But if he did it, I did it, too.”

When Katerina Ivanovna heard that, she got up wordlessly, went to her desk, opened a box, and took out a sheet of paper, which she laid in front of Ivan. This was the document Ivan later called “conclusive proof” that Dmitri had killed his father. It was a letter that Mitya had written to Katerina while drunk, on the same night he met Alyosha at the crossroads on the way to the monastery, after the scene at Katerina’s house when Grushenka insulted her. After leaving Alyosha, Mitya rushed to Grushenka. Whether he saw her or not, he ended up at the Metropolis tavern that night, where he got very drunk. There, he asked for pen and paper and wrote a wild, rambling, desperate letter. It was the kind of letter a drunk person might write—jumping from one thought to the next, full of emotion and confusion, with angry rants, tears, and pounding on the table. The letter was on a cheap, dirty piece of paper from the tavern, and there were even numbers scribbled on the back. Mitya filled up every inch, even writing the last line across the rest. The letter went like this:

Fatal Katya: Tomorrow I’ll get the money and pay you back your three thousand, and goodbye, angry woman—but goodbye, my love, too! Let’s end it! Tomorrow I’ll try to borrow from everyone, and if I can’t, I swear I’ll go to my father and smash his head and take the money from under his pillow, if Ivan has left. Even if I have to go to Siberia, I’ll pay you back the three thousand. Goodbye. I bow down to you, because I’ve been a scoundrel. Forgive me! No, don’t forgive me—it’s better for us both. Better Siberia than your love, because I love another woman, and you met her today, so how can you forgive me? I’ll kill the man who robbed me! I’ll leave everyone and go east, so I never see anyone again—not even her, because she tortures me, too. Goodbye!

P.S.—I curse you, but I adore you! I feel it in my heart. There’s only one string left, and it aches. Better to rip my heart in two! I’ll kill myself, but first that cur. I’ll rip the three thousand from him and throw it at you. Even though I’ve been a scoundrel, I’m not a thief! You’ll get the three thousand. That cur keeps it under his mattress, tied with pink ribbon. I’m not a thief, but I’ll kill my thief. Katya, don’t look down on me. Dmitri isn’t a thief! But a murderer! He murdered his father and destroyed himself just to stand up to your pride. And he doesn’t love you.
P.P.S.—I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S.—Katya, pray to God someone gives me the money. Then I won’t be covered in blood, and if no one does—I will! Kill me!
Your slave and enemy,
D. Karamazov.

When Ivan read this “document,” he was convinced. So it was his brother, not Smerdyakov. And if it wasn’t Smerdyakov, then it wasn’t Ivan, either. To Ivan, the letter was rock-solid proof. He never even considered the idea that Mitya and Smerdyakov might have done the murder together; in fact, that didn’t fit the facts at all. Ivan felt totally reassured. The next morning, he just thought of Smerdyakov’s accusations with scorn. A few days later, he actually wondered why he’d been so upset and suspicious. He decided to ignore Smerdyakov and forget about him. A month went by. He didn’t ask about Smerdyakov, though he heard twice that Smerdyakov was now very sick and seemed insane.

“He’ll go mad in the end,” said Varvinsky, the young doctor, and Ivan remembered that. In the last week of that month, Ivan himself started feeling really sick. He went to see a doctor from Moscow whom Katerina Ivanovna had brought in just before the trial. At the same time, things between Ivan and Katerina Ivanovna got very tense. It was like they were enemies who still loved each other. Katerina’s sudden “returns” to Mitya—her brief but intense moments of feeling for him—drove Ivan crazy. Strangely, until that last scene with Alyosha, Ivan had never heard Katerina doubt Mitya’s guilt, even during those “returns.” It’s worth noting that Ivan hated Mitya more and more every day, not because of Katerina’s feelings, but because he thought Mitya killed their father. He knew this about himself and admitted it.

Still, ten days before the trial, Ivan went to see Mitya and proposed a plan to help him escape—a plan he’d clearly thought about for a long time. Part of his reason was that old sore spot Smerdyakov had poked, about how it was in Ivan’s interest for Mitya to be found guilty, because then Ivan and Alyosha would get more money. Ivan decided to give up thirty thousand roubles to help Mitya escape. Afterward, he felt sad and depressed, and realized that he wanted Mitya to escape, not just to ease his own guilt by giving up the money, but maybe for another reason, too. “Is it because I’m also a murderer at heart?” he wondered. Deep down, something was burning inside him. His pride was hurt most of all that month. But more about that later....

After his talk with Alyosha, Ivan suddenly decided—his hand already on his doorbell—to go see Smerdyakov. He was driven by a burst of anger. He remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had just cried, in front of Alyosha, “It was you, you, who convinced me of Mitya’s guilt!” Ivan was shocked when he remembered that. He had never tried to convince her that Mitya was the murderer; if anything, he’d doubted himself in front of her, especially after coming back from Smerdyakov’s. It was Katerina who had produced the “proof” and shown Mitya’s guilt. Now, suddenly, she’d said, “I’ve been to Smerdyakov’s myself!” When had that happened? Ivan hadn’t known. So she wasn’t so sure about Mitya’s guilt, after all! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What did he say? Ivan’s heart burned with anger. He couldn’t believe he’d let her words pass half an hour ago without reacting. He let go of the bell and rushed out to see Smerdyakov. “Maybe I’ll kill him this time,” he thought on his way.

Halfway to his destination, a sharp, dry wind picked up again, and fine snow started falling thickly, swirling everywhere instead of settling on the ground. Soon, it was a full-on snowstorm. There were hardly any streetlights in this part of town where Smerdyakov lived. Ivan walked alone in the darkness, barely noticing the storm, instinctively finding his way. His head pounded, and there was a sharp pain in his temples. He realized his hands were twitching uncontrollably. Not far from Marya Kondratyevna's cottage, Ivan suddenly ran into a drunken little peasant. The man wore a rough, patched coat, staggered from side to side, muttering and cursing to himself. Every now and then, he would break into a hoarse, drunken song:

But every time, he stopped after the second line and went back to swearing—then started the same song again. Even before he really thought about it, Ivan felt a deep hatred for the man. Suddenly, Ivan became aware of him and felt a strong urge to knock him down. As they met, the peasant lurched violently and crashed into Ivan, who shoved him back hard. The peasant went flying and hit the frozen ground like a log. He let out a sad little “O—oh!” and then lay silent. Ivan stepped closer. The man was flat on his back, completely still and unconscious. “He’ll freeze to death,” Ivan thought, and kept walking to Smerdyakov’s.

In the hallway, Marya Kondratyevna hurried out with a candle to open the door. She whispered that Smerdyakov was very ill. “It’s not that he’s bedridden, but he seems not himself. He even told us to take the tea away; he wouldn’t have any.”
“Why, is he making a scene?” Ivan asked roughly.
“Oh no, not at all—he’s very quiet. Just, please, don’t talk to him too long,” Marya Kondratyevna begged. Ivan opened the door and stepped into the room.

The room was as overheated as before, but some things had changed. One of the benches had been replaced by a big, old, leather-covered mahogany sofa, now made up as a bed with almost clean white pillows. Smerdyakov sat on the sofa, wearing the same dressing gown as before. The table was now right in front of the sofa, leaving little space to move. On the table was a thick book with a yellow cover, but Smerdyakov wasn’t reading it. He just sat there, doing nothing, and looked at Ivan silently, almost as if Ivan’s visit was no surprise. Smerdyakov’s face was very different now—he looked much thinner and more sallow, with sunken eyes and dark circles underneath.
“Wow, you really are sick,” Ivan said, stopping short. “I won’t stay long. I won’t even take off my coat. Is there anywhere to sit?”
He walked to the other end of the table, pulled up a chair, and sat down.
“Why are you just staring at me? I only came here for one thing, and I swear I won’t leave without an answer. Did the young lady, Katerina Ivanovna, come to see you?”
Smerdyakov still said nothing, just quietly kept his eyes on Ivan. Then, suddenly, he turned his face away with a flick of his hand.
“What’s wrong with you?” Ivan demanded.
“Nothing.”
“What do you mean, ‘nothing’?”
“Yes, she came. That’s none of your business. Leave me alone.”
“No, I won’t leave you alone. Tell me—when was she here?”
“Why, I’d actually forgotten about her,” Smerdyakov said, giving a scornful smile and turning to face Ivan again, his eyes filled with the same wild hatred as during their last meeting a month ago.
“You look really sick yourself—your face is sunken. You don’t look like yourself,” he told Ivan.
“Forget about me. Answer my question.”
“Why are your eyes so yellow? The whites are all yellow. Are you that stressed?” Smerdyakov sneered, then suddenly burst out laughing.
“Listen, I told you—I won’t leave without an answer!” Ivan shouted, getting more and more irritated.
“Why do you keep bothering me? Why do you torture me?” Smerdyakov said, looking hurt.
“I don’t care about you. Just answer my question, and I’ll leave.”
“I have no answer for you,” Smerdyakov mumbled, eyes down.
“You can be sure I’ll make you answer!”

“Why are you so nervous?” Smerdyakov looked at him, full of not just contempt, but disgust. “Is it because the trial starts tomorrow? Nothing will happen to you; can’t you believe that? Go home, get some sleep, and don’t worry about anything.”
“I don’t get you.... What do I have to be afraid of tomorrow?” Ivan said in confusion, and suddenly he felt a cold shiver of fear run through him. Smerdyakov stared at him.
“You don’t get it?” Smerdyakov said accusingly. “It’s strange—a smart man like you, pretending to play dumb.”
Ivan stared back, speechless. Smerdyakov’s arrogant tone was shocking, especially coming from someone who used to be his servant. He hadn’t spoken this way even at their last meeting.

“I’m telling you—you have nothing to be afraid of. I won’t say anything about you; there’s no proof against you. But look—your hands are shaking! Why are your fingers twitching like that? Go home, you didn’t kill him.”
Ivan started. He thought of Alyosha.
“I know it wasn’t me,” he said, almost whispering.
“Do you?” Smerdyakov interrupted again.
Ivan jumped up and grabbed Smerdyakov by the shoulder.
“Tell me everything, you snake! Tell me everything!”
Smerdyakov wasn’t scared at all. He just stared at Ivan with crazy hatred.
“Well, you’re the one who killed him, if that’s what you want,” he spat out in a furious whisper.
Ivan fell back into his chair, as if deep in thought. He let out a harsh laugh.
“You mean because I left? Like we talked about last time?”
“You stood right in front of me last time and knew exactly what was going on, and you know now, too.”
“All I know is that you’re insane.”

“Aren’t you tired of this act? Here we are, face to face—why keep pretending with each other? Are you still trying to pin it all on me? You killed him; you’re the real murderer. I was just your tool, your loyal servant. I did it because of what you told me.”
“Did it? Wait—did you actually kill him?” Ivan went cold all over.
Something seemed to snap in Ivan’s mind, and he shivered with dread. Even Smerdyakov looked at him in surprise—maybe Ivan’s shock seemed real to him.
“You mean you really didn’t know?” Smerdyakov asked, watching him closely and forcing a smile. Ivan just stared at him, unable to speak.
suddenly echoed in his head.
“You know, I’m starting to think you’re just a dream, a ghost sitting in front of me,” Ivan muttered.
“There’s no ghost here—just the two of us, and one more. I’m sure he’s here, the third, between us.”
“Who’s that? Who’s here? What third person?” Ivan cried, panicked, looking around the room, his eyes searching the corners.
“That third person is God Himself—Providence. He’s here with us right now. But don’t bother looking for Him; you won’t find Him.”
“You’re lying! You didn’t kill him!” Ivan shouted wildly. “You’re crazy, or just messing with me again!”
Smerdyakov watched him with curiosity, not a trace of fear. He still seemed unsure—maybe he still thought Ivan knew everything and was just trying to blame it all on him.

“Wait a second,” Smerdyakov said in a weak voice. Suddenly, he lifted his left leg from under the table and started rolling up his pant leg. He wore long white socks and slippers. He slowly removed his garter and fumbled around at the bottom of his sock. Ivan watched, suddenly shuddering with terror.

“He’s lost it!” Ivan cried, jumping up so fast he banged his back against the wall and stood stiff and straight, staring wide-eyed at Smerdyakov. But Smerdyakov wasn’t bothered by Ivan’s fear. He kept searching in his sock, as if he was struggling to grab something. Finally, he pulled out what looked like a piece of paper or maybe a bundle. Smerdyakov laid it on the table.
“Here,” he said quietly.
“What is it?” Ivan asked, shaking.
“Take a look,” Smerdyakov said in the same low voice.
Ivan stepped up to the table, picked up the bundle, and started unwrapping it, but suddenly pulled his hand back, almost as if it burned him.
“Your hands keep twitching,” Smerdyakov said, and calmly unfolded the package himself. Inside were three packets of hundred-rouble notes.
“It’s all here—all three thousand roubles. You don’t need to count it. Take it,” Smerdyakov said, nodding at the money. Ivan slumped back in his chair, white as a sheet.
“You scared me ... with your sock,” Ivan said, forcing a strange grin.
“You really didn’t know until now?” Smerdyakov asked again.
“No, I didn’t know. I kept thinking of Dmitri. My brother, my brother! Ugh!” He clutched his head in both hands.
“Listen. Did you kill him alone? With my brother’s help or without?”
“It was only with you—with your help—that I killed him. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is totally innocent.”
“Fine, fine. We’ll talk about me later. Why can’t I stop shaking? I can barely talk.”

“You were brave enough before. You said ‘everything’s allowed,’ but now look how scared you are,” Smerdyakov said, surprised. “Want some lemonade? I’ll ask for some right now. It’s refreshing. But first I need to hide this.”

He motioned toward the money. He was about to get up and call for Marya Kondratyevna to bring lemonade, but looked around for something to cover the bills so she wouldn’t see them. He pulled out his handkerchief, but it was filthy, so instead he grabbed the big yellow book Ivan noticed earlier and put it on top of the money. The book was The Sayings of the Holy Father Isaac the Syrian. Ivan read the title automatically.
“I don’t want lemonade,” Ivan said. “We’ll talk about me later. Sit down and tell me how you did it. I want everything.”
“You’d better take off your coat or you’ll get too hot.” Ivan seemed to realize this for the first time, took off his coat, and threw it on the bench without getting up.
“Go on, talk.”
He seemed calmer now. He waited, certain Smerdyakov would tell him everything.
“How it happened?” Smerdyakov sighed. “It happened naturally—exactly following your words.”

“We’ll talk about what I said later,” Ivan cut in, sounding more in control now, his voice steady instead of yelling. “Just tell me exactly how you did it. Everything, in detail. Don’t skip anything. The details matter most—don’t leave anything out.”
“You’d gone away, and then I fell into the cellar.”
“Was it a real fit, or were you faking?”
“Of course I was faking. I slipped quietly down the steps, lay down at the bottom, and as soon as I was down I started screaming and thrashing around until they carried me out.”
“Wait—so were you faking the whole time after, even at the hospital?”
“No, not at all. The next morning, before they took me to the hospital, I had a real fit—worse than I’ve had in years. I was totally out of it for two days.”
“Okay, okay. Go on.”

“They put me on the bed. I knew I’d be on the other side of the wall, because whenever I was sick, Marfa Ignatyevna always put me there, near them. She’s been kind to me since I was born. That night I moaned quietly, waiting, because I was sure Dmitri Fyodorovitch would come.”
“Waiting for him? You thought he’d come to you?”
“Not to me. I thought he’d come into the house. I was certain of it—he’d get no news, he’d be desperate, so he’d climb over the fence like before and do something.”
“And if he hadn’t come?”
“Then nothing would have happened. I never would’ve gone through with it without him.”
“Okay, okay, just be clear—don’t rush; don’t leave anything out!”

“I expected he’d kill Fyodor Pavlovitch. I thought that was certain, since I’d been getting him ready for it lately.... He knew about the secret knocks—that was the key. With how suspicious and furious he’d become, he was bound to break in when he heard those taps. So I waited for him.”
“Hold on,” Ivan interrupted. “If he killed him, he’d take the money and run. What would you get out of it? I don’t get it.”

“He never would’ve found the money. I only told him it was under the mattress—but that was a lie. The cash was actually in a box. Later, I convinced Fyodor Pavlovitch—since I was the only one he trusted—to hide the envelope with the money behind the icons in the corner. No one would think to look there, especially not in a rush. So that’s where it was. It would be silly to keep it under the mattress—a box could be locked. But everyone believes it was under the mattress. If Dmitri had killed him and found nothing, he’d either run away in a panic or get caught. Then I could always go up to the icons and take the money later, and everyone would blame Dmitri. I could count on that.”
“But what if he didn’t kill him, just knocked him out?”

“If he didn’t kill him, I wouldn’t have dared to take the money, and nothing would’ve happened. But I figured he’d beat him unconscious, and I’d have time to take the cash, then tell Fyodor Pavlovitch Dmitri had taken it after attacking him.”
“Wait ... I’m getting confused. So it was Dmitri who killed him, and you just took the money?”

“No, he didn’t kill him. I could say he did, but I won’t lie to you, because ... because if you honestly didn’t know until now, and aren’t pretending to put the blame on me, then you’re still responsible, since you knew about the murder and told me to do it, and left knowing everything. So tonight I want to prove to your face that you’re the only real murderer, and I’m not—even though I killed him. You’re the true murderer.”

“Why? Why am I a murderer? Oh, God!” Ivan cried, unable to hold back, forgetting he’d promised to talk about himself later. “You still mean that [pg 709] Tchermashnya? Wait, tell me—why did you want my approval, if you really thought Tchermashnya meant yes? How do you explain that now?”

“Once I was sure you agreed, I knew you wouldn’t make a fuss about the missing three thousand if I got suspected instead of Dmitri, or as his helper. You’d even protect me. And when you got your inheritance, you’d reward me when you could, for the rest of your life. Because you’d get your inheritance thanks to me—if he’d married Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka), you wouldn’t have gotten a penny.”
“Ah! So you planned to blackmail me for the rest of my life,” Ivan growled. “And what if I hadn’t left, but told on you?”

“What could you tell? That I talked you into going to Tchermashnya? That’s nothing. Anyway, after our talk, you’d either leave or stay. If you stayed, nothing would happen—I’d know you didn’t want it done, and I’d do nothing. But when you left, it meant you promised not to rat me out at the trial, and you’d ignore me taking the money. And you couldn’t have come after me later, because then I’d reveal everything in court—not that I stole or killed him, but that you pushed me to do it. That’s why I needed your agreement—so you couldn’t trap me, but I could always trap you. I’d tell everyone how eager you were for your father’s death, and people would believe me. You’d be ashamed forever.”
“Was I really that eager?” Ivan snapped.
“You sure were. By agreeing, you silently approved of what I did.” Smerdyakov stared at Ivan, weak and tired but pushed on by some inner force. Ivan could tell he had some plan.
“Go on,” Ivan said. “Tell me what happened that night.”

“What else is there? I lay there and thought I heard the master shout. Before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch got up and ran out—then he screamed, and after that, it was quiet and dark. I lay there, my heart pounding—I couldn’t take it. I got up and went outside. I saw the window open on the left, into the garden, so I stepped there to listen if he was alive. I heard the master moving and sighing, so I knew he was okay. ‘Ah,’ I thought. I went to the window and called, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he ran away.’ He meant Dmitri had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he pointed, also whispering. ‘Wait a minute,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden and found Grigory lying by the wall, bleeding and unconscious. So it was true that Dmitri had been here, I thought, and I decided right then to go through with it, because Grigory, even if he lived, wouldn’t see anything—he was out cold. The only risk was Marfa Ignatyevna waking up. I felt that, but I wanted to get it done so badly I could barely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come—Agrafena Alexandrovna wants in.’ He jumped like a child. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but didn’t really believe it. ‘She’s standing there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out at me, half believing, half suspicious, too scared to open the door. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought, and it was funny. I decided to knock the signal on the window—the one we agreed was for Grushenka—right in front of him. He didn’t believe me at first, but as soon as he heard the knocks, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I tried to go in, but he blocked me. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking. ‘If he’s this scared, this could go bad,’ I thought, and my legs went weak—I was afraid he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or Marfa Ignatyevna would come, or something else would go wrong. I don’t remember exactly, but I must have stood there, pale, facing him. I whispered, ‘She’s there, under the window—can’t you see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her!’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said, ‘she’s hiding in the bushes. Go call her from the study.’ He ran to the window, put a candle there. ‘Grushenka!’ he called, ‘Grushenka, are you here?’ Even then, he didn’t want to lean out—he was terrified of me, too scared to turn his back. ‘She’s right here,’ I said. I leaned out the window. ‘She’s in the bushes, laughing at you. Don’t you see her?’ Suddenly, he believed me—he was nuts about her—and leaned way out. I grabbed the heavy iron paperweight from his desk—you remember it, about three pounds?—and hit him on the head with the corner. He didn’t even cry out, just sank down, so I hit him again, then a third time. The third blow broke his skull. He rolled onto his back, face up, covered in blood. I checked—no blood on me. I wiped the paperweight, put it back, went to the icons, took the money from the envelope, threw the envelope and the pink ribbon on the floor, and left. Out in the garden, shaking, I went straight to the apple tree with the hollow—you know the one. I’d hidden a rag and a piece of paper there before. I wrapped the money up and stuffed it deep inside the hole. It stayed there more than two weeks—I got it out after I left the hospital. Then I went back to bed and thought, ‘If Grigory is dead, this could be bad for me, but if he lives and recovers, he’ll testify that Dmitri was here—so everyone will blame Dmitri for the murder and the money.’ Then I started groaning, trying to wake up Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as possible. Finally she got up, and when she saw Grigory was missing, she ran outside. I heard her scream in the garden. That got everything started and made me feel safe.”

He stopped. Ivan had listened the whole time in total silence, not moving or looking away. While telling his story, Smerdyakov sometimes glanced at Ivan but mostly avoided his eyes. When he finished, he was clearly shaken and breathing hard. Sweat stood out on his face, but it was impossible to tell if it was from guilt or something else.
“Wait,” Ivan said, thinking hard. “What about the door? If he only opened the door for you, how did Grigory see it open before? He saw it before you went in.”
Interestingly, Ivan spoke calmly now, in a friendly tone, not angry like before. If anyone had looked in just then, they’d have thought they were just having a normal, if intense, conversation.

“That door and Grigory Vassilyevitch thinking he saw it open—that’s just in his imagination,” Smerdyakov said with a crooked smile. “He’s not a man, he’s a stubborn mule. He didn’t really see it, but you’ll never convince him otherwise. We’re lucky he thinks that, because now they’ll definitely blame Dmitri.”

“Listen ...” Ivan seemed confused again, struggling to keep his thoughts straight. “I have so many questions, but I keep forgetting them ... I’m getting mixed up. Yes—at least tell me this: why did you open the envelope and leave it there on the floor? Why not just take the whole thing? When you told me, it sounded like you had a good reason ... but why? I don’t get it....”

“I did that for a reason. If someone really knew about the money, like me, if he’d seen the notes before and maybe put them in the envelope himself, and saw it sealed and labeled, why would he tear open the envelope after killing, especially if he was in a hurry? He’d just grab it and run. But Dmitri only knew about the envelope by rumor—he’d never seen it. If he’d found it under the mattress, he would’ve ripped it open right away to check the cash was in there, and then just dropped the envelope, not thinking it’d be evidence. Because he’s not a real thief, and if he did steal, it would just be taking what he thought was his, since he’d told everyone in town he’d take his property from Fyodor Pavlovitch. I didn’t say this to the prosecutor directly—instead, I hinted at it, so he’d come up with it himself. The prosecutor was thrilled with my suggestion.”
“But could you really think of all that in such a rush?” Ivan said, stunned. He looked at Smerdyakov with new fear.
“Come on! Who could think all that up in a panic? I planned it out ahead of time.”
“Well ... the devil helped you!” Ivan cried. “You’re not stupid—you’re a lot smarter than I thought....”

He stood up, clearly wanting to walk around. He was obviously distressed. But the table blocked his way, and there was barely room to move, so he just turned in place and sat down again. Maybe being stuck made him angrier, because he suddenly shouted almost as loud as before.

“Listen, you miserable, disgusting creature! Don’t you get it? If I haven’t killed you, it’s only because I need you to testify tomorrow at the trial. God knows,” Ivan raised his hand, “maybe I am guilty—maybe I did secretly want my father dead, but I swear I wasn’t as guilty as you think, and maybe I didn’t push you at all. No, I didn’t! But it doesn’t matter—I’ll confess everything at the trial tomorrow. I’m determined! I’ll tell everything. But we’ll go together. Whatever you say about me, I’ll admit it—I’m not afraid of you. I’ll confirm it all! But you have to confess, too! You must—we’ll go together. That’s how it’s going to be!”
Ivan said this with a serious, determined look. Just from his fiery eyes, you could tell he meant it.
“You’re sick, I see it. You’re really sick. Your eyes are yellow,” Smerdyakov said, without any sarcasm—he almost sounded sympathetic.
“We’ll go together,” Ivan repeated. “And if you won’t go, I’ll go alone.”
Smerdyakov paused, thinking.
“That won’t happen. You won’t go,” he finally said, certain.
“You don’t understand me,” Ivan said, hurt.

“You’ll be too ashamed to confess everything. And anyway, it won’t help, because I’ll just say I never said any of this to you, and that you’re either sick (which you look like), or you feel sorry for your brother and are making all this up to save him, inventing it against me—since you always treated me like I was nothing. Who’ll believe you? What proof do you have?”
“But you showed me the money just now to convince me.”
Smerdyakov lifted the book off the notes and set it aside.
“Take the money with you,” Smerdyakov sighed.
“Of course I’ll take it. But why give it to me, if you killed him for it?” Ivan asked, surprised.

“I don’t want it,” Smerdyakov said, voice shaking, waving it away. “I did dream of starting a new life with that money, in Moscow or maybe abroad. I dreamed about it, mainly because ‘everything is allowed.’ That was what you taught me—you talked about it a lot. If there’s no eternal God, there’s no such thing as virtue, and no need for it. You were right. That’s how I saw it.”
“You came to that on your own?” Ivan said, with a twisted smile.
“With your help.”
“And now, I guess, you believe in God, since you’re giving the money back?”
“No, I don’t believe,” Smerdyakov whispered.
“Then why are you giving it back?”

“Stop ... that’s enough!” Smerdyakov waved his hand. “You used to say everything was allowed—so why are you so worked up now? You even want to confess against yourself.... But you won’t. You won’t testify,” Smerdyakov said with confidence.
“You’ll see,” Ivan replied.

“No way. You’re too smart. You love money, I know that. You like being respected, too, because you’re proud; you’re obsessed with women, and what you want most is a comfortable life without depending on anyone. That’s what matters to you. You won’t ruin your life by disgracing yourself. You’re like Fyodor Pavlovitch, more than any of his kids—you have the same soul as he did.”
“You’re not stupid,” Ivan said, surprised. His face flushed. “You’re serious now!” he said, looking at Smerdyakov differently.
“It was your pride that made you think I was a fool. Take the money.”
Ivan took the three packets of bills and stuffed them in his pocket without wrapping them up.
“I’ll show these in court tomorrow,” he said.
“No one will believe you. You have plenty of your own money—they’ll just think you brought it from your cash box.”
Ivan stood up.
“I repeat—the only reason I haven’t killed you is because I need you for tomorrow. Remember that—don’t forget it!”

“Then kill me. Do it now,” Smerdyakov said, suddenly staring at Ivan in a strange way. “But you won’t do it!” he added with a bitter smile. “You’re too scared to do anything, you, who used to be so bold!”
“Till tomorrow!” Ivan shouted, heading for the door.
“Wait ... show me the money again.”
Ivan took out the notes and showed them. Smerdyakov stared at them for ten seconds.
“Okay, you can go,” he said, waving his hand. “Ivan Fyodorovitch!” he called as Ivan left.
“What?” Ivan stopped but didn’t turn.
“Goodbye!”
“Till tomorrow!” Ivan called again, and left the cottage.

The snowstorm was still raging. Ivan started off confidently, but suddenly began to stagger. “It’s something physical,” he thought with a strange grin. He almost felt happy—he was filled with determination, finally putting an end to all his doubts. His mind was set; “and now it won’t change,” he thought with relief. Right then, he tripped over something and nearly fell. He stopped and realized it was the peasant he had knocked down earlier, still lying there, almost buried by the snow. Ivan picked him up. Seeing a light in a nearby house, he walked over, knocked on the shutters, and asked the man inside to help carry the peasant to the police station, promising him three roubles. The man got ready and came out. I won’t go into detail about how Ivan got the peasant to the police and arranged for a doctor, paying generously. It took a whole hour, but Ivan was satisfied. His mind kept racing.

“If I hadn’t made up my mind so firmly for tomorrow,” he thought, pleased, “I wouldn’t have spent a whole hour helping the peasant—I would have just walked by and let him freeze. I’m definitely able to watch myself,” he thought, even more satisfied, “even though people think I’m losing my mind!”

Just as he reached his house, he stopped, suddenly wondering if he should go right then to the prosecutor and tell him everything. But he answered his own question by turning back to his house. “Everything together tomorrow!” he whispered, and, strangely, all his happiness and satisfaction vanished in an instant.

When he entered his room, he felt as if a blast of cold air touched his heart—a reminder of something awful and disgusting that was in the room right now, and had been there before. He slumped onto his sofa. The old lady brought him a kettle for tea; he made some, but didn’t touch it. He sat there, dizzy and weak. He was starting to drift off, but got up and paced the room to shake off his sleepiness. Sometimes, he thought he was hallucinating, but what bothered him most wasn’t being sick. He sat down again, looking around as if searching for something. He did this several times, until finally his eyes locked onto one spot. Ivan smiled, but his face turned red with anger. He sat there a long time, leaning on both arms, glaring sideways at the same spot—the sofa against the opposite wall. Clearly, something there irritated and tormented him.

I’m not a doctor, but I think I have to tell you about Ivan’s illness now. Skipping ahead a bit, I can say this: Ivan was just about to have a really serious mental breakdown—what they used to call “brain fever.” His health had been shaky for a while, but he’d managed to fight off the sickness up until now. I’m not a medical expert, but I think maybe, through pure willpower, Ivan managed to hold off the breakdown, hoping he could stop it altogether. He knew he was sick, but he hated the idea of being ill—especially now, right when his whole life was coming to a crisis, when he needed to be at his sharpest and prove himself to himself.

Still, Ivan did see the new doctor—the one Katerina Ivanovna (Katya) had brought from Moscow, as I mentioned before. The doctor listened to Ivan, checked him over, and decided that Ivan really did have something wrong with his brain. Ivan even admitted, reluctantly, that he was seeing things. “Hallucinations are very possible in your condition,” the doctor said. “But you should get checked out right away—don’t wait, or things will get much worse.” But Ivan ignored the advice and didn’t go to bed to rest. “If I’m still walking around, then I’m fine. If I collapse, anyone who wants can take care of me then,” he decided, and dropped the subject.

So now Ivan was sitting there, half aware that he was losing touch with reality, and staring at something—or someone—on the sofa across from him. There seemed to be a person sitting there, though Ivan had no idea how he got in, since he hadn’t been there when Ivan came back from seeing Smerdyakov. This person looked like a certain type of Russian gentleman—not young, maybe around fifty, with shaggy dark hair going gray and a small pointed beard. He wore an old-fashioned brown jacket that had once been expensive, but was now shabby, and at least three years out of style. His shirt and scarf were meant to look fancy, but if you looked closely, they weren’t very clean and the scarf was worn out. His checked pants were nicely cut but too tight and too light in color for current fashion. He even wore a fluffy white hat that was totally wrong for the season.

In short, he looked like a well-bred man who had fallen on hard times. He seemed like one of those old landowners from the days of serfdom. He’d clearly been part of high society once and maybe still had a few connections, but after a wild youth and losing his money when serfdom ended, he’d become the sort of poor relative who drifts from one old friend’s house to another, always welcome for his good manners and because he could fit in anywhere—just not at the head of the table. People like him, who can tell stories, play cards, and avoid responsibility, usually end up alone, either bachelors or widowers. If they do have kids, the kids are raised far away, maybe by an aunt, and these men never mention them in polite company—almost like they’re embarrassed. Over time, they forget about their children altogether, except for maybe a birthday or Christmas letter.

The visitor’s face didn’t look exactly kind, but rather ready to look friendly whenever needed. He didn’t wear a watch, but had a pair of glasses on a ribbon. On his right hand he wore a big gold ring with a cheap opal.

Ivan sat silently, refusing to start a conversation. The visitor waited, sitting exactly like a poor relative who comes down to keep his host company at tea, but says nothing because the host looks busy and grumpy. Still, he was ready to chat if Ivan wanted. Suddenly, the visitor’s face looked concerned.

“Hey,” he said to Ivan, “sorry to bring this up, but just to remind you: you went to see Smerdyakov to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, but you left without learning anything about her. You probably forgot—”

“Oh, right,” Ivan blurted out, his face going dark with worry. “I did forget—but it doesn’t matter now. I’ll deal with it tomorrow,” he muttered to himself. Then, turning to the visitor, he added, “I would have remembered that myself in a minute—that’s exactly what was bothering me! Why do you act like you’re the one reminding me, like I wouldn’t have remembered on my own?”

“Then don’t believe it,” said the gentleman with a friendly smile. “Why believe something you don’t want to? Besides, proof doesn’t always help you believe—especially proof you can touch. Look at Thomas: he didn’t believe in Christ just because he saw him risen, but because he wanted to believe. Or spiritualists—they think they’re helping religion by seeing devils and talking to the dead. They say that’s proof of the other world. But does proving there’s a devil mean there’s a God? I’d love to join a club of idealists and argue with them—I’d claim I’m a realist, but not a materialist! Ha ha!”

“Listen,” Ivan suddenly stood up. “I think I’m losing my mind. In fact, I know I am. Say whatever nonsense you want—I don’t care! You won’t make me angry like last time. But I do feel kind of ashamed... I want to walk around the room. Sometimes I don’t even see you or hear your voice, but I always know what you’re saying, because it’s really just me talking to myself. I can’t even tell if I was awake or dreaming the last time you showed up. Maybe if I put a wet towel on my head, you’ll disappear.”
Ivan went to the corner, got a towel, wet it, put it on his head, and started pacing around the room.
“I’m so glad you feel comfortable around me,” the visitor said.

“Idiot,” Ivan laughed. “You think I’d be polite with you? I’m in a good mood now, even though my head hurts... just don’t start babbling philosophy like last time. If you can’t disappear, at least talk about something funny. You’re a poor relative—you should gossip! What a nightmare you are! But I’m not scared of you. I’ll beat you. I’m not going to an asylum!”

“That’s charming, poor relative. Yes, I’m in my natural form. What am I on earth if not a poor relation? By the way, I’m a little surprised to see you’re starting to see me as real, not just in your head like you insisted last time—”

“Not for a second do I think you’re real!” Ivan snapped. “You’re a lie, you’re my illness, you’re a hallucination. I just don’t know how to get rid of you, and I see I have to put up with you for a while. You’re just a part of me—my thoughts and feelings, but only the ugliest, dumbest ones. You might even be interesting if I had time to waste on you—”

“Excuse me, excuse me, I caught you! When you yelled at Alyosha under the streetlight tonight—‘You learned it from him! How do you know he visits me?’—you were thinking of me then. So, for a second, you did believe I’m real,” the gentleman said, grinning.
“Yeah, that was just a moment of weakness... but I couldn’t really believe in you. I don’t even know if I was awake or dreaming last time. Maybe I just imagined you then and didn’t see you at all.”
“And why were you so rude to Alyosha just now? He’s a good guy; I’ve treated him badly about Father Zossima.”
“Don’t talk about Alyosha! Who do you think you are, you servant!” Ivan laughed again.
“You scold me, but you laugh—that’s a good sign. But you’re much more polite than last time, and I know why: it’s that big decision of yours—”
“Don’t talk about my decision,” Ivan snapped, furious.
“I get it, I get it, it’s noble, it’s charming—you’re going to defend your brother and sacrifice yourself... very heroic.”
“Shut up or I’ll kick you!”

“I wouldn’t really mind, because then my goal would be reached. If you kick me, you must believe I’m real—because who kicks a ghost? But seriously, I don’t care; scold if you like, though it’s better to be a little more polite even to me. ‘Idiot, servant!’—what words!”
“Scolding you, I scold myself,” Ivan laughed again. “You’re just me, with a different face. You say what I’m thinking... and nothing new!”
“If I think like you, that’s a compliment to me,” the gentleman said, acting all dignified.
“You only pick out my worst thoughts, and the stupidest ones. You’re dumb and tasteless. You’re so dumb. No, I can’t deal with you! What do I do, what do I do?” Ivan said, grinding his teeth.

“My friend, all I want is to act like a gentleman and be seen as one,” the visitor said, sounding humble and proud at the same time—like a true poor relative. “I’m poor, but... well, I won’t say I’m honest, but... everyone says I’m a fallen angel. I can’t imagine how I was ever an angel. If I was, it was so long ago it doesn’t matter. Now I just care about being seen as a decent person and try to get along. I really like people, I’ve been lied about a lot! When I stay with you, it makes my life feel more real, and that’s what I like most. Like you, I’m a dreamer, so I love the reality of earth. Here, everything is neat and organized; in our world, it’s just endless equations. I like it here; I even get superstitious on earth. I’ve picked up your habits: I like going to the public baths now, would you believe it? I even dream about being born as a merchant’s wife, weighing three hundred pounds, and believing everything she believes. My dream is to go to church and light a candle with simple faith—really, that would end my suffering. I like going to doctors, too. Last spring there was smallpox, and I got a vaccination at a hospital—if you only knew how much I enjoyed it. I gave ten roubles to help the Slavs! But you’re not listening. You know, you’re not well tonight? You saw the doctor yesterday—so, what did he say?”
“Idiot!” Ivan snapped.
“But you’re smart, at least. Scolding again? I didn’t ask out of sympathy. You don’t have to answer. Now rheumatism has started up again—”
“Idiot!” Ivan repeated.
“You keep repeating yourself! But I had such a bad case of rheumatism last year I still remember it.”
“The devil gets rheumatism!”
“Why not, if I take on a body sometimes? If I have a body, I get the side effects. ‘Satan sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto.’”
“What, what, ‘Satan sum et nihil humanum...’? That’s not bad for the devil!”
“I’m glad you finally like something I said.”
“But you didn’t get that from me.” Ivan stopped, surprised. “That never occurred to me before. That’s strange.”

“That’s new, right? I’ll be honest and explain. Listen: in dreams—especially nightmares, maybe from eating something bad—you can see the most amazing things, whole worlds, plots with detail down to the last button on a cuff, better than Tolstoy could imagine. And regular people have these dreams, not just writers. It’s a mystery. A politician told me all his best ideas came to him in his sleep. Well, it’s like that now: even though I’m your hallucination, I still say things you never thought of, just like in a nightmare. So, I’m not just repeating your ideas, but I’m still only your nightmare, nothing else.”
“You’re lying. You just want me to believe you’re real and not my own dream, and now you’re pretending you’re just a dream.”
“My friend, I’m using a special method today. I’ll explain later. Where was I? Oh yes, I caught a cold then, but not here—over there.”

“Where’s ‘over there’? Tell me, are you going to stay long? Can’t you leave?” Ivan cried, almost desperate. He stopped pacing and sat on the sofa, elbows on the table, squeezing his head. He pulled off the wet towel and threw it away, annoyed—it was useless.

“You’re just nervous,” the gentleman said, sounding casual but polite. “You’re even mad at me for catching a cold, though it happened naturally. I was racing to a party at a high-ranking lady’s house in Petersburg—she wanted to influence the government. Well, I was in an evening suit, white tie, gloves, but I was God knows where and had to fly through space to get to earth. It only took an instant, but you know sunlight takes eight minutes to reach earth! And in an evening suit, with my vest open. Spirits don’t freeze, but with a fleshly body... well, I didn’t think, and set off. In those spaces, in the waters above the clouds, it’s so cold—like 150 degrees below zero! You know how village girls dare people to lick an axe in the cold and their tongue freezes to it? Well, that’s just at minus 30—at minus 150, you’d only have to touch an axe and your finger would freeze solid... if there was even an axe there.”
“Could there even be an axe there?” Ivan interrupted, annoyed. He was trying as hard as he could not to believe his own hallucination, not to go completely mad.
“An axe?” the guest asked, surprised.
“Yeah, what would happen to an axe there?” Ivan demanded, almost obsessively.

“What would happen to an axe in space? What a question! If it fell from far up, it would just end up orbiting the earth, like a satellite. Astronomers would track its rise and setting, and Gatzuk would put it in his calendar, that’s all.”
“You’re so dumb, unbelievably dumb,” Ivan grumbled. “If you’re going to make things up, at least be clever about it. You’re just trying to convince me you’re real, but I refuse to believe it!”
“But I’m not making things up; it’s all true. The truth, unfortunately, is hardly ever interesting. I see you expect something impressive from me, but I can only give what I have—”
“Don’t talk philosophy, idiot!”

“Philosophy? When my whole right side is numb and I’m moaning in pain? I’ve tried every doctor: they can diagnose everything, but they never know how to cure you. One young student told me, ‘You may die, but at least you’ll know exactly what you’re dying of!’ And then they send you to specialists: ‘We only diagnose, but go to this specialist—he’ll cure you.’ The old-fashioned doctor who treated everything is gone; now there are only specialists, and they all advertise in the papers. If you have a nose problem, they send you to Paris: ‘There’s a European specialist for noses.’ In Paris, he’ll say, ‘I only treat your right nostril; for the left, go to Vienna.’ So what do you do? I tried home remedies—a German doctor told me to rub myself with honey and salt in the bathhouse. I just wanted an extra bath, so I did it, but it didn’t help. In desperation I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan. He sent me a book and some drops—thank you, Count! But, funny enough, Hoff’s malt extract cured me! I found it by accident, drank a bottle and a half, and I was ready to dance, it felt so good. I even wrote a thank-you letter to the newspapers, but they wouldn’t print it. ‘That would be too old-fashioned,’ they said. ‘No one believes in the devil these days. You’d better stay anonymous.’ But what good is a thank-you letter if no one knows who wrote it? I laughed with the editors: ‘It’s old-fashioned to believe in God these days, but I’m the devil—you believe in me!’ ‘We get that,’ they said. ‘Who doesn’t believe in the devil? But we still can’t print it. Maybe as a joke?’ But I thought it wasn’t funny. So it never got printed. And you know, it still bothers me. My best feelings—like gratitude—are denied to me, just because of who I am.”
“Philosophy again?” Ivan snarled.

“God forbid, but sometimes you have to complain. I’m misunderstood. You keep calling me dumb. You must be young. Listen, intelligence isn’t everything! I have a kind and cheerful heart. ‘I also write comedy sketches.’ You think I’m just like Hlestakov grown old, but my situation is much more serious. Long ago, for reasons I never understood, I was supposed to ‘deny’—even though I’m not inclined to be negative. ‘No, you must go and deny,’ they told me. ‘Without denial, there’s no criticism—and what would a newspaper be without criticism?’ Without criticism, it would be just endless praise. But that’s not enough for life; praise must be tested by doubt. But I didn’t make the rules. They picked me as the scapegoat, made me write criticism, and that’s what made life possible. We get the joke. I, for one, just want to be erased. ‘No, live,’ they tell me, ‘because without you, there’s nothing.’ If everything made sense, nothing would ever happen. So I have to do things that make no sense, because that’s my job. And even though people are smart, they take all this seriously, and that’s their tragedy. They suffer, but that means they’re alive—suffering is life. Without suffering, life would just be an endless church service—holy, but boring. But what about me? I suffer, but I don’t really live. I’m x in an equation without an answer. I’m a ghost, lost, who’s even forgotten his own name. You’re laughing—no, you’re angry again. You care about intelligence, but I’d give up all this cosmic life, all the honors, to be a merchant’s wife, heavy as a barrel, and light candles at church.”
“So even you don’t believe in God?” Ivan asked, with a twisted smile.
“What can I say?—if you’re serious—”
“Is there a God or not?” Ivan demanded fiercely.
“Ah, you are serious! Honestly, I don’t know. There! I said it.”
“You don’t know, but you say you see God? No, you’re not someone else, you’re just me—nothing more! You’re trash, just my imagination!”

“Well, if you want, I have the same philosophy as you. That’s true. ‘I think, therefore I am’—that much I know. Everything else—these worlds, God, even the devil—none of that is proven, in my opinion. Maybe it all exists by itself, or maybe it’s just a result of my own ego, which has always existed. But I’ll stop, or you might jump up and hit me any second.”
“Just tell me a story!” Ivan said miserably.

“Funnily enough, I have a story about our topic—a legend, not an anecdote. You accuse me of not believing, but I’m not the only one. We’re all confused over there, and it’s your fault—with your science. It used to be simple: atoms, five senses, four elements, and it all made sense. But now, with molecules and protoplasm, we’ve had to admit we don’t know everything. There’s a lot of confusion and even more gossip among us than among you. We even have a secret police! This legend comes from our own middle ages—not yours. Even among us, only the old ladies believe it now. But I’ll share it as a secret, just for you. It’s about Paradise. There was once a thinker and philosopher on earth. He denied everything—laws, conscience, faith, and especially the afterlife. He died, expecting darkness and nothingness. Instead, he found an afterlife waiting for him! He was shocked and upset. ‘This goes against my principles!’ he said. And as punishment—well, excuse me, I’m just repeating what I heard—he was sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometers in darkness (we use the metric system now), and when he finished, he’d be let into heaven and forgiven—”
“What kinds of punishments do you have over there, besides the quadrillion kilometers?” Ivan asked, suddenly interested.

“What punishments? Oh, don’t ask. In the old days there were all kinds, but now it’s mostly mental suffering—‘pricks of conscience’ and such. We got that from you, with your more ‘civilized’ ways. Who does it help? Only people without a conscience, since they can’t be bothered by it. But decent people with honor suffer more than ever. When reforms come in before people are ready, especially if they just copy them from other countries, it just makes things worse! The old fire was better. Well, this guy sentenced to walk the quadrillion kilometers? He lay down across the road and said, ‘I refuse, on principle!’ He was like a mix of an enlightened Russian atheist and the prophet Jonah sulking in the whale.”
“What did he lie on, exactly?”
“Well, I guess there was something to lie on. Aren’t you laughing?”
“Bravo!” Ivan cried, still strangely interested. Now he was actually curious. “So, is he still lying there?”
“That’s the thing—he isn’t. He lay there almost a thousand years, then got up and walked on.”
“What an idiot!” Ivan said with a nervous laugh, still thinking hard. “Does it matter if he lies there forever or walks the quadrillion kilometers? It would take billions of years to walk that far!”
“More than that! I’d need paper and a pencil to work it out. But he reached the end long ago—and that’s where the story really starts.”
“Wait, he got there? But how did he have enough time?”

“You keep thinking of our earth! Our earth could have been repeated a billion times. It might have died, frozen, broken apart, turned to water, become a comet, then a sun, then earth again—over and over, always the same, endlessly boring—”
“Okay, but what happened when he got there?”

“The moment he walked into Paradise, before two seconds had passed (though I think his watch must have dissolved on the way), he shouted that those two seconds were worth not just a quadrillion kilometers, but a quadrillion quadrillions! He sang hosannah so loudly that some of the other people there wouldn’t talk to him at first—they said he’d become too much of a reactionary. That’s the Russian temperament for you. I repeat, it’s just a legend, take it or leave it. But that’s what some of us think about these things even now.”

“I caught you!” Ivan cried, almost like a little kid who just remembered something. “That story about the quadrillion years—I made that up myself! I was seventeen, in high school, in Moscow. I told it to my friend Korovkin. It’s so unique, I couldn’t have gotten it anywhere else. I thought I’d forgotten it, but I just remembered it again—I remembered it myself, not you! People remember weird things like that, even right before they die... it’s come back to me in a dream. You’re just a dream! You’re not real!”
“From how much you deny my existence,” the gentleman laughed, “I’m sure you believe in me.”
“Not even a tiny bit! Not even one percent of a percent!”
“But you do, even if it’s only one tiny part in ten thousand. Admit it!”
“Not for a second!” Ivan shouted. “But I wish I could believe in you,” he added, strangely.
“Aha! That’s an admission. But I’m nice, so I’ll help you out. Listen, I was the one who reminded you of your old story, not you. I did it on purpose, to make you doubt me completely.”
“You’re lying. Your whole reason for being here is to make me believe you’re real!”

“Exactly. But this back-and-forth—believing, not believing—is so hard on someone like you that it’s almost unbearable. Since you’re tempted to believe in me, I threw in some doubt by reminding you of your own story. I want you to swing between belief and disbelief. That’s my plan. It’s a new method. As soon as you totally stop believing in me, you’ll start telling me I’m real. I know you! Then my work is done. I’ll plant a tiny seed of faith in you, and it’ll grow into a huge oak tree—and you’ll want to become a saint, living alone in the wilderness. You’ll eat bugs, wander off to save your soul!”
“So you’re working for my soul’s salvation, are you, you jerk?”
“You have to do a good deed sometimes. Why are you so grumpy?”
“Idiot! Did you ever tempt those saints who ate bugs and prayed for years until they were covered in moss?”

“My dear boy, that’s all I ever do. You forget everything else in the world and focus on one saint, because he’s a real gem. One soul like that is sometimes worth a whole constellation. That’s how we measure things. The challenge is priceless! And some of those saints, believe it or not, are as smart as you. They can believe and doubt so deeply, they’re almost ready to flip upside down, as the actor Gorbunov says.”
“So, did you get your nose pulled?”9

“It’s better to get off with just your nose pulled than to lose it completely,” the visitor said wisely. “As a suffering marquis said to his priest—a Jesuit, I was there, it was great. ‘Give me back my nose!’ he cried, beating his chest. ‘My son,’ said the priest, ‘sometimes what seems bad leads to hidden good. If fate took your nose, at least no one can pull it anymore.’ ‘Father, that’s no comfort,’ the marquis said. ‘I’d be glad to have my nose pulled every day if I still had it!’ ‘My son,’ sighed the priest, ‘you can’t have every blessing at once. But when you lost your nose, you were led by the nose anyway.’”
“Idiot, that’s so dumb!” Ivan yelled.

“My friend, I just wanted to make you laugh. But I swear, that’s real Jesuit logic, and it really happened. The young man shot himself that same night. I was with him until the end. Those Jesuit confessionals are my favorite thing when I’m feeling down. Here’s another story from just the other day. A pretty young French girl, only twenty, comes to confess. She tells the old priest her sin. ‘Why, my daughter, have you fallen again? Not the same man this time? Aren’t you ashamed?’ ‘Ah, father,’ she says, crying, ‘it makes him so happy and it hardly hurts me at all!’ Just imagine! I stepped back. It was the cry of nature—better than innocence, really. I forgave her right there. But I had to turn back, because I heard the priest asking her to meet that evening—though he was old and strict, he fell instantly! It was just nature, the truth of nature taking over! What, you’re frowning again? Angry again? I don’t know how to make you happy—”
“Leave me alone, you’re pounding in my head like a nightmare,” Ivan moaned, helpless. “I’m so bored of you, it’s unbearable. I’d give anything to get rid of you!”

“I keep telling you—don’t expect ‘everything great and noble’ from me, and you’ll see we’ll get along,” said the gentleman seriously. “You’re mad at me for not showing up in a red cloud, with thunder and lightning and burned wings, but instead looking so plain. You’re upset, first, for aesthetic reasons, and second, out of pride—how could such a boring devil visit someone as great as you! You’ve got that romantic streak in you, just like Byelinsky mocked. I can’t help it. When I came here, I almost dressed up as a retired general with a medal on my coat, but I was afraid you’d beat me up for wearing the wrong medal. And you keep saying I’m dumb, but I know I’m not as smart as you. Mephistopheles told Faust he wanted evil but did only good—well, with me, it’s the opposite. I’m probably the only being who truly loves the truth and wants good. I was there when the Word died on the cross and rose to heaven carrying the soul of the thief. I heard the angels singing and the seraphim shouting hosannah—so loud it shook the universe. I swear I wanted to join in and shout hosannah too. The word was on my lips... you know how sensitive I am. But my common sense—a terrible trait—held me back. I let the moment pass. Because I thought, what would happen if I joined in? Everything would end, and nothing would ever happen again. So, out of duty and my role in the universe, I had to hold back. Someone else gets all the credit for the good; I get stuck with all the nasty stuff. But I don’t envy the honor of being the hero, I’m not ambitious. Why am I, of everyone, doomed to be cursed and even kicked? If I have a body, I get kicked sometimes. I know there’s a secret, but no one will tell me. If I knew, I might shout hosannah and then the minus would disappear, and only good sense would be left. But then everything would end—even magazines and newspapers, because who would need them? I know that at the end, I’ll be forgiven too. I’ll walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But until then, I sulk and do my job, even if I hate it: ruining thousands to save one. How many souls have had to be destroyed, how many reputations ruined, just for the sake of one righteous man—like Job, when they made such a joke of me! Until the secret is revealed, I have two kinds of truth: their truth (which I don’t know yet), and my own. Who knows which is better... Are you asleep?”
“I wish I was,” Ivan groaned angrily. “All my dumb old ideas—long since outgrown and thrown away—you bring up like they’re something new!”
“There’s no making you happy! And I thought you’d be impressed by my style. That hosannah in the sky was good, wasn’t it? And the irony, like Heine?”
“No, I was never such a servant! How could my soul create a flunkey like you?”
“My friend, I know a very smart and charming young Russian—a writer, an art lover, and author of a poem called ‘The Grand Inquisitor.’ I was just thinking of him!”
“Don’t you dare talk about The Grand Inquisitor!” Ivan shouted, blushing with shame.
“And the Geological Cataclysm. Remember? That was a poem, too!”
“Shut up or I’ll kill you!”

“You’ll kill me? No, sorry, I’m going to talk. That’s why I came—I wanted the pleasure. Oh, I love the dreams of passionate young men, eager for life! ‘There are new men,’ you thought last spring, when you planned to come here. ‘They want to destroy everything and start with cannibalism. Idiots! They didn’t ask me! I say, don’t destroy anything—just destroy the idea of God in people, that’s the real work. Once everyone denies God—and I think that’ll happen, just like geological periods—the old view of the world will collapse on its own, without any cannibalism. The old morals will disappear, and everything will begin again. People will come together to get the most out of life, just for happiness in this world. Man will feel divine pride and become the man-god. As he conquers nature, he’ll feel such joy that it will make up for all his old dreams of heaven. Everyone will know they’re mortal and accept death calmly, like gods. Their pride will teach them it’s pointless to complain about life being short, and they’ll love others with no thought of reward. Love will be enough, even just for a moment, and knowing it’s short will make it burn even brighter, instead of being wasted on dreams of eternal love after death... and so on, and so on. Lovely!’”
Ivan sat staring at the floor, hands over his ears, but he started shaking all over. The voice kept going.

“The question now, our young thinker wondered, is could this ever really happen? If it could, then everything would be decided and humanity would be set forever. But since people are so stubbornly stupid, it can’t happen for at least a thousand years. So anyone who sees the truth now can live however they want, by the new rules. In that sense, ‘everything is allowed.’ Even if that time never comes, since there’s no God and no afterlife, the new man can become the man-god, even if he’s the only one. Promoted to his new position, he can break all the old moral rules if he needs to. There’s no law for God. Where God stands is holy. Wherever I stand will be the best place—‘everything is allowed’ and that’s that! All very charming. But if you’re going to cheat, why do you need a moral reason? That’s our modern Russian: he can’t even cheat without wanting a moral excuse. He loves the truth so much—”
The visitor kept talking, clearly getting carried away and speaking louder and louder, glancing ironically at Ivan. But he didn’t finish—suddenly, Ivan grabbed a glass and threw it at him.

“Ah, but that’s so silly,” the visitor cried, jumping up and shaking off the tea. “He remembered Luther’s inkstand! He thinks I’m a dream and throws glasses at a dream! Typical! I knew you were only pretending to block your ears.”
Suddenly there was a loud, persistent knocking at the window. Ivan jumped up.
“Do you hear that? You’d better open up,” the visitor said. “It’s your brother Alyosha, and I bet he’s got big news!”
“Quiet, liar! I knew it was Alyosha—I could feel he was coming, and of course he’s got news,” Ivan shouted, almost frantic.
“Open up for him. There’s a snowstorm and he’s your brother. Does monsieur know what the weather’s like? You wouldn’t even send a dog out in this.”

The knocking went on. Ivan tried to run to the window, but it was like his arms and legs were chained. He tried to break free, but couldn’t. The knocking grew louder and louder. At last, the chains broke and Ivan leapt up. He looked around wildly. Both candles were almost gone, the glass he’d just thrown was still on the table, and there was no one on the sofa. The knocking at the window was still there, but it wasn’t as loud as it seemed in his dream; actually, it was pretty soft.
“It wasn’t a dream! No, I swear it wasn’t a dream—it just happened!” Ivan yelled. He ran to the window and opened it.
“Alyosha, I told you not to come,” he shouted at his brother. “Just tell me what you want, in two words. In two words, do you hear?”
“An hour ago, Smerdyakov hanged himself,” Alyosha said from outside.
“Come around to the steps, I’ll open the door,” Ivan replied, going to let his brother in.

Alyosha came in and told Ivan that just over an hour ago, Marya Kondratyevna had run to his rooms in a panic. She told him that Smerdyakov had killed himself. “I went in to clear away the samovar and found him hanging from a nail in the wall.” When Alyosha asked if she’d called the police, she said she hadn’t told anyone yet—“but I ran straight to you, I haven’t stopped running.” She was totally panicked, Alyosha said, shaking all over. Alyosha went with her to the cottage and found Smerdyakov still hanging there. On the table was a note: “I end my life by my own choice, so no one else is to blame.” Alyosha left the note where it was, then went right to the police captain and explained everything. “And I came to you right after,” Alyosha finished, staring hard at Ivan. He hadn’t looked away from Ivan’s face the whole time, as if he noticed something strange about Ivan’s expression.
“Brother,” Alyosha suddenly said, “you must be really sick. You’re looking at me but it’s like you don’t even understand what I’m saying.”
“It’s a good thing you came,” Ivan replied, sounding distant, as if he hadn’t even heard Alyosha’s words. “I already knew he’d hanged himself.”
“Who told you?”
“I don’t know. But I knew. Did I really know? Yes, he told me. He just told me.”
Ivan stood in the middle of the room, still speaking in that lost, thoughtful way, staring at the floor.
“Who are you talking about?” Alyosha asked, glancing nervously around the room.
“He’s gone now.”
Ivan lifted his head and gave a small, strange smile.

“He was scared of you. Of someone as gentle as you. You’re like an angel. Dmitri calls you a ‘cherub.’ Cherub!... the singing of the seraphim. What are seraphim anyway? Maybe a whole group of stars. Or maybe it’s just a chemical molecule. There’s the constellation Leo, the Lion, and the Sun. Don’t you know about that?”

“Brother, please sit down,” said Alyosha, worried. “Come on, sit on the sofa! You’re not making sense. Put your head on the pillow, okay? Do you want me to get you a wet towel for your head? Maybe it’ll help.”
“Give me the towel—it’s right there on the chair. I just threw it there.”

“It’s not here. Don’t worry, I know where it is—here,” Alyosha said, finding a clean, folded towel by Ivan’s dressing-table in the corner. Ivan stared at the towel strangely, like he suddenly remembered something.
“Wait,” Ivan said, standing up from the sofa. “Just an hour ago I took that towel, got it wet, and wrapped it around my head. I threw it down here… Why is it dry now? There wasn’t another one.”
“You put that towel on your head?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes, and I walked around the room an hour ago… Why are the candles so low? What time is it?”
“Almost midnight.”

“No, no, no!” Ivan suddenly shouted. “It wasn’t a dream. He was here; he was sitting right there, on that sofa. When you knocked at the window, I threw a glass at him… this one. Wait. I was asleep the last time, but this time it wasn’t a dream. This has happened before. I have dreams now, Alyosha… but they aren’t dreams, they’re real. I walk, talk, see things—while I’m asleep. But he was sitting right there, on that sofa… He’s unbelievably stupid, Alyosha, unbelievably stupid.” Ivan suddenly laughed and started pacing the room.
“Who is stupid? Who are you talking about, brother?” Alyosha asked, more anxious than ever.

“The devil! He’s started visiting me. He’s been here twice, almost three times. He made fun of me for being upset he’s just an ordinary devil, not Satan with burnt wings and lightning. But he isn’t Satan—that’s a lie. He’s a fraud. He’s just a devil—a pathetic, boring devil. He goes to public baths. If you undressed him, you’d probably see he has a tail, long and smooth, like a Danish dog’s—about a yard long, brownish color… Alyosha, you must be freezing. You’ve been out in the snow. Want some tea? Is it cold? Should I ask her to bring some? It’s weather not fit for a dog…”
Alyosha hurried to the washstand, wet the towel, convinced Ivan to sit down again, and wrapped the cool towel around his head. Then Alyosha sat next to him.

“What were you just telling me about Lise?” Ivan asked, suddenly chatty. “I like Lise. I said something mean about her. That wasn’t true. I like her… I’m worried about Katya tomorrow. I’m more scared of her than anything. It’s about what’s going to happen. Tomorrow she’ll reject me and crush me. She thinks I’m ruining Mitya because I’m jealous about her! Yes, she really thinks that! But it’s not true. The cross tomorrow, but not the gallows. No, I won’t kill myself. You know, Alyosha, I could never commit suicide. Is it because I’m weak? I’m not a coward. Maybe I just love life too much? How did I know Smerdyakov hanged himself? Yes, he told me.”
“And you’re completely sure someone was here?” Alyosha asked.

“Yes, right there on that sofa in the corner. You would have chased him away. Actually, you did—he disappeared when you came in. I love your face, Alyosha. Did you know I love your face? And he’s really me, Alyosha. All the worst parts of me, all the low, disgusting things. Yes, I’m a romantic. He figured that out—even if it’s not true. He’s so stupid, but it helps him. He’s sly, like an animal—he knew how to make me mad. He kept teasing me for believing in him, and that’s how he got me to listen. He tricked me like a little kid.
