But he did say a lot of true things about me, things I’d never admit to myself. You know, Alyosha,” Ivan said suddenly, super serious and secretive, “I honestly wish it was him, not me.”
“He’s worn you out,” Alyosha said, looking at his brother with pity.

“He’s been messing with me. And he’s so good at it, so clever. ‘Conscience! What is conscience? I just make it up for myself. Why does it bother me? Just from habit. People have done it for thousands of years. Let’s just give it up and we’ll be gods.’ That’s what he said, that’s what he said!”
“And it wasn’t you, it wasn’t you,” Alyosha said, looking his brother right in the eyes. “Forget him. Just let him go, and let him take everything you hate with him. Make sure he never comes back!”

“But he’s so mean. He laughed at me. He was rude, Alyosha,” Ivan said, shuddering at the memory. “He was unfair about a lot of things. He lied about me right to my face. ‘Oh, you’re planning to be a hero: you’ll confess you made the valet kill your father.’”
“Brother,” Alyosha broke in, “calm down. You didn’t kill him. That’s not true!”

“That’s what he says, he does, and he knows it. ‘You want to be heroic, but you don’t really believe in doing the right thing; that’s what really tortures you and makes you angry, makes you so bitter.’ He said that about me and he knows exactly what he’s saying.”
“You’re saying that, not him,” Alyosha said sadly. “You’re saying it because you’re sick and delirious, hurting yourself.”

“No, he knows what he’s talking about. ‘You’re doing this out of pride,’ he says. ‘You’ll stand up and say “I killed him,” and then you’ll act all horrified. You’re lying! I don’t care what you think, I don’t care about your horror!’ He said that about me. ‘And you secretly want people to praise you—‘he’s a criminal, a murderer, but he’s got a big heart; he wanted to save his brother and he confessed.’ That’s a lie, Alyosha!” Ivan suddenly shouted, his eyes blazing. “I don’t want those people to praise me, I swear I don’t! That’s a lie! That’s why I threw the glass at him and it smashed on his ugly face.”
“Brother, calm down, please!” Alyosha begged him.

“He just knows how to get to me. He’s cruel,” Ivan went on, ignoring him. “I had a feeling from the start what he wanted. ‘Even if you’re doing this out of pride, you were hoping Smerdyakov would get convicted and sent to Siberia, and Mitya would go free, while you’d only get told off.’ (‘Do you hear?’ he laughed then)—‘and some people would praise you. But now Smerdyakov’s dead, he hanged himself, so who will believe you now? But you’ll still go, you’ve decided to go. Why are you going now?’ That’s terrible, Alyosha. I can’t stand those questions. Who has the right to ask me that?”

“Brother,” Alyosha interrupted—his heart was pounding with fear, but he still hoped he could make Ivan see sense—“how could he have told you Smerdyakov was dead before I even came, when nobody knew yet and there wasn’t time for anyone to know?”

“He told me,” Ivan said firmly, not willing to doubt it. “That’s all he talked about, really. ‘And it would be fine if you actually believed in being good,’ he said. ‘Even if no one believes you, at least you’re doing it for the right reason. But you’re just like Fyodor Pavlovitch, a little pig, so what do you care about being good? Why are you getting involved if your sacrifice isn’t helping anyone? The truth is you don’t even know yourself! Oh, you’d give anything to know why you’re really going! And can you even decide? You haven’t made up your mind. You’ll spend the whole night debating whether to go or not. But you will go; you know you will. You know that no matter what, you can’t decide not to. You’ll go because you’re too scared not to. Why? Figure that out for yourself. That’s the riddle for you!’ He got up and left. You came, and he disappeared. He called me a coward, Alyosha! The answer to the riddle is that I’m a coward. ‘Eagles like you aren’t meant to fly above the earth.’ He said that—he did! And Smerdyakov said the same thing. He should die! Katya thinks I’m worthless. She’s felt that way for a month. Even Lise will start to hate me! ‘You’re only going so people will praise you.’ That’s a terrible lie! And you hate me too, Alyosha. Now I’m going to start hating you again! And I hate that monster, too! I don’t want to save the monster. Let him rot in Siberia! He’s started singing hymns! Tomorrow I’ll go, stand in front of them, and spit in their faces!”

Ivan jumped up, frantic, yanked off the towel, and started pacing the room again. Alyosha remembered what Ivan had just said: “I feel like I’m awake but dreaming… I walk, I talk, I see, but I’m asleep.” It seemed true now. Alyosha didn’t leave him. He thought about running for a doctor, but he didn’t want to leave Ivan alone—there was no one else to help. Little by little, Ivan lost touch with reality completely. He kept talking, but now it was just rambling, and his words were hard to understand. Suddenly he nearly collapsed, but Alyosha caught him in time. Ivan let Alyosha lead him to bed. Alyosha got him undressed and into bed as best he could. For another two hours, Alyosha sat by him. Ivan slept deeply, breathing softly, not moving at all. Alyosha finally took a pillow and lay down on the sofa, still fully dressed.

As Alyosha drifted off, he prayed for both Mitya and Ivan. He was starting to understand Ivan’s illness. “It’s the pain of being proud and trying to do what’s right.” God, even though Ivan didn’t believe in Him, and the truth, were starting to win over Ivan’s heart, even though he kept fighting it. “Yes,” Alyosha thought as he lay on the pillow, “if Smerdyakov is dead, no one will believe Ivan’s story; but Ivan will still tell it.” Alyosha smiled a little. “God will win!” he thought. “Either Ivan will rise up and find the truth, or… he’ll be destroyed by hate, punishing himself and everyone else for doing something he doesn’t really believe in,” Alyosha added sadly, and prayed for Ivan again.
At ten o’clock the next morning, after everything that happened before, Dmitri Karamazov’s trial began at our local courthouse.

I want to say right away that I’m not pretending I can remember or describe every single thing that happened at the trial, or even in the exact order. Honestly, if I tried to talk about everything in detail, it would fill a huge book. So I hope no one will blame me for only sharing the parts that stood out to me. Maybe I’m leaving out some important things and focusing too much on minor details, but I won’t keep apologizing for it. I’ll do my best, and you’ll see for yourself that I tried as hard as I could.

Before we go into the courtroom, I have to talk about something that really surprised me that day. Later, I found out everyone else was shocked too. We all knew this case had grabbed everyone’s attention—people had been talking and guessing about it for two months. It was a huge topic, not just in our town, but all over Russia. Still, I don’t think anyone realized just how intense people’s interest was until the trial actually started.

People came not just from our regional capital, but from other cities, and even from Moscow and St. Petersburg. There were lawyers, ladies, and even a few important people. Every ticket to get in was gone instantly. The court made a special area behind the judges’ table for the most important male guests, with a row of armchairs—something that had never happened before. At least half the audience were women. There were so many lawyers from all over that they didn’t know where to seat them; all the tickets had been snapped up long ago. At the back of the room, behind the raised platform, they’d quickly put up a partition to hold all these lawyers, and they considered themselves lucky just to have standing room, since all the chairs had been taken away to make space. The crowd behind the partition stood packed together the whole time.

Some of the women, especially those from out of town, dressed up for the occasion. But most didn’t care what they wore—they just looked wildly curious, even a little obsessed. Something interesting, as people later noticed: almost all the women in the audience were rooting for Mitya (Dmitri) and wanted him to be found not guilty. That was probably because he was known for charming women. Plus, everyone knew that two women who were rivals would be taking part in the case. One of them, Katerina Ivanovna, was especially fascinating to the crowd. There were all kinds of crazy stories about her deep love for Mitya, even after his crime. People talked about her pride and her “high-class connections” (she barely visited anyone in town). Some even said she planned to ask the government for permission to follow Mitya to Siberia and marry him in the mines. Grushenka showing up in court was just as big a deal—everyone was dying to see what would happen when the proud, elegant Katerina met “the hetaira” (Grushenka). But Grushenka was more familiar to the local women—they’d seen “the woman who ruined Fyodor Pavlovitch and his poor son,” and most of them wondered how father and son could have both fallen for “such an ordinary Russian girl, who wasn’t even that pretty.”

In short, people talked about it nonstop. I know for a fact that families in town had serious fights because of Mitya. Many women got into big arguments with their husbands about the case, and naturally, those husbands came to court already biased against Mitya. In fact, you could say most of the men in the audience were against him. A lot of them looked angry, even spiteful. Mitya had managed to offend many people while he was in town. Of course, some visitors didn’t really care about Mitya himself—they were just here for the trial. But most of the men seemed to want him convicted, except maybe the lawyers, who were more interested in the legal side of things than the moral one.

Everyone was buzzing about the famous defense lawyer, Fetyukovitch. He was known for his skills, and he’d handled big criminal cases before. Whenever he took a case, it became famous all over Russia. There were also rumors about our prosecutor and the President of the Court. People said Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, was nervous about facing Fetyukovitch, and that they’d been rivals since their early days in St. Petersburg. Our sensitive prosecutor always felt underappreciated, and he was hoping the Karamazov case would boost his career. But Fetyukovitch was his biggest worry. Still, that wasn’t totally fair—our prosecutor wasn’t the type to panic in tough situations. Actually, he got more confident when things got risky. He was a bit too quick to react and put his whole heart into every case, acting like his entire life depended on it. This made him famous in the legal world, sometimes as a bit of a joke, especially because he was obsessed with psychology. I think people underestimated him—he was a deeper person than most thought. But because of his fragile health, he never really made a name for himself at the start of his career and couldn’t catch up after that.

As for the President of the Court, he was a kind, smart man who really knew his job and liked progressive ideas. He was ambitious but didn’t worry too much about his own career. What mattered most to him was being seen as someone with advanced thinking. He was well-connected and had money. We later found out he felt strongly about the Karamazov case, but mostly as a social issue, not a personal one. He saw it as a sign of the times—a reflection of society and the national character, and so on. He didn’t get emotionally involved with the people in the case, not even the prisoner, which was probably how a judge should be.

The courtroom was packed long before the judges arrived. Ours is the best hall in town—big, tall, and with good acoustics. To the right of the judges’ raised platform was a table and two rows of chairs for the jury. On the left were seats for the prisoner and his lawyers. In the middle, near the judges, was a table holding the “evidence.” There was Fyodor Pavlovitch’s white silk dressing-gown stained with blood, the brass pestle that was supposedly the murder weapon, Mitya’s blood-stained shirt and coat, his handkerchief (now stiff and yellowed with blood), the pistol he’d loaded to kill himself, which Trifon Borissovitch secretly took from him at Mokroe, the envelope with the three thousand roubles for Grushenka, the pink ribbon it was tied with, and other things I don’t remember. The public sat farther back, but in front of the rail there were a few chairs for witnesses who stayed after testifying.

At ten o’clock, the three judges came in—the President, a justice of the peace, and another judge. The prosecutor came in right after. The President was short, stout, about fifty, with a sickly-looking face, dark hair going gray, cut short, and a red ribbon from some order I can’t remember. The prosecutor looked especially pale, almost green, and his face seemed thinner than usual—maybe just since yesterday. The President started by asking if all the jurors were present.

But I can’t keep going into this much detail—some things I didn’t hear or notice, and some I’ve forgotten. Mostly, though, there’s just not enough space or time to cover everything. I do remember that neither side objected to many jurors. There were twelve: four were minor town officials, two were merchants, and six were peasants or tradesmen from town. Before the trial, people (especially women) kept asking, “Can such an intense, complicated case be decided by minor officials and even peasants? What can they possibly understand?” The four officials on the jury were all older, low-ranking, and not well-known, probably with big families and very little money. They probably spent their free time playing cards and had never read a book. The merchants looked respectable but were strangely silent and serious—one was clean-shaven and dressed in modern European style, the other had a small gray beard and wore a medal. The tradesmen and peasants from our town were almost the same as the country peasants and even worked the land. Two of the tradesmen wore European clothes, but that just made them look even messier. Looking at them, I really did wonder, “What could these men possibly make of this case?” But their faces were serious and even a little intimidating—they looked very stern.

Finally, the President officially opened the case of the murder of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. I can’t remember exactly what he said about him. The court usher was told to bring in the prisoner, and Mitya came in. The whole room went silent—you could’ve heard a pin drop. I don’t know about everyone else, but Mitya made a really bad impression on me. He looked like he was trying to show off, wearing a brand-new suit he’d ordered from his tailor in Moscow just for this day. He had spotless black gloves and perfect linens. He walked in with long, stiff strides, staring straight ahead, and sat down looking completely calm.

At that moment, the famous lawyer Fetyukovitch, the defense attorney, walked in, and a quiet buzz went through the crowd. He was tall and thin, with very long legs and pale, thin fingers. His face was clean-shaven, his hair short and neatly brushed, and his lips sometimes curled in a way that was somewhere between a sneer and a smile. He looked about forty. His face would have been nice if it weren’t for his eyes, which were small, set very close together, and separated only by a long, thin nose. He actually looked a bit like a bird. He wore formal evening clothes and a white tie.

I remember the President’s first questions for Mitya—his name, his job, and so on. Mitya answered quickly and so loudly that the President was startled and stared at him. Then came a long list of witnesses and experts who would take part. Four of the witnesses weren’t there—Miüsov, who had already given evidence but was now in Paris; Madame Hohlakov and Maximov, who were sick; and Smerdyakov, who had suddenly died (an official police statement confirmed this). News of Smerdyakov’s death caused a stir and whispering in the courtroom; many people hadn’t heard he’d killed himself. What shocked people the most was Mitya’s sudden outburst as soon as Smerdyakov’s death was mentioned:
“He was a dog and died like a dog!”

I remember how his lawyer rushed over to him, and how the President warned Mitya that he’d take serious action if this happened again. Mitya nodded and kept repeating to his lawyer, not sounding sorry at all:
“I won’t do it again, I won’t. It just slipped out. I won’t do it again.”

Of course, this little scene didn’t help Mitya’s case with the jury or the crowd. It showed his true character, loud and clear. While everyone was still thinking about what just happened, the opening statement was read. It was short but detailed, explaining the main reasons for Mitya’s arrest and trial. It really made an impression on me. The clerk read it out loud and clear. Suddenly, the whole tragedy was right in front of us, shining in a harsh, unforgiving light. Right after it was read, the President asked Mitya in a loud, serious voice:
“Prisoner, do you plead guilty?”
Mitya suddenly stood up.

“I plead guilty to being drunk and wild,” he shouted, his voice shaky and almost desperate. “To being lazy and living badly. I was just about to turn my life around when fate struck me down. But I’m not guilty of killing that old man, my enemy and my father. No, no—I didn’t rob him! I couldn’t do it. Dmitri Karamazov is a scoundrel, but not a thief.”

He sat down again, shaking all over. The President quickly but firmly told him again to only answer questions and not to go off on wild speeches. Then he told them to continue. All the witnesses came up to take the oath. I saw them all together then. The prisoner’s brothers were allowed to give evidence without swearing an oath. After the priest and the President spoke to them, the witnesses were sent to sit as far from each other as possible. Then they began calling them up, one by one.

I’m not sure if the President of the court had the witnesses for the defense and prosecution separated into groups, or if they arranged the order in which they’d be called, but I’m sure there was some plan. What I do know is that the prosecution’s witnesses went first. I’m not going to go through every single question and answer, since both sides summed up the evidence in their big final speeches, and I’ll include important parts of those later on—along with one really wild and unexpected event that happened before the closing arguments, which definitely affected how the trial turned out.

Right from the start, there was something very obvious about the trial: the prosecution seemed way stronger than the defense. As soon as the facts started piling up, it looked like everything pointed to one terrible, bloody crime. Everyone in the courtroom felt, almost immediately, that the case was basically settled. It seemed like there was no way to argue against it, and that defending Dmitri (Mitya) was just a formality—the evidence made him look totally guilty. Even the ladies in the crowd, who were dying to see the “interesting prisoner” go free, actually believed he was guilty. Honestly, I think they would have been disappointed if the crime hadn’t been proved so well, since it would ruin the drama of a possible last-minute acquittal. All the women were convinced he’d be found not guilty in the end, though—“He’s guilty, but he’ll be pardoned for humanitarian reasons, because that’s the modern, fashionable thing to do,” they said. That’s why they packed the courtroom. The men, on the other hand, were focused on seeing the famous lawyer Fetyukovitch work his magic against the strong prosecutor. Everyone wanted to see what Fetyukovitch could do with such a hopeless case, so they watched his every move closely.

But Fetyukovitch was a real mystery, right up until his speech at the end. People who knew the law suspected he had some kind of plan, but it was impossible to guess what it was. He was clearly confident and sure of himself. People were impressed by how quickly he’d gotten up to speed on the case—he’d only been in town for about three days, but he seemed to know every detail. People later talked about how cleverly he’d questioned the prosecution’s witnesses, confusing them and making their testimonies seem less reliable. Still, most people thought he was just showing off—using all the tricks defense lawyers are supposed to use, even though they didn’t think it would help. They guessed he had some secret strategy he’d pull out at the right moment. Meanwhile, he seemed to be enjoying himself, knowing he was in control.

For example, when Grigory, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s old servant (who had given the most damaging testimony about the open door), was questioned, the defense lawyer really focused on him. Grigory came into the courtroom looking calm and almost dignified, not bothered at all by the judge or the big crowd. He answered questions with confidence, just like he might talk to his wife, Marfa—though maybe a bit more politely. No one could catch him in a contradiction. The prosecutor first asked him lots of questions about the Karamazov family’s home life, and Grigory described it honestly, making it clear that, while he respected his late master, Fyodor Pavlovitch, he still thought he’d treated Dmitri unfairly and hadn’t raised his children right. “He would have been eaten alive by lice as a child if it weren’t for me,” Grigory said about Mitya’s childhood. He also said the father had cheated Mitya out of his mother’s property, which should have belonged to him.

When the prosecutor asked Grigory to explain why he thought Fyodor Pavlovitch had cheated Mitya with money, Grigory surprised everyone by admitting he had no proof at all—he just insisted the arrangement was unfair and that Mitya should have gotten several thousand rubles more. The prosecutor asked this question about the inheritance to every possible witness, even Alyosha and Ivan, but no one had any solid evidence; everyone just thought it was true. Grigory described the dinner-table fight when Mitya burst in, beat his father, and threatened to come back and kill him, and this made a big impression on the court. Grigory was so calm and straightforward that his story seemed even more convincing. He said he’d forgiven Mitya long ago for hitting him. About Smerdyakov, the dead servant, Grigory said he was smart but also sick and an atheist—he blamed Fyodor Pavlovitch and Ivan for that. Still, he defended Smerdyakov’s honesty, telling how Smerdyakov once found the master’s money in the yard and returned it, earning Fyodor’s trust forever. Grigory insisted, stubbornly, that the door to the garden had been open that night. He was asked so many questions, I can’t remember them all.

Finally, the defense lawyer started his cross-examination, beginning with the envelope that supposedly held three thousand rubles for “a certain person.” He asked Grigory, “You were so close to your master for so many years—did you ever see this envelope?” Grigory said he’d never seen it or even heard about that money until everyone started talking about it. Fetyukovitch asked this same question about the envelope to everyone who might know about it, just as persistently as the prosecutor asked about the inheritance, and got the same answer: no one had seen it, but many had heard rumors. Everyone noticed how Fetyukovitch kept coming back to this point.

Then Fetyukovitch suddenly changed topics. “With your permission, I’d like to ask you something,” he said. “What exactly was in that balm—or, actually, herbal mix—you used to rub your back for your lumbago that evening?”
Grigory stared blankly and, after a moment, mumbled, “There was saffron in it.”
“Only saffron? Are you sure there wasn’t anything else?”
“There was milfoil, too.”
“And maybe pepper?” Fetyukovitch asked.
“Yes, pepper was in it too.”
“And so on. All mixed with vodka?”
“With spirits.”
Some people laughed quietly in the courtroom.
“So, in spirits. And after rubbing your back, I believe you drank whatever was left in the bottle, saying a special prayer only your wife knows?”
“I did.”
“Did you drink a lot? Like, a wine glass or two?”
“It could have been a whole tumbler.”
“A whole tumbler—even a tumbler and a half, maybe?”
Grigory didn’t answer. He seemed to realize where this was going.
“A glass and a half of straight spirits—that’s quite a bit, don’t you think? Maybe you saw the gates of heaven open, not just the door to the garden?”
Grigory stayed quiet. There was more laughter. The President shifted in his seat.
Fetyukovitch pressed on: “Are you sure you were awake when you saw the open door?”
“I was on my feet.”
“That doesn’t prove you were awake,” the lawyer said, and the audience laughed again. “Could you have answered a question right then—like, do you remember what year it was?”
“I don’t know.”
“Do you know what year it is now?”
Grigory stood there, looking confused, staring at his questioner. Strangely, it really seemed like he didn’t know the year.
“Maybe you can at least tell me how many fingers you have?”
“I am a servant,” Grigory suddenly said loudly and clearly. “If my betters want to make fun of me, it’s my duty to put up with it.”

Fetyukovitch was a bit surprised, and the President stepped in, reminding him to ask more relevant questions. Fetyukovitch bowed and said he had no more questions. Still, the jury and the crowd now had their doubts about a witness who might have been a little tipsy from his “medicine” and didn’t even know what year it was. But before Grigory left, something else happened. The President turned to Dmitri and asked if he wanted to comment on Grigory’s testimony.

“Everything he said is true—except about the door,” Mitya shouted. “For combing lice off me, I thank him; for forgiving me for hitting him, I thank him. That old man’s been honest all his life and as loyal to my father as seven hundred poodles.”
“Prisoner, watch your language,” the President warned him.
“I’m not a poodle,” Grigory muttered.
“Fine, then I’m the poodle,” Mitya cried. “If that’s an insult, I’ll take it. I apologize. I was terrible to him. I was terrible to Æsop, too.”
“Who’s Æsop?” the President asked sternly.
“Oh, Pierrot ... my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
The President kept warning Mitya, more and more seriously, to be careful how he spoke.
“You’re hurting yourself in the eyes of your judges.”

Fetyukovitch was just as clever with Rakitin’s testimony. Rakitin was an important witness, and the prosecutor thought he was key. He acted like he knew everything—he’d been everywhere, talked to everyone, and seemed to know every detail about Fyodor Pavlovitch and the Karamazovs. He’d only heard about the envelope from Mitya, but he described in detail all of Mitya’s wild adventures in “the Metropolis,” including what happened with Captain Snegiryov’s “wisp of tow.” Still, Rakitin couldn’t say anything definite about the inheritance—he just made vague, mocking comments.

“Who could say which of them was at fault, or who owed who, with their crazy Karamazov way of messing things up so much no one could figure it out?” Rakitin blamed the whole tragedy on old habits from serfdom and the sad state of Russia, which he said was caused by a lack of good institutions. He was allowed to talk pretty freely. This was the first time Rakitin really showed what he could do, and people noticed. The prosecutor knew Rakitin was writing a magazine article about the case, and later quoted ideas from it in his own speech. Rakitin painted a dark, dramatic picture that helped the prosecution a lot. People loved his speech for its independence and big ideas, and he even got applause when he talked about serfdom and Russia’s hard times.

But in his excitement, Rakitin slipped up, and the defense lawyer immediately took advantage. When answering questions about Grushenka, Rakitin got carried away and said something rude about Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka), calling her “the kept mistress of Samsonov.” He probably wished he could take it back, because Fetyukovitch caught him right away. Rakitin hadn’t expected the lawyer to know so much about everyone’s private business.

“Excuse me,” the defense lawyer started, smiling politely, “you’re the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima, was published by the diocese—full of deep and religious thoughts, with a lovely dedication to the bishop? I just read it and enjoyed it very much.”
“I didn’t write it to be published ... it came out afterward,” Rakitin mumbled, looking nervous and embarrassed.

“Oh, that’s great! A thinker like you should look at the big picture. Your pamphlet has really helped people, thanks to the bishop. But here’s what I want to know—you just said you knew Madame Svyetlov very well.” (I should mention that I learned Grushenka’s last name was Svyetlov for the first time that day.)
“I can’t answer for all my acquaintances.... I’m young—how can anyone be responsible for everyone they meet?” Rakitin said, blushing.

“I understand, of course,” Fetyukovitch said, acting embarrassed too. “Anyone would be interested in meeting a young, beautiful woman who likes to host the best young men in town. But... what I really want to know is this: I’ve heard that a couple months ago, Madame Svyetlov really wanted to meet the younger Karamazov, Alexey Fyodorovitch (Alyosha), and promised you twenty-five rubles if you’d bring him to her in his monk’s clothes. And you did bring Alexey to her—the very night of the terrible crime we’re talking about. Did you get the twenty-five rubles from Madame Svyetlov as a reward?”
“It was just a joke.... I don’t see why that matters.... I took it as a joke—planning to pay it back...”
“So you did take it—but you haven’t paid it back yet… or have you?”
“That doesn’t matter,” Rakitin muttered. “I refuse to answer that.... Of course I’ll pay it back.”

The President stepped in, but Fetyukovitch said he had no more questions. Rakitin left the witness stand not quite as spotless as before—his high-minded speech had lost some of its shine. Fetyukovitch’s expression seemed to say, “This is the kind of ‘noble’ person accusing my client.” I remember that Mitya couldn’t let this pass. Angry at the way Rakitin had talked about Grushenka, he suddenly shouted, “Bernard!” When the President asked Mitya if he had anything to add after Rakitin’s cross-examination, Mitya yelled:
“Since I was arrested, he’s borrowed money from me! He’s a sneaky Bernard and an opportunist, and he doesn’t even believe in God; he tricked the bishop!”

Of course, Mitya was scolded again for his wild language, but Rakitin was finished. Captain Snegiryov’s testimony was a failure too, but for a different reason. He showed up in filthy, torn clothes and muddy boots, and, even though the police tried to keep him in line, he was totally drunk. When they asked about Mitya attacking him, he refused to answer.
“God bless him. Ilusha told me not to. God will reward me later.”
“Who told you not to talk? Who are you talking about?”
“Ilusha, my little son. ‘Father, father, how he insulted you!’ He said that at the stone. Now he’s dying....”
Suddenly, the captain started sobbing and dropped to his knees in front of the President. He was quickly led out, while the crowd laughed. The prosecutor’s plan for his testimony totally fell apart.

Fetyukovitch kept using every chance he got and impressed everyone with how well he knew the case. For example, Trifon Borissovitch made a big impact—bad for Mitya. He counted up, almost on his fingers, that on his first trip to Mokroe, Mitya must have spent three thousand rubles, or almost that much. “Just think how much he threw away on the gypsy girls! And for our lousy peasants, he didn’t just toss them a few coins—he gave them each at least twenty-five rubles! And tons of money was just stolen from him too. You can’t keep track of who took what when someone’s throwing money everywhere. Our peasants are thieves—they don’t care about their souls. And the way he acted with the girls—now they’re rich! They used to be poor.” Trifon listed every expense and added it up, making it seem impossible that Mitya had only spent 1,500 rubles and hidden the rest in a bag.
“I saw three thousand clear as day in his hands. I know how to count money,” Trifon Borissovitch said, trying hard to please the important people.

When Fetyukovitch cross-examined him, he didn’t really try to challenge his main story, but instead asked about a specific incident at a party in Mokroe, a month before the arrest. That night, Timofey and another peasant named Akim had found one hundred rubles Mitya dropped when he was drunk, gave it to Trifon Borissovitch, and Trifon gave them a ruble each for their trouble. “Did you give that hundred rubles back to Mr. Karamazov?” the lawyer asked. Trifon tried to dodge the question, but after the peasants were called in and confirmed the story, he had to admit it had happened—though he claimed he returned all the money to Mitya “honestly, but Mitya was drunk and wouldn’t remember.” But since Trifon had denied the story until the peasants proved it, the jury doubted his claim about returning the money. So one of the prosecution’s most dangerous witnesses was discredited, too.

The same thing happened with the Polish witnesses. They acted all proud and important, saying they’d both worked for the government and that “Pan Mitya” tried to bribe them with three thousand rubles, and that they’d seen a lot of money in his hands. Pan Mussyalovitch kept throwing in Polish words, and when he saw the judge and prosecutor seemed impressed, he got even more dramatic and ended up speaking Polish altogether. But Fetyukovitch trapped them, too. Trifon Borissovitch, called back, had to admit that Pan Vrublevsky had switched the deck of cards for a marked one, and Pan Mussyalovitch had cheated at the game. Kalganov backed this up, and both Poles left the stand with ruined reputations, while the public laughed.

The same thing happened with almost all the prosecution’s most dangerous witnesses. Fetyukovitch managed to make them all look bad or unreliable, and dismissed them with a bit of mockery. The other lawyers and experts were amazed, though they couldn’t see how it would actually help, since everyone still felt the prosecution’s case was crushing and impossible to beat. But Fetyukovitch seemed so calm and sure of himself that people started to wonder if he had something big planned—after all, “a man like that” didn’t come all the way from Petersburg just to lose.

The testimony from the medical experts didn’t really help Mitya (Dmitri) much. It turned out that Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, hadn’t been counting on it anyway. The only reason the medical experts were brought in was that Katerina Ivanovna insisted, even sending for a well-known doctor from Moscow. The defense figured it couldn’t hurt and might help a little. But the whole thing ended up being a bit ridiculous because the doctors couldn’t agree with each other. The medical experts included the famous Moscow doctor, Doctor Herzenstube (the town’s respected old doctor), and the young Doctor Varvinsky. The last two were actually there as witnesses for the prosecution, not the defense.

Doctor Herzenstube was the first expert to take the stand. He was an old man, around seventy, with gray hair and bald patches, not very tall but solidly built. Everyone in town respected him, not just as a good doctor, but as a genuinely kind, religious, and upright man. He was either a Moravian brother or a Hernguter, but no one was sure. He’d lived in the town for many years, always carrying himself with real dignity. Doctor Herzenstube helped poor people and peasants for free, even leaving money for their medicine, but he was also extremely stubborn. Once he made up his mind, nothing could change it. Almost everyone knew that when the famous Moscow doctor arrived, he’d immediately started saying rude things about Doctor Herzenstube’s skills. The Moscow doctor charged twenty-five roubles a visit, and lots of people rushed to see him, even though they’d been Herzenstube’s patients before. He criticized Herzenstube harshly and would ask new patients, “Who’s been feeding you these weird remedies? Herzenstube? Ha!” Of course, Doctor Herzenstube heard about this, and now all three doctors were coming in, one after another, to be questioned.

Doctor Herzenstube stated plainly that it was obvious that Mitya’s mind wasn’t normal. He explained his reasons in detail (which are left out here), saying that Mitya’s strange thinking had shown up many times before and was visible even now, right in the courtroom. When asked how it was obvious right now, the old doctor said, in his usual direct way, that Mitya had walked into the court “with a strange look, not what you’d expect.” He entered like a soldier, staring straight ahead, when, according to the doctor, it would have been more natural for him to look to the left, where the ladies were sitting, especially since Mitya liked women and must be curious about what they thought of him at that moment.

Doctor Herzenstube spoke Russian pretty well, but he always sounded like he was translating from German. He didn’t mind, though; he believed he spoke better Russian than most Russians. He loved to use Russian proverbs and was convinced they were the most expressive in the world. Sometimes, when he talked, he’d forget common words—he did the same thing in German—and would wave his hand like he was trying to grab the missing word out of thin air, refusing to go on until he remembered it. His comment about Mitya looking at the ladies made the audience giggle. All the women in town liked Doctor Herzenstube. They knew that, even though he’d always been a bachelor and lived a very proper life, he thought women were wonderful. So his comment just seemed extra funny coming from him.

When the Moscow doctor was questioned, he said strongly that he believed Mitya’s mind was seriously disturbed. He talked for a long time, using lots of medical terms like “aberration” and “mania,” and said that, based on all the facts, Mitya had obviously not been thinking straight for days before his arrest. If Mitya did commit the crime, then—even if he knew what he was doing—it would have been almost against his will, because he couldn’t control the sick urge that pushed him.

Besides the temporary “aberration,” the Moscow doctor diagnosed Mitya with mania, which, he said, would likely turn into full insanity later. (This is a summary, since the doctor used very technical language.) “None of his actions make sense,” the doctor went on. “Even aside from the crime itself, just the day before yesterday, when I spoke with him, his eyes had a strange stare. He laughed out of nowhere, when nothing was funny. He was constantly irritable, using odd words like ‘Bernard!’ and ‘Ethics!’ for no reason.” The doctor especially saw mania in the way Mitya couldn’t talk about the three thousand roubles he felt cheated out of without getting extremely upset, even though he could talk about other problems much more calmly. Apparently, this had happened before—any time the money was mentioned, Mitya would explode in anger, even though he wasn’t greedy.

“As for what my learned colleague said,” the Moscow doctor added with sarcasm, “about Mitya looking at the ladies when he entered the court—well, aside from being a playful idea, it’s just not true. I agree that someone in Mitya’s position might not stare straight ahead when coming into court, and that this could show something’s wrong. But really, if he looked anywhere, it would be to the right, to find his lawyer, since that’s the person his future depends on.” The doctor said this with confidence.

But then Doctor Varvinsky surprised everyone and made the doctors’ disagreement seem almost like a joke. He said that Mitya was perfectly normal now and had always been normal. Sure, Mitya had been nervous and extremely upset before his arrest, but that could have been caused by obvious things: jealousy, anger, lots of drinking, and so on. But that didn’t mean he had the mental problems the others mentioned. As for whether Mitya should have looked left or right when entering the court, Doctor Varvinsky said, “In my opinion, he would naturally look straight ahead, just like he did, because that’s where the judges are—the people deciding his fate. So, by looking ahead, he actually showed he was perfectly sane.” The young doctor finished his statement with real passion.
“Bravo, doctor! Exactly!” Mitya shouted from his seat.

Mitya was quickly told to be quiet, but Doctor Varvinsky’s opinion really influenced the judges and the crowd, and later, almost everyone agreed with him. But Doctor Herzenstube, when he later testified as a witness, actually ended up helping Mitya in an unexpected way. As someone who’d lived in the town for years and knew the Karamazov family well, he shared some valuable facts. Then, as if remembering something suddenly, he added:

“But this poor young man could have had a totally different life, because he had a good heart as a child and even after that—I know it for a fact. There’s a Russian saying, ‘One head is good, but if another smart person joins you, that’s even better—then there are two heads instead of one.’”

“One head is good, but two are better,” the prosecutor interrupted impatiently. He was used to the old doctor’s slow, careful way of talking, which always delayed things, and his dull but cheerful German jokes. The old man liked making puns.

“Yes, that’s what I mean,” the doctor insisted. “One head is good, but two are better. But he never met that other smart head, and so he lost his wits. Where did his wits go? I’ve forgotten the word.” He waved his hand in front of his eyes, thinking. “Oh yes, spazieren.”
“Wandering?”

“Yes, wandering, that’s it. His wits went wandering and fell into such a deep hole that he lost himself. And yet, he was a grateful and sensitive boy. I remember him very well, just a little fellow, left alone by his father in the backyard, running around with no shoes, his pants barely held up by one button.”
Suddenly, the old doctor’s voice turned gentle and full of feeling. Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, sat up straight as if he sensed something important and paid extra attention.

“I was a young man then, about forty-five, and I’d just moved here. I felt so sorry for the boy. I thought, why not buy him a pound of—what? I can’t remember the word. A pound of something kids love. What is it? It grows on trees, and people gather it and give it to others...”
“Apples?”
“No, not apples. You’d have a dozen apples, not a pound. No, these are small, and you put them in your mouth and crack them.”
“Nuts?”

“That’s right—nuts, yes.” The doctor repeated this calmly, as if he’d never forgotten the word. “So I bought him a pound of nuts, because no one had ever done that for him before. I raised my finger and said, ‘Boy, Gott der Vater.’ He laughed and repeated it, ‘Gott der Vater.’... ‘Gott der Sohn.’ He laughed again and said, ‘Gott der Sohn.’ ‘Gott der heilige Geist.’ He tried to say it, too. I left, and two days later, as I was passing by, he called out to me, ‘Uncle, Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn,’ though he’d forgotten ‘Gott der heilige Geist.’ I reminded him, and I felt sorry for him again. But soon after, he was taken away, and I didn’t see him again for 23 years. One morning, when I was old and gray, a grown man walked into my study. I never would have recognized him, but he held up his finger and said, laughing, ‘Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn, and Gott der heilige Geist. I just arrived and came to thank you for the nuts, because you’re the only one who ever bought me a pound.’ It made me remember my younger days and that poor barefoot boy, and my heart was touched. I told him he was grateful to have remembered the nuts all his life. I hugged him and gave him my blessing, and I cried. He laughed, but he cried too. Russians often laugh when they really want to cry. But he did cry—I saw it. And now, sadly...”
“And I’m crying now, too, Doctor. I’m crying, too, you good man,” Mitya suddenly called out.

The story made the audience feel more sympathetic toward Mitya. But the main thing that really helped him was Katerina Ivanovna’s testimony, which will be described soon. In fact, as soon as the witnesses for the defense started talking, things seemed to be turning in Mitya’s favor—even surprising his own lawyer. But before Katerina Ivanovna took the stand, Alyosha (Alexey) was called, and he brought up a fact that went against one of the prosecutor’s main points.

Even Alyosha (Alexey) was surprised when he was called to testify. He didn’t have to swear an oath, and both the defense and prosecution spoke to him kindly and respectfully. Alyosha’s reputation for being good had clearly spread. When he gave his testimony, he was modest and careful, but it was obvious he cared deeply for his troubled brother. When asked about Dmitri (Mitya), Alyosha described him as a man with a quick temper, swept up by his emotions, but also as someone honorable, proud, generous, and willing to sacrifice himself for others if needed. He did admit that because of Mitya’s obsession with Grushenka and his competition with their father, Mitya’s situation had become unbearable lately. But Alyosha strongly denied any suggestion that his brother would murder for money, even though he admitted that the three thousand roubles had become an obsession for Mitya. Mitya saw the money as part of his inheritance that his father had stolen, and, although he usually didn’t care about money, he got furious whenever it was mentioned. When they asked about the rivalry between Grushenka and Katerina Ivanovna (Katya), Alyosha avoided the questions and even refused to answer some.
The prosecutor asked, “Did your brother ever tell you directly that he planned to kill your father? You don’t have to answer if you feel it’s not right.”
Alyosha replied, “He never told me that directly.”
“What do you mean? Did he say it in another way?” the prosecutor pressed.
“He once told me he hated our father,” Alyosha said, “and that he was afraid that, in a fit of rage, he might end up killing him.”
“Did you believe him?” the prosecutor asked.

“I’m afraid I did,” Alyosha admitted. “But I always trusted that something better in him would stop him at the crucial moment, just like it did in the end—because he didn’t kill my father.” Alyosha said this loud enough for everyone in the courtroom to hear.
The prosecutor reacted sharply, like a soldier hearing a battle trumpet.

“Let me say that I believe you’re being completely honest,” the prosecutor said. “I’m not saying your feelings for your brother are making you believe this. We already know your unusual point of view from the earlier investigation. But your view is very personal, and it goes against all the other evidence. So I have to ask—what facts make you so sure your brother is innocent, and that someone else is guilty? Especially Smerdyakov, whom you mentioned before?”
Alyosha answered slowly and calmly, “I only answered the questions they asked me in the earlier investigation. I never accused Smerdyakov on my own.”
“But you did give evidence that pointed to him?”

“That was only because of what Mitya said. I heard what happened when he was arrested, how he pointed to Smerdyakov before I was questioned. I completely believe my brother is innocent, and if he didn’t do it, then—”
“Then Smerdyakov did it? Why do you think it was him? And why are you so sure your brother is innocent?”
“I can’t help it—I just believe my brother. I know he wouldn’t lie to me. I could see it on his face.”
“Just from his face? Is that all the proof you have?”
“I have no other proof,” Alyosha admitted.
“So you also have no proof that Smerdyakov is guilty, except for your brother’s words and the look on his face?”
“No, I have no other proof,” Alyosha repeated.

At that, the prosecutor stopped questioning him. The people watching were disappointed. There had been rumors before the trial that Alyosha had real evidence proving Mitya was innocent and Smerdyakov was guilty, but in the end, all he had were his personal beliefs, which made sense for a brother but weren’t real evidence.

Now it was Fetyukovitch’s (the defense lawyer) turn to question Alyosha. He asked when exactly Mitya had said he hated his father and might kill him—had he said it during their last meeting before the murder? Alyosha seemed to remember something suddenly.
“I just remembered something I’d forgotten,” Alyosha said. “It didn’t make sense to me at the time, but now—”

Looking like he was just realizing it, Alyosha explained how, during his last talk with Mitya under the tree near the monastery, Mitya had hit himself on the upper chest and kept saying he had a way to regain his honor, and that the way was ‘here, here on his chest.’ “At the time,” Alyosha went on, “I thought he was talking about his heart—that he’d find the strength there to keep himself from doing something terrible, something he was too ashamed to tell me about. Honestly, I thought he might hurt our father, and that was the disgrace he was afraid of. But now I remember he pointed to a spot high up on his chest—just below his neck—not where the heart is. It seemed silly to me then, but maybe he was pointing to that little bag where he kept the fifteen hundred roubles!”
“Yes!” Mitya suddenly called out. “That’s right, Alyosha. I hit the bag with my fist.”

Fetyukovitch rushed over to quiet Mitya, then turned back to Alyosha. Alyosha, now excited by his memory, explained that the ‘disgrace’ was probably the fifteen hundred roubles he still had—money he could have returned to Katerina Ivanovna, paying back half of what he owed her, but he decided not to do it and instead wanted to use it to run away with Grushenka if she agreed.

“That’s it, that has to be it,” Alyosha said, getting worked up. “My brother kept saying that half the disgrace, half of it—he repeated the word—he could get rid of right away, but he felt so weak that he wouldn’t do it. He knew in advance he just couldn’t bring himself to do it.”
“And you’re sure he pointed right there, at that spot on his chest?” Fetyukovitch pressed.

“I’m sure,” Alyosha said. “I wondered at the time, ‘Why is he pointing so high up when your heart is lower?’ It seemed stupid, but now I remember. He was pointing to the little bag with the fifteen hundred roubles. And when he was arrested at Mokroe, I heard he shouted that the worst thing he’d ever done was not giving back half of what he owed Katerina Ivanovna, even when he had the money. He just couldn’t bring himself to do it, and he’d rather be seen as a thief than give it back. That debt tormented him so much!” Alyosha finished.
The prosecutor interrupted, asking Alyosha to describe everything again and kept asking, “Did the prisoner point to anything, or just hit his chest with his fist?”
“It wasn’t with his fist,” Alyosha insisted. “He pointed with his fingers, right up here. How did I forget this until now?”

The President of the court then asked Mitya what he thought of Alyosha’s testimony. Mitya confirmed it, saying he had pointed to the fifteen hundred roubles in the bag under his neck, and that this was his disgrace. “It’s the worst thing I’ve ever done,” Mitya shouted. “I could have paid her back but didn’t. I knew I wouldn’t. You’re right, Alyosha! Thank you!”

That ended Alyosha’s cross-examination. The important thing was that, for the first time, there was actual evidence—just a little, but still something—that the bag with the fifteen hundred roubles really existed, and that Mitya wasn’t lying when he said at Mokroe that the money was his own. Alyosha was happy. As he returned to his seat, his face was red, and he kept thinking, “How could I have forgotten? Why did I remember now?”

Next, Katerina Ivanovna (Katya) was called to the witness stand. When she came in, the whole courtroom became tense. The women picked up their opera glasses to get a better look, and the men stood for a clear view. People later said Mitya turned pale as a ghost when she entered. Katya was dressed in all black and walked in quietly, almost shyly. Her face didn’t show her emotions, but her dark eyes looked determined. Many people said she looked especially beautiful. She spoke softly but clearly, and everyone could hear her. She tried to look calm. The President questioned her gently and respectfully, as if he didn’t want to hurt her feelings. Early on, Katya said firmly that she had once been engaged to Mitya, “until he left me on his own…” When they asked about the three thousand roubles she had given Mitya to send to her family, she said, “I didn’t just give him the money to send off. I knew he needed money and gave it to him saying he could send it within a month if he wanted. He didn’t have to worry about paying me back.”
I won’t repeat every question and answer, but I’ll sum up what she said.

“I was sure he’d send the money as soon as he got some from his father,” she continued. “I never doubted his honesty, especially with money. He was sure he’d get money from his father, and he talked about it a lot. I knew he was fighting with his father and always thought his father treated him unfairly. I never heard him threaten his father, at least not in front of me. If he had come to me then, I would have told him not to worry about the three thousand, but by that time he’d stopped visiting me, and my own situation was such that I couldn’t invite him. And honestly, I had no right to demand that money from him,” she added, sounding determined. “I once borrowed more than three thousand roubles from him myself, when I couldn’t know if I’d ever be able to pay it back.”
There was a challenging edge to her voice. That’s when Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination.

“Did that happen at the start, when you first met?” Fetyukovitch asked carefully, sensing this could help the case. I should mention that, even though Katya herself had helped bring Fetyukovitch from St. Petersburg for the trial, he didn’t know about the incident when Mitya gave her four thousand roubles, or about her “bowing to the ground” to thank him. Katya had hidden this from him, maybe because she hadn’t decided until the last second whether she would talk about it in court.

I’ll never forget what happened next. Katya started telling everything—just like Mitya had once told Alyosha—about how she desperately went to Mitya for money to save her father, and how she bowed down to him in gratitude. She left out the detail that Mitya himself, through her sister, had suggested she come, letting it look like it was all her own idea. It was incredible—she was so honest, so self-sacrificing, especially for someone as proud as she was. And for what? To help the man who’d betrayed her, to save him even a little, by making people feel sympathy for him. The story made Mitya look very generous: a young officer who gave away his last four thousand roubles to help an innocent girl. But I worried that people might twist the story later (which they did), joking that maybe there was more to it than Katya admitted.
“And even if that was the whole story,” some of the society ladies said later, “it still wasn’t right for a young girl to act that way, even to save her father.”

Katya was smart and sensitive—she must’ve known people would gossip like that. Still, she decided to tell everything. At first, everyone was moved by her honesty, and the judges and lawyers listened quietly and respectfully. The prosecutor didn’t ask a single question. Fetyukovitch bowed low to her, almost triumphant. After all, if Mitya had once given away his last four thousand roubles just to help someone, how could he kill his father for three thousand? The whole case looked different now. People felt sorry for Mitya; during Katya’s testimony, he even jumped up a couple of times, then sat down with his face in his hands. When she finished, he suddenly cried out, sobbing:
“Katya, why have you ruined me?” His sobs filled the courtroom. But he quickly got control of himself and shouted:
“Now I’m doomed!”
Then he sat stiffly, teeth clenched, arms crossed. Katya stayed in the courtroom, sitting with her head down, pale and shaking as if she had a fever. Next, Grushenka was called.

Now I’m getting to the sudden disaster that might have sealed Mitya’s fate. Later, everyone said that if this incident hadn’t happened, the jury might have had mercy on him. But first, a bit about Grushenka.

Grushenka was also wearing all black, with a beautiful black shawl. She walked to the witness stand gracefully, looking straight ahead without glancing at anyone. I thought she looked beautiful, not pale as some ladies later claimed. They also said she looked angry or spiteful, but I think she was just annoyed by all the judging looks from the crowd. Grushenka was proud and hated being looked down on—if she felt insulted, she’d get angry and want to strike back. She was also nervous, and a bit ashamed of her nerves, so her tone kept changing—sometimes angry and rough, sometimes regretful. She sometimes spoke like she was just going to say whatever she wanted, no matter what happened. When asked about her relationship with Fyodor Pavlovitch, she said sharply, “That’s nonsense. Was it my fault he wouldn’t leave me alone?” But then, a minute later, she admitted, “It was all my fault. I was playing with both of them—the old man and Mitya—and I’m the reason all of this happened.”

Someone mentioned Samsonov, and she immediately snapped, “That’s nobody’s business! He helped me when I had nothing and my own family kicked me out.” The President politely reminded her to answer only the questions asked, not to go off-topic. Grushenka blushed and her eyes flashed.

She said she never saw the envelope with the money, just heard from “that wicked wretch” that Fyodor Pavlovitch had an envelope with three thousand roubles. “But that was all silly. I was just joking. I wouldn’t have gone to him for anything.”
“Who do you mean by ‘that wicked wretch’?” the prosecutor asked.
“The servant, Smerdyakov, who murdered his master and hanged himself last night,” Grushenka replied.
They immediately asked why she accused him so directly, but it turned out she had no real evidence.

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch told me so himself; you can believe him,” Grushenka said. “The woman who came between us ruined him; she’s the cause of all this.” She was shaking with anger, her voice sharp and bitter.
They asked again who she meant.
“That young lady, Katerina Ivanovna,” Grushenka said. “She sent for me, gave me chocolate, tried to win me over. She’s not as innocent as she acts…”
The President sharply told her to calm down, but Grushenka was too upset to care.

The prosecutor asked, “When Mitya was arrested at Mokroe, everyone saw and heard you run out and shout, ‘It’s all my fault. We’ll go to Siberia together!’ Did you already believe he’d killed his father?”

“I don’t remember what I felt then,” Grushenka answered. “Everyone was saying he killed his father, and I thought it was my fault, that he’d done it because of me. But as soon as he said he wasn’t guilty, I believed him, and I still do. He’s not the kind of man to lie.”
Fetyukovitch started his cross-examination. I remember he asked about Rakitin and the twenty-five roubles “you paid him for bringing Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov to see you.”

“It wasn’t strange for him to take the money,” Grushenka said angrily. “He was always asking me for money—he got thirty roubles a month from me, mostly for treats. He could have managed without my help.”
“Why were you so generous to Rakitin?” Fetyukovitch asked, even though the President looked uncomfortable.
“He’s my cousin,” Grushenka replied. “His mother was my mother’s sister. But he’s always begged me not to tell anyone—he’s so embarrassed about me.”

This shocked everyone—no one, not even Mitya, knew that Rakitin and Grushenka were related. I heard Rakitin turned bright red where he sat. Grushenka had learned before coming in that Rakitin had testified against Mitya, so she was angry. All the high-minded talk in his testimony, about justice and Russia’s problems, was now ruined in everyone’s eyes. Fetyukovitch was pleased; it was a lucky break for the defense. Grushenka wasn’t questioned much longer, and there was nothing new in her evidence. She left the court with many people looking at her with contempt, and she sat far from Katya. Mitya sat silent, staring at the floor, as if he were made of stone.
Then it was Ivan’s turn to testify.

I should mention that Ivan had actually been called to testify before Alyosha. But the court usher told the President that Ivan was having some kind of medical episode or seizure and couldn't come in right away. He would be able to testify as soon as he felt better. No one seemed to pay much attention to this at the time—it only became clear later.

When Ivan finally entered the courtroom, barely anyone noticed at first. The main witnesses—including the two women who were rivals—had already been questioned, so most people’s curiosity was satisfied and the crowd felt tired. There were still a few more witnesses, but people didn’t expect them to say anything new. Time was dragging on. Ivan walked in extremely slowly, not looking at anyone, his head down like he was lost in dark thoughts. His clothes were perfect, but his face looked awful—almost like someone very ill, with dull eyes and an ashen tone. He glanced around the court with lifeless eyes. Alyosha jumped up and gasped, "Ah!" I remember that clearly, but hardly anyone else seemed to notice.

The President told Ivan that he would be testifying as a witness, not under oath, so he could choose to answer or not answer questions. But, of course, he was expected to be truthful. Ivan stared blankly at him while he spoke, but then his face relaxed and he smiled a little. As soon as the President finished—looking confused by Ivan’s reaction—Ivan suddenly laughed out loud.
"So, what else do you want?" Ivan said loudly.
The courtroom went completely silent. People felt that something strange was happening. The President started to look a little nervous.
"You... are you still not feeling well?" he asked, looking around for the usher.
"Don’t worry about it, sir. I’m fine and I have something interesting to tell you," Ivan replied, suddenly speaking calmly and respectfully.
"You have something special to say?" the President asked, still sounding suspicious.
Ivan looked down and waited a few moments. Then he looked up and, almost stammering, said:
"No... I don’t. Nothing special."

The questioning began. Ivan answered in the shortest way possible, almost like it disgusted him to be there, though his answers made sense. He said "I don’t know" to many questions. He didn’t know anything about his father’s money dealings with Dmitri. "I wasn't interested," he added. He said he’d heard Dmitri threaten to kill their father, and that Smerdyakov told him about the money in the envelope.
"It’s always the same questions," Ivan said suddenly, looking tired. "I don’t really have anything new to tell the court."
"I can see you’re not well and I understand how you feel," the President began.
He turned to the prosecutor and defense attorney to see if they wanted to question Ivan, but then Ivan suddenly said in a weak voice:
"Please let me go, sir. I feel very sick."
Without waiting for permission, Ivan turned and started to walk away. But after only a few steps, he stopped, as if changing his mind, gave a slow smile, and walked back.

"I’m like that peasant girl, sir—you know the story? ‘I’ll stand up if I want, and I won’t if I don’t.’ They were trying to put her dress on to take her to church to be married, and she said, ‘I’ll stand up if I want, and I won’t if I don’t.’ It’s from a book about peasants."
"What are you trying to say?" the President asked, sounding stern.

"This is what I mean," Ivan suddenly pulled out a roll of bills. "Here’s the money... the same money that was in that envelope," he nodded toward the table with the evidence, "the money my father was killed for. Where should I put it? Mr. Superintendent, take it."
The court usher took the money from Ivan and handed it to the President.
"How did you get this money—if it really is the same money?" the President asked, surprised.

"I got it from Smerdyakov, from the real murderer, yesterday. I was with him just before he hanged himself. He was the one who killed our father, not my brother. He did it, and I encouraged him... Who doesn’t wish their father was dead?"
"Are you in your right mind?" the President blurted out.

"Of course I’m in my right mind... as much as any of you, or anyone else here," Ivan replied, suddenly turning to look at the crowd. "My father is dead, and you all pretend to be shocked," he sneered, full of anger. "But you’re all lying. Everyone wishes their father was dead. One snake eats another... If there hadn’t been a murder, you’d all be disappointed and go home in a bad mood. You just want a show! Bread and circuses. And I’m no better! Is there any water? Give me a drink, for Christ’s sake!" Ivan suddenly grabbed his head.

The usher hurried over to help. Alyosha jumped up and cried, "He’s sick! Don’t listen to him, he has brain fever!" Katerina Ivanovna stood up, frozen with horror, staring at Ivan. Mitya (Dmitri) got up too, watching his brother with a wild, strange smile.
"Don’t worry, I’m not crazy, I’m just a murderer," Ivan began again. "No one expects a murderer to give a good speech," he added for some reason, then let out a weird laugh.

The prosecutor leaned towards the President, obviously worried. The two other judges whispered nervously. Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, was paying close attention. The whole room was tense, waiting. Suddenly the President seemed to snap out of it.
"Witness, what you’re saying doesn’t make sense here. Please calm down and tell your story—if you actually have one. How can you prove what you’re saying—if you’re not just imagining things?"

"That’s just it. I have no proof. That bastard Smerdyakov isn’t going to send you proof from the afterlife... in an envelope. You only care about envelopes—one should be enough. I have no witnesses... except maybe one," Ivan said with a strange smile.
"Who’s your witness?"

"He has a tail, sir, so that would be a problem! The devil doesn’t exist! Don’t pay attention: he’s just a pathetic devil," Ivan suddenly got serious, almost like he was sharing a secret. "He’s probably here somewhere—maybe under that table with the evidence. Where else would he sit? Listen to me. I told him I wouldn’t keep quiet, and he started talking about a geological disaster... nonsense! Come on, let him out—he’s been singing a hymn. His heart is light! Like a drunk man in the street yelling about ‘Vanka went to Petersburg,’ and I’d give anything for two seconds of happiness. You don’t know me! This is all so stupid! Just take me instead! I didn’t come here for nothing... Why is everything so stupid?..."
Ivan started talking more slowly, almost thoughtfully, looking around again. But by now the whole court was in chaos. Alyosha ran toward him, but the usher had already grabbed Ivan’s arm.

"What are you doing?" Ivan yelled, staring into the usher’s face. Suddenly, he grabbed the man’s shoulders and threw him to the floor. But the police were there and quickly held Ivan down. He screamed in rage and kept shouting random things as they dragged him out.

The whole courtroom was in chaos. I can’t remember everything that happened since I was pretty shaken up myself. Later, when things calmed down and people realized what had happened, the usher got scolded. He explained that Ivan had seemed fine before, that the doctor had seen him an hour earlier when he was just a little dizzy, but Ivan had been talking clearly and insisted on testifying. No one could have expected what happened. But before anyone had really recovered from all this, something else happened. Katerina Ivanovna had a hysterical fit. She sobbed and screamed loudly, but refused to leave the courtroom, fighting and begging not to be taken out. Suddenly she shouted to the President:

"There’s more evidence I need to give right now! Here, here’s a document—a letter! Take it, read it quickly! It’s a letter from that monster—him!" she pointed at Mitya. "He killed his father, you’ll see. He wrote to me about how he would do it! But the other one is sick—he’s sick and delirious!" she kept shouting, out of control.

The usher took the letter from her and gave it to the President. Katerina dropped into her chair, hid her face in her hands, and cried silently, her whole body shaking, trying not to make a sound so she wouldn’t be thrown out. The letter was the one Mitya wrote at the "Metropolis" tavern, which Ivan had called "mathematical proof." Sadly, everyone saw it as proof, and if it weren’t for that letter, Mitya might have escaped such a terrible fate—or at least had a lighter sentence. I can’t remember every detail after that. I think the President passed the letter to the judges, the jury, and the lawyers. I only remember they started questioning Katerina Ivanovna. The President gently asked if she was well enough, and Katerina replied passionately:
"I’m ready! I’m fine—I can answer your questions," she insisted, clearly still afraid they might stop her from testifying. They asked her to explain what the letter was and how she got it.

"I got it the day before the murder, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—so, two days before he killed his father. Look, it’s written on some bill!" she cried, nearly out of breath. "He hated me then, because he’d acted horribly and was chasing after that woman... and because he owed me three thousand rubles. Oh! He was ashamed because of that money and his own actions! Here’s what happened with the three thousand: three weeks before the murder, he came to me in the morning. I knew he needed money, and why. Yes, yes—to win over that woman and run away with her. I already knew he’d betrayed me and planned to leave me, and I was the one who gave him that money, pretending it was for him to send to my sister in Moscow. As I handed it to him, I looked him in the eye and said he could send it whenever, ‘even a month from now.’ How could he not get that I was really saying, ‘You want money to betray me with that woman—here it is, take it if you have so little honor!’ I wanted to see what kind of person he was, and what did he do? He took it and spent it all on her in one night... But he knew, he knew I understood. I swear he knew I gave him the money as a test, to see if he would really take it. I stared into his eyes and he stared back—and he took my money!"
"That’s true, Katya," Mitya suddenly shouted, "I looked into your eyes and I knew you were humiliating me, and I still took your money. Call me a scoundrel, all of you! I deserve it!"
"Prisoner," the President yelled, "one more word and I’ll have you removed!"

"That money haunted him," Katya continued quickly. "He wanted to pay it back, that’s true, but he also needed money for that woman. So he killed his father, but never paid me back, and ran off with her to that village where he was arrested. There, he wasted the money he stole after the murder. And the day before, he wrote me this letter. He was drunk when he wrote it—I knew right away. He wrote it out of spite, and he was sure I’d never show it to anyone, even if he killed his father. Otherwise, he wouldn’t have written it! He knew I wouldn’t want revenge or to ruin him! But read the letter—read it carefully—and you’ll see he explains everything, how he would kill his father and where the money was hidden. Look, don’t miss that part where he writes, ‘I’ll kill him as soon as Ivan has gone away.’ So he planned it all in advance," Katerina said, almost with cruel satisfaction. She had clearly analyzed every line of the letter. "If he hadn’t been drunk, he wouldn’t have written it. But look—it’s all there, exactly how he did it! The whole plan!" she cried frantically.

Now she didn’t care what would happen to her, though she’d probably been thinking about this moment for weeks, maybe debating whether to show the letter at the trial. Now she’d finally done it. I remember the clerk read the letter out loud right after that. It had a huge impact. They asked Mitya if he admitted writing it.

"It’s mine, mine!" Mitya shouted. "I wouldn’t have written it if I hadn’t been drunk!... We hated each other for so many reasons, Katya, but I swear I loved you even when I hated you, and you never loved me!"

He dropped back into his seat, wringing his hands in despair. The prosecutor and defense lawyer began questioning Katerina, mostly to figure out why she hid the letter and had spoken so differently earlier.

"Yes, yes, I was lying before. I lied against my own honor and conscience because I wanted to save him, even though he hated and despised me so much!" Katya cried out wildly. "Oh, he’s always despised me, ever since I bowed down to him for that money. I saw it—I felt it then, but I didn’t want to believe it for a long time. I’ve seen it in his eyes so many times: ‘You came to me yourself, though.’ Oh, he never understood why I came to him, he thinks everyone is as low as he is!" Katya hissed, almost out of control. "And he only wanted to marry me because I had a fortune, because of that! I always suspected it! Oh, he’s cruel! He thought I’d be ashamed for the rest of my life because I went to him then, and that he’d always be better than me, and that’s why he wanted to marry me! That’s it, that’s all of it! I tried to win him over with my love, love with no limits. I even tried to forgive his betrayal, but he never understood! How could he? He’s a monster! I got the letter the next evening—it was brought to me from the tavern—and that morning, just that morning, I wanted to forgive him for everything—even his cheating!"

The President and prosecutor tried to calm her down. I think they were embarrassed to be taking advantage of her while she was so emotional, and to listen to such personal confessions. I remember them telling her, "We understand how hard this is for you; we feel for you," and things like that. Still, they kept questioning her. Finally, she explained, with a sudden unusual clarity, how Ivan had almost lost his mind in the past two months trying to save "the monster and murderer," his brother.

"He tortured himself," she said. "He kept trying to lessen his brother’s guilt and told me he himself never loved his father, and maybe even wished for his death. Oh, he has such a tender conscience! He told me everything, every day, like I was his only friend. I am his only friend!" she suddenly declared with pride, her eyes flashing. "He visited Smerdyakov twice. One day he told me, ‘If it wasn’t my brother, but Smerdyakov who did it’—since people were already saying Smerdyakov had done it—‘maybe I’m guilty too, because Smerdyakov knew I didn’t like my father and maybe thought I wanted him dead.’ Then I showed him that letter. He became sure his brother had done it, and it crushed him. He couldn’t stand the thought that his own brother was a killer! Just a week ago, I saw it was making him sick. Lately, he spoke nonsense around me. I saw his mind breaking down. He wandered around, talking to himself in the streets. The Moscow doctor checked him for me two days ago and said he was about to get brain fever—all because of this monster! And last night he found out Smerdyakov was dead! It was such a shock it drove him insane... and all because he wanted to save the monster!"

Of course, someone can only pour out their heart like that once in their life—maybe right before death, or on the way to the gallows. But that was Katya’s character, and this was that kind of moment. She was the same impulsive Katya who had once begged a wild young man to save her father; the same Katya who had just now, in front of everyone, told about Mitya’s generosity, hoping to help him. And now she sacrificed herself again, but this time for someone else—and maybe, only now, did she realize how much she cared for him! She gave up her pride to protect him, to save his name, his reputation!

And yet, one terrible question came to mind—was she telling the truth about her past with Mitya? No, she wasn’t lying on purpose when she said Mitya despised her for bowing down to him. She truly believed it. Ever since that day, she was sure that honest, passionate Mitya, who adored her, was actually laughing at her and looking down on her. She loved him in a wild, painful way—almost out of pride and wounded feelings, not true love, but more like revenge. Maybe, given time, she would have grown to really love him—maybe that’s what she wanted most. But Mitya’s betrayal hurt her too deeply, and she couldn’t forgive him. When her chance for revenge came, all her bottled-up anger exploded at once. She betrayed Mitya—but she betrayed herself, too. As soon as she let out all her feelings, the tension broke, and she was filled with shame. She had another hysterical fit, fell to the floor, sobbing and screaming, and had to be carried out. At that moment, Grushenka rushed towards Mitya, wailing, before anyone could stop her.

"Mitya," she cried, "that snake has destroyed you! See what she’s like!" she screamed at the judges, shaking with fury. The President signaled for people to remove her, but she wouldn’t go quietly. She fought to stay with Mitya. Mitya cried out and tried to reach her, but he was held back.

Well, I guess the ladies who came to watch got the spectacle they wanted—there was certainly enough drama. Then I remember the doctor from Moscow came in, probably because the President had asked the usher to call for medical help for Ivan. The doctor told the court that Ivan was suffering from a dangerous brain fever and needed to be removed right away. When the prosecutor and defense lawyer asked questions, the doctor said Ivan had come to see him two days earlier, and he’d warned Ivan about his illness, but Ivan refused to be treated. "He wasn’t in his right mind: he told me he saw visions while awake, met dead people in the street, and that the devil visited him every night," the doctor finished. After giving his statement, the famous doctor left. The letter Katerina brought was added to the evidence. After talking it over, the judges decided to keep going with the trial and officially record both Ivan’s and Katerina’s unexpected evidence.

I won’t go into detail about the rest of the witnesses, since they mostly just repeated what had already been said, each in their own way. Everything was summed up in the prosecutor’s speech, which I’ll quote next. Everyone was tense and electrified after all the drama, and they waited eagerly for the speeches from the prosecution and defense. Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, was obviously shaken by Katerina’s evidence, but the prosecutor looked confident. When all the evidence had been heard, the court took a break for almost an hour. I think it was around eight o’clock when the President came back to his seat, and our prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, began his speech.

Ippolit Kirillovitch started his speech shaking with nerves, sweating, and feeling both hot and cold. Later, he would say this speech was the best thing he ever did—his life’s masterpiece, his “swan song.” He actually died nine months later from a fast-moving illness, so it turned out he was right to call it that.
