He put everything he had into this speech—his heart and all his intelligence. People were surprised to see that he did care about society and the so-called “big questions" of life. What really stood out in his speech was how honest he was. He truly believed that the prisoner was guilty; he wasn’t just doing his job, but was personally upset and wanted justice “for the safety of society.” Even though most of the women in the audience didn’t like Ippolit Kirillovitch, they admitted he made a powerful impression. He started speaking with a shaky voice, but it got stronger and stronger until the end. Then, as soon as he finished, he almost fainted from exhaustion.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor began, “everyone in Russia has heard about this case. But why are we so shocked—why does it seem so terrifying to us? Maybe it shouldn’t, because we’re actually used to these kinds of crimes now! That’s the real horror—not the crime itself, but that we barely react to things like this anymore. Why are we so numb, so uncaring about these signs of trouble for our future? Is it because we’re cynical, or maybe because our society is already falling apart, even though it’s still young? Have our morals completely collapsed, or did we never really have any? I don’t know the answers, but these questions should bother all of us. Our new, still-nervous newspapers have already done some good, because without them, we wouldn’t even know about all the violence and moral collapse happening around us. The papers tell us about things far worse than this case, things that make it seem almost ordinary. But what really matters is that most of our national crimes are part of a much bigger problem—something so widespread that it’s hard to fight against.

“One day, we hear about a promising young army officer, just starting out in life, who murders an official—a man who once helped him—and also kills a servant girl, just to steal some cash and a piece of paper promising money. He does it secretly, with no guilt, just so he can enjoy himself in high society. After the murders, he even puts pillows under their heads and calmly leaves. Next, we hear about a young ‘hero,’ decorated for bravery, who kills the mother of his boss and benefactor, just like a common criminal. To convince his friends to help, he says, ‘She loves me like a son, so she’ll do whatever I say and won’t be careful.’ That’s monstrous, but sadly, I can’t say that kind of person is rare anymore. Someone else might not actually commit murder, but they might think just as dishonorably. Alone with their thoughts, they might ask themselves, ‘What is honor, anyway? Is thinking killing is wrong just an old-fashioned idea?’

“Maybe some people think I’m overreacting, that I’m being dramatic or unfair, or that I’m exaggerating everything. If you think so, fine—honestly, I wish I was wrong! But even if only a tenth, or a twentieth, of what I’m saying is true, it’s still terrible! Just look at how often young people kill themselves these days, without even stopping to wonder what happens after death, as if all questions about the soul or an afterlife have been erased from their minds. Look at how much vice and wild behavior there is. Fyodor Pavlovitch—the victim in this case—was almost innocent compared to some people out there. And yet, we all knew him. He lived among us...

“Someday, the best minds in Russia and Europe will study why so many crimes happen in Russia, because it’s a subject worth exploring. But that will be in the future, when this current chaos is behind us and people can look at things more clearly and fairly than I can now. Right now, we either act horrified or pretend to be, but secretly we enjoy the excitement of it all, because we’re bored and spoiled. Or we act like little kids, hiding from scary things and then going back to playing as soon as they’re gone. But eventually, we’ll have to grow up and look honestly at ourselves as a society. We need to start understanding our situation, or at least make a real effort to do so.

“A great writer from the last generation compared Russia to a fast-moving troika—a traditional Russian carriage pulled by three horses—racing toward an unknown destination. He cried, ‘Oh, troika, who invented you!’ and proudly added that all the peoples of the world stand aside in awe to let Russia speed by. Maybe that’s true, maybe they do move aside, but I think the writer ended his book that way because he was either naïvely optimistic or afraid of the government censors. After all, if the troika was being driven by the characters he wrote about—Sobakevitch, Nozdryov, Tchitchikov—it would never reach any sensible goal, no matter who was steering. And those characters were from the older generation; our generation is even worse...”

At this point, people in the courtroom started to clap. They understood the hidden message in his story. The applause didn’t last long, so the judge didn’t feel the need to warn anyone, though he did glare at them. But Ippolit Kirillovitch felt encouraged; no one had ever applauded him before! All his life, people had ignored him, and now suddenly, he had everyone’s attention.

“So, what is this Karamazov family, which is now so infamous across Russia?” he continued. “Maybe I’m exaggerating, but I think this family shows, in a small way, some of the main problems of our educated class today—it’s like seeing the sun reflected in a drop of water. Look at that unhappy, wild old man who met such a sad end—the head of the family. He was born into a noble family but was poor and depended on others. Then, thanks to a lucky marriage, he got a small fortune. He was a petty cheat, a flatterer, and a clown, not stupid but never really using his brain. More than anything, he was a moneylender, getting bolder as he got richer. His cowardly side disappeared, but his mean, sarcastic attitude stayed. He never grew as a person, but he had endless energy. He saw nothing in life except pleasure, and he raised his sons to be the same. He didn’t care about being a father—he even made fun of the idea. He left his kids to the servants and was happy to forget about them. His motto was ‘After me, the flood’—he didn’t care what happened to the world as long as he was comfortable. He even cheated his own son out of his inheritance to try to steal his son’s girlfriend. I’m not going to leave the defense of the prisoner only to my talented colleague from Petersburg. I’ll tell the truth myself. I can understand why his son was so angry with him.

“But that’s enough about the old man; he’s already paid for his actions. Still, let’s remember he was a father, and a typical one for today. Am I being unfair to say that? Maybe, but I think many modern fathers are just like him, except they hide their selfishness better because they’re more educated. Deep down, though, their beliefs are the same. Maybe I’m being too negative, but you agreed to let me speak my mind. You don’t have to believe everything I say, but please, at least listen and remember some of it.
“Now let’s talk about his sons. The main focus is the prisoner here—Dmitri Karamazov. I’ll talk mostly about him, but I’ll mention the other two briefly.

“The oldest brother is a modern young man—smart, well-educated, but he’s lost faith in everything. He has rejected a lot, just like his father. We’ve all heard him talk; he was popular in local society and never hid his opinions. That’s why I can talk openly about him now, not as just an individual, but as part of the Karamazov family. Another person connected to this case died here last night by suicide—Smerdyakov, a mentally troubled man, once a servant, and possibly the illegitimate son of Fyodor Pavlovitch. During the investigation, Smerdyakov cried and told me how Ivan Karamazov scared him with his bold ideas. ‘He always told me that anything is allowed, and in the future, nothing will be forbidden.’ I think Smerdyakov went crazy because of this idea, though his epilepsy and the terrible events lately also helped push him over the edge. But he did notice one very interesting thing, and that’s why I mention it: he said, ‘If any of the sons is like Fyodor Pavlovitch in character, it’s Ivan Fyodorovitch.’

“That’s all I’ll say about Ivan’s character—I don’t want to go further and sound like I’m predicting doom for him. We’ve seen today that Ivan still has good feelings in his heart; his lack of faith and his cynicism aren’t entirely his fault—they’re passed down from his father more than they’re his own ideas.

“Now the third son. He’s a religious and humble young man, not sharing his older brother’s gloomy, destructive worldview. He tries to stick to ‘the people’s ideas,’ at least what some educated people call that. He joined the monastery and almost became a monk. I think, without realizing it, he already shows the kind of quiet despair that makes some people in our troubled society run away from cynicism and blame everything bad on European influences. They try to ‘return to their roots,’ as they say—like scared children wanting to sleep forever in their old mother’s arms, just so they can escape the scary things in life.

“Personally, I wish this good, talented young man all the best. I hope his youthful idealism and love for ‘the people’s ideas’ never turn, as sometimes happens, into dark mysticism or blind patriotism—two things that threaten Russia even more than the early decay caused by misunderstanding and copying European ideas, which is what his older brother suffers from.”

A couple of people clapped when he mentioned patriotism and mysticism. Ippolit Kirillovitch had really gotten caught up in his speech. Honestly, this didn’t have much to do with the case, and it was a bit vague, but the sick, dying man just wanted to express himself for once in his life. Later, some people said he was only criticizing Ivan because Ivan had beaten him in arguments before, and Ippolit Kirillovitch wanted to get back at him. But who knows if that’s true. In any case, all of this was just the introduction—soon, he got to the actual issues of the trial.

“But let’s get back to the oldest son,” Ippolit Kirillovitch continued. “He’s the one on trial. We have all the facts of his life and his actions in front of us. This is the day of truth. While his brothers seem to stand for ‘Europeanism’ and ‘the people’s values,’ he seems to represent Russia as it really is. Not all of Russia, of course—heaven forbid—but he’s got that unique Russian mixture in him. He’s spontaneous, a strange blend of good and evil, a lover of culture and poetry, but also someone who fights in bars and pulls out people’s beards. He can be noble and good, but only when things are going well for him. He can get swept up by noble ideas, but only if they fall into his lap—he doesn’t want to work for them. He doesn’t like paying for anything, but he loves being given things, and that’s true for everything in his life. If you give him everything he wants and never stand in his way, he’ll show you how generous he can be. He’s not greedy, but he needs money—lots of it—and if he gets it, he’ll spend it all in one crazy night. But if he doesn’t have money, you’ll see what he’s willing to do to get it when he’s desperate. But let’s take things in order.

“First, we see a poor, neglected child running around barefoot in the yard, as our respected local citizen of foreign origin described it earlier. I want to be fair—I’m here to accuse, but also to defend. I know how much childhood and home life matter for someone’s character. But the boy grows up, becomes an army officer, and because of a duel and other wild behavior, is sent far away to a border town. There, he lives a wild life as an officer. Of course, he needs money—money is everything for him. After long arguments, he makes a deal with his father, and finally gets the last six thousand roubles. There’s a letter where he basically gives up his claim to more money, agreeing to end the fight with his father if he gets those six thousand.

“Then he meets a young woman with a great personality and good education. I won’t repeat the details—you just heard them. There was real honor and self-sacrifice there, and I’ll say no more. The young officer, wild and reckless, showed real respect for true goodness and high ideals, and we all saw him in a sympathetic light. But then, right after, everything changed—right here in this courtroom. I don’t know exactly why, but there were reasons. The same woman, now crying with anger she’d hidden for a long time, said that he—of all people—looked down on her for what she did, even though her actions, while maybe reckless, came from good motives. He, her fiancé, gave her a mocking smile that hurt more coming from him than anyone. And knowing that he had already cheated her—because he thought she would put up with anything, even betrayal—she offered him three thousand roubles, and made it clear she was testing him: ‘Will you take it, or are you really that shameless?’ was the question in her eyes. He understood what was happening (he’s admitted that to you), took the money without hesitation, and blew it all in two days on the new woman he was interested in.

“So what should we believe? The first story, where he gives away his last penny out of generosity and respect for virtue, or this ugly second story? Usually, the truth is somewhere in the middle, but not in this case. I think he was truly noble the first time and truly low the second time. Why? Because he has that Karamazov character—that’s my point—he can be both things at once: the best and the worst. Remember what Mr. Rakitin, who knows the Karamazovs well, said: ‘They need to feel both their own greatness and their own shame—it’s part of who they are.’ And it’s true—they’re only happy with this weird mix. They go to both extremes at once, or they’re miserable. They’re wide, wide as Russia itself—they include everything, accept everything.

“By the way, gentlemen of the jury, we’ve just mentioned those three thousand roubles, so I’ll jump ahead a little. Can you believe that a man like this—after taking that money in such a shameful way—could have set aside half of it, sewn it into a little bag, and carried it with him for a whole month without ever touching it, even though he was desperate for money? Even when he was drinking in bars or running all over trying to find money to keep his girlfriend away from his father, he never touched that bag! If only to keep her from being tempted by his father, you’d think he’d use that money and stay home to guard her, waiting for her to say, ‘I’m yours,’ and then run away with her.

“But no, he didn’t touch his lucky charm. Why? He says the main reason was so that if she finally agreed to run away with him, he’d have the money to do it. But even he admits that wasn’t the real reason. The real reason, as he said, was this: As long as I have that money, I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief, because I can always go back to my hurt fiancée and give her half the money I took. I can say, ‘See, I wasted half your money—I’m weak, maybe even a scoundrel—but I’m not a thief. If I were a thief, I would have taken all of it!’ What an explanation! This wild but weak man, who couldn’t resist taking the money in the first place, suddenly has the willpower to carry around a thousand roubles for weeks without spending any of it. Does that really fit the character we’ve just described? No, and I’ll tell you what the real Dmitri Karamazov would have done, if he’d actually put the money away.

“At the first temptation—say, he wanted to impress the woman he’d already blown half the money on—he’d open the bag and take out a hundred roubles. Why would he have to bring back exactly half the money, fifteen hundred roubles? Why not fourteen hundred? He could just as easily have said he wasn’t a thief because he brought back fourteen hundred. Then, another time, he’d take out another hundred, then a third, then a fourth, and by the end of the month there’d only be one note left, and he’d think, ‘Why give back just one hundred? Might as well spend it, too!’ That’s what the real Dmitri Karamazov, as we know him, would have done. It’s impossible to believe this story about the little bag. It just doesn’t make sense. But we’ll talk more about that later.”

After talking about the money issues between father and son, and saying again and again that no one could really tell who was right, Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to the medical experts’ testimony about Mitya’s obsession with the three thousand roubles he thought was owed to him.

“The medical experts have tried to convince us that the prisoner is insane, even calling him a madman. But I say he is perfectly sane—and if he wasn’t, he would have acted more carefully. Sure, I’ll admit he’s a bit crazy about one thing: his obsession with the three thousand roubles. But I think there’s a much simpler explanation than insanity. Personally, I agree with the young doctor who said the prisoner has always had a normal mind—he’s just been angry and frustrated. His anger wasn’t really about the money itself; there was something deeper driving him. That deeper reason is jealousy!”

Here, Ippolit Kirillovitch explained in detail how the prisoner became desperately obsessed with Grushenka. He started with the moment the prisoner went to Grushenka’s place planning “to beat her”—“those are his own words,” the prosecutor clarified—“but instead, he ended up at her feet. That’s when his obsession began. At the same time, the prisoner’s father fell for Grushenka too—a weird and tragic coincidence, because they both fell in love with her at once, even though they already knew her. She inspired a wild, classic Karamazov passion in both of them. Grushenka even admitted: ‘I was laughing at both of them.’ Yes, she wanted to mess with them for her own amusement, and she managed to completely win over both men. The old man, who loved money, immediately set aside three thousand roubles to reward her for just one visit, but soon after, he was ready to give up all his property and even his name if she would just agree to marry him. There’s strong evidence for this. As for the prisoner, his tragic story is clear as day. But this was all part of Grushenka’s ‘game.’ She never gave the poor young man any hope until the very last moment, when he was on his knees before her, his hands already stained with the blood of his father and his rival. That’s when he was arrested. ‘Send me to Siberia with him! I brought him to this. I’m the one most to blame,’ Grushenka cried out in real regret when he was taken away.

“The clever young man I mentioned before, Mr. Rakitin, described Grushenka with a few powerful words: ‘She was disappointed early in life. Her fiancé seduced and dumped her. She ended up poor, cursed by her proper family, and was taken in by a wealthy old man, whom she still sees as her savior. She probably had a lot of good in her heart, but it was soured too soon. She became careful with money. She grew sarcastic and angry at society.’ After hearing this, it’s easy to see why she might laugh at both men, just for mischief or out of spite.

“After a month of hopeless love and moral ruin—during which he betrayed his fiancée and spent money he was supposed to guard—the prisoner was pushed to the edge, nearly losing his mind with jealousy. And jealous of who? His own father! The worst part was that the old man was tempting Grushenka with the very three thousand roubles the son thought was rightfully his—part of his inheritance from his mother, which he believed his father was cheating him out of. Yes, it was a lot to handle! It could drive anyone insane. It wasn’t just about the money—it was about the fact that it was being used so shamelessly to destroy his happiness!”
Then, the prosecutor described how the idea of killing his father first entered the prisoner’s mind, and he backed up his theory with facts.

“At first, he just talked about it in taverns—he talked about it all month long. He loves being around people and telling them everything, even the darkest and most dangerous ideas. For some reason, he expects everyone he confides in to agree with him, support him, and never argue. If they don’t, he gets angry and causes a scene in the tavern. [Here followed the story about Captain Snegiryov.] Eventually, those who heard the prisoner talk started to think he might actually mean what he said, and that his wildness might turn threats into real actions.”
The prosecutor then described the family meeting at the monastery, the conversations with Alyosha, and the terrible moment when the prisoner burst into his father’s house right after dinner.

“I can’t say for sure,” the prosecutor continued, “that the prisoner had fully decided to kill his father before that incident. But the idea had come to him several times, and he’d thought it over—there’s proof, witnesses, and even his own words. I admit, gentlemen of the jury,” he added, “that until today, I wasn’t sure if the prisoner had really planned everything out. I was convinced he had pictured the deadly moment, but only as a possibility—not as something he’d definitely do, or planned exactly when or how.

“But I was only unsure until today, until that important letter was brought to court just now. You all heard the young woman yell, ‘It’s the plan—the plan for murder!’ That’s how she described the sad, drunken letter written by the prisoner. And, in fact, from that letter we can see that the whole idea of murder was planned ahead. It was written two days before, so now we know for sure that forty-eight hours before the crime, the prisoner swore that if he couldn’t get the money the next day, he would kill his father to get the envelope with the cash from under his pillow, as soon as Ivan left. ‘As soon as Ivan had gone’—you heard that. He had thought everything through, planned every detail, and then did exactly what he wrote. The proof of planning is undeniable; the crime was for the money, and that’s written and signed. The prisoner doesn’t deny his signature.

“Some might say he was drunk when he wrote it. But that doesn’t make the letter less important—it actually makes it more valuable. He wrote while drunk what he had already planned while sober. If he hadn’t already planned it, he wouldn’t have written it while drunk. You might ask: Then why did he talk about it in taverns? Wouldn’t a real criminal keep his plans secret? Yes—but he talked about it before he had an actual plan, back when it was just a desire, an impulse. After he made his plan, he talked about it less. The night he wrote that letter at the Metropolis tavern, he was quiet, even though he was drinking—a big change for him. He didn’t play billiards; he just sat in the corner, not talking to anyone. Sure, he did kick a shopkeeper out of his seat, but that was almost automatic, because he always made a scene in taverns. After he finally made his decision, he probably worried that he’d talked too much about it before and that it might get him caught later. But there was nothing he could do—he couldn’t take his words back, but he figured he’d been lucky before and would be lucky again. He always believed in his own good luck! I have to admit, he did a lot to avoid the disaster. ‘Tomorrow I’ll try to borrow money from everyone,’ he wrote in his own strange way, ‘and if they don’t give it to me, there will be blood.’”

Next, Ippolit Kirillovitch gave a detailed account of all Mitya’s attempts to borrow the money. He described his visit to Samsonov, his trip to Lyagavy. “He was exhausted, mocked, starving, and had to sell his watch just to pay for the trip (even though he claimed he still had fifteen hundred roubles—a pretty unbelievable story). He was tortured by jealousy, thinking Grushenka would go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was gone. But when he got back, he was thrilled to find out she hadn’t gone near his father. He even took her himself to see her protector. (Weirdly, he didn’t seem jealous of Samsonov, which is interesting from a psychological point of view.) Then he rushed back to his hiding spot in the back gardens, and found out Smerdyakov was having a fit, and the other servant was sick—so the coast was clear, and he knew the ‘signals.’ What a temptation! Still, he resisted and went to see Madame Hohlakov, a respected lady who had been living in town for a while. She had watched him with sympathy and gave him good advice: to give up his wild lifestyle, end his messy love affair, stop wasting his youth and strength in drunken parties, and head off to Siberia to work in the gold mines: ‘That would give you an outlet for your energy, your romantic nature, your thirst for adventure.’”

After describing what happened in that conversation, and the moment when the prisoner learned that Grushenka wasn’t at Samsonov’s after all, Ippolit Kirillovitch talked about the sudden frenzy that overtook the poor man, worn out by jealousy and nerves, when he thought she’d betrayed him and was now with his father. He ended this part by talking about the terrible role that chance played in everything. “If the maid had simply told him that her mistress was at Mokroe with her old lover, none of this would have happened. But the maid panicked and could only swear and insist she didn’t know where Grushenka was. If the prisoner didn’t kill her right then, it was only because he was too busy running after his unfaithful lover.

“But notice—even in his madness, he grabbed a brass pestle. Why that? Why not something else? But since he’d been thinking about his plan for a whole month, he was ready to use anything as a weapon, and he recognized instantly that the pestle would work. So he didn’t just grab it by accident; it was a conscious choice. Then we find him in his father’s garden—the path is clear, no witnesses, darkness, and jealousy burning inside him. The suspicion that Grushenka was there, with his father, his rival, maybe even laughing at him right then, left him breathless. And it wasn’t just suspicion; the evidence was clear. She had to be there, in that lit-up room, behind the screen. And now the prisoner wants us to believe that he just peeked in the window politely and left, because he was afraid something bad might happen. And he expects us to believe that, even though we know what he’s really like and what he was thinking at the time, and that he knew the signals to get into the house.” At this point, Ippolit Kirillovitch paused to dive into the possible involvement of Smerdyakov in the murder. He went into a lot of detail, and even though he acted like he didn’t think Smerdyakov was important, it was clear that he actually thought the topic mattered a lot.

“First, where did this suspicion even come from?” Ippolit Kirillovitch began. “The very first person to accuse Smerdyakov of the murder was the defendant himself, right when he was arrested. But since then, he hasn’t given us a single fact to back it up—not even a hint. Only three people have supported this accusation—the defendant’s two brothers and Madame Svyetlov. The older brother only spoke up today, and he was clearly very ill, possibly delirious. We also know that, for the past two months, he totally believed his brother was guilty and never argued against it. But more on that later. The younger brother admits he has no evidence at all for thinking Smerdyakov is guilty—he just says he got that idea from what the defendant said and how he looked. Yes, that’s actually his main argument, and he’s mentioned it twice today. Madame Svyetlov was even more surprising. She said, ‘Whatever the defendant tells you, you should believe—he never lies.’ That’s all the evidence these three people have given against Smerdyakov, and they’re all deeply involved in what happens to the defendant. Still, people keep repeating the idea that Smerdyakov is guilty. Does that make any sense? Is it even possible?”

At this point, Ippolit Kirillovitch thought he needed to talk about who Smerdyakov was. He mentioned that Smerdyakov had “ended his life in a fit of insanity.” He described Smerdyakov as not very smart, only somewhat educated, and easily pushed off balance by big philosophical ideas that were too much for him. He’d picked up these ideas from the wild lifestyle of his boss—who might also have been his father—Fyodor Pavlovitch, and from strange conversations about philosophy with Fyodor Pavlovitch’s older son, Ivan Fyodorovitch (sometimes called Ivan), who liked to mess with Smerdyakov, maybe just because he was bored. “Smerdyakov told me himself how he was feeling, spiritually, during those last days at his father’s house,” Ippolit Kirillovitch explained. “But others said the same thing—the defendant, his brother, and the servant Grigory. That is, everyone who knew him well.”

“Also, Smerdyakov was in bad health because of his epilepsy, and he was a total coward. ‘He fell at my feet and kissed them,’ the defendant himself told us—before he realized this made him look bad. He even called him ‘an epileptic chicken.’ The defendant chose Smerdyakov as his confidant (he said so himself) and scared him into agreeing to spy for him. In that role, Smerdyakov lied to his boss, telling the defendant about the envelope with the money and the signals that would let him get into the house. Did he have any choice? ‘He would have killed me—I could see it,’ Smerdyakov said during the investigation, shaking with fear even though the defendant was already arrested and couldn’t hurt him. ‘He suspected me every second. I told him every secret just to calm him down, so he’d see I wasn’t lying and let me live.’ That’s what he said, and I wrote it down. ‘When he started shouting, I’d drop to my knees.’”

“Smerdyakov was actually very honest by nature. His boss trusted him completely, especially after Smerdyakov once returned some lost money. So, it’s likely Smerdyakov felt terrible about betraying the man who’d helped him so much. People with bad epilepsy, doctors say, are often haunted by guilt, even when they’ve done nothing wrong—they make up faults and worry about being ‘wicked.’ But in this case, Smerdyakov really had done something wrong, because he was terrified and bullied into it.”

“On top of that, Smerdyakov had a strong feeling that something terrible was about to happen. Right before the murder, when Ivan Fyodorovitch was about to leave for Moscow, Smerdyakov begged him to stay—but he was too scared to say clearly what he was afraid of. He just dropped hints, but Ivan didn’t pick up on them.”

“Smerdyakov saw Ivan Fyodorovitch as his protector. As long as Ivan was in the house, Smerdyakov believed nothing bad would happen. Remember what Dmitri Karamazov wrote in his drunken letter: ‘I’ll kill the old man, if only Ivan goes away.’ So, to everyone in the house, Ivan’s presence meant safety and order.”

“But Ivan left, and not even an hour later, Smerdyakov had an epileptic fit. That makes sense. I should mention that Smerdyakov, overwhelmed by fear and despair, had felt for days that he might have another fit—he’d had them before during stressful times. No one can predict the exact moment, but epileptics often sense one coming. That’s what doctors say. So, right after Ivan left, Smerdyakov, scared and feeling alone, went to the cellar. He went down the stairs, wondering if he was about to have a fit, and that very worry brought on the attack. He collapsed, unconscious. Now, some people try to claim this means he faked the fit on purpose. But if he did, what was his reason? What did he hope to gain? The doctors couldn’t tell if he was faking or not, but even if they couldn’t, what would be the point of pretending? If he was planning murder, would he really want to attract everyone’s attention by having a fit just before?”

“Listen, gentlemen of the jury, on the night of the murder, there were five people in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house: Fyodor Pavlovitch himself (and he obviously didn’t kill himself); his servant Grigory (who was almost killed himself); Grigory’s wife, Marfa Ignatyevna (but it’s ridiculous to think she could have killed her boss). That leaves two people—the defendant and Smerdyakov. If we believe the defendant’s claim that he’s not the murderer, then Smerdyakov must be, because there’s no one else. That’s why the clever but ridiculous accusation against the poor man who just killed himself has spread. If even a shadow of suspicion had fallen on anyone else—a sixth person—I bet the defendant would have blamed them instead, because blaming Smerdyakov is just absurd.”

“Let’s forget about psychology, medicine, and even logic for a moment, and just look at the facts. If Smerdyakov killed him, how did he do it? Did he act alone, or did the defendant help him? Let’s consider the first option: he did it alone. If so, what was his reason? He didn’t have any of the motives the defendant had, like hatred or jealousy. The only possible reason would be for money—the three thousand roubles he saw his boss put in the envelope. But then, he told someone else—all the details about the money and the signals to get into the house—and not just anyone, but the defendant, who wanted that envelope for himself. Did Smerdyakov do this just to betray himself, or to invite someone else to steal the money? You might say, ‘He told out of fear.’ But think about it: could a person brave enough to plan and carry out a murder also be foolish enough to reveal these secrets to the one person who would want the money most?”

“No matter how cowardly he was, if Smerdyakov had planned such a crime, nothing would have made him tell anyone about the envelope and the signals—he’d be giving himself away! If he’d been forced to talk, he could have lied, but he wouldn’t have given up the secret. And if he’d kept quiet about the money, even if he killed and robbed his boss, no one would know—only he knew about the envelope. Even if he’d been accused, it wouldn’t be for robbery, and since everyone knew Fyodor Pavlovitch liked and trusted him, no one would suspect him. They’d first suspect the person who had a motive—a person who’d admitted to having such motives: the murdered man’s son, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. If Smerdyakov had killed and robbed Fyodor Pavlovitch, and Dmitri was blamed, that would have been perfect for Smerdyakov. So, why would he tell Dmitri about the money and the signals? Does that make any sense?”

“So, according to this theory, on the day Smerdyakov planned the murder, he pretended to have a fit and fell down the stairs. Why? First, so Grigory, who planned to take his medicine, would stay in the house instead, keeping watch since there was no one else to do it. Second, so his boss, realizing no one was guarding him, would be even more careful. And most importantly, so Smerdyakov, now ‘sick,’ would be moved from the kitchen (where he could go in and out freely) to Grigory’s room at the other end of the house, separated by a screen. That was always the routine when he had a fit. There, behind the screen, he’d probably keep up the act by groaning all night, keeping Grigory and Marfa awake. And we’re supposed to think all this was to make it easier for him to get up and murder his boss?”

“Maybe some people will say he faked being sick so he wouldn’t be suspected, and that he told the defendant about the money and the signals to tempt him to commit the murder. Then, after the defendant had done it, making plenty of noise and waking people, Smerdyakov would get up—what for? To kill his boss a second time and steal money that was already gone? Gentlemen, are you joking? I’m embarrassed to even mention such an idea, but, believe it or not, this is exactly what the defendant claims. He says that after he left the house, after knocking down Grigory and raising an alarm, Smerdyakov got up, went in, killed his boss, and stole the money! I won’t even get into how unlikely it is that Smerdyakov could have predicted all this, or that Dmitri would just look in the window and then leave. Gentlemen, I ask you seriously: when, exactly, could Smerdyakov have committed this crime? Name the moment, or you can’t accuse him.”

“But maybe the fit was real, and Smerdyakov suddenly woke up, heard a shout, and went out. Then what? Did he just look around and think, ‘Why not go kill my boss?’ And how would he even know what was happening, since he’d been unconscious the whole time? There’s a limit to how far we can stretch our imagination.”

“‘But what if they were in it together?’ some clever people might ask. ‘What if they both killed him and split the money?’ That’s a big question! But the facts supporting it are pretty ridiculous. One person commits the murder, while the other just lies around faking a fit, making everyone suspicious and scaring both the boss and Grigory. What possible reason would two partners have for making such a crazy plan?”

“Maybe it wasn’t active teamwork, but just Smerdyakov passively allowing it—maybe he was too scared to stop the murder and got Dmitri’s permission to get out of the way by pretending to have a fit—‘Go ahead and murder him if you want; it’s not my business.’ But since Smerdyakov’s attack would throw the whole house into confusion, Dmitri would never have agreed to such a plan. But let’s say he did. It would still mean Dmitri was the murderer and the one who planned it, and Smerdyakov just passively let it happen out of fear.”

“But what actually happened? As soon as he was arrested, the defendant immediately blamed Smerdyakov—not as an accomplice, but as the murderer. ‘He did it alone,’ the defendant says. ‘He killed and robbed him. He did it.’ That’s a strange way for accomplices to act—accusing each other right away! And think about the risk for Dmitri. After committing murder while his ‘accomplice’ lay in bed, he blames the sick man, who could easily have turned around and told the truth to protect himself. Smerdyakov could have admitted his part, knowing he’d be punished much less than the real killer. But he never did—he never even hinted that they were in it together, even though Dmitri kept accusing him.”

“Even more, at the investigation, Smerdyakov volunteered that he was the one who told the defendant about the envelope of money and the signals. If he’d been guilty, would he really have admitted that so easily? No—he would have tried to hide it or downplay it. But he didn’t. Only an innocent person, who isn’t afraid of being blamed, would do that. And, in a fit of depression from his illness and everything that happened, he killed himself yesterday. He left a note in his own strange wording: ‘I destroy myself by my own will and choice so as to blame no one else.’ Why didn’t he add: ‘I am the murderer, not Karamazov’? Did his guilty conscience push him to suicide, but not to confess?”

“And then what happened? The three thousand roubles were brought into court just now, and we were told they were the very same notes that had been in the envelope, and that the witness got them from Smerdyakov the day before. I won’t go over the whole painful scene, but I will point out a few details that might not be obvious. First, Smerdyakov must have returned the money and then hanged himself out of guilt. And only yesterday, supposedly, he confessed to Ivan Karamazov, according to Ivan himself. If that’s true, then why did Ivan keep silent until now? And if Smerdyakov confessed, why didn’t he admit everything in his final letter, knowing that the defendant would be facing trial today?”

“But the money alone doesn’t prove anything. Just a week ago, I, along with two other people in this court, learned by chance that Ivan Fyodorovitch had sent two coupons, each worth five thousand, to be cashed in the main city—a total of ten thousand. I only mention this to show that anyone can have money, and we can’t prove these notes were the same ones from Fyodor Pavlovitch’s envelope.”

“After hearing such important news from the real killer yesterday, why didn’t Ivan Karamazov do anything right away? Why did he wait until morning? I think I know why. His health had been failing for a week; he told his doctor and closest friends he was seeing things and imagining dead people. He was just about to have a mental breakdown when he heard Smerdyakov had died. He suddenly thought, ‘The man is dead, I can blame him and save my brother. I have money. I’ll bring some notes and say Smerdyakov gave them to me before he died.’ You might say that’s a terrible thing to do—even to save your brother, it’s wrong to accuse a dead man. True. But what if Ivan really believed it, because he was losing his mind? You saw what he was like just now—he was standing and talking, but was his mind really there?”

“Then we have the letter—the defendant’s own letter, written two days before the crime, laying out the whole plan. So why do we need any other theory? The crime happened exactly as he described, and by the person who wrote it. Yes, gentlemen, it all went off without a hitch! He didn’t run away from his father’s window, all shy and respectful, even though he thought his beloved might be there. That’s ridiculous! No, he went inside and murdered him—probably in a rage, as soon as he saw his hated rival. But after killing him—probably with one blow from the brass pestle—and making sure she wasn’t there, he didn’t forget to check under the pillow and take the envelope, the torn cover of which is right here on the table.”

“I point out this detail because it’s very important. If he’d been an experienced thief, killing just for money, would he have left the torn envelope on the floor next to the body? If Smerdyakov, for example, had killed his boss to rob him, he would have just taken the envelope without even opening it there—he knew the notes were inside. If he’d taken the envelope, no one would ever have known about the robbery. So, would Smerdyakov have left the envelope behind?”

“No, leaving the envelope was something only a desperate murderer would do—not a thief, and not someone used to stealing. Dmitri Karamazov was obsessed with the idea that the money belonged to him. He grabbed the envelope, which he’d never seen before, tore it open to make sure the money was really there, and ran off with it, not even thinking that he’d left obvious evidence behind. Why? Because he was Karamazov, not Smerdyakov—he wasn’t thinking straight. He ran, heard Grigory shout behind him, the old man caught him, tried to stop him, and was knocked down by the brass pestle.”

“The defendant says that, feeling sorry for Grigory, he jumped down to check on him. Do you really believe that? Was that the time for compassion? No—he just wanted to make sure the only witness to his crime was dead or alive. Any other explanation doesn’t make sense. Notice that he took time to wipe Grigory’s head with a handkerchief, and after making sure he was dead, ran to his lover’s house, confused and covered in blood. Why didn’t he realize he’d be recognized right away? But the defendant says he didn’t even notice the blood. That’s believable—criminals often miss the obvious. Sometimes they’re cunning about one thing but totally clueless about another. But at that moment, he was thinking only about one thing: where was she? He rushed to her place and found out something shocking—she had gone to Mokroe to meet her first lover.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch decided to use the “historical method” to make his case, a favorite trick for nervous speakers, because it keeps their emotions in check. Right now, in his speech, he started talking about Grushenka’s “first lover” and shared some interesting ideas about that part of her life.

“Karamazov, who’d been insanely jealous of everyone, just seemed to give up and disappear when it came to this first lover. What’s even stranger is that he barely seemed to think about that rival, even though this man was actually a real threat. Maybe he thought the guy wasn’t real or was far away. But once he realized Grushenka had been hiding this lover from him and tricking him, because this man was truly important to her—her only hope—Karamazov instantly accepted it.

“Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, I have to point out this surprising part of the defendant’s character. Suddenly, he shows a strong sense of fairness, respect for women, and even admits she has the right to love someone else. And this happens right after he’s allegedly killed his own father for her! It’s true that the blood on his hands is demanding justice, and after destroying his own life, he has to ask himself what he is to her now. What can he be to the woman he loves so much, especially compared to her old lover who came back to her with new promises and a better life? And what could poor Karamazov give her now?

“Karamazov understood all of this. He knew his crime had closed off every path for him—he wasn’t a free man anymore, just a criminal waiting for judgment. This thought crushed him, so he jumped to a desperate solution that a person like him would see as the only way out: suicide. He ran to get the pistols he’d left with his friend Perhotin. On the way, he pulled out the money he’d taken by killing his father, money he now needed more than ever. Karamazov would die, he’d shoot himself, and he wanted to make sure everyone remembered it! He was always dramatic, living life to the fullest. ‘To her, to her!’ he thought, ‘I’ll throw a huge party, the wildest anyone’s ever seen! There’ll be singing, dancing, and I’ll toast to the woman I love and her new happiness. Then, right there at her feet, I’ll shoot myself. She’ll remember Mitya Karamazov, she’ll know how much I loved her!’

“Here we see his need for attention, his romantic sadness, and the wildness that runs in the Karamazov family. But there’s something deeper, ladies and gentlemen—something eating away inside him. That’s his conscience, the pain and guilt that never lets up. The gun seemed like the only way to end everything. But did Karamazov even wonder what happens after death, like Hamlet? No, that’s not his style. They have their Hamlets, but we have our Karamazovs!”

At this point, Ippolit Kirillovitch described in detail how Mitya (Dmitri) got ready, what happened at Perhotin’s, at the store, and with the drivers. He quoted things witnesses had said. The story was so powerful that the whole audience felt how desperate and guilty Mitya seemed when all the facts were put together.

“Why would he bother hiding anything? He almost confessed several times—he hinted, he nearly said it outright.” (Then he went over what the witnesses had said.) “He even told the peasant driving him, ‘You’re driving a murderer!’ But he couldn’t just come out with it yet; he had to get to Mokroe and finish his ‘romance’ there. But what did he find waiting for him? Almost right away, he realized his rival might not be unbeatable after all, and that his toast to Grushenka’s new happiness wasn’t wanted. But you know all this from the investigation. Karamazov totally outshined his rival, and then his mind shifted into a whole new, even scarier mood.

“We can be sure, ladies and gentlemen,” the prosecutor continued, “that guilt and the criminal mind punish themselves more than any court ever could. In fact, punishment here on earth actually helps criminals—it can even save them from total despair. Imagine how horrible it must have been for Karamazov when he learned Grushenka loved him, that she’d turned down her first lover for him, that she was calling Mitya to a new life, promising him happiness. And all of this happened when it was already too late for him!

“By the way, let me mention something important about the accused’s situation. This woman, his great love, had always seemed out of reach, someone he wanted desperately but couldn’t have. So why didn’t he shoot himself then? Why did he give up his plan and even forget about the pistol? Because he still hoped for love. During their wild party, he stuck close to Grushenka, who was more beautiful and charming than ever. He wouldn’t leave her side, totally devoted to her.

“His passion might have drowned out not just his fear of getting caught, but even his guilt—for a little while, at least. Imagine the state of mind of someone trapped by these feelings: first, the effect of drinking, noise, excitement, music, and Grushenka herself—singing, dancing, laughing. Second, the hope in the back of his mind that maybe he still had some time left, that maybe they wouldn’t arrest him until morning. A few hours can mean a lot; in that time, you can think about everything. I imagine it was like what a criminal feels on the way to execution: the journey is long, and at first, it feels like life will go on forever. The houses go by, but the end seems far away. Only bit by bit does it hit him that the end is coming, step by step, until the very last moment.
“That’s probably how it was for Karamazov. ‘They haven’t had time yet,’ he must have thought. ‘Maybe I can still figure something out. There’s still time, and right now—she’s so amazing!’

“His mind was a mess, but somehow he managed to hide half his money somewhere—I can’t explain how only half of the three thousand roubles he took from his father was found on him. He’d been to Mokroe before, partied there for days, and knew the house well. I think he hid some of the money in the house, just before he was arrested—maybe in a crack, under the floor, or in some corner. Why? The crisis could come at any time. He hadn’t decided what to do yet—his head hurt and his heart was with her—but he knew he needed money. Maybe it seems strange to plan ahead at a time like that, but he said himself that a month earlier, in another tense moment, he split his money and sewed half into a little bag. Even though that wasn’t true, it shows the idea was already in his mind. When he told the investigators he put fifteen hundred roubles in a bag (that never existed), maybe he just made it up on the spot, because he’d actually hidden half the money at Mokroe a couple hours earlier, just in case. Remember, Karamazov could imagine two totally different things at once.

“We’ve searched the house, but haven’t found the money. Maybe it’s still hidden, or maybe it disappeared and is with the prisoner now. Either way, when it all happened, he was at Grushenka’s side, on his knees in front of her, with his hands stretched out. He was so lost in the moment that he didn’t even hear the police coming to arrest him. He hadn’t had time to think up any defense. He was caught by surprise and had to face his judges right away.

“Ladies and gentlemen, there are moments in our work that are really hard, even for us. It’s terrible to look at someone when they realize everything is lost but still try to fight. You see the fear in their eyes as they try to figure out what you’re thinking, coming up with a thousand plans in a second but too scared to say anything. This is a kind of hell for the spirit—the desperate instinct to survive. Sometimes, even lawyers feel both horror and pity for the accused. That’s what we all saw then.

“At first, he was shocked and blurted out some incriminating things. ‘Blood! I deserve this!’ But he quickly pulled himself together. He hadn’t thought about what to say, so all he could do was deny it: ‘I’m not guilty of my father’s death.’ That was his first defense, and he tried to build on it. He explained his first guilty-sounding words by saying he was only responsible for hurting the servant, Grigory. ‘I’m guilty of that, but who killed my father, gentlemen? Who could have done it, if not me?’ Imagine—he asked us that, the very people sent to question him! Do you hear how quickly he said, ‘if not me’—that impatience, that mix of cleverness and naivety that Karamazovs always have? ‘I didn’t kill him, and you shouldn’t think I did! I wanted to kill him, I admit that, but I’m not the killer.’ He admits he wanted to do it, like he’s saying, ‘See how honest I am? So believe me when I say I didn’t.’ Sometimes, criminals are surprisingly shallow and trusting in moments like this.

“Then, one of the lawyers casually asked, ‘Wasn’t it Smerdyakov who killed him?’ As we expected, he got really angry—because we’d guessed what he was planning to say before he could bring it up himself. He quickly went to the other extreme and insisted Smerdyakov couldn’t have done it. But don’t believe that—it was just a trick. He wasn’t giving up the idea of blaming Smerdyakov. He meant to bring it up again later, because he had no one else to blame. He just needed to wait for a better opportunity, maybe the next day or after a few days. For now, he fell back on denial, getting moody and irritable. All this impatience led him to make up a silly story about looking through the window and respectfully leaving. The worst part was, he didn’t know what Grigory had told us.

“When we searched him, he got angry but also hopeful, because we didn’t find all three thousand roubles on him, just half. I’m sure that’s when he first thought up the little bag story. He knew it sounded unlikely, so he tried to make it more believable, weaving it into a story. Our job as investigators is to catch suspects by surprise so they blurt out their real ideas, no matter how unlikely or inconsistent. The best way is to hit them with a new fact they couldn’t have expected. We had such a fact: Grigory’s story about the open door the night of the murder. Karamazov had forgotten all about it and didn’t know Grigory had seen it.

“The effect was huge. He jumped up and yelled, ‘Then Smerdyakov murdered him, it was Smerdyakov!’ He showed his whole strategy, but in the least believable way, because Smerdyakov could only have killed Fyodor Pavlovitch after Karamazov had knocked Grigory down and run away. When we told him Grigory saw the door open before he fell and had heard Smerdyakov behind the screen—Karamazov was crushed. My smart colleague, Nikolay Parfenovitch, even said he was almost moved to tears seeing him. To make things worse, the defendant quickly told us about the famous little bag—so let’s talk about that story!

“Ladies and gentlemen, I’ve already explained why I think the story of the little bag is not just silly, but the most unlikely thing he could have invented. If you tried to make up the least believable excuse, you couldn’t do better. The problem with such stories is that real life is full of details, and when you skip over those, they trip you up. The suspect was asked, ‘Where did you get the material for the bag, and who made it?’ ‘I made it myself.’ ‘And where did you get the cloth?’ He was actually offended by such a simple question! But that’s how these people are. ‘I tore it from my shirt.’ ‘Then we’ll find a shirt with a piece missing, right?’ Imagine if we really had found it! But he didn’t think that far. ‘Maybe it wasn’t my shirt. Maybe I sewed it from my landlady’s old cap.’ ‘What cap?’ ‘Just some old cotton rag lying around.’ ‘Do you remember that clearly?’ ‘No, I don’t.’ He got angry—how can you not remember something like that? At the worst moments, people remember the tiniest details. He hid making that bag from everyone, must have been terrified someone would catch him with a needle. If he heard someone come, he’d hide behind the screen in his room.

“But why am I telling you all these details, all these little things?” Ippolit Kirillovitch suddenly cried out. “Because the defendant still clings to these ridiculous stories, even now. He hasn’t explained anything new in two months—nothing but these wild tales. ‘You have to believe me, on my honor,’ he says. We’d love to believe him, but only if there’s real proof—something besides what his brother guesses or what he did in the dark. If there was a real fact in his favor, we’d be happy to admit it and drop our accusation. But right now, justice demands we stand by our case.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to his final dramatic conclusion. He seemed almost feverish as he talked about the blood of a father crying for vengeance, murdered by his own son for money. He emphasized how all the facts fit together so perfectly.

“And no matter what you hear from the famous defense lawyer,” Ippolit Kirillovitch added, “no matter how moving or clever his speech is, remember, you’re in a court of justice. You are defenders of our justice, of Russia, of our families and everything we value! Your verdict will echo not just in this room, but all across Russia. Don’t let Russia down. Our ‘troika’—our wild, racing country—may be heading for disaster, and people everywhere are begging for a stop to this reckless ride. Other countries may not be standing aside out of respect, but out of horror or even disgust. Maybe one day they’ll decide to intervene for their own safety and progress. We’ve already heard voices from Europe worrying about us. Don’t give them more reason to hate us by letting a son get away with murdering his father!”

Even though Ippolit Kirillovitch was honestly emotional, he finished his speech with this big appeal, and it had a huge effect. When he finished, he left quickly and almost fainted in the next room. There was no applause, but serious people were impressed. The women weren’t quite as pleased, but they still admired his speech, especially since they trusted the famous defense lawyer, Fetyukovitch, to win in the end. “He’ll speak last, and of course he’ll win everyone over,” they said.

Everyone looked at Mitya (Dmitri). He sat through the whole prosecutor’s speech without saying a word, clenching his teeth, hands tight together, head down. Sometimes he looked up, especially when Grushenka was mentioned. When the prosecutor brought up Rakitin’s opinion of her, Mitya’s face twisted in contempt and anger, and he muttered loudly, “The Bernards!” When Ippolit Kirillovitch described questioning and pressuring him at Mokroe, Mitya listened very closely. At one point, it looked like he might jump up and shout, but he held back and just shrugged angrily. Later, people talked about the end of the speech, how the prosecutor bragged about questioning Mitya at Mokroe, and they teased Ippolit Kirillovitch about it. “He just couldn’t help boasting about how clever he was,” they said.
The court took a short break, just fifteen or twenty minutes. Everyone started talking at once. I remember some of the things people said.
“That was a powerful speech,” one man said seriously in a group.
“He used too much psychology,” someone else said.
“But it was all true, every bit of it!”
“Yes, he’s really good at this.”
“He wrapped it all up nicely.”
“Yeah, and he summed us up, too,” another voice chimed in. “Remember at the start, how he compared us all to Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“And at the end, too. But that part was nonsense.”
“And a bit confusing.”
“He got too carried away.”
“It wasn’t fair, not fair at all.”
“Still, it was a clever speech. He waited a long time, but he finally got to say his piece, ha ha!”
“What will the defense lawyer say?”
In another group, I heard:
“He shouldn’t have taken a shot at the Petersburg lawyer like that—‘appealing to your feelings,’ did you catch that?”
“Yeah, that was awkward.”
“He was in too much of a rush.”
“He’s a nervous guy.”
“We’re laughing, but imagine what the prisoner must be feeling.”
“Yeah, how must it feel for Mitya?”
In a third group:
“Who’s that lady—the heavyset one with the fancy glasses, sitting at the end?”
“She’s a general’s ex-wife. I know her.”
“That’s why she’s got those glasses.”
“She’s not much to talk about.”
“Oh, I think she’s got a certain charm.”
“Two seats over there’s a little blonde woman—she’s prettier.”
“They really caught him well at Mokroe, didn’t they?”
“Yeah, that part was smart. And he’s told that story at people’s houses before!”
“And he couldn’t resist telling it again. That’s just vanity.”
“He always takes things personally, ha ha!”
“Yeah, and he gets offended so easily. And all those long, dramatic sentences.”
“He kept trying to scare us. Did you catch the part about the troika? And, ‘They have Hamlets, but we only have Karamazovs!’ That was clever!”
“He just wanted to make the liberals happy. He’s scared of them.”
“And he’s scared of the defense lawyer, too.”
“Yeah, what will Fetyukovitch say?”
“Whatever he says, he won’t be able to fool our jury.”
“You think so?”
In a fourth group:
“What he said about the troika was good—that part about the other nations.”
“And it’s true, what he said about other countries not putting up with things like this.”
“What do you mean?”

“Well, in the English Parliament last week, someone got up and, talking about the Nihilists, asked the government if it wasn’t time to step in and ‘educate these barbaric people.’ I bet Ippolit was thinking of that. He mentioned it last week.”
“Not an easy job.”
“Not easy? Why not?”
“We’d just close Kronstadt and not send them any grain. What would they do then?”
“They’d get it from America. They already do.”
“No way!”
But then the bell rang, everyone hurried to their seats, and Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, stood up to speak.

Everything was silent as the famous defense lawyer began to speak. Everyone in the courtroom stared at him. He started off simply and confidently, with no sign of arrogance. He didn’t try to sound dramatic or emotional. Instead, he spoke like someone talking to a group of close friends who understood him. His voice was strong and warm, and there was something honest and straightforward in the way he spoke. Still, everyone could sense he might suddenly become passionate and really move the audience. His words weren’t as smooth as Ippolit Kirillovitch’s, but he was more precise, using short, clear sentences. Some of the women didn’t like how he kept leaning forward as he spoke, almost like he was about to pounce on the listeners. His long back bent so much it seemed like he had a spring in the middle and could fold himself in half.

At first, his speech was a bit scattered, with facts coming one at a time and not in any clear order. However, by the end, all the facts came together to form a complete picture. His speech had two main parts—the first was full of sharp criticism against the charges, sometimes even sarcastic. In the second part, his tone and style changed suddenly, and he became much more emotional and moving. The audience seemed to be waiting for this, and they listened with excitement.

He got right to the point, saying that even though he usually worked in Petersburg, he had often come to small towns to defend people he believed were innocent—or at least people he thought might be innocent. “That’s what happened to me this time,” he explained. “From the very first newspaper stories, something made me feel I should trust the defendant. What interested me most was something that sometimes happens in court cases, but almost never in such an extreme way as this. I should probably save that detail for the end, but I’ll say it now, because I like to be direct, even if that’s not always the best strategy. At least it shows I’m honest. Here’s what I mean: There’s a huge chain of evidence against the defendant, but not a single piece of it stands up to close examination on its own. As I read more in the papers, I felt more and more certain. Then, when the defendant’s family asked me to take the case, I hurried here. After looking at everything myself, I was completely convinced. I took this case to break that chain of evidence and show that every single piece of it is unproven and unbelievable.”
That’s how Fetyukovitch began his defense.

“Ladies and gentlemen of the jury,” he suddenly said, “I’m new in this town. I had no opinions about anyone before this. The defendant, who has a wild and uncontrolled temper, never insulted me. But he has insulted maybe hundreds of people here, so a lot of you already don’t like him. I understand why local society feels strongly against him. He really does have a violent temper. Still, people welcomed him around here; he was even invited into the family of my talented colleague, the prosecutor.”

(Note: At these words, some people in the audience laughed quietly, but everyone noticed. We all knew that the prosecutor only let Mitya visit because his wife—who was very moral but also stubborn and liked to do the opposite of her husband—insisted on it. Even so, Mitya didn’t visit often.)

“Even so,” Fetyukovitch continued, “I think that even someone as fair and smart as my opponent might have let himself develop a bias against my unlucky client. Of course, my client has done plenty to deserve that. When our sense of right and wrong is shocked, and our sense of taste even more so, we can be very unforgiving. The prosecutor’s speech was a harsh breakdown of the defendant’s character, and you could tell he was taking a tough, critical approach. He even got into complex ideas about the defendant’s psychology—ideas he probably wouldn’t have explored if he’d had a truly unfair or hateful attitude. But sometimes, things are even worse when we get carried away by our creative instincts, wanting to turn real life into a kind of story—especially if we’re talented at understanding people’s minds. Before I came here, people in Petersburg warned me, and I already knew, that I’d be up against a very sharp opponent who was famous for his psychological insight. But psychology is tricky—it can be used for good or bad.” (There was laughter in the audience.) “Excuse my comparison; I’m not a fancy speaker. Let’s look at an example from the prosecutor’s argument.

“He says the defendant ran away in the dark, climbed over the fence, was caught by the servant, and hit him with a brass pestle. Then he jumped back into the garden and spent five minutes checking if he’d killed the man or not. The prosecutor doesn’t believe the defendant’s claim that he went back out of pity for the old servant. ‘No,’ he says, ‘no one would feel that way at a moment like that. It’s unnatural; he went back to make sure the only witness to his crime was dead, which proves he committed the murder. He wouldn’t have gone back for any other reason.’

“This is psychology at work; but let’s use that same method and flip it around. The prosecutor says the killer went back to check if the witness was alive, but he also argues that the killer left behind obvious evidence in his father’s study—a torn envelope marked with ‘three thousand roubles.’ If the killer had just taken that envelope, no one would ever have known about the money or who took it. That’s the prosecutor’s own argument. So on one hand, we have someone so careless he leaves a huge clue behind, running away in a panic. But two minutes later, after attacking another man, we’re supposed to believe he’s suddenly ice-cold, thinking ahead to every detail. Are we really to accept that a person can be terrified and clueless one minute, and then as sharp and ruthless as a hunting eagle the next? If this was a cold-blooded killer, only thinking about himself, why would he spend five minutes checking on a man he’d just attacked, risking being caught? Why wipe the blood off the servant’s head with his own handkerchief, leaving more evidence? If he was so calculating, why not just hit the servant again and again to make sure he was dead and couldn’t testify against him?

“Also, if he really went back to see if the servant was alive, he left another clue—the brass pestle he’d taken from the two women, which they could easily recognize as theirs and prove he took. And it’s not like he just dropped it by accident—he threw it, because it was found fifteen steps from where Grigory lay. Why would he do that? Most likely because he felt terrible for hurting the old servant, so he threw away the weapon in disgust. That’s the only thing that makes sense. And if he could feel sorry about hurting someone, that means he didn’t kill his father. If he had committed murder, he wouldn’t have had room in his mind for pity—he would have been focused only on saving himself. In that case, he would have finished the job and killed the servant to keep him quiet, rather than spending five minutes worrying over him. There was room for pity because his conscience was clear up until then. This is a different psychological explanation. I’m using this example, ladies and gentlemen, to show you that psychology can be twisted to prove anything—it all depends on who’s using it. Even smart, serious people can let their imaginations run wild with it, often without realizing. I’m talking about how psychology can be misused, everyone.”
The crowd laughed and applauded again, this time at the prosecutor’s expense. I won’t repeat the entire speech here; I’ll just share some important parts of it.
One thing in Fetyukovitch's speech really stood out to everyone. He completely denied that the famous three thousand roubles even existed, and so, he argued, it wasn’t possible for them to be stolen.

“Ladies and gentlemen of the jury,” he began, “anyone looking at this case with fresh eyes has to notice something odd: the whole charge of robbery depends on money that nobody can prove even existed. They say three thousand roubles were stolen, but who actually saw this money? The only person who ever claimed to have seen the notes was the servant, Smerdyakov. He told the defendant and his brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch, about the money before the crime happened. Madame Svyetlov (Grushenka) heard about it, too. But out of those three, only Smerdyakov actually saw the notes. Nobody else had seen them.”

“So here’s the big question: if the money really did exist, and Smerdyakov saw it, when was the last time he saw it? What if Fyodor Pavlovitch took the notes out from under his bed and put them back in his cashbox without telling Smerdyakov? Remember, Smerdyakov said the notes were under the mattress. The defendant would have had to pull them out, but the bed was perfectly neat—no sign it had been disturbed. That’s in the official report. How could the defendant have taken the notes without messing up the bed? How could he have avoided getting blood on the clean sheets, since the bed was made up so carefully?”

“Now, what about the envelope found on the floor? I was surprised to hear the prosecutor say that if it weren’t for that envelope, nobody would have known about the money or the theft, and so nobody would have accused the defendant of robbery. So, according to the prosecutor, that torn piece of envelope is basically the only proof that a robbery happened. But just because there was an envelope on the floor, does that prove there was money in it, or that the money was stolen? Maybe Smerdyakov saw money in the envelope, but when was the last time he saw it? I talked to Smerdyakov myself, and he said he saw the notes two days before the crime. So why couldn’t Fyodor Pavlovitch, while waiting alone for the woman he was obsessed with, have opened the envelope and taken out the money himself? Maybe he thought, ‘She won’t believe the money is real unless I show her all the colorful notes at once—it’ll impress her.’ So he opens the envelope, takes out the money, and throws the empty envelope on the floor, not worried about leaving clues because it’s his own money.”

“Isn’t that a totally reasonable theory? Why shouldn’t it be possible? If something like that happened, then there was no robbery at all—no money, no theft. If you want to say the envelope proves there was money inside, why can’t I say the envelope was there because the owner took the money out himself?”

“But then you’ll ask: if Fyodor Pavlovitch took the money out, why didn’t the police find it when they searched the house? First, they did find some money in his cashbox. Second, maybe he took it out that morning or the night before to use it for something else—to give away, or to send to someone. Maybe he changed his mind about what he wanted to do with it and didn’t tell Smerdyakov. If there’s even a small possibility of this, how can anyone be so sure the defendant murdered for money, and actually stole it? That’s just making up stories. If you say something was stolen, you have to show the thing, or at least prove for sure that it existed. No one ever actually saw the notes.”

“Let me tell you about a case in Petersburg: a young man, just eighteen, sold fruit and vegetables for a living. In broad daylight, he went into a moneychanger’s shop with an ax, killed the shop owner, and stole fifteen hundred roubles. Five hours later, he was caught, and except for fifteen roubles he’d already spent, all the money was found on him. The shop assistant could tell the police exactly how much was stolen and even describe the notes and coins—and the police found those exact notes and coins on the criminal. He confessed, too. That’s what I call real evidence! In that case, you know the money was real—you can see it, touch it. Is that the case here? This is a question of life and death!”

“Yes, people say, but he was out spending lots of money that night—fifteen hundred roubles—where did he get it? But the fact that only fifteen hundred was found, and not the full three thousand, proves it wasn’t the same money and was never in any envelope. It was shown at the investigation that the defendant went straight from the women servants to Perhotin’s and didn’t go home, so he couldn’t have split the three thousand and hidden half somewhere else. That’s why the prosecutor now says maybe the money is hidden at Mokroe. Why not say it’s hidden in a castle dungeon, too? Isn’t that just way too wild and made-up? And if that idea falls apart, then the whole robbery charge disappears. What else could have happened to the other fifteen hundred? How could it just vanish if the defendant went straight from one place to another? Are we really going to ruin a man’s life over stories like this?”

“Some will say he couldn’t explain where he got the fifteen hundred roubles, and everyone ‘knew’ he was broke before that night. But who really knew that? The defendant has clearly explained where the money came from, and honestly, it makes perfect sense given his personality. The prosecutor prefers his own dramatic story: that a weak-willed man who accepted three thousand from his fiancée wouldn’t have put half aside and sewn it up, and even if he did, he would have kept taking out hundreds and spent it all in a month. The prosecutor said this like it was absolutely certain. But what if things happened differently? What if you’ve just made up a story about a completely different kind of person? That’s the point—you’ve invented a different Dmitri!”

“Maybe someone will say there are witnesses who saw him spend the whole three thousand from his fiancée all at once, so he couldn’t have hidden half. But who are these witnesses? We’ve already seen in court how shaky their stories are. Besides, when it’s someone else’s money, it always seems like more than it is. None of the witnesses actually counted the money—they just guessed. One witness, Maximov, even said he saw the defendant with twenty thousand! See, psychology can cut both ways. Let’s look at the other side for a minute.”

“A month before the crime, Katerina Ivanovna gave the defendant three thousand roubles to mail. But was it really given to him in such a humiliating, insulting way as we just heard? The first time the young lady told the story, it was different. The second time, she was angry and upset, shouting about old grudges. The fact that she told the story differently the second time means her memory could be off. The prosecutor won’t touch this topic, but I’ll just say: if a smart, principled person like her can suddenly contradict her first statement in court, obviously trying to hurt the defendant, then her evidence wasn’t calm or fair. Isn’t it likely she exaggerated? Maybe she made the insult sound worse than it was. Maybe the money was given in a way that made it possible for him to accept it—especially since he was expecting his father to give him the same amount soon. Maybe it was foolish of him, but he believed his father would pay him, so he thought he could always send off Katerina’s money and repay her.”

“But the prosecutor insists the defendant wouldn’t have set aside half the money and sewn it up in a little bag—that’s not his style, he says. But the prosecutor himself talked about the wild Karamazov personality, able to swing between extremes. That’s exactly the point—a Karamazov can go from wild partying to suddenly stopping himself if something important comes up. And the most important thing for him was love—the new love he felt, for which he needed money way more than for drinking with his girlfriend. If she said, ‘I’m yours, I won’t have Fyodor Pavlovitch,’ he’d need money to take her away. That mattered more than partying. Is it really so unlikely that he hid the money for an emergency?”

“But time passed, and Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t give the defendant the three thousand he expected. Instead, the defendant heard his father planned to use that money to win over the woman he loved. ‘If my father doesn’t give me the money, Katerina Ivanovna will think I’m a thief,’ he thought. Then he got the idea: he’d go to Katerina, show her the fifteen hundred roubles he still had hidden, and say, ‘I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief.’ So there are two big reasons he’d guard that money closely—he wouldn’t spend it a little at a time. Why can’t you believe he has a sense of honor? Maybe it’s a weird kind of honor, and maybe he makes mistakes, but it’s real, and he’s proven it.”

“But things got even more complicated. His jealousy and anxiety grew worse and worse: ‘If I pay back Katerina Ivanovna, where can I get money to run away with Grushenka?’ If he acted crazy, drank a lot, and caused trouble in that month, maybe it was because he was miserable and stressed out. Those two questions drove him to despair. He sent his younger brother to ask his father for the three thousand one last time, but before he got an answer, he barged in himself and ended up beating his father in front of witnesses. After that, he had no hope of getting the money; his father would never give it to him after being attacked.”

“That same evening, he hit himself on the chest—right where the little bag was—and swore to his brother that he had a way not to be a scoundrel, but he’d stay a scoundrel anyway, because he didn’t have the willpower to do the right thing. Why does the prosecutor refuse to believe Alexey Karamazov (Alyosha), who gave such honest, heartfelt, and convincing testimony? And why does he want me to believe money is hidden in some secret spot, like in a storybook dungeon?”

“That same night, after talking with his brother, the defendant wrote the letter everyone keeps talking about—the main ‘proof’ that he committed robbery! ‘I’ll beg from everyone, and if I don’t get the money, I’ll kill my father and take the envelope with the pink ribbon from under his mattress after Ivan leaves.’ The prosecutor calls this the whole plan for the murder, and says, ‘He did exactly what he wrote!’”

“But first, it was written by a drunk man who was really upset. Second, he only wrote about the envelope because he’d heard about it from Smerdyakov—he never saw it himself. Third, even if he wrote the letter, how can you prove he actually did what he wrote? Did he really take the envelope from under the pillow? Did he find the money? Did the money even exist? And was it really for the money that he ran off that night? He ran off in a hurry, not to steal, but to find the woman who broke his heart. He didn’t run off to carry out some careful plan—he ran suddenly, full of jealousy. And even if you say he took the money after the murder, are you sure he even committed the murder?
