I absolutely reject the robbery charge. You can’t accuse someone of robbery if you can’t even say for sure what was stolen. That’s just common sense. And as for murder—did he even do it? Is that proven? Or is that just another story?”

“Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, let me remind you that a man’s life depends on your decision, so you must be very careful. Even the prosecutor admitted that, until today, he wasn’t sure if the accused had fully planned the crime. He only decided that after seeing the drunken letter in court—the one that said, ‘All was done as written.’ But, I’ll say it again: the accused was running to her, to find out where she was. That’s a fact. If she had been home, he would have stayed with her and never would have done what he threatened in the letter. He acted on impulse and probably didn’t even remember that drunken letter by then. People say, ‘He grabbed the pestle,’ and the prosecutor built a whole theory around why he would see it as a weapon. But here’s a simple point: what if the pestle hadn’t been out in the open? What if it was put away in a cupboard? He wouldn’t have seen it, would have run away empty-handed, and there would have been no killing. So how can the pestle be proof that he planned the murder?

“Yes, I know he talked in taverns about killing his father. Two days before the crime, on the night he wrote that drunken letter, he only got into a fight with a shopkeeper—because, apparently, a Karamazov just can’t help causing trouble! But if he was truly planning a murder like the letter says, he wouldn’t have fought with anyone or even gone to the tavern—people planning horrible crimes try to stay out of sight, not be noticed, and that’s not even something they think about, it’s just instinct. The psychological arguments go both ways, and we can use them too. And all that tavern shouting—don’t we hear drunk people or even kids yell, ‘I’ll kill you!’ all the time? But they don’t actually kill anyone. That letter—wasn’t that just drunken ranting, like yelling outside a bar? Why can’t it be just that? Why do we call the letter ‘fatal’ just because his father was later found murdered, because a witness saw the accused running from the garden with a weapon and got knocked down? Is that enough to say everything happened exactly as in the letter, and that the letter was a real plan instead of just nonsense?

“Now, finally, we get to the main point: ‘Since he was in the garden, he must have killed his father.’ That’s the whole case against him: if he was there, then he must have done it. But what if that’s not true? I admit the evidence and coincidences look suspicious. But let’s look at the facts one by one. For example, why won’t the prosecution believe the accused when he says he ran away after looking in his father’s window? Remember how the prosecutor mocked the idea that the murderer suddenly felt ‘pious’ or respectful? But what if he really did feel some religious fear or family respect? At the preliminary hearing, the accused said, ‘My mother must have been praying for me at that moment,’ and that’s why he ran away when he realized Madame Svyetlov wasn’t in the house. The prosecutor says he couldn’t have known that just by looking through the window. But why not? The window opened when the accused signaled. Maybe Fyodor Pavlovitch said something, maybe he made a noise showing she wasn’t there. Why do we have to imagine everything just one way? In real life, all kinds of things happen that we can’t even imagine.

“‘But Grigory saw the door open, so the accused was in the house, so he killed his father.’ Let’s talk about that door. Only one person says it was open, and he wasn’t exactly in great shape at the time. But let’s say the door was open, and maybe the accused lied about it to protect himself. Maybe he did go inside. But what does that prove? He could have rushed in, run through the rooms, maybe pushed his father or even hit him. But as soon as he saw Madame Svyetlov wasn’t there, maybe he ran away, happy that she was safe and that he hadn’t killed his father. And maybe, because he’d resisted the urge to kill, because his conscience was clear, he was able to feel pity and jump over the fence a minute later to help Grigory after accidentally knocking him down in all the chaos.

“The prosecutor described in great detail the accused’s awful state of mind at Mokroe, saying he couldn’t enjoy love because of his father’s murdered body haunting him and the punishment waiting for him. And yet, the prosecutor said he still wanted love, explaining it away by saying he was drunk or comparing it to a criminal waiting for execution. But, Mr. Prosecutor, are you inventing a new personality for him? Could the accused really be so heartless as to think about love or escaping punishment if he’d just killed his father? No! If he realized the woman he loved cared for him, he’d feel even more desperate, maybe even want to kill himself if he really had his father’s murder on his conscience. He wouldn’t have forgotten where his pistols were! I know this man—the cold-hearted monster the prosecutor describes doesn’t match his character. If he were guilty, he would have killed himself, I’m sure of it. He didn’t because, as he said, ‘his mother’s prayers saved him,’ and he was innocent. That night at Mokroe, he was upset only about old Grigory, praying that the old man would recover, hoping he wouldn’t have to suffer for hurting him. Why can’t we see the facts that way? What solid proof do we have that the accused is lying?

“But people will say again, ‘Look at his father’s dead body! If the accused ran away without killing him, who else could have done it?’ That’s the main argument from the prosecution: If not him, then who? There’s no one else.

“But is that really true? Is there really no one else? We heard the prosecutor count everyone who was in the house that night: five people. Three of them—Fyodor Pavlovitch, old Grigory, and his wife—obviously couldn’t have done it. That leaves the accused and Smerdyakov. The prosecutor said the accused only blamed Smerdyakov because he had no one else to accuse, and if there had been anyone else, he would have blamed them instead. But why can’t I say the opposite? There are two people left: the accused and Smerdyakov. Why can’t I say you’re blaming my client just because you have no one else? And the only reason you have no one else is because you’ve decided Smerdyakov can’t be guilty.

“It’s true, only the accused, his two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov suspect Smerdyakov. But there are others with doubts—rumors, hints, suspicions, a general feeling that something is off. And we have several facts that point to Smerdyakov, even if they’re not absolutely conclusive. First, on the very day of the murder, he had one of his attacks, which the prosecutor went out of his way to explain as real. Then, Smerdyakov’s sudden suicide right before the trial. Then today, Ivan Karamazov, the accused’s brother, who used to believe his guilt, brought in a stack of notes and accused Smerdyakov of the murder. I agree, Ivan is suffering from brain fever, and maybe he’s desperately trying to save his brother by blaming a dead man. But Smerdyakov keeps coming up, there’s a feeling of mystery, of something we don’t understand. Maybe someday we’ll know the truth. But let’s leave that for now.

“The court has decided to keep going with the trial, but I want to say something about the prosecutor’s description of Smerdyakov, which was clever but, in my opinion, wrong. I visited Smerdyakov and talked to him, and he seemed very different to me. He was physically weak, yes, but his character wasn’t weak at all. I didn’t see any of the fearfulness or simplicity the prosecutor talked about. On the contrary, he was extremely suspicious, pretending to be simple, and actually pretty smart. The prosecutor underestimated him. I left with the strong feeling that Smerdyakov was spiteful, ambitious, vengeful, and jealous. I asked around: he hated his background and would get angry remembering he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He was rude to Grigory and his wife, who raised him. He cursed Russia, wished he could go to France and be French, but complained he couldn’t afford it. I think he only loved himself and thought very highly of himself. For him, culture just meant wearing good clothes and polished boots. He believed he was Fyodor Pavlovitch’s illegitimate son and probably resented his position compared to the real sons. They had everything; he was just the cook. He told me himself that he helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the money in the envelope, and it must have made him angry to see so much money going somewhere else. It was the first time he’d seen that much cash. Anyone jealous and ambitious might be deeply affected by that.

“The prosecutor cleverly went over all the reasons for and against Smerdyakov’s guilt, especially questioning his motive for faking a fit. But maybe he didn’t fake it; maybe he really had a fit, and then started waking up, as sometimes happens with people with epilepsy.

“The prosecutor asks: when could Smerdyakov have committed the murder? That’s easy to figure out. After an epileptic fit, people fall into a deep sleep, but maybe he started waking up when Grigory yelled, ‘Parricide!’ Maybe that loud shout woke him up, even if he was still half-asleep.

“He could have gotten out of bed, not fully aware, drawn toward the noise to see what was happening. His mind still foggy, he goes into the garden, walks toward the lit windows, and hears the terrible news from his master, who would be happy to see him. As he listens, his mind starts working, and a dangerous idea forms: kill the old man, take the three thousand rubles, and blame his young master. The temptation of money and the chance to get away with it might have been overwhelming. Sudden, powerful urges like this often come when the opportunity is right, especially for people who haven’t planned murder before. Smerdyakov might have used any stone from the garden as a weapon. Why would he do it? For the money—three thousand rubles could change his life. Maybe only Smerdyakov knew where the money was hidden. And what about the torn envelope found on the floor?

“Earlier, the prosecutor said only an amateur thief like Karamazov would leave the envelope behind, while someone like Smerdyakov would never leave such obvious evidence. But, as I listened, I realized I’d heard this same argument two days ago—from Smerdyakov himself! He seemed almost too eager for me to think that way, as if he was planting the idea. Didn’t he do the same thing during the investigation and with the prosecutor?

“‘But what about Grigory’s wife?’ people might ask. ‘She heard Smerdyakov groaning all night.’ Yes, but that evidence isn’t reliable. I once knew a woman who said a dog kept her awake all night, but it had only barked a couple times. It’s normal—if you wake up at night to a noise, you get annoyed, then fall right back asleep. If it happens a few times, you remember being woken up, but not the hours in between. The next morning, it feels like you were awake all night, but really, you were only woken up a few times.

“But then, why didn’t Smerdyakov confess in his last letter? Why would his conscience make him do one thing but not confess everything? But, you see, conscience means feeling sorry, and maybe Smerdyakov wasn’t sorry—just desperate. Despair and regret aren’t the same. Someone who kills themselves out of despair might actually feel even more hatred for the people they envied all their life.

“Ladies and gentlemen, be careful not to make a mistake! Is anything I’ve said really impossible or absurd? If what I’m saying is even a little bit possible, you shouldn’t convict. And my explanation isn’t just a tiny possibility—I truly believe it’s the truth. What upsets me most is that, out of all the evidence the prosecution has piled up, not one fact is completely certain. And yet, the accused’s life might be ruined by all these suspicions added together. Yes, the overall effect is powerful—bloody hands, a bloody shirt, the night filled with the shout ‘Parricide!’ and the old man’s death. But all the statements, gestures, shouts—they make things look worse than they are. But, jury, can you let that sway you? Remember, you have the serious power to decide this man’s fate, and with great power comes great responsibility.

“I stand by everything I said, but just for a moment, let’s imagine the prosecution is right, and my poor client did kill his father. This is just a theory—I still believe he’s innocent. But even if he were guilty, let me say one more thing. I’m sure you’re all struggling with this decision in your hearts and minds. Please forgive me for mentioning your feelings, but I want to be honest and sincere to the end. Let’s all be sincere!”

At this point, the speech was interrupted by loud applause. The last words were spoken so sincerely that everyone felt he really had more important things to say. But the President, hearing the applause, threatened to clear the court if it happened again. The room went silent, and Fetyukovitch began again, his voice now full of emotion, very different from before.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he began, “it’s not just all the evidence that makes things look bad for my client. What really hurts him is one simple fact—his father’s dead body. If this was just a regular murder case, you’d probably reject the charges, since all the evidence is so weak and strange if you look at it piece by piece. Or at least, you’d hesitate to ruin a man’s life just because he already has a bad reputation—which, sadly, he does deserve. But this isn’t just any murder case. It’s about a son killing his father—parricide. That shakes people up so much that even the small and flimsy bits of evidence start to seem more serious. How could anyone let a prisoner like this go free? What if he really did kill his father and gets away with it? That’s the fear everyone feels deep down inside.

“Yes, it’s an awful thing to kill your own father—the man who brought you into this world, cared for you, worried about you when you were sick, and tried to make you happy. To murder someone like that seems impossible, doesn’t it? But let’s ask ourselves: what does ‘father’ really mean? What is so special about that word? We’ve just talked about what a true father is supposed to be. But in this case, the father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, didn’t fit that picture at all. That’s what’s so sad. Sometimes, having a father can actually be a misfortune. Let’s look at that honestly—after all, you have a big decision to make, and we can’t be afraid to face the truth, just like the prosecutor said.

“But during his passionate speech, my opponent—who was already arguing against me before I even started—kept saying, ‘Oh, I won’t let this defense lawyer from Petersburg take over! I’m both the accuser and the defender!’ He said that a few times. But he forgot to mention that if this ‘terrible’ prisoner could remember for twenty-three years a single pound of nuts given to him by the only kind person in his childhood home, don’t you think he could also remember for twenty-three years how he ran around his father’s backyard, barefoot, with his pants barely held up by one button—just like Dr. Herzenstube described?

“Gentlemen of the jury, do we really need to dig into this sad situation again? Why paint my client as a heartless monster? Yes, he’s wild and undisciplined, but whose fault is that? Who’s to blame for the way he was raised, for him turning out this way, even though he’s actually sensitive and thankful by nature? Did anyone ever teach him right from wrong? Did he get a good education? Was he ever shown any love as a child? He was left alone, like an animal. Maybe he even hoped to see his father again after all those years apart, and maybe he wanted to forgive him. But what did he find when he arrived? He was met with cruel jokes, suspicion, and constant arguments about money. All he heard was disgusting talk and bad advice, and then he saw his own father stealing his girlfriend from him with his own money. That’s horrible! And the old man kept complaining that his son was disrespectful and mean, spreading lies about him, ruining his reputation, and buying up his unpaid debts to get him thrown into jail.

“Juries, people like my client—who seem fierce and wild—are often the most sensitive deep down, even if they don’t show it. Please don’t laugh at this idea. The prosecutor just made fun of my client for loving Schiller and poetry—for loving things that are noble and beautiful! I wouldn’t have laughed at that. People like him, who seem rough on the outside, often secretly long for kindness, for goodness, and for justice, almost as a way to balance out their wild side. They can love deeply—especially women—with a kind of pure, spiritual love. Don’t laugh; it’s true for people like this. Sure, sometimes their feelings are obvious and not very refined, and people notice that, but their real selves are hidden. Their wild feelings burn out quickly, but when they meet someone good and noble, they want to change, to become better, ‘sublime and beautiful,’ even if others make fun of those words.

“I said earlier I wouldn’t talk about my client’s engagement, but let me say just a little. What we heard before wasn’t real evidence—it was just the angry outburst of a woman who was hurt and wanted revenge. And she, of all people, shouldn’t call him a traitor—she was the one who betrayed him! If she’d stopped to think, she never would have said those things. Please, don’t believe her. My client is not the monster she called him!

“On the night before He was crucified, the Savior said: ‘I am the Good Shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep so that none of them are lost.’ Let’s not be the ones who let a man’s soul be lost!

“I asked earlier what ‘father’ means, and called it a great and precious word. But we have to be honest, gentlemen. I believe in calling things by their real names: someone like old Karamazov doesn’t deserve to be called a father. Loving a father who doesn’t deserve it is foolish and impossible. Love can’t come from nowhere—only God can create something from nothing.

“‘Fathers, don’t make your children angry,’ the apostle wrote, out of love. I’m not saying this just for my client—I’m saying it for all fathers. Who gave me the right to preach to fathers? No one. But as a person and as a citizen, I have to say this—vivos voco! We’re not here long, and we do and say a lot of bad things. So let’s take this chance, while we’re all together, to say something good to each other. That’s what I’m doing now. This platform gives us a chance to be heard across Russia! I’m not just speaking to the fathers in this courtroom—I’m speaking to all fathers: ‘Fathers, don’t drive your children to anger.’ Let’s do what Christ told us first, and only then expect the same from our kids. If we don’t, we’re not fathers—we’re our children’s enemies, and they become ours, and it’s our own fault. ‘The measure you give will be the measure you get’—that’s not just my idea, it’s what the Gospel says. How can we blame our kids if they treat us the way we treated them?

“Not long ago in Finland, a maid was suspected of secretly having a baby. People watched her, and they found a box hidden in the attic, behind some bricks. When they opened it, they found the body of a newborn baby she had killed. In that same box, they found two tiny skeletons—the remains of two other babies she admitted to killing right after they were born.

“Was she a mother to those children? Sure, she gave birth to them, but was she really their mother? Would anyone dare call her that sacred name? Let’s be brave, gentlemen. It’s our duty right now to not be scared of tough truths, like those women in Ostrovsky’s play who panic at certain words. Let’s show we’re not afraid to say it: a father isn’t just someone who makes a child—he has to act like a real parent, too.

“Of course, there’s another way to look at ‘father’—that even if a father is a monster, even if he’s his child’s enemy, he’s still a father just because he created them. But that’s a mystical idea I can’t really understand—I can only accept it on faith, like other things religion asks us to believe. But that idea should stay out of real life. In real life, with its own rules and responsibilities, if we want to be humane—Christian, really—we need to base our actions on reason and experience, using ideas we’ve truly thought through. We need to act rationally, not like we’re dreaming or out of our minds, so we don’t hurt people or ruin someone’s life. That’s real Christian work—not just mystical, but reasonable and kind.”

As he finished that point, loud applause broke out from many people in the courtroom, but Fetyukovitch raised his hands, asking for silence so he could continue. The room quickly grew quiet again, and he went on.

“Do you think our children, as they grow up and start to think for themselves, won’t ask these tough questions? Of course they will, and we can’t expect them not to. When a young person sees their own father acting badly—especially compared to their friends’ good fathers—they can’t help but wonder. The usual answer is: ‘He made you, you’re his flesh and blood, so you have to love him.’ But the child thinks, ‘But did he love me when he made me? Did he do it for my sake? He didn’t even know me back then—not even if I’d be a boy or girl. Maybe it happened in a moment of passion, maybe drunk, and all he passed on was his own bad habits. Why am I supposed to love him just for creating me if he never cared about me afterward?’

“Maybe you think these are cruel questions, but you can’t expect kids to never ask them. ‘Push nature out the door and it comes in the window.’ Let’s not be scared of words—let’s use reason and kindness to answer. How should we decide? Like this: the son should be able to ask his father, ‘Father, why should I love you? Show me why I should.’ If the father can answer and give him a good reason, then that’s a real, healthy parent-child relationship—not just based on old superstitions, but on something solid and good. But if the father can’t answer, then the family bond is broken. He’s not a true father anymore, and the son has the right to see him as a stranger or even an enemy. This courtroom, gentlemen, should be a place where real, honest ideas are taught.”

(Here, the speaker was interrupted by wild applause. Not everyone clapped, but a lot of people did—fathers and mothers in the audience, people in the gallery, even some important-looking old men in special seats behind the judges. Handkerchiefs were waved, people shouted, and the President rang his bell as hard as he could, clearly irritated but not brave enough to kick everyone out like he’d threatened earlier. When things finally quieted down, the President just repeated his warning, and Fetyukovitch, both excited and proud, kept going.)

“Gentlemen, remember that terrible night we’ve talked about so much, when the son climbed over the fence and came face to face with the man who had always been his enemy, even though he was his father. I say again: he didn’t go there for money—the robbery charge is ridiculous, as I’ve already shown. And he didn’t go there to kill his father. If he had, he would have brought a weapon. He grabbed the brass pestle by instinct, without thinking. If he really did trick his father by tapping at the window and sneaking inside—though I don’t believe that story, but let’s just pretend for a moment—even then, I swear to you, if it had been anyone else, just a normal enemy and not his father, he would have just checked the rooms, seen the woman wasn’t there, and run away without hurting anyone. Maybe he would have shoved his rival or hit him, but nothing more. He was only looking for her. But it was his father—his enemy since childhood, his rival in love. Just seeing him was enough to make all his anger and hatred explode in a moment, clouding his mind. It was a burst of madness—a wild, natural reaction, like nature itself demanding revenge for its laws being broken.

“But I insist—my client didn’t murder him, not really! I say it loud and clear. He only swung the pestle in a wave of disgust and anger, not wanting or even knowing he would kill him. If he hadn’t picked up that heavy object, maybe he would have only knocked his father down. When he ran away, he didn’t know if the old man was dead. This kind of killing isn’t murder—it’s not parricide. Only prejudice can call it that.

“But I ask you again, from the bottom of my heart—did this murder really happen? If you find him guilty and punish him, he’ll think: ‘These people did nothing to raise me, to educate me, to help me become better. They never fed me, visited me in prison, or clothed me, and now they send me away to hard labor. I don’t owe them anything anymore. They were cruel, so I’ll be cruel too.’ That’s what he’ll feel, gentlemen. And by finding him guilty, you’ll actually make things easier for him—he’ll feel less guilty, and he won’t regret what he’s done. At the same time, you’ll destroy any chance for him to change and become a better person, because he’ll stay angry and blind for the rest of his life.

“But if you really want to punish him and save his soul at the same time, then show him mercy! You’ll see how shocked and shaken he’ll be. He’ll say, ‘How can I handle this kindness? Do I even deserve it?’ That’s what he’ll feel.

“I understand his heart, gentlemen. It may be wild, but it’s grateful. He’ll be humbled by your mercy—he longs for a great, loving act. He’ll regret his past, because deep down, he has good in him. Your kindness will open his heart and show him that God and people can be forgiving and just. He’ll be overwhelmed by guilt and responsibility, and instead of saying, ‘I owe nothing,’ he’ll say, ‘I’m more guilty than anyone, and everyone else is better than me—they wanted to save me, not destroy me!’ He’ll cry with real regret. This act of mercy is easy for you, especially since there’s no real evidence. How could you possibly say: ‘Yes, he’s guilty’?

“It’s better to let ten guilty people go than to punish one innocent person! Do you hear the voice of our great history? Our courts aren’t just for punishing, but for saving people. Let other countries focus on revenge and strict laws—we should care about the spirit of the law, about saving and changing lost people. If Russia and her justice are truly like this, then we should be proud! Don’t let anyone scare us with wild stories. Russia’s justice should move forward with dignity. The fate of my client—and the honor of Russian justice—are in your hands. You will protect it, you will save it, and you will show the world that justice is in good hands!”

This is how Fetyukovitch (the defense lawyer) finished his speech, and the crowd exploded with excitement like a storm. There was no way to stop it: the women cried, and many of the men cried too—even two important officials had tears in their eyes. The President just let it happen and didn’t even ring his bell for order. Later, the ladies said stopping such emotion would be like stopping something sacred. Even Fetyukovitch himself was honestly moved.

Right then, Ippolit Kirillovitch (the prosecutor) got up to make some objections. People stared at him angrily. The ladies whispered, “What? How dare he object after that speech?” But even if every woman in the courtroom—including his own wife—had tried to stop him, they couldn’t have. He was pale and shaking with emotion. At first, he stumbled over his words and could barely speak, but after a moment, he recovered. I’ll only share a few parts of his new speech.

“... I’m accused of making up a story. But isn’t the defense’s story just another wild tale—only without the poetry? Fyodor Pavlovitch, while waiting for his girlfriend, supposedly rips open the envelope and throws it on the floor. We’re even told exactly what he said while doing it. Isn’t that just imagination? What proof do we have that he took the money out? Who heard what he said? The feeble-minded Smerdyakov is turned into some kind of tragic hero, getting revenge for being born out of wedlock—isn’t that a made-up story too? And the son who breaks into his father’s house and kills him—without killing him? That’s not just a story, that’s a riddle no one can solve. If he killed him, then he killed him. What’s this about killing him without killing him? Who can make sense of that?”

“Then we’re told that this courtroom stands for real, honest ideas, and in the same speech, someone says that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is just an old-fashioned belief! But if parricide is just a silly superstition, and every child starts asking why they should love their father, what will happen to society? What about the family? Now, parricide is only a scary story for Moscow merchants’ wives, apparently. The most important things that keep Russian justice strong are being twisted around, just to justify something that can’t be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ says the defense lawyer—but that’s exactly what the criminal wants, and tomorrow we’ll see how crushed he really is. And isn’t the defense lawyer too modest, just asking for an acquittal? Why not make a charity in the murderer’s honor, so future generations can remember his ‘achievement’? Religion and the Gospel are changed around—that’s just called ‘mysticism’ now, and only the defense lawyer knows the real Christianity, which has been analyzed by reason and common sense. So we’re given a false version of Christ! The defense lawyer shouts, ‘What measure you use will be used against you,’ and then claims that Christ tells us to treat others as they treat us—and this is supposed to be truth and common sense! We only look at the Gospel before making speeches to impress the crowd with our knowledge of a strange old book, just to make a point! But Christ actually taught something very different: He said we shouldn’t do what the wicked world does; we should forgive and turn the other cheek, not take revenge. That’s what our God taught us—not that saying children shouldn’t murder their fathers is just an old belief. And from this place of truth and reason, we shouldn’t try to rewrite the Gospel, which the defense lawyer calls just ‘the crucified lover of humanity,’ instead of what all of Russia calls Him: ‘For Thou art our God!’ ”

At this, the President interrupted Ippolit Kirillovitch, asking him not to get carried away or go too far—like presidents always do in court. The audience was restless and uncomfortable; some even muttered angrily. Fetyukovitch didn’t bother to answer; he just went up to the podium, put his hand on his heart, and in an offended but dignified voice, spoke a few words. He made a light, joking comment about “making up stories” and “psychology,” and at the right moment quoted, “Jupiter, you’re angry, so you must be wrong,” which made everyone laugh, because Ippolit Kirillovitch was nothing like Jupiter. When the prosecutor accused him of encouraging kids to kill their fathers, Fetyukovitch said, with dignity, that he wouldn’t even answer that. As for being accused of unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted this was a personal attack and that he expected not to have his reputation insulted in court. But the President stopped him there, too, and Fetyukovitch finished his speech with a polite bow, while the crowd hummed with approval. The ladies thought Ippolit Kirillovitch was now “totally defeated.”

Then the accused, Mitya (Dmitri), was allowed to speak. He stood up, but said very little. He was completely exhausted, both in body and mind. The confidence and strength he’d had that morning were almost gone. It seemed like he’d gone through something that had taught him a huge lesson he’d never understood before. His voice was weak, and he didn’t shout like earlier. Everything he said sounded humbled, defeated, and ready to accept his fate.

“What can I say, gentlemen of the jury? My judgment day has come, and I feel God’s hand on me! The end has come for a man who has made mistakes. But, before God, I swear to you, I am innocent of my father’s blood! For the last time, I repeat—I didn’t kill him! I’ve made mistakes, but I loved what’s good. I tried to get better every moment, but I lived like a wild animal. I thank the prosecutor—he told me things about myself I didn’t know; but he’s wrong, I didn’t kill my father. I thank my lawyer, too. I cried listening to him; but he didn’t need to suggest I killed my father, because it’s not true. And don’t believe the doctors. I’m perfectly sane—just sad. If you let me go, I’ll pray for you. I’ll be a better man—I promise before God! But if you condemn me, I’ll break my sword over my own head and kiss the pieces. But please, spare me, don’t take my God away! I know myself—I’ll fight back! My heart is heavy, gentlemen... have mercy!”
He almost collapsed into his seat; his voice broke, and he could barely say the last words. After that, the judges started asking questions and both sides gave their final statements.

I won’t go into all the details. Finally, the jury stood up and went off to decide. The President was very tired, so his final instructions to the jury were pretty weak: “Be fair, don’t get carried away by the defense’s fancy words, but do consider their arguments. Remember, you have a big responsibility,” and so on.

The jury left, and the court took a break. People stood up, moved around, talked about everything they’d seen, and grabbed snacks from the buffet. It was really late—almost one in the morning—but nobody left. The tension was so strong that no one could even think about going home. Everyone waited, nervous and anxious—though honestly, most of the ladies were just impatient and excited, not really worried. They were sure there would be an acquittal and were ready for a dramatic celebration. Many men also believed Mitya would be found not guilty; some were happy about it, others looked upset, and some just looked sad because they didn’t want him acquitted. Fetyukovitch was confident he’d won, and people crowded around him, congratulating him and trying to get close.

“There are,” he told a group (I heard later), “invisible threads connecting the defense lawyer and the jury. You can feel them during your speech. I felt them today. They’re real. We’ve won. Don’t worry.”
“What will our peasants say now?” asked a chubby, grumpy, pock-marked landowner, joining a group of men talking nearby.
“But not all of them are peasants. Four of them are government clerks,” someone replied.
“That’s right, there are clerks,” added a district council member, joining in.
“And did you know that Nazaryev, the merchant with the medal, is one of the jurymen?”
“So what?”
“He’s a smart guy.”
“But he never talks.”
“He doesn’t say much, but that’s a good thing. We don’t need someone from Petersburg teaching him—he could teach the whole city himself. He’s got twelve kids. Imagine that!”
“Come on, you don’t really think they’ll convict him, do you?” a young official said in another group.
“They’ll acquit him for sure,” someone answered confidently.

“It would be shameful, even disgusting, not to acquit him!” the official cried. “Even if he did kill his father—there are fathers and then there are fathers! Plus, he was in such a wild state... Maybe he just swung the pestle and accidentally knocked the old man down. But it was stupid to get the valet involved. That was just a silly theory! If I were Fetyukovitch, I’d just have said: ‘He killed him, but he’s not guilty, that’s all!’ ”
“That’s basically what he did, just without saying, ‘that’s all!’ ”
“No, Mihail Semyonovitch, he pretty much said that too,” a third person chimed in.
“Remember last Lent? An actress here was found not guilty after she cut her lover’s wife’s throat.”
“Oh, but she didn’t finish cutting it.”
“Doesn’t matter—she started to.”
“What did you think about what he said about children? Wasn’t that great?”
“Amazing!”
“And the part about mysticism too!”
“Oh, enough about mysticism!” someone else said. “Think about Ippolit and what’s going to happen to him now. His wife will scratch his eyes out tomorrow for what he did to Mitya.”
“Is she here?”
“Of course not! If she were here, she’d have scratched them out in court. She’s at home with a toothache. Ha ha ha!”
“Ha ha ha!”
In another group nearby:
“I bet they really will acquit Mitenka.”
“Wouldn’t be surprised if he turns the city upside down tomorrow. He’ll be drinking for ten days straight!”
“Oh, the devil!”
“Of course the devil’s involved. Where else would he be if not here?”
“Well, I’ll admit the speech was amazing. But still, it’s not right to smash your father’s head in with a pestle! What’s the world coming to?”
“The chariot! Remember the chariot?”
“Yeah, he turned a cart into a chariot!”
“And tomorrow he’ll turn a chariot back into a cart, just to fit his story.”
“People are so clever these days! Is there any real justice left in Russia?”

But then the bell rang. The jury had been gone for exactly an hour—no more, no less. The courtroom went silent as everyone sat down again. I remember how the jurymen walked in. Finally! I won’t repeat all the questions—they’ve slipped my mind anyway. But I do remember the answer to the President’s first and most important question: “Did the accused commit the murder for money and plan it ahead of time?” (I don’t remember the exact words.) The room was completely silent. The foreman of the jury, the youngest of the clerks, said in a loud, clear voice, in the total silence:
“Yes, guilty!”

And the answer was the same for every question: “Yes, guilty!”—with no mention of mercy or anything to make it less harsh. No one expected this; almost everyone thought they’d at least recommend mercy. For a moment, the whole courtroom was frozen—people who wanted Mitya convicted and those who wanted him freed were both shocked. But that only lasted a second; then everyone started talking at once. Many men looked happy and even rubbed their hands, not hiding their delight. Those who disagreed with the verdict seemed crushed and confused, whispering and shrugging. But the women were the most upset—I thought they might start a riot. At first, they couldn’t believe their ears. Then suddenly the whole room was filled with shouts: “What does this mean? What happens now?” They jumped up from their seats, almost as if the verdict could be changed on the spot. Right then, Mitya suddenly stood up and cried out in a heartbroken voice, stretching his arms out in front of him:
“I swear to God and on the terrible Day of Judgment, I am not guilty of my father’s blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends, please have pity on the other woman!”

He couldn’t say more and broke down into loud, terrible sobs that echoed through the courtroom in a voice that didn’t even sound like him. From the far back of the gallery came a piercing scream—it was Grushenka. She had managed to get back into the courtroom before the lawyers’ speeches began. Mitya was taken away. The final sentence would be decided the next day. The whole court was in chaos, but I didn’t stay to watch. I only remember a few things people said as I was leaving.
“He’ll get twenty years in the mines!”
“Not less than that.”
“Well, our peasants held strong.”
“And they’ve finished off our Mitya.”

Early in the morning, around nine o’clock, five days after the trial, Alyosha (Alexey) went to see Katerina Ivanovna. He needed to talk with her about something very important for both of them, and he had a message to deliver. They sat together in the same room where Katerina Ivanovna had once received Grushenka. In the next room, Ivan Fyodorovitch was lying unconscious with a high fever. Right after what happened at the trial, Katerina Ivanovna had insisted that the sick and barely conscious Ivan be brought to her house, even though she knew people would gossip and disapprove. Of her two relatives living with her, one had left for Moscow as soon as the court scene was over, but the other stayed. Even if both had left, Katerina Ivanovna would have still stuck to her decision, caring for Ivan day and night. Doctors Varvinsky and Herzenstube were treating him. The famous doctor from Moscow had already left, refusing to say how the illness would end. Though the doctors tried to encourage Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, it was clear they couldn’t promise that Ivan would recover.

Alyosha had been visiting his sick brother twice every day. But this visit was especially urgent, and he knew it would be hard to bring up what he had to say. Still, he was in a hurry. He had another appointment that morning that he couldn’t miss, so he really needed to get things done quickly.

They had been talking for about fifteen minutes. Katerina Ivanovna looked pale and completely worn out, but she was also extremely tense, almost hysterical. She had a feeling she knew why Alyosha had come.

“Don’t worry about his decision,” she said, her voice full of confidence as she looked at Alyosha. “No matter what, he’ll have to go through with it. He must escape. That poor man, that hero with so much pride and honesty—not Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but the man in the next room, who’s giving up everything for his brother,” Katya added, her eyes shining. “He told me the whole escape plan a while ago. You know he’s already started making arrangements... I’ve told you some of this before... The escape will probably happen at the third stage, when the prisoners are being taken to Siberia. That’s still a long way off. Ivan Fyodorovitch has already met with the supervisor of the third étape. But we don’t know yet who will actually be in charge of the group, and there’s no way to find out this early. Maybe tomorrow I’ll show you all the details of the plan that Ivan Fyodorovitch left me right before the trial, in case it was needed... That was when—you remember?—you caught us arguing. He had just gone downstairs, but when I saw you, I made him come back up. Do you remember? Do you know what we were fighting about?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha.

“Of course, he didn’t tell you. We were fighting about the escape plan. He’d told me the main idea three days earlier, and we started arguing right away—we argued for three days straight. I was angry because, when he told me that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch was found guilty, he would run away with that woman, I got furious—I don’t even know exactly why... Oh, of course, I was angry about that woman, and that she would go abroad with Dmitri!” Katerina Ivanovna burst out, her lips shaking with anger. “As soon as Ivan Fyodorovitch saw that I was upset about her, he immediately thought I was jealous of Dmitri, that I still loved him. That’s how our first fight started. I didn’t want to explain, I couldn’t ask for forgiveness. I couldn’t stand that someone like him might think I still loved Dmitri, especially when I’d told him long ago that I only loved him! It was just my anger at that woman that made me so mad at him. Three days later, the night you came, he gave me a sealed envelope that I was supposed to open if anything happened to him. Oh, he knew he might get sick! He said the envelope had all the details of the escape, and if he died or got seriously ill, I was supposed to save Mitya by myself. He also left me nearly ten thousand—that money the prosecutor talked about, since someone had told him Ivan sent it to be exchanged. I was really moved that Ivan Fyodorovitch hadn’t given up on saving his brother, and that he trusted me with this plan, even though he was still jealous and still thought I loved Mitya. That’s real sacrifice! No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, you can’t imagine how big of a sacrifice that is. I wanted to fall at his feet out of respect, but I thought he’d just think I was happy about Mitya being saved (and he definitely would have thought that!), so I got angry again, just at the thought of him misunderstanding me, and instead of thanking him, I blew up again! Oh, I’m so miserable! It’s my character, my terrible, unhappy character! You’ll see, I’ll end up making him leave me too, for someone better, just like Dmitri did. But... no, I couldn’t take it, I’d rather die. And when you came in that time, and I called you and told him to come back, I was so furious at the look of disgust and hate he gave me that—do you remember?—I shouted to you that he was the one who convinced me Dmitri was a murderer! I said that on purpose to hurt him again. He never, ever convinced me Dmitri was a murderer. Actually, I convinced him! My awful temper was behind everything! I set up that horrible scene at the trial. He wanted to prove he was honorable, that even if I loved his brother, he wouldn’t destroy him out of jealousy or revenge. So he came to the court... I’m the cause of it all, it’s all my fault!”

Katya had never told Alyosha these things before, and he realized she had reached a level of pain so deep that even her pride was crushed by grief. Alyosha also knew there was another terrible reason for her suffering, even though she had hidden it from him since the trial; but it would have hurt him too much if she started talking about it now. She was tormented by guilt over her “betrayal” at the trial, and Alyosha could feel that her conscience was pushing her to confess everything to him, maybe even break down crying on the floor. But he dreaded that moment and wanted to spare her. That made the message he had to deliver even harder. He shifted the subject back to Mitya.

“It’s all right, it’s all right, don’t worry about him!” she said again, sharply and stubbornly. “All this is just temporary, I know him, I know his heart too well. I’m sure he’ll agree to escape. It’s not happening right away; he’ll have time to get used to the idea. Ivan Fyodorovitch will be better by then and will handle everything, so I won’t have to do anything. Don’t worry—he’ll agree to run away. He already has: do you think he would let go of that woman? And they won’t let her go to him, so of course he’ll escape. The one he’s most afraid of is you—he’s worried you won’t approve of him running away, that you’ll think it’s wrong. But you should allow it, if your approval is so important,” Katya added with a bitter smile. She paused and smiled.

“He talks about some hymn,” she continued, “some cross he has to bear, some duty; I remember Ivan Fyodorovitch told me all about it, and you wouldn’t believe how he talked!” Katya suddenly cried, full of emotion she couldn’t hide. “If you knew how much he loved that wretched man when he told me, and maybe at the same time how much he hated him. And when I heard his story and saw his tears, I just laughed at him. I was awful! Yes, I was awful. I’m the reason he’s so sick. But that man in prison can’t even suffer,” Katya finished angrily. “Can someone like him even feel pain? Men like him never suffer!”

There was real hatred and disgust in her words. And yet she was the one who had betrayed him. “Maybe it’s because she knows she’s hurt him that she sometimes hates him,” Alyosha thought. He hoped it was only “sometimes.” He could tell that Katya was challenging him with her last words, but he didn’t react.

“I asked you to come this morning to make you promise that you’ll persuade him yourself. Or do you also think that escaping would be dishonorable, cowardly, or maybe... unchristian?” Katya said, looking even more defiant.
“Oh, no. I’ll tell him everything,” Alyosha muttered. “He wants you to come see him today,” he suddenly blurted out, staring right at her. She jumped back a little on the sofa, looking shocked.
“Me? Really?” she whispered, turning pale.

“Yes, really! You should go!” Alyosha said, suddenly sounding more energetic. “He especially needs you right now. I wouldn’t have brought this up if it weren’t necessary. He’s sick, he’s not himself, and he keeps asking for you. He doesn’t want you to forgive him—‘It’s impossible to forgive me,’ he says—but he just wants you to show up at his door. So much has happened to him since that day. He realizes now just how badly he’s hurt you—he never understood it before. All he wants is for you to come to his doorway.”
“It’s so sudden...” Katya whispered. “I’ve had a feeling for days that you would come with that message. I knew he’d ask me to come. But it’s impossible!”

“Even if it feels impossible, do it. Just think about it—he finally realizes how much he’s hurt you, maybe for the first time in his life. He told me, ‘If she refuses to come, I’ll be unhappy for the rest of my life.’ Do you see? Even though he’s been sentenced to twenty years of hard labor, he’s still hoping to be happy—doesn’t that make you feel sorry for him? Please, you have to go see him; even though he’s ruined, he’s innocent,” Alyosha insisted. “His hands are clean—there’s no blood on them! For the sake of all the pain he’s going to go through, go now. Greet him as he heads into a dark future—just stand at his door, that’s all... You should do it, you have to!” Alyosha finished, putting extra force into the word “ought.”
“I should... but I can’t...” Katya moaned. “He’ll look at me... I can’t do it.”
“You need to look each other in the eye. How will you go on living if you don’t face this now?”
“It would be better to suffer forever,” she said.
“You have to go, you have to go,” Alyosha repeated, not backing down.
“But why today, why right now?... I can’t leave Ivan—”
“You can, just for a moment. It’ll only take a minute. If you don’t come, he’ll be completely delirious by tonight. I promise I’m not lying—please, have pity on him!”
“Have pity on me!” Katya cried out, hurt, and she started to sob.
“Then you’ll come,” Alyosha said firmly when he saw her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you’re coming right away.”
“No, don’t tell him that, please,” Katya said in alarm. “I’ll come, but don’t tell him ahead of time, because maybe I’ll go and then not go in... I just don’t know yet—”
Her voice broke off. She gasped for air. Alyosha stood up to leave.
“And what if I run into someone?” she said quietly, turning pale again.
“That’s exactly why you should go now, so you don’t meet anyone. There won’t be anyone there, I promise you. We’ll be waiting for you,” he said firmly, and left the room.

He rushed straight to the hospital, where Mitya (Dmitri) was staying. The day after his sentence, Mitya had become very sick with a nervous fever and was moved to the prison section of the town hospital. But thanks to people like Alyosha, Madame Hohlakov, and Lise, Doctor Varvinsky made sure Mitya wasn’t put with the other prisoners. Instead, he got a small private room—the same one Smerdyakov had used. There was still a guard at the end of the hallway and bars on the window, so Varvinsky didn’t have to worry too much about bending the rules. He was a kind and compassionate young doctor. He understood how hard it would be for someone like Mitya to suddenly be thrown in with criminals, so he wanted Mitya to get used to things slowly. Friends and family were allowed to visit, even though it was unofficial—Alyosha and Grushenka were the only ones who came. Rakitin tried to force his way in twice, but Mitya always begged Varvinsky not to let him in.

Alyosha found Mitya sitting on his bed, wearing a hospital robe. He looked a bit feverish, with a towel soaked in vinegar and water wrapped around his head. When Alyosha came in, Mitya stared at him with a strange, worried look. Ever since the trial, Mitya seemed lost in thought, sometimes going half an hour without saying a word, completely absorbed in whatever was bothering him. When he did talk, he was abrupt and never seemed to talk about what he really felt. He often looked at Alyosha with pain in his eyes, but oddly, he seemed more relaxed with Grushenka—even though he barely spoke to her, his whole face lit up when she arrived.

Alyosha sat silently next to him on the bed. Mitya was nervous, waiting for Alyosha to speak, but he didn’t dare ask the question on his mind. He could hardly imagine that Katya (Katerina Ivanovna) would agree to visit, but at the same time, he felt that if she didn’t, something terrible would happen. Alyosha understood exactly how he felt.

“Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began nervously, “has torn his whole inn apart, they say. He’s pulled up the floors, ripped apart the planks, even taken down the gallery. He’s looking for treasure—the fifteen hundred roubles the prosecutor said I hid there. He started all this as soon as he got back home. Serves him right, the cheat! The guard told me yesterday—he’s from there.”
“Listen,” Alyosha started, “she will come, but I don’t know when. It could be today, or it could take a few days. I can’t say for sure. But I know she will come. That’s certain.”

Mitya twitched, about to say something, but stayed quiet. The news hit him hard. He clearly wanted to know what Katya had said, but he was too scared to ask. Anything harsh or scornful from Katya would have hurt him deeply right now.
“One thing she said was that I must make sure you don’t feel guilty about escaping,” Alyosha continued. “If Ivan isn’t better by then, she’ll handle everything herself.”
“You already told me that,” Mitya said, lost in thought.
“And you told Grusha the same thing,” Alyosha pointed out.

“Yes,” Mitya admitted. “But she’s not coming this morning.” He looked nervously at his brother. “She won’t come until tonight. When I told her yesterday that Katya was making plans, she was quiet, but she pressed her lips together. She just whispered, ‘Let her!’ She knew it was important. I didn’t dare push her for more. I think she understands now that Katya doesn’t love me anymore, but loves Ivan.”
“Does she?” Alyosha blurted out.
“Maybe not. But she’s not coming this morning,” Mitya said quickly. “I asked her to do something for me. You know, Ivan is better than all of us. He should live, not us. He’ll get better.”
“Would you believe it, even though Katya is worried about him, she’s pretty sure he’ll recover,” Alyosha said.
“That just means she’s convinced he’ll die. She’s so afraid, she keeps telling herself he’ll get well.”
“Ivan’s strong, and I really believe he’ll recover too,” Alyosha said, sounding worried.
“Yes, he’ll recover. But she’s sure he’ll die. She’s got a lot of pain to deal with...” Mitya fell silent, clearly upset.
“Alyosha, I love Grusha so much,” he suddenly said, his voice shaking and his eyes filling with tears.
“They won’t let her come out there with you,” Alyosha said right away.

“And there’s something else I need to tell you,” Mitya continued, his voice suddenly louder. “If they hit me on the way or when I’m out there, I won’t just take it. I’ll kill someone, and then they’ll shoot me for it. And this is supposed to go on for twenty years! They already talk to me like I’m nothing. I spent all night judging myself. I’m not ready! I can’t just accept it. I wanted to sing a hymn or something, but if a guard insults me, I just can’t take it. For Grusha, I’d bear anything... anything except being beaten… But they won’t let her come.”
Alyosha smiled gently.

“Listen, brother, let me say this once and for all,” he said. “Here’s what I think. And you know I wouldn’t lie to you. You’re not ready for this, and you don’t need to carry such a heavy burden if you’re not ready. If you’d actually killed our father, I’d feel bad if you tried to run away from your punishment. But you’re innocent, and this is too much for you. You wanted to change yourself by suffering. I say—just remember the person you want to become, all your life, wherever you go. That will be enough. Escaping will make you feel even more responsible your whole life, and that feeling will change you more than suffering in Siberia ever could. If you went there, you wouldn’t last, you’d complain, and maybe even decide you’ve paid your debt. The lawyer was right about that—some burdens are just too heavy for some people. If someone else had to get in trouble for your escape, I wouldn’t let you do it,” Alyosha smiled. “But the head of the transport told Ivan himself that if it’s planned well, there won’t be a big investigation, and the guards can get off easy. Of course, bribery is wrong, even then, but if Ivan and Katya asked me to act for you, I know I’d be the one handing out the bribes. I have to be honest. So I can’t judge your actions. But I promise you, I’ll never condemn you. And it would be weird if I could. I think I’ve said everything now.”

“But I do condemn myself!” Mitya cried. “I’m going to escape, that was decided without you; what else could Mitya Karamazov do but run? But I’ll never forgive myself, and I’ll pray for my sin forever. Isn’t this what the Jesuits say? Just like we’re doing now?”
“Yes.” Alyosha smiled kindly.

“I love you for always telling the truth, for never hiding anything,” Mitya said, suddenly laughing with relief. “So I caught my Alyosha sounding like a Jesuit! I have to give you a kiss for that. Now listen to the rest; I’ll show you the other side of my heart. Here’s my plan: even if I escape with money and a passport, even if I go to America, I won’t be happy. It’ll be just as bad as Siberia, maybe worse. I can’t stand America, damn it, even if Grusha is with me. Look at her—is she American? She’s as Russian as they come. She’ll miss Russia so much, and I’ll see her suffering every day, carrying my burden. What did she do to deserve this? And how will I deal with the people over there, even if they’re better than me? I already hate America! Even if they’re all geniuses at making machines, they’re not like us. I love Russia, Alyosha, I believe in the Russian God, even if I’m a scoundrel myself. I’ll suffocate over there!” His eyes suddenly filled with tears. “So here’s my decision: as soon as Grusha and I arrive, we’ll start working the land, far away from everyone, maybe where there are still wild bears. I hear there are even some Native Americans left in the wild parts. So we’ll go to the land of the Last of the Mohicans, and right away start learning grammar—Grusha and me, just work and studying. After three years, we’ll speak English like natives. And then—we’ll come back to Russia as American citizens. Don’t worry, we won’t come back here. We’ll hide somewhere far away, maybe in the north or south. By then, we’ll both have changed. The doctors can give me a fake wart, or I’ll lose an eye, grow a huge beard, turn gray with homesickness. Maybe no one will recognize us. And if they do, let them send us to Siberia—I don’t care, it’ll be fate. We can work the land here too, somewhere wild, and I’ll pretend to be American forever. But at least we’ll die at home. That’s my plan, and I won’t change it. What do you think?”
“Yes,” Alyosha said, not wanting to argue. Mitya waited for a moment, then suddenly said:
“And wow, did they ever twist things at the trial! Didn’t they?”
“Even if they hadn’t, you would have been convicted anyway,” Alyosha sighed.
“Yeah, people here are sick of me! God bless them, but it’s hard,” Mitya groaned miserably. There was silence for a minute.
“Alyosha, just tell me the truth!” he burst out. “Is she coming now or not? What did she say? How did she say it?”
“She said she’d come, but I don’t know if it’ll be today. It’s hard for her, you know,” Alyosha said, looking nervously at his brother.

“Of course it’s hard for her! Alyosha, it’s driving me crazy. Grusha keeps watching me. She knows what’s going on. God, calm my heart—what do I even want? I want Katya! Do I even understand what I want? It’s just the wild Karamazov side of me! No, I can’t handle suffering. I’m just a scoundrel, that’s all.”
“She’s here!” Alyosha cried.

At that moment, Katya appeared in the doorway. For a second, she just stood there, looking at Mitya with a stunned expression. Mitya jumped up, looking scared, his face pale, but he managed a timid, pleading smile and reached both hands out to her. Seeing this, Katya rushed over, grabbed his hands, and almost forced him to sit back on the bed. She sat down next to him, gripping his hands tightly. They both tried to speak several times but couldn’t; they just stared at each other with strange smiles. Two minutes passed like that.
“Have you forgiven me?” Mitya finally whispered, and at the same time turned to Alyosha, his face full of joy. “Do you hear what I’m asking? Do you hear?”

“That’s why I always loved you—you have a generous heart!” Katya burst out. “My forgiveness doesn’t matter, nor yours to me; whether we forgive each other or not, we’ll always be a pain in each other’s hearts, and that’s just how it is....” She paused to catch her breath. “Why did I come?” she went on quickly, “to fall at your feet, to grip your hands till it hurts—you remember how in Moscow I used to squeeze them? To tell you again that you are my god, my joy, to tell you I love you madly,” she sobbed, suddenly kissing his hand. Tears poured down her face. Alyosha was stunned and speechless—he had never expected this.

“Love is over, Mitya,” Katya said, “but the past still means so much to me. You’ll always be important to me. But let’s pretend, just for a minute, that things could have been different,” she said with a forced smile, looking at him happily again. “You love another woman, and I love another man, but I’ll always love you, and you’ll always love me—do you know that? Do you hear me? Love me, love me all your life!” Her voice was trembling, almost threatening.

“I’ll love you, and... you know, Katya,” Mitya said, pausing to breathe between each word, “five days ago, that same night, I loved you... When you collapsed and were carried out... All my life! That’s how it will be, always—”
They whispered desperate words to each other, words that probably didn’t even make sense or weren’t even true, but at that moment, they both believed every bit of it.
“Katya,” Mitya suddenly asked, “do you think I killed him? I know you don’t believe it now, but back then… when you testified... You didn’t really believe it, did you?”

“I never really believed it. Not even then. I hated you, and for a moment I convinced myself. While I was testifying, I convinced myself and believed it, but the moment I finished, I stopped believing it. Don’t doubt that! I almost forgot I came here to punish myself,” she said, her voice suddenly different, not loving anymore.
“That’s a heavy burden, Katya,” Mitya said quietly, almost without meaning to.
“Let me go,” she whispered. “I’ll come again. I can’t take any more right now.”

She started to get up, but suddenly screamed and stumbled back. Grushenka walked quietly and unexpectedly into the room. No one was expecting her. Katya quickly headed for the door, but when she reached Grushenka, she stopped, went pale as a ghost, and whispered softly,
“Forgive me!”
Grushenka stared at her, and after a pause, said in a cold, angry voice,
“We’re both full of hate, you and I! We both are! As if we could forgive each other! Save him, and I’ll worship you forever.”
“You won’t forgive her?” Mitya cried out, hurt and shocked.
“Don’t worry, I’ll save him for you!” Katya said quickly, and ran out of the room.
“And you couldn’t forgive her, even when she asked you herself?” Mitya said, bitterly.
“Mitya, don’t blame her; you have no right!” Alyosha shouted, upset.
“Her proud lips spoke, not her heart,” Grushenka said with disgust. “If she saves you, I’ll forgive her everything—”
She stopped, like she was trying to hold something back. She was still shaken. Later, it turned out she’d just come in by accident, not knowing who she’d run into.
“Alyosha, go after her!” Mitya called to his brother. “Tell her... I don’t know... don’t let her leave like this!”
“I’ll come back at nightfall,” Alyosha said, and hurried after Katya. He caught up with her just outside the hospital. She was walking fast, but as soon as Alyosha reached her, she said quickly,

“No, I can’t punish myself in front of that woman! I asked her forgiveness because I wanted to punish myself all the way. She wouldn’t forgive me... I actually like her for that!” she added, her voice sounding strange and angry, her eyes flashing.
“My brother had no idea this would happen,” Alyosha muttered. “He was sure she wouldn’t come—”

“Probably. Let’s leave it at that,” she snapped. “Listen: I can’t go with you to the funeral now. I’ve sent flowers. I think they still have money. If they need anything, tell them I’ll never abandon them.... Now please, leave me. You’re already late—the church bells are ringing for the service.... Please, just go!”

He really was late. They had already decided to carry the small, flower-covered coffin to the church without waiting for him. It was the coffin of poor little Ilusha, who had died two days after Dmitri (Mitya) was sentenced. When Alyosha (also called Alexey) arrived at the gate, Ilusha’s classmates—about twelve boys—were waiting for him. They all had their schoolbags slung over their shoulders and looked relieved to see him. Ilusha had told them as he was dying, “Father will cry, be with father,” and the boys remembered his words. Kolya Krassotkin was leading the group.

“I’m so glad you’re here, Karamazov!” Kolya said, reaching out to shake Alyosha’s hand. “It’s terrible here. It’s really hard to see. Snegiryov isn’t drunk—we know for sure he hasn’t had anything to drink today—but he acts like he is… I always try to be strong, but this is awful. Karamazov, before you go in, can I ask you something?”
“What is it, Kolya?” Alyosha asked.
“Is your brother innocent or guilty? Did he kill your father, or was it the servant? However you answer, that’s what I’ll believe. I haven’t slept for four nights thinking about it.”
“The servant did it. My brother is innocent,” Alyosha replied.
“That’s what I said!” shouted Smurov.
“Then he’ll be ruined as an innocent victim!” Kolya exclaimed. “But he’s still happy! I almost envy him!”
“What do you mean? How can you say that? Why?” Alyosha said, surprised.
“Oh, if only I could give up myself someday for the sake of truth!” Kolya said, full of energy.
“But not for something like this—not with so much shame and pain,” Alyosha said.
“Of course… I’d want to die for humanity. And as for disgrace, that doesn’t matter—our names could be forgotten. I respect your brother a lot!”
“And so do I!” said the boy who had once claimed he knew who founded Troy, suddenly blurting it out and blushing all the way to his ears, just like before.

Alyosha went into the room. Ilusha lay with his hands folded and eyes closed in a blue coffin with a white frill. His thin face barely looked different, and oddly, there was no smell at all. His expression was serious and thoughtful. His hands crossed over his chest looked almost like they were carved from marble. Flowers were tucked in his hands and all around the coffin, thanks to Lise Hohlakov, who had sent them that morning, and Katerina Ivanovna, who sent some too. When Alyosha entered, Captain Snegiryov was holding a bunch of flowers, trembling, and gently covering his son with them again. He barely glanced at Alyosha, not looking at anyone—not even his heartbroken wife, “mamma,” who tried to stand on her crippled legs to get closer to her dead boy. Nina, in her chair, had been pushed up close to the coffin by the boys. She sat with her head leaning against it, quietly crying. Snegiryov’s face showed a mix of eagerness, confusion, and frustration. He kept repeating, “Old man, dear old man!” as he looked at Ilusha. He’d always called Ilusha “old man” as a loving nickname.

“Father, give me a flower too; take that white one from his hand and give it to me,” the grieving mother begged, whimpering. Maybe the little white rose in Ilusha’s hand caught her eye, or maybe she wanted one from his hand as a keepsake. She moved around, reaching toward the flower.
“I’m not giving anything to anyone! They’re his flowers, not yours! Everything is his, nothing is yours!” Snegiryov snapped harshly.
“Father, give mother a flower!” Nina said, lifting her tear-streaked face.

“I won’t give anything away—and definitely not to her! She didn’t love Ilusha. She took his little cannon away, and he gave it to her,” the captain sobbed loudly at the thought of Ilusha handing over his toy cannon to his mother. The poor, broken woman silently cried, hiding her face in her hands.
The boys, seeing that the father wouldn’t leave the coffin and it was time to go, gathered around and began to lift it.
“I don’t want him buried in the churchyard,” Snegiryov suddenly wailed. “I’ll bury him by the stone, by our stone! Ilusha told me to. I won’t let you carry him away!”
For the last three days, he’d insisted on burying Ilusha by the stone, but Alyosha, Kolya Krassotkin, the landlady, her sister, and all the boys tried to stop him.

“What a thing to suggest, burying him by some unholy stone, as if he’d hanged himself!” the old landlady said sternly. “In the churchyard, the ground is blessed. There he’ll be prayed for. You can hear the singing from the church, and the deacon reads so clearly, it’ll be like he’s reading right over Ilusha’s grave.”

Finally, the captain waved his hand in defeat, as if saying, “Do what you want.” The boys picked up the coffin, but as they passed the mother, they paused and lowered it so she could say goodbye. But as she saw her beloved son’s face up close—something she hadn’t done in three days—she started trembling, her gray head jerking over the coffin.

“Mother, make the sign of the cross over him, bless him, kiss him,” Nina pleaded. But her head just kept twitching, and with a face twisted by grief, she started hitting her chest with her fist without saying a word. They carried the coffin past her. Nina kissed her brother for the last time as the coffin passed by. As Alyosha left the house, he asked the landlady to look after those who stayed behind, but the old woman interrupted him.
“Of course I’ll stay with them. We’re Christians too,” she said, crying.

They didn’t have far to go—only about three hundred steps to the church. It was a clear, cold day, and the church bells were still ringing. Snegiryov hurried after the coffin, wearing his thin old summer coat, his head bare, and his old floppy hat in his hand. He seemed nervous and confused, sometimes reaching out to touch the coffin and getting in the way, sometimes running alongside, trying to find a spot for himself. When a flower fell onto the snow, he rushed to get it as if the whole world depended on that flower.
“And the bread crust—we forgot the bread crust!” he suddenly cried, panicked. But the boys reminded him that he already had it in his pocket. He quickly pulled it out and calmed down.

“Ilusha told me to bring it, Alyosha,” he explained. “One night I was sitting with him, and he suddenly said, ‘Father, when my grave is filled up, crumble some bread on it so the sparrows will come. I’ll hear them and it will cheer me up, because I won’t feel alone.’”
“That’s a good idea,” Alyosha said. “We should do it often.”
“Every day, every day!” the captain replied quickly, looking happier at the thought.

They finally reached the church and set the coffin in the middle. The boys gathered around and stood respectfully during the whole service. The church was old and poor, many icons had no decoration, but these kinds of churches are the best for praying. During the mass, Snegiryov calmed down a little, though sometimes he acted nervously and confused. He would go up to fix the coffin cover or wreath, or fuss over a candle that had fallen, then stand quietly by the coffin with a lost and worried look. After the Epistle, he whispered to Alyosha that it hadn’t been read correctly but didn’t explain why. When the hymn “Like the Cherubim” was sung, he joined in but didn’t finish. He fell to his knees, pressed his forehead to the stone floor, and stayed that way for a long time.

Finally, the funeral service began and candles were handed out. The distracted father started fussing again, but the moving funeral prayers seemed to touch him deeply. He suddenly hunched over and began sobbing quickly and quietly, then finally cried out loud. When it was time to say goodbye and close the coffin, he threw his arms out, as if refusing to let them cover Ilusha, and kissed his dead son over and over. At last, they gently pulled him away, but he suddenly grabbed a handful of flowers from the coffin. Staring at them, he seemed to forget his grief for just a moment, lost in thought. When the coffin was lifted and carried to the grave, he didn’t fight it. The grave was a good one, close to the church—Katerina Ivanovna had paid for it. After the usual prayers, the gravediggers lowered the coffin. Snegiryov bent so low over the grave with his flowers that the boys had to pull him back, afraid he’d fall in. He didn’t seem to really understand what was happening. As they started filling the grave, he pointed anxiously at the falling dirt, trying to say something, but no one understood and he stopped. Then someone reminded him about the bread, and he got excited, grabbed the bread, and started crumbling it over the grave.
“Come, fly down, birds, fly down, sparrows!” he muttered anxiously.

One boy noticed it was hard for Snegiryov to crumble the bread with his hands full of flowers and suggested he let someone hold them. But Snegiryov wouldn’t let go, suddenly afraid they’d take his flowers away. After checking the grave and making sure the bread was crumbled, he surprised everyone by turning around calmly and heading home. But as he walked, he sped up almost to a run, with the boys and Alyosha following behind.
“The flowers are for mamma, the flowers are for mamma! I was mean to her,” he suddenly exclaimed.

Someone called out, reminding him to put on his hat because of the cold. But he tossed the hat into the snow angrily, repeating, “I won’t wear the hat, I won’t wear the hat.” Smurov picked it up and carried it after him. All the boys were crying, especially Kolya and the boy who knew about Troy. Even Smurov, carrying the captain’s hat, was crying hard, but he still managed to grab a piece of red brick from the snow and throw it at a flock of sparrows flying by. He missed, of course, and kept crying as he ran. Halfway home, Snegiryov suddenly stopped, stood still for a moment, then turned back toward the church and Ilusha’s grave. The boys quickly caught up and grabbed him from all sides. Snegiryov collapsed in the snow, sobbing and wailing, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man!” Alyosha and Kolya tried to comfort him and help him up.
“Captain, that’s enough—a brave man has to be strong,” Kolya said quietly.
“You’ll ruin the flowers,” Alyosha added. “And mamma is waiting for them; she’s crying because you didn’t give her any before. Ilusha’s little bed is still there—”

“Yes, yes, mamma!” Snegiryov said, suddenly remembering. “They’ll take away the bed, they’ll take it away,” he added, as if scared they would. He jumped up and ran home. It wasn’t far, so they all reached the house together. Snegiryov burst in and called out to his wife, with whom he’d just argued so harshly:

“Mamma, my poor crippled darling, Ilusha sent you these flowers!” he cried, holding out the bunch that had gotten frozen and broken in the snow. But then he saw Ilusha’s little boots in the corner by the bed, set neatly by the landlady. He ran to them, fell to his knees, grabbed one boot, and started kissing it desperately, crying, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man, where are your little feet?”
“Where did you take him? Where did you take him?” the grieving mother cried out. Nina started sobbing too. Kolya ran out of the room, the other boys followed, and finally Alyosha left as well.
“Let them cry,” Alyosha told Kolya. “There’s no point trying to comfort them right now. Let’s wait a minute, then we’ll go back in.”
“No, it’s no use, it’s terrible,” Kolya said. He lowered his voice so no one else could hear. “You know, Karamazov, I feel so sad, and if it were possible to bring Ilusha back, I’d give up anything.”
“So would I,” Alyosha replied.
“What do you think, Karamazov? Should we come back tonight? He’ll probably be drunk, you know.”
“Maybe he will,” Alyosha said. “Let’s come together, you and me, and spend an hour with them—with the mother and Nina. If we all go in at once, it’ll just remind them of everything again.”
“The landlady is setting the table for them now—there’ll be a funeral meal, and the priest is coming. Should we go back for that, Karamazov?”
“Definitely,” Alyosha said.
“It’s all so strange, Karamazov—so much sadness, and then pancakes afterwards. It just seems weird in our religion.”
“They’re having salmon too,” the boy who knew about Troy said loudly.
“Please, Kartashov, don’t interrupt with stupid comments, especially when no one asked you,” Kolya snapped. Kartashov turned bright red but didn’t say anything else.
While they walked slowly down the path, Smurov suddenly shouted:
“There’s Ilusha’s stone—the one they wanted to bury him under.”

They all stopped by the big stone. Alyosha looked at it and remembered what Snegiryov had told him—how Ilusha, crying and hugging his father, had said, “Father, father, how he insulted you.” The whole scene appeared vividly in his mind.
Suddenly, Alyosha felt moved. With a serious look, he glanced at each of Ilusha’s friends and said:
“Boys, I want to say something to you all, right here.”
The boys gathered around and looked at him, waiting and listening closely.

“Boys, we’ll soon have to go our separate ways. I’ll be with my two brothers for a while—one is going to Siberia, the other is very sick. Soon I’ll leave this town, maybe for a long time. So let’s make a promise here, at Ilusha’s stone, that we’ll never forget Ilusha or each other. No matter what happens, even if we don’t see each other for twenty years, let’s always remember burying the boy we once threw stones at by the bridge—remember? But then we all became friends with him. He was a great kid—kind, brave, and he stood up for his father’s honor. So first, let’s promise to remember him for the rest of our lives. Even if we become busy or important, or if we fall into trouble, let’s remember how good it felt to be together here, united by kindness. My little doves—let me call you that, because you really seem like doves to me as I look at your faces. Maybe you won’t understand everything I’m saying now—I know I’m not always clear—but you’ll remember it and someday agree. There’s nothing better or stronger in life than a good memory, especially from childhood or home. People talk a lot about education, but a good, sacred memory from childhood is maybe the best education. If a person has many such memories, he’ll be safe for life. Even if he only has one, it might save him someday. Maybe we’ll become bad, unable to stop ourselves from doing wrong, or laugh at people who want to help others, like Kolya said just now. But even if that happens—which I hope it doesn’t—when we remember how we buried Ilusha, how we loved him, and how we were all friends here, even the worst of us won’t be able to mock being kind at this moment. Maybe that memory will keep him from doing something terrible, and he’ll think, ‘I was good and brave then!’ Even if he laughs, it’s just thoughtlessness. But I promise you, as he laughs, he’ll feel in his heart, ‘No, I shouldn’t laugh, because that’s not something to make fun of.’”
“Yes, that’s true—I understand, Karamazov!” Kolya said, his eyes shining.
The boys were moved and wanted to speak, but they held back, looking at Alyosha with emotion.

“I’m only saying this in case we turn bad,” Alyosha continued. “But there’s no reason we have to, right? Let’s always be kind first, then honest, and never forget each other. I promise I’ll never forget any of you. I’ll remember every face I see now, even thirty years from now. Earlier, Kolya told Kartashov that we didn’t care if he existed. But I can’t forget that Kartashov exists, and he isn’t blushing now like when he talked about Troy, but looking at me with his happy, kind eyes. Boys, let’s all be generous and brave like Ilusha, smart and brave like Kolya (who will be even smarter when he grows up), and as humble and sweet as Kartashov. But honestly, you’re all special to me, and I hope I have a place in your hearts too! Who brought us together in this good feeling? Who, if not Ilusha—the good boy, precious to us forever! Let’s never forget him. May his memory live in our hearts forever from now on!”
“Yes, yes, forever, forever!” the boys shouted, their faces soft and shining.
“Let’s remember his face and his clothes, his little boots, his coffin, his sad father, and how bravely he defended him, even when the whole school was against him.”
“We’ll remember, we will!” the boys called back. “He was brave, he was good!”
“Oh, how I loved him!” Kolya cried.
“Ah, my friends, don’t be afraid of life! Life is good when you do something good and just!” Alyosha said.
“Yes, yes!” the boys replied, full of energy.
“Karamazov, we love you!” someone—probably Kartashov—shouted suddenly.
“We love you, we love you!” all the boys echoed. Many of them had tears in their eyes.
“Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya shouted with excitement.
“And may Ilusha’s memory live forever!” Alyosha added, his voice full of feeling.
“Forever!” the boys shouted together.
“Karamazov,” Kolya asked, “is it really true, like we’re taught, that we’ll all rise from the dead and see each other again—Ilusha too?”
“Of course we will! We’ll all rise again and see each other, and share everything that’s happened with joy!” Alyosha replied, half laughing, half excited.
“How amazing that will be!” Kolya cried out.

“Okay, let’s finish talking and go to his funeral dinner. Don’t be upset about the pancakes—it’s an old tradition, and there’s something nice about it!” Alyosha said, laughing. “Come on, let’s go! And let’s walk hand in hand.”
“And always, for the rest of our lives, hand in hand! Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya shouted again, and the boys all joined in: “Hurrah for Karamazov!”
the end
